chapters.summary: Set up Packet Tracer, build a first LAN, navigate Cisco IOS, and distinguish the active configuration, the saved configuration, and the lab project. Establish a repeatable method for studying and verifying your work.

sections.body:
Network work depends on a few habits that are worth establishing from the start: know which device you are changing, understand what the change should accomplish, and verify the result. A command being accepted is only one part of that process.

This chapter prepares your study environment and introduces those habits. By the end, you should be able to build a small LAN in Packet Tracer, move confidently between Cisco IOS command modes, and preserve a working configuration. You do not need to understand every field in the output yet. Addressing, switching, and packet forwarding are developed in the following chapters.

The first practical pass is deliberately small: build a working LAN, correct a device name, and save it. Later CLI and reload examples remain reference material; they are not all required tasks in the opening lab.

sections.title: Which exam you are sitting
sections.body:
Cisco's published exam topics are the scope reference for this course. They describe the knowledge and skills that can be assessed; they are not a list of actual exam questions. Read the topic list alongside your study plan, and pay attention to the verb at the start of each objective.

As checked on **19 September 2026**, the current exam is **CCNA 200-301 v1.1**, with a duration of **120 minutes**. Cisco states that **2 February 2027** is the last testing day for v1.1 and that **v2.0 begins on 3 February 2027**. Select the track that matches your planned exam date. Recheck Cisco's exam page before booking, especially if your date changes.

| Exam track | Published domains and weights |
|---|---|
| v1.1 | Network Fundamentals 20%; Network Access 20%; IP Connectivity 25%; IP Services 10%; Security Fundamentals 15%; Automation and Programmability 10% |
| v2.0 | Network Infrastructure and Connectivity 25%; Switching and Network Access 25%; IP Routing 20%; Network Services and Security 20%; AI, Network Operations, and Management 10% |

The weights help you allocate study time; they do not justify skipping a domain or predict the exact questions on an individual exam. Both versions require a working understanding of addressing, forwarding, device configuration, and verification. The first eight chapters establish that foundation.

| Objective wording | What your study should enable you to do |
|---|---|
| Describe or explain | Explain a function accurately and relate it to a practical example. |
| Compare | Identify meaningful differences and choose an appropriate option for a stated requirement. |
| Configure and verify | Translate requirements into a configuration, then prove that the intended behavior occurs. |
| Troubleshoot | Interpret evidence, identify the cause, make an appropriate correction, and test again. |

A multiple-choice score alone does not demonstrate all four skills. Use the labs and output interpretation exercises as part of your preparation. Cisco may assess practical skills as well as conceptual knowledge. Use its current exam guidance for the delivery format and test-day rules; this course does not assume a fixed question count, passing score, or placement of practical items.

:::note
This opening chapter teaches prerequisite skills rather than a separate exam domain. Foundation chapters remain part of your study path even when a blueprint does not name a concept, such as the OSI model, as its own objective. Coverage tags identify relevant objectives; they do not certify complete mastery of an objective.
:::

sections.title: Install Packet Tracer and learn its workspace
sections.body:
**Cisco Packet Tracer** is a network simulator. It lets you build a topology, configure simulated devices, and inspect selected protocol events without buying equipment. It implements a subset of device features and commands. A command supported on a physical Catalyst switch or a current IOS XE router may be unavailable or behave differently in a particular Packet Tracer device.

Use the software version and operating-system requirements currently listed in the [Networking Academy Resource Hub](https://www.netacad.com/resources/lab-downloads). Cisco provides desktop installation packages for supported Windows, macOS, and Linux systems. Do not use an unofficial download or assume that an old course's version number is a current requirement.

1. Sign in to Cisco Networking Academy, creating an account if needed, and open the Resource Hub's lab downloads.
2. Select the Packet Tracer package for your operating system. Follow Cisco's installation instructions and the installer prompts. On Windows, run the downloaded installer; on macOS, open the downloaded disk image and installer package. For the Ubuntu package, use the package-installation command in Cisco's guide with your actual downloaded filename.
3. Start Packet Tracer and complete its sign-in flow. If authentication opens in a browser, finish there and return to the application.
4. Create a folder for your exercises, with a separate project file for each chapter. Save this chapter as **00-first-lan.pkt**.
5. Open a blank project and locate the device palette, connection tools, device configuration windows, and the Realtime/Simulation controls.

The first labs use devices within a local simulated topology. You do not need Packet Tracer's multiuser server features for them. If asked about enabling multiuser services or allowing inbound connections, those features are optional for this exercise; the application may still need Internet access for download and sign-in.

| Workspace feature | How you will use it |
|---|---|
| Logical workspace | Place devices and see how they connect. |
| Device palette | Select routers, switches, PCs, and other supported models. |
| Connections | Choose a cable and its ports. Inspect the endpoints rather than relying only on the cable's appearance. |
| Device window | Open a router or switch CLI, or a PC's IP Configuration and Command Prompt. |
| Realtime mode | Let the simulation run normally while you configure and test. |
| Simulation mode | Filter events and advance through selected packet exchanges. |
| Save / Save As | Preserve the topology as a Packet Tracer project. |

For the first lab, use a **2960 switch** and two **PC-PT** devices. The lab specifies the ports so you can compare your work with its output. If you choose another model, inspect its interface names and adjust the instructions consistently. A router's GigabitEthernet0/0 is not interchangeable with a switch's FastEthernet0/1 simply because both are Ethernet ports.

Link indicators are useful observations, but they are not a complete diagnosis. A port may take time to become ready because of link negotiation or spanning tree. A red link can have several causes, including a disconnected cable, the wrong port, an incompatible connection, or an administratively disabled interface. Later chapters show how to distinguish these causes.

sections.title: The command line: modes, help and the pager
sections.body:
Cisco IOS uses command modes to separate monitoring from configuration. The **prompt** shows the device name and current mode. Read it before entering a command, particularly when switching between several devices.

| Prompt example | Mode | Common work |
|---|---|---|
| Switch> | User EXEC | Limited monitoring; enter privileged EXEC with `enable`. |
| Switch# | Privileged EXEC | Run verification commands, save configurations, and enter configuration mode. |
| Switch(config)# | Global configuration | Change device-wide settings or enter a more specific configuration mode. |
| Switch(config-if)# | Interface configuration | Change the selected interface. |
| Switch(config-line)# | Line configuration | Configure console or remote terminal lines; covered later. |

This sequence names a new switch. The prompts are shown for orientation; type only the commands after them.

```ios S1
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname S1
S1(config)# interface FastEthernet0/1
S1(config-if)# exit
S1(config)# end
S1#
```

`exit` moves out of the current configuration level. From interface configuration it returns to global configuration. `end`, or the usual Ctrl+Z shortcut, returns from configuration mode to privileged EXEC. From EXEC, `exit` can end a session, so it is not a universal synonym for “go back.”

IOS provides **context-sensitive help**. Enter `?` to see choices at the current position; it does not execute the command. Compare `show ?`, which lists possible next keywords, with `show ip ?`, which narrows the list. A help response containing `<cr>` indicates that pressing Enter can complete the command at that point.

You may abbreviate a command when the entered characters identify it uniquely. For example, `conf t` commonly resolves to `configure terminal`. The full form is used in explanations so its meaning remains clear. An abbreviation accepted on one software image may be ambiguous on another.

| Message or behavior | What to check |
|---|---|
| Invalid input with a caret | Check the mode, spelling, position of the caret, and whether this platform supports the command. |
| Incomplete command | The command needs another argument. Use a space followed by `?`. |
| Ambiguous command | Supply more characters to distinguish the possible commands. |
| --More-- | Output has paused at the pager. Space advances a page; Enter advances a line; `q` normally stops the display. |

On images that support it, `terminal length 0` disables paging for the current terminal session. It is a convenience, not a prerequisite: use the pager if your simulated device does not implement it. Similarly, common IOS output filters such as `show running-config | include hostname` help find a line, but filtered output can hide context. Read the complete relevant section before making a diagnosis.

From configuration mode, the supported `do` form lets you run common EXEC verification commands without leaving that mode:

```ios S1
S1(config)# do show ip interface brief
S1(config)# end
S1# show running-config
```

sections.title: Saving, reloading and the domain-lookup trap
sections.body:
The **running configuration** is the active configuration. The **startup configuration** is the saved configuration used at startup. On the classic IOS devices used in these introductory labs, running configuration is held in RAM and startup configuration is conventionally stored in NVRAM. Storage implementation varies across platforms; the operational distinction is active versus saved.

The configuration commands in this lab take effect when accepted. Leaving configuration mode does not save them. Use the direction of the copy command to check your intent:

```ios S1
S1# copy running-config startup-config
```

Representative response:

```output Save confirmation
Destination filename [startup-config]?
Building configuration...
[OK]
```

At the destination prompt, Enter accepts the name in brackets. Then inspect `show startup-config` and confirm that the intended setting appears. `write memory` is a common alternative save command on these devices; learning the full copy command makes the source and destination explicit.

:::trap
`copy startup-config running-config` is the opposite direction. On conventional IOS it merges saved commands into the active configuration; it is not a general “undo everything” operation. Do not use it as a substitute for understanding which setting must be corrected.
:::

A reload restarts the device and interrupts its operation. Practice it only on the isolated lab device. If the running configuration differs from startup configuration, IOS may ask whether to save the changes. The answer changes what you will see after the restart. Read the prompt rather than pressing Enter through it.

There are three separate things to preserve:

| Item | How to preserve it | What it represents |
|---|---|---|
| Device startup configuration | `copy running-config startup-config` | Configuration the simulated device uses when it starts. |
| Packet Tracer project | Save the .pkt file | Your topology and the project state stored by Packet Tracer. |
| Course progress | Use the app's progress export/backup feature | Your study records in this browser profile. |

Saving the project is not a replacement for practicing the device's save procedure. Saving a device also does not export your study history. Keep working project files and progress backups somewhere you can find them again.

Another common surprise occurs when an unrecognized word at an EXEC prompt is treated as a hostname. The device may attempt a DNS lookup, appearing to pause. On an isolated practice device, `no ip domain-lookup` in global configuration disables this behavior. It changes that device's name-lookup behavior; it does not disable DNS for the entire network. Do not apply it automatically to a system that needs name resolution.

Ctrl+Shift+6 is a common IOS escape sequence for interrupting a running operation. Its handling can depend on the terminal or simulator. If a lookup does not respond to the shortcut, allow it to time out, correct the input, and use context help before retrying.

sections.title: How to study with this site
sections.body:
Work through the foundation chapters in order. They build from device operation and packet forwarding to addressing, transport protocols, and Ethernet switching. If a later explanation is unclear, return to the prerequisite concept and reproduce a small example.

For each chapter, first read for the main mechanism: what decision is being made, which information is used, and what changes as a result. Then use the lab to observe that mechanism. Before issuing a command, predict what the output should show. Afterward, compare your prediction with the evidence.

Keep a short lab record with the requirement, addressing or interface plan, commands you changed, and the outputs that verify the result. When a test fails, record the symptom before changing anything. Make one justified correction at a time and repeat the same test. This makes it much easier to distinguish the actual cause from a coincidental improvement.

Use flashcards for recall, checkpoint questions for reasoning, and command drills for syntax. Review the explanations for incorrect options as well as the correct answer. A useful check is whether you can explain why an option fails under the stated conditions, without relying on the position of the answer.

After completing a guided lab, rebuild it from the topology and requirements with the instructions closed. Change one address range or interface assignment and verify the revised result. This tests whether you understand the configuration, rather than whether you remember one sequence of keystrokes.

No course can guarantee an exam result. Readiness is better demonstrated by consistent performance across the published objectives, including unfamiliar examples and practical verification, than by a particular number of study hours.

sections.title: Reading the output
sections.body:
The following is a **representative excerpt**, not a required byte-for-byte result from your Packet Tracer version:

```output show ip interface brief
Interface              IP-Address      OK? Method Status                Protocol
FastEthernet0/1         unassigned      YES unset  up                    up  ← The local interface reports operational physical and line-protocol states.
FastEthernet0/2         unassigned      YES unset  down                  down  ← No operational link is reported; inspect the connection and peer.
FastEthernet0/3         unassigned      YES unset  administratively down down  ← The interface has been disabled in configuration.
Vlan1                  unassigned      YES unset  down                  down  ← The switch virtual interface has no IP address here.
```

An access switch can forward Layer 2 traffic without an IP address on each physical port or a configured management address. The Vlan1 row concerns a logical interface; it does not, by itself, say that every physical port is down.

**Up/up** is useful local evidence. It does not prove that the host has the correct address, that every switch setting is appropriate, or that an application works. Similarly, a successful ping proves that the tested source received ICMP replies from the destination at that time. It does not validate every service or every possible path.

To check whether a hostname is saved, inspect both configurations. If running configuration contains `hostname S1` but startup configuration contains `hostname Switch`, the active name has not been saved to that startup configuration. This is stronger evidence than simply remembering that you pressed a Save button somewhere in the application.

sections.title: Exam focus
sections.body:
- Recognize IOS modes from their prompts and choose commands appropriate to the mode.
- Use context help and interpret common parser messages.
- Distinguish running configuration, startup configuration, and a simulator project file.
- Save deliberately, verify the saved setting, and understand the effect of an unsaved reload.
- Interpret interface status without claiming that one command proves the whole network works.
- Build the habit of checking requirements, predicting behavior, observing evidence, and testing after a correction.

lab.title: Build and save your first LAN
lab.intro:
Practice revised September 2026. If you completed an earlier version, repeat the revised exercise and update its checkmarks.

Build a small working network, give the switch its intended name, and save your work. The goal is to become comfortable finding the right device window and checking a result. Allow extra time for the initial Packet Tracer download and sign-in.

Use the chapter's official installation guide before starting. The addresses below are supplied settings; you do not need to calculate a subnet yet. Output and interface timing vary by simulator version.
lab.topology:
Start with a blank project and the listed device models.

```diagram
{"type":"topology","title":"Your first LAN","caption":"Two PCs exchange traffic through one switch; no router or gateway is needed for this local test.","nodes":[{"id":"A","kind":"pc","label":"PC-A","sub":"192.168.10.10/24","x":2,"y":3},{"id":"S","kind":"switch","label":"S1","sub":"2960","x":6,"y":3},{"id":"B","kind":"pc","label":"PC-B","sub":"192.168.10.20/24","x":10,"y":3}],"links":[{"from":"A","to":"S","fromLabel":"Fa0","toLabel":"Fa0/1"},{"from":"S","to":"B","fromLabel":"Fa0/2","toLabel":"Fa0"}]}
```

| Connection | Cable |
|---|---|
| PC-A FastEthernet0 → S1 FastEthernet0/1 | Copper straight-through |
| PC-B FastEthernet0 → S1 FastEthernet0/2 | Copper straight-through |

| PC | IPv4 address | Mask | Gateway and DNS |
|---|---|---|---|
| PC-A | 192.168.10.10 | 255.255.255.0 | Leave blank |
| PC-B | 192.168.10.20 | 255.255.255.0 | Leave blank |

steps.title: Place, label and save the project
steps.body:
Place the 2960 and two PC-PT devices. Open each device and change its workspace display name to match the drawing. Find the switch's **CLI** tab and each PC's **Desktop** tab, then return to the workspace.

Create a lab folder and use **File → Save As** to save **00-first-lan.pkt** there. A workspace display name is a label; it does not necessarily set the IOS hostname.

:::expected
You can find all three devices and the saved project file. No communication has been tested yet.
:::

steps.title: Cable and address the PCs
steps.body:
Select **Copper Straight-Through**, then click the exact ports from the connection table. On each PC, open **Desktop → IP Configuration**, choose **Static**, and enter its address and mask. Leave gateway and DNS blank.

Read each entry back against the table. Allow the links to initialize in Realtime mode. A brief amber indication while a switch port becomes ready is not a reason to change the addressing.

:::expected
Both cables use the intended switch ports, and the PCs have different addresses with the same supplied mask. These separate PCs need distinct host addresses; reusing the same address on both creates an address conflict. The switch needs no management address for this exchange.
:::

steps.title: Confirm communication
steps.body:
On PC-A, open **Desktop → Command Prompt**:

```text
ping 192.168.10.20
```

Wait for completion. If an initial request times out, repeat once after the links are ready. On PC-B, test the other direction:

```text
ping 192.168.10.10
```

:::expected
Both PCs receive replies on the repeated tests. Record the source, destination and result, for example: “PC-A to 192.168.10.20: replies received.” These tests establish this communication at this time; they do not test an Internet connection.
:::

steps.title: Read the prompt and inspect a naming mistake
steps.body:
Open S1's CLI. If the initial configuration dialog appears, answer **no**. Press Enter to reach the prompt. Type the commands after the displayed prompts, one line at a time. The temporary name below is a deliberate, harmless mistake: the required name is **S1**.

```ios S1
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname TEMP
TEMP(config)# end
TEMP# show running-config
```

If the display pauses at **--More--**, Space advances a page and **q** stops the remaining display. Find the hostname line. At the returned `TEMP#` prompt, try `show ?` to see the available next keywords; clear the unfinished input with Backspace. Help does not execute the command.

:::expected
The CLI now says TEMP, and running configuration contains `hostname TEMP`. This is the active device setting. The workspace label may still say S1, so the label alone did not prove that configuration was correct. Leave the mistake in place until the next step.
:::

steps.title: Correct the name and check it
steps.body:
The requirement is S1. Correct that one setting:

```ios S1
TEMP# configure terminal
TEMP(config)# hostname S1
S1(config)# end
S1# show running-config
```

:::expected
The prompt and active hostname now both say S1. You corrected the configuration without changing cables, PC addresses or restarting the switch. The setting is active; saving is a separate action.
:::

steps.title: Save and inspect the saved setting
steps.body:
```ios S1
S1# copy running-config startup-config
```

At `Destination filename [startup-config]?`, press Enter to accept the suggested destination. Wait until the copy finishes and the EXEC prompt returns. Then enter:

```ios S1
S1# show startup-config
```

:::expected
The saved configuration contains `hostname S1`. A copy-completed message is useful, but inspecting the required setting establishes what was saved. The wording of the completion message can vary.
:::

steps.title: Leave a working checkpoint
steps.body:
Repeat PC-A's ping to PC-B. Save the project as **00-first-lan-complete.pkt**. Record its location and the saved hostname in your notes. If you use this app's progress export, keep that file with your study backups; it is separate from the network project.

:::expected
Your checkpoint contains a working two-PC network and the saved switch hostname S1. You can distinguish the active configuration, the device's startup configuration, the .pkt project and your study-progress backup.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
| Symptom | First check |
|---|---|
| Persistent ping failure | Compare both PC entries with the table; inspect the two cable endpoints and link readiness. |
| A CLI command is rejected | Read the device prompt. Use `enable` from `>` before the privileged commands shown here. Check spelling and context help. |
| Output appears stuck | Look for `--More--`. Use the pager keys; do not restart the device. |
| The CLI still says TEMP | Correct the IOS hostname in configuration mode; the workspace label is separate. |
| Startup configuration is absent or has the wrong name | Check the active name, copy in the running-to-startup direction, then inspect startup configuration again. |
lab.challenge:
With the instructions closed, add PC-C on S1 FastEthernet0/3 using copper straight-through. Give it **192.168.10.30**, mask **255.255.255.0**, with gateway and DNS blank. Test it against both existing PCs and save a separate **00-first-lan-challenge.pkt** file.

Keep three pieces of evidence: the new cable endpoints, PC-C's address settings, and the results of its two tests.

:::solution
PC-C receives replies from 192.168.10.10 and 192.168.10.20 after the link is ready. Its address is distinct from the other PCs. No router or switch management address is needed. Completion means the settings and tests agree with the requirements, not just that three device icons appear.
:::

exhibit.title: First LAN test record
exhibit.text:
PC-A: 192.168.10.10, mask 255.255.255.0
PC-B: 192.168.10.20, mask 255.255.255.0
Both PCs connect to the same switch.
PC-A ping to 192.168.10.20: replies received

questions.prompt: What does the successful test establish?
options: PC-A received ICMP replies from PC-B during this test.
PC-A can reach Internet destinations through the switch.
Every application on PC-B is available to PC-A.
The switch has saved the PCs’ addresses in startup configuration.
questions.explanation: The result establishes the tested ICMP exchange between the two local addresses at that time. Other destinations, applications and saved configuration require their own checks.

whyWrong.1: No Internet destination or router path was tested.
whyWrong.2: A ping tests ICMP, not every service on the destination.
whyWrong.3: PC addressing is endpoint configuration; a ping does not verify any device’s saved configuration.

exhibit.title: Context help
exhibit.text:
S1# show ip interface brief ?
  |     Output modifiers
  <cr>

questions.prompt: What does `<cr>` in this context-help response mean?
options: The command just completed successfully.
Another required argument must follow.
Enter can complete the command here.
Enter will display another page of output.
questions.explanation: The `<cr>` marker represents a carriage return. It indicates that the command can be completed by pressing Enter; other listed choices may be optional continuations.

whyWrong.0: Context help lists valid choices; it has not executed the command.
whyWrong.1: The completion marker means a required argument is not missing at this point.
whyWrong.3: This is command help, not the --More-- output pager.

questions.prompt: Which command saves the active configuration to the normal startup configuration?
options: copy startup-config running-config
copy running-config startup-config
show startup-config
show running-config
questions.explanation: The copy command names the source first and destination second. Copy running configuration to startup configuration, accept the intended destination, and verify the saved setting.

whyWrong.0: The source and destination are reversed; this does not save the active configuration.
whyWrong.2: This displays the saved configuration rather than updating it.
whyWrong.3: This displays the active configuration rather than saving it.

questions.prompt: On the classic IOS lab device, which two statements describe running and startup configuration? Choose two.
options: Running configuration contains only changes since the last save.
Running configuration represents the currently active settings.
Startup configuration changes whenever you enter end.
Startup configuration supplies saved settings for a normal boot.
Displaying startup configuration copies it into running configuration.
questions.explanation: The active configuration and the saved startup configuration serve different purposes. Leaving configuration mode or displaying a configuration does not copy it. The Packet Tracer project is another separate item.

whyWrong.0: Running configuration represents the active configuration, not just the unsaved difference.
whyWrong.2: end changes command mode; saving requires a separate action.
whyWrong.4: A show command displays the saved settings without applying them.

questions.prompt: Both PCs share one switch LAN. Which correction matches the supplied plan?
options: Keep both addresses because their subnet masks match.
Enter PC-A’s address as PC-B’s default gateway.
Change PC-B’s address to 192.168.10.20.
Rename PC-B’s workspace label without changing its address.
questions.explanation: PC-B repeats PC-A’s address instead of using its own assigned value. These separate hosts need distinct addresses on this LAN. Correct PC-B to the supplied value before interpreting a communication test.

whyWrong.0: Matching masks do not make a duplicate host address correct.
whyWrong.1: A gateway setting would not remove the duplicate address, and this local test needs no gateway.
whyWrong.3: A workspace name does not change the address configured on the endpoint.

exhibit.title: Representative CLI excerpt
exhibit.text:
Switch> show running-config
             ^
% Invalid input detected at '^' marker.

questions.prompt: Why is this command rejected on a default lab switch?
options: The display command belongs in global configuration.
The displayed command needs an interface selected first.
The command requires privileged EXEC on this device.
The hostname argument must follow running-config.
questions.explanation: The > prompt indicates user EXEC. Enter enable to reach privileged EXEC, then run show running-config. Check the prompt before treating a parser error as a spelling problem.

whyWrong.0: Global configuration changes settings; this display is a privileged EXEC command on the lab switch.
whyWrong.1: The whole running configuration is not selected through an interface context.
whyWrong.3: The hostname is a setting inside the configuration, not an argument to this show command.

exhibit.title: Separate device and project checks
exhibit.text:
Workspace label: S1
Saved project filename: 00-first-lan.pkt
Current CLI prompt: S1#

questions.prompt: You need evidence that hostname S1 is in the switch’s startup configuration. Which additional check directly supplies it?
options: Find S1 in the workspace device label.
Find S1 in show running-config.
Close and reopen the CLI tab to read its prompt.
Find hostname S1 in show startup-config.
questions.explanation: Inspect startup configuration to verify the saved device setting. The prompt verifies the active name, while the file and workspace names describe the simulator project.

whyWrong.0: The workspace label is separate from the IOS configuration.
whyWrong.1: Running configuration shows the active name, which may still be unsaved.
whyWrong.2: Reopening the tab shows the currently active name, not whether it was saved.

cards.front: What does a successful ping to the other lab PC establish?
cards.back: That the source received ICMP replies from that destination during the test. It does not test every application or Internet access.

cards.front: Can two separate PCs use the same IPv4 address on this simple LAN?
cards.back: No. Give each PC its own address from the supplied plan; a different device name does not prevent an address conflict.

cards.front: What do >, # and (config)# identify in IOS?
cards.back: User EXEC, privileged EXEC and global configuration. Read the prompt before entering a command.

cards.front: How do you save and verify a conventional IOS startup configuration?
cards.back: copy running-config startup-config saves it. After the copy completes, use show startup-config to check the required setting.

cards.front: What is the operational difference between running and startup configuration?
cards.back: Running configuration is active now. Startup configuration contains the saved settings used for a normal boot.

cards.front: What does `<cr>` mean in IOS context help?
cards.back: Enter can complete the command at this position. Displaying help has not executed it.

cards.front: Must a Layer 2 switch have a management IP to forward local frames?
cards.back: No. Ordinary Layer 2 forwarding does not require a switch management address.

cards.front: What three kinds of saved work should you distinguish in this course?
cards.back: Save the device’s startup configuration, the Packet Tracer .pkt project, and the app’s study-progress export separately.

commands.task: Enter privileged EXEC on this fresh lab switch.
commands.note: The expected prompt is Switch#. A configured device may require authentication.

commands.task: Enter global configuration mode.
commands.note: The prompt becomes Switch(config)#.

commands.task: Set the IOS hostname to S1.
commands.note: The prompt changes immediately. Save separately when the configuration is ready.

commands.task: Leave global configuration and return to privileged EXEC.
commands.note: The expected prompt is S1#. This action does not save the configuration.

commands.task: Save the active configuration as the normal startup configuration.
commands.note: Accept the intended destination and verify the required settings with show startup-config.

commands.task: Display the saved configuration used for a normal startup.
commands.note: Compare the saved setting with running configuration; an absent startup file means it has not been created there.

chapters.summary: Explain OSI and TCP/IP functions, distinguish frames from packets, and trace an IPv4 exchange through switches and a router. Use ARP, interface status, and forwarding tables as evidence without overstating what they prove.

sections.body:
When a user reports that a service is unavailable, several different failures can produce the same symptom. The cable might be disconnected, the host might have an incorrect gateway, or the application might not be listening. Network models give you a way to separate these functions and choose useful tests.

This chapter follows an IPv4 packet across two Ethernet LANs. The aim is to understand which addresses each device uses, which fields change at a router, and what you can learn from the device tables. Detailed subnet calculations, TCP behavior, and switch learning follow in later chapters.

The lab supplies router addresses and their commands as setup for observing traffic. You are not yet expected to design subnets or reproduce that setup from memory; Chapter 04 teaches addressing and Chapter 08 extends the IOS workflow.

sections.title: Why we need a model
sections.body:
A **layer model** organizes communication into related functions. Applications exchange meaningful data; transport protocols provide services to applications; IP addresses and routes support delivery between networks; link technologies carry data across each local connection.

This separation supports interoperability. An application does not need to implement Ethernet signaling, and an Ethernet switch does not need to understand the contents of a web page to forward its frames. Real devices can perform functions at several layers, so a layer number describes a function rather than everything a device can do.

The models are also a troubleshooting framework. Begin with the symptom and select a test that narrows the possibilities. If an interface reports no operational link, physical connectivity deserves attention. If a remote IP address responds to ping but its application does not work, examine the application and relevant transport or policy behavior. The successful ping is useful evidence about that exchange; it does not establish that all Layer 1–3 conditions are correct for every kind of traffic.

For the CCNA, use the models to explain forwarding and interpret evidence. Memorizing the layer names is a starting point. Being able to distinguish a MAC address lookup from an IP route lookup is the more useful skill.

sections.title: Seven layers, four layers, five PDUs
sections.body:
The **OSI reference model** has seven layers. Read this table from the top down to follow data toward the medium, or from the bottom up to follow received data toward an application.

| OSI layer | Main function | Useful example |
|---|---|---|
| 7 Application | Network services used by applications | HTTP, DNS, and SSH |
| 6 Presentation | Representation and transformation of data | Character encoding, compression, encryption functions |
| 5 Session | Establishing and managing a dialogue | Session establishment and coordination |
| 4 Transport | Communication between application endpoints | TCP and UDP; port numbers |
| 3 Network | Logical addressing and forwarding between networks | IPv4, IPv6, and routing |
| 2 Data link | Delivery across a local link | Ethernet frames and MAC addresses |
| 1 Physical | Transmission of signals | Copper electrical signals, optical signals, and radio |

The **TCP/IP model** groups these functions into four layers: **Application, Transport, Internet, and Link**. Its Application layer includes functions discussed across the upper three OSI layers. Its Internet layer corresponds broadly to OSI Layer 3, and its Link layer includes data-link and physical functions. Some teaching materials split Link into two layers and call this a five-layer model.

These are ways of describing functions, not competing packet formats. For example, encryption can be discussed as a presentation function, but that does not mean every encrypted protocol exists exclusively at OSI Layer 6. Modern protocol implementations do not always fit a single neat box.

:::facts
- **PDU** means protocol data unit: the unit handled by a protocol at a particular layer.
- Common teaching names are **data** at the upper layers, a TCP **segment** or UDP **datagram** at Layer 4, an IP **packet** at Layer 3, and an Ethernet **frame** at Layer 2.
- Physical interfaces represent bits using signals. “Bits” describes the information, not a particular voltage or optical encoding.
- Ethernet MAC addresses are 48 bits; IPv4 addresses are 32 bits; IPv6 addresses are 128 bits.
- TCP and UDP use 16-bit port fields. A port identifies a transport endpoint; it is not a physical switch socket.
:::

**ICMP** carries IP control and diagnostic messages. IPv4 ping uses ICMP Echo Request and Echo Reply messages carried directly in IPv4, without a TCP or UDP header. An ARP exchange on Ethernet is also not a TCP or UDP conversation, and ARP is not carried inside an IPv4 packet.

sections.title: Encapsulation and de-encapsulation
sections.body:
**Encapsulation** adds the information needed by each protocol as data moves toward the medium. For an application exchange using TCP over IPv4 over Ethernet, the host creates a TCP segment, places it inside an IPv4 packet, and carries that packet inside an Ethernet frame. The receiving endpoint interprets and removes the corresponding encapsulation to deliver the data to the appropriate application.

| Protocol information | Purpose in this example |
|---|---|
| TCP source and destination ports | Identify the application endpoints of the transport exchange. |
| IPv4 source and destination addresses | Identify the IP endpoints of the packet. |
| Ethernet source and destination MAC addresses | Identify sender and intended receiver on the current Ethernet link. |
| Ethernet frame check sequence (FCS) | Detect corruption of the received frame; it does not repair the data. |

A minimum IPv4 header is **20 bytes**, and a minimum TCP header is **20 bytes**; options can make either larger. UDP has an **8-byte header**. Recognize that headers add overhead, but do not treat these minimums as the length of every observed header.

For ordinary Ethernet without VLAN tags, the MAC frame from destination address through FCS is normally **64–1518 bytes**, with up to **1500 bytes** of payload. VLAN tags and other supported frame formats affect frame length. The preamble and interframe gap are not part of that 64–1518-byte count. **MTU** refers to the maximum network-layer packet size carried by the link in this context, not to every byte transmitted on the medium. Frame details are developed in Chapter 07.

A host delivering an IPv4 packet to another subnet does not put the remote host's MAC address into the local frame. It uses a reachable **next hop** on its own link. The distinction between the packet's destination and the frame's destination explains why the same IP packet can cross several different link technologies.

sections.title: Local or remote: the host's first decision
sections.body:
A host uses its routing information to choose how to send a packet. In our introductory topology, each PC has one interface, one connected subnet, and a default gateway, with no additional routes. Under those conditions, the subnet mask determines whether the destination belongs to the connected subnet. Later routing chapters extend this decision to more-specific routes.

For **192.168.10.10/24**, the mask is **255.255.255.0** and the connected subnet is **192.168.10.0/24**. A destination of **192.168.10.20** is local. A destination of **192.168.20.20** is outside that subnet and is sent toward the configured gateway, **192.168.10.1**.

| Destination in this topology | IP next hop | MAC address needed before sending the IPv4 frame |
|---|---|---|
| 192.168.10.20 | The destination host itself | MAC for 192.168.10.20 |
| 192.168.20.20 | Gateway 192.168.10.1 | MAC for 192.168.10.1 |

**ARP**, Address Resolution Protocol, resolves the IPv4 address of a next hop to a MAC address on an Ethernet LAN. A host first checks its ARP cache. If it lacks a usable mapping, it normally sends an ARP request to the Ethernet broadcast address, **ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff**. The request names the IPv4 address being resolved. A normal solicited reply is sent back to the requester as a unicast frame.

For the remote destination above, the request asks for **192.168.10.1**, not 192.168.20.20. The subsequent IPv4 packet still has destination **192.168.20.20**. Learning the gateway's MAC address does not change the final IP destination.

ARP requests remain within the local Layer 2 broadcast domain. A switch floods a broadcast to eligible forwarding ports in the same VLAN, excluding the receiving port. A router does not route that Ethernet broadcast into the next subnet. Its outgoing interface can perform a separate ARP exchange when it needs a next-hop mapping there.

:::trap
A default gateway is used when the selected route requires it. Two hosts in the same correctly configured subnet can communicate directly without sending their traffic through a router. Conversely, a host can reach local neighbors while failing to reach remote networks because its gateway is missing or incorrect.
:::

An incorrect mask can make the host choose the wrong next hop. Features such as **proxy ARP**, where a router answers certain ARP requests on another host's behalf, can sometimes conceal an addressing error. Do not use one successful ping as proof that the configured mask is correct. Read the actual settings and compare them with the addressing plan. Proxy ARP configuration and platform defaults are not memorization targets for this chapter.

sections.title: The packet walk: PC-A to Server-B and back
sections.body:
Use the following topology throughout the example. Both router interfaces are operational, both connected routes exist, and no NAT, filtering, tunneling, or fragmentation affects the exchange. PC-A and Server-B have the gateways shown.

```diagram
{ "type": "topology", "title": "One routed IPv4 exchange",
  "caption": "The switches forward within their LANs. R1 routes between 192.168.10.0/24 and 192.168.20.0/24.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "PCA", "kind": "pc", "label": "PC-A", "sub": "192.168.10.10/24", "x": 1, "y": 3 },
    { "id": "SW1", "kind": "switch", "label": "SW1", "x": 3.5, "y": 3 },
    { "id": "R1", "kind": "router", "label": "R1", "sub": "Gi0/0: .10.1 · Gi0/1: .20.1", "x": 6, "y": 3, "highlight": true },
    { "id": "SW2", "kind": "switch", "label": "SW2", "x": 8.5, "y": 3 },
    { "id": "B", "kind": "server", "label": "Server-B", "sub": "192.168.20.20/24", "x": 11, "y": 3 }
  ],
  "links": [
    { "from": "PCA", "to": "SW1" },
    { "from": "SW1", "to": "R1", "toLabel": "Gi0/0" },
    { "from": "R1", "to": "SW2", "fromLabel": "Gi0/1" },
    { "from": "SW2", "to": "B" }
  ],
  "packet": { "path": ["PCA", "SW1", "R1", "SW2", "B"], "label": "ICMP Echo Request" } }
```

| Interface | IPv4 address | Illustrative MAC address |
|---|---|---|
| PC-A | 192.168.10.10/24; gateway 192.168.10.1 | 0060.2f3e.1b22 |
| R1 Gi0/0 | 192.168.10.1/24 | 0001.9641.7a01 |
| R1 Gi0/1 | 192.168.20.1/24 | 0001.9641.7a02 |
| Server-B | 192.168.20.20/24; gateway 192.168.20.1 | 00d0.ba2c.5e01 |

**1. PC-A selects its next hop.** The destination is outside its connected /24, so PC-A uses its default gateway. If necessary, it resolves 192.168.10.1 through ARP. It then sends an Ethernet frame with source MAC **0060.2f3e.1b22** and destination MAC **0001.9641.7a01**. Inside that frame, the IPv4 addresses are **192.168.10.10 → 192.168.20.20**.

**2. SW1 forwards the frame.** It learns the source MAC against the incoming port and VLAN, and looks up the destination MAC in that VLAN's table. If the gateway's MAC is known on the router-facing forwarding port, SW1 sends the frame there. If it is unknown, SW1 floods it to eligible ports in that VLAN except the incoming port. Ordinary Layer 2 forwarding preserves the source and destination MAC addresses and does not decrement the packet's TTL.

**3. R1 routes the packet.** The frame is addressed to R1's receiving interface. R1 processes the contained IPv4 packet and selects a route for **192.168.20.20**. In this example the destination is on the subnet directly connected to Gi0/1. Normal forwarding decrements **TTL**, the IPv4 Time to Live field, by one and updates the IPv4 header checksum. If forwarding would exhaust TTL, the router discards the packet and normally generates an ICMP Time Exceeded message, subject to the rules and limits for ICMP responses.

**4. R1 builds the outgoing frame.** It resolves Server-B's MAC on LAN-B if needed. The new frame has source MAC **0001.9641.7a02** and destination MAC **00d0.ba2c.5e01**. The source and destination IPv4 addresses remain **192.168.10.10 → 192.168.20.20** under our stated assumptions. The outgoing frame has an FCS for its own contents.

**5. Server-B receives the request and sends a reply.** SW2 forwards the frame within LAN-B. Server-B recognizes its own destination addresses and processes the ICMP Echo Request. The reply is a new packet with source **192.168.20.20** and destination **192.168.10.10**. Because that destination is remote to Server-B, its reply uses gateway **192.168.20.1**. R1 then routes the reply toward LAN-A.

The reply has its own initial TTL. A ping display usually reports the TTL of the received reply, not the original request's remaining TTL. Initial values vary. You can calculate a hop count from a received TTL only when you know the starting value and the relevant forwarding assumptions; do not infer an exact path from a guessed operating-system default.

sections.title: Where the layers live: devices and commands
sections.body:
Keep three tables distinct:

| Table | Main relationship | What it helps decide |
|---|---|---|
| IP routing table | Destination prefix to a forwarding action, interface, and possibly next hop | Where to send an IP packet |
| ARP cache | IPv4 address to MAC address on a local link | How to address an Ethernet frame to the selected IPv4 next hop |
| Switch MAC address table | VLAN and MAC address to switch port | Where to forward a frame inside a VLAN |

These tables have different contents and learning mechanisms. A learned MAC entry does not prove that the host has the right IP address. An ARP entry does not prove that a TCP service works. A route does not, by itself, prove that the next-hop link is operational or that return traffic is permitted.

Useful IOS commands include `show ip interface brief`, `show interfaces GigabitEthernet0/0`, `show ip route`, `show arp`, and `show mac address-table`. On a Windows PC or the Packet Tracer PC command prompt, `arp -a` displays the ARP cache. Command availability and output vary by platform.

Use **ping** for an ICMP reachability test. Use **traceroute** on IOS, or **tracert** on Windows, to collect responses from probes with increasing TTL values. Implementations use different probe types, and intermediate devices may filter or rate-limit replies. A missing traceroute response does not by itself prove that the device cannot forward traffic, and the displayed forward path does not establish the return path.

sections.title: Reading the output
sections.body:
These excerpts are illustrative and use the MAC addresses from the example.

```output SW1: show mac address-table
Vlan    Mac Address       Type        Ports
----    -----------       --------    -----
   1    0060.2f3e.1b22    DYNAMIC     Fa0/1   ← Frames with this source MAC were learned on Fa0/1 in VLAN 1.
   1    0001.9641.7a01    DYNAMIC     Fa0/24  ← The gateway MAC is reachable through the router-facing port.
```

For a known unicast addressed to 0001.9641.7a01 in VLAN 1, SW1 selects Fa0/24 if that port is eligible to forward. The destination IP can be remote; this ordinary Layer 2 decision uses the destination MAC and VLAN.

```output R1: show arp
Protocol  Address          Age (min)  Hardware Addr   Type   Interface
Internet  192.168.10.1            -   0001.9641.7a01  ARPA   GigabitEthernet0/0
Internet  192.168.10.10           2   0060.2f3e.1b22  ARPA   GigabitEthernet0/0
Internet  192.168.20.1            -   0001.9641.7a02  ARPA   GigabitEthernet0/1
Internet  192.168.20.20           1   00d0.ba2c.5e01  ARPA   GigabitEthernet0/1
```

In this known configuration, the .1 entries correspond to R1's own interfaces. The numbered ages belong to dynamically learned neighbor entries. A dash in the Age field alone is not enough to distinguish every possible static or local entry; use the address and configuration as well. ARP entries can age out, so a missing entry alone does not prove that communication never occurred.

After a failed remote ping, first compare the hosts' addresses, masks, and gateways with the plan. Inspect interface states and the relevant connected routes. Then examine ARP and MAC learning on the path. This sequence is a practical starting point, not a requirement to run every command regardless of the evidence.

sections.title: Exam focus
sections.body:
- Explain the functions of OSI and TCP/IP layers and use frame, packet, segment, and datagram accurately.
- Identify the IP next hop and the MAC address needed for a local or remote destination.
- Explain why ARP for a remote destination normally resolves the local gateway, while the packet keeps the remote destination IP.
- Distinguish source-MAC learning and destination-MAC lookup from IP route selection.
- Describe the new Ethernet frame, TTL decrement, and IPv4 checksum update at a router.
- Account for the return path and its gateway when investigating a failed exchange.
- Interpret ping, traceroute, interface status, ARP, and MAC-table evidence within the limits of each test.

lab.title: Follow an IPv4 exchange across two LANs
lab.intro:
Practice revised September 2026. If you completed an earlier version, repeat the revised exercise and update its checkmarks.

Build two Ethernet LANs connected by one router. Observe address resolution and packet forwarding, then introduce a return-path fault. PC-B fills the destination-host role called Server-B in the lesson; no application server is needed for an ICMP test.

The router addressing commands in Steps 1–2 are supplied setup, not a command-memory test. Read what each line selects or changes, then use the network to observe forwarding. Chapter 04 develops IPv4 addressing, and Chapter 08 develops a fuller IOS workflow. For this /24 example, addresses with the same first three decimal numbers belong to the same subnet; use the given plan rather than designing your own yet.

Use a new project with the listed device models. The commands assume their interface names. Record the actual MAC addresses assigned by your simulator: they will differ from the illustrative addresses in the lesson. Event order, packet counts, and timing may also vary.
lab.topology:
```diagram
{ "type": "topology", "title": "Two LANs joined by R1",
  "caption": "SW1 and SW2 provide separate Layer 2 LANs. R1 has one interface in each subnet.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "PCA", "kind": "pc", "label": "PC-A", "sub": "192.168.10.10/24", "x": 1, "y": 3 },
    { "id": "SW1", "kind": "switch", "label": "SW1", "x": 3.5, "y": 3 },
    { "id": "R1", "kind": "router", "label": "R1", "sub": "2911", "x": 6, "y": 3, "highlight": true },
    { "id": "SW2", "kind": "switch", "label": "SW2", "x": 8.5, "y": 3 },
    { "id": "PCB", "kind": "pc", "label": "PC-B", "sub": "192.168.20.20/24", "x": 11, "y": 3 }
  ],
  "links": [
    { "from": "PCA", "to": "SW1", "fromLabel": "Fa0", "toLabel": "Fa0/1" },
    { "from": "SW1", "to": "R1", "fromLabel": "Fa0/24", "toLabel": "Gi0/0" },
    { "from": "R1", "to": "SW2", "fromLabel": "Gi0/1", "toLabel": "Fa0/24" },
    { "from": "SW2", "to": "PCB", "fromLabel": "Fa0/1", "toLabel": "Fa0" }
  ] }
```

Use copper straight-through cables for all four PC-to-switch and router-to-switch links shown. Select the ports explicitly.

| Device | Interface | IPv4 address | Mask | Gateway |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PC-A | FastEthernet0 | 192.168.10.10 | 255.255.255.0 | 192.168.10.1 |
| R1 | GigabitEthernet0/0 | 192.168.10.1 | 255.255.255.0 | — |
| R1 | GigabitEthernet0/1 | 192.168.20.1 | 255.255.255.0 | — |
| PC-B | FastEthernet0 | 192.168.20.20 | 255.255.255.0 | 192.168.20.1 |

The switches use their default access VLAN for these separate LANs. They need no management IP address for this exercise. R1 needs no static or default route to reach its two directly connected subnets.

steps.title: Build and label the topology
steps.body:
Place and cable the devices as shown. Set their workspace display names. Open each network device's CLI and decline the initial configuration dialog if it appears. Configure the hostnames:

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# end
```

On SW1 and SW2, use the same sequence with `hostname SW1` and `hostname SW2`, respectively. Inspect the cable endpoints before continuing. Router interfaces may initially remain administratively disabled.

:::expected
There are two separate switch LANs with R1 between them. The CLI hostnames match the labels, and you can identify R1's interface toward each subnet.
:::

steps.title: Apply the supplied router setup
steps.body:
Each interface needs the address from its own row. The `interface` command selects a port; `ip address` gives it an address and mask; `no shutdown` enables it. `description` is a label. These two active local interfaces give R1 routes to the attached LANs without a routing protocol or static route.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/0
R1(config-if)# description LAN-A
R1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/1
R1(config-if)# description LAN-B
R1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.20.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
R1# show ip route
R1# copy running-config startup-config
```

Accept the save command's default destination. Once links are ready, verify that both configured interfaces report **up/up** and that the routing table contains connected routes for **192.168.10.0/24** and **192.168.20.0/24**. Some IOS versions also display local /32 routes for the router's own addresses.

:::expected
R1 has an operational interface and a connected route for each LAN. No route learned from another router is required in this topology. If a connected route is absent, check the address and interface state before adding unrelated routing commands.
:::

steps.title: Configure the hosts and record the baseline
steps.body:
On each PC, use **Desktop → IP Configuration** to enter the table's address, mask, and gateway. Read the settings back to catch typing errors.

Save each switch's configuration, then save the project as **01-models-ready.pkt**. Do not initiate test traffic yet: the next step is intended to capture the first exchange. Normal background traffic or earlier tests may already have populated some tables; that is an observation to record, not an error.

Before starting the ping, predict:

- Which IPv4 address PC-A will resolve through ARP for a packet destined for PC-B.
- The source and destination IPv4 addresses of the request.
- Which device will replace the Ethernet header and decrement the IPv4 TTL.

:::expected
Your prediction is: PC-A uses gateway 192.168.10.1 as its next hop; the request's IP addresses are 192.168.10.10 and 192.168.20.20; R1 performs the routed forwarding step.
:::

steps.title: Observe the first remote exchange
steps.body:
Switch to **Simulation** mode. Open the event filters and select **ARP** and **ICMP** to keep the display manageable. From PC-A's Command Prompt, run:

```text
ping 192.168.20.20
```

Use **Capture/Forward**, or the equivalent step control in your version, to advance events. Open the event or PDU details at PC-A, R1's incoming side, and R1's outgoing side. Inspect the available Layer 2 and Layer 3 fields.

Before opening the outgoing event, predict which incoming fields must change. Then record the request's source MAC, destination MAC, source IP, destination IP, and TTL on both sides of R1. Also record the ARP target addresses if requests appear. A cached mapping can eliminate an ARP exchange; do not invent a missing packet or assume that every ping must generate fresh ARP.

:::expected
On LAN-A, the ICMP request frame is addressed to R1's LAN-A MAC. On LAN-B, the outgoing frame uses R1's LAN-B MAC as source and PC-B's MAC as destination. The request's IP addresses remain unchanged, and normal forwarding through R1 reduces its TTL by one. Any necessary ARP on LAN-B is a separate local exchange initiated there.
:::

If your version does not expose all fields, use this **supplied worksheet** for the missing comparison. It is not an observed capture. The device labels stand for interface MAC addresses.

| Location of the same request | Ethernet source → destination | IPv4 source → destination | TTL |
|---|---|---|---|
| LAN-A, before R1 | PC-A → R1 Gi0/0 | 192.168.10.10 → 192.168.20.20 | 128 |
| LAN-B, after R1 | R1 Gi0/1 → PC-B | 192.168.10.10 → 192.168.20.20 | 127 |

Classify each change as **unchanged**, **new local-link encapsulation**, or **decremented**. Keep supplied values separate from actual observations.

steps.title: Compare local and remote delivery
steps.body:
Allow the first test to finish, then use Realtime mode for a repeat ping from PC-A to PC-B. Also test PC-A to **192.168.10.1**, its local gateway address. Return to Simulation mode if needed to inspect that local request.

Compare the two packets. Their outgoing frames can use the same destination MAC, but their destination IP addresses differ. A packet addressed to 192.168.10.1 is for R1 itself; a packet addressed to 192.168.20.20 is to be forwarded toward PC-B.

:::expected
Both tests receive replies after the topology is ready. You can distinguish “using the router as next hop” from “addressing the router as the IP destination.” A gateway MAC in a frame does not imply that the packet's destination IP is the gateway.
:::

steps.title: Read the three tables
steps.body:
Collect the following evidence:

```ios R1
R1# show ip route
R1# show arp
```

```ios SW1
SW1# show mac address-table
```

```ios SW2
SW2# show mac address-table
```

On each PC, run `arp -a`. Match actual MAC addresses to the devices using the tables and the device interface information. For each table, record one row and label its relationship: prefix with forwarding information, IP with MAC, or VLAN/MAC with switch port. Learn which question a table answers, rather than memorizing every column.

:::expected
SW1 learns PC-A's MAC on Fa0/1 and R1's LAN-A MAC on Fa0/24 when it receives frames from them. SW2 makes the equivalent local observations. R1 can hold ARP mappings for neighbors on both LANs. PC-A normally needs the local gateway mapping for the remote test, not PC-B's MAC.
:::

steps.title: Introduce a return-path fault
steps.body:
In PC-B's IP Configuration, change only the gateway from **192.168.20.1** to the unused address **192.168.20.254**. Keep its address and mask unchanged. Allow existing tests to finish.

From PC-B, ping its local router interface, **192.168.20.1**. Then, from PC-A, ping PC-B again. If helpful, inspect ICMP and ARP events in Simulation mode.

:::expected
PC-B can still reach 192.168.20.1 directly because that destination is local. The remote PC-A-to-PC-B exchange fails: PC-B's reply to 192.168.10.10 needs an off-subnet next hop, and its configured gateway is unavailable. A request arriving at PC-B does not guarantee a reply can return.
:::

If your results differ, verify that no extra routes, gateways, devices using .254, or previous topology changes exist. Compare the actual host settings and event details before drawing a conclusion.

steps.title: Restore and verify
steps.body:
Restore PC-B's gateway to **192.168.20.1**. Test PC-A to PC-B and PC-B to PC-A. Inspect the addressing settings and router interface summary once more. Save the completed project as **01-models-complete.pkt**.

:::expected
Both remote tests receive replies, and the configuration matches the original plan. Your lab record identifies the fault, the evidence that isolated it, the single setting corrected, and the successful retest.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
| Symptom | Useful checks |
|---|---|
| Router link stays down | Actual cable endpoints, peer port, interface address context, and `no shutdown`; inspect `show ip interface brief`. |
| A connected subnet is missing | Verify the address/mask and operational state of that subnet's router interface. |
| Local gateway replies but the remote host does not | Check both hosts' settings, both LANs, R1's routes, and the return path. |
| No ARP request appears during a later ping | Inspect existing ARP entries; cached mappings can be reused. |
| Packet details differ from the lesson | Use your actual MACs and initial TTL; compare the forwarding changes, not fixed sample values. |
| One early timeout followed by replies | Note the timing and resolution events; investigate if loss persists instead of treating the first timeout as a diagnosis. |
lab.challenge:
Your evidence record should contain a before/after frame comparison, one labeled row from each table, and local/remote tests before and after the gateway repair. Identify any supplied rather than observed values.

Add PC-C on SW1 Fa0/2 with **192.168.10.30/24** and gateway **192.168.10.1**. Predict the ARP target and frame destination for PC-A sending to PC-C, then compare them with PC-A sending to PC-B.

Before changing a setting, predict whether each test should work if PC-A has no default gateway. Temporarily remove PC-A's gateway, repeat the local PC-C and remote PC-B tests, and record the results. Restore PC-A's gateway to 192.168.10.1, verify both tests again, and save only the restored state. Complete these predictions and observations before opening the answer below.

:::solution
For PC-C, PC-A resolves 192.168.10.30 and sends directly to PC-C's MAC. For PC-B, it resolves or reuses the gateway mapping. With PC-A's gateway removed, communication with PC-C should remain possible, while PC-A has no route to PC-B in this simple host configuration. Restoring 192.168.10.1 as PC-A's gateway restores its remote next hop; verify both tests before saving.
:::

questions.prompt: For TCP over IPv4 over Ethernet, which PDU names correspond to Layers 4, 3, and 2, in that order?
options: Packet, frame, bits
Segment, frame, packet
Frame, packet, segment
Segment, packet, frame
questions.explanation: A TCP segment is carried in an IP packet, which is carried in an Ethernet frame. UDP uses the term datagram at the transport layer.

whyWrong.0: These begin at Layer 3 and continue downward.
whyWrong.1: A frame carries the packet, not the reverse.
whyWrong.2: This lists the requested layers in reverse order.

questions.prompt: Which layer of the four-layer TCP/IP model covers IP addressing and routing?
options: Application
Transport
Internet
Link
questions.explanation: The TCP/IP Internet layer provides IP addressing and packet forwarding functions, corresponding broadly to OSI Layer 3.

whyWrong.0: Application protocols provide application-level services.
whyWrong.1: Transport includes TCP and UDP services to application endpoints.
whyWrong.3: Link handles communication across the local link.

questions.prompt: Which two statements describe a normal ARP request and solicited reply on an Ethernet LAN? Choose two.
options: The request normally uses a unicast Ethernet destination.
The request normally uses the Ethernet broadcast destination.
ARP is carried inside the IPv4 packet it helps deliver.
The solicited reply is normally unicast to the requester.
The reply maps the final remote destination to the gateway’s MAC.
questions.explanation: ARP uses Ethernet directly to resolve an IPv4 next-hop address on the local link. A normal request is broadcast and its solicited reply is unicast; it does not distribute a remote route.

whyWrong.0: A normal request without a usable mapping is broadcast on the local Ethernet LAN.
whyWrong.2: ARP uses the Ethernet link directly; it is not a header inside the pending IPv4 packet.
whyWrong.4: For remote delivery, the host resolves the local gateway’s own IPv4 address to its MAC.

questions.prompt: PC-A is 192.168.10.10/24 and PC-C is 192.168.10.30/24 on the same VLAN. PC-A has no additional routes and no cached mapping for PC-C. What does it normally do before sending an IPv4 packet to PC-C?
options: Resolve PC-C’s MAC, then address the frame to the gateway.
Resolve the gateway’s MAC, then send through that gateway.
Send a unicast IP packet using a broadcast Ethernet destination.
Resolve PC-C’s MAC, then send directly to that MAC.
questions.explanation: The destination is on the connected /24. PC-A resolves the destination host's MAC and sends directly on the LAN. The configured gateway is not needed for this exchange.

whyWrong.0: A mapping for PC-C does not supply a reason to send this local exchange through the gateway.
whyWrong.1: The stated local destination is directly reachable on the connected LAN.
whyWrong.2: The ARP request may be broadcast, but the ordinary resolved unicast IPv4 frame is addressed to PC-C.

questions.prompt: PC-A has one interface and only the connected and default routes shown. After resolving the required MAC, which destination addresses belong in its ICMP request to PC-B?
questions.explanation: PC-B is outside PC-A's /24, so the local frame goes to the gateway interface on LAN-A. The enclosed packet still names PC-B as its destination.

whyWrong.0: That MAC is on the remote LAN, not the local next hop.
whyWrong.2: The request would then be addressed to the router itself.
whyWrong.3: This is R1's interface on the remote LAN, not PC-A's local gateway.

questions.prompt: A router forwards an ordinary IPv4 packet between two Ethernet LANs. No NAT, tunnel, or fragmentation is involved. Which two actions describe normal forwarding? Choose two.
options: It decrements TTL by one and updates the IPv4 header checksum.
It changes the source IPv4 address to its outgoing interface address.
It creates a new Ethernet frame using its outgoing interface's MAC as source.
It replaces the destination IPv4 address with the next-hop IPv4 address.
It sends the incoming Ethernet frame unchanged onto the second LAN.
questions.explanation: The router performs a new link-layer encapsulation for the outgoing Ethernet LAN. Normal IPv4 forwarding reduces TTL and updates the affected header checksum, while preserving the source and destination IP addresses under these assumptions.

whyWrong.1: Ordinary routing in this example does not translate the source address.
whyWrong.3: The route identifies a forwarding action without replacing the packet's final destination address.
whyWrong.4: The outgoing link needs a frame addressed for that link.

exhibit.title: Capture after R1
exhibit.text:
Ethernet source: R1 GigabitEthernet0/1 MAC
Ethernet destination: PC-B MAC
IPv4 source: 192.168.10.10 (PC-A)
IPv4 destination: 192.168.20.20 (PC-B)

questions.prompt: R1 routes between LAN-A and LAN-B without NAT. A capture on LAN-B shows the request below. Which explanation fits?
options: R1 translated the packet’s source to its LAN-B address.
R1 built a new frame for the outgoing Ethernet link.
SW2 routed the packet and changed its source MAC.
PC-A addressed the original frame directly to PC-B.
questions.explanation: On the outgoing LAN, the link-layer sender is R1, but the packet still identifies PC-A as its original IP source. This is normal routed forwarding.

whyWrong.0: The exhibit still names PC-A as the source IP; no translation is shown.
whyWrong.2: R1 supplied the outgoing source MAC during routing; ordinary SW2 bridging does not do this.
whyWrong.3: The original LAN-A frame went to PC-A’s local gateway; PC-B’s MAC is used on the outgoing LAN.

questions.prompt: A capture at the sender records an IPv4 packet with TTL 128. The same packet arrives with TTL 126. Assume ordinary forwarding, one decrement per routed hop, and no other TTL changes. How many routers forwarded it?
questions.explanation: The observed reduction is 128 − 126 = 2. The initial TTL is explicitly known here; a received TTL by itself is insufficient for an exact hop count.

whyWrong.0: The captured TTL decreased, so this was not a zero-hop exchange under the stated assumptions.
whyWrong.1: One decrement would leave 127.
whyWrong.2: Three decrements would leave 125.

exhibit.title: Representative R1 show arp excerpt
exhibit.text:
Protocol  Address          Age (min)  Hardware Addr   Type  Interface
Internet  192.168.10.10           2   0060.2f3e.1b22  ARPA  GigabitEthernet0/0
Internet  192.168.20.20           1   00d0.ba2c.5e01  ARPA  GigabitEthernet0/1

questions.prompt: Which neighbor mapping does the displayed ARP table contain?
options: 192.168.20.20 → 00d0.ba2c.5e01 on GigabitEthernet0/1
192.168.20.20 → 0060.2f3e.1b22 on GigabitEthernet0/0
192.168.20.0/24 → a route through GigabitEthernet0/1
00d0.ba2c.5e01 → a learned switch port in VLAN 1
questions.explanation: Read one complete row: address 192.168.20.20 maps to MAC 00d0.ba2c.5e01 on the router’s GigabitEthernet0/1 link. This is local-neighbor information, not a route or a switch-port entry.

whyWrong.1: That MAC and interface belong to the other displayed neighbor.
whyWrong.2: The exhibit is an ARP table; it does not display a destination-prefix route.
whyWrong.3: A VLAN/MAC-to-switch-port entry belongs to the switch MAC address table.

exhibit.title: Representative SW1 show mac address-table excerpt
exhibit.text:
Vlan  Mac Address       Type     Ports
1     0060.2f3e.1b22    DYNAMIC  Fa0/1
1     0001.9641.7a01    DYNAMIC  Fa0/24

questions.prompt: A frame in VLAN 1 arrives on Fa0/1 with destination MAC 0001.9641.7a01. All shown ports are forwarding. What is the normal Layer 2 forwarding action?
options: Forward through Fa0/24 using the existing destination MAC.
Forward through Fa0/1 because it learned the source there.
Flood the frame because the destination IP is remote.
Forward through Fa0/24 using the switch’s own source MAC.
questions.explanation: The destination MAC is known on Fa0/24 in VLAN 1. Ordinary Layer 2 forwarding selects that eligible port and preserves the endpoint MAC addresses; it does not perform an IP routing hop.

whyWrong.1: The source entry tells the switch where return traffic can go; this frame’s destination selects its egress port.
whyWrong.2: The known destination MAC determines this Layer 2 action, regardless of the packet’s remote IP destination.
whyWrong.3: Ordinary Layer 2 forwarding does not replace the frame’s source MAC with the switch’s address.

exhibit.title: Two observations from a fresh test
exhibit.text:
R1 LAN-A interface: up/up
PC-A ping to R1 LAN-A address: request timed out

questions.prompt: What can these two observations establish without further evidence?
options: R1 reports a working local link, but the failed ping needs more investigation.
PC-A must have the wrong mask because R1’s interface is operational.
The timeout proves R1 cannot receive frames on this interface.
The local up/up state proves that PC-A received an Echo Reply.
questions.explanation: Up/up describes the local interface's operational states. Host settings, routes, policy, and applications require additional evidence.

whyWrong.1: A mask error is one possibility, not established by this pair of observations.
whyWrong.2: The interface state and timeout do not prove which stage failed.
whyWrong.3: The stated ping result reports no reply; link state is a different observation.

questions.prompt: PC-A's remote ping reaches PC-B, but PC-B has an unused address configured as its default gateway. PC-B can still ping its actual local router interface. Which explanation best fits?
options: PC-B selects an unavailable next hop for its remote reply.
PC-B cannot send any frame through its local switch port.
R1 must change PC-A’s source IP before PC-B can reply.
PC-B’s successful local test validates its default gateway.
questions.explanation: A local router-interface ping uses direct delivery on PC-B's subnet. Replying to remote PC-A requires the selected off-subnet next hop, so a wrong gateway can prevent the return traffic even when the request arrives.

whyWrong.1: The successful local test demonstrates that the port can carry that exchange.
whyWrong.2: Ordinary routing does not require source translation; PC-B needs a valid route back to PC-A.
whyWrong.3: The local router address can be reached directly, so that test does not exercise the default gateway.

cards.front: Name the seven OSI layers from Layer 7 to Layer 1.
cards.back: Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data link, Physical.

cards.front: What PDU names are commonly used for TCP, UDP, IP, and Ethernet?
cards.back: TCP segment; UDP datagram; IP packet; Ethernet frame.

cards.front: How does the four-layer TCP/IP model relate to OSI?
cards.back: Application groups OSI 5–7; Transport matches 4; Internet matches 3; Link groups 1–2.

cards.front: How do a MAC address, an IP address, and a transport port differ?
cards.back: MAC: the Ethernet link endpoint. IP: the logical network endpoint. TCP/UDP port: the transport endpoint for an application exchange.

cards.front: What changes during ordinary IPv4 routing between Ethernet LANs without NAT or tunneling?
cards.back: The outgoing Ethernet frame is new; TTL decreases and its IPv4 checksum changes. Source and destination IP stay the same under these assumptions.

cards.front: Can a received TTL alone establish the exact routed hop count?
cards.back: No. You also need the packet’s initial TTL and the assumptions about how it changed.

cards.front: How does a simple host with a connected route and default gateway choose a next hop?
cards.back: With only a connected route and default gateway: send directly to local destinations; send other destinations to the gateway.

cards.front: Does ordinary Layer 2 switching rewrite endpoint MAC addresses or decrement IP TTL?
cards.back: No. Ordinary bridging preserves the source/destination MAC addresses and does not decrement IP TTL.

cards.front: Which commands display ARP mappings on IOS and a Windows or Packet Tracer PC?
cards.back: IOS: show arp. Windows or Packet Tracer PC: arp -a. They display present IP-to-MAC mappings; entries can age out.

cards.front: What does a dynamic switch MAC-table entry associate?
cards.back: A VLAN and source MAC with the port where a frame arrived. The switch then looks up destination MACs to select egress ports.

cards.front: Does IPv4 ping use TCP or UDP ports?
cards.back: Neither. ICMP Echo is carried directly in IPv4. Its success does not establish that a TCP or UDP service works.

cards.front: Which address does ARP resolve before a correctly configured host sends to a remote subnet through its default gateway?
cards.back: The local gateway’s IPv4 address. The frame uses that gateway’s MAC; the IP packet keeps the remote destination.

cards.front: What limits the scope of a normal Ethernet ARP request?
cards.back: It stays in the local Layer 2 broadcast domain. Routers can originate separate ARP exchanges on their other links.

cards.front: Why must you consider the return path when troubleshooting a ping?
cards.back: The source needs an Echo Reply. A remote host can receive the request but fail to return its reply through an incorrect gateway.

commands.task: Display R1's IPv4-to-MAC mappings.
commands.note: Read the address, MAC, interface, and age together. An entry does not test an application.

commands.task: Display the switch's MAC address table.
commands.note: This table associates VLAN/MAC entries with switch ports. Command spelling varies on older images.

commands.task: Display IPv4 addresses and a brief summary of router interface states.
commands.note: Check both Status and Protocol, then investigate the relevant interface if needed.

commands.task: Display the IPv4 routing table.
commands.note: In the two-LAN lab, expect connected routes for both operational, addressed router interfaces.

commands.task: Display this PC's ARP cache.
commands.note: This is a Windows/Packet Tracer PC command, not an IOS command. Cached entries may be reused without new ARP requests.

commands.task: From PC-A, test ICMP reachability to remote PC-B at 192.168.20.20.
commands.note: This tests the actual client’s path and its return path. Wait for completion and record the result.
