chapters.summary: Learn what switches, routers, firewalls, access points, controllers, endpoints, and servers do. Compare common network designs and check the power and connectivity a device needs.

sections.body:
Before configuring a network, you need to recognize what each device contributes. This chapter follows a user reaching a server, then shows how the same functions fit into larger designs. The lab uses an office LAN to distinguish working local communication from a stopped application service, then compares larger designs on paper.

This directly covers the v1.1 component and architecture objectives. For v2.0, it provides the background needed for later interface, edge-port, wireless, and management configuration. Identifying an AP or a PoE port here does not replace those later configuration labs.

sections.title: Why roles matter more than boxes
sections.body:
:::facts
- A Layer 2 switch forwards Ethernet frames within a local network using MAC addresses.
- A router, including the routing function of a Layer 3 switch, forwards IP packets between networks.
- An access point connects wireless clients; a controller coordinates the devices it manages.
- A firewall enforces traffic policy. An inline IPS can detect and block suspicious traffic.
- PoE provides electrical power over a suitable copper Ethernet connection.
- A topology describes connections and paths. A device's position alone does not prove its configuration.
:::

Suppose a desktop opens a page hosted on a server in the same office. The desktop is the client, the server provides the page, and an Ethernet switch connects them. If they are in the same local IP network, the traffic can pass through the switch without being routed. If the server is in another network, the desktop sends the traffic to its **default gateway**, the local router interface used to reach other networks.

A **physical topology** shows equipment, ports, and cables. A **logical topology** shows how traffic is organized, including IP networks and paths through routing or security devices. Both are useful. A cable may be installed correctly while an interface is disabled; two devices may connect to the same switch but belong to different logical networks.

Read a drawing by tracing one specific exchange. Identify the source and destination, their local connections, and any device that must move traffic between networks. Then ask what would happen if one link failed. This is more useful than deciding what a device does from its shape, position, or product name alone.

sections.title: Routers, switches, endpoints and servers
sections.body:
An **endpoint** sends or receives the traffic that the network exists to carry. Desktops, printers, phones, cameras, and sensors are endpoints. A **server** is an endpoint that provides a service to other devices: a web page, a shared file, a name lookup, or an address assignment. “Client” and “server” describe the roles in an exchange; the same computer can perform both roles in different exchanges.

An **interface** is a device's connection to a network. On a PC it may be an Ethernet adapter or a Wi-Fi adapter. A switch has many interfaces because it connects many devices. Interface names such as `FastEthernet0/1` and `GigabitEthernet0/0` identify the particular connection you are inspecting, so record both ends of a cable when building or troubleshooting a network.

A **Layer 2 switch** learns which source MAC addresses are reachable through its ports. For a known unicast destination, it can forward the frame toward the correct port instead of copying it to every device. An unknown destination may need to be flooded within the relevant **VLAN**, a logical Layer 2 network. Broadcast traffic is also confined to that VLAN; the Ethernet switching chapter explains the forwarding rules in detail.

A switch does not need a management IP address merely to switch Ethernet frames. A management address lets an administrator reach the switch itself. This distinction matters in the lab: the PCs can communicate through an otherwise unconfigured switch even though the switch has no address you can ping.

A **router** uses a routing table to choose where an IP packet should go next. It connects networks, such as an office LAN and a provider connection. As it forwards a packet, it removes the incoming link-layer framing and places the packet in framing suitable for the outgoing connection. A router does not simply extend an Ethernet broadcast domain into the next network.

A **Layer 3 switch**, also called a multilayer switch, can perform both Ethernet switching and IP routing. It is often used to route between local networks in a campus. A router is often selected for a branch or WAN edge because of the interfaces and services it supports. These are typical roles, not a rule that every product labeled “switch” lacks a particular routing, security, or WAN feature; check the actual platform and software.

| Device or role | Main task in this chapter | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Layer 2 switch | Connect devices in a local Layer 2 network | Desktop and printer on the same LAN |
| Router | Forward packets between IP networks | Office LAN reaching another site |
| Layer 3 switch | Switch locally and route between local networks | Several department networks in a campus |
| Client endpoint | Request or use a service | Browser requesting a web page |
| Server endpoint | Provide a service | Server returning that page |

The lab keeps PC-A and Server-A on one network, where SW1 can carry their exchange locally. Chapter 01's routed example shows the additional gateway role for a remote destination. Using a router does not mean every endpoint requires a direct cable to it.

sections.title: Firewalls, IPS, access points and controllers
sections.body:
A **firewall** allows or blocks traffic according to a security policy. A stateful firewall also tracks connection state, helping it distinguish traffic belonging to an allowed exchange from unrelated traffic. Allowing a connection is a policy decision; the presence of a route does not mean that the connection is permitted.

A **next-generation firewall (NGFW)** adds capabilities such as application identification and integrated intrusion prevention. This allows an organization to distinguish applications that may use the same transport port and to inspect traffic for threats. Available inspection depends on the product, configuration, and visibility into the traffic. Encrypted content is not automatically readable merely because the device is called an NGFW.

An **intrusion prevention system (IPS)** examines traffic for signs of attacks. When deployed inline, it is in the forwarding path and can drop traffic according to its policy. An **intrusion detection system (IDS)** typically examines a copy and raises alerts. The useful distinction is whether that inspection point can directly stop the traffic passing through it; avoid assuming that every alert proves a successful attack.

An **access point (AP)** provides a wireless connection for clients and connects that wireless network to the rest of the network. A standalone AP is administered individually. A controller-based AP is managed as part of a larger wireless system. A wireless LAN controller can coordinate settings such as network names, security policy, and radio behavior across multiple APs.

A **controller** provides a central place to coordinate or manage network devices. It may distribute configuration, collect operational information, and help apply consistent policy. That does not imply that every user packet passes through every kind of controller. Some wireless deployments tunnel client traffic through a controller, while others switch it locally at the AP's site. The later wireless chapters examine those options.

The v1.1 topic list includes **controllers**. Two useful examples are **Cisco Catalyst Center**, formerly Cisco DNA Center, and a **wireless LAN controller (WLC)**. Catalyst Center provides network management, automation and operational-health information across supported campus devices. A WLC coordinates its wireless APs and their operation. Recognize the different roles; the objective does not require a catalog of controller models.

:::trap One enclosure can perform several roles
A home wireless router often combines a router, a small Ethernet switch, an AP, and services such as DHCP. Its AP function gives a laptop wireless access; its routing function reaches another network. Identify the function involved in the problem rather than treating all failures as “the router is down.”
:::

For example, if wired devices can reach an office server but wireless devices cannot associate with the wireless network at all, begin with wireless settings and the AP. If both wired and wireless devices can reach the local server but cannot reach another network, investigate their gateway and the path beyond it. This narrows the investigation without pretending that the symptom alone proves one failed component.

sections.title: Power over Ethernet
sections.body:
**Power over Ethernet (PoE)** carries electrical power and Ethernet data over the same suitable copper cable. A PoE-capable switch or injector is the **power sourcing equipment (PSE)**. The phone, AP, camera, or other device receiving power is the **powered device (PD)**. This is useful when the endpoint is mounted somewhere without a nearby electrical outlet.

Standards-based PoE detects a compatible powered device before supplying its operating power. You can connect an ordinary non-PoE Ethernet endpoint to a compatible standards-based PoE switch port without requiring it to consume PoE. Do not apply that statement to an unspecified passive injector: verify the equipment's documented compatibility.

| IEEE standard | Type | Maximum power supplied at the PSE port |
|---|---|---|
| 802.3af | Type 1, commonly PoE | 15.4 W |
| 802.3at | Type 2, commonly PoE+ | 30 W |
| 802.3bt | Type 3 | 60 W |
| 802.3bt | Type 4 | 90 W |

Power supplied at the switch and power available at the endpoint are different quantities because the cable introduces loss. Do not compare an endpoint's required input power directly with a switch's headline wattage without checking the relevant standard and device specifications. For this chapter, concentrate on the equipment roles, the four supplied-power limits, and the two checks below.

First, check the **per-port capability**: does this port support the standard and power allocation the endpoint requires? Second, check the switch's **total PoE budget**: how much power remains available across all powered ports? A port might support 30 W while the entire switch has only 15 W left to allocate.

For a simple budget example, a switch has 120 W available for PoE and three connected devices are each allocated 30 W. That leaves 30 W. A fourth 30 W allocation fits; a fifth does not. This calculation uses switch-side allocations throughout, not a mixture of allocation and device-side consumption. Actual power accounting and priorities depend on the platform.

On a supported Cisco PoE switch, `show power inline` is a useful first check. It reports the budget and per-port power information. An administratively disabled PoE port is different from a port denied power because the budget is exhausted. `power inline auto` enables normal detection and allocation; `power inline never` disables PoE on the selected port. These are reading and command-recognition examples here, not a claim that every Packet Tracer switch implements the feature.

sections.title: Campus designs: two-tier, three-tier and spine-leaf
sections.body:
A **campus network** connects users and services within a site, which might be one building or several nearby buildings. A hierarchical design separates responsibilities so that the network remains understandable as it grows. **Access** connects endpoints, **distribution** brings access networks together, and the **core** provides connectivity between distribution areas.

In a **two-tier** design, the distribution and core responsibilities are combined in a **collapsed core**. In a **three-tier** design, the core is a separate layer. Count functional layers, not switches: two collapsed-core switches providing redundancy still belong to one layer. The choice depends on scale, required resilience, geography, and operational needs.

```diagram
{"type":"topology","title":"Fig 2.1 — A two-tier campus example","caption":"Access switches connect endpoints; the upper pair provides the combined distribution and core role. The drawing shows physical paths, not a particular forwarding configuration.","nodes":[{"id":"c1","kind":"l3switch","label":"Collapsed core 1","x":4,"y":1},{"id":"c2","kind":"l3switch","label":"Collapsed core 2","x":8,"y":1},{"id":"a1","kind":"switch","label":"Access 1","x":2,"y":3.5},{"id":"a2","kind":"switch","label":"Access 2","x":6,"y":3.5},{"id":"a3","kind":"switch","label":"Access 3","x":10,"y":3.5},{"id":"pc","kind":"pc","label":"Desktop","x":2,"y":5.5},{"id":"ap","kind":"ap","label":"AP","x":10,"y":5.5}],"links":[{"from":"a1","to":"c1"},{"from":"a1","to":"c2"},{"from":"a2","to":"c1"},{"from":"a2","to":"c2"},{"from":"a3","to":"c1"},{"from":"a3","to":"c2"},{"from":"c1","to":"c2"},{"from":"pc","to":"a1"},{"from":"ap","to":"a3"}]}
```

Redundant links can provide another path after a failure, but only when the network is designed and configured to use that path safely. Two cables into the same switch do not protect against failure of that switch. Also, additional Ethernet links can create loops; do not copy the diagram into a live network without the switching design. Spanning tree and link aggregation are later topics, not prerequisites for this chapter's lab.

**Spine-leaf** is a common data-center topology. In the basic design, each leaf connects to each spine, and servers attach to leaves. Traffic between devices on different leaves can follow leaf → spine → leaf. This provides a consistent structure for **east-west traffic**, meaning traffic between systems within the data center.

```diagram
{"type":"topology","title":"Fig 2.2 — Basic spine-leaf design","caption":"Each leaf has a connection to each spine. Server A reaches Server B through a leaf, a spine, and the other leaf.","nodes":[{"id":"s1","kind":"switch","label":"Spine 1","x":4,"y":1},{"id":"s2","kind":"switch","label":"Spine 2","x":8,"y":1},{"id":"l1","kind":"switch","label":"Leaf 1","x":2,"y":3.5},{"id":"l2","kind":"switch","label":"Leaf 2","x":6,"y":3.5},{"id":"l3","kind":"switch","label":"Leaf 3","x":10,"y":3.5},{"id":"a","kind":"server","label":"Server A","x":2,"y":5.5},{"id":"b","kind":"server","label":"Server B","x":10,"y":5.5}],"links":[{"from":"l1","to":"s1"},{"from":"l1","to":"s2"},{"from":"l2","to":"s1"},{"from":"l2","to":"s2"},{"from":"l3","to":"s1"},{"from":"l3","to":"s2"},{"from":"a","to":"l1"},{"from":"b","to":"l3"}],"packet":{"path":["a","l1","s1","l3","b"],"label":"One possible server-to-server path"}}
```

Adding a leaf provides more attachment ports; adding a spine provides more interconnection capacity and possible paths, subject to the equipment and configuration. Recognize this basic arrangement for CCNA. Detailed fabric protocols and larger variations of the topology belong beyond this introductory objective.

sections.title: WAN, SOHO and cloud
sections.body:
A **wide-area network (WAN)** connects networks across a wider geographic area, often through a service provider. A company might connect branch offices to a main office using provider Ethernet, a private WAN service, or an encrypted connection across the Internet. A line drawn through a provider cloud represents a service or logical path; it does not necessarily mean one dedicated physical cable between the offices.

In a **point-to-point** arrangement, a connection joins two sites. In **hub-and-spoke**, branches connect through a central site. A **mesh** provides multiple inter-site connections. Read the paths shown: if two branches must communicate through a hub, losing that hub affects their communication unless another path is available. Do not assume that using a private provider network automatically encrypts the traffic.

**Small office/home office (SOHO)** networks serve relatively few users and often combine several functions in one appliance. The LAN ports, Wi-Fi radio, and Internet-facing connection have different jobs. A failed Internet connection does not necessarily stop a desktop from reaching a local printer. Conversely, a working wireless association does not prove that the user can reach the Internet.

**On-premises** describes equipment operated at the organization's own site. A cloud service makes computing resources available through a service model rather than requiring the customer to install and operate every underlying component. Moving a server to a provider changes who manages parts of the service and how users reach it; it does not remove the need for addressing, connectivity, and security.

NIST's cloud definition includes self-service provisioning, network access, shared resources, elasticity, and measured usage. **Elasticity** means capacity can expand and contract with demand. For introductory recognition, IaaS supplies infrastructure on which the customer manages operating systems and applications; PaaS supplies an application platform; SaaS supplies a ready-to-use application. A private cloud serves one organization, a public cloud offers services to customers generally, and a hybrid arrangement connects distinct cloud environments.

Treat those cloud terms as useful context for comparing deployments. Detailed provider products, WAN service catalogs, fabric configuration, and memorized product model lists are not required to understand the architecture objectives here.

sections.title: Reading the output
sections.body:
Start with the question you need to answer. To identify a router's interface addresses and operational states, use `show ip interface brief`. To inspect a switch's physical port status, use `show interfaces status`. Neither command, by itself, proves that a server application works.

The following is a **representative IOS-style excerpt**, not a captured Packet Tracer run. Interfaces and formatting vary by model. This is a separate routed example; the practical lab needs only its local 192.0.2.0/24 LAN.

```output R1# show ip interface brief — representative excerpt
Interface              IP-Address      OK? Method Status                Protocol
GigabitEthernet0/0     192.0.2.1        YES manual up                    up   ← LAN containing PC-A and Server-A
GigabitEthernet0/1     198.51.100.1     YES manual up                    up   ← LAN containing PC-B
```

The address column identifies the local router interface on each LAN. The two state columns show that the interfaces are operational. These are not PC addresses, and an interface address is not a list of every destination the router knows. `show ip route` is the separate view of its forwarding information.

For a PoE fault, first establish whether the device has power. This representative budget excerpt is a reading exercise for a supported PoE switch; the lab's 2960 model is not required to produce it.

```output SW-POE# show power inline — representative budget excerpt
Module   Available     Used     Remaining
          (Watts)     (Watts)    (Watts)
------   ---------   --------   ---------
1           120.0       90.0        30.0   ← 30 W remains for additional allocations
```

Work from the symptom to the relevant function. A dark AP needs a power check before wireless troubleshooting. A local server that works while remote destinations fail suggests checking the gateway path. A topology with two links still needs inspection of where those links terminate and whether a usable alternative exists. Write down the observation before changing configuration; it becomes your baseline for deciding whether the change helped.

sections.title: Exam focus
sections.body:
- Identify endpoints and servers by their role in an exchange.
- Distinguish MAC-based Layer 2 switching from IP routing; a Layer 3 switch supports both.
- Explain a firewall's policy role and the blocking capability of an inline IPS.
- Distinguish the AP's client connection role from a controller's coordination role.
- Identify the PSE, PD, per-port PoE limit, and total power budget.
- Recognize access, distribution, core, and the combined role in a two-tier campus.
- Trace a path through a basic spine-leaf design and identify its endpoint connections.
- Compare WAN, SOHO, on-premises, and cloud arrangements without assuming that a device name or drawing proves its configuration.

lab.title: Separate a network path from an application service
lab.intro:
Practice revised September 2026. If you completed an earlier version, repeat the revised exercise and update its checkmarks.

Build an office LAN and prove that its switch and server do different jobs. Then investigate a web-service failure while the same network still carries ping traffic. Finish by reading larger topology plans and checking a PoE allocation.

Chapter 01 already followed traffic through a router. Here the practical setup stays on one LAN so you can concentrate on device roles. The design worksheets extend those roles to a campus, WAN and wireless expansion without requiring their later configuration commands.
lab.topology:
Start a new Packet Tracer file. Use a 2960, PC-PT and Server-PT. The switches in this exercise do not need PoE simulation; the power case uses supplied values.

```diagram
{"type":"topology","title":"Office client and web server","caption":"SW1 forwards local frames; Server-A supplies the requested web page.","nodes":[{"id":"A","kind":"pc","label":"PC-A","sub":"192.0.2.10/24","x":2,"y":3},{"id":"SW1","kind":"switch","label":"SW1","sub":"2960","x":6,"y":3},{"id":"S","kind":"server","label":"Server-A","sub":"192.0.2.20/24","x":10,"y":3}],"links":[{"from":"A","to":"SW1","fromLabel":"Fa0","toLabel":"Fa0/1"},{"from":"SW1","to":"S","fromLabel":"Fa0/2","toLabel":"Fa0"}]}
```

| Connection | Cable |
|---|---|
| PC-A FastEthernet0 → SW1 FastEthernet0/1 | Copper straight-through |
| Server-A FastEthernet0 → SW1 FastEthernet0/2 | Copper straight-through |

| Device | IPv4 address | Mask | Gateway and DNS |
|---|---|---|---|
| PC-A | 192.0.2.10 | 255.255.255.0 | Leave blank |
| Server-A | 192.0.2.20 | 255.255.255.0 | Leave blank |

Both endpoints share the supplied local subnet. There is no router, Internet path, DNS service or DHCP requirement. Use the numeric server address in each test.

steps.title: Build and document the office LAN
steps.body:
Place, label and cable the three devices. On each endpoint, use **Desktop → IP Configuration → Static** and enter its row from the table. Read it back before continuing.

Open SW1's CLI, decline the initial configuration dialog if offered, and name the switch. The descriptions below document the intended cable endpoints; they do not configure a web service or establish that the cables are correct.

```ios SW1
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW1
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# description PC-A
SW1(config-if)# exit
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/2
SW1(config-if)# description Server-A
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces status
```

:::expected
The two ports reach `connected` after initialization. If the compact command is unavailable, use `show interfaces fastethernet0/1` and `show interfaces fastethernet0/2`. Match the real cable endpoints to the descriptions rather than treating a description as proof.
:::

steps.title: Establish two different baseline tests
steps.body:
On Server-A, open **Services → HTTP** and set **HTTP On**. Keep its supplied page, or change a short line of its index page to **Office service baseline** and save that page.

On PC-A's **Desktop → Command Prompt**, run:

```text
ping 192.0.2.20
```

Repeat once if the first attempt loses an initial request while the topology becomes ready. Then use **Desktop → Web Browser** and visit **http://192.0.2.20**. Record the visible page text. Save the project as **02-office-baseline.pkt**.

:::expected
The repeated ping receives replies and the browser obtains the page. Ping tests this ICMP exchange; the browser tests the HTTP service. The path for both is PC-A → SW1 → Server-A. Server-A is an endpoint supplying a service, while SW1 forwards the local frames.
:::

steps.title: Stop the service and collect evidence
steps.body:
On Server-A, change **Services → HTTP → Off**. Keep its power, Ethernet connection and address unchanged. On PC-A, repeat the same ping. Close and reopen the Web Browser and request **http://192.0.2.20** again.

Leave HTTP off while recording the results. An already displayed page may be cached; its presence is not proof of a new successful request. If the browser retains it, inspect events for the fresh request in Simulation mode if available. Use the supplied fallback below if a new response cannot be distinguished.

:::expected
New ping requests still receive replies, while a fresh HTTP request cannot obtain a response from the stopped service. The precise browser error or timeout depends on the simulator. The service's Off setting is direct evidence of the controlled change; a timeout alone would not identify this cause on an unknown network.

If the simulator does not let you distinguish a new response from a retained page, record that limitation. For the written exercise, use the supplied observations: ICMP replies arrive; a new HTTP request gets no service response; the server's HTTP setting is Off.
:::

steps.title: Restore the application and retest
steps.body:
On Server-A, return HTTP to **On**. Close and reopen PC-A’s browser, request **http://192.0.2.20**, and compare the page with your baseline. Repeat the ping. If your simulator retains a page without showing a distinguishable new response, record that limitation and use the supplied recovery result: after HTTP is enabled, a fresh HTTP request receives the server page and ping continues to receive replies.

:::expected
Both tests work again. Your explanation identifies the stopped HTTP service and the evidence for it. Changing the switch's address, replacing the cable or introducing a router would not have restored the service setting.
:::

steps.title: Choose functions for an office expansion
steps.body:
Complete this worksheet without adding devices or commands. For each requirement, name the needed function and explain its role in one sentence.

| Requirement | Function to identify |
|---|---|
| Laptops need wireless access to this office LAN | Wireless attachment |
| The office needs to reach another IP network | Routing between networks |
| Administrators need consistent settings across many managed APs | AP coordination |
| Traffic between the office and an outside network must follow a security policy | Traffic-policy enforcement |
| Staff need a device that supplies shared web content | Application service |

:::expected
An AP supplies wireless attachment; a router or appropriately configured Layer 3 switch routes; a WLC coordinates supported APs; a firewall enforces traffic policy; a server supplies the application. One enclosure can combine roles, but naming it does not prove that every needed role is configured. An inline IPS may add prevention according to the required security design.
:::

steps.title: Read paths and failure dependencies
steps.body:
Draw these three small plans on paper. Trace the stated exchange, then cross out the failed device and decide whether another listed path remains.

| Plan | Connections and test |
|---|---|
| Campus | Access-A and Access-B each connect to CC1 and CC2. Both CC devices provide combined distribution/core functions. Trace Access-A to Access-B; then remove CC1. |
| Data center | Leaves L1 and L2 each connect to spines S1 and S2. Server-X attaches to L1; Server-Y attaches to L2. Trace X to Y; then remove S1. |
| WAN | Branch-A and Branch-B each connect only to HQ. Trace Branch-A to Branch-B; then remove HQ. |

These are verified connection records, not a demand to configure redundant Ethernet links. Assume the normal design can forward on the surviving listed path; do not infer a recovery time.

:::expected
The campus is two-tier despite having two CC switches; a path can remain through CC2. The spine-leaf path is X → L1 → a spine → L2 → Y; S2 remains after S1 fails. The WAN's only interbranch path uses HQ, so that path is lost. Local communication inside an unaffected branch can remain possible. Physical alternatives are necessary evidence, but their actual forwarding and failover must be verified in a real design.
:::

steps.title: Check a proposed PoE allocation
steps.body:
A proposed PoE switch has **120 W available**, with **60 W already allocated**. Each proposed compatible AP needs **30 W allocated at the source**, and each selected port can supply that allocation. Decide whether two more APs fit and whether a third would fit.

Then consider a separate switch with 60 W remaining whose selected port can supply only 15.4 W. Would that port satisfy one 30 W allocation?

:::expected
Two additional 30 W allocations use the 60 W remainder exactly. A third would exceed the budget. The second switch fails the per-port requirement despite its sufficient aggregate remainder. Compare source-side allocations consistently; endpoint input power and source allocation are different quantities.

On supported PoE hardware, `show power inline` helps inspect allocation. This worksheet does not require that command to work on the simulated 2960.
:::

steps.title: Save and explain the working result
steps.body:
Save the switch's configuration:

```ios SW1
SW1# copy running-config startup-config
```

Accept the destination filename with Enter and wait for completion. Save **02-components-complete.pkt** with HTTP enabled. Keep your baseline, failure and recovery observations together.

:::expected
The final file contains the restored service, and the notes distinguish three kinds of evidence: port state, an ICMP exchange and an HTTP response. The architecture worksheet names the roles and shows where each remaining or missing path goes.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
| Symptom | Useful check |
|---|---|
| Neither ping nor HTTP works | Inspect endpoint address/mask entries, cable endpoints, power and port states before focusing on HTTP. |
| Ping works but a fresh page request fails | Read the actual HTTP setting and numeric URL; a ping result does not prove application availability. |
| An old page remains after HTTP is off | Request a fresh URL and inspect events if supported; record the simulator limitation if no new response can be distinguished. |
| A diagram looks redundant | Trace the actual surviving connections and identify shared dependencies. Do not infer redundancy from two lines alone. |
| An AP allocation does not fit | Check per-port capability and remaining total budget separately, using the same source-side units. |
lab.challenge:
Add **PC-B** to SW1 FastEthernet0/3 with copper straight-through. Assign **192.0.2.30**, mask **255.255.255.0**, and no gateway or DNS. Verify its ping and HTTP request to Server-A.

Without changing the configuration, predict which tests would fail for both clients if HTTP stopped, and which would fail if Server-A were powered off. Explain which evidence would distinguish the two cases.

:::solution
PC-B reaches the server locally through SW1. With HTTP stopped but the host/network otherwise working, both clients can still receive ping replies but cannot obtain new HTTP responses. With Server-A powered off, neither client receives ping replies or new HTTP responses from it.

A complete answer gives the two predictions and checks the server's actual service/power state. An unknown host's failed ping alone would not prove that it was powered off. Leave the server powered on with HTTP On, verify both clients, and save a separate challenge file.
:::

questions.prompt: A computer supplies web pages to other computers on the network. Which description is most accurate?
options: It performs a transit role because several clients use it.
It performs a client role while returning the requested pages.
It performs a switching role when it receives Ethernet frames.
It performs a server role while remaining a network endpoint.
questions.explanation: A server supplies a service such as HTTP to clients and is also an endpoint on the network. Server and endpoint describe compatible roles, not mutually exclusive hardware categories.

whyWrong.0: Supplying an application is different from forwarding other hosts’ traffic as transit.
whyWrong.1: For this exchange, the computer supplies rather than requests the web content.
whyWrong.2: Receiving its own frames does not mean it switches transit frames between ports.

questions.prompt: A PC must send an IP packet to a different IP network. Which function selects the next hop using the destination IP address?
options: A Layer 2 switch forwarding within one VLAN
An access point accepting a wireless association
A router consulting its IP routing table
A hub repeating the received electrical signal
questions.explanation: Routing selects an outgoing path using the destination IP network and the routing table. A router or a Layer 3 switch with routing configured can supply this function.

whyWrong.0: Layer 2 forwarding uses MAC addresses within the local VLAN rather than selecting an IP next hop.
whyWrong.1: Wireless association establishes a client's connection to an AP; it does not by itself choose routes between IP networks.
whyWrong.3: A hub repeats signals and does not inspect an IP routing table.

questions.prompt: A company wants a consistent wireless configuration across many access points. What is the main role of a wireless LAN controller?
options: Coordinate the configuration and operation of supported APs.
Provide each wireless client’s physical radio attachment itself.
Supply power allocation independently of the AP’s PoE switch.
Choose every client’s IP next hop as the campus core.
questions.explanation: A wireless LAN controller provides centralized coordination for supported APs, including configuration and monitoring. The traffic-forwarding path depends on the wireless deployment; controller management does not mean every data frame follows the same path.

whyWrong.1: The AP supplies the client’s radio attachment; the controller coordinates AP operation.
whyWrong.2: The actual power source still needs sufficient per-port capability and total budget.
whyWrong.3: Controller coordination is not the same function as campus routing; forwarding depends on the deployment.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of the core in a three-tier campus design?
options: Connect individual users and APs to the campus.
Provide transport between distribution blocks.
Combine the roles of distribution and access.
Connect each leaf to every other leaf directly.
questions.explanation: The core interconnects distribution blocks and provides a reliable transport path across the campus. Access connects endpoints; distribution aggregates access and commonly provides routing or policy boundaries.

whyWrong.0: Direct endpoint attachment is the access layer’s main function.
whyWrong.2: A separate core interconnects distribution blocks; it is not the combined access/distribution layer described here.
whyWrong.3: That is not the core’s role in the stated hierarchical campus design.

questions.prompt: A hosted application automatically adds capacity as demand grows and releases it when demand falls. Which cloud characteristic does this illustrate?
options: Rapid elasticity
Resource pooling
Broad network access
Measured service
questions.explanation: Rapid elasticity is the ability to expand and reduce provisioned resources in response to demand. It differs from simply hosting a server in someone else's building.

whyWrong.1: Resource pooling concerns shared provider resources; the described change is capacity expanding and contracting.
whyWrong.2: Network access describes how the service can be reached, not this adjustment to demand.
whyWrong.3: Measured service concerns metering usage, which is different from changing provisioned capacity.

questions.prompt: Which two statements accurately describe a next-generation firewall and an inline IPS? (Choose two.)
options: An NGFW can apply policy using identified applications.
An inline IPS can drop traffic according to its threat policy.
A stateful firewall uses only the destination IP, ignoring connection state.
An inline IPS inspects only an out-of-path traffic copy.
An NGFW’s encrypted-payload visibility is independent of decryption.
questions.explanation: An NGFW combines traffic-policy enforcement with capabilities such as application visibility and intrusion prevention. An inline IPS sits in the traffic path and can block a detected threat, subject to its configuration and inspection capability.

whyWrong.2: Stateful inspection also uses connection-state information; this option describes too narrow a function.
whyWrong.3: Inline placement puts the IPS in the traffic path; an out-of-path copy describes a different inspection arrangement.
whyWrong.4: Encrypted content visibility depends on the traffic and available decryption, not just the NGFW label.

exhibit.title: Documented forwarding behavior — teaching evidence, not CLI output
exhibit.text:
SW3 forwards frames between local ports in each VLAN.
SW3 is configured with IP routing and serves as gateway for two IP networks.
Traffic between those networks is routed by SW3.

questions.prompt: Which device role best matches the documented behavior of SW3?
options: A Layer 2 switch providing management access
A wireless controller managing radio settings
A hub connecting a shared Ethernet segment
A Layer 3 switch performing routing and switching
questions.explanation: SW3 both forwards Ethernet frames within each LAN and routes between the IP networks. Those documented functions justify identifying a Layer 3 switching role; the label on a diagram alone would not establish that routing is configured.

whyWrong.0: A management IP address alone would not provide the documented forwarding between networks.
whyWrong.1: The evidence describes wired switching and IP routing, not AP management.
whyWrong.2: A hub neither learns destination MAC forwarding entries nor makes IP routing decisions.

questions.prompt: An office adds compatible controller-managed access points on PoE switch ports. Which two statements describe the design correctly? (Choose two.)
options: The AP uses its wired uplink only for power, with no Ethernet data.
The AP connects wireless clients to the wired network through its uplink.
The controller’s budget replaces the switch’s PoE power budget.
The switch can supply power and Ethernet connectivity on the AP’s cable.
Controller management means client forwarding always bypasses the AP’s site.
questions.explanation: The AP supplies wireless access, while a compatible PoE switch can supply both its wired connection and electrical power. A controller coordinates AP operation, but forwarding and power requirements still depend on the chosen design.

whyWrong.0: The compatible uplink carries Ethernet as well as supplying power in the stated design.
whyWrong.2: The switch’s actual source budget governs the power available on its PoE ports.
whyWrong.4: Management and forwarding are different roles; some designs switch client traffic locally.

exhibit.title: Campus design notes
exhibit.text:
Access switches connect users and APs.
Their uplinks reach a redundant pair of switches.
That pair performs both distribution and core functions.
There is no separate core layer.

questions.prompt: Which campus architecture matches the described design?
options: A two-tier campus with a collapsed distribution/core layer
A three-tier campus because the upper layer has two switches
A spine-leaf fabric because every access switch has two uplinks
A single access layer because all switches share one site
questions.explanation: A two-tier campus combines distribution and core functions into a collapsed layer above access. Redundant devices can exist within that layer without turning the architecture into three tiers.

whyWrong.1: Tier count follows functional layers, not the number of redundant devices.
whyWrong.2: Two uplinks alone do not establish the endpoint/leaf/spine roles of that architecture.
whyWrong.3: A site can contain several functional layers; the description explicitly gives access and combined distribution/core roles.

exhibit.title: Basic spine-leaf plan
exhibit.text:
Spines: S1, S2
Leaves: L1, L2, L3
Each leaf connects to S1 and S2.
Servers attach to leaf ports.

questions.prompt: Which two additions fit the basic spine-leaf connection pattern in the plan? Choose two.
options: Add L4 with one link to S1 and one to S2.
Connect a new server to S1 instead of a leaf.
Attach a new server to an available L2 port.
Connect L4 only to L3, using L3 as its transit leaf.
Replace L2’s two spine links with one L1–L2 link.
questions.explanation: A new leaf needs connectivity to each spine in the stated basic pattern, and endpoint attachment belongs on a leaf. These choices describe the physical pattern; forwarding capacity and configuration still need to be checked.

whyWrong.1: The reference pattern places endpoints on leaves, rather than directly on spines.
whyWrong.3: The new leaf would depend on another leaf instead of connecting to every spine.
whyWrong.4: Replacing the spine connections with a leaf-to-leaf path changes the stated topology.

exhibit.title: PoE allocation worksheet — supplied values
exhibit.text:
Available budget: 120 W
Existing allocations: 90 W
Remaining budget: 30 W
Each proposed AP allocation: 30 W

questions.prompt: Each additional AP needs a 30 W allocation, and each selected port supports it. Based on the stated total budget, how many more such APs can the switch support?
options: Three additional APs
Two additional APs
No additional APs
One additional AP
questions.explanation: The remaining allocation budget is 120 − 90 = 30 W, enough for one more 30 W AP. Per-port capability and aggregate available power must both be sufficient.

whyWrong.0: Three APs would require 90 W of additional available budget.
whyWrong.1: Two APs would require 60 W, more than the stated remainder.
whyWrong.2: The given 30 W remainder does fit one compatible 30 W allocation.

questions.prompt: On a home device combining routing, switching and an AP, wired clients still reach the Internet. Nearby wireless clients cannot find the configured network name. Which function should be investigated first?
options: The WAN routing function that the wired clients are using
The wireless access-point function and its radio configuration
The Ethernet switching function serving the wired clients
The remote Internet server used by both kinds of client
questions.explanation: The symptom is failure to discover the wireless network, while the wired forwarding path works. Start with the AP's radio, network-name settings and wireless environment before changing a working wired path.

whyWrong.0: Successful wired Internet use is evidence that the WAN path is working for those clients.
whyWrong.2: The failed step is wireless discovery rather than the wired clients' Ethernet attachment.
whyWrong.3: Clients must first discover and join the local wireless network before reaching a remote server.

questions.prompt: Three branches reach headquarters through separate WAN links. Each branch's only path to the others passes through headquarters. What is the effect of losing the headquarters transit function?
options: Branch-A loses local switching as well as its WAN path.
The branches retain communication through their local gateways alone.
Communication between branches loses its only designed path.
Only requests addressed to HQ itself are affected.
questions.explanation: In this hub-and-spoke design, interbranch communication depends on the hub's transit role. A failure there removes that path even if each branch's local LAN continues operating.

whyWrong.0: An HQ transit failure does not by itself stop switching within Branch-A.
whyWrong.1: The local gateways do not create an alternative interbranch connection.
whyWrong.3: Traffic using HQ as transit is affected even when HQ is not its final destination.

exhibit.title: Office test record — supplied evidence
exhibit.text:
PC-A and Server-A: same local subnet, different addresses
PC-A → Server-A ping: replies received
PC-A → Server-A new HTTP request: no service response
Server-A Services → HTTP: Off

questions.prompt: Which change directly addresses the confirmed cause while preserving the working path?
options: Assign a management IP address to the switch.
Enable HTTP on Server-A, then repeat the fresh request.
Give PC-A a default gateway for this local destination.
Move Server-A to a different subnet before testing.
questions.explanation: The actual server setting shows that HTTP is stopped. Enabling the service and retesting addresses that confirmed cause; ping already provides evidence that the same client can exchange ICMP with the server.

whyWrong.0: Local switching and the working ping do not require a switch management address.
whyWrong.2: The server is in the client’s connected subnet, so a default gateway is not needed for this exchange.
whyWrong.3: Changing the subnet adds a different requirement without starting the stopped service.

cards.front: Can a server also be an endpoint?
cards.back: Yes. An endpoint originates or receives traffic; a server is an endpoint supplying a service such as HTTP to clients.

cards.front: What addresses guide Layer 2 switching and IP routing?
cards.back: Layer 2 switching uses destination MAC addresses within a VLAN. Routing uses the destination IP address and a routing table.

cards.front: What makes a switch a Layer 3 switch?
cards.back: It supports IP routing as well as Ethernet switching. Routing must be configured; a management IP alone does not establish a forwarding role.

cards.front: Which functions can one SOHO wireless router combine?
cards.back: Ethernet switching, wireless access, IP routing and security functions. Diagnose the failed function rather than treating the whole enclosure as one role.

cards.front: How do Catalyst Center and a wireless LAN controller differ?
cards.back: Catalyst Center manages and monitors supported campus devices. A WLC coordinates supported APs and their wireless operation.

cards.front: What does a next-generation firewall add to stateful filtering?
cards.back: Capabilities such as application-aware policy and intrusion prevention. Inspectable traffic and enforcement depend on configuration and visibility.

cards.front: How do IDS and inline IPS differ?
cards.back: IDS detects and reports suspicious activity. An inline IPS can block traffic as it passes, according to policy; detection is not a guarantee against every attack.

cards.front: In standards-based PoE, what are PSE and PD?
cards.back: PSE supplies power; PD receives it. Detection checks for a compatible powered device before supplying normal operating power.

cards.front: What two power limits must a PoE design satisfy?
cards.back: The port must support the required allocation, and all allocations must fit the switch’s available total power budget.

cards.front: Campus access, distribution and core: primary roles?
cards.back: Access attaches endpoints; distribution aggregates access and often supplies routing/policy boundaries; core interconnects distribution blocks.

cards.front: Two-tier versus three-tier campus design?
cards.back: Two-tier combines distribution and core functions. Three-tier separates access, distribution and core; device count alone does not define the tiers.

cards.front: Why do two physical uplinks not automatically guarantee redundancy?
cards.back: They may share a failed device or other dependency. Trace both complete paths and verify that the design can use the surviving path.

cards.front: What connects to what in a basic spine-leaf design?
cards.back: Endpoints normally attach to leaves. Each leaf connects to every spine. This is the basic reference pattern, not a universal rule for every fabric variant.

cards.front: What distinguishes a WAN from a local LAN?
cards.back: A WAN connects networks across a wider geographic area, often through provider services. Local switching can remain operational when the WAN path fails.

cards.front: How do on-premises hosting and cloud services differ?
cards.back: On-premises names a location. Cloud names a service model with on-demand resources and elasticity; a private cloud can be on premises.

commands.task: Display the switch's compact table of port state, VLAN, duplex and speed.
commands.note: Compare the named ports with the physical cable table. This is a read-only check.

commands.task: Label the selected switch interface as the connection to PC-A.
commands.note: The label records intent. Check that the actual cable on FastEthernet0/1 reaches PC-A.

commands.task: On a supported PoE switch, display total power budget and per-port power state.
commands.note: Hardware command recognition. The Packet Tracer 2960 lab does not require or promise PoE simulation.

tickets.title: A third-floor switch loses its path when another floor reboots
tickets.scenario: The building uses access switches and a collapsed distribution/core pair. Users on A3 can reach their local printer, but lose access to the server network whenever A2 is powered off. A cable inspection confirms the connections below. There are no unlisted links or wireless alternatives.

exhibits.title: Verified physical connection record
exhibits.text:
A1 uplink 1 → CC1
A1 uplink 2 → CC2
A2 uplink 1 → CC1
A2 uplink 2 → CC2
A3 uplink 1 → A2
A3 uplink 2 → no cable
Server network → collapsed distribution/core layer

exhibits.title: Tests while A2 is powered off
exhibits.text:
A3 user → printer attached to A3: succeeds
A3 user → server network: fails
A1 user → server network: succeeds

tickets.question: Which dependency explains A3's loss of server access?
options: A3’s local printer needs a gateway for traffic within its LAN.
A3’s only path to the server network passes through A2.
A3 has two independent paths because its switch has two uplink ports.
The evidence shows CC1 and CC2 both lost power.
tickets.explanation: The verified cable record gives A3 only one uplink, and it leads through A2. Local traffic on A3 can continue, but traffic toward the server network loses its path while A2 is off. This is a specific single-path dependency; it does not establish that every access-switch chain is forbidden or that an unused port is administratively shut down.
tickets.fix: Record A3's dependency in the diagram and restore A2 to recover the existing path. Verify local and server tests again. For a planned improvement, connect A3 to the intended distribution/core layer using a reviewed design that supplies appropriate independent paths and forwarding configuration. Do not create extra Layer 2 links casually: later switching chapters explain loop prevention. After an approved redesign, update the port records and test each intended failure separately; two cables alone do not prove resilience.

tickets.title: Two compatible phones receive no PoE power
tickets.scenario: Two compatible IEEE PoE phones remain dark on a supported PoE Catalyst switch. A controlled test confirms both phones power on through a known-good cable on another compatible port. The switch has sufficient remaining budget for both phones. The following excerpts are representative teaching evidence, not a claim of a completed hardware test.

exhibits.title: Selected running configuration
exhibits.text:
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/7
 description Conference-phone-A

tickets.question: Which finding directly explains why the switch is not supplying power on these ports?
options: The phones’ combined allocations exhaust the remaining budget.
The selected interfaces await IP addresses before detecting power.
The selected ports are configured not to supply PoE power.
The working test proves every cable path to the phones is healthy.
tickets.explanation: The selected configuration explicitly disables power delivery. The supplied port compatibility and remaining budget meet the stated requirements, so those do not explain the failure here. A phone need not obtain an IP address before standards-based PoE can power it.
tickets.fix:
Record the disabled PoE setting and identify the two intended interfaces. On supported hardware, an authorized technician restores automatic power detection with power inline auto on each selected port, then inspects show power inline. Chapter 09 develops that configuration; this ticket assesses the device role and the evidence, not new syntax.

Verify detection and an appropriate allocation for each phone, allow it to boot, and check its operation. The known-good test does not certify the original cable paths; inspect them separately if power still fails. This is supplied hardware evidence, not an executed Packet Tracer PoE test.
