chapters.summary: Compare copper and fiber links, understand speed and duplex, and use interface state and counters to investigate a fault without jumping to a conclusion.

sections.title: Why the wire still matters
sections.body:
Before investigating routing or an application, establish whether the network interface can carry traffic. A disconnected cable, disabled port or incompatible pair of transceivers prevents communication regardless of the IP addresses. A link can also come up and then lose or corrupt traffic. That second case requires more than looking for a green light.

Ask two separate questions: **is the link operational, and is it carrying frames cleanly?** Interface state answers the first. Speed, duplex, error counters and tests from both ends help answer the second. Start by identifying the exact port and its far-end device. Otherwise, a perfectly valid command can show you the wrong link.

In v1.1, you compare media and identify interface problems. The announced v2.0 objective also explicitly includes diagnosing distance, signal level and pinout problems. This chapter teaches those basic diagnostic decisions. Optical planning calculations and the detailed electrical design of Ethernet are outside this lesson.

sections.title: Copper: standards, categories and pinouts
sections.body:
:::facts
- Common twisted-pair Ethernet channels are designed for up to **100 m** with the specified cable category. Check the actual port or module specification; some copper transceiver modules have shorter limits.
- **100BASE-TX** uses two pairs; **1000BASE-T** uses all four pairs. Cat5e is the normal minimum choice for new 1 Gbps cabling.
- **Cat6A** supports 10GBASE-T over a 100 m channel. Cat6 does not guarantee that same 10 Gbps distance.
- A straight-through cable keeps the same pin numbers at both ends. A conventional 10/100 crossover exchanges pins **1 with 3** and **2 with 6**.
- On a full-duplex Ethernet link, normal operation has **no collisions**.
:::

**Twisted-pair cable** contains insulated copper conductors arranged in pairs. The twists help the pair reject interference; they are part of the cable's electrical design, not just a way to bundle wires. An Ethernet cable that looks intact may still have a broken conductor, damaged termination or excessive interference. The printed category indicates a performance specification, not the speed currently negotiated by the devices.

| Link type | Practical cable choice | Pairs used | Typical channel limit |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10BASE-T, 10 Mbps | Cat3 or better | 2 | 100 m |
| 100BASE-TX, 100 Mbps | Cat5 or better | 2 | 100 m |
| 1000BASE-T, 1 Gbps | Cat5e or better | 4 | 100 m |
| 10GBASE-T, 10 Gbps | Cat6A for the full distance | 4 | 100 m on supporting ports |

A channel includes the installed cable and patch leads. The usual structured-cabling arrangement allows 90 m of permanent link plus 10 m of patch cords. Do not treat the table as permission to extend every pluggable copper module to 100 m: for example, Cisco's SFP-10G-T-X supports a shorter 30 m 10 Gbps reach over Cat6A/7. Cable and interface specifications both matter.

The common eight-position Ethernet connector is often called **RJ-45**. Numbered conductors must arrive at the intended pins. The physical pairs occupy pins 1–2, 3–6, 4–5 and 7–8. Notice that pins 3 and 6 form a pair even though they are not adjacent. Keeping the two wires of each pair together is essential.

For traditional 10/100 Ethernet without automatic pair correction, a PC, server or router port uses one transmit/receive arrangement, called **MDI**, while a switch or hub uses **MDI-X**. A straight-through cable connects unlike arrangements, such as a PC to a switch. A crossover connects like arrangements, such as two switches or a PC directly to a router. These are electrical arrangements, not a rule that every pair of differently named devices uses straight-through.

**Auto-MDIX** detects the pair arrangement and compensates for it on supported ports. One working auto-MDIX end can remove the need to choose between straight-through and crossover. Cisco's documented 2960 procedure uses `speed auto`, `duplex auto` and `mdix auto`. Support depends on interface and software; it is not a feature of every fiber or copper port. In Packet Tracer, use the cable specified by the lab rather than assuming a particular simulated auto-MDIX implementation.

A cable tester can identify an **open** conductor, a **short** between conductors and a wrong pin connection. A **split pair** can preserve pin-to-pin continuity while using conductors from different twisted pairs. A simple continuity check may therefore pass a cable that performs badly. Check its wire map and, when quality or distance is in doubt, use a suitable cable qualification or certification test.

:::trap A connector does not identify the protocol
A traditional rollover console cable reverses pins and carries a serial console connection. It is not an Ethernet crossover cable, even if the device end uses a similar-looking connector. Connect it to a port labeled Console, not an Ethernet port. USB console connections are another management option; check the device's installation guide.
:::

sections.title: Fiber: single-mode, multimode and optics
sections.body:
**Fiber-optic cable** carries light rather than an electrical Ethernet signal. A **transceiver** converts between the device's electrical interface and the optical signal. The cable, transceivers and ports must form a compatible system: connector fit alone is insufficient. Check the module part number, supported Ethernet standard, fiber type, distance and switch support.

**Multimode fiber**, or MMF, has a larger core and supports multiple light paths. It is common for shorter building and data-center links. **Single-mode fiber**, or SMF, has a smaller core and supports longer-distance optical designs. Do not identify the supported distance from jacket color alone; use the cable's marking, documentation and transceiver specification.

| Example module or standard | Fiber and wavelength | Documented reach to recognize |
|---|---|---|
| Cisco 1000BASE-SX SFP | MMF, 850 nm | Depends on fiber grade; commonly up to 550 m |
| Cisco 1000BASE-LX/LH SFP | SMF, 1310 nm | Up to 10 km on the specified SMF |
| 10GBASE-SR SFP+ | MMF, 850 nm | 300 m on OM3; 400 m on OM4 |
| 10GBASE-LR SFP+ | SMF, 1310 nm | 10 km on the specified SMF |

These are examples, not interchangeable distance promises. An older multimode cable may support much less distance than OM3 or OM4. Cisco's LX/LH module specification is also not a reason to assign its 10 km reach to every product labeled LX. For a real link, read the exact module's data sheet.

**SFP** and **SFP+** describe common pluggable module formats; 1 Gbps SFP and 10 Gbps SFP+ modules are familiar examples. A physically similar module does not guarantee that a port supports its speed or optical standard. Many duplex modules use LC connectors, but other connector arrangements exist. Use the device's compatibility information rather than forcing a module into an apparently suitable slot.

A common duplex fiber link has two strands. The local transmitter must connect to the remote receiver, and the remote transmitter to the local receiver. If transmit is connected to transmit, both devices can be operational but no usable signal reaches the receivers. This is a **polarity** problem. Single-strand bidirectional modules are a separate design and require a compatible complementary pair.

```diagram
{"type":"topology","title":"Fig 03.1 — A duplex optical path","caption":"Each transmitter reaches the other device's receiver; connector fit alone does not establish correct polarity.","nodes":[{"id":"AT","kind":"switch","label":"Switch A · Tx","x":2,"y":1},{"id":"AR","kind":"switch","label":"Switch A · Rx","x":2,"y":5},{"id":"BT","kind":"switch","label":"Switch B · Tx","x":10,"y":1},{"id":"BR","kind":"switch","label":"Switch B · Rx","x":10,"y":5}],"links":[{"from":"AT","to":"BR","label":"strand 1"},{"from":"BT","to":"AR","label":"strand 2"}]}
```

Optical power is often displayed in **dBm**, a logarithmic value relative to 1 milliwatt. Here you need to compare a reading with the module's supported receive range, not memorize a fiber-engineering calculation. A reading of −16 dBm is lower power than −8 dBm. If a question supplies a low receive threshold of −12 dBm, −16 dBm is below that threshold.

Low received power suggests checking the far-end transmitter, fiber continuity, connectors, bends, polarity, distance and compatibility. It does not identify one unique cause. Excessive received power can also be a problem; use the module's upper limit rather than assuming more is always better. Never look into a live fiber or transceiver. Use the approved inspection and cleaning equipment for the installation.

sections.title: Shared media, point-to-point and duplex
sections.body:
A **shared-media** Ethernet segment places multiple devices on the same transmission medium. A historical Ethernet hub repeats signals between its ports; it does not learn MAC addresses or select one destination port. Devices on that segment must take turns transmitting. If two transmit at once, their signals can collide.

**Half duplex** allows transmission in one direction at a time. Traditional shared Ethernet uses carrier sense multiple access with collision detection, or **CSMA/CD**, to detect a collision and retry. Collisions can occur during normal half-duplex operation. They are not normal on a correctly operating full-duplex switched link.

**Full duplex** allows both ends to transmit and receive simultaneously. A modern switch-to-PC connection is normally a point-to-point, full-duplex link. Each switch port separates its attached Ethernet segment from the others; devices on different switch ports do not share one hub-style collision domain. A hub connected to one switch port still leaves the devices behind that hub sharing their segment.

Keep collision domains separate from **broadcast domains**. A switch can forward broadcasts across ports in the same VLAN while keeping those ports on separate Ethernet segments. A router does not normally forward an Ethernet broadcast from one interface to another. VLANs and switching behavior are developed in later chapters; here, remember that eliminating collisions does not eliminate broadcasts.

sections.title: Autonegotiation and the mismatch
sections.body:
**Autonegotiation** lets supported Ethernet interfaces exchange capabilities and choose compatible operating settings. For ordinary 10/100/1000 copper links, leaving both ends automatic is the usual starting point. Both sides must support the selected speed, and the cable must support it. An interface negotiating 100 Mbps does not by itself prove that the cable is defective: the far endpoint may only support 100 Mbps.

A useful CCNA case is a **10/100 link with one end forced to 100 Mbps full duplex and the other automatic**. The automatic end can detect speed without receiving a full negotiation exchange, but it cannot determine the forced end's duplex that way. It can settle at 100 Mbps half duplex. The link may be up even though its ends disagree.

With a **duplex mismatch**, the full-duplex side transmits without the half-duplex side's collision-handling rules. Communication may work intermittently or become slow under load. The half-duplex end may record collisions and late collisions; the full-duplex end may record damaged received frames. Compare both operational settings before blaming a cable. Do not apply this 10/100 fallback example as a universal rule for every gigabit, fiber or multigigabit interface.

For this lab's 2960 FastEthernet link, restore both ends to automatic settings. Apply the following to SW1, and apply the equivalent block to SW2 separately.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/24
SW1(config-if)# speed auto
SW1(config-if)# duplex auto
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces fastethernet0/24
```

If both 10/100 ends are manually set to the same supported speed and duplex, they can also work correctly. A manual speed mismatch, such as one end forced to 10 Mbps and the other to 100 Mbps, can prevent link establishment entirely. The right repair is a deliberate matching configuration at both ends, followed by a traffic test.

sections.title: Reading the output
sections.body:
Use `show interfaces status` for a compact switch-port overview, `show interfaces <interface>` for detailed operational state and counters, and `show running-config` to inspect configured values. Some IOS versions support a narrower `show running-config interface <interface>` command; use the full configuration if your simulator does not. Always compare the named physical connection at both ends.

The excerpts below are **representative IOS-style teaching output**, not a capture from an executed Packet Tracer lab. Columns, supported counters and wording vary by platform. The observations and relationships are what you need to interpret.

```output Representative: SW1# show interfaces status
Port      Name               Status       Vlan       Duplex  Speed Type
Fa0/24    To-SW2              connected    1          a-half  a-100 10/100BaseTX  ← Automatically selected half duplex
```

```output Representative: SW2# show interfaces status
Port      Name               Status       Vlan       Duplex  Speed Type
Fa0/24    To-SW1              connected    1          full    100   10/100BaseTX  ← Forced full duplex at the other end
```

Both ends report a link, but SW1 operates half duplex and SW2 full duplex. The `a-` prefix indicates an automatically selected setting; it does not prove a complete negotiation exchange succeeded. Neither `connected` nor a matching speed proves the duplex settings match.

```output Representative: selected lines from show interfaces fastethernet0/24
FastEthernet0/24 is up, line protocol is up (connected)
  Half-duplex, 100Mb/s, media type is 10/100BaseTX
     0 input errors, 0 CRC, 0 frame, 0 overrun, 0 ignored
     12 output errors, 86 collisions, 12 interface resets
     0 babbles, 0 late collision, 0 deferred
```

This excerpt shows counters since the last reset, not necessarily new errors. Record a baseline, generate controlled traffic and compare a later reading. A **CRC error** means a received frame failed its error check; damaged cabling, interference, hardware faults or duplex issues can contribute. A **late collision** occurs later than the permitted collision window on half-duplex Ethernet and warrants investigation of duplex and physical conditions. No single counter identifies every cause.

**Runts** are undersized frames; **giants** exceed the permitted frame size for the interface's configuration and encapsulation. Do not blindly use 1518 bytes as the giant threshold on every port: VLAN tags and configured larger frames affect what is accepted. **Output drops** often indicate an egress queue that could not hold traffic. Investigate load and queue behavior rather than treating them as automatic proof of a broken cable.

An `administratively down` interface is locally shut down. A disconnected or incompatible physical link usually presents a down state without that administrative wording. `err-disabled` indicates that a protection mechanism disabled the port; investigate its recorded cause before re-enabling it. Conversely, `up/up` establishes local link operation, not correct addressing, routing or application service.

Use a repeatable sequence: identify both ends; check administrative and physical state; compare media, speed and duplex; compare counters over a test interval; change one justified item; retest. Keep the original readings. If you choose to reset counters in an isolated lab, target only the intended interface and answer the confirmation prompt. A supported `show interfaces transceiver detail` command adds physical optical measurements on suitable hardware; Packet Tracer and virtual routers do not provide a trustworthy replacement for real optical power testing.

sections.title: Exam focus
sections.body:
- Choose copper or fiber using speed, distance, environment and the actual interface/module specification.
- Recognize straight-through, crossover, console and auto-MDIX roles; a connector's shape does not prove compatibility.
- Know the common 100 m copper design limit and the Cat6A requirement for a full-distance 10GBASE-T channel.
- Compare single-mode and multimode fiber; match modules, fiber grade, reach and transmit-to-receive polarity.
- Distinguish shared half-duplex Ethernet from point-to-point full-duplex Ethernet.
- Recognize a 10/100 forced-versus-auto duplex mismatch by comparing both ends.
- Treat CRC, collisions, late collisions and drops as evidence to investigate, not a one-counter diagnosis.
- Compare optical receive power with supplied limits and verify the result of a repair.

lab.title: Establish a baseline and diagnose Ethernet link faults
lab.intro:
Practice revised September 2026. If you completed an earlier version, repeat the revised exercise and update its checkmarks.


Build one small LAN in Packet Tracer, verify it, and introduce one interface fault at a time. You will compare both ends of the same link, restore service between tests, and finish with supplied fiber and cable-test evidence.

Packet Tracer does not reproduce every hardware counter, physical cable defect or optical power measurement. The configured speed/duplex and administrative states are the main observations in this lab. If the simulated traffic or error counters do not behave like hardware, record that limit and use the lesson's representative examples to explain the real mechanism. The optical exercise is paper-based; no optical meter or transceiver is required.
lab.topology:
Use two **2960** switches, named SW1 and SW2, and two standard **PC** end devices, named PC-A and PC-B. Start a new file. The interswitch link deliberately uses FastEthernet ports so the 10/100 duplex exercise applies.

```diagram
{"type":"topology","title":"Fig 03.L1 — One LAN with a testable interswitch link","caption":"Both PCs share one subnet; the tests require switching but no router or default gateway.","nodes":[{"id":"A","kind":"pc","label":"PC-A","sub":"10.0.30.11/24","x":1,"y":3},{"id":"S1","kind":"switch","label":"SW1","x":4,"y":3},{"id":"S2","kind":"switch","label":"SW2","x":8,"y":3},{"id":"B","kind":"pc","label":"PC-B","sub":"10.0.30.12/24","x":11,"y":3}],"links":[{"from":"A","to":"S1","toLabel":"Fa0/1","label":"straight-through"},{"from":"S1","to":"S2","fromLabel":"Fa0/24","toLabel":"Fa0/24","label":"crossover"},{"from":"S2","to":"B","fromLabel":"Fa0/1","label":"straight-through"}]}
```

| Device and interface | Connection or address | Cable or mask |
|---|---|---|
| PC-A FastEthernet0 | SW1 FastEthernet0/1 | Copper straight-through |
| SW1 FastEthernet0/24 | SW2 FastEthernet0/24 | Copper crossover |
| SW2 FastEthernet0/1 | PC-B FastEthernet0 | Copper straight-through |
| PC-A | `10.0.30.11` | `255.255.255.0` |
| PC-B | `10.0.30.12` | `255.255.255.0` |

Leave both PCs' default gateway and DNS fields blank. No switch management IP, trunk, VLAN change or route is needed. The switch ports remain in their default VLAN 1. Do not add a second interswitch link.

steps.title: Cable, name and address the network
steps.body:
Connect the three cables exactly as listed. On each PC, open **Desktop → IP Configuration**, choose **Static**, and enter its address and mask. Clear any leftover gateway or DNS address if you reused a device.

Open SW1's CLI, press Enter and decline the initial configuration dialog if present. Enter its baseline configuration.

```ios SW1
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW1
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# description PC-A
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# interface fastethernet0/24
SW1(config-if)# description To-SW2
SW1(config-if)# speed auto
SW1(config-if)# duplex auto
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# end
```

Configure SW2 separately.

```ios SW2
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW2
SW2(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
SW2(config-if)# description PC-B
SW2(config-if)# no shutdown
SW2(config-if)# interface fastethernet0/24
SW2(config-if)# description To-SW1
SW2(config-if)# speed auto
SW2(config-if)# duplex auto
SW2(config-if)# no shutdown
SW2(config-if)# end
```

:::expected
The device prompts and cable endpoints match the diagram. After the switch ports initialize, all three links should be usable. A crossover is specified so the lab does not depend on auto-MDIX support during forced-setting tests. Do not deliberately use a wrong cable and assume it must fail; supported auto-MDIX can make either copper arrangement work.
:::

steps.title: Record the working baseline
steps.body:
On PC-A's **Desktop → Command Prompt**, enter `ping 10.0.30.12`. Retry once if initial address resolution loses a first request. Repeat the test from PC-B to `10.0.30.11`. Then inspect the interswitch port at both ends.

```ios SW1
SW1# show interfaces status
SW1# show interfaces fastethernet0/24
SW1# show running-config
```

```ios SW2
SW2# show interfaces status
SW2# show interfaces fastethernet0/24
SW2# show running-config
```

Write down each end's administrative state, operational speed, duplex and displayed error counters. Find the FastEthernet0/24 stanza in each running configuration. Default automatic settings may be omitted from that display.

:::expected
Both PCs receive replies on a repeated test. Both interswitch ends should operate at 100 Mbps full duplex, with the compact display commonly showing `a-full` and `a-100`. Detailed output should show an up physical and line-protocol state. If a compact display command is unavailable, use the detailed interface output.

Save the working topology as `03-interfaces-baseline.pkt`. Keep your first counter readings; later comparisons need a baseline. No conclusion should depend on all counters being exactly zero or on one particular simulator output layout.
:::

steps.title: Identify an administrative shutdown
steps.body:
Disable **SW1's** interswitch port without touching the cable.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/24
SW1(config-if)# shutdown
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces fastethernet0/24
```

Inspect the far end separately.

```ios SW2
SW2# show interfaces fastethernet0/24
SW2# show running-config
```

:::expected
SW1 should identify its interface as `administratively down`. SW2 loses the link but has not been administratively shut down; its configuration still lacks `shutdown` on this port. A down state at SW2 therefore does not tell you whether SW1 was disabled, disconnected or powered off. Inspecting both ends resolves that ambiguity. PC-A's ping to PC-B fails while the port is disabled.
:::

steps.title: Restore the administratively disabled port
steps.body:
Enable the SW1 port you just identified.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/24
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces fastethernet0/24
```

On SW2, run `show interfaces fastethernet0/24`. Repeat the PC-to-PC ping after the links become ready.

:::expected
Both interswitch ports return to an operational state, and repeated pings receive replies. The repair targeted the port whose administrative state was wrong. If the test still fails, collect fresh evidence rather than assuming that command acceptance completed the repair.
:::

steps.title: Introduce a controlled duplex mismatch
steps.body:
This is an isolated lab fault, not a recommended production configuration. Force **SW1** FastEthernet0/24 to 100 Mbps half duplex.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/24
SW1(config-if)# speed 100
SW1(config-if)# duplex half
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces fastethernet0/24
```

Now force **SW2** FastEthernet0/24 to 100 Mbps full duplex.

```ios SW2
SW2# configure terminal
SW2(config)# interface fastethernet0/24
SW2(config-if)# speed 100
SW2(config-if)# duplex full
SW2(config-if)# end
SW2# show interfaces fastethernet0/24
```

Leave both settings in place while you inspect them. Repeat pings in each direction and compare new counter readings with Step 2. Do not assume a few small ping requests provide enough traffic to expose every performance symptom.

:::expected
The two configurations and operational displays should show matching speed but opposing duplex settings. A real Ethernet link can remain up in this condition. Under traffic, the half-duplex end may accumulate collisions or late collisions, while the other end may see receive errors.

The simulator may show successful pings and unchanged counters. That does not make the mismatch correct. The decisive evidence is the half/full disagreement on the two ends of this one connection. Record the actual behavior rather than inventing a target counter value.

If the simulator omits useful counter behavior, interpret this supplied example separately: before a transfer the half-duplex end has 10 collisions and 0 late collisions; afterward it has 420 and 180. The increases are 410 collisions and 180 late collisions. These readings are consistent with the documented mismatch, but the opposing duplex settings establish it directly. Do not record these supplied totals as measurements.
:::

steps.title: Restore duplex agreement and test again
steps.body:
Restore automatic settings on each switch, using the block for that device.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/24
SW1(config-if)# speed auto
SW1(config-if)# duplex auto
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces fastethernet0/24
```

```ios SW2
SW2# configure terminal
SW2(config)# interface fastethernet0/24
SW2(config-if)# speed auto
SW2(config-if)# duplex auto
SW2(config-if)# end
SW2# show interfaces fastethernet0/24
```

:::expected
Both ends return to 100 Mbps full duplex after the link settles, and repeated pings work in both directions. Old error totals need not disappear: they are historical counters. Compare new readings over a new test interval. If the display still shows half duplex, inspect the configuration at both physical ends before proceeding.
:::

steps.title: Diagnose supplied physical-layer evidence
steps.body:
These cases are paper exercises. Use the module facts in the lesson and the readings supplied here; do not attempt to generate optical measurements in Packet Tracer.

| Case | Evidence | Decision to make |
|---|---|---|
| A | A 350 m OM3 path with 10GBASE-SR modules at both ends; the documented OM3 limit is 300 m | Is this path within the specified reach? |
| B | Compatible duplex modules are documented, but strand 1 connects Tx to Tx and strand 2 connects Rx to Rx | What connection must be corrected? |
| C | Receive reading −16 dBm; supplied acceptable range −12 through −1 dBm | Is received power within range, and what should be investigated? |
| D | A basic continuity tester passes pins 1–8, but a better tester reports a split pair | Why does the basic result not clear the cable? |
| E | A new 1 Gbps copper run measures 130 m including patch leads | What should be checked before blaming the IP configuration? |
| F | One FastEthernet end is forced to 10/full; its peer is forced to 100/full | Can the physical link operate with these settings? |

:::expected
A exceeds the supplied OM3 reach; use a design whose fiber and optics support the distance, such as suitable OM4 within the stated SR specification, after verifying the whole installation. B requires Tx at each end to reach Rx at the other. C is below the low limit: inspect the transmitter, path, connectors, polarity and compatibility rather than naming one unproven cause. D has the wrong physical pairing despite pin continuity, which can harm signal performance. E exceeds the normal 100 m channel design limit; verify measurement and redesign the physical path or select suitable fiber. F has a forced-speed mismatch despite matching duplex; coordinate compatible settings at both ends before retesting. Changing an IP address cannot repair it.
:::

steps.title: Preserve the restored baseline
steps.body:
Confirm both interswitch ends still use automatic speed and duplex and that neither is shut down. Repeat PC-A to PC-B and the reverse ping, then save each device separately:

```ios SW1
SW1# copy running-config startup-config
```

Accept the destination with Enter and wait for completion before opening SW2.

```ios SW2
SW2# copy running-config startup-config
```

:::expected
Accept SW2's destination and save the project as `03-interfaces-complete.pkt`. Keep the baseline, fault-state and recovery readings. A useful record names both ends, identifies the changed setting, distinguishes new counter increments from historical totals, and includes a successful retest.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- **No baseline ping:** verify PC addresses and masks, device power and all three cable endpoints. These PCs are on the same LAN and do not need a gateway.
- **A CLI command is rejected:** verify the prompt and port. Use the 2960 FastEthernet0/24 interfaces for these 10/100 tests, not a fixed-speed fiber interface.
- **A port is up but pings fail:** inspect the other ports in the path and endpoint settings. Local link-up is only one part of reachability.
- **Counters do not change during the mismatch:** record the simulator result. A mismatch is identified by comparing duplex at both ends, not by waiting for a specific synthetic error total.
- **Recovery commands seem ineffective:** inspect both switches' running configurations and detailed interface state. Changing only one end can leave the previous fault in place.
- **A physical optical link remains down after a repair:** recheck compatible module part numbers, supported ports, fiber grade, distance, polarity and measured receive levels. A successful command cannot prove an optical path is healthy.
lab.challenge:
With the recovery instructions closed, state which observations would justify calling a link repaired: matching operational settings on both ends and successful fresh traffic tests. Then attempt the optional variation below in a separate copy.

On paper first, predict the result of setting SW1 FastEthernet0/24 to `speed 100` and `duplex full` while leaving SW2 automatic. Which end may operate half duplex on a real 10/100 link, and why?

Test this optional variation in a copy of your Packet Tracer file. Compare the two operational displays, document any simulator limitation, then restore both ends to `speed auto` and `duplex auto`. Finish by proving communication works. Do not change the PCs' addresses or cable type during this test.

:::solution
The automatic SW2 end can detect 100 Mbps but cannot infer full duplex from the nonnegotiating forced end, so it can use half duplex. SW1 remains full duplex. The link can be up despite disagreement. After both ends are restored to automatic settings, they should agree on 100 Mbps full duplex and repeated pings should succeed. If Packet Tracer does not model that fallback, the correct written explanation still distinguishes the documented hardware behavior from what the simulation displayed.
:::

questions.prompt: Which comparison of single-mode and multimode fiber is accurate?
options: Multimode supports longer links because it has a larger core.
Either fiber type is interchangeable when the connector is LC.
Single-mode has a smaller core and is common on longer links.
Jacket color alone proves the installed fiber's speed and reach.
questions.explanation: Single-mode fiber has a smaller core and is commonly used by longer-distance optical systems. Reach depends on the compatible module-and-fiber design, not the core description alone.

whyWrong.0: A larger core does not mean longer reach; multimode light paths can limit supported distance.
whyWrong.1: Matching connectors do not establish fiber and optical-standard compatibility.
whyWrong.3: Use cable markings and verified specifications; color alone is insufficient.

questions.prompt: An office plans 90 m of installed cable plus 10 m of patch leads for supported 10GBASE-T switch ports. Which category supports that full 100 m channel?
options: Cat6A
Cat6 for an unspecified installation
Cat5 rated for 100BASE-TX
Cat5e rated for 1000BASE-T
questions.explanation: Cat6A supports a 100 m 10GBASE-T channel on suitable interfaces. The permanent link and patch leads together consume the channel distance, and actual module reach must still be checked.

whyWrong.1: Cat6 does not guarantee the same full 100 m 10GBASE-T channel requirement.
whyWrong.2: A category sufficient for 100BASE-TX is not the specified full-distance 10GBASE-T choice.
whyWrong.3: Cat5e is a normal 1 Gbps choice but does not meet this full-distance 10 Gbps requirement.

questions.prompt: A conventional 10/100 Ethernet crossover exchanges the transmit and receive pairs. Which pin mapping describes that exchange?
options: Pins 1↔2 and 3↔6, without moving pairs
Pins 1↔3 and 2↔6 between the ends
Pins 1↔1 through 8↔8 between the ends
questions.explanation: A conventional 10/100 crossover swaps the pair using pins 1–2 with the pair using pins 3–6. This connects the intended transmit and receive arrangements where crossover wiring is required.

whyWrong.0: Reversing all pins describes a rollover arrangement used by some serial console cables.
whyWrong.1: Exchanging conductors within each pair is not the required transmit/receive pair crossover.
whyWrong.3: Keeping each pin number unchanged describes a straight-through cable.

questions.prompt: Which Cisco switch command provides a compact table of port status, VLAN, duplex, speed and media type?
options: show ip route
show running-config
show power inline
show interfaces status
questions.explanation: The switch's `show interfaces status` command provides the compact port overview. Use the detailed interface command for the named port's counters or physical and line-protocol state.

whyWrong.0: The routing table does not provide the requested switch-port status columns.
whyWrong.1: The running configuration shows configured commands rather than this operational table.
whyWrong.2: PoE status describes electrical power allocation rather than the requested Ethernet state.

questions.prompt: What does a late collision on a half-duplex 10/100 Ethernet link mean?
options: A frame waited in the output queue beyond its allowed time.
A receive frame failed the Ethernet FCS check.
The peer advertised an unsupported link speed during negotiation.
A collision occurred beyond the permitted collision window.
questions.explanation: A late collision occurs later than the allowed collision-detection window. Investigate duplex agreement and physical or hardware conditions; it does not independently prove one specific defect.

whyWrong.0: Egress queuing and collision timing describe different mechanisms.
whyWrong.1: An FCS failure is received-frame corruption, not the definition of a late collision.
whyWrong.2: Autonegotiation capabilities do not define this collision counter.

questions.prompt: Assume traditional 10/100 MDI/MDI-X ports with no auto-MDIX. Which two connections require a crossover cable? (Choose two.)
options: PC to switch
Switch to switch
Router Ethernet port to switch
PC to router Ethernet port
Server Ethernet port to switch
questions.explanation: Two switch MDI-X ports need a crossover, as do a PC and router whose ports both use MDI. PC, server and router connections to a switch use unlike arrangements and therefore straight-through wiring in this stated case.

whyWrong.0: A PC-to-switch connection pairs MDI with MDI-X, so straight-through is appropriate.
whyWrong.2: A router-to-switch connection pairs MDI with MDI-X.
whyWrong.4: A server-to-switch connection uses straight-through under the stated assumptions.

spec.title: One switch and a shared hub segment
spec.caption: PC-C and PC-D share the hub segment; all switch ports belong to VLAN 1.

questions.prompt: All switch ports are in VLAN 1, and there are no routers or additional links. How many Ethernet collision domains and broadcast domains are represented?
options: One collision domain and three broadcast domains
Four collision domains and one broadcast domain
Three collision domains and three broadcast domains
Three collision domains and one broadcast domain
questions.explanation: Each of the switch's three connected ports separates an Ethernet segment, giving three collision domains. The two PCs behind HUB1 share one of those segments, and all devices remain in one VLAN and therefore one broadcast domain.

whyWrong.0: The switch separates the segments; one VLAN does not create three broadcast domains.
whyWrong.1: The two PCs attached to the hub share one collision domain rather than having one each.
whyWrong.2: Switch ports do not create separate broadcast domains when they share the same VLAN.

questions.prompt: A 350 m path will use 10GBASE-SR modules. The supported reaches are 300 m on OM3 and 400 m on OM4. Which choice meets the stated distance?
options: OM4 multimode fiber within the specified SR design
OM3 multimode fiber because both ends use SR
Single-mode fiber because its core is smaller
Cat6A copper because the connectors can be adapted
questions.explanation: The 350 m path exceeds the supplied OM3 reach but is within the 400 m OM4 specification. Module compatibility and the actual fiber path still need verification.

whyWrong.1: Matching modules do not extend OM3 beyond the stated 300 m reach.
whyWrong.2: SR is specified here for multimode fiber; a different fiber type is not automatically supported.
whyWrong.3: SR is optical, and this distance exceeds the normal copper channel limit.

questions.prompt: A duplex fiber patch connects Switch A Tx to Switch B Tx and Switch A Rx to Switch B Rx. Both modules are otherwise compatible. What should be corrected first?
options: Connect each transmitter to the far receiver.
Leave the mapping and replace one module with a different optical standard.
Leave the mapping and clean both connectors before any other change.
Loop each transmitter to its own receiver instead of the far device.
questions.explanation: A duplex optical link requires each transmitter to connect to the other end's receiver. The documented arrangement is a polarity fault; correct the physical path, then verify light levels and link state.

whyWrong.1: The modules are stated to be compatible; substituting a different standard does not correct the strand mapping.
whyWrong.2: Cleaning is useful maintenance but does not correct a documented Tx-to-Tx connection.
whyWrong.3: A local loopback does not establish communication between the two switches.

exhibit.title: Supplied optical measurements — teaching example
exhibit.text:
Receive power: -16.0 dBm
Acceptable range for this exercise: -12.0 to -1.0 dBm
Link state: down

questions.prompt: The optical receiver's supplied acceptable range is −12 through −1 dBm. What conclusion is supported by a receive reading of −16 dBm?
options: The signal exceeds the receiver's upper power limit.
The receive power is below the supplied lower limit.
The fiber polarity is definitely the only fault.
Both transmit modules are confirmed healthy.
questions.explanation: −16 dBm is less received power than the −12 dBm lower limit. Investigate the optical path and far-end transmitter; the receive value alone does not isolate the cause.

whyWrong.0: A value above −1 dBm would exceed the supplied upper limit.
whyWrong.2: Polarity, distance, connectors, incompatible modules or a transmitter fault can contribute.
whyWrong.3: A receive reading at one end does not establish the health of both transmitters.

exhibit.title: Two ends of one physical cable — representative state
exhibit.text:
SW1 FastEthernet0/24: administratively down, protocol down
SW2 FastEthernet0/24: down, protocol down
SW1 interface configuration: shutdown
SW2 interface configuration: no shutdown

questions.prompt: The cable directly connects the two listed ports. The intended design enables both. What does the evidence establish?
options: Both switches are administratively shut down because both links are down.
SW2 must have a cable defect because its port is administratively enabled.
SW2 should also be shut down to match SW1 before testing traffic.
SW1 is administratively disabled; SW2’s down state does not identify a separate fault.
questions.explanation: SW1’s configuration and administrative state identify the local shutdown. SW2 loses its link when its peer is disabled, even though SW2 remains administratively enabled. Restore the intended SW1 setting and retest before claiming an additional failure.

whyWrong.0: Only SW1 has the shutdown setting in the supplied configuration.
whyWrong.1: A down far end is consistent with SW1’s shutdown; it does not prove a separate cable defect.
whyWrong.2: The intended working design enables both ports; disabling the other end would not restore communication.

exhibit.title: Representative: SW1# show interfaces status
exhibit.text:
Port      Name          Status       Vlan       Duplex  Speed Type
Fa0/3     Appliance     connected    1          a-half  a-100 10/100BaseTX

questions.prompt: The appliance is manually set to 100 Mbps full duplex. Its connected switch port is automatic and shows the following state. What has been established?
options: The link reports a matching speed but an undetermined duplex.
The two ends report matching speed but opposing duplex.
The a- prefix means the switch follows the forced full-duplex setting.
The connected state establishes matching speed and duplex.
questions.explanation: The appliance is full duplex while the switch displays half duplex, so their operational settings disagree. In this 10/100 case, an automatic end can detect the forced end's speed without learning its duplex.

whyWrong.0: The switch explicitly reports half duplex; its duplex is not unknown in this output.
whyWrong.2: The a-half value says half duplex was selected automatically; it does not mean full duplex.
whyWrong.3: A link can remain connected despite a duplex mismatch.

questions.prompt: On the half-duplex end of a 10/100 duplex mismatch, which two observations are consistent with its collision-handling behavior? (Choose two.)
options: The collision count increases during simultaneous traffic.
The late-collision count increases during the test.
The CRC count identifies the exact damaged cable segment.
The output-drop count measures collisions at the far receiver.
The collision count must fall when the duplex setting is repaired.
questions.explanation: The half-duplex end applies collision handling while the full-duplex peer does not. Collisions and late collisions can result; compare the two duplex settings because counters alone do not exclude cable or hardware faults.

whyWrong.2: A CRC counter records received-frame corruption; it does not locate a particular cable segment.
whyWrong.3: Output drops commonly relate to egress queuing, not a remote collision count.
whyWrong.4: Repair stops a cause; historical totals do not automatically decrease.

questions.prompt: A 10/100 link has a forced 100/full endpoint and an automatic switch port operating at 100/half. Both support autonegotiation. What is the preferred starting repair?
options: Leave the current settings and inspect only the next IP hop.
Return both ends to auto and verify speed, duplex and traffic.
Return only the forced end’s speed to auto but leave its duplex forced.
Clear the counters on both ends without changing their settings.
questions.explanation: Returning both supported ends to automatic settings lets them agree on compatible speed and duplex. Verify the result and traffic afterward; matching manual settings at both ends are another deliberate option where required.

whyWrong.0: The confirmed interface-setting disagreement still requires correction.
whyWrong.2: Restoring only one attribute can leave inconsistent duplex behavior; use a coordinated configuration.
whyWrong.3: Clearing counters does not correct the opposing operational duplex settings.

exhibit.title: Printer port before and after an authorized correction
exhibit.text:
Before: administratively down, protocol down
Change applied: no shutdown
After: up, protocol up
Printer address and mask: match the documented plan

questions.prompt: The printer was unreachable before its port was enabled. Which verification best establishes that the required service is restored?
options: Read the interface again and stop because up/up establishes printing.
Save the configuration immediately because no shutdown was accepted.
Retest reachability and a new print request, then record the result.
Clear all interface counters so the display begins with zero errors.
questions.explanation: The port is operational again, but the intended outcome is communication with a working printer. Retest reachability and the actual service from the affected client, then preserve the verified configuration.

whyWrong.0: Link state is necessary evidence but does not test a printer’s application.
whyWrong.1: Command acceptance and saving do not establish that the service is available.
whyWrong.3: Resetting counters neither tests nor repairs application service.

exhibit.title: Representative counter comparison — same interface
exhibit.text:
Start of test: 4 input errors, 4 CRC
End of test:   89 input errors, 89 CRC
Both ends: 1000 Mbps, full duplex

questions.prompt: Both ends of a copper link show 1 Gbps full duplex. During a controlled transfer, received CRC errors increase on the switch. What is the best next action?
options: Clear the counters and conclude the physical path is repaired.
Replace the cable immediately without collecting another reading.
Test the cable path and compare the far-end error readings.
Treat matching duplex as proof that these errors are harmless.
questions.explanation: Rising CRC errors establish that received frames are failing their error check. With the documented speed and duplex agreement, investigate the physical path and endpoint hardware while collecting far-end evidence; the counter does not identify one unique failed component.

whyWrong.0: Clearing a total removes evidence without correcting whatever caused the errors.
whyWrong.1: A cable fault is possible, but the displayed counter does not prove that one component is the cause.
whyWrong.3: Full-duplex agreement does not make received-frame corruption acceptable.

cards.front: What is the usual copper Ethernet channel limit, and what must you check?
cards.back: 100 m for the specified category on supporting ports, commonly 90 m installed plus 10 m patch leads. Some copper modules have shorter limits.

cards.front: Cable choices for 1 Gbps and for a full 100 m 10GBASE-T channel?
cards.back: Cat5e or better is the normal new 1 Gbps choice. Use Cat6A for 10GBASE-T at 100 m on supporting interfaces.

cards.front: Which pin groups form the four physical twisted pairs?
cards.back: 1–2, 3–6, 4–5 and 7–8. A split pair can pass simple pin continuity while using the wrong physical pairing.

cards.front: Which pairs does a conventional 10/100 crossover exchange?
cards.back: Pins 1–2 exchange with pins 3–6: 1↔3 and 2↔6. This is the 10/100 crossover mapping, not a complete rule for every four-pair interface.

cards.front: Without auto-MDIX, when is crossover used on traditional 10/100 ports?
cards.back: Between like electrical arrangements: switch–switch or PC–router, for example. PC/router/server–switch uses straight-through.

cards.front: How does a rollover console cable differ from an Ethernet cable?
cards.back: A traditional rollover reverses pins for a serial console connection. Connect it to the Console port; similar-looking connectors do not make it Ethernet.

cards.front: How do single-mode and multimode fiber differ?
cards.back: Single-mode has a smaller core and commonly supports longer-distance optical designs. Multimode has a larger core and commonly serves shorter links; use specifications, not jacket color alone.

cards.front: What do common 1 Gbps SFP and 10 Gbps SFP+ examples teach about module choice?
cards.back: Match form factor, supported port speed, Ethernet optical standard and fiber. Physical fit and matching connectors alone do not establish compatibility.

cards.front: Hub versus switch: collision and broadcast domains?
cards.back: A hub's devices share one collision domain. A switch separates port segments, while ports in one VLAN share a broadcast domain. Full-duplex Ethernet has no normal collisions.

cards.front: What can an automatic 10/100 end do when its peer is forced to 100/full?
cards.back: Detect 100 Mbps but not the forced duplex setting, then operate at half duplex. The resulting link can be up with a duplex mismatch.

cards.front: What evidence supports a duplex-mismatch diagnosis?
cards.back: Opposing operational duplex settings at the two ends. Collisions/late collisions or received-frame errors may support it, but counters alone are not conclusive.

cards.front: What does the a- prefix in a-full or a-100 mean?
cards.back: The setting was selected automatically, rather than explicitly forced. It can reflect negotiation or sensed/defaulted behavior, so compare both ends.

cards.front: Administrative shutdown versus a lost physical link: what evidence matters?
cards.back: Administratively down identifies the local shutdown. A down/notconnect state can have several causes, including the far end; inspect both ends.

cards.front: What are runts and giants?
cards.back: Runts are undersized Ethernet frames. Giants exceed the permitted frame size for that interface and encapsulation; tags and larger configured frames affect the limit.

cards.front: What does a late collision suggest on a half-duplex 10/100 link?
cards.back: A collision occurred beyond the permitted window. Investigate duplex agreement and physical/hardware conditions; it is not proof of one specific defect.

cards.front: What do increasing output drops commonly suggest?
cards.back: An egress queue cannot hold all offered traffic. Examine load and queue behavior; drops do not automatically prove a cable fault.

cards.front: Is −16 dBm within a supplied receive range of −12 through −1 dBm?
cards.back: No. −16 dBm is lower power than the −12 dBm limit. Check transmitter, path, connectors, distance and compatibility; the reading alone does not isolate the cause.

cards.front: How do you restore automatic speed and duplex in interface configuration?
cards.back: Use speed auto and duplex auto on both supported ends. Verify matching operational settings and a fresh traffic test.

commands.task: Show the switch's compact port-state, VLAN, duplex, speed and media table.
commands.note: Compare the two ends of the same connection, especially a-half versus full.

commands.task: Inspect the detailed state and counters for the interswitch FastEthernet0/24 port.
commands.note: Inspect the same physical link at both ends and compare counters over a recorded test interval.

commands.task: On the 2960 FastEthernet lab port, set the speed to 100 Mbps.
commands.note: A deliberate manual configuration must match the peer. Do not assume auto-MDIX will compensate during forced-setting tests.

commands.task: On the 2960 FastEthernet lab port, set full duplex.
commands.note: Compare the peer's setting. A forced 100/full end with an automatic 10/100 peer can produce a mismatch.

commands.task: Return the selected 2960 FastEthernet port's speed to automatic selection.
commands.note: Restore automatic duplex as well on both ends, then verify operation.

commands.task: Return the selected 2960 FastEthernet port's duplex to automatic selection.
commands.note: A default automatic setting may be omitted from the running configuration.

commands.task: Disable the selected FastEthernet0/24 port for an isolated administrative-fault test.
commands.note: Leave the fault in place while inspecting both ends. Use the separate recovery step afterward.

commands.task: Restore the intended enabled state of the selected FastEthernet0/24 port.
commands.note: Wait for readiness, inspect both ends, and retest the affected traffic before saving.

tickets.title: Backups slow down after an endpoint replacement
tickets.scenario: An appliance's replacement NIC is manually set to 100 Mbps full duplex. The connected switch interface supports 10/100/1000 and remains automatic. Pings work, but larger transfers are slow. You identify the exact two ends, collect a baseline and repeat a transfer. The excerpts are representative IOS-style diagnostic evidence.

exhibits.title: Representative: ASW2# show interfaces status
exhibits.text:
Port      Name               Status       Vlan       Duplex  Speed Type
Gi1/0/12  Backup-appliance   connected    1          a-half  a-100 10/100/1000BaseTX

exhibits.title: Counter comparison on Gi1/0/12
exhibits.text:
Before transfer: 10 collisions; 0 late collisions
After transfer:  420 collisions; 180 late collisions
Operational speed: 100 Mbps
Operational duplex: half

exhibits.title: Verified endpoint settings
exhibits.text:
Adapter mode: manually configured
Speed: 100 Mbps
Duplex: full

tickets.question: Which fault has the evidence established?
options: The rising late-collision count uniquely identifies damaged cabling.
The two ends use opposite duplex settings at the same speed.
The matching 100 Mbps rates rule out an interface-setting fault.
Successful small pings demonstrate that the larger-transfer fault is an IP route.
tickets.explanation: The switch operates at 100/half while the endpoint is set to 100/full. That direct comparison establishes a duplex mismatch, and the increasing collision counters are consistent with it. The counters do not independently prove or exclude a cable fault; the operational settings are the decisive evidence here.
tickets.fix:
Coordinate the endpoint change so its NIC returns to automatic speed and duplex. Then restore the switch side:
```ios ASW2
ASW2# configure terminal
ASW2(config)# interface gigabitethernet1/0/12
ASW2(config-if)# speed auto
ASW2(config-if)# duplex auto
ASW2(config-if)# end
ASW2# show interfaces gigabitethernet1/0/12
```
Verify matching operational speed and full duplex on both ends. Record current counters, repeat the same transfer and compare new increments and completion time. Old totals do not disappear when the cause is fixed. If the endpoint must remain manually configured for a documented reason, deliberately match both ends instead; do not force only one and assume the peer follows. Save the working configuration only after verification.

tickets.title: An optical uplink uses incompatible module types
tickets.scenario: A new 180 m OM3 multimode path joins DSW1 and CORE1. Both intended interfaces are administratively enabled, but the link is down. You inspect the module labels and verify the fiber record. These are supplied inventory and measurement observations, not fabricated output from an executed switch session.

exhibits.title: Verified component record
exhibits.text:
DSW1 optical port: 10GBASE-SR, 850 nm, supported by DSW1
CORE1 optical port: 10GBASE-LR, 1310 nm, supported by CORE1
Installed path: OM3 multimode, 180 m
Both interfaces: administratively enabled

exhibits.title: Specification comparison
exhibits.text:
10GBASE-SR over OM3: up to 300 m for the specified modules
10GBASE-LR: specified for single-mode fiber
Connector shape at both ends: LC
No completed end-to-end optical qualification test is available

tickets.question: Which confirmed incompatibility should be corrected before further link testing?
options: The OM3 distance exceeds the supplied limit for SR modules.
The matching connector shape is sufficient for this module pair.
The design pairs SR over MMF with LR intended for SMF.
The enabled administrative states establish that both optical directions work.
tickets.explanation: The inventory identifies incompatible optical designs: SR over OM3 at one end and LR at the other. The 180 m path is within the supplied SR-on-OM3 distance, but distance alone does not make the module pair compatible. Connector fit does not prove that a supported optical link exists.
tickets.fix:
For the intended OM3 design, select a compatible 10GBASE-SR module supported by CORE1 so both ends use the appropriate SR design. Follow the equipment's module replacement and fiber-handling procedure. Alternatively, an LR design requires a correctly specified single-mode path and compatible modules at both ends; changing a label does not change the installed fiber.

After the component correction, verify transmit-to-receive polarity, inspect and clean connectors using approved equipment, and measure received power against each actual module's permitted range. Never look into a live fiber. On supported hardware, use the interface and transceiver displays, then test traffic and watch for new errors. Do not predict an exact receive dBm value or declare both transmitters healthy from one reading; other faults may remain after the confirmed mismatch is corrected.

chapters.title: IPv4 addressing
chapters.subtitle: Read an address and mask, decide what is local, and verify the configuration.

sources.title: Cisco: Configure IP Addresses and Unique Subnets
RFC 1122: Host requirements, section 3.3.1.1 local/remote decision
Cisco: Local Host Routes Installed in the Routing Table

chapters.summary: Build an IPv4 address from binary, calculate subnet boundaries and usable ranges, then configure router and host addresses and diagnose mask and gateway errors.

sections.body:
An address by itself does not tell you which network a device belongs to. You need its subnet mask as well. Once you can use those two values together, you can choose valid addresses, understand when a host uses its gateway, and explain several common connection failures.

Work through the calculations before trying to do them quickly. The lab uses the same two subnets throughout so that you can compare your paper answers with the configuration and the router's routing table.

sections.title: Why the mask decides everything
sections.body:
A PC on Ethernet needs to choose the next device to receive a packet. If the destination is on its own IP subnet, the PC normally uses **Address Resolution Protocol (ARP)** to find that destination's MAC address. If the destination is remote, the PC uses an appropriate route, usually its **default gateway** on a simple workstation. The gateway is a router address reachable on the local LAN.

Consider PC-A at `192.168.44.130/26`. Its subnet contains addresses `192.168.44.128` through `192.168.44.191`. A destination of `192.168.44.150` is local, so PC-A resolves that host's MAC address. A destination of `192.168.44.194` is outside the subnet, so PC-A resolves its gateway's MAC address and sends the frame there. The packet's destination IP address is still `192.168.44.194`; using a gateway does not replace it with the gateway's IP.

Change only PC-A's mask to `/24` and it now considers `192.168.44.194` local. It may send ARP requests for a device that is physically on a different LAN. This is why a correct-looking address does not prove a correct configuration. Check the address, mask, and gateway together.

For these examples, assume a workstation with one network connection and no manually added routes. Real hosts have routing tables, and a more specific route can change the next-hop decision. You do not need those exceptions to configure the basic LAN correctly.

sections.title: Binary and the 32-bit address
sections.body:
:::facts
- IPv4 addresses contain 32 bits, written as four 8-bit octets. Each octet is 0–255.
- Octet bit values, left to right: `128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1`.
- A prefix length counts network bits. Host bits = `32 − prefix length`.
- Network address = address AND mask. A mask has consecutive ones followed by zeros.
- On an ordinary subnet through /30: total addresses = `2^host bits`; usable addresses = total − 2.
- A /31 point-to-point subnet uses both addresses; /32 identifies one address.
:::

A **bit** has two possible values: 0 or 1. In an address, the position of a bit tells you how much it contributes to the number. A 1 in the leftmost position contributes 128; a 1 in the rightmost contributes 1. Add the values of the positions containing 1. Eight ones add to 255, which explains the largest possible decimal octet.

| Position from left | Value | Bit in 173 |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 128 | 1 |
| 2 | 64 | 0 |
| 3 | 32 | 1 |
| 4 | 16 | 0 |
| 5 | 8 | 1 |
| 6 | 4 | 1 |
| 7 | 2 | 0 |
| 8 | 1 | 1 |

For `173`, start with 128 and subtract it: 45 remains. Skip 64 because it is too large. Subtract 32, leaving 13; skip 16; subtract 8, 4, and 1. The result is `10101101`. To check it, add `128 + 32 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 173`. Keep all eight positions, including zeros; otherwise the place values change.

The reverse operation uses the same table. Binary `11010010` contains `128 + 64 + 16 + 2`, which equals 210. Practice with individual octets first. An entire address is simply four of these conversions separated by dots.

An **AND** operation compares corresponding bits in two values. Its result is 1 only when both bits are 1: `1 AND 1 = 1`; all other combinations produce 0. A mask bit of 1 therefore retains the address bit, while a mask bit of 0 clears it. That is how the mask separates the network portion from the host portion.

```text
Address, last octet: 173 = 10101101
Mask, last octet:    192 = 11000000
                            AND
Network octet:      128 = 10000000
```

The first three octets of a /26 mask are all ones, so they remain unchanged. Applying this operation to `192.168.44.173/26` produces network address `192.168.44.128`. The remaining six bits identify the position of a device within that subnet.

```diagram
{ "type": "binary", "ip": "192.168.44.173", "prefix": 26, "title": "Address bits and the /26 boundary", "caption": "The first 26 bits identify the subnet; the final six bits vary between addresses within that subnet." }
```

sections.title: Masks, prefixes and block sizes
sections.body:
A **subnet mask** marks network bits with ones and host bits with zeros. A **prefix length**, such as `/26`, is another way to write the same boundary: 26 network bits, then 6 host bits. In dotted notation, `/26` is `255.255.255.192`, because its final octet is `11000000`.

The ones must be consecutive from the left. `255.0.255.0` is not a valid contiguous subnet mask: it resumes network bits after host bits have already begun. Do not confuse a subnet mask with the wildcard masks used later in access lists; their rules and purpose differ.

| Ones within one octet | Binary value | Decimal value |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | `00000000` | 0 |
| 1 | `10000000` | 128 |
| 2 | `11000000` | 192 |
| 3 | `11100000` | 224 |
| 4 | `11110000` | 240 |
| 5 | `11111000` | 248 |
| 6 | `11111100` | 252 |
| 7 | `11111110` | 254 |
| 8 | `11111111` | 255 |

To convert `/20`, fill two complete octets with ones: that accounts for 16 bits. Put four ones in the third octet, giving 240, and zeros in the fourth. The result is `255.255.240.0`. In the other direction, `255.255.254.0` contains `8 + 8 + 7 = 23` ones, so it is `/23`.

For a partial octet, the **block increment** is `256 − mask value`. With 192 in the fourth octet, the increment is 64. Subnets therefore start at fourth-octet values 0, 64, 128, and 192. With 240 in the third octet, they start at 0, 16, 32, 48, and so on in the third octet; the whole fourth octet varies inside each block.

An increment is not always the total number of addresses. A /20 increment of 16 covers 16 complete fourth-octet ranges: `16 × 256 = 4,096` addresses. At an octet boundary such as /24, there is no partial octet: retain the first three octets and vary the fourth from 0 through 255.

:::trap Use the stated mask
Modern addressing is classless. You cannot infer a device's configured prefix from its first octet. An address starting with 10 can use /25, /30, or another valid prefix. Historical class A, B, and C defaults were /8, /16, and /24; they are background terminology, not a substitute for reading today's configuration.
:::

sections.title: Network, broadcast and usable hosts
sections.body:
The **network address** identifies the subnet as a whole. All host bits are zero. The **subnet broadcast address** has the same network bits with all host bits set to one. On an ordinary LAN, neither address is assigned to a workstation or gateway. Addresses between them are available for interfaces.

For `192.168.44.173/26`, the final-octet increment is 64. The boundaries are 0, 64, 128, and 192; 173 lies in the block starting at 128. Its network is `192.168.44.128`, broadcast is `192.168.44.191`, and usable range is `192.168.44.129–192.168.44.190`. Six host bits provide `2^6 = 64` total addresses and 62 usable addresses.

A gateway consumes one of those 62 addresses. It does not have to be the first or last usable address; that is an administrative convention. If a requirement says “62 PCs plus a router interface,” a /26 is too small because you need 63 usable addresses. Establish what the device count includes before choosing a mask.

For `172.20.77.210/20`, the third-octet boundaries are multiples of 16. The value 77 falls in the 64–79 block. Set the host bits to zero for `172.20.64.0`; set them to one for `172.20.79.255`. The usable range is `172.20.64.1–172.20.79.254`, with 4,094 usable addresses. Both the low four bits of the third octet and all eight bits of the fourth octet are host bits.

The method also works in the second octet. For `10.203.15.77/13`, the mask is `255.248.0.0`, with an increment of 8 in the second octet. The containing block begins at 200 and ends at 207, giving network `10.200.0.0` and broadcast `10.207.255.255`. Do not stop the calculation at an octet that still contains host bits.

| Prefix | Mask | Total addresses | Usable on an ordinary subnet |
|---|---|---|---|
| /24 | `255.255.255.0` | 256 | 254 |
| /25 | `255.255.255.128` | 128 | 126 |
| /26 | `255.255.255.192` | 64 | 62 |
| /27 | `255.255.255.224` | 32 | 30 |
| /28 | `255.255.255.240` | 16 | 14 |
| /29 | `255.255.255.248` | 8 | 6 |
| /30 | `255.255.255.252` | 4 | 2 |

A **/31** is a specific exception for a point-to-point link with two endpoints. RFC 3021 treats both addresses as endpoint addresses; neither is reserved as that subnet's directed broadcast. For `10.0.0.0/31`, the endpoints can use `10.0.0.0` and `10.0.0.1`. Do not apply the ordinary subtraction of two, and do not use /31 for a multi-device user LAN. Both devices must support this use.

A **/32** identifies exactly one address. It is common on router loopbacks and in host routes. Loopbacks can be configured with other masks, so “loopback” does not automatically mean /32. The important calculation is that /32 leaves no varying host bits.

:::trap An ending of .0 or .255 is not enough
Within `10.4.8.0/22`, the network is `10.4.8.0` and the broadcast is `10.4.11.255`. Addresses such as `10.4.9.0` and `10.4.8.255` are valid hosts. Judge the complete host portion, using the actual mask.
:::

sections.title: Practice problems
sections.body:
For each row, write the mask, locate the block, and identify the network and broadcast before reading the answer. Then check the result by counting the total addresses. If you can explain your result in binary, the quicker block method is working correctly.

| Address | Network | Broadcast | Usable range |
|---|---|---|---|
| `192.168.1.77/28` | `192.168.1.64` | `192.168.1.79` | `.65–.78` |
| `10.10.10.200/25` | `10.10.10.128` | `10.10.10.255` | `.129–.254` |
| `172.16.33.19/27` | `172.16.33.0` | `172.16.33.31` | `.1–.30` |
| `192.168.100.250/29` | `192.168.100.248` | `192.168.100.255` | `.249–.254` |
| `10.1.1.130/30` | `10.1.1.128` | `10.1.1.131` | `.129–.130` |
| `172.30.150.9/22` | `172.30.148.0` | `172.30.151.255` | `172.30.148.1–172.30.151.254` |
| `10.66.77.88/18` | `10.66.64.0` | `10.66.127.255` | `10.66.64.1–10.66.127.254` |
| `192.168.200.130/23` | `192.168.200.0` | `192.168.201.255` | `192.168.200.1–192.168.201.254` |

To choose a mask for 50 total interface addresses, compare capacities. A /27 gives 30 usable addresses and is too small. A /26 gives 62 and is the smallest subnet that fits. “Smallest subnet” means the fewest total addresses that satisfy the requirement, which corresponds to the longest suitable prefix.

To check whether two hosts share a subnet, calculate each host's network using its configured mask. With matching masks, matching network addresses mean the addresses belong to the same subnet. If masks differ, also evaluate what each host believes about the destination; one may send directly while the other uses a gateway. Matching the first three decimal numbers is not a valid general test.

sections.title: Configuring addresses on IOS
sections.body:
On the Cisco 2911 used here, configure an IPv4 address on the routed Ethernet interface. The `ip address` command takes an address and dotted mask. Enter `no shutdown` to remove an administrative shutdown, then check that the physical link and line protocol are actually up. The command enables the interface; it cannot repair a disconnected cable.

These commands create two separate LANs. Start at `Router>`; if the router already has a hostname, its prompt will use that name.

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.44.129 255.255.255.192
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.44.193 255.255.255.224
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
```

Each LAN needs its own nonoverlapping subnet. In this example, Gi0/0 uses `.128/26` and Gi0/1 uses `.192/27`. Configuring Gi0/1 with a /24 instead would include the first LAN's entire range. IOS normally rejects this overlap between routed interfaces in the same routing table. Read any error before continuing, then verify the configuration that was actually retained.

A Catalyst 2960's physical switch ports operate at Layer 2. You do not assign these LAN gateway addresses to its ordinary access ports. A switch management address belongs on a switch virtual interface, a subject covered later. The switch needs no management IP merely to forward frames between the PC and R1 in this lab.

sections.title: Verify and troubleshoot
sections.body:
Use different commands for different questions. A saved configuration proves what is configured, while operational output proves whether the interface is currently usable. The following examples are representative, abbreviated IOS-style output for the stated topology, not a captured Packet Tracer run. Interface lists, spacing, and other details vary by software image.

```output R1# show ip interface brief
Interface              IP-Address      OK? Method Status                Protocol
GigabitEthernet0/0      192.168.44.129  YES manual up                    up  ← LAN-A is operational
GigabitEthernet0/1      192.168.44.193  YES manual administratively down down  ← administrative shutdown
```

The brief table shows addresses and state, but not masks. Use `show ip interface gigabitethernet0/0` to read the prefix, or `show running-config` to find the interface's `ip address` line. Some simulator images support fewer filtered forms of these commands; the full running configuration remains a useful fallback.

```output R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/0
GigabitEthernet0/0 is up, line protocol is up
  Internet address is 192.168.44.129/26  ← verify /26, not merely .129
...
```

After both LAN interfaces are up/up, `show ip route` should contain connected routes for `192.168.44.128/26` and `192.168.44.192/27`. A `C` route identifies the connected subnet. Images displaying `L` local routes also show each router interface's own address as a /32. An `L` /32 does not mean that the attached LAN uses a /32 mask.

Check a PC with `ipconfig` or its network settings. Ping its gateway first, then a remote host. If the gateway responds but remote communication fails, inspect the far host as well: the reply needs a return path. A gateway need not be involved in a same-subnet exchange, so working local traffic does not prove the gateway setting.

| Evidence | What to check next |
|---|---|
| Interface says administratively down | Enter `no shutdown` on the intended interface |
| Interface is enabled but link remains down | Cable, peer port, device power, and physical state |
| Correct address, uncertain mask | Detailed IP interface output and host configuration |
| Local traffic works; remote traffic fails | Both hosts' masks and gateway addresses, then router routes |
| Address command rejected | Network/broadcast selection, mask validity, and overlap |

A wrong mask can sometimes remain unnoticed because of **proxy ARP**: a router may answer an ARP request on behalf of a remote destination and then route the packet. A successful ping therefore does not certify the mask. Read the configuration. Proxy ARP behavior depends on the receiving interface and available route; do not assume it is enabled everywhere or depend on it to correct a bad address plan.

sections.title: Exam focus
sections.body:
- Convert an octet between decimal and binary, and explain what AND does.
- Convert between dotted masks and prefix lengths without assuming an address class.
- Calculate network, broadcast, usable range, and usable count with the actual prefix.
- Include gateway and other infrastructure addresses in host requirements.
- Distinguish /30, the /31 point-to-point exception, and a /32 host route.
- Explain when a basic workstation ARPs for a destination versus its gateway.
- Configure an interface with a dotted mask and verify both its prefix and operational state.
- Diagnose an invalid host address, overlapping subnet, wrong mask, or incorrect gateway from evidence.

lab.title: Configure two LANs and isolate address, mask, and gateway faults
lab.intro:
Calculate two directly connected LANs, compare your predictions with the configured devices, and isolate a gateway fault without changing unrelated settings. Finish by adding a third LAN from a fresh prefix. The IOS commands are supplied as guided setup; address calculations and verification are your work. No VLAN, static-route, routing-protocol or DNS configuration is needed.

Practice revised September 2026. If you completed an earlier version, repeat the revised exercise and update its checkmarks.

Keep a worksheet with four parts: calculated address plan, predicted next hops, actual test results, and the independent challenge. Before opening an answer, write a result and the rule that produced it. Correct an error in the worksheet before applying its values to a device. The estimated time includes that reasoning; this is not a speed test.

This procedure has been checked against the address plan and Cisco command documentation, but was not executed in Packet Tracer during this review. Output excerpts are representative. Compare addresses, prefixes, and interface state rather than exact spacing, message timing, or TTL values.
lab.topology:
```diagram
{ "type": "topology", "title": "Two LANs with one router", "caption": "PC-A and PC-C share LAN-A; PC-B is reached through R1 on LAN-B.",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "A", "kind": "pc", "label": "PC-A", "sub": "192.168.44.130/26", "x": 1, "y": 1 },
    { "id": "C", "kind": "pc", "label": "PC-C", "sub": "192.168.44.150/26", "x": 1, "y": 5 },
    { "id": "S1", "kind": "switch", "label": "SW1", "x": 3.5, "y": 3 },
    { "id": "R", "kind": "router", "label": "R1 · 2911", "x": 6, "y": 3 },
    { "id": "S2", "kind": "switch", "label": "SW2", "x": 8.5, "y": 3 },
    { "id": "B", "kind": "pc", "label": "PC-B", "sub": "192.168.44.194/27", "x": 11, "y": 3 }
  ],
```
