cards.front: Which three blocks are RFC 1918 private space?
What is the last address inside RFC 1918 block 172.16.0.0/12?
cards.back: 172.31.255.255. An address beginning 172.32 is outside that private block.

cards.front: How do /20, /26, and octet-aligned /24 boundaries differ?
cards.back: /20 varies within the third octet; /26 within the fourth. /24 has three full network octets and one full host octet.

cards.front: How do you count equal-size child subnets and usable addresses?
cards.back: Parent /p to child /q: 2^(q−p) subnets. Each ordinary child through /30: 2^(32−q) − 2 usable addresses.

cards.front: What checks make a VLSM allocation valid?
cards.back: Enough capacity, correct boundary, containment in the parent, and no overlap. Allocate larger blocks first in empty space.

cards.front: How do you find a single containing summary?
cards.back: Find the shared leading bits of the full address range. Use them as the prefix and clear the remaining bits; check extra covered space.

cards.front: Why can’t 10.44.9.0/24 through 10.44.12.0/24 form one exact /22?
cards.back: They straddle the /22 boundary between third-octet values 11 and 12. The smallest containing /21 also covers extra /24s.

cards.front: What does an automatically assigned 169.254.x.x address suggest?
cards.back: IPv4 link-local fallback. Investigate why normal DHCP configuration was not obtained; the address alone does not identify the cause.

cards.front: Do modern subnet counts exclude subnet zero and the all-ones subnet?
cards.back: No. All 2^s subnet numbers are available after adding s prefix bits. Do not confuse this with reserving host network/broadcast addresses.

cards.front: Which IPv4 blocks identify loopback and multicast addresses?
cards.back: 127.0.0.0/8 is loopback; 224.0.0.0/4 is multicast. Neither is ordinary unicast addressing for a workstation LAN.
0.0.0.0 can mean unspecified; 0.0.0.0/0 is the default-route prefix. 255.255.255.255 is the limited broadcast.

cards.front: How do invalid host addresses differ from overlapping allocations?
cards.back: Network/broadcast selection makes the host address unsuitable. Overlap means two proposed routed subnet ranges share addresses; inspect the relevant masks.

cards.front: What should you verify when local pings work but remote pings fail?
cards.back: Both endpoints' masks and gateways, followed by router routes. A too-wide mask can make remote addresses appear local.

cards.front: Can nonoverlapping RFC 1918 LANs communicate through ordinary internal routing?
cards.back: Yes. Appropriate routes and usable paths can connect them without NAT; private addressing does not itself block forwarding.

cards.front: What distinguishes FLSM from VLSM?
cards.back: FLSM uses one child-subnet size; VLSM uses different sizes to suit separate requirements. Both still require valid, nonoverlapping allocations.

cards.front: What must an addressed-interface requirement include before you choose a subnet size?
cards.back: Count end devices, router interfaces and any stated growth or reservations. Do not add a gateway twice when the given total already includes it.

cards.front: How do you choose the smallest ordinary subnet for a usable-address requirement?
cards.back: Choose the fewest host bits h for which 2^h − 2 meets the requirement, then use prefix 32 − h. Check placement separately.

cards.front: What happens to capacity when a prefix grows from /26 to /27?
cards.back: The address block halves from 64 to 32 total addresses; ordinary usable capacity drops from 62 to 30. A longer prefix cannot fix a capacity shortage.

cards.front: Why can 128 free addresses still fail to provide a /26?
cards.back: The addresses may be split into gaps. A /26 requires one aligned, contiguous 64-address block with no occupied addresses inside.

cards.front: What proves that a proposed subnet is contained in its approved parent?
cards.back: Its entire network-to-broadcast range lies within the parent. Checking only the gateway or the first few octets is insufficient.

cards.front: How do you choose gateway and test-host addresses after allocating a LAN?
cards.back: Choose distinct usable addresses in that subnet, reserve the router’s address, and give each host the matching mask and actual local gateway.

cards.front: Does changing a router interface’s address or mask update static PC settings?
cards.back: No. Update and verify the affected PCs separately against the new allocation. Check their address, mask and gateway.

cards.front: When does allocating largest first simplify VLSM placement?
cards.back: In an empty contiguous parent. Existing assignments still require checking the actual free intervals; sorting requirements does not remove fragmentation.

cards.front: What should a small subnet-renumbering verification record include?
cards.back: The new router prefix, each changed PC’s settings, local gateway tests and both directions to unchanged LANs. Test the new addresses, not the retired ones.

tickets.title: The Devices subnet overlaps an existing interface
tickets.scenario: The approved plan is Users 10.44.8.0/25 on Gi0/0, Operations 10.44.8.128/26 on Gi0/1, and Devices 10.44.8.192/27 on Gi0/2. While configuring Devices, IOS reports an overlap with Gi0/1. Its exact message is not needed: the configuration below shows the relevant evidence.

exhibits.title: Existing Gi0/1 configuration excerpt
exhibits.text:
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip address 10.44.8.129 255.255.255.128

exhibits.title: Proposed Gi0/2 configuration
exhibits.text:
interface GigabitEthernet0/2
 ip address 10.44.8.193 255.255.255.224

tickets.question: Which correction follows the approved plan?
options: Move the Devices gateway to .192 but retain its /27 mask.
Change Operations from its configured /25 to the planned /26.
Change Devices to /24 so it includes the Operations interface.
Shrink Devices to /28 while retaining the existing Operations /25.
tickets.explanation: Operations was configured as 10.44.8.128/25, spanning .128–.255 and including the proposed Devices range .192–.223. The intended /26 ends at .191, so correcting that mask removes the overlap. Address .192 is not a valid Devices gateway; widening Devices would worsen the overlap. Shrinking Devices to .192/28 would still place its entire range inside the incorrect Operations /25 and would abandon the approved Devices size.
tickets.fix:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.44.8.129 255.255.255.192
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.44.8.193 255.255.255.224
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip route
```
With both links operational, verify C prefixes `10.44.8.128/26` and `10.44.8.192/27`. Also compare Operations clients with the planned /26; the router correction does not update their static masks.

tickets.title: A broad host mask sends ARP onto the wrong LAN
tickets.scenario: PC-OPS belongs on 10.44.8.128/26, gateway 10.44.8.129. R1 directly connects Users 10.44.8.0/25 and Devices 10.44.8.192/27 as well. PC-OPS reaches local peer 10.44.8.150 and its gateway, but fails to reach Users printer 10.44.8.20 and Devices scanner 10.44.8.200. A correctly configured Operations peer reaches both. Proxy ARP is disabled on the Operations-facing router interface, and there are no extra host routes.

exhibits.title: R1 configuration excerpt
exhibits.text:
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip address 10.44.8.129 255.255.255.192
 no ip proxy-arp

exhibits.title: Representative first-hop observations
exhibits.text:
PC-OPS ARP target for printer test: 10.44.8.20
PC-OPS ARP target for scanner test: 10.44.8.200
No device on the Operations LAN answers either target.
R1’s three planned LAN interfaces are up/up.

tickets.question: Which diagnosis accounts for the observed pattern?
options: R1 needs static routes for its two directly connected LANs.
R1's /26 should be widened to match the incorrect host mask.
The host's /24 treats the printer and scanner as local destinations.
The .129 gateway lies outside the PC's configured /24 subnet.
tickets.explanation: The host’s /24 covers .0–.255, so both .20 and .200 appear local even though they are on R1’s other LANs. The observed ARP targets support that incorrect decision. The PC cannot resolve either target on Operations, and R1 is not acting as a proxy. Its .129 gateway is valid, and the correctly configured peer plus R1’s directly connected LANs rule out the proposed need for new static routes.
tickets.fix: Set PC-OPS to `10.44.8.140`, mask `255.255.255.192`, gateway `10.44.8.129`. Read the settings and repeat the local-peer, gateway, printer and scanner tests. Under the correct /26, .20 and .200 are remote and use .129 as next hop. Keep the router’s approved prefixes and proxy-ARP policy unchanged.

chapters.title: TCP, UDP & ports
chapters.subtitle: How transport protocols deliver application data and identify the service at each end.

sources.title: IETF RFC 1122: TCP push is not a record marker
IANA: Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry

chapters.summary: Compare TCP and UDP, follow connections and DNS exchanges, interpret ports and acknowledgments, and distinguish network reachability from application availability.

sections.body: A PC can browse a website, request a DNS answer, and maintain a remote management session at the same time. IP addresses identify the endpoints, but they do not identify which application should receive each piece of data. Transport protocols provide that distinction and determine what happens when data is lost or arrives out of order. This chapter develops those ideas before you use ports in access lists, NAT, and network services.

sections.title: Why IP alone is not enough
sections.body:
**IP** provides best-effort packet delivery. A packet can be lost, delayed, duplicated, or delivered after a packet sent later. IP does not promise to recover a missing part of a file for an application. A transport service must either provide that recovery or leave the application responsible for deciding what to do.

**TCP**, the Transmission Control Protocol, provides a reliable, ordered **byte stream** between applications. It establishes a connection, numbers the bytes, acknowledges received data, and retransmits when necessary. **UDP**, the User Datagram Protocol, sends individual **datagrams** without establishing a transport connection or providing its own acknowledgments and retransmissions. Both identify application endpoints with source and destination ports.

:::facts
- TCP provides connection establishment, ordered byte delivery, loss recovery, and flow control. Its minimum header is **20 bytes**.
- UDP preserves datagram boundaries and provides no transport-level delivery or ordering guarantee. Its header is **8 bytes**.
- Each TCP or UDP port field is **16 bits**: numerical values run from `0` to `65535`. Port `0` is reserved, not a normal service destination.
- TCP and UDP have separate port spaces. `TCP 53` and `UDP 53` are different transport endpoints.
- An ordinary TCP opening is **SYN → SYN/ACK → ACK**. ICMP echo traffic does not perform this handshake and has no TCP or UDP ports.
:::

Reliability does not mean that TCP can overcome an indefinite outage. If the path remains unavailable, the connection can fail and the application must handle that failure. Nor does a TCP acknowledgment prove that a business transaction was completed: it acknowledges transport data, not that the server saved a file or accepted an order. Keep transport delivery and application success separate when interpreting tests.

The CCNA v1.1 objective is to **compare TCP to UDP**. Learn the behavior well enough to explain a capture and choose an appropriate test. The header details below support that understanding; memorizing congestion algorithms or operating-system timer defaults is unnecessary for this foundation.

sections.title: Ports, sockets and multiplexing
sections.body:
A **port number** identifies a transport endpoint within a host. A server usually waits on a known service port, while a client chooses a temporary **ephemeral port** for its end of an exchange. For example, a client at `192.168.40.10` could connect from TCP port `51514` to `192.168.40.20` on TCP port `80`. The server's reply reverses the source and destination addresses and ports.

| Direction | Source endpoint | Destination endpoint |
|---|---|---|
| Client request | `192.168.40.10:51514` | `192.168.40.20:80` |
| Server reply | `192.168.40.20:80` | `192.168.40.10:51514` |

The **five-tuple** consists of transport protocol, source IP address, source port, destination IP address, and destination port. It distinguishes conversations for packet analysis and traffic policy. For two simultaneous TCP connections using the same client IP, server IP, and server port, the client ports distinguish the connections. Do not equate connections with browser tabs: modern applications can carry multiple requests over a shared connection.

The term **socket** refers to an application endpoint exposed by the operating system. In diagrams you will often see it represented as an IP address and port, with the transport understood from context. A TCP connection joins two endpoints. Thousands of clients can therefore connect to one server port without requiring a different listening port for each client.

| IANA range | Numbers | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| System, also called well-known | `0–1023` | Familiar assignments such as SSH `22` and DNS `53` |
| User, also called registered | `1024–49151` | Additional registered application services |
| Dynamic/private | `49152–65535` | Available for dynamic use; IANA does not assign individual services here |

These are registry categories, not a rule that every operating system must choose ephemeral ports from the final range. Selection ranges and policies vary. The important capture-reading skill is recognizing which endpoint initiated an exchange and which port identifies the requested service. A low port is a useful clue, not proof of the application's identity.

:::trap A port assignment is not an application test
Traffic to TCP `443` is consistent with HTTPS, but another program can use that port. A successful TCP connection also does not prove that TLS negotiation, authentication, or the requested page works. Read ports together with the protocol exchange and the application's result.
:::

sections.title: Two headers, two philosophies
sections.body:
TCP carries more control information because it performs more work. Its header includes source and destination ports, sequence and acknowledgment numbers, control flags, an advertised receive window, and a checksum. Options can extend the header beyond its 20-byte minimum. UDP contains four 16-bit fields: source port, destination port, length, and checksum; the length includes both its header and data.

| Property | TCP | UDP |
|---|---|---|
| Data presented to application | Ordered stream of bytes | Separate datagrams |
| Opening exchange | Establishes connection state | No UDP handshake |
| Missing data | TCP can detect loss and retransmit | UDP itself does not recover it |
| Ordering and duplicates | TCP orders bytes and handles duplicates | Application handles these if needed |
| Receiver flow control | Advertised receive window | No equivalent UDP window |
| Examples in this course | SSH, HTTP over TCP, FTP | DHCP, NTP, ordinary DNS over UDP |

**Byte stream** is an important qualification. If an application writes 200 bytes and then 300 bytes, TCP may carry them in one segment or several. The receiving application uses its own message format to determine where a request ends. The PSH flag does not create a message boundary, and a segment boundary does not reliably identify a complete application message.

With UDP, the application supplies a datagram and the receiver is given a datagram, if it arrives. UDP has no sequence-number field with which to order several datagrams. However, an application can put its own identifiers in the data, detect missing messages, and retry. TFTP uses UDP and implements acknowledgments and retransmission above it. “UDP application” therefore does not mean “application incapable of reliable transfer.”

Neither TCP nor UDP inherently encrypts application data. SSH and TLS provide security above the underlying transport; a TCP checksum detects errors rather than protecting against an attacker. UDP's small header also does not establish that every UDP application is faster. Performance depends on application design, network conditions, and mechanisms built above UDP.

sections.title: Opening and closing a connection
sections.body:
A TCP server first needs a **listening** endpoint. The client sends a segment with **SYN** set to request synchronization of sequence numbers. The server replies with SYN and **ACK**, acknowledging the client's initial sequence number and supplying its own. The client then acknowledges the server's SYN. Data exchange can follow once the connection is established.

```diagram
{ "type": "sequence", "title": "Fig 6.1 — An ordinary TCP opening", "actors": ["Client · port 51514", "Server · port 80"],
  "steps": [
    { "from": 0, "to": 1, "label": "SYN · seq 1000", "note": "Client proposes its initial sequence number", "accent": true },
    { "from": 1, "to": 0, "label": "SYN, ACK · seq 5000 · ack 1001", "note": "Server acknowledges the client and supplies its own number" },
    { "from": 0, "to": 1, "label": "ACK · seq 1001 · ack 5001", "note": "Client acknowledges the server's SYN", "accent": true }
  ], "caption": "These are illustrative absolute sequence numbers; each SYN consumes one sequence number." }
```

The **sequence number** identifies a position in one direction's byte stream. The **acknowledgment number** states the next byte expected in the other direction. Here, the first client data byte is numbered `1001`. A segment containing 200 data bytes occupies `1001–1200`, so successful in-order reception is acknowledged with `1201`. The directions have independent numbering: do not add the server's starting value to the client's.

ACK does not mean “I received one packet.” Acknowledgments are **cumulative**: acknowledgment `1201` says all preceding stream bytes through `1200` have been received, with no earlier gap remaining. They may originally have arrived out of order. An ACK-only segment consumes no data sequence space. SYN and **FIN** each consume one sequence number, even when no application data accompanies them. These rules are enough to work introductory sequence examples without studying the entire TCP state machine.

A normal close uses FIN to say that one endpoint has no more bytes to send. Each direction closes separately, and acknowledgments are required; the server can still finish sending after the client closes its sending direction. Textbooks often draw four segments, but an acknowledgment and FIN can be combined, so four is not a mandatory packet count. **RST** resets a connection or rejects an attempt rather than carrying out an orderly close.

If a SYN receives a reset, the attempt was actively rejected. A closed listening port is one possible cause, but a security device can also generate a reset. If no response appears, the capture alone does not identify whether the request was filtered, the destination was unavailable, or the reply was lost. Use evidence from both endpoints or intermediate devices before selecting a cause.

sections.title: Windowing, flow control and congestion control
sections.body:
TCP does not have to stop after every data segment and wait for an individual acknowledgment. It can have multiple bytes outstanding while acknowledgments return. **Windowing** describes this controlled amount of data in flight. It allows useful throughput while still limiting what the sender may send.

**Flow control** protects the receiving endpoint. The receiver advertises how much additional data it is prepared to accept, based on available receive capacity. A small receive window can limit the sender even on an otherwise fast network. A zero advertised window tells the sender that the receiver cannot currently accept additional stream data; this differs from a failed cable or an unknown destination.

**Congestion control** concerns the network path. The sender limits traffic in response to indications of congestion, such as loss or explicit congestion signaling. It must respect both receiver capacity and its congestion-control limit. A larger receive window therefore does not permit sending without regard to network conditions. Detailed algorithms and window-scaling calculations are beyond the comparison required here.

Consider data bytes `1001–1100`, `1101–1200`, and `1201–1300`. If the middle range is lost, later data does not make the gap disappear: the cumulative acknowledgment remains `1101`. TCP can retransmit missing data after detecting loss, including through a retransmission timeout. Once the gap is filled and all three ranges are present, an acknowledgment can advance to `1301`. The application receives an ordered stream rather than a file with an unexplained missing section.

This recovery has a cost: later bytes can wait behind missing earlier bytes. An interactive voice application may prefer to discard a late audio sample rather than delay later samples. That helps explain why many media systems use UDP-based transport, but it is not a universal rule for video or voice. The application chooses whether to retry, conceal loss, adjust its rate, or use another transport above UDP.

sections.title: Which application uses which transport, and why
sections.body:
Learn these ports with the services they identify. They recur in management, services, security, and troubleshooting tasks. This table describes conventional transports used in the course, not every registered or modern variant. On a real system, confirm the configured service and transport before writing a firewall rule.

| Service | Conventional transport and ports | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| FTP | TCP `21`; active data typically TCP `20` | Separate control/data connections; passive data uses a server-selected port |
| SSH / Telnet | TCP `22` / TCP `23` | Remote CLI; SSH protects the session, Telnet does not |
| SMTP | TCP `25` | Server-to-server mail transfer; useful TCP example |
| TACACS+ | TCP `49` | Device administration AAA |
| DNS | UDP **and** TCP `53` | Both transports support DNS queries |
| DHCPv4 | UDP `67` server, `68` client | Initial address discovery can be broadcast |
| TFTP | UDP `69` for the initial request | Server selects another transfer port for the exchange |
| HTTP / HTTPS | TCP `80` / TCP `443` | Conventional web traffic; HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP |
| NTP | UDP `123` | Time synchronization |
| SNMP | UDP `161` agent, `162` notification receiver | Management queries and notifications |
| Syslog | UDP `514` in the conventional UDP transport | Other transports exist; UDP itself does not acknowledge delivery |
| RADIUS | UDP `1812` authentication, `1813` accounting | Conventional AAA transport |

DNS needs particular care. Many small lookups use UDP, but TCP is a normal supported DNS transport, not something reserved exclusively for zone transfers. A resolver can retry over TCP after receiving a truncated UDP answer, and can use TCP for other queries. Do not apply a universal “anything over 512 bytes uses TCP” rule: DNS extensions support larger UDP messages. A policy permitting only UDP `53` can therefore break valid DNS operations.

FTP also needs two separate ideas. The control connection carries commands on TCP `21`; the data connection carries a directory listing or file. In active mode, the server traditionally initiates that data connection from TCP `20`. In passive mode, the client connects to a server-selected data port. Knowing only `20/21` is insufficient to explain why a login succeeds while a file transfer fails.

TFTP starts with a read or write request addressed to UDP `69`. The server responds from its chosen **transfer identifier**, carried as a UDP port, and the remaining exchange uses that port rather than continuously targeting `69`. TFTP messages add block numbers and acknowledgments. These are TFTP fields inside UDP's data, not evidence that UDP gained TCP's reliability features.

DHCP illustrates another use of UDP. During initial address acquisition, a client can send from `0.0.0.0:68` toward `255.255.255.255:67` before it has a usable address. Subsequent DHCP exchanges are not all broadcasts. Study the detailed sequence in the services chapter; here, recognize the server/client ports and the absence of a TCP opening.

sections.title: Reading the output
sections.body:
Read a transport exhibit in this order: protocol, addresses, ports, flags or state, then sequence details if needed. Establish which device initiated the connection before deciding whether a displayed port is local or remote. The following summary uses representative values for teaching; it is not a recording of the Packet Tracer lab.

```output Representative TCP exchange · absolute sequence numbers
Client 192.168.40.10:51514 -> Server 192.168.40.20:80  SYN      Seq=1000  Len=0  ← request to the listening port
Server 192.168.40.20:80 -> Client 192.168.40.10:51514  SYN,ACK  Seq=5000  Ack=1001  ← reverse ports; acknowledges client SYN
Client 192.168.40.10:51514 -> Server 192.168.40.20:80  ACK      Seq=1001  Ack=5001  ← completes the ordinary opening
Client 192.168.40.10:51514 -> Server 192.168.40.20:80  ACK      Seq=1001  Len=200  ← data occupies bytes 1001 through 1200
Server 192.168.40.20:80 -> Client 192.168.40.10:51514  ACK      Seq=5001  Ack=1201  ← next client byte expected
```

On Windows, `netstat -an` lists numeric endpoints, including listening sockets and active TCP connections. `LISTENING` means the local host has a listening endpoint; `ESTABLISHED` means a TCP connection is established. `TIME_WAIT` is a TCP closing state, not by itself a failure. UDP entries do not have the equivalent TCP state. Packet Tracer implements only part of a real operating system, so its display and supported switches can differ.

On an IOS router, `show tcp brief` describes connections in which the router itself is an endpoint, such as a management session. It is not a list of all TCP conversations merely routed through the device. This representative row identifies local port `22` and remote port `51522`; it is consistent with an SSH client connected to the router.

```output Representative R1# show tcp brief
TCB       Local Address          Foreign Address        (state)
6640A3C8  10.10.10.1.22          10.10.10.50.51522       ESTAB  ← ports follow the final dots; the router is the local endpoint
```

On a real Windows PC, PowerShell’s `Test-NetConnection 192.168.40.20 -Port 80` tests a TCP opening and reports `TcpTestSucceeded`. On supported IOS, `telnet 10.1.1.10 443` can similarly test TCP acceptance at an authorized lab target; it does not perform a useful HTTPS request or authenticate TLS. Packet Tracer support differs, so the lab uses its browser and PDU inspection as the primary tests.

For a failed website, compare three tests: ping the server address, browse to the address with the correct URL scheme, and browse to the name. Ping success provides evidence that ICMP echo traffic can make a round trip; it does not verify TCP, TLS, DNS, or HTTP. If address-based HTTP works but the name fails, investigate name resolution. If the TCP opening succeeds but the application fails afterwards, continue with application evidence rather than declaring the entire path healthy.

sections.title: Exam focus
sections.body:
- Compare TCP's reliable, ordered byte stream with UDP's datagrams and lack of built-in loss recovery.
- Separate transport behavior from features an application implements above it.
- Read both source and destination ports; replies reverse the endpoints.
- Explain SYN, SYN/ACK, ACK and simple next-byte acknowledgment calculations.
- Distinguish receive-window flow control from congestion control; advanced congestion mathematics is unnecessary here.
- Recognize the conventional service ports, particularly DNS's two transports and FTP/TFTP data-port behavior.
- Treat successful ping, a listening socket, an established TCP connection, and a successful application request as different evidence.

lab.title: Watch a TCP handshake and a UDP lookup in Simulation mode
lab.intro:
Build a local LAN, enable HTTP and DNS, and compare a TCP opening with a UDP query. Then disable one service and use separate tests to identify what still works. These are guided simulator observations, not a claim that a particular Packet Tracer release was manually tested; record the actual ports, sequence values, labels, and behavior shown by your installed version.

Practice revised September 2026. If you completed an earlier version, repeat the revised exercise and update its checkmarks.
lab.topology:
```diagram
{ "type": "topology", "title": "TCP and UDP on one subnet",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "A", "kind": "pc", "label": "PC-A", "sub": "192.168.40.10/24", "x": 2, "y": 3 },
    { "id": "S", "kind": "switch", "label": "SW1", "sub": "2960 · VLAN 1", "x": 6, "y": 3 },
    { "id": "V", "kind": "server", "label": "SRV1", "sub": "192.168.40.20/24", "x": 10, "y": 3 }
  ],
  "links": [
    { "from": "A", "to": "S", "fromLabel": "Fa0", "toLabel": "Fa0/1" },
    { "from": "S", "to": "V", "fromLabel": "Fa0/2", "toLabel": "Fa0" }
  ], "caption": "HTTP and DNS share one server address; ports and transport identify the requested service." }
```

| Device | Interface / peer | IP address / mask | DNS / gateway |
|---|---|---|---|
| PC-A | FastEthernet0 to SW1 Fa0/1 | `192.168.40.10`, `255.255.255.0` | DNS `192.168.40.20`; gateway blank |
| SRV1 | FastEthernet0 to SW1 Fa0/2 | `192.168.40.20`, `255.255.255.0` | DNS not needed; gateway blank |
| SW1 | Fa0/1 and Fa0/2 | No management address required | No routing required |

Use copper straight-through cables for both host-to-switch links. Start with new devices rather than a reused switch with unknown configuration. All traffic stays within one IPv4 subnet, so a router and default gateway are unnecessary. The `.test` names below are lab examples, not public sites.

steps.title: Prepare the single LAN
steps.body:
Place new devices and connect the ports in the table. On both endpoints, open **Desktop → IP Configuration**, select **Static**, and enter the address and mask. Enter PC-A's DNS server as shown. Leave the gateways blank because both endpoints are on the same subnet. The new switch's default access ports are sufficient; no switch management address or router configuration is part of this transport exercise.

On PC-A, open **Desktop → Command Prompt**:

```text
ipconfig /all
ping 192.168.40.20
```

Record the address, mask and DNS server. Wait for the links to forward and repeat an initial ping if necessary.

:::expected
The settings match the table and the repeated ping receives replies. This establishes an ICMP round trip for the test; it does not yet establish a working HTTP service. If repeated requests fail, check the cable endpoints, link state and two host addresses before investigating transport behavior.
:::

steps.title: Establish services and make predictions
steps.body:
On SRV1, open **Services → HTTP** and set **HTTP On**. Under **Services → DNS**, set **On** and add an A record named `www.lab.test` with address `192.168.40.20`. Click **Add** and confirm the record appears.

On PC-A, request `http://192.168.40.20` in **Desktop → Web Browser**, then run:

```text
nslookup www.lab.test
```

Finally browse to `http://www.lab.test`. Use HTTP explicitly; this exercise does not require HTTPS.

Before reading the expected result, write the conventional transport and server port for (a) this HTTP exchange and (b) a small DNS lookup. Predict whether the server reply uses a new client destination port or reverses the request endpoints.

:::expected
Both pages should load and the name should return the intended address. HTTP here uses TCP destination port 80. A small DNS lookup ordinarily uses UDP destination port 53, although real DNS also supports TCP. Replies reverse the relevant client/server endpoint pair; the actual client source port must be observed rather than guessed.
:::

steps.title: Inspect one TCP opening
steps.body:
Enter **Simulation** mode. In **Edit Filters**, select ARP, TCP, HTTP and DNS; also select UDP if your release lists it separately. Clear old events with **Reset Simulation**, which does not guarantee application or address-resolution caches are erased.

Close and reopen PC-A's browser and request `http://192.168.40.20`. Advance using **Capture/Forward** and inspect the TCP PDUs. Read source/destination IP, source/destination port and flags.

Use this worked row only as a format:

| Direction | Source endpoint | Destination endpoint | TCP flags |
|---|---|---|---|
| Illustrative request | `192.168.40.10:51000` | `192.168.40.20:80` | SYN |

Replace `51000` with the client port in your own exchange. Complete the server reply and client's next row yourself before comparing with the expected result. Record why the sequence-number field is not a port number.

:::expected
An ordinary opening shows client SYN, server SYN/ACK and client ACK. The server reply has source `192.168.40.20:80` and destination `192.168.40.10:<observed-client-port>`. The third segment returns to the server port. Sequence numbers identify positions in each direction's byte stream; ports identify transport endpoints.

A reused connection might show data without a new opening. Start a new connection or use this explicitly representative opening worksheet if the release cannot show one. Mark worksheet evidence separately from observed PDUs.
:::

steps.title: Compare a fresh UDP lookup
steps.body:
Add `lookup.lab.test` on SRV1 with the same correct address. Clear the Simulation event list and run `nslookup lookup.lab.test` on PC-A. Advance and inspect the DNS query and reply. A fresh name avoids assuming a particular cache-clearing command.

Complete two rows: query source/destination endpoints and reply source/destination endpoints. Then answer: where would you expect to find SYN, SYN/ACK and ACK in this UDP exchange?

:::expected
For the ordinary UDP query in this exercise, the destination is server port 53 and the reply's source is port 53. The other port is the client's observed query port. There is no UDP transport opening, so no TCP SYN sequence belongs to this exchange. A DNS response is application data carried in UDP; it does not mean UDP itself added acknowledgments or reliability.

If the simulator's client command is unavailable, request a newly added name in its browser and inspect the resulting DNS events. If your release cannot expose the fields, use this explicitly illustrative worksheet: PC-A sends UDP from 192.168.40.10:53000 to 192.168.40.20:53. Write the reply endpoints and state whether a transport opening is required. The answer is source 192.168.40.20:53 to destination 192.168.40.10:53000, with no UDP opening. Port 53000 is supplied for the worksheet, not claimed as the simulator’s chosen value. Record that limitation.
:::

steps.title: Interpret a new connection snapshot
steps.body:
Without referring to Step 3's completed rows, interpret this representative snapshot. It belongs to a different Windows PC and is a paper exercise, not claimed output from Packet Tracer.

```output Representative Windows netstat -an excerpt
Proto  Local Address         Foreign Address        State
TCP    10.6.0.10:22          10.6.0.30:52000        ESTABLISHED
TCP    10.6.0.10:52100       10.6.0.20:80           ESTABLISHED
TCP    10.6.0.10:52101       10.6.0.20:80           TIME_WAIT
```

The documented services are SSH on 22 and HTTP on 80. Identify the PC's server role, its client role and the number of currently established HTTP connections. State the reply endpoints for the established HTTP connection.

Optionally use `netstat` on PC-A if supported, or `netstat -an` on an authorized real Windows computer. A short HTTP connection may close before inspection. Do not count a missing row as proof that your earlier captured exchange never happened.

:::expected
The PC accepts SSH from `10.6.0.30:52000` at local port 22. It has one established HTTP connection from `10.6.0.10:52100` to `10.6.0.20:80`. The other HTTP row is closing, not established. The reply endpoints are source `10.6.0.20:80` to destination `10.6.0.10:52100`.
:::

steps.title: Observe a known service fault
steps.body:
Save the working project as `06-transport-baseline.pkt`. On SRV1, set **Services → HTTP → Off**. Keep DNS and addressing unchanged. This is a guided mechanism experiment: you know which setting changed.

Before testing, predict the outcome of ping, a fresh name lookup and a new address-based HTTP request. Add `faultcheck.lab.test` pointing to SRV1 for a fresh DNS name, then run:

```text
ping 192.168.40.20
nslookup faultcheck.lab.test
```

Open a new browser request to `http://192.168.40.20`. Do not rely on previously displayed page content. Record the actual response or lack of response; do not demand a particular reset or timeout string.

:::expected
ICMP and the fresh DNS lookup can still succeed while the new HTTP request fails. The known HTTP Off setting explains this controlled failure. Without that server evidence, ping success plus HTTP failure would justify checking transport and application evidence, not automatically diagnosing a stopped service. DNS and HTTP share a server IP but are separate services.
:::

steps.title: Restore and verify the original service
steps.body:
Set **SRV1 → Services → HTTP → On**. Start fresh browser requests to the address and to `http://www.lab.test`. Repeat the fresh name query if needed. Save the repaired project as `06-transport-complete.pkt` only after the intended service works.

:::expected
Both new HTTP requests load the page, and the name resolves to the intended server. The correction restores the actual failed service rather than merely producing another successful ping. No router, default gateway or switch configuration change was required.
:::

steps.title: Submit evidence and attempt the independent variation
steps.body:
Prepare a short record using the following rubric. Mark unavailable simulator checks as **worksheet** or **not yet observed**, not as passed.

| Evidence to submit | Satisfactory explanation |
|---|---|
| TCP three-row exchange | Correct directions, server port, observed client port and flags |
| UDP query/reply | Correct endpoint reversal; no invented UDP opening |
| New socket snapshot | Correct listening/client role and established count |
| Known fault and recovery | Predictions, actual tests, changed service and fresh application retest |
| Independent variation below | Your answer before the reference and any correction afterward |

Attempt the challenge before reading its expected box. A copied configuration or a checked step without an explanation is not the submission.

:::expected
Your record distinguishes address reachability, transport behavior, name resolution and useful application success. Errors are recorded with the corrected rule, not hidden by replacing the first answer.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- Repeated ping failure: inspect the two addresses/masks, cable ports and link state first.
- Address-based HTTP works but a fresh lookup fails: inspect the selected DNS server and record, then use the name again.
- No new TCP opening in the event list: check whether a previous connection is reused; clear events and initiate a new session.
- No DNS event for an old name: use a newly added name and inspect the query, rather than assuming Reset Simulation clears caches.
- A connection disappears before `netstat`: use the previously captured PDU evidence; the snapshot is not a traffic-history log.
- An unsupported client command: use the named GUI/Simulation alternative or the paper worksheet, and label the evidence accurately.
lab.challenge:
In a separate project copy, add Server-PT SRV2 to SW1 Fa0/3 using straight-through copper. Give it `192.168.40.30/24`, leave the gateway blank and turn **HTTP On**. On the original SRV1 DNS service, add `second.lab.test → 192.168.40.30`. Keep PC-A's DNS server at `192.168.40.20`.

Before generating traffic, predict the destination IP/port for the name lookup and the subsequent HTTP connection. Then test both, record the actual client ports, and explain why the two destination server addresses differ. Finally, on paper, give the cumulative ACK after in-order data beginning at sequence `8001` with length `1200` and no SYN/FIN.

:::solution
The DNS query goes to the configured resolver `192.168.40.20`, ordinarily UDP port 53 in this small lab query. Its answer identifies SRV2. The later HTTP connection goes to `192.168.40.30` TCP port 80, using a separately observed client port. The DNS server and requested application server need not be the same device.

If the address works but the name does not, verify SRV1's record and a fresh lookup; if the new server is unreachable by address, check its cable, address and HTTP setting independently. The data covers bytes `8001–9200`, so the next expected byte is `9201`. Save the variation separately, or remove SRV2 and its exact DNS record to return to the original baseline.
:::

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly compares the transport service supplied to an application?
options: TCP supplies an ordered byte stream; UDP supplies separate datagrams.
TCP preserves each application write; UDP combines writes into a byte stream.
TCP guarantees application success; UDP reports whether the service accepted data.
TCP encrypts its data by default; UDP relies on application encryption.
questions.explanation: TCP recovers and orders stream bytes, while UDP delivers individual datagrams without its own delivery guarantee. Application framing, security and successful processing remain separate concerns.

whyWrong.1: TCP does not preserve write boundaries, and UDP does not create a byte stream.
whyWrong.2: Transport delivery does not guarantee that an application completed its work.
whyWrong.3: Neither transport inherently encrypts the application data.

questions.prompt: Which comparison distinguishes TCP flow control from congestion control?
options: Flow control tracks network loss; congestion control advertises receiver space.
Flow control respects receiver capacity; congestion control responds to the path.
Flow control establishes a connection; congestion control closes each direction.
Flow control selects service ports; congestion control identifies application data.
questions.explanation: The advertised receive window limits data according to receiver capacity. Congestion control limits the sender in response to network-path conditions; the sender must respect both.

whyWrong.0: The receiver and network roles are reversed.
whyWrong.2: Connection opening and closing are different TCP functions.
whyWrong.3: Ports identify endpoints rather than controlling receiver capacity or network congestion.

questions.prompt: Which two services conventionally use TCP in this course? Choose two.
options: Initial DHCPv4 discovery
SMTP server-to-server mail transfer
NTP time synchronization
SSH remote management
questions.explanation: SMTP mail transfer conventionally uses TCP 25, and SSH uses TCP 22. DHCPv4 discovery and NTP are conventional UDP examples.

whyWrong.0: Initial DHCPv4 discovery uses UDP client/server ports 68 and 67.
whyWrong.2: NTP uses UDP 123 in the conventional exchange.

questions.prompt: Which two statements correctly describe ordinary DNS transport? Choose two.
options: DNS queries can use UDP destination port 53.
TCP port 53 is reserved exclusively for zone transfers.
DNS queries can use TCP destination port 53.
A UDP DNS query first establishes a UDP transport connection.
questions.explanation: DNS supports both UDP and TCP queries. Many small queries use UDP, while TCP can carry normal queries and retry after a truncated UDP response.

whyWrong.1: TCP also carries ordinary DNS queries; it is not exclusive to zone transfers.
whyWrong.3: UDP provides no transport connection-establishment handshake.

questions.prompt: Which endpoint interpretation follows from this TCP opening?
options: The server requests a service on TCP 51514 at 10.20.0.15.
The server listens on TCP 9000 and the client selects TCP 3000.
The client requests TCP 22 at 10.20.0.5 from local port 51514.
The client requests TCP 22 and receives replies on local port 22.
questions.explanation: The initial SYN goes from client port 51514 to server port 22. Replies reverse those endpoints; the displayed sequence numbers are not ports.

whyWrong.0: The initial SYN identifies the opposite initiator and destination service.
whyWrong.1: 9000 and 3000 are sequence numbers, not transport ports.
whyWrong.3: The server replies to the client-selected port 51514.

questions.prompt: A DHCPv4 client has no usable IPv4 address and begins discovery. Which initial transport exchange matches this task?
options: UDP source port 67 to destination port 68, sent by the new client.
TCP source port 68 to destination port 67, after a TCP opening.
UDP source port 68 to destination port 53, requesting its address.
UDP source port 68 to destination port 67, which can be broadcast.
questions.explanation: The initial client discovery uses UDP client port 68 toward server port 67. It can be sent before the client has a usable address, without a TCP opening.

whyWrong.0: The client/server port roles are reversed.
whyWrong.1: DHCPv4 uses UDP for this exchange, not TCP.
whyWrong.2: Port 53 identifies DNS, not DHCP address discovery.

questions.prompt: A client uses the same local IP address to open two separate simultaneous TCP connections to the same server address on TCP 443. Which difference distinguishes the two connections?
options: The server uses a different listening port for the second connection.
The client uses a different local source port for the second connection.
The client uses a different TCP protocol number for the second connection.
The server uses a different MAC address for the second connection.
questions.explanation: With the same client/server IP addresses and server port, distinct client source ports produce distinct TCP endpoint pairs. The server can serve many connections on one listening port.

whyWrong.0: Both connections can use the stated server port 443.
whyWrong.2: Both use TCP; its IP protocol identifier does not change per connection.
whyWrong.3: MAC addresses are not part of the transport connection identity.

exhibit.title: Representative application writes
exhibit.text:
Write 1: 200 bytes
Write 2: 300 bytes
Transport: TCP

questions.prompt: The application makes the writes shown. What must its receiving application assume?
options: It receives a byte stream and must use its message format to find boundaries.
It receives two messages whose boundaries match the two sending writes.
It receives a message boundary wherever the TCP PSH flag is present.
It receives one application message for each arriving TCP segment.
questions.explanation: TCP preserves byte order rather than the sender’s write boundaries. The application needs its own framing, such as a length or delimiter, to recognize messages.

whyWrong.1: Two writes need not become two separately delivered messages.
whyWrong.2: PSH does not define application-message boundaries.
whyWrong.3: A message may span segments, and a segment may contain several messages.

spec.title: Complete the TCP opening
spec.caption: No application data is included in the opening segments.

questions.prompt: The client has received the second segment. Which third segment completes this ordinary TCP opening?
options: Server to client: FIN, ending the server’s sending direction.
Client to server: SYN, starting another independent connection.
Server to client: ACK, acknowledging its own initial sequence.
Client to server: ACK, acknowledging the server’s SYN.
questions.explanation: After receiving SYN/ACK, the client acknowledges the server’s SYN. This completes the ordinary SYN, SYN/ACK, ACK opening shown.

whyWrong.0: FIN closes a sending direction rather than completing this opening.
whyWrong.1: Another SYN is not the expected third step in this ordinary opening.
whyWrong.2: The client must acknowledge the server’s SYN; the server cannot acknowledge it on the client’s behalf.

questions.prompt: A TCP data segment begins at sequence 20001 and contains 1460 bytes, with no SYN or FIN. All earlier bytes arrived in order and no later data is buffered. Which cumulative acknowledgment follows?
questions.explanation: The bytes occupy sequence positions 20001 through 21460. The acknowledgment identifies the next expected byte, 21461.

whyWrong.0: This ignores the newly received data.
whyWrong.2: This is the last received byte, not the next expected byte.
whyWrong.3: No SYN or FIN consumes an additional position in this segment.

exhibit.title: Representative Windows netstat -an excerpt
exhibit.text:
Proto  Local Address         Foreign Address        State
TCP    0.0.0.0:22            0.0.0.0:0              LISTENING
TCP    172.16.5.20:22        172.16.5.99:50210       ESTABLISHED
TCP    172.16.5.20:50344     198.51.100.10:443       ESTABLISHED
TCP    172.16.5.20:50351     198.51.100.10:443       TIME_WAIT

questions.prompt: SSH uses local TCP 22 and HTTPS uses remote TCP 443. Which reading of this snapshot is correct?
options: Two HTTPS connections are established, and the local host initiates SSH.
The local host has one SSH listener but no accepted SSH connection.
The local host serves HTTPS and connects outward from SSH port 22.
One SSH connection is accepted and one HTTPS connection is established.
questions.explanation: The local port-22 row is an accepted SSH connection. Only the port-50344 HTTPS row is ESTABLISHED; the other is closing in TIME_WAIT.

whyWrong.0: TIME_WAIT is not ESTABLISHED, and local port 22 is the server endpoint here.
whyWrong.1: The ESTABLISHED port-22 row shows a current accepted connection.
whyWrong.2: The local temporary HTTPS port is the client endpoint; the remote service port is 443.

questions.prompt: What does this client-side observation establish about the connection attempt?
options: The attempt received an active reset and did not complete a TCP opening.
The opening completed, but an established session then timed out.
The SYN was acknowledged normally and the client should send login data.
The request received no response before its retransmission timer expired.
questions.explanation: The matching RST/ACK actively rejects the attempt. A closed server port is possible, but this one capture does not prove whether the server or an intermediary generated the reset.

whyWrong.1: No SYN/ACK and final ACK are shown to establish a connection.
whyWrong.2: A reset is not the accepting SYN/ACK response.
whyWrong.3: The second segment is a response, so this is not simply silence.

exhibit.title: Representative receive state
exhibit.text:
1001–1100: received
1101–1200: missing
1201–1300: received and retained

questions.prompt: The receiver has all earlier bytes and retains the shown later range. Which cumulative acknowledgment stays in place, and when may it advance to 1301?
options: 1301 now; the arrival of the highest-numbered range proves all earlier bytes.
1201 now; only another copy of 1201–1300 allows the acknowledgment to advance.
1101 now; receiving the missing 1101–1200 range completes the contiguous data.
1001 now; every original segment must be received again in its original order.
questions.explanation: The cumulative acknowledgment cannot skip the missing middle range. Once that gap arrives, the retained later bytes complete the stream through 1300 and ACK can advance to 1301.

whyWrong.0: Later-byte arrival does not establish receipt of an earlier gap.
whyWrong.1: 1201 would incorrectly acknowledge the absent middle range.
whyWrong.3: The receiver already has the earlier and later ranges; they need not all be resent.

exhibit.title: Representative combined client evidence
exhibit.text:
Approved server: 192.168.40.20, HTTP on TCP 80
Fresh DNS answer www.lab.test: 192.168.40.20
Ping 192.168.40.20: replies received
TCP capture at client: SYN to 192.168.40.20:80; retry SYN; no reply seen
Fresh HTTP request: fails

questions.prompt: All tests are fresh and target the intended server. Which next investigation best fits the combined evidence?
options: Correct DNS first because the browser used a name rather than an address.
Correct the client subnet because TCP and ICMP require different gateways.
Check TCP 80 service and path evidence; ICMP success does not prove the opening.
Begin HTTP content diagnosis because a successful ping proves TCP acceptance.
questions.explanation: The correct name response and successful ICMP exchange narrow the problem, but the capture does not show a completed TCP opening. Check the listener and relevant transport-path evidence before attributing one unique cause or diagnosing HTTP content.

whyWrong.0: The shown name response already returns the approved server address.
whyWrong.1: The transport choice does not by itself imply a different gateway or wrong subnet.
whyWrong.3: A ping does not perform the required TCP opening, and none is shown.

cards.front: What is the central TCP-versus-UDP comparison?
cards.back: TCP supplies a reliable ordered byte stream. UDP sends separate datagrams without its own delivery, ordering, or retransmission guarantee.

cards.front: What identifies a transport flow?
cards.back: The five-tuple: transport protocol, source IP, source port, destination IP, and destination port. A socket is an application endpoint.

cards.front: A request is 10.6.0.10:51000 → 10.6.0.20:80. What are the reply endpoints?
cards.back: Source 10.6.0.20:80 → destination 10.6.0.10:51000, using the same transport. Source and destination swap.

cards.front: Two simultaneous TCP connections share both IPs and the server port. What differs?
cards.back: The client source ports differ, giving distinct TCP endpoint pairs. This assumes both connections use the same client IP, server IP and server listening port.

cards.front: TCP opening with client ISN 1000 and server ISN 5000?
cards.back: SYN seq 1000; SYN/ACK seq 5000 ack 1001; ACK seq 1001 ack 5001. Each SYN consumes one sequence number.

cards.front: How do TCP FIN and RST differ?
cards.back: FIN closes one sending direction in an orderly shutdown. RST resets an existing connection or rejects an attempt rather than performing that orderly close.

cards.front: What does cumulative TCP acknowledgment 1301 mean?
cards.back: All preceding stream bytes through 1300 have arrived without an earlier gap. Byte 1301 is next expected; this does not prove application processing.

cards.front: Does TCP preserve application-write or message boundaries?
cards.back: No. The application must define its message format within the byte stream. Neither a TCP segment boundary nor PSH is a message marker.

cards.front: TCP flow control versus congestion control?
cards.back: Flow control respects the receiver’s advertised capacity. Congestion control limits the sender according to conditions on the network path.

cards.front: Can an application use UDP and still recover lost data?
cards.back: Yes. The application can add numbering, acknowledgments, and retries, as TFTP does. UDP itself does not provide that recovery.

cards.front: Does a successful ping verify HTTP or HTTPS?
cards.back: No. ICMP echo success is round-trip reachability evidence; it does not verify DNS, a TCP port, TLS, or the web application.

cards.front: Which IANA port range is dynamic/private?
cards.back: 49152–65535. This registry category does not require every operating system to select ephemeral ports from that range.

cards.front: Which ports identify conventional SSH and Telnet?
cards.back: SSH uses TCP 22; Telnet uses TCP 23. SSH protects the management session; Telnet carries it without that protection.

cards.front: Conventional HTTP and HTTPS ports, and the HTTP/3 exception?
cards.back: HTTP commonly uses TCP 80 and HTTPS TCP 443. HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP, commonly UDP 443.

cards.front: Which transports does ordinary DNS support on port 53?
cards.back: UDP and TCP. Small lookups often use UDP; TCP also handles normal queries and retry after a truncated UDP response.

cards.front: What are the DHCPv4 client and server ports?
cards.back: UDP 68 is the client port; UDP 67 is the server port. Initial discovery can be broadcast; later exchanges are not all broadcasts.

cards.front: FTP control and data connections?
cards.back: Control uses TCP 21. Active data traditionally comes from server TCP 20; passive data uses a server-selected destination port.

cards.front: What does UDP port 69 mean in TFTP?
cards.back: It receives the initial read/write request. The server selects a transfer identifier port used for the remaining exchange.

commands.task: From a PC command prompt, send ICMP echo requests to 192.168.40.20.
commands.note: ICMP replies are reachability evidence, not a test of a TCP/UDP service.

commands.task: On Windows, display numeric TCP/UDP endpoints, including listening TCP sockets.
commands.note: LISTENING and ESTABLISHED are TCP states. This is a Windows command; simulator switches may differ.

commands.task: Resolve www.lab.test using the PC's configured DNS server.
commands.note: Inspect the returned address. A small query often uses UDP 53, but DNS also supports TCP.

commands.task: Display the PC's full IP settings before troubleshooting the lab connection.
commands.note: Compare address, mask, and DNS server with the addressing table.

commands.task: In Windows PowerShell, test whether a TCP connection to 192.168.40.20 port 80 succeeds.
commands.note: Read TcpTestSucceeded. Success alone does not establish that the HTTP page works; this is not a Packet Tracer PC command.

tickets.title: HTTP fails while ping and DNS still work
tickets.scenario: PC-A and SRV1 share a working VLAN and IPv4 subnet. A fresh HTTP request fails. The technician collects the following client and server observations; they are representative teaching evidence.

exhibits.title: PC-A test results
exhibits.text:
ping 192.168.40.20: replies received
nslookup www.lab.test: returns 192.168.40.20
Fresh request to http://192.168.40.20: fails
Fresh request to http://www.lab.test: fails

exhibits.title: SRV1 Services settings
exhibits.text:
HTTP: Off
DNS: On
A record www.lab.test: 192.168.40.20

tickets.question: Which diagnosis is directly supported by all the evidence?
options: The client needs a different default gateway for the HTTP service.
The name record points to a different host from the approved server.
The HTTP service is disabled while the other tested services still work.
A failed TCP opening is impossible because the ICMP round trip succeeds.
tickets.explanation: The server setting explicitly identifies HTTP Off, while the fresh lookup returns the approved address and ICMP replies. An incorrect gateway is not needed for this same-subnet exchange, and successful ICMP does not establish a TCP opening. Without the server-setting exhibit, the failed-browser symptom alone would not identify one cause.
tickets.fix: On SRV1, open Services → HTTP and set HTTP On. Start fresh requests to both http://192.168.40.20 and http://www.lab.test, verify that the page loads, then save the restored Packet Tracer topology. Do not change addressing or routing to repair a deliberately stopped service.

tickets.title: The server address works but its name does not
tickets.scenario: The isolated LAN contains PC-A at 192.168.40.10/24 and SRV1 at 192.168.40.20/24. No device uses 192.168.40.99. HTTP and DNS are enabled on SRV1, and its www.lab.test A record correctly points to 192.168.40.20. The technician checks a fresh browser request and the PC configuration.

exhibits.title: PC-A configured settings
exhibits.text:
IPv4 address: 192.168.40.10
Subnet mask: 255.255.255.0
DNS server: 192.168.40.99

exhibits.title: Observed tests
exhibits.text:
http://192.168.40.20: page loads
nslookup www.lab.test using configured DNS: fails
http://www.lab.test: name cannot be resolved

tickets.question: Which correction addresses the demonstrated cause?
options: Set PC-A’s DNS server to 192.168.40.20 and repeat the fresh lookup.
Replace the server’s correct A record with a pointer to 192.168.40.99.
Change SRV1’s HTTP port to 53 so that the browser can request the name.
Set a default gateway on PC-A before attempting its on-link DNS server.
tickets.explanation: The client sends name queries to an explicitly unused address, while direct-IP HTTP already works. Correct the selected resolver, then requery and repeat the original named request. Changing the valid A record or the HTTP port confuses separate services; a default gateway does not make the unused on-link resolver exist.
tickets.fix: Open PC-A Desktop → IP Configuration, change DNS Server to 192.168.40.20, and run nslookup www.lab.test. Confirm the returned address, open http://www.lab.test, and save the repaired topology. Leave the working server IP, subnet mask, and HTTP service unchanged.

chapters.title: Ethernet switching
chapters.subtitle: How source addresses build the MAC table and destination addresses determine forwarding.

sources.title: Cisco: Catalyst 2960 IOS 15.0(2)SE — Managing the MAC address table
Cisco: Unicast Flooding in Switched Campus Networks
Cisco: Catalyst 2960 — Configuring IGMP Snooping and MVR
Cisco: Configure Jumbo/Giant Frame Support on Catalyst Switches
