chapters.summary: Follow frames through a switched LAN, distinguish learning from forwarding, read the MAC address table, and investigate flooding, aging, and an incorrect static entry.

sections.body: When two computers communicate through a switch, the switch must decide which port should transmit each frame. It does not need a manually configured location for every computer. Instead, it builds a table by observing the source addresses of arriving frames. This chapter follows that process carefully, because the same reasoning explains normal forwarding, temporary flooding, and several common connectivity faults.

sections.title: Why a switch and not a hub
sections.body:
A **hub** repeats received signals to its other ports. Devices connected through the hub share one Ethernet medium and its available capacity. With half-duplex Ethernet, simultaneous transmissions can collide, and CSMA/CD manages contention and retransmission on that shared medium. Hubs are useful as a comparison, but modern wired access networks use switches.

A **switch** receives Ethernet frames and makes forwarding decisions. Each switched link can operate independently, and a correctly operating full-duplex point-to-point link has no collisions. A known unicast frame can go only toward its destination instead of being repeated to every attached computer. Total throughput still depends on link speeds, destination-port capacity, and the switch's hardware; full duplex does not remove every bottleneck.

:::facts
- A MAC address is **48 bits**, written as **12 hexadecimal digits**. The Ethernet broadcast destination is `ffff.ffff.ffff`.
- For normal dynamic learning, record the **source MAC**, **ingress port**, and **VLAN**. For forwarding, look up the **destination MAC in that VLAN**.
- Flood ordinary broadcast and unknown-unicast traffic to eligible forwarding ports in the same VLAN, excluding the ingress port.
- A MAC table maps **MAC + VLAN → port**. An IPv4 ARP table maps an on-link **IP address → MAC address**. They are separate tables.
- The documented default dynamic MAC aging time on the Catalyst 2960 IOS 15.0(2)SE used as the CLI reference is **300 seconds**. Verify the timer on the actual platform.
:::

The **MAC address table**, also called the forwarding or CAM table, is the starting point for this chapter. Basic Layer 2 forwarding uses that table rather than selecting an IP route. This does not mean a switch is incapable of inspecting IP information: switches may support ACLs, QoS, or Layer 3 routing. Here, we isolate ordinary bridging within a VLAN so that the learning process is clear.

sections.title: Anatomy of an Ethernet frame
sections.body:
An **Ethernet frame** carries a destination address, a source address, information identifying the payload, the payload itself, and an error-detection trailer. In ordinary Ethernet II, the **EtherType** identifies the payload protocol. For example, `0x0800` identifies IPv4, `0x0806` identifies ARP, and `0x86DD` identifies IPv6. The receiving protocol stack uses that distinction; the basic MAC lookup still concerns the destination MAC and VLAN.

| Field in an untagged Ethernet II frame | Size (bytes) | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Destination MAC | `6` | Identifies the intended recipient or group |
| Source MAC | `6` | Identifies the sender on this Ethernet link; used for learning |
| EtherType | `2` | Identifies the payload protocol |
| Data and any padding | `46–1500` for the basic frame described here | Carries the packet or other payload |
| Frame check sequence | `4` | Detects corruption using a CRC |

```diagram
{ "type": "bits", "title": "Fig 7.1 — Basic untagged Ethernet II frame",
  "fields": [
    { "label": "Destination MAC", "bits": 48, "note": "6 bytes · forwarding lookup", "highlight": true },
    { "label": "Source MAC", "bits": 48, "note": "6 bytes · learning", "highlight": true },
    { "label": "Type", "bits": 16, "note": "2 bytes" },
    { "label": "Data + padding", "bits": 368, "note": "minimum 46 bytes illustrated" },
    { "label": "FCS", "bits": 32, "note": "4 bytes · error detection" }
  ], "caption": "The 64-byte minimum includes destination MAC through FCS; preamble, start delimiter, and interframe gap are excluded." }
```

For the basic untagged frame with a 1500-byte maximum payload, the frame length is **64–1518 bytes**, measured from destination MAC through FCS. The physical transmission also uses a preamble and start frame delimiter, which are outside that count; an interframe gap is not payload or a frame field. A typical capture may omit the FCS, so its reported length need not equal the complete on-wire frame length. Always establish what a measurement includes before diagnosing a size error.

An ARP message provides a simple calculation. A 28-byte ARP message needs padding to reach the 46-byte minimum data area in this untagged frame. Add 14 bytes of header and 4 bytes of FCS: `14 + 46 + 4 = 64`. The **MTU** refers to the maximum Layer 3 packet size carried without fragmentation on that link, not the total frame including Ethernet header and trailer.

The **frame check sequence**, or FCS, contains a cyclic redundancy check calculated by the sender. A receiver can use it to detect corruption; it does not repair damaged bits. A store-and-forward switch checks the complete frame and discards one that fails that check. Recovery, if any, comes from another mechanism such as TCP or application retry, not from the FCS itself.

:::note Frame size depends on the framing and platform
An 802.1Q VLAN tag adds four bytes of tagging information, allowing a 1522-byte tagged frame with the same 1500-byte payload. Platforms may also support larger frames. A giant/error counter must be interpreted against the interface's supported size and configuration; “anything over 1518 is always bad” is incorrect. Small-frame and CRC counters also need context rather than an automatic diagnosis of collisions.
:::

sections.title: MAC addresses: OUI, unicast, multicast, broadcast
sections.body:
A MAC address such as `0050.56be.1a2b` can also be written as `00:50:56:be:1a:2b` or `00-50-56-BE-1A-2B`. The punctuation and capitalization change the presentation, not the value. Record the complete address when matching a host to a table entry. Similar-looking suffixes are not enough to identify the correct computer.

A **unicast** address identifies an individual interface; a **multicast** address identifies a group. The all-ones **broadcast** address, `ffff.ffff.ffff`, addresses the broadcast domain. In the first octet, the least-significant bit is the individual/group bit: a set bit indicates a group address. Thus `01` as the first octet indicates a group, while `00` indicates an individual address. Valid ordinary Ethernet source addresses are individual addresses, so switches do not dynamically learn a broadcast destination as a host source.

An **organizationally unique identifier**, or OUI, is a registered organizational prefix. The familiar manufacturer allocation uses a 24-bit OUI followed by an organization-assigned portion, but the IEEE also supplies other allocation sizes. **Locally administered** addresses can be assigned by software, including virtual systems and address-randomization features. An OUI lookup can be a useful clue; it is not proof of the physical manufacturer, device type, ownership, or trustworthiness.

| Destination type | Example | Forwarding consideration |
|---|---|---|
| Individual unicast | `0050.56be.1a2b` | Look up that MAC within the VLAN |
| Broadcast | `ffff.ffff.ffff` | Flood to eligible forwarding ports in the VLAN |
| IPv4 multicast | `0100.5e01.0203` | Multicast forwarding state can restrict delivery |
| Link-local bridge group | `0180.c200.0000` | Reserved control traffic has special bridge handling |

Do not treat all multicast as ordinary unknown unicast. **IGMP snooping** can use receiver-membership information to restrict IPv4 multicast delivery. Reserved link-local group addresses, including the standard spanning-tree bridge group, are handled specially rather than blindly relayed like a user broadcast. For introductory forwarding questions, read the stated assumptions about multicast, forwarding state, and policy.

sections.title: Learn, forward, filter, flood
sections.body:
A switch makes two separate decisions when a valid frame is eligible for ordinary bridging. First, it learns or refreshes the **source** address on the ingress port in the frame's VLAN. Second, it looks up the **destination** in that VLAN. The fact that a sender is new does not require flooding if the destination is already known.

| Operation | Condition | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Learn or refresh | Valid source received with learning enabled | Associate source MAC and VLAN with ingress port |
| Forward known unicast | Destination is on another forwarding port | Send toward that port |
| Filter same-port traffic | Destination is known through the ingress port | Do not send it back onto the same segment |
| Flood unknown unicast | No destination entry in this VLAN | Send copies to eligible forwarding ports except ingress |
| Flood ordinary broadcast | Destination is Ethernet broadcast | Send copies within the VLAN, subject to port state and policy |

Imagine PC-A on `Fa0/1`, PC-B on `Fa0/2`, and PC-C on `Fa0/3`, all in VLAN 1. All three ports are up and forwarding, no filtering policy is configured, and both the host ARP caches and switch's dynamic table start empty. PC-A knows PC-B's IPv4 address from the ping command but must first obtain its MAC address. Follow the sequence below without skipping the source-learning decision.

| Frame arriving at the switch | Source learned | Destination decision | Egress ports |
|---|---|---|---|
| A's ARP request to broadcast | A on `Fa0/1` | Broadcast | `Fa0/2`, `Fa0/3` |
| B's ARP reply to A | B on `Fa0/2` | A already known | `Fa0/1` |
| A's ICMP echo request to B | Refresh A | B known | `Fa0/2` |
| B's ICMP echo reply to A | Refresh B | A known | `Fa0/1` |

PC-C receives the broadcast but does not answer an ordinary ARP request for PC-B's address. Merely receiving a frame does not put C into the switch's dynamic table: the switch needs to see a frame with C as its source. The ARP reply is already known unicast because the preceding request taught the switch where A is. There is no requirement to flood the first reply simply because B is a newly observed sender.

Now clear the switch's dynamic entries while A retains B's mapping in its ARP cache. A can immediately construct a unicast Ethernet frame addressed to B, without sending ARP again. The switch has no destination entry for B, so it floods that **unknown unicast** to B's and C's eligible ports. B's reply teaches B's location again, after which the next request can use known-unicast forwarding.

:::trap Flooding does not rewrite the destination
An unknown-unicast frame keeps its original unicast destination MAC. Flooding describes the switch making copies, not the sender addressing a broadcast. In ordinary host operation, C rejects the copy addressed to B. Exclude the ingress port, other VLANs, down ports, and ports not forwarding for this VLAN when listing flood destinations.
:::

A single switch port can lead to many hosts. If B and C sit behind a second switch reached through `Fa0/24`, the first switch can learn both addresses on `Fa0/24`. That entry means “the path toward this address,” not “the address is physically plugged into this port.” If a frame arrives from that segment for another address already known through the same ingress port, the switch filters it instead of sending it back.

sections.title: Aging, static entries and the table commands
sections.body:
**Dynamic** entries are learned from traffic and can age out after inactivity. Seeing frames from a source refreshes its learned location. Traffic merely addressed to a host does not demonstrate where that host is currently attached. This explains how a quiet destination can disappear from the dynamic table even while another device keeps sending traffic toward it.

The Catalyst 2960 IOS reference for this chapter documents a **300-second** default aging timer. Other platforms and configurations can differ. Aging is not the only way an entry can change: a new source frame on a different port can update a dynamic location, and interface events, topology changes, or an administrator can remove entries. Do not wait for the timer to expire before expecting a legitimate host move to be learned.

Use privileged EXEC mode to examine the table before changing it. The first command displays all entries; the filtered commands answer narrower questions. Keyword support differs among simulators and IOS releases, so use the full table if a display filter is unavailable. These commands inspect existing state; they do not send traffic from the host you are looking for.

```ios SW1
SW1# show mac address-table
SW1# show mac address-table dynamic
SW1# show mac address-table address 0050.56be.1a2b
SW1# show mac address-table interface fastethernet0/24
SW1# show mac address-table vlan 10
SW1# show mac address-table aging-time
```

A **static entry** explicitly associates an address and VLAN with an interface. It does not age like an ordinary dynamic entry and survives a dynamic-table clear. A wrongly placed static entry can therefore keep sending destination traffic toward the wrong port. Static entry configuration is a useful controlled lab demonstration; ordinary access-switch hosts normally rely on dynamic learning.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# mac address-table aging-time 600
SW1(config)# mac address-table static 0050.56be.1a2b vlan 10 interface fastethernet0/5
SW1(config)# end
SW1# show mac address-table
```

The snippet demonstrates syntax, not a complete VLAN 10 topology. In the lab you will use the actual host MAC and the existing VLAN 1 ports, then remove the change. `clear mac address-table dynamic` removes learned entries; it does not remove a configured static entry. Use the matching `no mac address-table static ...` command for that configuration and verify the result before saving.

sections.title: Switching methods and domains
sections.body:
**Store-and-forward** switching receives the complete frame before forwarding it and can check the FCS first. **Cut-through** forwarding can begin after sufficient header information arrives, before the whole frame and FCS have arrived. It therefore cannot wait for the complete frame's FCS result before that initial forwarding. Specific switches may use different behavior depending on their architecture, ports, or operating conditions; do not infer a universal forwarding method from the Catalyst or Nexus family name alone.

The practical distinction is error checking before initial transmission versus starting earlier. Both approaches still need destination forwarding information. Neither means every received frame is copied to every port. Exact hardware latency, historical fragment-free switching, and internal ASIC behavior are outside this chapter's CCNA foundation.

A **collision domain** describes a shared area in which half-duplex transmissions can contend. Each switch port separates that area from the other ports; a hub and the devices attached through it share one. On a full-duplex link, collisions do not occur even though introductory diagrams still count the link as a separate collision domain. Do not confuse this diagram convention with a prediction that the link will suffer collisions.

A **broadcast domain** is the Layer 2 scope of ordinary broadcast delivery. One VLAN can span several switches without creating a new broadcast domain at each switch. Different VLANs are separate broadcast domains, and routing is needed for IP communication between them. In a simple diagram with one router interface in each of two separate LANs, count two broadcast domains; more elaborate routed subinterfaces and bridging require examining the actual configuration.

sections.title: Why VLANs and spanning tree exist
sections.body:
A **VLAN** keeps a group of switch ports in its own logical Layer 2 domain. A broadcast received in VLAN 10 is not simply copied into VLAN 20. VLAN membership is therefore part of every forwarding example, even before you learn to configure trunks. The same numerical MAC value can have separate forwarding entries in different VLANs.

Redundant Layer 2 paths create another problem. An ordinary Ethernet frame has no hop-count field equivalent to IP TTL to stop its circulation through a bridging loop. Flooded traffic can travel around the loop repeatedly, consume capacity, and make source locations appear to move between ports. **Spanning Tree Protocol** establishes a loop-free forwarding topology while retaining redundant physical links for recovery.

This is why a connected port is not automatically an eligible flood destination. A port that is not forwarding for the VLAN must be excluded. The later spanning-tree chapter teaches roles, states, and convergence; do not deliberately build an unprotected loop to test this foundation. Frequent MAC moves warrant investigation, but can also involve duplicate addressing or other topology behavior rather than proving one particular cause.

sections.title: Reading the output
sections.body:
Read the VLAN column first, then the MAC, entry type, and port. The following output is representative: the values illustrate a topology, and actual host MACs, reserved entries, totals, and formatting vary. PC-A is directly attached to `Fa0/1`; B and C are reached through the second switch on `Fa0/24`. Multiple distinct MACs on that uplink are expected.

```output Representative SW1# show mac address-table
          Mac Address Table
-------------------------------------------
Vlan    Mac Address       Type        Ports
----    -----------       --------    -----
   1    00aa.aaaa.aaaa    DYNAMIC     Fa0/1   ← PC-A has transmitted on this link
   1    00bb.bbbb.bbbb    DYNAMIC     Fa0/24  ← path toward PC-B, behind another switch
   1    00cc.cccc.cccc    DYNAMIC     Fa0/24  ← PC-C shares the uplink, not B's address
  10    0050.56be.1a2b    STATIC      Fa0/5   ← configured entry in a different VLAN
```

To investigate a missing host, first verify its link and VLAN, then generate traffic from that host and inspect the table again. If the address appears on an uplink, continue to the next switch; do not assume it is directly connected. If replies head toward an unexpected port, check whether the entry is static, whether the host moved, and whether the same source is appearing elsewhere. One table snapshot provides a location observation, not a complete diagnosis.

Keep **ARP** and switching evidence separate. A host uses ARP to find the MAC for an on-link IPv4 next hop; the switch uses its MAC table to select an egress port. Clearing the host's ARP cache does not directly clear the switch's MAC entries, and clearing the switch table does not clear the host's ARP cache. A switch may also have an ARP table for its own IP functions, which remains distinct from its bridging table.

sections.title: Exam focus
sections.body:
- Learn from source MAC, ingress port, and VLAN; forward using destination MAC in that VLAN.
- Work through initial ARP and ping traffic one frame at a time, updating the table after each source is observed.
- Distinguish known unicast, unknown unicast, and broadcast; apply VLAN, ingress-port, and forwarding-state exclusions.
- Recognize multicast forwarding and reserved-control-traffic exceptions to a simple flooding rule.
- Explain dynamic aging, source refresh, static entries, and why multiple MACs on one uplink are normal.
- Read `show mac address-table` and distinguish it from a host or router ARP table.
- Explain FCS as error detection, frame-length counting scope, VLAN broadcast domains, and the reason spanning tree prevents loops.

lab.title: Watch a switch learn, flood and forget
lab.intro:
Build a small LAN and follow the switch's table as hosts transmit. Separate host ARP state from switch MAC state, then move two hosts behind another switch and diagnose a deliberately incorrect static entry. Output below is representative teaching output, not a record of an executed Packet Tracer session; use the MAC addresses and supported commands shown by your installed version.

Practice revised September 2026. If you completed an earlier version, repeat the revised exercise and update its checkmarks.
lab.topology:
```diagram
{ "type": "topology", "title": "Initial topology: one switch and three PCs",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "A", "kind": "pc", "label": "PC-A", "sub": "192.168.90.10/24", "x": 2, "y": 1 },
    { "id": "B", "kind": "pc", "label": "PC-B", "sub": "192.168.90.20/24", "x": 2, "y": 5 },
    { "id": "S1", "kind": "switch", "label": "S1", "sub": "2960 · VLAN 1", "x": 6, "y": 3 },
    { "id": "C", "kind": "pc", "label": "PC-C", "sub": "192.168.90.30/24", "x": 10, "y": 3 }
  ],
  "links": [
    { "from": "A", "to": "S1", "fromLabel": "Fa0", "toLabel": "Fa0/1" },
    { "from": "B", "to": "S1", "fromLabel": "Fa0", "toLabel": "Fa0/2" },
    { "from": "S1", "to": "C", "fromLabel": "Fa0/3", "toLabel": "Fa0" }
  ], "caption": "All three hosts initially use VLAN 1 on S1; S2 is added in Step 7." }
```

| Host | IPv4 / mask | Initial port | Port after Step 7 |
|---|---|---|---|
| PC-A FastEthernet0 | `192.168.90.10 / 255.255.255.0` | S1 Fa0/1 | S1 Fa0/1 |
| PC-B FastEthernet0 | `192.168.90.20 / 255.255.255.0` | S1 Fa0/2 | S2 Fa0/2 |
| PC-C FastEthernet0 | `192.168.90.30 / 255.255.255.0` | S1 Fa0/3 | S2 Fa0/3 |
| Switch link added in Step 7 | No IP address | Not connected | S1 Fa0/24 ↔ S2 Fa0/24 |

Use straight-through copper for PCs. Use copper crossover or Packet Tracer's automatic connection tool for the switch-to-switch link. No host needs a default gateway or DNS server because the entire exercise stays in one subnet. Begin with new switches; do not add a second inter-switch link, which would introduce a spanning-tree exercise beyond this lab.

steps.title: Cable, address and record the MAC addresses
steps.body:
Create S1 and the three PCs, connect their initial ports, and set each static address under **Desktop → IP Configuration**. Open each PC's **Desktop → Command Prompt** and record its physical/MAC address alongside its name and IP:

```text Each PC
ipconfig /all
```

The interface-range and switchport commands below are supplied setup for one VLAN: they select several ports, make them ordinary access ports in VLAN 1, and enable them. You are not yet expected to design a VLAN configuration independently; Chapter 09 teaches that work.

On S1, decline an initial setup dialog if offered, enter the CLI, and configure the host ports explicitly:

```ios S1
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname S1
S1(config)# interface range fastethernet0/1 - 3
S1(config-if-range)# switchport mode access
S1(config-if-range)# switchport access vlan 1
S1(config-if-range)# no shutdown
S1(config-if-range)# end
S1# show interfaces status
S1# show vlan brief
```

:::expected
The selected ports belong to VLAN 1 and the cabled links become operational. Wait until the ports are forwarding before beginning captures. Record real MAC values from your PCs; the sample addresses used later are illustrations. Link initialization can take time, but no exact color-change timer is a success criterion.
:::

steps.title: Start from an empty table
steps.body:
Before generating test traffic, inspect and clear S1's dynamic table. This clears learned forwarding state on the switch, not the PCs' ARP caches. Do not clear or change configuration on any other device.

```ios S1
S1# show mac address-table
S1# clear mac address-table dynamic
S1# show mac address-table
```

:::expected
The dynamic host entries have been removed. Reserved/static rows can differ by platform and simulator; do not require a completely blank display. If a host transmits background traffic, a dynamic row can reappear immediately. Identify it by the source MAC you recorded and clear again just before the next controlled test if necessary.
:::

steps.title: One ping, one frame at a time
steps.body:
Before advancing a frame, write its source, destination, expected learned row and expected egress ports. Use the first ARP request as your worked example; predict the reply before clicking Capture/Forward again.


Enter **Simulation** mode and use **Edit Filters** to select ARP and ICMP. On PC-A, inspect `arp -a`; because this is a fresh topology, PC-B's mapping should be absent. If it is already present, restart with a fresh PC or clear that PC's ARP cache using its supported command (`arp -d` in versions that support it), and verify absence with `arp -a`. Clear S1's dynamic table again after any preparatory traffic.

Start the ping on PC-A and use **Capture/Forward** to follow events:

```text PC-A
ping 192.168.90.20
```

After the ARP request reaches S1, pause and inspect the table. Continue through the reply and inspect again. Return to Realtime mode to finish any remaining ping events.

```ios S1
S1# show mac address-table
```

:::expected
The ARP request teaches A on Fa0/1 and is flooded to Fa0/2 and Fa0/3. B replies; the source teaches B on Fa0/2, and the reply is forwarded only to A's known port. Subsequent ICMP request/reply frames use the learned ports. PC-C does not answer an ARP request for B's address, so receiving that request alone does not teach C's MAC.

Representative host rows after A and B communicate:
```output Representative S1# show mac address-table
Vlan    Mac Address       Type        Ports
----    -----------       --------    -----
   1    00aa.aaaa.aaaa    DYNAMIC     Fa0/1  ← use PC-A's actual recorded MAC
   1    00bb.bbbb.bbbb    DYNAMIC     Fa0/2  ← learned from B's source traffic
```
:::

steps.title: Bring PC-C into the table
steps.body:
From PC-A, ping C and then display the table. A successful reply requires C to transmit, providing a source from which the switch can learn.

```text PC-A
ping 192.168.90.30
```

```ios S1
S1# show mac address-table
S1# show mac address-table count
```

:::expected
C appears as a dynamic address on Fa0/3, and A and B may remain if their entries have not aged out. Count the three recorded host addresses rather than assuming all table rows are host rows. If `count` is unsupported, the plain display is sufficient; it is the MAC-to-port mapping that proves the result.
:::

steps.title: Prove unknown-unicast flooding
steps.body:
In Realtime mode, ping B once to refresh A's ARP entry, then use `arp -a` on A to confirm that `192.168.90.20` maps to B's recorded MAC. Clear only S1's dynamic table immediately before the next ping. Do not clear A's ARP cache.

```ios S1
S1# clear mac address-table dynamic
S1# show mac address-table
```

Switch to Simulation mode, clear old events, and start another ping from A to B. Inspect the first ICMP frame's Ethernet destination and the switch's outgoing copies. Then continue through B's reply and a second request.

```text PC-A
ping 192.168.90.20
```

:::expected
A already knows B's MAC, so it can send an ICMP frame addressed to that unicast MAC without a new ARP exchange. S1 learns A but does not know B's location; the first request is copied to both Fa0/2 and Fa0/3. Its destination remains B's unicast MAC. B's reply teaches B, allowing the following request to use Fa0/2 alone. If you instead observe ARP first, refresh A's mapping and repeat: the ARP reply would teach B before the ICMP request, defeating this demonstration.
:::

steps.title: Explain aging from source evidence
steps.body:
Inspect the currently configured timer if your image supports this command:

```ios S1
S1# show mac address-table aging-time
```

The following is a paper experiment, so no timer change or several-minute wait is required. Complete the last row before reading the answer.

| Time | Event on an otherwise quiet VLAN 1 |
|---|---|
| 0 s | S1 receives a frame sourced by B and learns B dynamically |
| 200 s | A sends a frame to B; B sends no response or other frame |
| 301 s | Inspect B's entry, with the dynamic aging interval explicitly set to 300 s |

Explain whether the frame **to** B refreshed B's entry. Then compare a static B entry with the dynamic one. If you choose to observe real aging, record your image's timer and all actual source traffic; do not assume the worksheet guarantees a simulator timing result.

:::expected
The frame from A refreshes A, not B. In this stated worksheet, B supplies no source frame after time 0, so its dynamic entry is eligible to age out after the configured interval. A configured static entry is different: it does not age and is not removed by clearing dynamic state. Unsupported timer displays can be replaced by this explicitly labeled worksheet.
:::

steps.title: Add a second switch and watch one port learn two MACs
steps.body:
Reuse the supplied one-VLAN setup pattern from Step 1; the learning task is the MAC path across the link.

Add a new 2960 named S2. Connect S1 Fa0/24 to S2 Fa0/24, then move B to S2 Fa0/2 and C to S2 Fa0/3. Keep A on S1 Fa0/1. Both ends of the inter-switch link are deliberately access ports in VLAN 1; this exercise carries one VLAN and does not require a trunk.

```ios S1
S1# configure terminal
S1(config)# interface fastethernet0/24
S1(config-if)# switchport mode access
S1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 1
S1(config-if)# no shutdown
S1(config-if)# end
```

```ios S2
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname S2
S2(config)# interface range fastethernet0/2 - 3
S2(config-if-range)# switchport mode access
S2(config-if-range)# switchport access vlan 1
S2(config-if-range)# no shutdown
S2(config-if-range)# exit
S2(config)# interface fastethernet0/24
S2(config-if)# switchport mode access
S2(config-if)# switchport access vlan 1
S2(config-if)# no shutdown
S2(config-if)# end
S2# show interfaces status
```

Wait for the links to forward. Clear dynamic entries on each switch, ping B and C from A in Realtime mode, and inspect both tables immediately afterwards. If a dynamic entry ages out while you work, repeat the relevant ping.

```ios S1
S1# clear mac address-table dynamic
```

```ios S2
S2# clear mac address-table dynamic
```

```text PC-A
ping 192.168.90.20
ping 192.168.90.30
```

```ios S1
S1# show mac address-table
```

```ios S2
S2# show mac address-table
```

:::expected
S1 reaches B and C through Fa0/24, so their two different MACs appear on that one port. A is learned DYNAMIC on S1 Fa0/1. S2 learns A through its Fa0/24, B on Fa0/2, and C on Fa0/3. Check the three known host addresses rather than predicting every control-plane entry the simulator may show.
:::

steps.title: Predict a source move and preserve the baseline
steps.body:
You now have A on S1 and B/C behind S2. Before generating more traffic, answer this on paper: if B broadcasts an ARP request for C and C returns a unicast reply, which switch sees each source? Assume both dynamic tables begin empty and no other host transmits.

Then perform a separate source-move experiment. Configure an additional port, using S1's console:

```ios S1
S1# configure terminal
S1(config)# interface fastethernet0/4
S1(config-if)# switchport mode access
S1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 1
S1(config-if)# no shutdown
S1(config-if)# end
```

Keep A's address and MAC unchanged. Move its cable from S1 Fa0/1 to Fa0/4, wait for forwarding, and **predict** the learned port before A pings B. After A transmits, inspect `show mac address-table`. Explain whether you needed to clear A's ARP cache or wait for the previous MAC timer.

Restore A's cable to Fa0/1, wait for forwarding, ping B and C, and inspect the learned path again. Save only the restored layout:

```ios S1
S1# copy running-config startup-config
```

```ios S2
S2# copy running-config startup-config
```

Press Enter at each destination-filename prompt. Save `07-switching-baseline.pkt`.

:::expected
For the paper exchange, S2 sees B on Fa0/2 and S1 sees B through Fa0/24 because the broadcast crosses the uplink. C's reply goes directly from S2 Fa0/3 to its known B port, so S1 does not learn C from that reply.

For the live move, A's first new source frame updates its dynamic entry to Fa0/4. Correct host ARP information can remain; the switch learns a new physical path for the same source MAC. After the explicit restoration and new source traffic, A should be learned on Fa0/1 again. Record actual table rows and any simulator limitation separately.
:::

steps.title: Introduce one incorrect static entry
steps.body:
In this isolated lab only, point B's MAC at S1 Fa0/1, which actually leads to A. Substitute **B's actual MAC for `00bb.bbbb.bbbb`**. This is one deliberate change; do not change addresses, cabling, or VLANs.

```ios S1
S1# configure terminal
S1(config)# mac address-table static 00bb.bbbb.bbbb vlan 1 interface fastethernet0/1
S1(config)# end
S1# show mac address-table
S1# clear mac address-table dynamic
S1# show mac address-table
```

From A, retry a ping to B and then to C. If supported, inspect B's unicast request in Simulation mode after address resolution. Read the STATIC row before attempting any repair.

```text PC-A
ping 192.168.90.20
ping 192.168.90.30
```

:::expected
Traffic for B is directed by the incorrect static row. In particular, a B-destined unicast frame arriving from A on Fa0/1 has a destination mapped to that same ingress port, so S1 filters it rather than forwarding toward S2. A-to-B ping fails while A-to-C can still work. Clearing dynamic entries does not remove this fault because the offending entry is static. If the simulator rejects static configuration, use this as a paper diagnosis from the displayed command rather than claiming to have reproduced the failure.
:::

steps.title: Recover the fault and confirm the baseline
steps.body:
Remove only the B static entry created in Step 9. Substitute B’s actual recorded MAC for 00bb.bbbb.bbbb in the removal command, exactly as you did when creating the fault. Generate traffic again to relearn the correct path and verify both hosts. Do not save until the correct behavior has returned.

```ios S1
S1# configure terminal
S1(config)# no mac address-table static 00bb.bbbb.bbbb vlan 1 interface fastethernet0/1
S1(config)# end
S1# clear mac address-table dynamic
```

```text PC-A
ping 192.168.90.20
ping 192.168.90.30
```

```ios S1
S1# show mac address-table
S1# copy running-config startup-config
```

:::expected
B is learned dynamically through Fa0/24, both pings succeed, and the wrong static row is absent. Accept the destination filename prompt when saving the device. Save the repaired topology as `switching-lab.pkt`. Your notes should connect the symptom, incorrect entry, failed dynamic clear, precise removal, and successful retest.
:::



Before saving completion, submit the following evidence. State whether each part was observed or completed from a supplied worksheet.

| Skill | Required evidence |
|---|---|
| Learning versus lookup | Identify the source that was learned and the destination that selected egress |
| Unknown unicast | Show a unicast destination, missing switch entry and eligible egress set |
| Host state versus switch state | Explain why a retained ARP mapping can coexist with an empty MAC table |
| Two-switch path | Give the MAC/port rows on both switches and explain any absent source |
| Source movement | Show the updated location after the host transmits |
| Fault and repair | Identify the static row, remove that exact entry, and verify correct relearning |

The fault in Step 9 was deliberately known. The challenge below is your independent prediction: write the result before consulting its answer key.

lab.troubleshooting:
- **Host absent from the MAC table:** verify the link and VLAN, generate traffic from that host, then inspect promptly. Merely connecting or receiving is insufficient evidence of learning.
- **ARP appears before the intended unknown-unicast test:** A lacks a current mapping for B; refresh ARP, clear only S1's dynamic entries, and repeat immediately.
- **Multiple hosts appear on Fa0/24:** compare with the final topology; this is expected for B and C behind S2.
- **Aging or a display keyword is unsupported:** record the simulator limitation; use the full table and controlled dynamic clear. CML images also differ, so do not assume every virtual image implements every hardware command.
- **Failure persists after clearing dynamic entries:** check for the deliberately configured STATIC row and remove its exact configuration.
- **Ping fails after moving cables:** check final port assignments, VLAN 1 on both inter-switch ends, and forwarding state. Do not add a second switch link to troubleshoot the first.
lab.challenge:
Work in a separate copy of the restored two-switch project. Before moving anything, have B ping C and verify that B knows C's actual MAC with `arp -a`. Move C from S2 Fa0/3 to **S1 Fa0/5**, leaving its IP and MAC unchanged. Configure S1 Fa0/5 as an enabled VLAN 1 access port, and wait for forwarding. Keep A on S1 Fa0/1 and B on S2 Fa0/2.

Clear only the dynamic MAC tables on both switches. Generate no other host traffic. Before B sends its next unicast request to C, predict the egress ports and learned rows on each switch. Then predict C's reply and explain whether S2 will learn C this time. Observe in Simulation mode; if a new ARP exchange occurs, record it and repeat the unicast test after confirming B's mapping rather than pretending it matched the intended initial state.

:::solution
Prepare the added port through S1's CLI:

```ios S1
S1# configure terminal
S1(config)# interface fastethernet0/5
S1(config-if)# switchport mode access
S1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 1
S1(config-if)# no shutdown
S1(config-if)# end
S1# clear mac address-table dynamic
```

```ios S2
S2# clear mac address-table dynamic
```

B's first unicast request teaches B on S2 Fa0/2. C is unknown there, so its copy leaves the only other connected forwarding host path, Fa0/24. S1 learns B on Fa0/24 and floods the still-unknown C destination toward A on Fa0/1 and C on Fa0/5. The Ethernet destination remains C's unicast MAC.

C's reply teaches C on S1 Fa0/5 and follows the known B path through Fa0/24. S2 now receives C's source frame on its Fa0/24 and learns C there before forwarding to B on Fa0/2. Unlike the earlier same-switch B/C exchange, this reply crosses the inter-switch link, so both switches can learn C.

To restore the baseline, move C back to S2 Fa0/3, wait for forwarding, generate traffic from C toward A, and verify the learned path and both client pings. Save the challenge separately or save only after restoring the original layout.
:::

questions.prompt: With normal dynamic learning enabled, which two observations create a learned MAC-to-port association within the frame’s VLAN? Choose two.
options: The source MAC address in the received frame
The destination MAC address in the received frame
The interface on which the frame arrived
The destination IP address inside the payload
The output interface selected after the lookup
questions.explanation: The switch observes a source address arriving through a particular ingress port in a VLAN. That evidence establishes a path toward the source. The destination is looked up separately and does not reveal its own location from this frame.

whyWrong.1: The current destination is not evidence of where that destination is connected.
whyWrong.3: An IP address is not the key used for ordinary dynamic MAC learning.
whyWrong.4: The egress interface is a result of forwarding, not the source-location observation.

questions.prompt: Which two statements distinguish store-and-forward from cut-through forwarding? Choose two.
options: Cut-through waits for the complete frame before beginning its transmission.
Store-and-forward can check the complete frame’s FCS before forwarding.
Store-and-forward identifies the destination using the source MAC address.
Cut-through can begin forwarding before the complete frame and FCS arrive.
Cut-through replaces damaged payload bits using information in the FCS.
questions.explanation: Store-and-forward has the full frame available for checking before forwarding it. Cut-through can begin earlier and therefore cannot wait for the entire frame’s FCS result before that initial transmission. Hardware behavior varies; family names alone are insufficient to select a mode.

whyWrong.0: Waiting for the complete frame describes store-and-forward rather than the defining early-start behavior.
whyWrong.2: Destination MAC is used for the destination lookup in either forwarding method.
whyWrong.4: The FCS detects corruption; it is not an error-correction code that repairs payload bits.

questions.prompt: In an untagged Ethernet II frame, which EtherType identifies an IPv4 payload?
options: 0x86DD
questions.explanation: EtherType 0x0800 identifies IPv4. It tells the receiving protocol stack what payload follows; it is distinct from the destination MAC used for basic forwarding.

whyWrong.0: 0x0806 identifies ARP.
whyWrong.1: 0x86DD identifies IPv6.
whyWrong.3: 0x8100 identifies an 802.1Q tag, not an untagged IPv4 payload.

questions.prompt: Which comparison correctly distinguishes the switch MAC table from an IPv4 ARP table?
options: The MAC table maps an IP prefix to a next hop; ARP maps a VLAN to a port.
The MAC table maps MAC/VLAN to a port; ARP maps an on-link IPv4 address to a MAC.
The MAC table maps a TCP port to a process; ARP maps a frame to its EtherType.
The MAC table maps IPv4 addresses to MACs; ARP maps learned MACs to switchports.
questions.explanation: A Layer 2 switch uses the MAC/VLAN entry to choose a forwarding port. IPv4 ARP supplies a host’s on-link IP-to-MAC association; they serve different lookups.

whyWrong.0: The first description resembles routing, and ARP does not map VLANs to ports.
whyWrong.2: Transport sockets and Ethernet payload types are separate from these tables.
whyWrong.3: The two table roles are reversed.

whyWrong.1: The destination is known, so unknown-unicast flooding is unnecessary.
whyWrong.2: Other learned addresses do not make their ports destinations for this frame.
whyWrong.3: A known source is normal; same-port filtering concerns the destination.

questions.prompt: With normal dynamic learning enabled, C (00cc.cccc.cccc) sends its first valid frame on VLAN 1 Fa0/3 to B (00bb.bbbb.bbbb). Fa0/2 is forwarding and no policy blocks the frame. What does SW1 do?
options: Learns B on Fa0/3 and floods toward all other forwarding ports.
Rejects C’s frame until an administrator adds C to the table.
Learns C on Fa0/3 and forwards only toward B on Fa0/2.
Learns C on Fa0/3 and floods because C was previously unknown.
questions.explanation: Source learning and destination lookup are separate decisions. The frame teaches C’s location, while the existing B entry directs forwarding to Fa0/2. An unfamiliar valid source is not by itself a reason to flood or reject ordinary traffic.

whyWrong.0: The switch learns the source C, not the destination B, from this arrival.
whyWrong.1: Normal dynamic learning does not require a preconfigured host entry.
whyWrong.3: Unknown-unicast flooding depends on an unknown destination, not an unknown source.

options: Fa0/2 and Fa0/4, because both physical links are operational.
Fa0/2 only, because it is the other forwarding port in VLAN 10.
Fa0/2 and Fa0/5, because both are in a forwarding state.
Fa0/1 and Fa0/2, because broadcast includes its ingress port.
questions.explanation: Flooding is limited to eligible forwarding ports in the same VLAN and excludes the ingress port. Fa0/3 is down, Fa0/4 is not forwarding for VLAN 10, and Fa0/5 belongs to VLAN 20. Only Fa0/2 qualifies.

whyWrong.0: An operational link is insufficient when it is not forwarding for the VLAN.
whyWrong.2: Fa0/5 is in another VLAN and is not an egress for this broadcast.
whyWrong.3: The switch does not send the ordinary flooded copy back through its ingress port.

questions.prompt: An untagged Ethernet II frame carries a 28-byte ARP message. What is its minimum frame length, counted from destination MAC through FCS, with ordinary Ethernet padding?
options: 42 bytes
46 bytes
60 bytes
64 bytes
questions.explanation: Padding extends the data area to 46 bytes. Adding the 14-byte untagged header and 4-byte FCS gives 64 bytes. Preamble, start frame delimiter, and interframe gap are excluded from this count.

whyWrong.0: 42 counts only the header and unpadded ARP message.
whyWrong.1: 46 is the padded data area, not the complete frame.
whyWrong.2: 60 leaves out the four-byte FCS required by the stated counting scope.

questions.prompt: What identifies 0100.5e01.0203 as an Ethernet group address?
options: The organizational prefix proves that one individual NIC owns it.
The low-order bit of the first octet is set, indicating a group.
The final octet is odd, indicating a locally administered address.
The first octet differs from 00, making the address a broadcast.
questions.explanation: The individual/group bit is the least-significant bit of the first octet. In 01 that bit is set, so the address is a group address; this example is an IPv4 multicast MAC. The Ethernet broadcast address is the separate all-ones value.

whyWrong.0: A group address is not an individual NIC’s ordinary unicast identifier.
whyWrong.2: The relevant classification bits are in the first octet, not the last.
whyWrong.3: Many valid unicast/group addresses do not begin with 00; broadcast is ffff.ffff.ffff.

questions.prompt: The switch’s dynamic aging timer is explicitly set to 300 seconds. B sends no frames for six minutes, while A continues sending toward B. No link or topology event occurs. Why can B’s dynamic entry disappear?
options: No source frame from B refreshed its learned location before the timer expired.
A’s traffic replaced B’s entry because the table keeps one source per VLAN.
The timer converted B into a static entry after receiving traffic for five minutes.
The switch required a TCP acknowledgment from B to retain its Ethernet entry.
questions.explanation: A received source frame is evidence of the sender’s location. Sending frames toward B does not provide new source evidence from B, so its inactive dynamic entry can age out. Subsequent traffic for an unknown B is flooded within the eligible VLAN ports until it is relearned.

whyWrong.1: A VLAN can contain entries for many distinct source MAC addresses.
whyWrong.2: Ordinary dynamic aging removes an entry rather than configuring it as static.
whyWrong.3: MAC learning is not maintained by TCP acknowledgment tracking.

questions.prompt: After the representative display, an administrator enters clear mac address-table dynamic. No new host frame arrives before the next display. Which host entry remains?
options: No host entry remains because clear removes configured and learned entries.
Only A remains because it is learned in the switch’s default VLAN.
Only 0050.56be.1a2b remains because its entry is configured as STATIC.
All three remain because clear changes only their aging countdowns.
questions.explanation: The dynamic clear removes the two learned entries while leaving the configured static entry. Static configuration requires its matching removal command; ordinary dynamic aging or clearing is insufficient. Reserved platform entries are omitted from this exhibit.

whyWrong.0: The command is restricted to dynamic entries.
whyWrong.1: VLAN 1 does not exempt a dynamic entry from the clear.
whyWrong.3: The clear deletes dynamic entries rather than merely resetting countdowns.

spec.title: All switch ports are in VLAN 1
spec.caption: Two routed interfaces attach separate LANs; all switch ports share VLAN 1 and the hub is one shared segment.

questions.prompt: The router’s two Ethernet interfaces are routed interfaces in separate LANs. SW1’s three PC links and router link are separate switch ports; the hub connects two PCs and the other router interface. Under introductory domain-counting conventions, what is the count?
options: 7 collision domains and 2 broadcast domains
5 collision domains and 1 broadcast domain
4 collision domains and 3 broadcast domains
5 collision domains and 2 broadcast domains
questions.explanation: SW1 creates four separate link domains: three PC links plus the router link. The hub and everything on its shared segment form one more, giving five collision domains by the diagram convention; correctly operating full-duplex switch links do not actually collide. The routed interfaces separate the two broadcast domains.

whyWrong.0: Hub ports do not each separate the shared collision domain.
whyWrong.1: The two distinct routed LANs do not share one broadcast domain.
whyWrong.2: This misses a link/shared segment and adds a broadcast domain not present in the topology.

questions.prompt: A technician clears a PC’s IPv4 ARP cache. Before the PC sends new traffic, what direct effect does this have on the access switch’s MAC table?
options: The switch removes the PC’s entry because its ARP mapping was removed.
No direct effect; the host’s ARP state and switch’s MAC state are separate.
The switch clears all entries associated with the PC’s access VLAN.
The switch converts the PC’s dynamic entry to a configured static entry.
questions.explanation: The ARP cache on the PC maps IPv4 next-hop addresses to MACs. The switch’s separate table maps MACs within VLANs to ports, so clearing the host cache does not directly delete switch entries. The PC’s later frames can refresh or establish its learned source location.

whyWrong.0: A host-cache deletion is not a switch MAC-table removal operation.
whyWrong.2: Deleting host ARP entries does not request a VLAN-wide switch clear.
whyWrong.3: Host ARP state does not create static switch configuration.

questions.prompt: An inventory shows Gi0/1 connects to another access switch. The representative table has several VLANs and 38 distinct source MACs on Gi0/1. What is the appropriate first interpretation?
options: The 38 distinct sources require a separate physical port for each learned address.
The expected uplink can learn downstream hosts; compare the observed paths with inventory.
The count establishes that one duplicate MAC is repeatedly moving between two ports.
The DYNAMIC label establishes that the learned entries have their aging timer disabled.
questions.explanation: An uplink carries frames whose sources are downstream hosts, so many distinct MACs on it are normal. The inventory supports that explanation. A count alone neither proves an attack nor proves that all traffic is benign; investigate additional evidence if the behavior differs from expectations.

whyWrong.0: An uplink carries source frames from many downstream hosts, so multiple learned addresses can legitimately share one physical port.
whyWrong.2: These are different addresses on one port, not evidence of one address alternating between ports.
whyWrong.3: DYNAMIC identifies learned entries; it does not display or prove an aging configuration.

questions.prompt: A switch receives ordinary user IPv4 multicast in VLAN 1. The destination is not a reserved link-local group. Snooping and multicast restrictions are disabled, and all listed VLAN 1 ports are forwarding. Which behavior matches ordinary multicast flooding?
options: Drop the frame because a group address cannot be dynamically learned as a host source.
Deliver only to the switch CPU because every group address is control-plane traffic.
Select receiver ports from membership information despite snooping being disabled.
Copy to the other eligible VLAN 1 ports, excluding the ingress port.
questions.explanation: With the stated restrictions absent, ordinary multicast is flooded within the VLAN, excluding ingress. Group delivery can differ when snooping, multicast forwarding state, policy, or reserved control addresses apply. The assumptions in the question make the forwarding decision unambiguous.

whyWrong.0: Lack of a learned unicast-source entry does not by itself require discarding ordinary multicast.
whyWrong.1: Only particular control addresses receive special handling; multicast as a whole is not CPU-only.
whyWrong.2: The question excludes the receiver-membership restrictions that would support this selection.

questions.prompt: PC-B is physically moved as shown and then sends the first new frame. No static entries, security policies or loop are present. Which forwarding result follows?
options: A’s next frame to B is flooded until the old timer expires.
A’s next frame to B is sent to Fa0/2 until its ARP entry is cleared.
A’s next frame to B is sent to both old and new ports during relearning.
A’s next frame to B is sent to Fa0/4 using the updated source location.
questions.explanation: A valid frame from B on Fa0/4 updates B’s dynamic MAC location immediately. A can keep its correct IP-to-MAC mapping; the switch’s updated destination lookup chooses the new port.

whyWrong.0: New source evidence can update a dynamic location without waiting for the old aging interval.
whyWrong.1: The host’s unchanged IP-to-MAC mapping does not prevent the switch from learning the new physical path.
whyWrong.2: Ordinary learning updates the entry rather than keeping both ports as simultaneous unicast destinations.

questions.prompt: Initially D and E are reached through Fa0/24. Apply the two received frames in order. What happens to the second frame?
options: It is filtered because the initial entry put E on its ingress port.
It is flooded because a learned source can have more than one location.
It is forwarded to Fa0/3 after E’s source frame updated the table.
It is returned through Fa0/24 because D was learned on that port.
questions.explanation: Frame 1 updates the dynamic location of source E to Fa0/3. Frame 2 then looks up destination E using that updated table, so it leaves Fa0/3 rather than being same-port filtered. The initial table is not a permanent forwarding rule.

whyWrong.0: The source frame from E changed its learned location before the second lookup.
whyWrong.1: The destination has a known current entry; a normal source move does not require unknown-unicast flooding.
whyWrong.3: Destination lookup selects E’s port, and ordinary bridging does not reflect the frame through its ingress.

All ports are forwarding in VLAN 1, with ordinary bridging.
A -- S1 Fa0/1     S1 Fa0/24 -- S2 Fa0/24
B -- S2 Fa0/2     C -- S2 Fa0/3

1. A sends a unicast Ethernet frame to B (A already knows B’s MAC).
2. B sends a unicast reply to A.
3. C sends a unicast Ethernet frame to B (C already knows B’s MAC).

questions.prompt: Both tables begin empty. The three frames below occur in order, and no other host transmits. Which host locations has S1 learned after frame 3?
options: A on Fa0/1 and B on Fa0/24; it has not learned C.
A on Fa0/1, with both B and C on Fa0/24.
B on Fa0/24 and C on Fa0/3; it has not learned A.
A on Fa0/1 and C on Fa0/24; B ages out after its reply.
questions.explanation: The first request teaches A on each switch along its path. B’s reply reaches S1 and teaches B on Fa0/24. C’s final frame is sent by S2 only to the already-known B port, so S1 never sees C transmit and cannot learn C from that frame.

whyWrong.1: C’s source frame stays on S2’s local path to B and does not reach S1.
whyWrong.2: Fa0/3 is C’s port on S2, not a learned S1 port; A already transmitted into S1.
whyWrong.3: B’s reply supplied source evidence; the stated immediate sequence includes no aging event.

cards.front: What is the basic untagged Ethernet frame size, and what is counted?
cards.back: 64–1518 bytes for the basic 1500-byte-payload framing, destination MAC through FCS. Preamble, SFD, and interframe gap are excluded.

cards.front: What is the data-area size in the basic untagged Ethernet II frame?
cards.back: 46–1500 bytes including any minimum-size padding. The 1500-byte payload limit is distinct from the total Ethernet frame length.

cards.front: What are the Ethernet II header and FCS sizes?
cards.back: Destination MAC 6 + source MAC 6 + EtherType 2 = 14-byte untagged header; FCS adds 4 bytes.

cards.front: Which Ethernet II types distinguish IPv4 from ARP?
cards.back: 0x0800 identifies IPv4; 0x0806 identifies ARP. The EtherType describes the Ethernet payload protocol.

cards.front: Is every frame longer than 1518 bytes invalid?
cards.back: No. VLAN tags and supported larger-frame configurations change valid sizes. Interpret size/error counters against the platform and interface configuration.

cards.front: How long is a MAC address, and what does an OUI identify?
cards.back: 48 bits, or 12 hexadecimal digits. An OUI identifies an organizational allocation; locally assigned MACs and other IEEE allocation sizes also exist.

cards.front: How do you identify an Ethernet group address and broadcast address?
cards.back: The low-order bit of the first octet is set for group addresses. The all-ones broadcast address is ffff.ffff.ffff.

cards.front: What information does ordinary switching learn and look up?
cards.back: Learn source MAC + VLAN → ingress port. Look up destination MAC in the VLAN to forward, filter, or flood.

cards.front: Does unknown-unicast flooding change the destination MAC?
cards.back: No. It copies the unicast frame to eligible forwarding ports in the same VLAN, excluding the ingress port.

cards.front: What refreshes a dynamic MAC entry, and what is the reference 2960 timer?
cards.back: Frames received from that source refresh its location. The documented 2960 IOS 15.0(2)SE default is 300 seconds; verify the actual device.

cards.front: What creates a static MAC entry for a VLAN and interface?
cards.back: mac address-table static H.H.H vlan N interface X. It does not age or disappear in a dynamic-table clear; remove the matching configuration to undo it.

cards.front: How do you clear learned MAC entries without removing static entries?
cards.back: At privileged EXEC: clear mac address-table dynamic. Hosts sending new frames can be learned again immediately.

cards.front: Which columns matter in show mac address-table?
cards.back: VLAN, MAC address, entry type, and port. Read the VLAN first; a dynamic row gives the learned path toward the source.

cards.front: Store-and-forward compared with cut-through?
cards.back: Store-and-forward receives the whole frame and checks FCS before forwarding. Cut-through can start before the complete frame/FCS arrives.

cards.front: How do switch ports and VLANs separate Ethernet domains?
cards.back: Switch ports separate collision domains; full-duplex links have no collisions. A VLAN is a broadcast domain that can span multiple switches.

cards.front: Why can a Layer 2 loop carry repeated flooded traffic?
cards.back: Ordinary Ethernet has no hop-count field to stop circulation. Spanning tree creates a loop-free forwarding topology.

cards.front: MAC address table versus ARP table?
cards.back: MAC table: MAC + VLAN → port. IPv4 ARP table: on-link IP → MAC. Clearing either table does not directly clear the other.

cards.front: Do many MAC addresses on one port prove a fault?
cards.back: No. An uplink can carry many hosts. Compare the topology; repeated moves of one MAC warrant investigation but do not alone identify the cause.

cards.front: Can the Ethernet FCS repair a corrupted frame?
cards.back: No. The CRC detects corruption; it is not error correction. A store-and-forward switch discards a frame that fails its FCS check.

cards.front: A learned host transmits on a new port. Must the old entry age out first?
cards.back: No. With ordinary dynamic learning and no restriction, the new source frame updates its MAC/VLAN location to the new ingress port.

commands.task: Display MAC table entries associated with FastEthernet0/24.

commands.task: Display the MAC aging timer currently in force.
commands.note: The referenced Catalyst 2960 IOS default is 300 seconds. Verify the actual platform and configuration.

commands.note: Removes dynamic entries; static entries remain. New source traffic can repopulate the table immediately.

commands.task: Create a static path for MAC 0050.56be.1a2b in VLAN 10 through FastEthernet0/5.

accept: mac address-table static 0050.56be.1a2b vlan 10 interface fa0/5

tickets.title: Unicast still fails after a dynamic clear
tickets.scenario: In VLAN 1, PC-A is directly attached to S1 Fa0/1. PC-B, MAC 00bb.bbbb.bbbb, is attached to S2; S1 reaches S2 through Fa0/24. Both links are forwarding. A can ping another host behind S2 but cannot ping B. The table was inspected after clearing dynamic entries and before new source traffic.

exhibits.title: Representative S1# show mac address-table
exhibits.text:
Vlan    Mac Address       Type        Ports
   1    00bb.bbbb.bbbb    STATIC      Fa0/1

exhibits.title: S1 configuration excerpt
exhibits.text: mac address-table static 00bb.bbbb.bbbb vlan 1 interface FastEthernet0/1

tickets.question: What explains the failed ping and persistence after a dynamic clear?
options: The static entry directs B’s traffic toward A’s port and survives the dynamic clear.
The previous dynamic location remains authoritative until its aging timer expires.
The table is correct because B’s frame destination is used to relearn its location.
The retained host ARP mapping forces the switch to transmit through the old port.
tickets.explanation: The configured B entry points to Fa0/1 rather than the actual path through Fa0/24. B-destined unicast from A therefore encounters same-port filtering, and the static entry survives a dynamic clear. This is not an old dynamic timer, destination-based learning or a host-ARP decision; remove the exact static configuration and verify the newly learned path.
tickets.fix:
```ios S1
S1# configure terminal
S1(config)# no mac address-table static 00bb.bbbb.bbbb vlan 1 interface fastethernet0/1
S1(config)# end
S1# clear mac address-table dynamic
```
Ping B from A, then run `show mac address-table` on S1. Confirm B is learned dynamically on Fa0/24 and connectivity returns before saving. On a different topology, substitute the actual host MAC and configured interface rather than copying this example blindly.

A retains B’s ARP mapping, but a technician clears only S1’s dynamic MAC entries. In Simulation mode, the first ICMP request for B reaches both B and C; later requests reach B alone.
