tickets.question: Which explanation fits this sequence?
options: A changed the destination to Ethernet broadcast when it sent the first ICMP request.
The switch learned B’s destination address from A before selecting both output ports.
Clearing S1’s table also deleted A’s ARP mapping and forced a new broadcast request.
The first destination was unknown to S1; B’s source reply then established its port.
tickets.explanation: A knows B’s MAC, so it can send an ordinary unicast frame immediately. S1 lacks B’s entry and floods within the eligible VLAN ports while learning A from the request. B’s reply teaches B on Fa0/2, so later requests use known-unicast forwarding; the frame never needs a broadcast destination.
tickets.fix: No repair is required for this controlled clear/relearn behavior. Confirm the destination MAC stays unicast, observe B’s reply creating the Fa0/2 entry, and verify subsequent requests use that port. If flooding continues unexpectedly, investigate why source learning is not retained rather than assuming the host ARP table and switch MAC table are the same.

chapters.title: Secure device access
chapters.subtitle: Local accounts, console and VTY lines, SSH, and a reliable way to verify access.

sources.title: Cisco: Protecting secrets on network devices
Cisco: Understand Cisco IOS password encryption
Cisco: Guide to harden Cisco IOS devices

chapters.summary: Build and verify local device access with named users and SSH. Distinguish session transport, authentication, privilege and saved configuration, then diagnose a failed login without losing console access.

sections.body: A working network must also be manageable. You need a dependable way to reach each device, identify the person signing in, and give that session the intended level of access. This chapter builds on the command-line introduction in Start here. The main task is now to configure local accounts and SSH, verify them from a second session, and diagnose failures in a deliberate order.

sections.title: Why management access needs protection
sections.body:
The **management plane** is the part of a device used to administer and monitor it. Console sessions, remote command-line sessions and a device's web interface are management paths. Protecting these paths matters because a user who can change the configuration can also change forwarding, credentials and access controls.

Separate four questions when reading a configuration. Can the client reach the device? Which session transport is accepted? How is the user authenticated? What may the authenticated session do? A correct password cannot repair a broken IP path, and a running SSH server does not mean its VTY lines accept SSH. These are separate checks.

For v1.1, this chapter covers management access methods, SSH configuration and local passwords. For v2.0, it supplies the local-user foundation for device management; [AAA: TACACS+ and RADIUS](#/chapter/aaa-tacacs-radius) adds centralized AAA configuration. Source-address filtering is developed in [Access control lists](#/chapter/acls), after wildcard masks and rule order are taught.

:::facts
- `login local` uses the local `username` database. With ordinary local authentication, a line's shared `password` is not its fallback.
- `enable secret` takes precedence over `enable password` for the same privilege level in the basic local configuration used here.
- SSH uses TCP `22`; Telnet uses TCP `23`. `transport input ssh` restricts the selected VTY lines to SSH.
- `show ip ssh` reports the SSH server configuration; `show ssh` reports SSH sessions; `show users` identifies active terminal lines and their users.
- A local account defaults to privilege `1`; `privilege 15` grants privileged EXEC access. These examples assume no AAA method lists or custom command authorization.
- Inspect the available VTY lines on the actual device. A five-line example is not proof that the device has only five lines.
:::

sections.title: Review the IOS workflow
sections.body:
Start here introduced prompts and configuration storage. Here, use that knowledge as an operating procedure: inspect, change, verify, and save. Know the mode before typing a command, especially when moving between interface configuration and line configuration.

| Prompt | Meaning | Typical action here |
|---|---|---|
| `R1>` | User EXEC | Basic monitoring; enter `enable` |
| `R1#` | Privileged EXEC | Inspect configuration, save, enter configuration mode |
| `R1(config)#` | Global configuration | Create a local user or enable SSHv2 |
| `R1(config-if)#` | Interface configuration | Configure the management-facing IP interface |
| `R1(config-line)#` | Line configuration | Set authentication, transport and idle timeout |

Most configuration commands affect the **running configuration** as you enter them. Saving copies that configuration into the **startup configuration**, which the normal boot process reads. Traditional IOS platforms expose startup configuration through NVRAM; storage details vary by platform. The useful distinction is active state versus saved boot configuration, rather than assuming every device stores the file on identical hardware.

```ios R1
R1# show running-config
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# end
R1# copy running-config startup-config
```

When the copy command asks `Destination filename [startup-config]?`, press Enter to accept the destination. That response is interactive input, not another IOS command. Saving a Packet Tracer project also preserves the simulator workspace; it is a separate action from saving the device configuration.

Output filters help you inspect the relevant configuration. `show running-config | section line vty` displays VTY sections on supporting images; `| include username` displays matching user lines. If a simulator does not support a filter, read the corresponding part of the full output. Do not confuse missing output caused by an unsuitable filter with proof that a feature is absent.

Erasing startup configuration is not a universal factory reset. VLAN databases, keys and other files may have separate persistence. Use a new blank simulator device for this chapter, rather than trying to reset an existing device that may hold useful work.

sections.title: Local accounts and privileged access
sections.body:
**Authentication** verifies an identity. **Privilege** determines the commands available to the resulting session. In this chapter, local usernames provide authentication, and the user's configured privilege controls the initial EXEC level. More detailed authorization and accounting are introduced with AAA.

```ios R1
R1(config)# enable secret EnableLabSecret8
R1(config)# username admin privilege 15 secret AdminLabSecret8
R1(config)# username trainee secret TraineeLabSecret8
```

These are example lab credentials. `admin` starts at privilege 15 when the line uses the local database. `trainee` defaults to privilege 1 and enters privileged EXEC with `enable` and the enable secret. `show privilege` confirms the current level; the prompt alone is a useful clue, but the command is a direct check.

The `secret` keyword stores a password verifier rather than a cleartext password. Its supported algorithms and defaults depend on the software. Older IOS and simulator configurations often display type 5; current software can support stronger types such as 8 and 9. A stored hash can still be attacked by guessing passwords, so hashing is not a substitute for strong credentials and restricted access to configuration files.

| Stored form | What to recognize | Practical implication |
|---|---|---|
| Type `0` | Cleartext password | Reading the configuration reveals the password |
| Type `7` | Reversible obfuscation | Does not provide strong protection for a stored credential |
| Type `5` | MD5-based password hash | Legacy verifier; prefer stronger supported types |
| Type `8` | PBKDF2-SHA-256 verifier | Availability and syntax depend on the image |
| Type `9` | scrypt verifier | Availability and syntax depend on the image |

On traditional IOS, `service password-encryption` obscures applicable cleartext password fields using type 7. It does not encrypt Telnet traffic and does not convert an enable secret into a stronger hash. Removing the command does not automatically recover plaintext for already converted fields. The important skill is distinguishing stored-password handling from protection of the session carrying the password.

:::trap Privileged access and login are separate
Setting `enable secret` does not create a local username or configure line authentication. Creating a local username does not make a line use it. Read the user, privilege and line settings together before deciding how a login will behave.
:::

sections.title: Console and VTY line settings
sections.body:
A **console line** is associated with the local console connection. A **VTY**, or virtual terminal line, supports remote terminal sessions such as SSH. Some devices also have an auxiliary port. Physical connectors, console speeds and the number of remote lines depend on the platform; a common serial-console setting on the lab router is 9600 baud, 8 data bits, no parity and 1 stop bit.

The console does not require a working IP interface. That makes it a useful recovery path while configuring remote access. It is still an authenticated management path once you protect it; a console cable does not bypass configured credentials or guarantee access during every boot or hardware failure.

| Line setting | Effect in the basic local configuration |
|---|---|
| `password` followed by `login` | Uses a shared line password |
| `login local` | Checks a named user in the local database |
| `exec-timeout 5 0` | Ends an idle EXEC session after five minutes |
| `logging synchronous` | Redisplays the prompt/input around unsolicited messages |
| `transport input ssh` | Accepts SSH as the incoming VTY transport |

Create and verify the account before applying `login local`. Keep the current console session open and test a separate login before disconnecting. An existing authenticated session is not proof that the next login will succeed.

```ios R1
R1(config)# line console 0
R1(config-line)# login local
R1(config-line)# exec-timeout 5 0
R1(config-line)# logging synchronous
R1(config-line)# exit
R1(config)# line vty 0 4
R1(config-line)# login local
R1(config-line)# transport input ssh
R1(config-line)# exec-timeout 5 0
R1(config-line)# end
```

The example covers VTY 0–4. Inspect `show line`, the VTY sections in `show running-config`, and `line vty ?` on your device. If it also has VTY 5–15, apply the same intended policy there. Different line ranges can have different authentication and transport settings, so verify each range without assuming a router-versus-switch rule.

A banner communicates an access notice; it is not an authentication mechanism. For example, `banner motd #Authorized lab users only#` uses `#` as the delimiter. Banner timing can differ with the protocol and platform. Learn what the banner does and how its delimiter works, rather than relying on one universal display order.

sections.title: Choose a management method
sections.body:
**In-band management** uses the production network or its forwarding infrastructure. **Out-of-band management** uses a separate management path. Ethernet and SSH can be part of either design; the protocol alone does not establish whether the path is separate. A direct serial console is the local out-of-band example in this lab.

| Method | Role | What must be considered |
|---|---|---|
| Console | Local CLI access | Physical access, console settings and authentication |
| Telnet | Remote CLI over TCP 23 | Carries session data without SSH-style protection |
| SSH | Protected remote CLI over TCP 22 | IP reachability, server keys, compatible algorithms, line policy and credentials |
| HTTP / HTTPS | Web management, commonly TCP 80 / 443 | HTTPS uses TLS; enable only the required web service and validate its identity |
| TACACS+ / RADIUS | Central AAA services consulted by the device | These support access decisions; they do not replace the administrator's SSH session |
| Cloud management | Administration through a vendor service | Connectivity, identity, supported functions and fallback access vary by product |

SSH protects the authenticated session, but encryption alone does not prove that you reached the intended server. A client may ask you to verify a host key on first connection. In a real environment, compare that identity with a trusted record. Do not teach yourself to accept unexpected key changes automatically.

Cloud-managed products use different control and management designs. Do not infer that every device uses only outbound HTTPS or lacks local access. For CCNA, recognize the management approach and its dependencies; product-specific ports and recovery procedures belong in the product documentation.

sections.title: Configure SSH step by step
sections.body:
Use the conventional hostname/domain/RSA-key workflow below on a supported IOS image. Some platforms support additional key-management methods; the point is to build one complete, verifiable configuration. Setting a domain name for device identity does not require a DNS server or a DNS query to generate the key.

```diagram
{"type":"topology","title":"Local and remote access to R1","caption":"The console remains available while the PC tests SSH over the directly connected subnet.","nodes":[{"id":"CON","kind":"laptop","label":"Console laptop","sub":"Serial console","x":2,"y":1},{"id":"PC","kind":"pc","label":"Admin PC","sub":"10.8.0.10/24","x":2,"y":5},{"id":"SW","kind":"switch","label":"SW1","sub":"Same LAN","x":6,"y":5},{"id":"R","kind":"router","label":"R1","sub":"Gi0/0 10.8.0.1/24","x":10,"y":3}],"links":[{"from":"CON","to":"R","label":"Console","style":"dashed"},{"from":"PC","to":"SW","label":"Ethernet"},{"from":"SW","to":"R","label":"SSH over IP","accent":true}]}
```

First establish the IP path. R1's address is `10.8.0.1/24`; the PC is `10.8.0.10/24`. They can communicate directly on this subnet, so no routed transit path is needed. A remote management subnet would also require correct forwarding and a return path. An IP address assigned to a Layer 2 switch's management SVI does not, by itself, enable that switch to route user traffic; Chapter 11 develops the distinction.

```ios R1
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.8.0.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# ip domain-name lab.test
R1(config)# crypto key generate rsa general-keys modulus 2048
R1(config)# ip ssh version 2
R1(config)# end
R1# show ip ssh
```

The local accounts and VTY policy from the previous sections complete this configuration. Key-generation syntax and supported sizes vary. If the full command is rejected, use contextual help; some images accept the shorter form or prompt for a modulus after `crypto key generate rsa`. Use 2048 bits for this lab where supported, rather than memorizing an obsolete minimum as a security recommendation.

From a Packet Tracer PC, use the following command and enter the configured password when asked. A desktop SSH client may instead use `ssh admin@10.8.0.1`.

```text
ssh -l admin 10.8.0.1
```

sections.title: Verify and troubleshoot
sections.body:
Inspect configuration and operational evidence separately. The following output is an abbreviated representative example, not a transcript from a simulator run.

```output R1# show ip ssh
SSH Enabled - version 2.0  ← server is enabled for SSHv2
Authentication timeout: 120 secs; Authentication retries: 3
```

This proves the reported server state. It does not prove that the PC can reach R1, that all VTY lines accept SSH, or that the account is valid. Verify those conditions, then open a new session and run `show privilege` as each test user. `show users` identifies sessions and may show the client's address in its Location column; `show ssh` supplies SSH-session details.

| Observation | Next check | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Interface is administratively down | Interface configuration and `no shutdown` | Remote access needs a usable IP path |
| SSH server reports disabled | Image support, key configuration and SSH settings | A local account alone does not start the SSH service |
| SSH is enabled, but connection is refused | All VTY transport settings and access policy | Server state and accepted line transports are separate |
| Credentials are rejected | Exact username, secret and authentication method | `login local` needs a matching local account |
| Login succeeds at `>` instead of `#` | `show privilege` and user privilege | Authentication succeeded; authorization level is the separate issue |
| Access breaks after reload | Saved configuration and actual boot state | The verified running configuration may not have been saved |

A successful ping is evidence of ICMP reachability under the test conditions. It is not an SSH test. Conversely, a blocked ICMP response does not alone prove that TCP 22 is unreachable. Test the service you intend to use, and keep configuration changes small enough that you can identify which one affected the result.

sections.title: Exam focus
sections.body:
- Distinguish console access, remote-session transport, authentication and privilege.
- Configure a local username and enable secret, then explain `login` versus `login local`.
- Configure the hostname/domain/key/SSHv2 workflow and restrict every intended VTY line to SSH.
- Verify the actual line range instead of assuming a fixed count by device family.
- Recognize the difference between a stored secret, type 7 obfuscation and session encryption.
- Use `show ip ssh`, `show ssh`, `show users` and `show privilege` for their different purposes.
- Test a new login before closing the working session; save the verified configuration.
- Leave centralized AAA and source-address ACL construction to their dedicated chapters.

lab.title: Configure local accounts and SSH, diagnose a refusal, and restore access
lab.intro:
Build this as a new Packet Tracer project. You will verify two privilege levels, restrict remote access to SSH, create a controlled transport fault, and recover through the console. All credentials shown are for this isolated exercise. Outputs are representative excerpts; record what your installed simulator actually reports.

Practice revised September 2026. If you completed an earlier version, repeat the revised exercise and update its checkmarks.
lab.topology:
```diagram
{"type":"topology","title":"SSH access lab","caption":"The laptop's console connection is independent of the PC's Ethernet management path.","nodes":[{"id":"L","kind":"laptop","label":"CONSOLE","sub":"RS-232 terminal","x":2,"y":1},{"id":"P","kind":"pc","label":"ADMIN","sub":"10.8.0.10/24","x":2,"y":5},{"id":"S","kind":"switch","label":"SW1","sub":"2960-24TT","x":6,"y":5},{"id":"R","kind":"router","label":"R1","sub":"2911 · 10.8.0.1/24","x":10,"y":3}],"links":[{"from":"L","to":"R","fromLabel":"RS-232","toLabel":"Console","style":"dashed"},{"from":"P","to":"S","fromLabel":"Fa0","toLabel":"Fa0/1"},{"from":"S","to":"R","fromLabel":"Gi0/1","toLabel":"Gi0/0","accent":true}]}
```

| Connection or device | Setting |
|---|---|
| CONSOLE RS-232 → R1 Console | Console cable |
| ADMIN Fa0 → SW1 Fa0/1 | Copper straight-through |
| SW1 Gi0/1 → R1 Gi0/0 | Copper straight-through |
| ADMIN IPv4 | `10.8.0.10`, mask `255.255.255.0`, gateway `10.8.0.1` |
| R1 Gi0/0 | `10.8.0.1/24` |
| SW1 | Default access VLAN for this single-LAN exercise; no management IP required |

The gateway is recorded for a complete host configuration; this lab's SSH destination is on ADMIN's own subnet. DNS is not needed because the SSH test uses an IP address.

steps.title: Open a console and identify the device
steps.body:
Place and cable the devices. On CONSOLE, open Desktop → Terminal and accept the displayed serial settings, using 9600 baud, 8 data bits, no parity and 1 stop bit for the 2911. Press Enter if needed. Decline the initial configuration dialog if it appears. Keep this terminal open throughout the exercise.

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# no ip domain-lookup
R1(config)# end
R1# show version
R1# show line
```

:::expected
The prompt is `R1#`. Record the model, image description and available console/VTY lines. `no ip domain-lookup` avoids accidental hostname lookups from mistyped commands; it does not prevent local RSA-key generation or change ADMIN's DNS settings. If the terminal is blank, check the console cable endpoints before investigating Ethernet.
:::

steps.title: Establish the IP path
steps.body:
On ADMIN, use Desktop → IP Configuration to enter the address table. Configure R1 through the console.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# description Management lab LAN
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.8.0.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
R1# show running-config
```

On ADMIN, open Desktop → Command Prompt:

```text
ping 10.8.0.1
```

:::expected
Gi0/0 should have `10.8.0.1` and become `up/up` after the link is operational. Repeat an initial ping if address resolution was still in progress. If repeated tests fail, verify cabling, address/mask and interface state. Record every VTY range shown in the running configuration; later steps must apply the intended policy to all available lines.
:::

steps.title: Create users and an enable secret
steps.body:
Configure one administrator and one lower-privilege account. Do this before making a line depend on the local database.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# enable secret EnableLabSecret8
R1(config)# username admin privilege 15 secret AdminLabSecret8
R1(config)# username trainee secret TraineeLabSecret8
R1(config)# end
R1# show running-config | include username
R1# show running-config | include enable
```

:::expected
Both usernames and the enable secret appear. The stored verifier strings and their type numbers may differ by image; do not compare them character for character with an example hash. The configuration explicitly gives `admin` privilege 15 and leaves `trainee` at the default local-user level of 1. If a filter is unsupported, inspect the full running configuration.
:::

steps.title: Protect the console line
steps.body:
Keep the existing console session open. Do not deliberately log out until a separate remote session has been tested. An open terminal window does not prevent the five-minute idle timeout: if the session times out, press Enter and sign in as `admin` with `AdminLabSecret8` from Step 3.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# line console 0
R1(config-line)# login local
R1(config-line)# exec-timeout 5 0
R1(config-line)# logging synchronous
R1(config-line)# end
R1# show running-config | section line con
```

:::expected
The console line uses `login local` and a five-minute idle timeout. The existing session remains available until it ends or the idle timeout expires; the next console login will need one of the accounts from Step 3. A missing user entry must be corrected now, before that session ends.
:::

steps.title: Configure the SSH server and VTY policy
steps.body:
Use the conventional RSA-key workflow. If your image rejects the complete key-generation command, inspect `crypto key generate rsa ?`; a supported alternative may prompt for the modulus after `crypto key generate rsa`. Enter `2048` at that prompt. Do not paste an interactive answer as a separate configuration command.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip domain-name lab.test
R1(config)# crypto key generate rsa general-keys modulus 2048
R1(config)# ip ssh version 2
R1(config)# line vty 0 4
R1(config-line)# login local
R1(config-line)# transport input ssh
R1(config-line)# exec-timeout 5 0
R1(config-line)# end
R1# show ip ssh
```

If Step 2 showed VTY 5–15, apply the same policy to that range as well. Run this additional block only when those lines exist:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# line vty 5 15
R1(config-line)# login local
R1(config-line)# transport input ssh
R1(config-line)# exec-timeout 5 0
R1(config-line)# end
```

:::expected
`show ip ssh` reports the server enabled for version 2.0. Inspect the VTY sections and confirm local authentication and SSH transport on every range. If the simulator lacks SSH support for the chosen device/image, use a supported router/image; reading an output example does not count as a successful login test.
:::

steps.title: Test both users from a new session
steps.body:
On ADMIN, enter:

```text
ssh -l trainee 10.8.0.1
```

Enter `TraineeLabSecret8` when prompted. Inside that remote session:

```ios R1
R1> show privilege
R1> enable
```

Enter `EnableLabSecret8` at the password prompt, then:

```ios R1
R1# show privilege
R1# exit
```

Open a new SSH session as `admin` using `AdminLabSecret8`, then check it:

```text
ssh -l admin 10.8.0.1
```

```ios R1
R1# show privilege
R1# show users
R1# exit
```

Finally try `telnet 10.8.0.1` from ADMIN.

:::expected
`trainee` initially reports privilege 1 and reaches 15 after the enable secret is accepted. `admin` begins at privilege 15. Telnet must not open an authenticated terminal session. Exact rejection wording varies; the result and the VTY configuration matter. If your simulator does not expose `show privilege`, record the prompts and check the username privilege in the configuration.
:::

steps.title: Complete a changed line requirement
steps.body:
The administrator now requires a **three-minute remote EXEC idle timeout**, while the console must remain at five minutes. Keep SSH-only transport and local-user authentication. This is a partially guided task: write the necessary configuration context and timeout command before reading the reference below, then apply it through the console to every existing VTY range.

Inspect the resulting console and VTY sections. Verify a fresh administrator login; you need not wait three minutes to document the configured timeout, and a successful login alone is not a measurement of timer expiry.

:::expected
The timeout is a property of the selected terminal lines. Configure VTY 0–4 as follows, and repeat for VTY 5–15 only if those lines were found earlier:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# line vty 0 4
R1(config-line)# exec-timeout 3 0
R1(config-line)# end
R1# show running-config | section line
```

The VTY ranges show `exec-timeout 3 0`, while the console still shows `exec-timeout 5 0`. If the filter is unavailable, inspect the full configuration. Do not change `login local`, the username entries or `transport input ssh` to satisfy a timeout requirement.
:::

steps.title: Introduce a remote-transport fault
steps.body:
Confirm that ADMIN has exited its SSH session. On the still-open console, replace the incoming transport with `none` on every VTY range you configured. Do not save this fault.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# line vty 0 4
R1(config-line)# transport input none
R1(config-line)# end
```

If VTY 5–15 exists, apply `transport input none` to that range too. From ADMIN, run the ping and SSH tests again.

```text
ping 10.8.0.1
ssh -l admin 10.8.0.1
```

:::expected
The IP interface remains operational and ping should still succeed. A new SSH terminal session is refused because the VTY lines accept no incoming transport. On the console, `show ip ssh` can still report an enabled SSH server. This combination demonstrates why server status, IP reachability and line policy must be checked separately.
:::

steps.title: Restore the intended transport
steps.body:
Use the console to restore SSH on every VTY range. Keep the fault and recovery as separate observations in your notes.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# line vty 0 4
R1(config-line)# transport input ssh
R1(config-line)# end
```

Apply the same recovery to VTY 5–15 if present. Open a new SSH session from ADMIN as `admin`.

:::expected
The new login succeeds with privilege 15. Telnet remains disallowed. If SSH still fails, compare all VTY ranges, user entries and the SSH server state before changing the interface address or regenerating keys.
:::

steps.title: Verify the complete access policy
steps.body:
From the console, inspect the active sessions while ADMIN's SSH session is open.

```ios R1
R1# show users
R1# show ssh
R1# show ip ssh
R1# show running-config | section line vty
```

Record the user, line and any displayed client address. Keep ADMIN's proven SSH session open while you test a fresh console login. At the console, enter `exit` from privileged EXEC (`R1# exit`), then press Enter to start a new session and sign in as `admin` with `AdminLabSecret8` so the next step begins at `R1#`. Closing and reopening the terminal window alone may leave the existing console session active. Both an open console window and an open SSH window can still reach their configured idle timeouts; log back in if either session ends before testing. After both paths have been verified, log out of the SSH session on ADMIN.

:::expected
The commands provide different evidence: terminal users, SSH sessions, SSH server state, and line configuration. The console login accepts a valid local account. A successful test on one VTY does not replace reviewing the other VTY ranges. On images with limited filters/session commands, inspect the full configuration and record the limitation instead of inventing missing output.
:::

steps.title: Save the verified configuration
steps.body:
Save only after the fault has been removed and both access paths work.

```ios R1
R1# copy running-config startup-config
```

Press Enter at the destination filename prompt and wait for the command to finish. Once `R1#` returns, inspect the saved configuration:

```ios R1
R1# show startup-config
```

Save the Packet Tracer project as `08-secure-device-access.pkt`.

:::expected
The saved configuration includes the intended username, interface, SSH and line settings. It must not contain `transport input none` on the VTY lines. The device save and project save are both complete. A reload is unnecessary for this exercise; if you later test one, retain the verified credentials and console path.
:::


Before checking this lab complete, submit a short acceptance record:

| Requirement | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Local recovery | New console login while another proven path remains available |
| Different user privileges | New trainee and admin sessions with their actual privilege levels |
| SSH-only admission | Fresh SSH success and fresh Telnet rejection |
| Complete line policy | Every available VTY range; console five minutes, VTY three minutes |
| Fault reasoning | Ping/server/line evidence, narrow correction and new-session retest |
| Persistence | Desired users and repaired line settings in startup-config |

The deliberately introduced fault is guided practice. Attempt the independent fresh build below before reading its answer key; record help used and corrected reasoning.

lab.troubleshooting:
- **No console prompt:** check the serial connection and terminal settings; the Ethernet IP address is not the first check.
- **Repeated ping failure:** check host addressing, cable endpoints and R1 Gi0/0 before changing user accounts.
- **SSH server disabled:** check support, RSA-key configuration and SSH settings.
- **Server enabled but session refused:** inspect every VTY range and its accepted transports; a reachable server can still reject terminal access.
- **Password rejected:** check exact username, secret and line authentication method. Do not assume an enable secret is the login password.
- **Unexpected privilege:** inspect the user entry and `show privilege`; an authenticated level-1 session is different from a failed login.
- **Change disappears after restart:** inspect the saved configuration and boot state rather than assuming the earlier save succeeded.
lab.challenge:
Build a **fresh** project using the same device models, cable types and physical ports from the topology. Name the router **R2**. Use router `10.8.1.1/24` and ADMIN `10.8.1.10/24`, gateway `10.8.1.1`; no DNS is needed. Keep the console laptop as a separate recovery path.

Produce a configuration from these requirements before looking at the answer:

- Local user `operator` starts at privilege 15; user `reviewer` starts at privilege 1.
- Use isolated-lab secrets `OperatorLab8`, `ReviewerLab8` and enable secret `EnableChallenge8`.
- The console uses local authentication and a five-minute EXEC idle timeout.
- All actual VTY lines use local authentication, SSH only and a three-minute idle timeout.
- Use the conventional RSA workflow with domain `challenge.test`, supported 2048-bit keys and SSHv2.
- Verify a new login for each account, a new console login, Telnet rejection, and the saved policy.

Write a six-row acceptance table with predicted and actual results. If you consult the reference, record which part needed help and repeat that part later with changed values.

:::solution
The new switch can use its default access VLAN; the host/router share one subnet. Configure through the console, creating users before making lines depend on them:

```ios R2
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R2
R2(config)# enable secret EnableChallenge8
R2(config)# username operator privilege 15 secret OperatorLab8
R2(config)# username reviewer secret ReviewerLab8
R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R2(config-if)# ip address 10.8.1.1 255.255.255.0
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# exit
R2(config)# line console 0
R2(config-line)# login local
R2(config-line)# exec-timeout 5 0
R2(config-line)# exit
R2(config)# ip domain-name challenge.test
R2(config)# crypto key generate rsa general-keys modulus 2048
R2(config)# ip ssh version 2
R2(config)# line vty 0 4
R2(config-line)# login local
R2(config-line)# transport input ssh
R2(config-line)# exec-timeout 3 0
R2(config-line)# end
R2# show line
R2# show ip ssh
R2# show running-config
```

Use the Step 5 key-generation fallback if required by the image. If VTY 5–15 exists, configure it as well:

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# line vty 5 15
R2(config-line)# login local
R2(config-line)# transport input ssh
R2(config-line)# exec-timeout 3 0
R2(config-line)# end
```

From ADMIN, test `ssh -l operator 10.8.1.1` and `ssh -l reviewer 10.8.1.1` in separate sessions. Verify privilege 15 and 1 respectively with `show privilege` where supported; the reviewer test must be before using `enable`. Test `telnet 10.8.1.1` and confirm that a terminal login is not admitted. While a proven SSH recovery session remains available, log out at the console prompt and verify a new local-user console login.

Inspect the line timeouts and all VTY ranges. Save with `copy running-config startup-config`, accept the filename prompt, and inspect `show startup-config`. The acceptance record should show operator privilege 15, reviewer privilege 1, fresh console authentication, SSH admission/Telnet rejection, correct console/VTY timeouts, and the saved intended policy. Record unsupported checks as limitations rather than invented output. Save this project separately from R1's guided baseline.
:::

questions.prompt: R1 uses ordinary local enable authentication. An enable secret and a different enable password both exist at privilege 15. Which credential permits the transition from `>` to `#`?
options: The password configured as the enable password
Either configured credential, tried in sequence
The password configured as the enable secret
The shared password under the console line
questions.explanation: For the same privilege level, the enable secret takes precedence over the enable password. This question assumes local enable authentication, with no AAA method list changing that behavior.

whyWrong.0: The enable secret takes precedence for the same level.
whyWrong.1: This local configuration does not fall back to the enable password.
whyWrong.3: Line authentication and the enable transition are separate.

questions.prompt: On traditional IOS, what does `service password-encryption` do to applicable cleartext password fields?
options: Stores those fields using reversible type 7 obfuscation
Replaces those fields with type 9 password verifiers
Encrypts terminal traffic for existing Telnet sessions
Converts the enable secret into a stronger hash
questions.explanation: The command obscures applicable cleartext password fields in the configuration. Type 7 is reversible, and removing the command does not automatically reveal plaintext for fields already converted.

whyWrong.1: That command does not select the scrypt algorithm for those fields.
whyWrong.2: Stored configuration formatting does not protect a Telnet session.
whyWrong.3: It does not upgrade the algorithm used by an enable secret.

questions.prompt: An IOS configuration contains `enable secret 5` followed by a stored verifier. What does the number identify?
options: The privilege level assigned to the enable session
The type of password verifier stored in the configuration
The number of failed logins permitted before disconnection
The minimum number of characters in the original password
questions.explanation: Type 5 identifies the legacy MD5-based verifier format. A one-way hash is still vulnerable to password guessing; do not describe it as impossible to crack or as a universal current default.

whyWrong.0: The type marker is not the requested privilege level.
whyWrong.2: Authentication retry settings are separate configuration.
whyWrong.3: The marker does not encode the original password length.

questions.prompt: A powered, normally running router has no usable IP interface. Which access method can still be used by an authorized technician with working credentials and the correct cable?
options: An SSH session to its previous interface address
An HTTPS session to its previous interface address
A Telnet session to its default gateway address
A direct connection to its serial console
questions.explanation: A direct serial console does not require a configured IP interface. Authentication and the console’s own operational state still matter, so this is not a claim that physical access bypasses credentials.

whyWrong.0: SSH requires an IP path to a currently reachable server address.
whyWrong.1: Web management also requires IP reachability.
whyWrong.2: The gateway is not a substitute for a reachable router management address.

questions.prompt: Which two identity settings are used by the conventional unnamed RSA-key workflow taught in this chapter? Choose two.
options: An available public DNS resolver
A configured nondefault hostname
An established Telnet session from the client
A configured management-interface IP address
A configured local domain name
questions.explanation: The conventional workflow uses a configured hostname and domain name for the device key identity. Other key-management forms exist, so this is a scoped workflow rather than a claim about every possible RSA command.

whyWrong.0: The identity settings do not require a live DNS query.
whyWrong.2: A Telnet session is not a key-generation prerequisite.
whyWrong.3: An IP address is needed for network reachability, but it is not one of the local identity settings used to generate this key pair.

questions.prompt: Which command saves the verified running configuration for the normal next boot?
options: `copy running-config startup-config`
`copy startup-config running-config`
`show startup-config`
`configure terminal`
questions.explanation: The direction of the copy matters: active configuration is the source, startup configuration the destination. The device’s persistent storage implementation may vary, but the active-versus-saved distinction remains.

whyWrong.1: That loads saved settings into the active configuration rather than saving active changes.
whyWrong.2: That displays the saved configuration without updating it.
whyWrong.3: That enters configuration mode without saving changes.

questions.prompt: With ordinary IOS privilege assignments, which two actions belong to privileged EXEC or require entering it first? Choose two.
options: Send a basic ping permitted in user EXEC
Read the device hostname from its prompt
Inspect the full running configuration
Enter a username at a login prompt
Enter global configuration mode
questions.explanation: Privileged EXEC provides access to configuration inspection and the entry point for configuration mode. Custom privilege or AAA policies can alter command access; this question uses the ordinary lab assignments.

whyWrong.0: A basic ping is normally available before privileged EXEC.
whyWrong.1: The prompt is visible without privileged access.
whyWrong.3: Logging in is separate from privileged EXEC.

questions.prompt: With local authentication and no custom authorization, which account and line combination begins a session at privilege 15?
options: A default-privilege local user on a line using `login local`
A shared line password with `login` and an enable secret
A local user with `secret` but no configured privilege
A privilege-15 local user on a line using `login local`
questions.explanation: Local user privilege and line authentication work together. A user configured with privilege 15 begins at privileged EXEC when authenticated by this local method.

whyWrong.0: The default local-user privilege is 1.
whyWrong.1: The existence of an enable secret does not by itself make line login start at privilege 15.
whyWrong.2: The secret controls password storage, not the initial privilege level.

questions.prompt: A client cannot obtain ping replies from R1, but a new SSH login to R1 succeeds. What does this evidence establish?
options: SSH access works even though this ICMP test did not receive replies
The successful SSH login proves ICMP is enabled on every interface
The failed ping proves the SSH session is connected to another subnet
The client must regenerate R1’s SSH host keys before continuing
questions.explanation: A service test answers a different question from a ping. Record the failed ICMP result separately; do not treat it as proof that all IP communication is broken.

whyWrong.1: SSH and ICMP are separate protocols and can be treated differently.
whyWrong.2: The ping result does not identify the subnet of an authenticated SSH session.
whyWrong.3: A successful session provides no basis for replacing the server keys.

exhibit.title: R1# show ip ssh — legacy image
exhibit.text:
SSH Enabled - version 1.99
Authentication timeout: 120 secs; Authentication retries: 3

questions.prompt: A legacy IOS image reports the SSH version shown. Which configuration restricts that server to SSHv2?
options: `transport input telnet` under the VTY lines
`service password-encryption` in global configuration mode
`ip ssh version 2` in global configuration mode
`login local` under the console and VTY lines
questions.explanation: On an image reporting this compatibility mode, version 1.99 indicates support for SSHv1 and SSHv2. Explicitly select version 2; do not assume every current image starts in this legacy mode.

whyWrong.0: That permits Telnet rather than selecting the SSH version.
whyWrong.1: That affects applicable stored passwords, not the SSH version.
whyWrong.3: That selects local authentication, not an SSH protocol version.

questions.prompt: Which two statements correctly distinguish management access methods? Choose two.
options: A direct serial console can work without a configured IP interface
SSH always proves that a physically separate management network is used
An HTTP management page protects credentials in the same way as HTTPS
TACACS+ and RADIUS support AAA decisions rather than replacing SSH
Cloud management requires every product to disable local access
questions.explanation: Console access does not depend on the device’s IP forwarding path. Central AAA can support authentication and authorization while the administrator still uses SSH for the terminal session.

whyWrong.1: Whether management is in-band or out-of-band depends on the network design.
whyWrong.2: HTTPS adds TLS; ordinary HTTP does not provide that protection.
whyWrong.4: Local access and recovery capabilities vary by product.

exhibit.title: Terminal sessions — representative excerpt
exhibit.text:
Line       User       Host(s)   Idle       Location
*  0 con 0                idle      00:00:00
   2 vty 0     admin      idle      00:00:05   10.8.0.10

questions.prompt: Which command most directly provides the terminal-session table shown, including the Location column?
options: `show ip ssh`
`show privilege`
`show users`
`show ip interface brief`
questions.explanation: The terminal-session table identifies active lines and users; remote sessions can include a client address under Location. The asterisk marks the session issuing the command.

whyWrong.0: That reports SSH server settings rather than this terminal-line table.
whyWrong.1: That reports the current session’s privilege level.
whyWrong.3: That reports interface addresses and state, not the users of terminal lines.

exhibit.title: Representative current mode
exhibit.text: R1(config)#

questions.prompt: The intended idle timeout is five minutes on VTY 0–4. You are at the prompt shown. Which next command selects the correct configuration context?
options: line vty 0 4
exec-timeout 5 0
interface gigabitethernet0/0
enable
questions.explanation: The global configuration prompt requires selecting the VTY lines before applying a line-specific timeout. Then enter exec-timeout 5 0 under the resulting config-line prompt.

whyWrong.1: The timeout belongs under line configuration, not directly at the shown global prompt.
whyWrong.2: An Ethernet interface is not the terminal-line context for an EXEC idle timeout.
whyWrong.3: Enable enters privileged EXEC from user EXEC; this session is already configuring the device.

questions.prompt: A previously trusted SSH server presents a different host key. A planned router replacement might explain it, but you have not verified the replacement record. What should you do before accepting the new key?
options: Accept the key because a successful IP test proves the server identity.
Verify the expected device and new key through the trusted management process.
Delete the old key record and retry with the same username and password.
Change the VTY transport to Telnet until the client stops reporting the warning.
questions.explanation: A legitimate replacement can change the host key, but the warning does not verify that explanation. Confirm the intended device and approved new identity before accepting it.

whyWrong.0: IP reachability does not authenticate the device presenting the key.
whyWrong.2: Deleting the record removes the comparison without resolving the identity question.
whyWrong.3: Switching to unprotected transport does not verify the server identity.

exhibit.title: Representative access checks
exhibit.text:
New SSH login: refused before authentication
Ping to management address: replies
SSH server: enabled, version 2.0
Local user: confirmed present
Only VTY range:
line vty 0 4
 login local
 transport input telnet

questions.prompt: Which narrow change meets the requirement to admit SSH and reject Telnet?
options: Replace local-user authentication with a shared VTY line password.
Replace transport input telnet with transport input ssh on the VTY range.
Create another administrator at privilege 15 in the local username database.
Save the current configuration, then repeat the same new-session test.
questions.explanation: The VTY range currently accepts Telnet only. Selecting SSH corrects the transport policy; verify a new session after the change and inspect any additional VTY ranges.

whyWrong.0: Changing the authentication method does not make this range accept SSH transport.
whyWrong.2: An additional user does not change the accepted transport.
whyWrong.3: Saving preserves the existing policy; it does not correct it.

exhibit.title: Abbreviated VTY configuration
exhibit.text:
line vty 0 4
 login local
 transport input ssh
line vty 5 15
 password 7 0822455D0A16
 login
 transport input telnet

questions.prompt: A device has VTY 0–15. Which problem is demonstrated by this abbreviated configuration?
options: Each VTY range needs its own independently generated SSH host key.
The ranges use different authentication methods and accept different transports.
The local username database applies only to the lowest numbered VTY range.
The higher VTY range inherits SSH-only policy when the first range is occupied.
questions.explanation: VTY 5–15 still permits Telnet with shared-line authentication. Apply the intended local-user and SSH policy to every available range; do not assume the policy on VTY 0–4 covers the rest.

whyWrong.0: One server key configuration can serve multiple VTY lines.
whyWrong.2: The database is not limited by line number; each line selects its authentication policy.
whyWrong.3: Each configured range retains its own transport settings.

exhibit.title: Representative console review and client evidence
exhibit.text:
ADMIN can reach R1 at its configured 10.8.0.1 address.
Hostname: R1
Local domain: not configured
RSA host-key inventory: no generated key pair
Local user admin: present, privilege 15
All VTY lines: login local; transport input ssh
SSH server: disabled

questions.prompt: R1 uses the conventional hostname/domain/RSA-key workflow. Which ordered correction addresses the missing SSH prerequisites without changing the working IP path or local login policy?
options: Set a reachable DNS server and default route, then retry the existing SSH server.
Create another privilege-15 user and save; the VTY settings generate the host key.
Replace login local with a line password, then permit SSH and Telnet together.
Set the local domain, generate the supported RSA host key, and require SSHv2.
questions.explanation: The working IP path and configured local user do not supply a host key. In the stated conventional workflow, configure the local domain before generating the supported RSA key, require SSHv2, and then verify the server and a fresh login. DNS resolution is not required merely to use the configured domain as identity data.

whyWrong.0: A DNS server and default route do not create the missing identity configuration or host key.
whyWrong.1: Another user duplicates authentication data; VTY transport selection does not generate an RSA key.
whyWrong.2: Changing authentication and allowing Telnet does not resolve the missing host key or meet SSH-only access.

exhibit.title: Representative console review and new-session test
exhibit.text:
Fresh SSH test: server reached; username/password authentication fails.
All VTY lines:
 login local
 transport input ssh
Complete username check: no username entries
AAA method lists: none configured
An enable secret exists; the console session remains open.

questions.prompt: Which correction addresses the failed login while preserving named-user authentication?
options: Add a shared line password while leaving the empty local database selected.
Change the interface subnet before another username/password attempt.
Use the enable secret as an implicit replacement for the missing username.
Create the intended local username and secret through the working console.
questions.explanation: The VTY lines request local-user authentication, but the local database has no accounts. Create the intended account through the working console, then verify a new remote session.

whyWrong.0: A shared line password is not the fallback for the local-user method.
whyWrong.1: The session already reaches authentication; the evidence identifies the local database.
whyWrong.2: The enable transition does not supply a missing login identity.

exhibit.title: Representative complete relevant VTY excerpts
exhibit.text:
RUNNING-CONFIG
line vty 0 4
 login local
 transport input ssh

STARTUP-CONFIG
line vty 0 4
 login local
 transport input telnet

Normal boot is configured to load startup-config.

questions.prompt: The policy requires SSH-only access after a normal reboot. Current new SSH succeeds and new Telnet is refused. What must be corrected before declaring the saved policy complete?
options: Generate another RSA key because running and startup transports differ.
Remove the local user because it appears in both configuration stores.
Save the verified running configuration and inspect the saved VTY policy.
Merge the startup configuration into running to make both stores agree.
questions.explanation: The desired active policy has been verified but is not reflected in startup-config. Save running to startup and inspect the result; agreement achieved by restoring the old Telnet policy would violate the requirement.

whyWrong.0: A differing saved transport is a persistence issue, not evidence of a missing or invalid host key.
whyWrong.1: The intended local account belongs in both active and saved configurations.
whyWrong.3: Merging the old saved VTY commands can restore the unwanted transport instead of preserving the verified policy.

exhibit.title: Representative policy review
exhibit.text:
REQUIREMENT
admin: initial privilege 15
auditor: initial privilege 1
Remote terminals: SSH only; local-user authentication
Only VTY lines 0–4 exist. No custom AAA authorization.

RUNNING-CONFIG
username admin privilege 15 secret <stored verifier>
username auditor privilege 15 secret <stored verifier>
line vty 0 4
 login local
 transport input telnet ssh

questions.prompt: Review the requirement and active configuration. Which pair of corrections meets the access policy while retaining the working admin account?
options: Set both local users to privilege 1 and leave both VTY transports enabled.
Delete auditor and replace login local with a shared line password.
Change the console timeout and save without changing the username or transports.
Set auditor to privilege 1 and restrict the VTY range to SSH.
questions.explanation: The requirement distinguishes initial privilege by local user and separately restricts the incoming transport. Correct auditor’s explicit privilege and the VTY transport, then test new auditor/admin sessions and Telnet refusal before saving.

whyWrong.0: Admin must still begin at privilege 15, and Telnet must be excluded.
whyWrong.1: Deleting the required named account and using a shared line password violates the policy.
whyWrong.2: The console timeout does not correct either demonstrated policy mismatch.

cards.front: What does the prompt R1(config-line)# identify?
cards.back: Line configuration mode, used for settings on the selected console or VTY lines. It is different from global configuration and privileged EXEC.

cards.front: How do `exit` and `end` differ in configuration mode?
cards.back: `exit` leaves the current configuration level; `end` returns to privileged EXEC.

cards.front: Running configuration versus startup configuration?
cards.back: Running is the active configuration; startup is the saved configuration read during normal boot. Traditional IOS exposes startup configuration through NVRAM; storage details vary.

cards.front: How do you save active changes for the next normal boot?
cards.back: `copy running-config startup-config`; `write memory` is a familiar alternative on supporting IOS devices.

cards.front: How should you determine which VTY lines to protect?
cards.back: Inspect `show line`, VTY sections in the configuration, and contextual help. Apply the intended policy to every available range; do not assume a fixed count by device family.

cards.front: What does `exec-timeout 5 0` configure?
cards.back: A five-minute idle EXEC timeout on the selected line. `exec-timeout 0 0` disables the idle timeout; choose settings deliberately.

cards.front: `login` with a line password versus `login local`?
cards.back: The former uses a shared line password; `login local` checks the local username database. Create the account before making the line depend on it.

cards.front: Enable secret and enable password at the same level: which is used?
cards.back: In the basic local enable configuration, the enable secret takes precedence. It is separate from the password used to log in to the line.

cards.front: Does `service password-encryption` secure Telnet?
cards.back: No. On traditional IOS it obscures applicable stored password fields with type 7. It does not encrypt the terminal session or upgrade an enable secret.

cards.front: Why does an SSH server need a host key?
cards.back: It supplies the server’s cryptographic identity for the protected session. A local username supplies authentication data; it does not create that host key.

cards.front: Which conventional TCP ports distinguish SSH and Telnet?
cards.back: SSH uses TCP 22; Telnet uses TCP 23. A port number is separate from the account and privilege used after connecting.

cards.front: Does a direct serial console require a working IP interface?
cards.back: No. It is a separate local management path, but the correct cable/settings and configured authentication are still required.

cards.front: How do show ssh and show ip ssh differ?
cards.back: show ssh reports SSH-session information; show ip ssh reports server configuration/state. Supported fields vary by image.

cards.front: Default local-user privilege and the effect of `privilege 15`?
cards.back: Default is 1. With basic local authentication, privilege 15 starts at privileged EXEC. `show privilege` verifies the current level.

cards.front: Which VTY command accepts SSH and excludes Telnet?
cards.back: `transport input ssh`. Apply and verify it on all intended VTY ranges.

cards.front: What should an unexpected SSH host-key change prompt you to do?
cards.back: Verify the server identity through a trusted record or management process before accepting the change. A key warning is not fixed by blindly trusting a new key.

cards.front: Does an enabled SSH server prove a user can log in?
cards.back: No. The IP path, compatible client/server algorithms, accepting VTY policy and valid authentication must also work. Test a new session.

cards.front: What does an IOS banner provide?
cards.back: An access notice or message. It does not authenticate the user; the chosen delimiter ends the text, and display timing can differ by protocol.

cards.front: Does the local domain used to generate an RSA key need a working DNS lookup?
cards.back: No. In the conventional workflow it supplies configured device identity data. This does not configure the client’s DNS or prove SSH reachability.

cards.front: What should you inspect after saving a verified access policy?
cards.back: Inspect startup-config for the intended user and line settings, including every VTY range. A save should preserve the repaired policy, not the deliberate fault.

cards.front: Does an existing SSH session verify a changed admission policy?
cards.back: No. Test a new session after the change and inspect every intended VTY range; an old session alone does not show that a new login is permitted.

cards.front: How do you verify the next console login while preserving recovery access?
cards.back: Keep a separately proven management session available, log out at the console prompt, then start a new console login. Reopening the terminal window alone may retain the old session.

commands.task: Set the local domain to lab.test for the conventional RSA-key workflow.

commands.note: Use contextual help on images with different syntax; an interactive modulus response is not a separate IOS command.

commands.task: Configure the SSH server to use version 2.
commands.note: Verify the reported version; older compatibility output and modern defaults may differ.

commands.task: Use local usernames to authenticate this line.
commands.note: Create a working user before making the line depend on the local database.

commands.task: Permit SSH as the only incoming VTY transport.

commands.task: Report the privilege level of the current session.

tickets.title: SSH server enabled, but remote sessions are refused
tickets.scenario: A change on an isolated lab router leaves its directly connected management PC able to ping 10.8.0.1. A new SSH session is refused. The account and key configuration are unchanged, and the console remains available. The complete VTY range is 0–4.

exhibits.title: R1# show ip ssh — excerpt
exhibits.text: SSH Enabled - version 2.0

exhibits.title: R1 VTY configuration
exhibits.text:
line vty 0 4
 login local
 transport input none

tickets.question: Which configuration is responsible for refusing new terminal sessions?
options: The unchanged host key must be regenerated for each new session.
The VTY range accepts no incoming transport despite the enabled server.
The valid local user needs a line password to supplement login local.
The active SSH configuration has to be saved before it can admit a login.
tickets.explanation: The VTY range explicitly selects transport input none; the reachable interface and enabled server do not override it. There is no evidence that the unchanged key needs replacement, and login local does not require a second shared line password. Saving the current configuration would preserve the fault rather than change active admission.
tickets.fix:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# line vty 0 4
R1(config-line)# transport input ssh
R1(config-line)# end
R1# show running-config | section line vty
```
Open a new SSH session from the management PC and verify its privilege. Save after the intended access works.

tickets.title: New sessions reach authentication but no local login succeeds
tickets.scenario: After a configuration cleanup, new SSH sessions reach username/password authentication but no intended local account is accepted. The working console remains open. The administrator collects the complete username check and VTY settings below; no AAA method lists exist.

exhibits.title: Complete username check
exhibits.text:
R1# show running-config | include username
R1#

exhibits.title: R1 VTY configuration
exhibits.text:
line vty 0 4
 login local
 transport input ssh

tickets.question: Which change restores the intended named-user authentication?
options: Replace SSH with Telnet while keeping the same empty local database.
Use the enable secret as an implicit local username credential.
Create the intended local username and secret through the console.
Save the current line configuration before retrying local authentication.
tickets.explanation: The selected login local method depends on the local username database, and the complete check shows no entries. Restore the intended account through the working console, then test a new session. Changing transport, using an enable secret or saving does not create the missing login identity.
tickets.fix:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# username admin privilege 15 secret AdminLabSecret8
R1(config)# end
```
Use this example secret only in the isolated lab. Verify a new SSH login, check show privilege, and save the corrected configuration.
