chapters.summary: Configure static 802.1Q trunks, interpret native and allowed VLAN settings, and diagnose a VLAN that cannot cross a link. Apply the same tagging rules to access points and virtual hosts.

sections.body:
VLANs separate Layer 2 traffic. A trunk lets you extend several of those VLANs across one Ethernet connection without joining their broadcast domains. This chapter builds on access-port membership: you will follow a frame across a trunk, configure both ends deliberately, and use the switch's evidence to distinguish a working link from a working VLAN.

Static 802.1Q configuration is the main skill. DTP is supporting knowledge for recognizing existing Cisco configurations. The endpoint examples teach the switch-side tagging requirements of APs, virtual hosts and appliances; their complete wireless, virtualization and security configurations come later.

sections.title: Why one link must carry many VLANs
sections.body:
:::facts
- An 802.1Q trunk carries the VLANs permitted and operational on that link.
- Tagging identifies a frame's VLAN; it does not route between VLANs.
- A normal 802.1Q tag adds **4 bytes**. Its VLAN ID field is **12 bits**.
- VLAN IDs **1–4094** are usable identifiers in the standard; platform reservations and VLAN support still apply.
- On the Catalyst configurations used here, the default native VLAN is **1**. Ordinary native-VLAN data is untagged unless native tagging is explicitly enabled on a supporting platform.
:::

Suppose SW1 has a PC in VLAN 10 and another in VLAN 20. SW2 has the same arrangement. Connecting an access port in VLAN 10 on each switch extends VLAN 10, but does nothing for VLAN 20. Two separate access links could carry the two VLANs, but that consumes another port and cable for every added VLAN. A trunk carries both on one connection while retaining their identities.

Follow a VLAN 20 frame from an ordinary PC. It enters SW1 without a VLAN tag. SW1 associates it with VLAN 20 because the receiving access port belongs to VLAN 20. If the destination is reachable through the trunk, SW1 transmits the frame with VLAN 20 identification. SW2 reads that identification, performs its Layer 2 forwarding decision within VLAN 20, and sends an untagged frame from the destination PC's access port.

```diagram
{"type":"topology","title":"Fig 10.1 — Two separate VLANs share one cable","caption":"PC-A reaches PC-C within VLAN 10; PC-B reaches PC-D within VLAN 20. The trunk does not connect VLAN 10 to VLAN 20.","nodes":[{"id":"a","kind":"pc","label":"PC-A","sub":"VLAN 10","x":1,"y":1},{"id":"b","kind":"pc","label":"PC-B","sub":"VLAN 20","x":1,"y":5},{"id":"s1","kind":"switch","label":"SW1","x":4,"y":3},{"id":"s2","kind":"switch","label":"SW2","x":8,"y":3},{"id":"c","kind":"pc","label":"PC-C","sub":"VLAN 10","x":11,"y":1},{"id":"d","kind":"pc","label":"PC-D","sub":"VLAN 20","x":11,"y":5}],"links":[{"from":"a","to":"s1","label":"access 10"},{"from":"b","to":"s1","label":"access 20"},{"from":"s1","to":"s2","label":"802.1Q: 10,20,99","accent":true},{"from":"s2","to":"c","label":"access 10"},{"from":"s2","to":"d","label":"access 20"}]}
```

VLAN-aware equipment can also send and receive tags. A router subinterface, an AP carrying locally switched client VLANs, or a virtual host may terminate a trunk. Conversely, a connection to a switch is not automatically a trunk. Select the port behavior from the traffic the peer must carry, then configure the peer to agree.

sections.title: The 802.1Q tag
sections.body:
The tag sits after the source MAC address and before the original EtherType field. It preserves the Ethernet source and destination addresses. Adding or removing the tag changes the frame contents, so the transmitter calculates the appropriate frame check sequence. An ordinary Ethernet frame with a 1,500-byte payload is 1,518 bytes from destination MAC through FCS; adding one tag makes that 1,522 bytes. This count excludes the preamble and start delimiter. Do not confuse the extra Layer 2 bytes with a larger IP payload.

```diagram
{"type":"bits","title":"Fig 10.2 — The four-byte 802.1Q tag","caption":"The VID carries VLAN identification. Priority and drop-eligibility fields serve different purposes.","fields":[{"label":"TPID","bits":16,"note":"0x8100"},{"label":"PCP","bits":3,"note":"priority 0–7"},{"label":"DEI","bits":1,"note":"drop eligibility"},{"label":"VID","bits":12,"note":"VLAN identifier","highlight":true}]}
```

The **tag protocol identifier**, or TPID, identifies the 802.1Q tag. The **priority code point** is a three-bit priority value; it does not choose a VLAN or guarantee that a packet receives priority throughout a network. The **drop eligible indicator** supports traffic treatment under congestion. The **VLAN identifier**, or VID, determines the tagged VLAN. Older documentation may call the one-bit field CFI; DEI is the terminology used here.

Twelve bits provide 4,096 numeric values. VID 0 is used for priority tagging without identifying a VLAN, and 4095 is reserved. That leaves identifiers 1 through 4094. This is an identifier range, not a promise that every switch supports 4,094 simultaneously active VLANs or allows you to create every number. For these labs, ordinary VLANs 10, 20, 30 and 99 avoid platform-specific reserved ranges.

sections.title: Native VLAN and untagged traffic
sections.body:
A receiving trunk needs a rule for a frame that has no VLAN tag. Under the default behavior used in this chapter, it assigns ordinary untagged data to the port's **native VLAN**. In the reverse direction, ordinary data belonging to that native VLAN leaves untagged. Data in the other allowed VLANs carries a tag. Configure native VLAN 99 at both ends and an untagged frame retains the intended VLAN 99 membership across the link.

A native mismatch breaks that agreement. If SW1 sends untagged VLAN 99 traffic but SW2 classifies untagged traffic as VLAN 999, the two switches interpret the same frame differently. This can misclassify traffic or trigger protective spanning-tree behavior. Cisco discovery protocols may report a mismatch, but the exact messages and consequences depend on the platform and features in use. Compare both ends instead of waiting for a particular warning.

| Setting | What it controls | What it does not establish |
|---|---|---|
| Native VLAN | Default classification and transmission of untagged data | Which VLAN contains an administrator |
| Management VLAN | Where device management IP connectivity is placed | Whether its frames must be untagged |
| Allowed VLAN list | Which VLANs are eligible to use a trunk | Whether each VLAN exists and is forwarding |
| Access VLAN | VLAN membership for ordinary data on an access port | Membership of all tagged traffic on a trunk |

Management traffic can be tagged. Calling VLAN 99 “management” does not make it native; setting it as native does not give any device an IP address. In the main lab, VLAN 99 is an unused native VLAN with no attached endpoints.

:::trap Native VLAN is a configuration agreement
Some platforms support explicit native-VLAN tagging. Those configurations change the default treatment described above and require compatible settings at the peer. Do not enable a new tagging feature or change a live native VLAN simply because an example uses VLAN 99. Establish the intended design and a recovery path first.
:::

sections.title: The allowed VLAN list
sections.body:
The **allowed list** is configured independently on each trunk port. It limits the VLANs eligible to cross that port. On the Catalyst defaults described by the cited guides, all supported VLAN IDs are allowed initially. Explicitly listing the required VLANs makes the intended connection easier to review. Both ends must permit a VLAN, and the VLAN must exist and be operational wherever the switching path needs it.

The difference between replacing and modifying a list matters. If the current list is `10,20,99`, the command `switchport trunk allowed vlan 30` replaces it with just 30. The command `switchport trunk allowed vlan add 30` preserves the existing list and adds 30. Likewise, `remove 20` removes only VLAN 20. The `all` keyword restores permission for all supported VLANs; it is not the intended restricted list for this lab. Before changing a live trunk, record its current list and identify which users and management sessions rely on it.

A configured VLAN can still be unable to forward. Think through three questions in order: is it allowed, is it active locally, and is this port forwarding it? Spanning tree may hold a redundant path out of forwarding to prevent a loop; you will learn those decisions in chapter 14. For now, recognize that physical link state and VLAN forwarding state are separate.

Removing VLAN 1 from the user VLAN list does not silence every link-control protocol. Cisco documents continued transmission of several control protocols despite that removal. Treat a VLAN filter as a user-traffic setting, not as a general instruction to disable discovery, negotiation or loop prevention.

sections.title: Configure a static trunk
sections.body:
A **static trunk** does not depend on a peer requesting trunk formation. The example below assumes VLANs 10, 20 and 99 already exist on both switches, and SW1 Gi0/1 connects to SW2 Gi0/1. Enter the same trunk settings on SW2. The full lab supplies both configurations.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# description Trunk-to-SW2-Gi0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 99
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,99
SW1(config-if)# switchport nonegotiate
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces trunk
SW1# show interfaces gigabitethernet0/1 switchport
```

The mode command establishes the local trunk configuration. The native and allowed commands define its VLAN behavior. `switchport nonegotiate` suppresses DTP messages; it does not disable 802.1Q tagging. `no shutdown` removes an administrative shutdown, but cannot fix a cable or power problem.

A Catalyst 2960 uses 802.1Q without an encapsulation-selection command. Some older interfaces that support a choice of trunk encapsulations require `switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q` before accepting static trunk mode. Use the actual interface's help and platform documentation; do not paste that selector into every model. ISL recognition is historical context, not a second trunk technology to deploy in this lab.

sections.title: Trunks to APs and virtual hosts
sections.body:
An AP does not require a trunk merely because it advertises several SSIDs. With centrally switched wireless traffic, client traffic may be tunneled to a controller while the AP's wired connection uses one access VLAN. With local switching, the AP can place client frames directly into local wired VLANs. If several such VLANs share its uplink, that uplink needs compatible tagging.

For a concrete local-switching design, assume the AP's management traffic is untagged in VLAN 100, staff clients are tagged 110, and guest clients are tagged 120. Configure the AP's native VLAN and WLAN-to-VLAN mappings to agree with those requirements. The switch-side template is:

```ios SW-EDGE
SW-EDGE# configure terminal
SW-EDGE(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
SW-EDGE(config-if)# description AP-management100-clients110-120
SW-EDGE(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
SW-EDGE(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 100
SW-EDGE(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 100,110,120
SW-EDGE(config-if)# switchport nonegotiate
SW-EDGE(config-if)# end
```

This template assumes those VLANs have been created and the port has suitable connectivity and power. It is not a complete wireless installation. If the AP instead tags management traffic, adjust the design accordingly; copying the untagged template would create a mismatch.

A **virtual host** runs virtual machines through a hypervisor. A virtual switch can associate a VM's virtual network adapter with a VLAN and carry multiple VLANs over the host's physical uplink. For example, assume the host explicitly tags management VLAN 100 and VM VLANs 110 and 120. Use a static trunk allowing `100,110,120`, with an agreed unused native VLAN such as 999. Do not make VLAN 100 native on the switch while the host expects its returning management frames tagged. A host serving only one untagged network may instead use an access port.

The same question applies to a firewall or other network appliance: does this particular interface expect one untagged network or several tagged logical interfaces? Match its documented interface configuration. Port aggregation, loop-protection features and complete appliance policy belong to later chapters; attaching several cables without understanding their forwarding design is not an extension of this single-link exercise.

sections.title: Recognize DTP negotiation
sections.body:
**Dynamic Trunking Protocol**, or DTP, is Cisco negotiation for trunk formation on supporting switch ports. It is distinct from 802.1Q, which identifies VLANs in frames. A device can understand 802.1Q without participating in DTP. Routers and ordinary virtual-host uplinks should therefore receive an explicitly configured switch trunk.

| Local mode | Meaning | Common peer result |
|---|---|---|
| `access` | Keep the local port nontrunking | Use for a single ordinary access VLAN |
| `trunk` | Keep the local port trunking | Configure the peer compatibly |
| `dynamic auto` | Willing to trunk if the peer initiates | Auto with auto remains nontrunking |
| `dynamic desirable` | Actively tries to negotiate a trunk | Desirable with auto can form a trunk |

These dynamic-mode results assume compatible, operational Cisco peers with DTP running. The cited Catalyst 2960 guide documents dynamic auto as its default; verify actual defaults rather than extending that claim to every Catalyst platform. `nonegotiate` is not another switchport mode. With static trunk mode, it stops sending negotiation messages while the trunk continues to carry tagged traffic.

For CCNA preparation, recognize why two passive ports do not form a trunk and why a non-DTP peer requires manual configuration. The lab deliberately builds static trunks. Memorizing negotiation timers, destination MAC addresses or every obsolete encapsulation combination adds little to that task.

sections.title: Verify and troubleshoot
sections.body:
Start with `show interfaces trunk`, then inspect a specific port with `show interfaces gigabitethernet0/1 switchport`. The first lists operational trunk information; the second helps compare configured and operational modes. If a configured trunk is absent from the first command, check the physical connection, administrative state and the detailed port output.

The following is a representative, abbreviated IOS-style example. Formatting, ranges and available fields vary by model and simulator release.

```output SW1# show interfaces trunk
Port        Mode         Encapsulation  Status        Native vlan
Gi0/1       on           802.1q         trunking      99  ← Check mode and native VLAN at both ends

Port        Vlans allowed on trunk
Gi0/1       10,20,30,99  ← Configured eligibility

Port        Vlans allowed and active in management domain
Gi0/1       10,20,99  ← VLAN 30 is not active locally

Port        Vlans in spanning tree forwarding state and not pruned
Gi0/1       10,20,99  ← These VLANs are forwarding on this local trunk
```

VLAN 30 is allowed but absent from the active list. Inspect `show vlan brief` before changing the trunk list: VLAN 30 may be absent or inactive locally. The output does not tell you which condition exists on SW2. If a VLAN is active but missing from the forwarding list, inspect its spanning-tree state and any applicable pruning configuration; do not assume the cable is broken.

Use endpoint tests to finish the diagnosis. If same-VLAN communication works locally but fails across the trunk, compare that VLAN's membership and forwarding along the link. If same-VLAN communication works across the trunk but communication to another VLAN fails, remember that no routing has been configured yet. A trunk extending VLANs is not an IP gateway.

sections.title: Exam focus
sections.body:
- Explain how tagging preserves VLAN identity across a shared link.
- Identify the four-byte tag, twelve-bit VID and usable identifier range.
- Configure static trunk mode and consistent native VLAN settings.
- Distinguish replacement of an allowed list from `add` and `remove`.
- Interpret allowed, active and forwarding VLAN lists separately.
- Match AP, host and appliance tagging to the peer's actual requirements.
- Recognize DTP auto/desirable behavior and the purpose of `nonegotiate`.
- Diagnose a specific VLAN with evidence from both ends and endpoint tests.

lab.title: Build and diagnose a static trunk
devices: Optional: 2 additional PC-PT for the challenge
lab.intro:
Build two working VLANs across one trunk. Then remove one allowed VLAN and introduce a native mismatch, recording each fault before restoring it. A final disconnected-port exercise applies trunk settings to an AP design.

Use a fresh Packet Tracer file and the devices' CLI tabs, which provide console access independent of the trunk. If the initial configuration dialog appears, answer `no` and press Enter. These instructions use the Packet Tracer 2960 model's `FastEthernet0/1`, `FastEthernet0/2` and `GigabitEthernet0/1` interfaces. Inspect the selected model before wiring. The examples were checked against Cisco documentation; this exact lab has not been executed in Packet Tracer. Treat shown output as representative and use the stated configuration and connectivity checks if the display differs.


Practice revised September 2026. If you completed an earlier version, repeat the revised exercise and update its checkmarks.
lab.topology:
```diagram
{"type":"topology","title":"Lab 10 — Four PCs across one static trunk","caption":"Each VLAN has one PC on each switch. No router or default gateway is needed for same-subnet tests.","nodes":[{"id":"a","kind":"pc","label":"PC-A","sub":"192.168.10.11","x":1,"y":1},{"id":"b","kind":"pc","label":"PC-B","sub":"192.168.20.11","x":1,"y":5},{"id":"s1","kind":"switch","label":"SW1","x":4,"y":3},{"id":"s2","kind":"switch","label":"SW2","x":8,"y":3},{"id":"c","kind":"pc","label":"PC-C","sub":"192.168.10.12","x":11,"y":1},{"id":"d","kind":"pc","label":"PC-D","sub":"192.168.20.12","x":11,"y":5}],"links":[{"from":"a","to":"s1","toLabel":"Fa0/1"},{"from":"b","to":"s1","toLabel":"Fa0/2"},{"from":"s1","to":"s2","fromLabel":"Gi0/1","toLabel":"Gi0/1","label":"trunk 10,20,99"},{"from":"s2","to":"c","fromLabel":"Fa0/1"},{"from":"s2","to":"d","fromLabel":"Fa0/2"}]}
```

| Device / port | Peer / port | VLAN | Address / mask |
|---|---|---|---|
| PC-A FastEthernet0 | SW1 Fa0/1 | 10 | `192.168.10.11 / 255.255.255.0` |
| PC-B FastEthernet0 | SW1 Fa0/2 | 20 | `192.168.20.11 / 255.255.255.0` |
| PC-C FastEthernet0 | SW2 Fa0/1 | 10 | `192.168.10.12 / 255.255.255.0` |
| PC-D FastEthernet0 | SW2 Fa0/2 | 20 | `192.168.20.12 / 255.255.255.0` |
| SW1 Gi0/1 | SW2 Gi0/1 | Trunk 10,20,99; native 99 | No IP address |

Use copper straight-through cables for PC-to-switch links and a copper crossover cable for the switch-to-switch link. Packet Tracer's automatic connection tool is an alternative if it selects the intended ports. Leave every PC's gateway and DNS fields blank. VLAN 99 has no host; it is the agreed unused native VLAN.

steps.title: Cable, address and name the devices
steps.body:
Place and connect the devices as listed. On each PC, open Desktop → IP Configuration, select Static, and enter its address and mask. Open Desktop → Command Prompt and run `ipconfig` to check your entries.

Name the switches from their CLI tabs. A new switch initially displays `Switch>`.

```ios SW1
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW1
SW1(config)# end
SW1# show interfaces status
```

```ios SW2
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW2
SW2(config)# end
SW2# show interfaces status
```

:::expected
The three cabled ports on each switch should establish a physical connection. Initial amber indicators may reflect spanning-tree startup; allow the simulator to advance before testing. Confirm that the port names match the table. Do not expect the default interswitch connection to carry VLANs 10 and 20 yet.
:::

steps.title: Create the VLANs and access ports
steps.body:
Create the same three VLANs locally on both switches. Explicit access mode removes dependence on default negotiation settings at the PC ports.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# vlan 10
SW1(config-vlan)# name USERS10
SW1(config-vlan)# exit
SW1(config)# vlan 20
SW1(config-vlan)# name USERS20
SW1(config-vlan)# exit
SW1(config)# vlan 99
SW1(config-vlan)# name UNUSED-NATIVE
SW1(config-vlan)# exit
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 10
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# exit
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/2
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 20
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show vlan brief
```

```ios SW2
SW2# configure terminal
SW2(config)# vlan 10
SW2(config-vlan)# name USERS10
SW2(config-vlan)# exit
SW2(config)# vlan 20
SW2(config-vlan)# name USERS20
SW2(config-vlan)# exit
SW2(config)# vlan 99
SW2(config-vlan)# name UNUSED-NATIVE
SW2(config-vlan)# exit
SW2(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
SW2(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW2(config-if)# switchport access vlan 10
SW2(config-if)# no shutdown
SW2(config-if)# exit
SW2(config)# interface fastethernet0/2
SW2(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW2(config-if)# switchport access vlan 20
SW2(config-if)# no shutdown
SW2(config-if)# end
SW2# show vlan brief
```

:::expected
Each switch lists VLAN 10 with Fa0/1 and VLAN 20 with Fa0/2. VLAN 99 exists and is active, with no PC access port. VLAN names are helpful labels; matching VLAN IDs are what preserve membership across the trunk.
:::

steps.title: Configure the trunk at both ends
steps.body:
Enter the complete settings on SW1, then SW2. Use the console tabs throughout; transient differences while configuring the two ends will not disconnect your console.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# description Trunk-to-SW2-Gi0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 99
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,99
SW1(config-if)# switchport nonegotiate
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces trunk
```

```ios SW2
SW2# configure terminal
SW2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW2(config-if)# description Trunk-to-SW1-Gi0/1
SW2(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
SW2(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 99
SW2(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,99
SW2(config-if)# switchport nonegotiate
SW2(config-if)# no shutdown
SW2(config-if)# end
SW2# show interfaces trunk
```

:::expected
Gi0/1 is an operational 802.1Q trunk with native VLAN 99 at both ends. The allowed list is 10,20,99. After startup convergence, those active VLANs should also appear in the forwarding list for this single interswitch path. The 2960 does not need an encapsulation-selection command. If your simulator rejects a command, record the model and rejection; do not substitute dynamic mode for the static trunk.
:::

steps.title: Prove a working baseline
steps.body:
Before the first test, predict both same-VLAN results and PC-A's result to PC-D. For a VLAN 20 frame, identify which two links carry untagged access traffic and which link carries its 802.1Q tag. Then test your predictions.

From PC-A's Command Prompt, ping PC-C. From PC-B, ping PC-D. Repeat after initial address resolution if the first echo is lost.

```text PC-A
ping 192.168.10.12
```

```text PC-B
ping 192.168.20.12
```

After generating traffic, inspect both switches:

```ios SW1
SW1# show interfaces trunk
SW1# show mac address-table
```

```ios SW2
SW2# show interfaces trunk
SW2# show mac address-table
```

:::expected
Both same-VLAN pairs communicate. SW1 learns PC-A and PC-B on their local access ports and remote PC-C and PC-D through Gi0/1, in their respective VLANs. A ping from PC-A to 192.168.20.12 is expected to fail: the destination is off subnet and there is no gateway. Record the successful tests and save the Packet Tracer file as `10-trunk-working.pkt` using File → Save As. This is a working checkpoint, not yet a startup-configuration save.
:::

For the VLAN 20 path, the PC-to-switch access links carry ordinary untagged frames. The interswitch trunk carries VLAN 20 tagged because its native VLAN is 99.

steps.title: Remove VLAN 20 and record the fault
steps.body:
Save a separate working copy as `10-trunk-experiments.pkt`. Write which client pair should be affected and which should remain usable. On SW1 only, remove VLAN 20 from the trunk. Do not repair it until you have collected evidence.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan remove 20
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces trunk
```

Repeat the two successful pings from step 4 and inspect SW2's trunk list.

```ios SW2
SW2# show interfaces trunk
```

:::expected
PC-A to PC-C still works; PC-B to PC-D fails. SW1's allowed list is now 10,99, while SW2 still allows 10,20,99. The link can remain up and trunking. Record those three facts together: physical operation, a VLAN-specific failure, and different allowed lists. A successful VLAN 10 ping does not prove VLAN 20 is permitted.
:::

steps.title: Restore VLAN 20 without replacing the list
steps.body:
Add VLAN 20 back on SW1. Predict the final list before entering the command.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan add 20
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces trunk
```

:::expected
The list again contains 10,20,99. After the VLAN is forwarding, both same-VLAN ping pairs succeed. `add 20` preserves VLANs 10 and 99; a bare `allowed vlan 20` would remove them. Check both pairs before moving to the next fault.
:::

steps.title: Introduce a native mismatch and inspect both ends
steps.body:
Change SW2's native VLAN to 999 while leaving SW1 at 99. Create VLAN 999 locally and allow it so its local existence is not an additional fault. Before the commands, predict the VLAN into which SW2 would classify an ordinary untagged frame from SW1. This exercise observes a configuration mismatch; no endpoint uses the native VLAN, so a particular ping failure is not required.

```ios SW2
SW2# configure terminal
SW2(config)# vlan 999
SW2(config-vlan)# name TEMP-NATIVE-FAULT
SW2(config-vlan)# exit
SW2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW2(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan add 999
SW2(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 999
SW2(config-if)# end
SW2# show interfaces gigabitethernet0/1 switchport
SW2# show interfaces trunk
```

```ios SW1
SW1# show interfaces gigabitethernet0/1 switchport
SW1# show interfaces trunk
```

:::expected
The explicit evidence is native VLAN 99 on SW1 versus 999 on SW2. If CDP warnings or spanning-tree protection appear, record them; their exact behavior is platform dependent. Tagged VLAN tests may continue working or be affected by protective behavior. Explain the fundamental fault: an ordinary untagged frame sent as VLAN 99 by SW1 would be classified into VLAN 999 by SW2. Do not disable spanning tree to make the symptom disappear.
:::

steps.title: Restore the native agreement
steps.body:
Restore the intended native VLAN and allowed list on SW2. Remove the temporary VLAN only after the port no longer uses it.

```ios SW2
SW2# configure terminal
SW2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW2(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 99
SW2(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan remove 999
SW2(config-if)# exit
SW2(config)# no vlan 999
SW2(config)# end
SW2# show interfaces trunk
```

:::expected
Both ends again use native VLAN 99 and allow 10,20,99. Allow convergence and repeat both successful baseline pings. If either pair still fails, compare both ends and PC settings with the working checkpoint before adding any new configuration.
:::

steps.title: Prepare a disconnected AP port
steps.body:
Leave SW1 Gi0/2 uncabled and administratively shut down. Configure only the switch side of an AP design: untagged management VLAN 100 and tagged client VLANs 110 and 120. This is a configuration inspection exercise; it does not simulate a FlexConnect AP. Write the required mode, native VLAN, allowed list and DTP setting before opening the reference. Then apply it to the disconnected port and record what configuration can prove without a working link.

:::solution Switch-side reference

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# vlan 100
SW1(config-vlan)# name AP-MANAGEMENT
SW1(config-vlan)# exit
SW1(config)# vlan 110
SW1(config-vlan)# name WIRELESS-STAFF
SW1(config-vlan)# exit
SW1(config)# vlan 120
SW1(config-vlan)# name WIRELESS-GUEST
SW1(config-vlan)# exit
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
SW1(config-if)# shutdown
SW1(config-if)# description Prepared-AP-untagged100-tagged110-120
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 100
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 100,110,120
SW1(config-if)# switchport nonegotiate
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces gigabitethernet0/2 switchport
SW1# show running-config
```

The administrative configuration is trunk, native 100, allowed 100,110,120, with DTP disabled. The disconnected, shut port is not an operational trunk. Write down the AP-side requirements: management untagged in 100, staff clients tagged 110, guests tagged 120. None of those VLANs has been extended over Gi0/1 or given a gateway, so the prepared port alone cannot deliver a wireless service. For a virtual host that tags all three VLANs, use an agreed unused native VLAN instead; leave this AP exercise unchanged.
:::

steps.title: Save the restored configuration
steps.body:
Verify the main trunk and both baseline pings once more. Save each switch from privileged EXEC mode, completing the interactive prompt before moving to the next device.

```ios SW1
SW1# copy running-config startup-config
```

If asked `Destination filename [startup-config]?`, press Enter. Wait for the completion message and the `SW1#` prompt.

```ios SW2
SW2# copy running-config startup-config
```

Complete the same destination prompt. Then save the Packet Tracer file as `10-trunk-complete.pkt`.

:::expected
The saved configuration has a working Gi0/1 trunk on each switch and a deliberately shut, disconnected AP preparation port on SW1. No temporary native mismatch remains. Keep your fault observations alongside the file so you can explain why the repairs worked without looking at the commands.
:::

Submit the following evidence before completion:

| Outcome | Evidence |
|---|---|
| VLAN frame path | Access versus trunk tagging for one predicted exchange |
| Healthy trunk | Allowed, active and forwarding sets at both ends |
| Selective failure | Failed VLAN 20 test and unaffected VLAN 10 test |
| Native agreement | Both native IDs and the predicted untagged classification |
| Recovery | Original tests restored before saving |
| Changed requirement | Independently add VLAN 30 while all original services remain usable |

lab.troubleshooting:
- No physical connection: inspect exact ports, cable type, power and administrative shutdown before VLAN settings.
- One VLAN fails across the trunk: compare its access membership, allowed list, local VLAN existence and forwarding at both switches.
- Gi0/2 is missing from operational trunks: expected in step 9 because it is shut and uncabled; inspect its administrative configuration.
- Pings between different VLANs fail: expected in this lab because no inter-VLAN gateway exists.
- First ping partly fails: repeat after ARP resolution and spanning-tree startup. Persistent failure needs investigation.
- A native mismatch produces a different warning or state: rely on the demonstrated settings at both ends, not a memorized message.
lab.challenge:
Add PC-E on SW1 Fa0/3 and PC-F on SW2 Fa0/3 using straight-through cables. Put them in VLAN 30 with `192.168.30.11/24` and `192.168.30.12/24`, leaving gateways blank. Extend VLAN 30 over the existing trunk without removing any current VLAN. Write your required VLAN database, access-port and trunk changes before opening the solution. Predict the final allowed lists and native setting. Prove all three same-VLAN pairs communicate, then save a separate challenge file.

:::solution
Create VLAN 30 and assign Fa0/3 on **both** switches. Add 30 to both existing allowed lists; leave native VLAN 99 unchanged.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# vlan 30
SW1(config-vlan)# name USERS30
SW1(config-vlan)# exit
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/3
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 30
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# exit
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan add 30
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces trunk
```

```ios SW2
SW2# configure terminal
SW2(config)# vlan 30
SW2(config-vlan)# name USERS30
SW2(config-vlan)# exit
SW2(config)# interface fastethernet0/3
SW2(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW2(config-if)# switchport access vlan 30
SW2(config-if)# no shutdown
SW2(config-if)# exit
SW2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW2(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan add 30
SW2(config-if)# end
SW2# show interfaces trunk
```

Both allowed lists become 10,20,30,99. PC-E should ping 192.168.30.12 after convergence; the original VLAN 10 and 20 pairs must still pass. VLAN 30 does not need a router for these same-subnet tests.
:::

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the VLAN identifier in an ordinary 802.1Q tag?
options: It is 16 bits, providing VLAN IDs 1 through 65534.
It is 12 bits, with usable VLAN identifiers 1 through 4094.
It is 8 bits, providing VLAN IDs 1 through 254.
It is 32 bits, with one separate identifier for each IP subnet.
questions.explanation: The VID is a 12-bit field. Values 0 and 4095 have special or reserved meaning, leaving identifiers 1–4094; individual platforms can impose additional restrictions.

whyWrong.0: The 16-bit TPID identifies the tag format, not the VLAN.
whyWrong.2: The VID has 12 bits, not eight.
whyWrong.3: The complete tag is 32 bits; VLAN identification is only part of it.

questions.prompt: Two operational Cisco switch ports are explicitly set to dynamic auto, with no other trunk-forcing configuration. What does their DTP interaction normally produce?
options: A trunk because each side advertises willingness to trunk.
An error-disabled link caused by a negotiation conflict.
A nontrunking link because neither side initiates trunk negotiation.
A trunk carrying only the common native VLAN.
questions.explanation: Dynamic auto is a passive negotiation mode. Auto paired with auto does not initiate the exchange needed to make the link a trunk.

whyWrong.0: Willingness alone is insufficient when both sides are passive.
whyWrong.1: This combination is a normal nontrunking outcome, not an error-disable trigger.
whyWrong.3: A single native VLAN is not the result of a partly negotiated trunk.

questions.prompt: Which two statements correctly describe switchport nonegotiate on a supported statically configured trunk? (Choose two.)
options: It suppresses DTP messages sent by the port.
It removes 802.1Q tags from all transmitted frames.
It requires both ends to use the same access VLAN.
It changes the native VLAN to VLAN 1.
It leaves the static trunk able to carry tagged VLAN traffic.
questions.explanation: The command controls DTP transmission, not the data-plane tag format. A static trunk can continue carrying its configured VLANs without negotiating them with a peer.

whyWrong.1: Disabling DTP does not disable 802.1Q tagging.
whyWrong.2: A trunk's allowed and native VLAN settings matter; matching access VLANs is not this command's requirement.
whyWrong.3: The native VLAN remains whatever the trunk configuration specifies.

questions.prompt: An engineer removes VLAN 1 from a Catalyst trunk's allowed list. Which conclusion is justified?
options: All Cisco discovery and negotiation messages stop on the link.
The trunk's native VLAN automatically becomes the lowest allowed VLAN.
VLAN 1 user forwarding is restricted, but some link-control protocols can still operate.
The trunk becomes an access port in its configured native VLAN.
questions.explanation: The allowed list controls VLAN forwarding eligibility. Cisco documents continued operation of several link-control protocols when VLAN 1 is removed; use each feature's own configuration to control it.

whyWrong.0: Removing a user VLAN does not disable every control protocol.
whyWrong.1: Native VLAN selection is a separate setting.
whyWrong.3: An allowed-list modification does not change static trunk mode.

exhibit.title: Representative excerpt — SW1# show interfaces trunk
exhibit.text:
Port        Mode         Encapsulation  Status        Native vlan
Gi0/1       on           802.1q         trunking      99

Port        Vlans allowed on trunk
Gi0/1       10,20,30,99

Port        Vlans allowed and active in management domain
Gi0/1       10,20,99

Port        Vlans in spanning tree forwarding state and not pruned
Gi0/1       10,20,99

questions.prompt: VLAN 30 cannot cross SW1's trunk. Which local condition does the exhibit establish?
options: VLAN 30 is allowed but is not active locally.
VLAN 30 is missing from the configured allowed list.
VLAN 30 is active but held out of forwarding by STP.
VLAN 30 is the trunk's untagged native VLAN.
questions.explanation: The first list includes VLAN 30, while the active list does not. Check the local VLAN database for an absent or inactive VLAN before changing the allowed list.

whyWrong.1: VLAN 30 is explicitly present in the allowed list.
whyWrong.2: It is absent from the active list, so the exhibit does not isolate STP as the cause.
whyWrong.3: The configured native VLAN is 99, not 30.

questions.prompt: A compatible Cisco peer is in dynamic auto with DTP enabled. Which two local modes can make that link become a trunk through DTP? (Choose two.)
options: Static access
Dynamic auto
Static trunk with DTP enabled
Dynamic desirable
Static access with VLAN 99
questions.explanation: Dynamic desirable actively negotiates. Static trunk with DTP running advertises a trunking state that a compatible auto peer can accept; manual trunk mode on both ends remains the clearer operational design.

whyWrong.0: Static access keeps the local port nontrunking.
whyWrong.1: Two auto ports are both passive.
whyWrong.4: Changing an access VLAN does not change the port into a trunk.

exhibit.title: Configuration excerpts from the two trunk ports
exhibit.text:
SW1 Gi0/1:

SW2 Gi0/1:

questions.prompt: The intended unused native VLAN is 99 at both ends. Which single change restores that agreement?
options: On SW1, change its allowed list to VLAN 999 only.
On SW2, add VLAN 99 as an access VLAN.
On SW1, change its switchport mode to dynamic auto.
On SW2, set switchport trunk native vlan 99.
questions.explanation: Native membership is configured per trunk port. Restoring SW2's native value to 99 makes its treatment of ordinary untagged data agree with SW1 and the stated design.

whyWrong.0: An allowed-list change does not set the intended native VLAN.
whyWrong.1: An access-VLAN command does not select the operational trunk's native VLAN.
whyWrong.2: Changing negotiation mode does not repair native VLAN agreement.

questions.prompt: Gi0/1 currently allows VLANs 10,20,99. Which command adds VLAN 30 while preserving that list?
options: switchport access vlan 30
switchport trunk allowed vlan 30
switchport trunk allowed vlan add 30
switchport trunk native vlan 30
questions.explanation: The add keyword modifies the existing list. A bare allowed-vlan list replaces the current selection, potentially interrupting existing users.

whyWrong.0: This selects access-port membership, not the trunk's allowed list.
whyWrong.1: This replaces the list with only VLAN 30.
whyWrong.3: This changes the native VLAN and does not add VLAN 30 to the allowed list.

exhibit.title: Representative older-platform configuration rejection
exhibit.text:
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
Command rejected: An interface whose trunk encapsulation is "Auto" can not be configured to "trunk" mode.

questions.prompt: On this older interface, command help confirms an encapsulation selector is supported. Which command addresses the displayed rejection before retrying static trunk mode?
options: switchport trunk native vlan 1
switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q
switchport nonegotiate
switchport access vlan 10
questions.explanation: An interface that supports an encapsulation choice may require a fixed encapsulation before static trunk mode. This is a platform-specific selector; a 2960's 802.1Q-only interface does not need it.

whyWrong.0: The native VLAN does not select the trunk encapsulation.
whyWrong.2: Suppressing DTP does not choose the encapsulation required by this rejection.
whyWrong.3: Access membership does not resolve an encapsulation choice.

questions.prompt: A trunk uses default native-VLAN treatment with native VLAN 99. It receives an ordinary untagged data frame. How does the switch classify that frame?
options: Into VLAN 1 because the frame has no explicit VID.
Into the access VLAN configured on that same trunk port.
Into every VLAN in the trunk's allowed list.
Into VLAN 99 according to the receiving trunk's native setting.
questions.explanation: Under the specified default behavior, the native VLAN supplies the membership for ordinary untagged data. The receiving port's configuration determines that classification.

whyWrong.0: VLAN 1 is a default native value, not an override of a configured native VLAN.
whyWrong.1: The native setting, not the access-VLAN setting, classifies ordinary untagged data on an operational trunk.
whyWrong.2: A frame is not assigned simultaneously to all allowed VLANs.

exhibit.title: Configured trunk settings
exhibit.text:
SW1 Gi0/1: mode trunk; native 99; allowed 10,99
SW2 Gi0/1: mode trunk; native 99; allowed 10,20,99

questions.prompt: VLANs 10 and 20 exist and are active on both switches, and the PC access assignments are correct. VLAN 10 works across the link, but VLAN 20 does not. What does this configuration show?
options: SW1 classifies all tagged VLAN 20 data into native VLAN 99.
SW1's trunk omits VLAN 20 from its allowed list.
The static trunks require DTP before they can carry VLAN 20.
SW2 has no active local VLAN 20 to receive the tagged traffic.
questions.explanation: The two ends do not both permit VLAN 20. Add 20 to SW1's existing list, then verify forwarding and repeat the VLAN 20 traffic test.

whyWrong.0: The native rule applies to the stated ordinary untagged traffic, not every tagged VLAN.
whyWrong.2: Static compatible trunks can carry data without DTP negotiation.
whyWrong.3: The question verifies VLAN 20 active on both switches.

questions.prompt: A standard untagged Ethernet frame is 1,518 bytes from destination MAC through FCS. What is its length after one four-byte 802.1Q tag is added, with the payload unchanged?
options: 1,522 bytes
1,514 bytes
1,526 bytes
1,500 bytes
questions.explanation: Adding one four-byte tag produces 1,522 bytes. The IP payload does not become four bytes larger, and the count given excludes preamble and start delimiter.

whyWrong.1: The tag adds bytes instead of removing four.
whyWrong.2: That adds eight bytes rather than the single tag's four.
whyWrong.3: 1,500 bytes describes the usual maximum payload in this example, not the complete frame.

questions.prompt: An ordinary PC should use only untagged VLAN 10 traffic and must not negotiate a trunk. Which port configuration fits?
options: switchport mode dynamic desirable; switchport access vlan 10
switchport mode access; switchport access vlan 10
switchport mode trunk; switchport trunk native vlan 10
switchport mode dynamic auto; switchport trunk allowed vlan 10
questions.explanation: Static access mode defines a nontrunking port, and the access-VLAN command assigns ordinary data to VLAN 10. This matches the PC's single untagged network requirement.

whyWrong.0: Desirable actively attempts to form a trunk.
whyWrong.2: A trunk remains a trunk even if its native VLAN matches the PC's intended VLAN.
whyWrong.3: Dynamic auto leaves trunk negotiation possible with a suitable peer.

questions.prompt: The AP requires untagged management VLAN 100 and tagged local client VLANs 110 and 120. Which switch-side change fixes the shown configuration?
options: Set the port to access VLAN 100.
Remove VLAN 100 from the allowed list.
Set the native VLAN to 110.
Set the native VLAN to 100.
questions.explanation: The port already permits all required VLANs, but ordinary untagged management traffic must be classified into VLAN 100. Client VLANs 110 and 120 remain tagged.

whyWrong.0: One access VLAN would not carry the two specified tagged client VLANs.
whyWrong.1: Removing management VLAN eligibility would not correct its classification.
whyWrong.2: That would classify untagged management traffic into the staff client VLAN.

exhibit.text:
Management interface: VLAN 100 tagged
VM group A: VLAN 110 tagged
VM group B: VLAN 120 tagged
No service uses untagged traffic; unused native VLAN 999 agreed.

questions.prompt: A virtual host expects management VLAN 100 and VM VLANs 110 and 120 to remain tagged on its uplink. With default native treatment, which matching switch profile avoids untagging a required VLAN?
options: Allow 100,110,120 and use an agreed unused native VLAN 999.
Allow 100,110,120 and make management VLAN 100 native.
Use access VLAN 110 because the virtual switch handles all VLANs.
Allow only VLAN 999 and make management VLAN 100 native.
questions.explanation: The host explicitly expects all three required VLANs tagged. Keeping the native VLAN outside that set preserves their tagging under the specified default behavior.

whyWrong.1: Management frames in the native VLAN would leave the switch untagged.
whyWrong.2: A single access VLAN cannot transport the required three tagged networks.
whyWrong.3: The required VLANs are absent from that allowed list.

questions.prompt: A firewall's Ethernet interface is configured with logical interfaces for tagged VLANs 10 and 20. It does not use DTP. What should you configure on the connected switch port?
options: Dynamic auto with access VLAN 10.
A routed switch port with no switchport and no IP address.
A static trunk permitting VLANs 10 and 20, with matching native treatment.
An access port in VLAN 20 with an additional allowed list.
questions.explanation: The peer requires multiple tagged VLANs, so the switch must provide a compatible static trunk. The appliance's documented tagging requirements determine the profile; its product category alone does not.

whyWrong.0: Auto relies on negotiation that this peer does not provide.
whyWrong.1: A routed port is not the Layer 2 trunk required by the peer's tagged logical interfaces.
whyWrong.3: An allowed list does not turn an access port into a trunk.

Vlans allowed: 10,20,99
Vlans allowed and active: 10,20,99

questions.prompt: What does the absence of VLAN 20 from only the last list establish?
options: VLAN 20 is not currently eligible to forward on this port.
VLAN 20 was removed from the configured allowed list.
VLAN 20 is absent from the local VLAN database.
VLAN 20 is being forwarded without an 802.1Q tag.
questions.explanation: The VLAN is allowed and active but missing from the effective forwarding list. Inspect its forwarding state and pruning evidence before naming the cause; the list alone does not distinguish them.

whyWrong.1: It appears in the configured allowed list.
whyWrong.2: It appears in the allowed-and-active list.
whyWrong.3: The lists do not make VLAN 20 native; the native VLAN is 99.

Gi0/2 interface state: administratively down

questions.prompt: The new link is approved for service, its peer is configured compatibly, and the cable is connected. Which next action follows from these checks?
options: Recreate VLANs 10 and 20 because native VLAN 99 prevents trunking.
Replace the allowed list with all VLANs to make the port operational.
Assign an IP address directly to the Layer 2 trunk interface.
Enable Gi0/2 with no shutdown, then verify its actual operational state.
questions.explanation: Administrative shutdown explains why a configured trunk is not operational. Enable the approved port, then check physical connection, trunk state and required VLANs rather than assuming the command itself proves success.

whyWrong.0: An unused native VLAN does not prevent the configured static trunk.
whyWrong.1: Expanding the list does not remove shutdown.
whyWrong.2: A Layer 2 trunk does not need a routed-interface IP address.

questions.prompt: Assume ordinary default native treatment and no protective blocking. SW1 sends a data frame from its native VLAN 99. SW2's native VLAN is 999; both IDs are allowed and active at both ends. Which two statements follow? Choose two.
options: SW1 sends this native-VLAN frame without an 802.1Q tag.
SW1 changes the frame's source MAC to identify VLAN 99.
SW2 uses VLAN 99 because the sender's original membership is retained invisibly.
SW2 classifies the received untagged frame into VLAN 999.
SW2 puts the frame into both native VLANs simultaneously.
questions.explanation: The sending port omits the native tag under the stated rule, and the receiving port assigns ordinary untagged data to its own native VLAN. The frame has no hidden VID that corrects the mismatch.

whyWrong.1: VLAN tagging does not require replacing the source MAC.
whyWrong.2: An untagged frame does not carry the sender's VLAN ID.
whyWrong.4: Ordinary ingress classification selects the receiving native VLAN.

questions.prompt: SW1 uses static trunk mode and nonegotiate. SW2 is dynamic auto and remains nontrunking. Both must carry VLANs 10 and 20 with native 99. Which design correction establishes the intended trunk without relying on DTP?
options: Configure SW2 as a static trunk with the matching native/allowed settings.
Change SW1's native VLAN to SW2's access VLAN without changing modes.
Keep both modes and clear the dynamic MAC tables.
Keep both modes and create management SVIs on the switches.
questions.explanation: SW1 is not sending DTP, so a passive auto peer has no negotiation that makes it a trunk. Configure the peer explicitly and verify both ends; MAC state and management addressing cannot substitute for the mode.

whyWrong.1: Matching an access VLAN does not make SW2 a multi-VLAN trunk.
whyWrong.2: A MAC-table clear does not change negotiation or administrative mode.
whyWrong.3: SVIs do not configure the physical link as a trunk.

VLAN 20

questions.prompt: The new VLAN 30 pair must communicate while existing VLANs 10 and 20 keep working. Which two corrections are required by the combined evidence? Choose two.
options: Set SW1 Fa0/3 to access VLAN 30.
Replace SW1's uplink allowed list with VLAN 30 only.
Set both uplink native VLANs to 30.
Add VLAN 30 to SW2's existing uplink allowed list.
Move SW2 Fa0/3 to access VLAN 10.
questions.explanation: SW1's new endpoint is in the wrong access VLAN, and SW2's trunk excludes the new VLAN. Correct both while preserving the existing trunk list and native agreement, then verify all three client pairs.

whyWrong.1: That disrupts the required existing VLANs and does not fix the endpoint membership.
whyWrong.2: Changing native membership fixes neither the wrong access port nor the missing allowed VLAN.
whyWrong.4: The documented new pair belongs to VLAN 30.

cards.front: 802.1Q versus DTP?
cards.back: 802.1Q identifies VLANs in frames. DTP negotiates trunk formation on supporting Cisco switch ports.

cards.front: Size and position of an ordinary 802.1Q tag?
cards.back: 4 bytes, after the source MAC and before the original EtherType field.

cards.front: What identifies an ordinary 802.1Q tag in the Ethernet frame?
cards.back: The 16-bit TPID value 0x8100.

cards.front: Usable VLAN identifiers in the 12-bit VID field?
cards.back: 1–4094. VID 0 supports priority tagging without a VLAN ID; 4095 is reserved. Platforms can impose additional restrictions.

cards.front: Under default native treatment, how is ordinary untagged trunk data classified?
cards.back: Into the receiving port's native VLAN. Ordinary data from that native VLAN is sent untagged.

cards.front: Which command selects native VLAN 99 on a trunk?
cards.back: Use `switchport trunk native vlan 99` in interface configuration mode, and agree with the peer.

cards.front: What is the most direct evidence of a native VLAN mismatch?
cards.back: The two trunk ports show different native VLAN IDs. Warnings or protective states may also appear; exact behavior depends on the platform.

cards.front: Default allowed VLAN selection in the cited Catalyst guides?
cards.back: All supported VLANs are initially allowed. Verify the actual list; permission alone does not mean each VLAN exists or forwards.

cards.front: allowed vlan 30 versus allowed vlan add 30?
cards.back: The first replaces the list with 30. The second preserves the current list and adds 30.

cards.front: What do the three VLAN lists in show interfaces trunk distinguish?
cards.back: Configured allowed VLANs; VLANs allowed and active locally; VLANs forwarding in spanning tree and not pruned.

cards.front: Does one switch's forwarding list prove the peer permits the same VLAN?
cards.back: No. Compare allowed, active and forwarding state at both ends, then test the intended endpoint path.

cards.front: Where do you inspect a configured port absent from show interfaces trunk?
cards.back: Use `show interfaces <port> switchport` to compare administrative and operational settings, then check link and shutdown state.

cards.front: DTP outcomes: auto with auto, and desirable with auto?
cards.back: With compatible operational DTP peers: auto/auto stays nontrunking; desirable/auto can form a trunk.

cards.front: Purpose of switchport nonegotiate on a static trunk?
cards.back: Suppress DTP messages while retaining the static trunk and its configured 802.1Q traffic.

cards.front: Does removing VLAN 1 from a trunk disable every link-control protocol?
cards.back: No. Cisco documents continued operation of several control protocols; configure each feature explicitly.

cards.front: When does an AP's wired connection need multiple VLANs?
cards.back: When its actual forwarding design carries multiple local VLANs over that link, such as locally switched client VLANs. Multiple SSIDs alone do not prove it.

cards.front: An AP sends management untagged in VLAN 100. What must its trunk peer match?
cards.back: The peer must classify that untagged traffic into VLAN 100 and allow the required management/client VLANs.

cards.front: A host expects all required VLANs tagged. Should one of them be native by default?
cards.back: No. With default untagged-native treatment, use an agreed unused native VLAN so required VLANs retain their tags.

commands.task: Make the selected switch port a static trunk.
commands.note: Configure the peer compatibly; this command does not create or route VLANs.

commands.task: Set the selected trunk's native VLAN to the agreed VLAN 99.
commands.note: Under default treatment, ordinary VLAN 99 data is untagged.

commands.task: Replace the selected trunk's allowed list with exactly 10,20,99.
commands.note: This is a replacement. Use the explicit approved list, particularly on a live trunk.

commands.task: Add VLAN 30 to the selected trunk without removing existing allowed VLANs.
commands.note: Verify the resulting list and the other end.

commands.task: Remove only VLAN 20 from the selected trunk's allowed list.
commands.note: This intentionally interrupts VLAN 20 over this port; the lab observes it before recovery.

commands.task: Suppress DTP messages on the selected statically configured trunk.
commands.note: This leaves the static 802.1Q trunk configured.

commands.task: On this older interface whose help offers a trunk encapsulation selector, explicitly choose 802.1Q.
commands.note: A 2960's 802.1Q-only interface does not need this platform-specific selector.

commands.task: List operational trunks and their native, allowed, active and forwarding VLAN information.
commands.note: Inspect both ends; a local display cannot prove the peer's configuration.

commands.task: Inspect administrative and operational switchport settings for GigabitEthernet0/1.
commands.note: Useful when a configured port is absent from the operational trunk list.

commands.task: Display local VLAN existence, activity and ordinary access-port membership.
commands.note: Use this when a VLAN is allowed on a trunk but absent from its active list.

tickets.title: Existing VLANs fail after VLAN 30 is added
tickets.scenario: SW1 Gi0/1 connects to SW2 Gi0/1. Each switch has one correctly addressed PC in VLAN 10 (192.168.10.0/24), VLAN 20 (192.168.20.0/24) and VLAN 30 (192.168.30.0/24). Same-VLAN communication across the link worked for VLANs 10 and 20 before a change intended to add VLAN 30. Now only the new VLAN 30 pair communicates across it. Both switch consoles are available. The following excerpts are representative teaching evidence.

exhibits.title: SW1 trunk summary
exhibits.text:
Port        Mode   Encapsulation   Status      Native vlan
Gi0/1       on     802.1q          trunking    99

Vlans allowed on trunk: 30
Vlans allowed and active: 30
Vlans forwarding and not pruned: 30

exhibits.title: Recorded configuration of SW1 Gi0/1
exhibits.text:
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 switchport mode trunk
 switchport trunk native vlan 99
 switchport trunk allowed vlan 30
 switchport nonegotiate

exhibits.title: Checks completed on both switches
exhibits.text:
VLANs 10,20,30,99 exist and are active locally.
PC access-port assignments and /24 addresses match the design.
SW2 Gi0/1 is trunking, native 99, with 10,20,30,99 allowed and forwarding.

tickets.question: Which diagnosis fits all the evidence?
options: Creating VLAN 30 replaced VLAN 20 in the VLAN database.
The allowed list on SW1 was replaced by 30 instead of extended.
The link changed into an access connection in VLAN 30.
The native VLAN on SW1 changed from 99 to 30.
tickets.explanation: SW1 remains an operational trunk with native VLAN 99. Its allowed list contains only 30, even though the original VLANs still exist. That selective filter explains why the new pair works and the old same-VLAN pairs fail.
tickets.fix:
Use SW1's console to restore the required VLANs while retaining 30.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan add 10,20,99
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces trunk
```

The allowed list should become 10,20,30,99. Verify local activity and forwarding, then repeat each same-VLAN pair's test in both directions. Do not assume the list alone proves host connectivity. Save after verification and correct the change instructions to distinguish replacement from add.

tickets.title: Native VLAN agreement is missing on a replacement switch
tickets.scenario: The intended native VLAN between SW1 Gi0/1 and SW2 Gi0/1 is 99. A test PC on each switch uses an access port in VLAN 99, with addresses 10.99.0.11/24 and 10.99.0.12/24 and no gateway. Their same-subnet test stopped working after SW2 was replaced. Separate tagged VLAN 10 tests still work in this reported incident. The displays below are representative configuration evidence, not a guarantee of identical protection behavior on every platform.

exhibits.title: SW1 Gi0/1 configuration
exhibits.text:
switchport mode trunk
switchport trunk native vlan 99
switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,99
switchport nonegotiate

exhibits.title: Replacement SW2 Gi0/1 configuration
exhibits.text:
switchport mode trunk
switchport trunk native vlan 1
switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,99
switchport nonegotiate

exhibits.title: Completed local checks
exhibits.text:
Both physical uplink ports are connected and configured as trunks.
VLAN 99 exists and is active on each switch.
The two test PC ports are static access VLAN 99 and linked.
PC addresses and masks match the stated 10.99.0.0/24 design.

tickets.question: What configuration defect must be repaired?
options: The test PCs need default gateways for their same-subnet traffic.
The switches must negotiate DTP before native frames can pass.
The replacement switch's native VLAN is 1 instead of the agreed 99.
VLAN 99 must be removed from both allowed lists.
tickets.explanation: The native settings differ explicitly. Under default treatment, an ordinary untagged frame sent from SW1 as VLAN 99 is not classified as VLAN 99 by SW2. Native mismatches may also trigger spanning-tree protection; neither a working tagged VLAN nor the absence of a particular warning makes this configuration correct.
tickets.fix:
Restore the documented native VLAN on the replacement switch through its console.

```ios SW2
SW2# configure terminal
SW2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW2(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 99
SW2(config-if)# end
SW2# show interfaces trunk
```

Compare both native and allowed settings, allow any protective state to recover, and repeat the VLAN 99 and VLAN 10 tests. If a state remains nonforwarding, inspect its evidence rather than disabling spanning tree. Update the replacement template and save the verified configuration.

chapters.title: Inter-VLAN routing
chapters.subtitle: Build gateways with router subinterfaces and SVIs, then follow a packet between them.

sources.title: Cisco: Configure Inter-VLAN Routing with an External Router
Cisco: Catalyst 3560 IOS 15.0(2)SE — Interface Characteristics and SVI Autostate
