exhibits.text:
interface GigabitEthernet0/0.30
!
No encapsulation or IP address is configured under this subinterface.

exhibits.title: SW1 verification worksheet
exhibits.text:
VLAN 30 exists and is active.
PC-C's connected access port belongs to VLAN 30.
The router-facing Gi0/1 trunk is operational.
VLAN 30 is allowed, active and forwarding on Gi0/1.
PC-C's address, /24 mask and gateway match the stated design.

tickets.question: Why is the router not providing the VLAN 30 gateway?
options: The new subinterface has neither encapsulation nor a gateway address.
SW1's uplink excludes VLAN 30 from its effective forwarding set.
The router's physical parent interface is shut down.
The gateway must be placed on the unaddressed physical parent.
tickets.explanation: Creating a subinterface name does not supply its VLAN mapping or address. Up/up can follow the operational parent without proving a usable gateway service. The evidence does not prove whether a paste failed or commands were omitted; it proves the two required settings are absent. The supplied switch evidence confirms VLAN 30 is active and forwarding on the trunk. The parent and subinterface are up/up; the missing encapsulation and address remain visible in the configuration.
tickets.fix:
Complete the new subinterface, setting encapsulation before addressing.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0.30
R1(config-subif)# encapsulation dot1Q 30
R1(config-subif)# ip address 192.168.30.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-subif)# no shutdown
R1(config-subif)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
R1# show ip route
```

Confirm the address is assigned, the interface is operational, and 192.168.30.0/24 appears as connected. Test PC-C's own gateway and a known reachable host in another VLAN. Older images may not show a separate local /32 entry; gateway and forwarding verification matter more than reproducing an exact display.

chapters.title: CDP & LLDP
chapters.subtitle: Identify adjacent devices, verify both ends of a link, and correct network documentation.

sources.title: Cisco: LLDP and LLDP-MED, Catalyst 2960 IOS 15.2(2)E
IEEE: 802.1AB Station and Media Access Control Connectivity Discovery

chapters.summary: Configure CDP and LLDP, interpret local and remote neighbor fields, assess cached evidence and management reachability, and build an accurate link inventory.

sections.body:
CDP and LLDP help you identify the device at the other end of a network link. You can use their advertisements to check a cable connection, find the correct neighboring port, and compare the operating network with its documentation. The result is evidence to investigate, rather than a complete test of the network.

In this chapter, start with the device where you ran the command. Read each neighbor entry as a relationship between that device's local port and the advertised port on another device. Then verify the relationship from the other end before correcting a diagram.

sections.title: What neighbor discovery tells you
sections.body:
A **neighbor discovery protocol** exchanges information over a local link. **Cisco Discovery Protocol (CDP)** is Cisco's discovery protocol; **Link Layer Discovery Protocol (LLDP)** is the vendor-neutral standard defined by IEEE 802.1AB. They are separate protocols. Enabling LLDP does not enable CDP, and a device running only one cannot discover advertisements sent only in the other format.

On Ethernet, these exchanges operate at Layer 2 and do not need a working IPv4 configuration. Two switches can learn about each other even when their management addresses are wrong. Conversely, two correctly addressed devices might exchange user traffic while their discovery protocols are disabled. Keep the discovery result separate from an IP connectivity test.

The information comes from the neighbor's own advertisements. Typical fields include device identity, sending port, capabilities, software, and a management address. Advertisements use **type-length-value fields (TLVs)**, which identify each piece of information and its size. Some fields are optional, so an absent management address or software string does not automatically mean the advertisement is defective.

In ordinary switch links, discovery describes adjacent protocol speakers, not an IP route through the network. Routers do not route these Ethernet advertisements between IP subnets. However, the table alone cannot certify one uninterrupted physical cable: a hub, transparent device, or deliberate Layer 2 protocol transport can complicate the path. Ordinary LLDP uses a reserved link-local destination that compliant bridges do not simply forward as user multicast. Do not assume every unmanaged switch forwards it.

sections.title: Configure and verify CDP
sections.body:
:::facts
- CDP and LLDP are Layer 2 discovery protocols; a neighbor entry does not prove IP reachability.
- Referenced classic IOS CDP defaults: advertisements every **60 seconds**, holdtime **180 seconds**, version **2** advertisements enabled.
- CDP controls: global `cdp run`; interface `cdp enable`. Both levels must permit operation.
- Referenced Catalyst LLDP timer defaults: **30-second** advertisements, **120-second** holdtime, **2-second** reinitialization delay.
- LLDP controls: global `lldp run`; interface `lldp transmit` and `lldp receive` are separate.
- Read a row as **local device/local interface → neighbor identity/neighbor port**.
:::

CDP is enabled by default on the supported classic IOS Ethernet interfaces described in Cisco's guide. This is a useful starting expectation, not a statement about every Cisco product, interface type, or saved configuration. Check `show cdp` for device-wide status and `show cdp interface` for the participating interfaces. Our lab explicitly enables the required settings.

A switch sending an advertisement every 60 seconds normally refreshes the receiver's entry before its advertised 180-second lifetime expires. The **holdtime** is the lifetime supplied by the sender, not a routing convergence timer. If advertisements stop arriving, the receiver eventually removes the cached entry. A local link-down event or explicit table clear can remove information earlier, so do not promise an entry will remain for exactly three minutes after every fault.

Use `no cdp run` to disable CDP globally. Use `no cdp enable` under an interface to disable it on that port. The positive interface command cannot override global disablement. The following starts CDP and sets familiar timer values on a selected switch link:

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# cdp run
SW1(config)# cdp timer 60
SW1(config)# cdp holdtime 180
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# cdp enable
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show cdp
SW1# show cdp interface
SW1# show cdp neighbors
```

CDPv2 can advertise native-VLAN and duplex information. A mismatch message is a reason to compare the actual interface settings on both ends. CDP does not correct them. Do not change a trunk merely to silence a log without first identifying which side differs from the approved design.

sections.title: Configure and verify LLDP
sections.body:
LLDP is especially useful when the network includes equipment from different vendors or endpoints with LLDP support. A server, phone, or appliance must actually implement and enable LLDP to appear. An ordinary PC with no discovery agent will not appear simply because it has an IP address or responds to ping.

Cisco's referenced Catalyst 2960 guide documents LLDP as globally disabled initially. Defaults vary across product families and software, so configure the intended directions explicitly. `lldp run` enables the process; `lldp transmit` allows advertisements out of the selected interface; `lldp receive` allows processing of incoming advertisements. Verify the effective interface state instead of assuming that one global command overrides previous interface settings.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# lldp run
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# lldp transmit
SW1(config-if)# lldp receive
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show lldp
SW1# show lldp interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1# show lldp neighbors detail
```

SW1 can learn SW2 only when SW2 transmits toward SW1 and SW1 receives on that link, with LLDP globally operating on both devices. SW1's own transmit setting determines what SW2 can learn. That distinction explains one-way visibility without requiring a broken cable or an IP-routing fault.

```diagram
{ "type": "matrix", "title": "Conditions for SW1 to learn SW2", "rows": ["SW2 transmits", "SW2 does not transmit"], "cols": ["SW1 receives", "SW1 does not receive"], "cells": [["Can refresh entry", "Cannot refresh entry"], ["Cannot refresh entry", "Cannot refresh entry"]], "tones": {"Can refresh entry":"accent", "Cannot refresh entry":"neutral"}, "caption": "Assume LLDP is globally enabled and the link works; existing cached entries can remain temporarily after a direction is disabled." }
```

LLDP identifies the sending device with a **chassis ID** and the sending interface with a **port ID**. Those IDs can use different representations; a chassis ID is not universally a MAC address, and a port ID is not universally a familiar IOS interface name. Use the advertised system name and port description as additional evidence. Do not substitute a guessed interface name for an unfamiliar identifier.

**LLDP-MED**, Media Endpoint Discovery, extends LLDP for compatible endpoints such as phones. It can communicate network policy, including voice VLAN and QoS parameters, along with power and location information. This helps a phone obtain the information needed for its role. It does not replace DHCP, assign an arbitrary IP address, or establish that a voice call will succeed.

sections.title: Read local and remote fields correctly
sections.body:
Always identify the command's execution point first. In an SW1 table, `Local Intrfce` belongs to SW1. `Device ID` describes the neighbor, and `Port ID` describes the neighbor's sending interface. Neither column is a path through subsequent routers. A second row for the same neighbor can represent a second physical connection, so retain the port identities when documenting parallel links.

The following is representative, abbreviated CDP output for the lab. Platform strings, capability combinations, spacing, and remaining lifetimes vary by image.

```output SW1# show cdp neighbors
Device ID   Local Intrfce  Holdtme  Capability  Platform  Port ID
R1          Gig 0/2        155      R           C2911     Gig 0/0  ← SW1 Gi0/2 reaches R1 Gi0/0
SW2         Gig 0/1        162      S I         WS-C2960  Gig 0/2  ← SW1 Gi0/1 reaches SW2 Gi0/2
```

The first row does not mean R1 uses Gi0/2. That is SW1's local port. Reverse the observation by logging in to R1: its local Gi0/0 should identify SW1's Gi0/2 if both ends are advertising and the records are current. Write the device name beside every port in your notes so this distinction survives when tables are combined.

Capability letters require the legend belonging to the command. In common Cisco CDP output, `S` means switch and `R` means router. In LLDP output, `B` means bridge, which includes ordinary Ethernet switching, while `S` means station. A phone is commonly `P` in CDP and `T` in LLDP. These are advertised capabilities, not proof that every supported function is enabled or carrying traffic.

| Field | Useful conclusion | Conclusion requiring other evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Local interface and remote port ID | Observed connection between protocol speakers | Complete physical cable path through passive or transparent equipment |
| Capability | Advertised device function | Actual routing configuration and forwarding success |
| Management address | An address the neighbor advertises | Address is reachable from your current source |
| Lifetime or time remaining | Entry is retained according to protocol state | Cable and peer are still working now |

sections.title: Check and correct network documentation
sections.body:
Begin with a table containing local device, local interface, neighbor identity, neighbor port, protocol, and observation time. Record the unmodified observations before correcting the diagram. This makes the change reviewable and avoids turning an uncertain inference into a documented fact.

Suppose the existing drawing says SW1 Gi0/1 connects to R1 Gi0/0, while SW1 Gi0/2 connects to SW2 Gi0/1. The preceding CDP output disagrees with both links. The candidate corrections are SW1 Gi0/2 to R1 Gi0/0 and SW1 Gi0/1 to SW2 Gi0/2. Confirm the reverse entries and inspect the actual ports before updating the document.

| Existing drawing | Current SW1 observation | Proposed correction |
|---|---|---|
| SW1 Gi0/1 → R1 Gi0/0 | R1 on local Gi0/2, remote Gi0/0 | Change SW1 end to Gi0/2 |
| SW1 Gi0/2 → SW2 Gi0/1 | SW2 on local Gi0/1, remote Gi0/2 | Correct both switch ends |

If only one direction appears, do not immediately change the cable. Check the relevant transmit and receive controls, the global process, interface state, and record age. If a name appears twice, retain chassis and port identities and investigate naming duplication. Two devices can share a hostname; the correct response is to establish identity, not discard one row.

A discovery entry and an interface description can disagree because either record is stale. An advertisement can also contain an incorrect or deliberately misleading identity. Corroborate it with the neighboring device's configuration, inventory, and physical evidence where available. Update a diagram when the evidence supports the correction, not simply because one source looks more authoritative.

sections.title: Choose where discovery should operate
sections.body:
Discovery shares information about the local device with connected equipment. Ordinary CDP/LLDP advertisements are not authenticated proof of identity and are not encrypted management sessions. This is useful on managed internal links, but can disclose information unnecessarily on an external connection.

Apply the organization's policy per interface. Keep the required discovery protocol on links used for internal documentation or phone policy. Disable unwanted advertisement and reception on a boundary where it serves no purpose. Disabling CDP globally to protect one ISP-facing port can also remove useful internal neighbor information and affect endpoints that depend on it.

For example, `no cdp enable` removes CDP on the selected interface. For LLDP, consider both `no lldp transmit` and `no lldp receive` when the intention is to disable participation entirely. Disabling transmission alone limits your advertisements, but the local device can still receive and display the neighbor's information.

Before changing a phone-facing link, determine whether CDP or LLDP-MED supplies its VLAN or power information. A discovery policy should account for that dependency. Neither protocol is a replacement for access control, and an absent neighbor entry does not demonstrate that a port is secure.

sections.title: Verify state, lifetime, and reachability separately
sections.body:
Use `show cdp neighbors detail` or `show lldp neighbors detail` to inspect available addresses and additional identifiers. A management address may belong to another interface or an SVI on the neighbor. Test it from an appropriate source only after checking that the source has the required addressing and route.

```output SW1# show lldp neighbors detail
Chassis id: 0011.2233.4455
Port id: Gi0/2
Port Description: GigabitEthernet0/2
System Name: SW2
System Capabilities: B
Enabled Capabilities: B
Management Addresses:
    IP: 192.168.12.12
Time remaining: 93 seconds  ← cached lifetime, not a ping result
```

This illustrative entry identifies SW2's advertised port and address. It does not prove that SW1 can reach 192.168.12.12. A wrong management VLAN or mask can prevent ping while LLDP still works over the Ethernet connection. Diagnose the failing function rather than disabling discovery to make the symptoms agree.

On CDP implementations that display remaining holdtime, an entry with 174 seconds left from an advertised 180-second lifetime was refreshed approximately six seconds earlier. Avoid treating the arithmetic as an exact timestamp. For LLDP, use the detail view's time remaining where available; brief-table holdtime presentation differs between platforms. Timers advertised by a neighbor need not equal your local timer settings.

When changing a discovery setting, record the change and allow cached information to expire, or use a documented clear command such as `clear cdp table` on the observation device. Then verify fresh learning. Clearing a local table does not clear the neighbor's table and does not immediately force the neighbor to send a new periodic advertisement.

:::trap An advertised address is not a reachability test
A neighbor can advertise a management address even when your device has no route to it. Verify the address, VLAN, routing, and permitted management service separately. A CDP or LLDP entry does not establish that ping or SSH will work.
:::

sections.title: Exam focus
sections.body:
- Configure CDP globally and per interface; verify both levels.
- Configure LLDP globally and check transmit and receive directions separately.
- Read local interface, remote port, identity, capability, and management address correctly.
- Recognize the referenced default timers without assuming all product defaults are identical.
- Distinguish cached neighbor information from current link state and IP reachability.
- Compare observations from both ends with a documented topology and justify corrections.
- Explain discovery policy on internal, endpoint, and external links.

lab.title: Discover neighbors and correct a link inventory
lab.intro:
Practice revised September 2026. If you completed an earlier version, repeat the revised exercise and update its checkmarks.

Build one small management LAN, collect neighbor evidence from both switches, and correct a deliberately inaccurate connection record. Then create one-way LLDP visibility and restore it without changing IP addressing.

This procedure was checked against the address plan and Cisco documentation, but was not executed in Packet Tracer during this review. Output is representative. Some Packet Tracer images omit LLDP or individual show commands. Complete CDP on the specified models; if LLDP is unavailable, use the clearly identified paper observations in Steps 6–9 or a supporting Catalyst image in CML/hardware. Do not treat a missing simulator command as a cabling fault.

## Evidence to keep

Keep a link table containing both device names, both ports, observation time and the source protocol. Include reverse observations and the separate management pings. For the LLDP fault, explain each learning direction before and after recovery. Mark any simulator fallback as supplied evidence, and preserve the old drawing alongside your justified correction.
lab.topology:

steps.title: Build, name, and address the devices
steps.body:
Start a new project, select the exact models, and connect the listed ports. Decline initial configuration dialogs if shown. Type commands after the prompts.

```ios SW1
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW1
SW1(config)# cdp run
SW1(config)# interface range gigabitethernet0/1 - 2
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport access vlan 1
SW1(config-if-range)# cdp enable
SW1(config-if-range)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if-range)# exit
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 1
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# exit
SW1(config)# interface vlan 1
SW1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.12.11 255.255.255.0
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# exit
SW1(config)# ip default-gateway 192.168.12.1
SW1(config)# end
```

```ios SW2
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW2
SW2(config)# cdp run
SW2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
SW2(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW2(config-if)# switchport access vlan 1
SW2(config-if)# cdp enable
SW2(config-if)# no shutdown
SW2(config-if)# exit
SW2(config)# interface vlan 1
SW2(config-if)# ip address 192.168.12.12 255.255.255.0
SW2(config-if)# no shutdown
SW2(config-if)# exit
SW2(config)# ip default-gateway 192.168.12.1
SW2(config)# end
```

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# cdp run
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.12.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# cdp enable
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
```

Set PC-A using **Desktop → IP Configuration → Static**, including the exact mask and gateway in the table.

:::expected
After the ports become operational, each switch SVI can become up/up because VLAN 1 has active forwarding members. R1 Gi0/0 is enabled. Check `show ip interface brief` on each network device and PC-A's `ipconfig` before continuing.
:::

steps.title: Read the CDP tables from both ends
steps.body:
Before collecting output, draw the expected rows for each network device using the cable table. Do not expect PC-A to advertise. Run the following on SW1, then run the same three show commands on SW2 and R1 at their privileged prompts.

```ios SW1
SW1# show cdp
SW1# show cdp interface
SW1# show cdp neighbors
```

:::expected
Allow periodic advertisements to arrive. SW1 should identify SW2 on its Gi0/1, remote Gi0/2, and R1 on its Gi0/2, remote Gi0/0. SW2 should identify SW1 on its Gi0/2, remote Gi0/1. R1 should identify SW1 on its Gi0/0, remote Gi0/2. PC-A is not expected to advertise CDP. If a row is absent, check both device-wide and interface CDP state before changing addresses.
:::

steps.title: Correct an inaccurate drawing
steps.body:
Treat this as the inherited record: **SW1 Gi0/1 → R1 Gi0/0**, and **SW1 Gi0/2 → SW2 Gi0/1**. Create a correction table with the old claim, your observation, the reverse observation, and the proposed connection. Keep the command's device name attached to each local interface.

:::solution Compare your correction table
Both records are wrong. The supported corrections are **SW1 Gi0/2 → R1 Gi0/0** and **SW1 Gi0/1 → SW2 Gi0/2**. Your table includes evidence from both ends, rather than merely copying the workspace drawing.
:::

steps.title: Separate advertised addresses from reachability
steps.body:
Before testing, state whether a fresh neighbor entry alone guarantees a successful management ping. Inspect detailed records, then test the management address independently.

```ios SW1
SW1# show cdp neighbors detail
SW1# ping 192.168.12.12
```

From PC-A, ping `192.168.12.11`, `.12`, and `.1` using the full addresses. Record whether the detailed record advertises the address you configured; optional fields and address selection may vary.

:::expected
With the given address plan and operational VLAN, repeated pings should receive replies. That is additional IP evidence. Discovery could still work if you introduced a management-address error, so the neighbor table is not the reason the ping succeeds.
:::

steps.title: Inspect the configured timers and cached lifetime
steps.body:
```ios SW1
SW1# show cdp
SW1# show cdp neighbors
```

Repeat the neighbor view after a short interval and record changes. Also inspect `show cdp` on SW2 to identify the timer and holdtime SW2 advertises. Do not change timers merely to make the observed number match the lesson.

:::expected
The referenced defaults are 60-second advertisements and 180-second holdtime. Remaining holdtime commonly decreases and refreshes when an advertisement arrives. A displayed value is not an exact packet timestamp; the relevant lifetime comes from the neighbor. Clearing SW1's local CDP table, if used for an additional experiment, does not instantly force SW2 to advertise again.
:::

steps.title: Enable LLDP explicitly and compare identities
steps.body:
Use these commands where supported. If `lldp run` is unavailable, read the subsequent observations as a paper exercise instead of entering guessed alternatives.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# lldp run
SW1(config)# lldp timer 30
SW1(config)# lldp holdtime 120
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# lldp transmit
SW1(config-if)# lldp receive
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show lldp
SW1# show lldp neighbors detail
```

```ios SW2
SW2# configure terminal
SW2(config)# lldp run
SW2(config)# lldp timer 30
SW2(config)# lldp holdtime 120
SW2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
SW2(config-if)# lldp transmit
SW2(config-if)# lldp receive
SW2(config-if)# end
SW2# show lldp
SW2# show lldp neighbors detail
```

:::expected
After advertisements arrive, each switch learns the other. A representative SW1 observation is **system name SW2, local Gi0/1, remote port Gi0/2, bridge capability B**. CDP may use capability S for the same switching function. LLDP IDs can differ in format; use the actual advertised IDs and descriptions. These stated observations are also the starting facts for the paper fallback.
:::

steps.title: Create one-way LLDP visibility
steps.body:
Write a two-row prediction first: whether SW1 can refresh SW2, and whether SW2 can refresh SW1. Then stop only SW2's advertisements toward SW1. Leave SW2 receiving and leave all settings on SW1 unchanged.

```ios SW2
SW2# configure terminal
SW2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
SW2(config-if)# no lldp transmit
SW2(config-if)# end
SW2# show lldp interface gigabitethernet0/2
SW2# show lldp neighbors
```

On SW1, inspect `show lldp neighbors detail` and `show cdp neighbors` over time. If a detail/interface form is unsupported, inspect the running configuration for the configured directions.

:::expected
SW1 can no longer refresh its LLDP entry for SW2; it disappears after any retained lifetime, or earlier if a shutdown advertisement is processed. SW2 can continue learning SW1. CDP remains independently configured. In the paper exercise, write these directional conclusions and identify which one setting caused them; do not report an unobserved simulator result. Record the fault before Step 9 restores it.
:::

steps.title: Limit discovery on the ordinary PC port
steps.body:
This lab PC has no phone or policy dependency. Disable unnecessary discovery on SW1 Fa0/1. Omit only the LLDP lines if that feature is unavailable in the image.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# no cdp enable
SW1(config-if)# no lldp transmit
SW1(config-if)# no lldp receive
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show cdp interface
```

:::expected
The policy affects the PC-facing port, not the interswitch uplink. PC-A can still ping the management addresses; removing discovery does not shut the port or implement a traffic-filtering policy. Record this intentional final difference from the original default configuration.
:::

steps.title: Restore the uplink and save the verified map
steps.body:
```ios SW2
SW2# configure terminal
SW2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
SW2(config-if)# lldp transmit
SW2(config-if)# end
SW2# show lldp neighbors
```

On supported images, inspect both switches and verify fresh two-way learning before saving. Then run `copy running-config startup-config` at SW2's privileged prompt. Complete SW2's save prompt: if `Destination filename [startup-config]?` appears, press Enter and wait for the `SW2#` prompt. In the paper fallback, state why reenabling SW2 transmission restores SW1's ability to refresh the entry. Save SW1 and R1 with `copy running-config startup-config`, accepting the destination filename if prompted. Save the project as `12-discovery-complete.pkt` and keep your corrected link table with it.

:::expected
Both uplink directions are restored, the PC-port policy remains intentional, and the corrected map identifies both endpoints of each link. The record distinguishes actual CDP/LLDP observations from any paper-only LLDP work.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- Missing neighbor: check link state, device-wide process, local receive policy, remote transmit policy, and cache lifetime.
- LLDP absent but CDP present: inspect LLDP settings independently; CDP does not enable it.
- Neighbor present but management ping fails: check SVI state, VLAN, address, mask, and source reachability.
- Unexpected port ID: compare from the far device and inspect the cable before changing documentation.
- Unsupported command: use the documented full-table/configuration alternative, or the marked paper workflow; do not claim the simulator executed it.
lab.challenge:
In a separate copy, move only SW2's cable end from Gi0/2 to Gi0/1. Configure the new SW2 interface as an enabled VLAN 1 access port with CDP, LLDP transmit, and LLDP receive where supported. Predict which fields change in both switches' neighbor tables. Verify them, revise the link record, and save this variation separately.

:::solution Check your changed topology
The physical connection becomes **SW1 Gi0/1 → SW2 Gi0/1**. In SW1's row for SW2, the local port remains Gi0/1 and the remote port changes to Gi0/1. In SW2's row, the local port changes to Gi0/1 and the remote port remains SW1 Gi0/1. Management IPs do not need to change because both ports still serve VLAN 1. Allow stale entries to clear and fresh advertisements to arrive before calling the map verified.

One suitable configuration of the newly connected SW2 port is:

```ios SW2
SW2# configure terminal
SW2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW2(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW2(config-if)# switchport access vlan 1
SW2(config-if)# cdp enable
SW2(config-if)# lldp transmit
SW2(config-if)# lldp receive
SW2(config-if)# no shutdown
SW2(config-if)# end
SW2# show cdp neighbors
SW2# show lldp neighbors
```

Omit LLDP commands only for the documented simulator fallback. Inspect SW1 as well, and repeat PC-A's management pings to confirm the cable move preserved the original IP service. Save the variation after these checks.
:::

questions.prompt: On the Cisco IOS CDP implementation documented in this chapter, the timers have not been changed. What are the default advertisement interval and advertised holdtime?
options: 60 seconds and 180 seconds
30 seconds and 120 seconds
60 seconds and 120 seconds
180 seconds and 60 seconds
questions.explanation: The referenced IOS guide specifies an advertisement every 60 seconds and an advertised holdtime of 180 seconds. A receiver ages its entry when advertisements stop; these values can be configured.

whyWrong.1: These are the LLDP interval and holdtime documented for the chapter’s Catalyst platform.
whyWrong.2: The first number is the CDP default interval, but the default CDP holdtime is 180 seconds.
whyWrong.3: This reverses the interval and holdtime. A timer value is not a count of neighbors.

exhibit.title: Representative SW1# show lldp neighbors
exhibit.text:
Capability codes: (R) Router, (B) Bridge, (T) Telephone, (S) Station
Device ID   Local Intf  Hold-time  Capability  Port ID
DIST1       Gi0/24     120        B           Te1/0/1

questions.prompt: Which interpretation is supported by this LLDP output?
options: DIST1 is advertising the LLDP station capability.
DIST1 advertises bridge capability and remote port Te1/0/1.
B means the receiving local port is blocked by STP.
The B code proves that DIST1 cannot also support routing.
questions.explanation: Read the legend belonging to this protocol. LLDP B means bridge, which includes Ethernet switching. The row maps the local Gi0/24 to the advertised remote Te1/0/1; it does not establish all configured features on DIST1.

whyWrong.0: The legend uses S for station, not B.
whyWrong.2: The capability field describes the neighbor’s advertised capability, not the local STP state.
whyWrong.3: A bridge capability does not rule out other capabilities or prove how every feature is configured.

questions.prompt: You must disable CDP only on SW1 Gi0/2 while retaining it on other intended ports. Which command belongs under interface Gi0/2?
options: no cdp run
no lldp transmit
no cdp enable
cdp timer 0
questions.explanation: no cdp enable disables CDP on the selected interface. Keep the global cdp run setting if CDP is still needed elsewhere.

whyWrong.0: no cdp run is a global command and disables CDP device-wide.
whyWrong.1: This affects LLDP transmission, a different discovery protocol.
whyWrong.3: A timer adjustment is not the per-interface enable/disable control.

questions.prompt: Which two privileged EXEC commands help inspect CDP advertisement/holdtime settings on the local IOS device? Choose two.
options: show cdp neighbors detail
show cdp
show cdp interface
show ip route
questions.explanation: show cdp reports local global settings; show cdp interface reports CDP status and timing for participating local interfaces. Neighbor detail is a record about received neighbors, not a substitute for inspecting the local sender settings.

whyWrong.0: Neighbor detail can include the remaining lifetime of a received entry, but the task asks for local CDP timer settings.
whyWrong.3: The IP routing table does not report CDP timer configuration.

questions.prompt: A supported IP phone uses LLDP-MED network-policy information from its switch. What can that information help the phone learn?
options: The phone's complete IPv4 address, subnet mask and default gateway.
The voice call server's successful registration response.
The switch's complete table of reachable IP subnets.
The intended voice VLAN and associated traffic-priority policy.
questions.explanation: LLDP-MED extends discovery for media endpoints, including network-policy information such as voice VLAN and priority. Advertisement does not replace configuring the required VLAN, power, and data path.

whyWrong.0: Network-policy information does not replace IP address configuration or DHCP.
whyWrong.1: Advertising policy is not proof of successful call-server registration.
whyWrong.2: LLDP-MED network policy is not an IP routing-table exchange.

exhibit.title: Supplied endpoint evidence
exhibit.text:
PC-A has no CDP or LLDP agent
Its access link is up in the intended VLAN
PC-A and a same-subnet peer exchange repeated successful pings
Switch CDP/LLDP uplink neighbors refresh normally

questions.prompt: PC-A exchanges traffic successfully but never appears in either discovery table. Which conclusion follows?
options: The user-traffic test is invalid because every host must advertise LLDP.
The access VLAN is inactive despite the successful local exchange.
The switch has proved PC-A's software is trustworthy.
Absence is expected for the stated host and does not contradict its traffic test.
questions.explanation: A host needs a discovery speaker to advertise its identity. IP traffic can work without CDP or LLDP, and a table's absence or presence is not device authentication.

whyWrong.0: Ordinary endpoint traffic does not require a discovery agent.
whyWrong.1: The successful tested path does not support that diagnosis.
whyWrong.2: Discovery state does not authenticate software.

exhibit.title: Representative SW1# show cdp neighbors
exhibit.text:
Device ID  Local Intrfce  Holdtme  Capability  Platform    Port ID
SW2        Gig 0/1       172      S I         WS-C2960-   Gig 0/2
R1         Gig 0/2       156      R S I       CISCO2911   Gig 0/0

questions.prompt: Which link record correctly interprets both rows?
options: SW1 Gi0/2 → SW2 Gi0/1; SW1 Gi0/0 → R1 Gi0/2
SW1 Gi0/1 → SW2 Gi0/1; SW1 Gi0/2 → R1 Gi0/2
SW1 Gi0/1 → SW2 Gi0/2; SW1 Gi0/2 → R1 Gi0/0
SW2 Gi0/1 → R1 Gi0/0; SW1 Gi0/2 has no neighbor
questions.explanation: The command ran on SW1. Local Intrfce belongs to SW1; Port ID is the interface advertised by the neighbor in that row. Record both device names and both ports.

whyWrong.0: This reverses local and remote port ownership and invents an SW1 Gi0/0 observation.
whyWrong.1: The remote ports are Gi0/2 on SW2 and Gi0/0 on R1, not copies of the local port numbers.
whyWrong.3: The table reports two SW1 adjacencies; it does not report a link between SW2 and R1.

exhibit.title: Recorded interface state on the connected ports
exhibit.text:
SW1 Gi0/1: LLDP Tx enabled; Rx enabled
SW2 Gi0/2: LLDP Tx disabled; Rx enabled

questions.prompt: LLDP runs globally on both switches, the cable is correct, and old entries have expired. What is the expected neighbor-table result?
options: Neither switch learns the other because LLDP requires bidirectional transmission.
Both switches learn each other because global enablement overrides interface settings.
SW1 learns SW2, but SW2 cannot learn SW1.
SW2 learns SW1, but SW1 cannot learn SW2.
questions.explanation: SW1 transmits, so SW2 can receive and learn SW1. SW2 does not transmit, so SW1 receives no new SW2 advertisement. Receive and transmit controls are independent.

whyWrong.0: One-way LLDP learning is possible when the corresponding sender and receiver are enabled.
whyWrong.1: Global enablement does not override a disabled per-interface transmit direction.
whyWrong.2: This reverses the direction: SW2 is the device with transmission disabled.

questions.prompt: A fresh CDP detail entry advertises SW2 management address 192.168.12.12, but SW1 cannot ping it. Which conclusion is justified?
options: Discovery works; IP reachability requires separate checks.
The management path is working because discovery crossed the link.
The management address must be on the port facing SW1.
CDP authenticated SW2 and verified its SSH service.
questions.explanation: CDP operates at Layer 2 and can advertise an address that is not on the facing interface. The entry is discovery evidence, not proof of IP reachability, identity authentication, or a working SSH service.

whyWrong.1: A received Layer 2 advertisement does not test the separate IP management path.
whyWrong.2: A device can advertise a management address from another interface.
whyWrong.3: Ordinary CDP advertisements do not authenticate the neighbor or test a management service.

questions.prompt: A policy prohibits discovery on an untrusted provider-facing Ethernet port. Internal switch and phone links still require their approved discovery features. Which change best matches the policy?
options: Disable both discovery protocols globally on the switch.
Disable CDP on the port while leaving LLDP participation enabled.
Disable both discovery protocols on the port and preserve approved internal use.
Disable only LLDP transmission on the port and leave other discovery enabled.
questions.explanation: Apply the boundary policy to the selected interface. Review both discovery protocols, because disabling one does not disable the other. Preserve approved dependencies on other ports and verify their behavior.

whyWrong.0: The requirement is port-specific; a global change removes approved internal discovery.
whyWrong.1: That leaves LLDP participating where all discovery is prohibited.
whyWrong.3: That leaves reception and CDP participation outside the stated policy.

questions.prompt: An IOS switch supports LLDP but show lldp reports that it is not enabled. You want discovery only on the approved Gi0/1 uplink. What is the appropriate next configuration?
options: Enter cdp run; LLDP automatically shares CDP’s state.
Enable lldp run, Gi0/1 transmit/receive, and verify port policy.
Add a default route; the LLDP process starts when a gateway is reachable.
Only enter lldp receive on Gi0/1; the global process can remain disabled.
questions.explanation: Enable the LLDP process and the intended interface directions. Inspect other interface states rather than assuming a universal default across models or releases.

whyWrong.0: CDP and LLDP have independent configuration.
whyWrong.2: LLDP is Layer 2 and does not need a default route.
whyWrong.3: An interface direction setting cannot make a globally disabled LLDP process operate.

questions.prompt: The sender advertises a 180-second CDP holdtime. A receiver’s countdown is now approximately 174 seconds. What does that indicate?
options: The link has been down for exactly 174 seconds.
The sender will transmit its next advertisement in 174 seconds.
The neighbor was discovered for the first time 174 seconds ago.
About 6 seconds have elapsed since the advertisement that last refreshed this entry.
questions.explanation: 180 − 174 = 6 seconds. The countdown describes the entry’s remaining lifetime after its last refresh; rounding and display timing make this an approximate observation. It does not establish physical link uptime.

whyWrong.0: The countdown is time remaining, not downtime.
whyWrong.1: The receiver’s cache countdown is separate from the sender’s advertisement schedule.
whyWrong.2: A refresh restarts the lifetime of an existing entry, so this is not an age-since-first-discovery value.

questions.prompt: Global configuration explicitly contains `no cdp run`, but Gi0/1 contains `cdp enable`. What should you conclude?
options: CDP remains disabled globally; the interface command does not override that.
Gi0/1 operates CDP while every other interface stays disabled.
Only CDP reception works on Gi0/1.
The device automatically changes to LLDP on Gi0/1.
questions.explanation: CDP needs the global process and the interface enabled. Global disablement prevents CDP operation even where the interface has cdp enable.

whyWrong.1: Per-interface enablement does not override the global state.
whyWrong.2: CDP does not use LLDP-style independent transmit and receive controls here.
whyWrong.3: One discovery protocol does not automatically substitute for the other.

questions.prompt: Two devices appear as CDP neighbors, but inspection finds an Ethernet hub between them. What is the correct documentation conclusion?
options: The hub must have an IP address in the CDP table before the observation can be valid.
Document the speakers and hub; discovery does not prove a single cable.
The hub is necessarily the Device ID shown in each CDP row.
Every unmanaged switch must forward LLDP in exactly the same way.
questions.explanation: A hub repeats the received signal and does not identify itself through CDP. Neighbor discovery can therefore omit an intermediate nonparticipating component. Record observed speakers separately from verified physical infrastructure.

whyWrong.0: A hub does not need an IP address or CDP identity to repeat signals.
whyWrong.2: The Device ID belongs to the advertising speaker, not automatically to an intermediate device.
whyWrong.3: Do not generalize this CDP/hub case to all bridges or to LLDP forwarding behavior.

exhibit.title: Supplied protocol checks
exhibit.text:
Physical connection up; intended interfaces verified
SW1: CDP enabled; LLDP globally disabled
SW2: LLDP globally enabled, Tx/Rx enabled; CDP disabled
Policy: use LLDP on this link

questions.prompt: Both images support both protocols, but their empty discovery tables persist after sufficient advertisement time. Which change establishes the approved LLDP discovery on this link?
options: Change both management gateways to the same router address.
Enable CDP on SW2 while leaving SW1's LLDP disabled.
Enable LLDP globally and in both directions on SW1's connected port.
Clear both tables repeatedly while keeping their protocol settings.
questions.explanation: The devices currently use different discovery protocols. Enable the approved common protocol, LLDP, at SW1 and verify both directions; IP addressing and table clears do not translate CDP into LLDP.

whyWrong.0: The Layer 2 protocol mismatch is independent of the management gateway.
whyWrong.1: That could provide CDP discovery, but the approved outcome requires LLDP and SW1's LLDP process remains disabled.
whyWrong.3: Clearing tables does not create compatible advertisements.

exhibit.title: Supplied complete relevant direction state
exhibit.text:
LLDP globally enabled on both devices; link up
SW1: transmit enabled, receive disabled
SW2: transmit disabled, receive enabled
Old entries have expired

questions.prompt: The required outcome is that SW1 receives fresh SW2 information. Which two interface changes are necessary under the stated configuration? Choose two.
options: Enable LLDP transmit on SW1.
Enable LLDP receive on SW1.
Enable LLDP receive on SW2.
Enable LLDP transmit on SW2.
Disable CDP on both switches.
questions.explanation: SW2 is the sender for this observation and SW1 is the receiver. Restore those two disabled directions; the reverse-direction controls already work and CDP is independent.

whyWrong.0: SW1 transmission is already enabled and sends information in the opposite direction.
whyWrong.2: SW2 reception is already enabled and concerns learning SW1.
whyWrong.4: CDP need not be disabled for LLDP to operate.

exhibit.title: Supplied maintenance records
exhibit.text:
09:00 drawing: SW1 Gi0/1 to SW2 Gi0/2
09:02 saved CDP record: same endpoints
09:10 cable move recorded, destination port not recorded
09:11 new SW1 LLDP record: neighbor name SW2, remote Gi0/1
No post-move SW2 observation or physical-port inspection has yet been recorded

questions.prompt: Which documentation action is justified now?
options: Replace the approved drawing with the oldest cached observation.
Record the disagreement and confirm current identities and both port ends before updating the drawing.
Declare Gi0/1 physically faulty because two records disagree.
Publish the new one-sided record immediately because it has the latest timestamp.
questions.explanation: The observations were taken at different times and the new local record lacks corroboration. Preserve the evidence and establish the current physical endpoints and peer identity before publishing a correction.

whyWrong.0: The old record predates the move and may no longer describe the current connection.
whyWrong.2: An identity or port-record conflict alone does not establish a physical-layer fault.
whyWrong.3: The newer record is useful evidence, but its identity and physical endpoint still need corroboration.

cards.front: What kind of protocol is CDP?
cards.back: Cisco Discovery Protocol discovers nearby participating devices at Layer 2. Its operation does not require a working IP route between them.

cards.front: What is LLDP?
cards.back: Link Layer Discovery Protocol is the vendor-neutral link-discovery standard IEEE 802.1AB.

cards.front: In show cdp neighbors, who owns Local Intrfce and Port ID?
cards.back: Local Intrfce belongs to the device where you ran the command. Port ID is advertised by the neighbor. Record local device/port → remote device/port.

cards.front: How do the switch/bridge capability codes differ between CDP and LLDP?
cards.back: CDP S means switch. LLDP B means bridge; LLDP S means station. Read each output’s legend rather than transferring letters between protocols.

cards.front: Why use show cdp neighbors detail after the brief table?
cards.back: It can expose advertised addresses, software/platform details, and additional TLVs that help identify the neighbor. Available fields depend on what the neighbor advertises and the image displays.

cards.front: Does an advertised management address prove that you can ping or SSH to it?
cards.back: No. CDP/LLDP receive advertisements at Layer 2. Verify IP addressing, VLANs, routing, policy, and the intended service separately; the address may belong to another interface on the neighbor.

cards.front: How do cdp run and cdp enable differ?
cards.back: cdp run controls the global process; cdp enable controls the selected interface. Both must permit CDP. A globally disabled process is not overridden by interface enablement.

cards.front: What global and interface controls permit LLDP on an intended link?
cards.back: `lldp run` enables the process; the selected interface's `lldp transmit` and `lldp receive` control its directions. Verify the actual state.

cards.front: Which LLDP directions allow SW1 to learn SW2?
cards.back: SW2 transmits on its connected port and SW1 receives on its connected port, with LLDP globally running. The reverse directions let SW2 learn SW1.

cards.front: What if show cdp or show lldp reports that the protocol is not enabled?
cards.back: Check global configuration first: cdp run or lldp run as appropriate. Then verify the intended interface settings and the peer’s corresponding protocol. Discovery protocols have independent state.

cards.front: Which LLDP commands inspect neighbor details and per-interface directions?
cards.back: show lldp neighbors detail shows received details; show lldp interface identifies local transmit/receive state on supporting IOS images. Inspect the actual fields and use the lesson’s paper fallback if the simulator omits LLDP.

cards.front: What does a discovery entry’s remaining lifetime tell you?
cards.back: How much longer the receiver may retain that entry without refresh. It is not link uptime or a guarantee that the neighbor is still connected. LLDP field labels/brief-display behavior vary; use detail output and the applicable command reference.

cards.front: Does an empty discovery table uniquely prove a broken cable?
cards.back: No. Inspect link state, common protocol support, global enablement, the relevant transmit/receive controls, and record freshness.

cards.front: What practical information can CDP version 2 add?
cards.back: The referenced IOS guide documents version 2 as enabled and includes information such as native VLAN and duplex. A mismatch warning is evidence to investigate, not an instruction to change either side without checking the design.

cards.front: What voice-network information can LLDP-MED advertise to a compatible phone?
cards.back: Network policy such as the voice VLAN and traffic priority. This does not replace DHCP or prove call-server registration.

cards.front: How should discovery be controlled at a network boundary?
cards.back: Follow the approved policy per port. Disable CDP and LLDP directions where discovery is prohibited; preserve verified dependencies such as approved phone network policy on trusted links. Disabling one protocol does not disable the other.

cards.front: Why might a CDP table omit a hub between its two speakers?
cards.back: A hub repeats signals and does not advertise a CDP identity. The speakers can be discovered across it. Document the inspected physical path separately; do not generalize this to every unmanaged bridge or to LLDP forwarding.

commands.note: The intended interfaces must also permit CDP.

commands.task: Disable CDP only on the currently selected untrusted interface.
commands.note: This does not disable LLDP; apply the separate LLDP policy if required.

commands.task: Enable the global LLDP process.
commands.note: Then explicitly configure and verify transmit/receive on the intended interfaces; global state alone is not the complete check.

commands.task: Disable LLDP reception on the selected interface while leaving its transmit setting unchanged.
commands.note: This stops learning new peer information on this port; it does not stop the peer learning your advertisements.

tickets.title: The uplink monitoring record points at the wrong port
tickets.scenario: The documentation and monitoring configuration claim that SW1 Gi0/1 connects to SW2 Gi0/1. The technician has just inspected the cable labels and sees its SW2 end on Gi0/2. Fresh CDP observations were collected at both ends. The exhibits are representative records, not live output from this app.

exhibits.text:
Device ID  Local Intrfce  Holdtme  Port ID
SW2        Gig 0/1       176      Gig 0/2

exhibits.title: SW2 discovery record
exhibits.text:
Device ID  Local Intrfce  Holdtme  Port ID
SW1        Gig 0/2       175      Gig 0/1

exhibits.title: Existing documentation
exhibits.text:

Monitor interface: SW2 Gi0/1

tickets.question: Which correction follows from the corroborated evidence?
options: Change only SW1's documented port to Gi0/2.
Correct the SW2 link and monitoring target to Gi0/2; retain SW1 Gi0/1.
Keep the old monitoring target because the remote Port ID describes a management SVI.
Change both documented ends to Gi0/2 because that remote port appears in the new record.
tickets.explanation: Both directions and the physical inspection identify SW1 Gi0/1 ↔ SW2 Gi0/2. The stale record uses the wrong SW2 port. Reversing the columns would move the error to SW1; interface numbers need not match. The observations support correcting this link record, but they do not prove that every VLAN or management service works. The Port ID is the neighbor's advertised sending port, not its management SVI. The reverse observation confirms SW1 remains on Gi0/1; changing both ends would introduce another error.
tickets.fix:
Update the local documentation to `SW1 Gi0/1 ↔ SW2 Gi0/2`, record when and how it was checked, and correct the intended monitoring interface using the monitoring system’s approved edit flow. This exercise does not change any real monitoring service. Preserve the original record in the change history.

```ios SW1
SW1# show cdp neighbors
SW1# show cdp neighbors detail
SW1# show interfaces gigabitethernet0/1
```

```ios SW2
SW2# show cdp neighbors
SW2# show interfaces gigabitethernet0/2
```

Verify refreshed observations and both physical port states. Test the required VLAN or management path separately before declaring the service healthy. If hostname or cable evidence disagrees, investigate identity and cache freshness instead of automatically overwriting the drawing.

SW1 has LLDP enabled globally and has explicitly enabled transmit and receive on Gi0/1. SW2’s recorded global output is below. Old entries have expired.

tickets.question: What is the most direct correction?
options: Enable SW2 LLDP globally and its Gi0/2 transmit/receive directions.
Enable only SW2 Gi0/2 transmit/receive while leaving its global process disabled.
Clear SW1's LLDP table without changing SW2's configuration.
Change SW1's LLDP holdtime while leaving SW2's global process disabled.
tickets.explanation: SW2 explicitly reports a disabled LLDP process. Its global process and intended interface directions must permit operation. Interface controls alone cannot override global disablement. Clearing SW1's table or adjusting a lifetime does not make SW2 send LLDP advertisements. CDP remains a separate working protocol.

Wait for an actual advertisement opportunity according to the configured timers, then verify each device receives the intended peer and remote port. Review interface discovery policy on other ports after globally enabling LLDP. Save the intended configuration after verification. If a simulator lacks LLDP, use these records as the paper exercise and do not label it an executed protocol test.

chapters.title: EtherChannel
chapters.subtitle: Build and verify LACP bundles without confusing aggregate capacity with one flow.

sources.title: Linux kernel: Ethernet bonding driver documentation
Cisco: EtherChannel load balancing and redundancy

chapters.summary: Explain LACP negotiation, compatible member settings, Layer 2 and Layer 3 port channels, endpoint teaming requirements, and traffic distribution; configure, verify, fault, and restore both bundle types.

sections.body:
An EtherChannel combines compatible Ethernet links into one logical interface. The arrangement can increase capacity across several traffic flows and keep a connection operating when one member fails. It also introduces a requirement: both ends must agree about which links belong to the bundle and how those links carry traffic.

You will first build a Layer 2 trunk bundle with LACP, then a routed Layer 3 bundle. Use the logical interface and member state together when verifying either design. Working traffic alone does not establish that every intended link has joined the channel.

sections.title: Why links are bundled
sections.body:
Without aggregation, two parallel switch links are separate Layer 2 paths. Ethernet has no general hop limit to stop a frame circulating around a switching loop. **Spanning Tree Protocol (STP)** prevents loops by placing redundant paths into nonforwarding roles. For now, understand that parallel cables do not automatically provide simultaneous usable forwarding capacity. Chapter 14 develops root selection, roles, and states in detail.

An **EtherChannel**, also called a **port channel**, groups its physical **member interfaces** into one logical link. STP handles a Layer 2 port channel as one interface for the relevant VLAN. The members are used by the bundle, rather than each becoming an independent competing STP path. STP can still block the entire logical port channel if it is redundant with another path. Aggregation does not disable loop prevention.

Two 1-Gbps members provide up to 2 Gbps of aggregate link capacity in each direction when traffic distribution uses both links. They do not turn every individual transfer into a 2-Gbps transfer. If one member fails, a normally configured bundle can continue through the surviving member with less capacity. Features that require a minimum number of active links can deliberately change that behavior.

Port channels are useful between switches, between routing-capable devices, and toward a server or appliance that supports the corresponding aggregation mode. A two-NIC server does not automatically need LACP. Its operating system, virtual switch, appliance configuration, and physical attachment must support the chosen design.

```diagram
{"type":"topology","title":"Two physical members, one logical port channel","caption":"Several traffic flows may use different members of Po1; an individual hash result selects one member.","nodes":[{"id":"A","kind":"switch","label":"SW1","sub":"Po1","x":3,"y":3},{"id":"B","kind":"switch","label":"SW2","sub":"Po1","x":9,"y":3}],"links":[{"from":"A","to":"B","label":"Po1: two 1-Gbps members","fromLabel":"Gi0/1 + Gi0/2","toLabel":"Gi0/1 + Gi0/2","accent":true}]}
```

sections.title: LACP negotiation and the alternatives
sections.body:
:::facts
- **LACP** is the standards-based Link Aggregation Control Protocol, now specified by IEEE 802.1AX; older references use IEEE 802.3ad.
- LACP `active` initiates negotiation; `passive` responds. Active/active and active/passive can form a bundle; passive/passive cannot initiate one.
- **PAgP** is Cisco's Port Aggregation Protocol: `desirable` initiates, `auto` responds.
- `on` uses static aggregation without LACP or PAgP negotiation. Both endpoints need compatible static configuration.
- `S` means Layer 2, `R` means Layer 3, and `U` means in use in common `show etherchannel summary` output. Member `P` means bundled.
- Configure a routed port channel's IP address on the logical interface, not on each member.
:::

LACP exchanges information about the sending system and its ports. The switches use that information, together with local interface compatibility, to select links for one aggregate. A physically up port is only a candidate; it must also join the correct partner and bundle. LACP active mode does not mean that the port is the only forwarding member, and passive mode does not mean a standby-only data link.

| Endpoint A | Endpoint B | Negotiation result, assuming compatible links |
|---|---|---|
| LACP active | LACP active | Can form a bundle |
| LACP active | LACP passive | Can form a bundle |
| LACP passive | LACP passive | No initiating LACP peer |
| PAgP desirable | PAgP desirable or auto | Can form a PAgP bundle |
| PAgP auto | PAgP auto | No initiating PAgP peer |
| Static on | Static on | Static bundle; no negotiation validation |
| LACP active | PAgP desirable or static on | Incompatible aggregation methods |

Use LACP for the main exercises. PAgP and static mode are useful comparisons, not alternative spellings of LACP. `channel-group 1 mode on` does not make the switch answer a neighbor's LACP packets. An asymmetric static/dynamic setup can cause loss or loops; do not create it casually on a production link.

The **channel-group number** identifies the local bundle. SW1 group 1 can connect to SW2 group 5; matching numbers are an administrative convenience, not an LACP requirement. What matters is that the intended links on each device belong to the correct local group and identify the same appropriate aggregation partner.

When LACP does not form, members may be suspended, down, or operate individually depending on platform and configuration. Do not promise that passive/passive will preserve user connectivity. Read the member flags and interface state. Cisco's referenced current Catalyst guide, for example, documents standalone forwarding as disabled by default.

sections.title: Check both ends before configuring
sections.body:
Start with a connection table. List every local member, the far device, and the far port. CDP or LLDP can help confirm the observed endpoints, but also inspect the actual cables. In the simple design used here, all members connect the same two switches. Connecting half the links to a separate independent switch does not create one valid remote LACP system.

Member interfaces need compatible operational characteristics. Check their speed, duplex, Layer 2 versus routed mode, and the supported interface types for that device. For a Layer 2 bundle, members must share the intended access VLAN or compatible trunk settings, including native VLAN and allowed VLANs. LACP negotiates aggregation; it does not automatically build the VLAN design.

| Check | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Same intended partner on all links | Prevents grouping unrelated physical paths |
| Compatible member speed and duplex | Gives the aggregate a supported set of physical links |
| Layer 2 or Layer 3 on all members | Avoids mixing switched and routed interfaces |
| Consistent access VLAN or trunk settings | Ensures frames receive the same treatment on any member |
| Compatible protocol and modes | Allows both ends to agree on aggregation |
| Required VLANs configured at both ends | Makes the intended traffic service available after formation |

Distinguish local member consistency from the service settings across the two switches. A local mismatch can prevent a member from joining. A VLAN mismatch between complete logical trunks may still leave a bundle up while particular traffic fails. Successful LACP negotiation is therefore necessary evidence for this design, but not the whole service test.

For a server, verify its actual teaming mode before selecting switch commands. An LACP team needs an LACP-capable host configuration. A supported static team needs matching static aggregation. A switch-independent team may require separate switch ports with no port channel. An access port or trunk is chosen separately according to the endpoint's VLAN requirements; do not infer the mode from a device label such as “hypervisor.”

For one LACP bundle, a server whose members attach to two physical switches needs those switches to offer a supported common logical aggregation system, such as an appropriate stack or multichassis design. Two unrelated switches are insufficient. This chapter does not configure those designs; it teaches the requirement so that a port-channel template is not applied to an incompatible endpoint. The same check applies to firewalls and other network appliances.

sections.title: Build Layer 2 and Layer 3 port channels
sections.body:
For a Layer 2 trunk bundle, define the VLANs, make both members consistent, and apply `channel-group ... mode active`. Keep new parallel links administratively shut while configuring both ends, then enable the finished bundle. This prevents the work-in-progress cabling from being mistaken for a verified channel.

The example below is one side of a two-member Catalyst 2960 trunk. The lab supplies both endpoints, PC settings, and verification. `interface range` selects the physical members; `interface port-channel 1` selects their logical interface.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# vlan 10
SW1(config-vlan)# exit
SW1(config)# vlan 99
SW1(config-vlan)# exit
SW1(config)# interface range fastethernet0/23 - 24
SW1(config-if-range)# shutdown
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport mode trunk
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport trunk native vlan 99
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,99
SW1(config-if-range)# channel-group 1 mode active
SW1(config-if-range)# exit
SW1(config)# interface port-channel 1
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 99
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,99
SW1(config-if)# end
```

Once the bundle exists, make common trunk changes on its logical interface and verify the resulting member settings. Do not edit only one member's allowed VLAN list as a way to add a VLAN to the channel. Configuration inheritance and consistency checks can vary by image; the running configuration and operational output show what actually took effect.

A **Layer 3 EtherChannel** is a routed connection. Its members are routed ports, and the logical port channel holds one IP address for the local end. It does not carry a switchport access VLAN or trunk allowed list. The far end has another usable address in the same transit subnet, just as with an ordinary routed Ethernet link.

On the Catalyst 3560 used for the routed lab, create the routed logical interface and make its members routed before assigning the group. A Layer 2-only 2960 is not a substitute for this part.

```ios D1
D1# configure terminal
D1(config)# ip routing
D1(config)# interface port-channel 1
D1(config-if)# no switchport
D1(config-if)# ip address 10.13.12.1 255.255.255.252
D1(config-if)# no shutdown
D1(config-if)# exit
D1(config)# interface range fastethernet0/1 - 2
D1(config-if-range)# shutdown
D1(config-if-range)# no switchport
D1(config-if-range)# no ip address
D1(config-if-range)# channel-group 1 mode active
D1(config-if-range)# end
```

D2 uses 10.13.12.2/30 on its corresponding logical interface. After both endpoints are ready, enable the members, inspect the bundle and connected route, and ping across it. This establishes the transit link; communication with additional remote networks would require the appropriate routes and return paths.

sections.title: Understand traffic distribution and capacity
sections.body:
A switch normally selects an outgoing member using a **hash** of selected frame or packet fields. Depending on hardware and configuration, the inputs can include source/destination MAC addresses, IP addresses, or transport ports. The same input values usually select the same member while membership is stable. Keeping related traffic together avoids routine packet reordering.

“Per flow” is a useful shorthand, but the configured hash may distinguish fewer fields than a full TCP connection. A source-MAC-only hash places all traffic with the same source MAC onto the same selected member. Several different conversations can therefore share one member. Two distinct inputs can also hash to the same member, so multiple clients do not guarantee equal distribution.

A four-member 1-Gbps bundle has up to 4 Gbps of aggregate capacity per direction across suitably distributed traffic. One conversation assigned to one member remains limited by that member's 1-Gbps line rate, with application throughput below it because of overhead and other limits. Adding members does not remove a server, disk, or remote-path bottleneck.

Suppose a distribution switch routes traffic toward many clients through an EtherChannel. Those outgoing Ethernet frames may all have the distribution switch's source MAC. If its selected method uses only that MAC, the downstream traffic can concentrate on one member. An available destination-based or source-and-destination IP method may provide more varied input. Verify the current method rather than assume a product-family default.

Use `show etherchannel load-balance` on a supporting image. The referenced Catalyst platforms configure the method with the global `port-channel load-balance` command, so a change can affect several bundles. Choose it deliberately and inspect actual counters under representative traffic. The two ends can make independent outbound selections; matching hash settings are not required for LACP formation.

Member-count limits also depend on platform. The referenced Catalyst 3560 guide describes up to eight active LACP members with additional configured links in standby, up to sixteen total. This is a platform example, not an IEEE-wide limit or a substitute for checking the target switch. The required labs use only two members and do not depend on standby-member selection.

sections.title: Read the bundle and partner state
sections.body:
Read the legend printed by `show etherchannel summary`. These are representative excerpts for the two lab topologies, not captured Packet Tracer output.

```output SW1# show etherchannel summary
Flags: D - down        P - bundled in port-channel
       I - stand-alone s - suspended
       R - Layer3      S - Layer2
       U - in use
Group  Port-channel  Protocol    Ports
------+-------------+-----------+-----------------------------------
1      Po1(SU)       LACP        Fa0/23(P) Fa0/24(P)  ← Layer 2, in use, two bundled members
```

```output D1# show etherchannel summary
Group  Port-channel  Protocol    Ports
------+-------------+-----------+-----------------------------------
1      Po1(RU)       LACP        Fa0/1(P) Fa0/2(P)  ← routed logical interface, two bundled members
```

`U` describes the logical interface, while `P` describes each member's participation. A channel may remain in use with only one intended member bundled. Count the participating members instead of stopping at the first reassuring flag. Lowercase `s` means suspended; uppercase `S` means a Layer 2 port channel. Case matters.

Use `show lacp neighbor` to compare the partner system and port information. Both intended links should identify the same appropriate partner system, with different partner ports. Do not memorize one hexadecimal state byte as proof for every platform. Use the summary, partner information, and interface configuration together. Where a simulator lacks this command, `show etherchannel port-channel` and inspection of both ends provide a partial alternative, not an identical protocol capture.

sections.title: Verify traffic and correct faults
sections.body:
For a Layer 2 trunk channel, check the bundle, then `show interfaces trunk` and the VLAN configuration on both ends. Confirm that the PCs are on the intended access VLAN and have compatible addresses. STP should see the logical port channel for that VLAN. Reading its detailed role and cost belongs to the next chapter; this lab does not require memorizing an aggregate STP cost.

For a Layer 3 channel, verify that the IP address belongs to `Port-channel1`, that the members are routed and unnumbered, and that the expected connected prefix appears when the interface is operational. Test both directions. A successful peer ping establishes the local transit exchange, not reachability to every network beyond the peer.

When a member fails, record the member flags, active member count, and logical state before restoring it. Brief packet loss can occur while traffic is reassigned; do not promise zero loss or a fixed recovery interval. In a two-member lab with no minimum-links requirement above one, the healthy member can maintain the channel while available capacity drops.

When an intended bundle fails completely, compare the actual configuration with the connection table. Check physical state, compatible LACP modes, partner identity, routed versus switched mode, and VLAN consistency. Make one justified change, then repeat the same checks. Do not force static `on` simply to obtain an up flag; that removes negotiation without correcting an incompatible design.

:::trap An up port channel can have reduced capacity
`Po1(SU)` tells you that a Layer 2 port channel is in use. It does not count the active members for you. If only one of two intended interfaces has `(P)`, investigate the other interface even when a ping succeeds.
:::

sections.title: Exam focus
sections.body:
- Explain why STP treats a Layer 2 bundle as one logical interface.
- Recognize compatible LACP modes and distinguish PAgP and static aggregation.
- Check physical members, partner identity, VLAN settings, and endpoint teaming requirements.
- Configure and verify both Layer 2 and Layer 3 LACP port channels.
- Interpret logical-interface flags separately from individual member flags.
- Explain aggregate capacity, hash-based distribution, and one-flow limitations.
- Diagnose a missing member or failed traffic service and verify recovery.

lab.title: Build, fault, and restore Layer 2 and Layer 3 LACP bundles
devices: 2 × Catalyst 3560-24PS (D1, D2) for a separate Layer 3 topology
lab.intro:
Practice revised September 2026. If you completed an earlier version, repeat the revised exercise and update its checkmarks.

Build a two-member Layer 2 trunk, verify each member, and observe a member failure separately from a negotiation failure. Then create a routed port channel in a second file. These instructions and representative states have been checked against Cisco configuration guidance; this exercise has not been executed in Packet Tracer during this review.

## Evidence to keep

Keep both-end summaries, participating-member counts and the separate VLAN or IP service checks. Compare your predictions with the observed member-failure and negotiation-failure states. Explain why a passing ping does not establish full capacity. Mark any supplied-evidence fallback clearly; neither ping nor a representative summary is a throughput measurement.
