| Device and port | Connected device and port | Cable | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| PC-A FastEthernet0 | SW1 Fa0/1 | Copper straight-through | VLAN 10 endpoint |
| PC-B FastEthernet0 | SW2 Fa0/1 | Copper straight-through | VLAN 10 endpoint |
| SW1 Fa0/23 | SW2 Fa0/23 | Copper crossover | First Po1 member |
| SW1 Fa0/24 | SW2 Fa0/24 | Copper crossover | Second Po1 member |
| D1 Fa0/1 | D2 Fa0/1 | Copper crossover | Separate Layer 3 topology, first member |
| D1 Fa0/2 | D2 Fa0/2 | Copper crossover | Separate Layer 3 topology, second member |

Use the named models so that these interfaces exist. Auto-connect is acceptable if you inspect the chosen ports afterward. Do not substitute 3650 interface names into the 3560 instructions. Begin with new, empty devices. All physical members in this lab are FastEthernet: each is 100 Mbps, not 1 Gbps.

| Interface | IPv4 address | Mask | Gateway |
|---|---|---|---|
| PC-A FastEthernet0 | 10.13.10.11 | 255.255.255.0 | Leave blank |
| PC-B FastEthernet0 | 10.13.10.12 | 255.255.255.0 | Leave blank |
| D1 Port-channel1, second file | 10.13.12.1 | 255.255.255.252 | Not applicable |
| D2 Port-channel1, second file | 10.13.12.2 | 255.255.255.252 | Not applicable |

The PCs share a subnet, so this exercise needs no default gateway. The Layer 2 trunk carries VLAN 10 and uses VLAN 99 as its native VLAN. The Layer 3 bundle carries an IP subnet directly and has no trunk or native VLAN configuration.

steps.title: Prepare the switches before connecting both uplinks
steps.body:
Place SW1, SW2, and the PCs. Connect the PC cables now; leave the two switch-to-switch cables disconnected until the selected members have been shut down below. This avoids creating temporary independent parallel links during configuration. Configure each device from its console.

```ios SW1
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW1
SW1(config)# no ip domain-lookup
SW1(config)# vlan 10
SW1(config-vlan)# name USERS
SW1(config-vlan)# vlan 99
SW1(config-vlan)# name NATIVE
SW1(config-vlan)# exit
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 10
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# interface range fastethernet0/23 - 24
SW1(config-if-range)# shutdown
SW1(config-if-range)# end
```

```ios SW2
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW2
SW2(config)# no ip domain-lookup
SW2(config)# vlan 10
SW2(config-vlan)# name USERS
SW2(config-vlan)# vlan 99
SW2(config-vlan)# name NATIVE
SW2(config-vlan)# exit
SW2(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
SW2(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW2(config-if)# switchport access vlan 10
SW2(config-if)# no shutdown
SW2(config-if)# interface range fastethernet0/23 - 24
SW2(config-if-range)# shutdown
SW2(config-if-range)# end
```

Connect the two crossover uplinks exactly as the port table specifies. On each PC, use Desktop → IP Configuration and enter its address and mask. Leave gateway and DNS blank.

:::expected
Both VLANs exist on each switch. The PC ports belong to VLAN 10. Both uplink members remain administratively down, so the PCs cannot yet communicate across the switches.
:::

steps.title: Configure LACP on both ends, then enable the links
steps.body:
Complete both configuration blocks before enabling any uplink. The 2960 uses 802.1Q; do not add a trunk encapsulation selection command that this model does not require.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface range fastethernet0/23 - 24
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport mode trunk
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport trunk native vlan 99
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,99
SW1(config-if-range)# channel-group 1 mode active
SW1(config-if-range)# exit
SW1(config)# interface port-channel 1
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 99
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,99
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# end
```

```ios SW2
SW2# configure terminal
SW2(config)# interface range fastethernet0/23 - 24
SW2(config-if-range)# switchport mode trunk
SW2(config-if-range)# switchport trunk native vlan 99
SW2(config-if-range)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,99
SW2(config-if-range)# channel-group 1 mode active
SW2(config-if-range)# exit
SW2(config)# interface port-channel 1
SW2(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
SW2(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 99
SW2(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,99
SW2(config-if)# no shutdown
SW2(config-if)# end
```

Now enable the members on both devices.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface range fastethernet0/23 - 24
SW1(config-if-range)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if-range)# end
```

```ios SW2
SW2# configure terminal
SW2(config)# interface range fastethernet0/23 - 24
SW2(config-if-range)# no shutdown
SW2(config-if-range)# end
```

:::expected
After link initialization, negotiation, and any STP transition, both physical links should join Po1. Exact timing varies; verify the state in the next step instead of assuming a fixed waiting period.
:::

steps.title: Prove the logical link and both members work
steps.body:
Before collecting output, predict the logical type, number of bundled members, allowed VLANs, and PC reachability. Keep those as four separate acceptance checks; one reassuring flag cannot answer all four.

```ios SW1
SW1# show etherchannel summary
SW1# show etherchannel port-channel
SW1# show interfaces trunk
SW1# show spanning-tree vlan 10
SW1# show lacp neighbor
```

```ios SW2
SW2# show etherchannel summary
SW2# show interfaces trunk
SW2# show spanning-tree vlan 10
SW2# show lacp neighbor
```

Some Packet Tracer images omit `show lacp neighbor` or detailed fields in `show etherchannel port-channel`. Use the available summary, member configuration, and trunk output for the formation checks; inspect partner details on supporting IOS/CML hardware if necessary. Do not treat an unsupported show command as a failed bundle.

On PC-A open Desktop → Command Prompt and run `ping 10.13.10.12`; on PC-B run `ping 10.13.10.11`. Repeat after address resolution if the first attempt loses a packet. This tests reachability, not aggregate throughput.

:::expected
A representative healthy summary is `Po1(SU) LACP Fa0/23(P) Fa0/24(P)`. Your device supplies the actual flags and formatting. Po1 is a trunk with native VLAN 99 and allowed VLANs 10,99. STP represents the bundle as Po1; in this isolated two-switch topology it forwards VLAN 10 after convergence. Both PC pings succeed. Two 100-Mbps members provide up to 200 Mbps aggregate capacity per direction across suitably distributed traffic, but this ping does not measure it.
:::

steps.title: Fail one member and inspect the remaining capacity
steps.body:
Predict whether the bundle can remain in use, how many members should participate, and the remaining aggregate capacity. Then shut one member on SW1. Stop here and observe before doing the recovery step.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/23
SW1(config-if)# shutdown
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show etherchannel summary
```

```ios SW2
SW2# show etherchannel summary
```

Repeat the PC-A ping to PC-B. Inspect whether Fa0/24 remains bundled on both ends.

:::expected
With this lab's default configuration and no extra minimum-links policy, Po1 should remain in use through Fa0/24. Fa0/23 is no longer a forwarding member; the exact flag depends on device state. Aggregate link capacity has fallen from two 100-Mbps members to one. A brief interruption may occur, but no particular number of lost packets is guaranteed. Successful ping does not mean the missing member is healthy.
:::

steps.title: Restore the failed member
steps.body:
```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/23
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show etherchannel summary
```

```ios SW2
SW2# show etherchannel summary
```

First verify both members are bundled on both switches and repeat both PC pings. Then run `copy running-config startup-config` on SW1, complete its destination prompt, and wait for completion. Do the same on SW2 in its own CLI window. Save a Packet Tracer checkpoint as `13-lacp-l2-working.pkt`.

:::expected
Both members return to `(P)` and Po1 remains in use on both switches. PC-A and PC-B communicate. Keep this checkpoint before changing negotiation modes.
:::

steps.title: Create a passive/passive negotiation fault
steps.body:
Before changing modes, predict whether the physical links can be up while no LACP bundle forms. This is an intentional fault in the isolated lab. On both switches, shut the members before removing and reapplying their group membership. Complete both blocks, then enable the members in the two subsequent blocks.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface range fastethernet0/23 - 24
SW1(config-if-range)# shutdown
SW1(config-if-range)# no channel-group
SW1(config-if-range)# channel-group 1 mode passive
SW1(config-if-range)# end
```

```ios SW2
SW2# configure terminal
SW2(config)# interface range fastethernet0/23 - 24
SW2(config-if-range)# shutdown
SW2(config-if-range)# no channel-group
SW2(config-if-range)# channel-group 1 mode passive
SW2(config-if-range)# end
```

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface range fastethernet0/23 - 24
SW1(config-if-range)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if-range)# end
SW1# show etherchannel summary
```

```ios SW2
SW2# configure terminal
SW2(config)# interface range fastethernet0/23 - 24
SW2(config-if-range)# no shutdown
SW2(config-if-range)# end
SW2# show etherchannel summary
```

Record the result before continuing. The physical trunk settings should remain as configured; inspect `show running-config` if the image behaves differently after group removal.

:::expected
Neither side initiates LACP, so a new LACP bundle cannot form. Your image may show individual, suspended, or down members. Whether an unbundled link forwards user traffic depends on platform and configuration; do not infer a universal result from this simulator. The fault is the passive/passive pairing even if some traffic still works.
:::

steps.title: Diagnose a static/LACP mismatch on paper
steps.body:
Do not apply this asymmetric configuration to the live topology. Consider a separate record in which SW1 uses `channel-group 1 mode on` on both members and SW2 uses `channel-group 1 mode active`. All VLAN, speed, and duplex settings otherwise match. Explain why changing a timer cannot make this an LACP bundle.

:::solution Compare your diagnosis
SW1 is using static aggregation and does not negotiate LACP. SW2 expects an LACP partner. These are incompatible methods, not a slow negotiation. The correct design is matching compatible aggregation methods, such as active/active LACP. Static/on on both ends is a different supported design when configured consistently; it does not provide LACP's partner checks. No exact traffic or interface-state outcome is assumed for the asymmetric case.
:::

steps.title: Restore LACP and save the Layer 2 exercise
steps.body:
Keep both pairs shut while changing their membership. Complete the configuration blocks before enabling either pair.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface range fastethernet0/23 - 24
SW1(config-if-range)# shutdown
SW1(config-if-range)# no channel-group
SW1(config-if-range)# channel-group 1 mode active
SW1(config-if-range)# end
```

```ios SW2
SW2# configure terminal
SW2(config)# interface range fastethernet0/23 - 24
SW2(config-if-range)# shutdown
SW2(config-if-range)# no channel-group
SW2(config-if-range)# channel-group 1 mode active
SW2(config-if-range)# end
```

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface range fastethernet0/23 - 24
SW1(config-if-range)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if-range)# end
SW1# show etherchannel summary
SW1# show interfaces trunk
```

```ios SW2
SW2# configure terminal
SW2(config)# interface range fastethernet0/23 - 24
SW2(config-if-range)# no shutdown
SW2(config-if-range)# end
SW2# show etherchannel summary
SW2# show interfaces trunk
```

:::expected
Both members return to `(P)` on both ends, and the original trunk settings remain consistent. Repeat both PC pings. Then save each running configuration with `copy running-config startup-config`, completing one device's prompt before starting the other, and save `13-lacp-l2-complete.pkt`. Do not save the passive/passive fault as your final working state.
:::

steps.title: Build and verify a routed port channel in a separate file
steps.body:
Create `13-lacp-l3.pkt` with two new Catalyst 3560-24PS switches. Connect Fa0/1 to Fa0/1 and Fa0/2 to Fa0/2 with crossover cables only after the member shutdown commands have been entered. The following blocks keep the members shut throughout configuration. Create the logical routed interface first, then add routed members. Addresses belong to Po1, not to Fa0/1 or Fa0/2.

```ios D1
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname D1
D1(config)# ip routing
D1(config)# interface range fastethernet0/1 - 2
D1(config-if-range)# shutdown
D1(config-if-range)# exit
D1(config)# interface port-channel 1
D1(config-if)# no switchport
D1(config-if)# ip address 10.13.12.1 255.255.255.252
D1(config-if)# no shutdown
D1(config-if)# exit
D1(config)# interface range fastethernet0/1 - 2
D1(config-if-range)# no switchport
D1(config-if-range)# no ip address
D1(config-if-range)# channel-group 1 mode active
D1(config-if-range)# end
```

```ios D2
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname D2
D2(config)# ip routing
D2(config)# interface range fastethernet0/1 - 2
D2(config-if-range)# shutdown
D2(config-if-range)# exit
D2(config)# interface port-channel 1
D2(config-if)# no switchport
D2(config-if)# ip address 10.13.12.2 255.255.255.252
D2(config-if)# no shutdown
D2(config-if)# exit
D2(config)# interface range fastethernet0/1 - 2
D2(config-if-range)# no switchport
D2(config-if-range)# no ip address
D2(config-if-range)# channel-group 1 mode active
D2(config-if-range)# end
```

Connect the links and enable both member pairs.

```ios D1
D1# configure terminal
D1(config)# interface range fastethernet0/1 - 2
D1(config-if-range)# no shutdown
D1(config-if-range)# end
```

```ios D2
D2# configure terminal
D2(config)# interface range fastethernet0/1 - 2
D2(config-if-range)# no shutdown
D2(config-if-range)# end
```

After both ends are enabled, predict the subnet route and location of the IP addresses, then verify each side separately:

```ios D1
D1# show etherchannel summary
D1# show ip interface brief
D1# show ip route
D1# ping 10.13.12.2
```

```ios D2
D2# show etherchannel summary
D2# show ip interface brief
D2# show ip route
D2# ping 10.13.12.1
```

Repeat the pings after any needed address resolution. If your Packet Tracer image rejects routed port-channel configuration despite using the named multilayer model, complete this step on a supporting 3560 IOS image in hardware or an equivalent IOS switching image in CML; retain the same logical design and map available ports. If no supporting environment is available, complete a supplied-evidence worksheet using the address table and representative summary below: identify the interface that owns each address, the connected prefix, the two bundled members, and why no remote route is needed for this peer test. Label that work as interpreted evidence. Do not replace the routed bundle with a Layer 2 trunk and claim to have tested Layer 3 EtherChannel.

:::expected
A representative summary is `Po1(RU) LACP Fa0/1(P) Fa0/2(P)`: routed and in use, with two bundled members. Po1 owns `.1/30` or `.2/30`; the physical members have no IP addresses. The connected route is `10.13.12.0/30` through Port-channel1, and each peer address responds to ping. No routing protocol or static route is required to reach the directly connected peer. Only after those checks pass, save D1 and D2 with `copy running-config startup-config`, completing each destination prompt separately, and save the second project.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- **Po1 is up but only one member has `(P)`:** inspect both ends of the missing link. Check shutdown state, physical connectivity, speed/duplex, group membership, and local compatibility. A successful ping does not clear this fault.
- **Both ends are passive:** choose an active initiator. Do not try to repair the pairing by changing VLANs or group numbers.
- **Members are suspended after a trunk change:** compare the logical interface and all members. Restore the intended native VLAN and allowed list consistently, then verify the far-end trunk too.
- **Po1 is bundled but PC ping fails:** verify PC addresses/masks, access VLAN 10, VLAN existence, and allowed/forwarding VLANs. LACP formation does not configure those services.
- **Routed Po1 is down or lacks its connected route:** confirm both Po1 and members use `no switchport`, member flags are correct, the logical interface is enabled, and its address/mask is correct.
- **A show command is unsupported:** use the stated simulator fallback for that observation, and record the limit. An unavailable command is different from an observed protocol failure.
lab.challenge:
If routed EtherChannel is unavailable in your environment, continue the Step 9 worksheet fallback: write both endpoint command sequences and predict the summary, IP ownership, connected route and capacity checks. Label the submission as a plan, not an executed test. Otherwise, work from a copy of the successful Layer 3 project. Add a third physical member using Fa0/3 on each 3560, keeping the same Po1 addresses. Plan the cable, configuration mode, and verification before entering commands. Predict aggregate capacity and the limit for one flow when the load-balancing inputs consistently choose one member.

:::solution Check your third-member design
Use a crossover cable from D1 Fa0/3 to D2 Fa0/3. On each switch, enter privileged EXEC, then global configuration and `interface fastethernet0/3`. Apply `shutdown`, `no switchport`, `no ip address`, and `channel-group 1 mode active`. After both ends are ready and connected, apply `no shutdown` on each new member. Leave the existing Po1 addresses unchanged. Verify `Po1(RU)` with Fa0/1, Fa0/2, and Fa0/3 all `(P)`, then repeat peer pings. Three 100-Mbps members provide up to 300 Mbps aggregate link capacity per direction across appropriately distributed traffic; one stable hash-selected flow remains limited to one 100-Mbps member before overhead. Adding members does not require another IP subnet.
:::

exhibit.title: Representative SW1# show etherchannel summary
exhibit.text:
Group  Port-channel  Protocol  Ports
1      Po1(SU)       LACP      Fa0/23(P) Fa0/24(P)

questions.prompt: Which statement is fully supported by the summary?
options: Po1 is routed and both members are passive.
Po1 is Layer 2 and in use; both listed members are bundled.
Po1 carries every VLAN on the switch.
One flow can necessarily use the sum of both member speeds.
questions.explanation: S means Layer 2, U means in use, and P on each member means bundled. The summary establishes formation, not VLAN service correctness or single-flow throughput.

whyWrong.0: R would identify a routed bundle; the member P flag means bundled, not passive mode.
whyWrong.2: The allowed and forwarding VLAN lists require separate trunk/STP checks.
whyWrong.3: Hash-based distribution normally selects one member for the same traffic inputs.

questions.prompt: Assuming compatible links and supported LACP implementations, which two mode pairs can initiate an LACP bundle? Choose two.
options: active / active
passive / passive
desirable / auto
active / passive
questions.explanation: LACP needs an active initiator. Active/active and active/passive meet that requirement. Mode names also identify the protocol; a successful PAgP pair is not an LACP pair.

whyWrong.1: Neither passive endpoint initiates LACP.
whyWrong.2: Desirable/auto is PAgP, not LACP.

questions.prompt: How does STP treat a correctly formed Layer 2 EtherChannel for a VLAN?
options: As one logical STP interface that can still be blocked when required.
As separate competing STP ports for every active member.
As an instruction to disable STP for the entire VLAN.
As a routed interface that never carries Layer 2 frames.
questions.explanation: The port channel is the STP interface. Bundling avoids treating its members as independent parallel paths, but it does not remove STP’s responsibility to prevent loops elsewhere in the topology.

whyWrong.1: Bundled members are represented by the logical port channel for this purpose.
whyWrong.2: EtherChannel does not disable STP throughout the VLAN.
whyWrong.3: A Layer 2 EtherChannel remains a switched interface; R identifies the separate routed bundle type.

exhibit.title: Representative D1# show etherchannel summary
exhibit.text:
Group  Port-channel  Protocol  Ports
1      Po1(RU)       LACP      Fa0/1(P) Fa0/2(P)

questions.prompt: What does RU mean in this summary?
options: Layer 2 and in use.
Layer 3 and down.
Layer 2 and suspended.
Layer 3 and in use.
questions.explanation: R means Layer 3 and U means in use. The physical P flags establish that both listed members have joined the routed bundle. Check IP addressing and connected routes separately.

whyWrong.0: S identifies Layer 2; this summary uses R.
whyWrong.1: U means in use, not down.
whyWrong.2: The logical flags are R and U; a lowercase member s would identify suspension.

questions.prompt: Which two conditions must be compatible among members of this ordinary Layer 2 EtherChannel? Choose two.
options: Every local group number must equal the group number at the far end.
Member speed and duplex.
Member trunk/access mode and relevant VLAN settings.
Every member must have a different IPv4 subnet.
questions.explanation: Members need supported compatible physical characteristics and consistent Layer 2 treatment. For trunks, inspect native and allowed VLAN settings as well as mode. A group number identifies the local bundle.

whyWrong.0: Matching group numbers between devices is a naming convenience, not an LACP requirement.
whyWrong.3: Layer 2 members are not individually addressed routed links.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly compares PAgP with LACP?
options: PAgP uses desirable and auto; LACP uses active and passive.
PAgP uses active and passive; LACP uses desirable and auto.
PAgP auto and LACP passive negotiate directly with each other.
Static on is the initiating mode of both protocols.
questions.explanation: PAgP is Cisco’s aggregation protocol and uses desirable/auto. LACP uses active/passive. An initiating mode is needed for each dynamic protocol, and the endpoints must use compatible protocols.

whyWrong.1: The mode pairs have been reversed.
whyWrong.2: They are different protocols, and both listed modes are responders rather than initiators.
whyWrong.3: on disables aggregation-protocol negotiation; it is not an initiating dynamic mode.

questions.prompt: Which command on a supporting IOS image displays the LACP partner information learned for bundle members?
options: show lacp neighbor
show ip route
show interfaces trunk
show vlan brief
questions.explanation: show lacp neighbor displays partner information such as system and port identifiers, with fields depending on the image. Compare intended partner identity across members; do not memorize a single hexadecimal state as universally healthy.

whyWrong.1: The route table identifies IP forwarding routes, not LACP partners.
whyWrong.2: Trunk output helps verify VLAN service but does not replace LACP partner inspection.
whyWrong.3: The VLAN database does not show LACP partner state.

questions.prompt: What does passive mean for an LACP endpoint after a compatible bundle forms?
options: It keeps all its members as backup-only data links.
It responds to negotiation; its bundled members can still forward data.
It switches the bundle to PAgP after the active peer is found.
It transmits data only if the active endpoint's links fail.
questions.explanation: Active and passive describe negotiation behavior, not primary/standby data forwarding. A formed bundle can use its compatible bundled members in either traffic direction.

whyWrong.0: Responding to negotiation does not make every member standby-only.
whyWrong.2: LACP does not turn into PAgP after formation.
whyWrong.3: Normal outbound member selection is not conditional on failure of the active peer's links.

questions.prompt: Both intended LACP members on each switch are configured mode passive. Physical links and VLAN settings are correct, but a new bundle does not form. Which targeted change addresses the cause?
options: Change only the remote channel-group number to match the local number.
Change both trunk native VLANs from 99 to 1.
Configure the intended members on at least one endpoint as LACP active.
Change one endpoint to mode on while leaving the other passive.
questions.explanation: At least one endpoint must initiate LACP. An active/passive pair can negotiate when the member settings and partner design are valid.

whyWrong.0: Channel-group numbers are locally significant and need not match between endpoints.
whyWrong.1: Changing already-compatible native VLANs does not create an LACP initiator.
whyWrong.3: Static on does not negotiate LACP and is incompatible with the remaining LACP endpoint.

questions.prompt: Four 1-Gbps members form a healthy EtherChannel. The selected algorithm consistently hashes one large TCP flow to one member. What is its member-link capacity ceiling before protocol overhead?
options: 1 Gbps
2 Gbps
4 Gbps
8 Gbps
questions.explanation: The flow is assigned to one 1-Gbps member. Four members can provide up to 4 Gbps aggregate link capacity per direction across suitably distributed traffic; that is not a promise for one transfer.

whyWrong.1: The stated hash result does not split this flow across two members.
whyWrong.2: 4 Gbps is the aggregate capacity of four members in one direction, not this flow’s selected link.
whyWrong.3: Adding both full-duplex directions does not give one unidirectional flow 8 Gbps.

questions.prompt: Which plan correctly creates a routed Layer 3 EtherChannel between two supporting multilayer switches?
options: Give every member the same IPv4 address and leave the port channel unnumbered.
Configure Po1 as an 802.1Q trunk and put the peer-link address on each member.
Assign a different subnet to every member; LACP combines the routes.
Create routed, addressed Po1 first; then add unnumbered routed members.
questions.explanation: The logical routed interface owns the IP configuration. Its physical members carry the aggregate’s traffic and are not separate addressed routed links. The referenced 3560 procedure creates the routed port channel before adding its members.

whyWrong.0: Repeating the logical link address on physical members is not the routed port-channel design.
whyWrong.1: A Layer 2 trunk and individually addressed members do not form the requested Layer 3 bundle.
whyWrong.2: LACP aggregates links, not unrelated routed subnets.

exhibit.title: Representative failure evidence
exhibit.text:
Po1(SU) LACP Fa0/23(P) Fa0/24(s)
Recorded log reason: vlan mask is different

questions.prompt: The recorded configuration on this switch shows Po1 and Fa0/23 allow VLANs 10,99, but Fa0/24 allows 10,20,99. The log cites incompatible VLAN masks. What should you investigate first?
options: The trunk allowed list only at the remote end.
Local trunk-setting consistency between Po1 and both physical members.
Whether the local and remote channel-group numbers are identical.
Whether passive mode is forbidden as an LACP response mode.
questions.explanation: The local consistency failure is explicitly identified by the configuration and log. Restore the intended allowed VLAN list across the logical interface and members, then check the far end and actual VLAN forwarding.

whyWrong.0: The log and local configuration identify a local member mismatch first; far-end service verification follows that repair.
whyWrong.2: Local group numbers can differ across the link.
whyWrong.3: Passive can respond to active; it is not inherently an invalid member mode.

questions.prompt: A virtualized server needs a two-link LACP connection to a switch. Which requirement must be confirmed before configuring the switch bundle?
options: The server has two NICs, which guarantees LACP support.
Each NIC reaches a different independent switch; that always creates one LACP partner.
The endpoint supports and uses LACP with compatible VLAN and partner configuration.
The host uses any teaming mode, because all teaming modes exchange LACP.
questions.explanation: Endpoint support and its selected mode matter. LACP is one teaming design; static and switch-independent approaches have different requirements. Links must terminate on the intended supported aggregation partner, not arbitrary independent switches.

whyWrong.0: NIC count alone says nothing about operating-system, virtual-switch, licensing, or configured LACP support.
whyWrong.1: Separate independent switches do not automatically present one logical LACP system.
whyWrong.3: Switch-independent teaming and static aggregation are not synonyms for LACP.

questions.prompt: SW1 members use mode on while SW2 members use mode active. The cables and VLAN settings match. Which statement is correct?
options: They form LACP after both sides choose the same group number.
SW1’s on mode cannot provide the LACP negotiation expected by SW2; use a compatible mode pair.
The pairing is identical to active/passive.
Both sides are guaranteed to continue forwarding safely through independent links.
questions.explanation: Static aggregation does not answer LACP. Use a supported matching design such as active/active. The mismatched design can cause loss or loops; exact forwarding behavior is platform dependent.

whyWrong.0: Group numbers do not make static aggregation speak LACP.
whyWrong.2: Passive is an LACP response mode; on is static aggregation.
whyWrong.3: Failed or asymmetric aggregation does not guarantee safe standalone forwarding.

exhibit.title: Recorded device and traffic observations
exhibit.text:
Configured hash method: src-mac
Most transmitted frames: source MAC 0011.2233.4455
Both members: bundled (P)

questions.prompt: Traffic crosses a port channel with source-MAC hashing. Most frames entering that bundle have the same source MAC: the upstream router’s interface. Why may one member carry most of that traffic?
options: The switch assigns each successive frame to the next member.
LACP requires the active side to use only one member.
The native VLAN automatically chooses the first member.
The repeated source-MAC hash input can repeatedly select the same member.
questions.explanation: Hashing is deterministic for the selected inputs. Many IP sessions can still present one source MAC at this hop, so this algorithm may not spread them evenly. Inspect supported alternative inputs and actual traffic before choosing a different method.

whyWrong.0: Round-robin per-packet distribution is not the stated hash method.
whyWrong.1: Active describes negotiation, not an exclusive forwarding member.
whyWrong.2: Native VLAN selection does not explain repeated source-MAC hash results.

questions.prompt: SW1 uses channel-group 1 and SW2 uses channel-group 5. Both ends use active, all member settings are compatible, and both links join the same intended partner. What should you expect?
options: The mismatch prevents LACP negotiation.
The group numbers must be changed before any traffic can pass.
The bundle can form; the numbers identify the local port channels.
Only the link with the lower physical interface number can join.
questions.explanation: Channel-group numbers have local significance. SW1 Po1 and SW2 Po5 can be the two logical ends of the same aggregate when the actual partner and member requirements are satisfied.

whyWrong.0: LACP does not require matching local administrative group numbers across the link.
whyWrong.1: Renumbering is not necessary for the stated compatible design.
whyWrong.3: Local group-number differences do not select a single physical member.

questions.prompt: A four-member bundle loses one 1-Gbps member. Three remain bundled, no minimum-links policy removes the channel, and a stable flow uses one surviving member. Which two capacity statements are correct before overhead? Choose two.
options: Aggregate capacity remains 4 Gbps per direction.
Aggregate capacity is up to 3 Gbps per direction.
The selected flow's member-link ceiling becomes 3 Gbps.
The selected flow's member-link ceiling remains 1 Gbps.
The two full-duplex directions give that one flow 6 Gbps.
questions.explanation: Three surviving 1-Gbps members provide up to 3 Gbps per direction across suitably distributed traffic. The one stable flow still uses a single 1-Gbps member; neither outcome is a measured application throughput.

whyWrong.0: The failed member no longer contributes capacity.

cards.front: What does an EtherChannel combine?
cards.back: Compatible physical Ethernet links into one logical port-channel interface.

cards.front: Which LACP mode pairs can initiate a bundle?
cards.back: Active/active and active/passive. Passive/passive has no initiator. Modes describe negotiation, not primary/standby data forwarding.

cards.front: What are PAgP’s two dynamic modes?
cards.back: Desirable initiates; auto responds. Desirable/desirable or desirable/auto can form compatible PAgP bundles. Auto/auto does not initiate. PAgP is separate from LACP.

cards.front: What does channel-group 1 mode on mean?
cards.back: Static aggregation without LACP or PAgP negotiation. Both ends need compatible static configuration. It is not a way to answer an LACP active peer.

cards.front: Why must Layer 2 bundle members share compatible VLAN treatment?
cards.back: Traffic can leave through any selected member. Access/trunk mode and the relevant access, native and allowed VLAN settings must be consistent with the logical bundle.

cards.front: What must be checked before using LACP toward a server or appliance?
cards.back: Its actual teaming/bonding or virtual-switch implementation must support and use LACP. Verify VLAN treatment and a supported logical partner design. Two NICs or a generic teaming option does not establish LACP compatibility.

cards.front: Where do you apply and verify shared trunk settings after forming a Layer 2 port channel?
cards.back: Configure the intended trunk policy on the logical port-channel interface and verify the resulting settings on every member and the far end. Do not leave one physical member with a different allowed or native VLAN setting.

cards.front: Can one stable hash-selected flow use four 1-Gbps members as a 4-Gbps link?
cards.back: No. That flow selects one member, so its member-link ceiling is 1 Gbps before overhead. Several suitably distributed flows can use up to 4 Gbps aggregate capacity per direction.

cards.front: Which command displays the EtherChannel member-selection method on a supporting Catalyst image?
cards.back: `show etherchannel load-balance`. Inspect the actual supported method instead of assuming a universal default.

cards.front: Where is the peer-link IP address configured in a routed EtherChannel?
cards.back: On the logical port-channel interface with no switchport. Members are also routed and do not have individual IP addresses. Create the routed logical interface before adding members in the documented 3560 workflow.

cards.front: What do S, R, and U mean in show etherchannel summary?
cards.back: S = Layer 2; R = Layer 3; U = in use. Read the legend supplied by the device and inspect the individual member flags as well.

cards.front: What does member flag P mean in show etherchannel summary?
cards.back: The member is bundled in the port channel. P does not mean LACP passive; inspect each intended member, not just the logical interface's U flag.

cards.front: Which command shows the LACP partner learned on member links?
cards.back: `show lacp neighbor` on supporting IOS images. Compare system and port identities; use documented alternatives if the simulator omits the command.

cards.front: Why can many sessions still concentrate on one member with source-MAC hashing?
cards.back: At this hop they may all use the same source MAC, such as a router interface. Repeated selected inputs can give the same member even when IP destinations differ. The chosen hash fields, not session count alone, control distribution.

cards.front: Can one ordinary LACP bundle connect a host to two unrelated independent switches?
cards.back: Not as one assumed partner. A multi-device design needs explicitly supported technology that presents the required logical aggregation system. Do not configure arbitrary independent switches as if they were one partner.

cards.front: Must the channel-group number match between endpoints?
cards.back: No. It identifies the local port channel. SW1 group 1 and SW2 group 5 can form a valid aggregate if their actual partner and member configuration are compatible.

cards.front: What happens when one of two 100-Mbps members fails?
cards.back: With a surviving member and no policy requiring more links, the bundle can remain in use with 100 Mbps aggregate capacity per direction instead of 200. Observe actual interruption; do not promise a fixed number of lost packets.

cards.front: Po1 is in use but a member is suspended after a VLAN-list change. What next?
cards.back: Compare the logical interface and every local member, correct the intended trunk settings consistently, then verify the far end and the required VLAN traffic. Formation alone does not guarantee VLAN service.

cards.front: Po1 is SU with both members P, but VLAN 10 traffic fails. What should you check?
cards.back: Verify VLAN 10 exists, endpoint access VLANs and addresses are correct, and both port channels allow and forward the intended VLAN with consistent native VLAN settings. Formation does not prove the VLAN service.

cards.front: Must both ends use the same EtherChannel hash method?
cards.back: No. Each endpoint selects its own outbound member; compatible LACP formation does not require identical hash inputs.

cards.front: Does Po1(RU) prove that the peer's IP address and mask are correct?
cards.back: No. Formation and logical-interface state need separate IP addressing, connected-route and peer-reachability checks.

cards.front: What partner relationship should all members of this ordinary two-switch LACP bundle identify?
cards.back: The same intended remote system, through its different member ports.

If the image retains a discrepant physical setting, shut the affected member, set its allowed list to the approved list, restore it, and recheck; do not assume propagation occurred. Confirm native VLAN 99 is unchanged, VLAN 40 exists, and the required VLAN is allowed and forwarding on both ends. Test the intended VLAN 40 endpoints after their access-port configuration is complete. No exact recovery log or delay is promised.

Layer 2 members do not need individual IPv4 addresses. The failure establishes lack of bundle formation, not a guaranteed standalone forwarding behavior. Different native VLANs would introduce a separate inconsistency, and replacing only one end with static aggregation would create a protocol mismatch rather than repair negotiation.

Do not impose a fixed formation time or fixed packet-loss count.

chapters.title: Spanning tree
chapters.subtitle: Build a redundant LAN and predict its root, forwarding paths, and standby ports.

sources.title: Cisco: Catalyst 9400 documented short path-cost table
Cisco: Understand Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol
Cisco: Catalyst 2960 STP configuration and defaults

chapters.summary: Learn how Rapid PVST+ prevents Ethernet loops, compare bridge IDs and path costs, select port roles, and verify a deliberate primary and secondary root design.

sections.title: Why redundant Ethernet needs spanning tree
sections.body:
You already know that a switch learns a frame's source MAC address and forwards according to its destination MAC address within a VLAN. Now connect three switches in a triangle. A broadcast entering one switch can leave through both interswitch links, return through the third switch, and be flooded again. Ethernet has no hop limit to expire that circulating frame. The TTL inside an IPv4 packet does not help because ordinary Layer 2 switching does not decrement it.

Repeated flooding can consume link capacity, deliver duplicate frames, and make a source MAC appear on different ports. That last symptom is **MAC address table instability**: the switch keeps updating an otherwise valid source entry because copies arrive through different paths. Unknown unicasts can circulate too. A loop does not need a large original traffic load to become disruptive, and a switch does not correct it merely by learning more MAC addresses.

**Spanning Tree Protocol (STP)** permits physical redundancy while selecting a loop-free forwarding topology. A redundant port can remain operational at the physical layer yet discard user frames for a particular VLAN. It still participates in the control protocol, allowing a standby path to become useful after a failure. Do not interpret an intentionally blocked port as a faulty cable or administratively shut interface.

The historical **802.1D STP** used timer-based transitions. **RSTP**, introduced as 802.1w, adds port roles and handshakes that allow faster transitions. Cisco's **Rapid PVST+** runs a rapid spanning-tree instance per VLAN; **PVST+** uses the classic behavior. The CCNA core here is Rapid PVST+: determine the root, calculate paths, and interpret roles and states. Classic STP provides useful comparison, but you do not need a second full legacy design workflow.

sections.title: Bridge IDs and the root election
sections.body:
:::facts
- Lowest bridge ID wins: compare priority plus extended system ID, then MAC address.
- Configurable priority defaults to `32768`; legal values are `0`–`61440` in steps of `4096`. VLAN 10 adds `10` to the displayed priority.
- A root bridge has root path cost `0` and no root port. Each other connected switch selects one root port per instance.
- Short path costs: 10 Mbps `100`, 100 Mbps `19`, 1 Gbps `4`, 10 Gbps `2`.
- RSTP states are discarding, learning, forwarding. Default hello/max-age/forward-delay timers are `2/20/15` seconds.
:::

A **Bridge Protocol Data Unit (BPDU)** carries the root identity, the sender's path cost to that root, the sender's identity, and a sending port identifier. Switches compare this information with what they currently know. A newly started, isolated switch initially identifies itself as root. After exchanges with its neighbors, it selects the best root it can hear about and advertises information consistent with that decision. Host IP addresses and default gateways do not participate in this election.

The **bridge ID (BID)** contains a two-byte priority/system-ID field and a six-byte bridge MAC address. In a per-VLAN instance, the field includes the configurable priority and the VLAN ID as the **extended system ID**. With priority `32768`, VLAN 10 displays `32778`; VLAN 20 displays `32788`. Compare switches within the same VLAN. Differences between VLAN instances do not cause VLAN 10 to defeat VLAN 20 in an election.

For example, SW1 advertises `32778` with MAC `0001.0001.0001`, while SW2 advertises `24586` with MAC `00ff.00ff.00ff`. SW2 wins VLAN 10 because the priority field is compared first. If both advertise `24586`, their MAC addresses decide. A priority of zero is the lowest configurable value, but another priority-zero switch with a lower MAC can still win. Likewise, `61440` can win if every competing BID is higher or no other switch participates.

Set root placement deliberately near the intended traffic paths. The root is the reference point used to construct the tree; it is not a requirement that every frame travel through that switch. Once the tree is established, normal destination-MAC forwarding still applies. Two hosts on the same access switch can communicate locally without sending their traffic to the root first.

sections.title: Port roles and path selection
sections.body:
Calculate the topology in order: elect the root, select each non-root switch's root port, then select a designated port on each segment. A **root port** offers the best received path toward the root. A **designated port** advertises the best path onto its segment. These are related decisions, but they compare costs from different viewpoints.

For a root-port candidate, add the neighbor's advertised root path cost to the cost of the local port receiving that information. If SW3 hears cost `0` from SW2 on a Gigabit port with cost `4`, SW3's total is `4`. SW1 hearing SW3's advertised `4` on another cost-`4` port obtains `8`. SW1's direct FastEthernet path to SW2 costs `0 + 19 = 19`; the two-link Gigabit route wins even though it has more hops.

```diagram
{"type":"topology","title":"Fig 14.1 — Calculate the received cost","caption":"SW1 selects 8 through SW3 instead of 19 directly to SW2. SW2 remains designated on the direct link.","nodes":[{"id":"SW2","kind":"switch","label":"SW2 · root","sub":"priority 24576 · cost 0","x":2,"y":3,"highlight":true},{"id":"SW1","kind":"switch","label":"SW1","sub":"priority 32768 · cost 8","x":10,"y":1},{"id":"SW3","kind":"switch","label":"SW3","sub":"priority 28672 · cost 4","x":10,"y":5}],"links":[{"from":"SW2","to":"SW1","label":"19 at each end","fromLabel":"Fa0/24","toLabel":"Fa0/24","fromBadge":"DP","toBadge":"ALT","style":"blocked"},{"from":"SW2","to":"SW3","label":"4 at each end","fromLabel":"Gi0/1","toLabel":"Gi0/2","fromBadge":"DP","toBadge":"RP"},{"from":"SW3","to":"SW1","label":"4 at each end","fromLabel":"Gi0/1","toLabel":"Gi0/1","fromBadge":"DP","toBadge":"RP","accent":true}]}
```

When candidates describe the same root, compare total root path cost first, then the sending bridge ID, then the sending port ID, and finally the local receiving port ID if everything received still ties. The last case is unusual on ordinary direct switch links: it can occur when two local ports hear the same sender through a shared segment. Do not choose the lowest local interface number before comparing the information advertised by neighbors.

A **port ID** combines port priority and port number. Default port priority is `128`; configurable values are `0`–`240` in steps of `16`. In `128.25`, `128` is the priority and `25` is the platform's STP port number. It need not match the final digit in an interface name. A common 2960 reports `Gi0/1` as port `25`; use the displayed number instead of assuming a mapping across models.

Suppose SW1 has two equal-cost links to the same root switch. SW1's `Gi0/1` hears sender port ID `128.26`, and its `Gi0/2` hears `128.25`. The second local interface wins. Changing the root switch's sending port priority to `64` on the first link would reverse that tie. Changing SW1's receiving port priority would not override an already different sending port ID.

For the designated-port decision, compare the information each switch would advertise onto the segment: root ID, advertised root path cost, sender BID, then sender port ID. Do not add the cost of crossing that segment to both advertisements. In Figure 14.1, SW2 advertises `0` and SW1 advertises `8` on the direct link, so SW2's end is designated. Between two non-root switches with equal root cost, their BIDs decide the designated end.

| Role | What it provides | Stable data state |
|---|---|---|
| Root | Best path toward the root on a non-root switch | Forwarding |
| Designated | Best advertised path on that segment | Forwarding |
| Alternate | Another path toward the root through another bridge | Discarding |
| Backup | Redundant attachment to the same segment as this bridge's own designated port | Discarding |

An **alternate port** can replace a failed root path. A **backup port** is different: imagine two ports of the same switch attached to one hub, receiving that switch's own BPDUs. One can back up the other designated port's attachment to that shared segment. Two separate cables between two switches ordinarily create root/alternate roles downstream, not a backup role. On normal point-to-point links the root's active ports are designated; shared or self-connected arrangements explain why that statement is not universal.

sections.title: Port states and convergence
sections.body:
A **role** describes the port's job; a **state** describes what it currently does. A newly selected designated port may still be discarding while the protocol establishes that forwarding is safe. A blocked alternate is therefore normal, but a designated role does not prove that the port already forwards. Read both columns in operational output.

| State | Learns source MAC addresses from user frames? | Forwards user frames? |
|---|---|---|
| Discarding | No | No |
| Learning | Yes | No |
| Forwarding | Yes | Yes |

Classic STP separates blocking and listening from learning and forwarding; disabled interfaces do not participate. RSTP groups the nonforwarding, nonlearning behavior under discarding. Cisco displays stable rapid alternate ports as `Altn BLK`, even though discarding is the RSTP state name. A healthy blocked port can process BPDUs: blocking user traffic does not mean blocking the protocol that maintains the tree.

Classic transitions can require `15` seconds listening and `15` seconds learning. If stale information must first expire, the default `20`-second max age can add delay. An alternate may remain blocked indefinitely while redundancy is healthy; max age is not a maximum permitted time in blocking. Treat `30` or `50` seconds as conditional timer examples, not a countdown applied to every link event.

RSTP uses **proposal/agreement** on point-to-point links to confirm a safe transition. A receiver synchronizes other relevant non-edge forwarding ports before agreeing, preventing a temporary loop while the topology changes. Full-duplex links are considered point-to-point by default; half-duplex links are considered shared. An agreement is not a TCP acknowledgment: these are spanning-tree control messages between bridges.

RSTP also uses periodic BPDUs to detect neighbor loss. Three missed hellos at the default two-second interval correspond to about six seconds; a physical link-down event can be detected earlier. Detection time and completed reconvergence are different measurements. Legacy neighbors, link type, topology, and implementation affect the result, so do not promise zero lost pings or a fixed two-second failover.

**Edge ports**, configured using PortFast, can forward immediately when connected to end devices. Receiving a BPDU removes operational edge status unless another feature, such as BPDU guard, shuts the port down. RSTP detects topology changes when non-edge ports enter forwarding; an edge port's ordinary link transitions do not create those changes. Chapter 15 explains safe edge configuration and protection. A legacy PVST+ neighbor can also cause classic interoperability behavior on the connecting port.

sections.title: Configure the root and path preferences
sections.body:
Configure Rapid PVST+ explicitly when building the lab rather than relying on a platform default. Cisco documents PVST+ as the older 2960 default and Rapid PVST+ on current Catalyst 9300 software. The operational mode in `show spanning-tree summary` is the useful evidence. All switches in the example use VLAN 10, matching trunks, and known priorities.

```ios SW2
SW2# configure terminal
SW2(config)# spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst
SW2(config)# spanning-tree vlan 10 root primary
SW2(config)# end
SW2# show spanning-tree vlan 10
```

The `root primary` command is a configuration macro, not a permanent election privilege. It uses `24576` when that makes the switch root; for an already lower current root priority, it attempts a value `4096` lower. Verify the resulting priority and root identity, especially near priority zero where no lower value exists. It does not keep lowering its priority if another switch arrives later. `root secondary` sets `28672`, which is useful behind a primary at `24576` when other switches use `32768`; it does not reserve second place against arbitrary configurations.

```ios SW3
SW3# configure terminal
SW3(config)# spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst
SW3(config)# spanning-tree vlan 10 root secondary
SW3(config)# end
```

For deterministic exercises, explicit priorities make the intended ordering visible. Per-interface cost changes tune a local candidate path; if that changes the switch's root cost, the new advertised cost can affect downstream switches too. Port-priority changes appear in transmitted BPDUs and primarily influence a neighbor's equal-cost choice. Neither setting changes the physical speed of the link.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# spanning-tree vlan 10 priority 32768
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/24
SW1(config-if)# spanning-tree vlan 10 cost 2
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show spanning-tree vlan 10
```

Short costs are sufficient for this lab. Long-cost implementations use a different scale, for example `200000` at 100 Mbps and `20000` at 1 Gbps. Read the configured method and displayed costs before doing arithmetic; do not mix a short-cost table with long-cost output. Leave timers unchanged and adjust only the planned VLAN/interface parameter.

sections.title: Reading the output
sections.body:
The following is representative, abbreviated 2960-style output using the Figure 14.1 design. MAC addresses illustrate the comparison and will differ on your devices. It is a worked exhibit, not a capture from an executed Packet Tracer lab.

```output SW1# show spanning-tree vlan 10
VLAN0010
  Spanning tree enabled protocol rstp  ← Rapid PVST+ for this VLAN
  Root ID    Priority    24586
             Address     0002.0002.0002
             Cost        8  ← total root path cost, not just Gi0/1 cost
             Port        25 (GigabitEthernet0/1)
             Hello Time   2 sec  Max Age 20 sec  Forward Delay 15 sec
  Bridge ID  Priority    32778  (priority 32768 sys-id-ext 10)
             Address     0001.0001.0001  ← local bridge; differs from Root ID
...
Interface           Role Sts Cost      Prio.Nbr Type
------------------- ---- --- --------- -------- --------------------------------
Gi0/1               Root FWD 4         128.25   P2p
Fa0/24              Altn BLK 19        128.24   P2p  ← intended standby path
Fa0/5               Desg FWD 19        128.5    P2p
```

Read the VLAN and protocol first, compare Root ID with Bridge ID, then inspect root cost and root port. Matching IDs and the message `This bridge is the root` identify the local root. The priority `24586` proves a configurable value of `24576` plus VLAN 10; it does not prove whether someone used a macro or an explicit priority command.

:::trap A blocked path is not automatically a fault
Check whether an alternate forwarding path exists before changing STP. If every redundant port were forced to forward, the original Ethernet loop would return. Diagnose the intended root and cost calculation before treating `Altn BLK` as the cause of an outage.
:::

Use `show spanning-tree root` for a per-VLAN root summary and `show spanning-tree interface gigabitethernet0/1 detail` for received/sent BPDU and designated information. A missing VLAN may indicate a VLAN or trunk problem rather than an election error. Compare `show interfaces trunk`, `show vlan brief`, interface status, and the running configuration before changing priorities. Save a confirmed baseline so the next fault exercise starts from known evidence.

sections.title: Exam focus
sections.body:
- Compare BIDs within one instance: priority/system ID, then MAC. Priority zero still has a MAC tie-breaker.
- Add the receiving port cost for root-port candidates; compare advertised costs for designated-port selection.
- Break equal-cost root-port ties using sender BID, sender port ID, then receiving port ID.
- Distinguish root, designated, alternate, and backup roles from discarding, learning, and forwarding states.
- Know default `32768`, increments `4096`, short costs `100/19/4/2`, and timers `2/20/15` in context.
- Explain why Rapid PVST+ can converge quickly without assigning every failure the same duration.
- Configure and verify a primary/secondary design; the macros do not guarantee permanent election positions.
- Use the root ID, local bridge ID, total cost, and interface role/state together to justify a conclusion.

lab.title: Build and verify a three-switch Rapid PVST+ topology
lab.intro:
Practice revised September 2026. If you completed an earlier version, repeat the revised exercise and update its checkmarks.

Start with a new Packet Tracer file. You will establish a complete VLAN and trunk baseline, predict port roles, alter one parameter at a time, and restore each change before the next exercise. Keep a worksheet containing the root BID, local BID, total root cost, root port, and alternate ports for every switch.

This is an authored lab with representative observations; it has not been manually executed in Packet Tracer. Interface names match the 2960-24TT model. On CML or hardware, map these connections to the interfaces on your licensed switch image and retain the explicit VLAN 10 costs. Display formatting and convergence timing can differ.
lab.topology:
```diagram
{"type":"topology","title":"Lab topology — a triangle with one slower link","caption":"Use the listed ports on three 2960-24TT switches. VLAN 10 carries both PCs; VLAN 999 is the unused native VLAN.","nodes":[{"id":"PCA","kind":"pc","label":"PC-A","sub":"10.0.10.11/24","x":1,"y":1},{"id":"SW1","kind":"switch","label":"SW1","x":4,"y":1},{"id":"SW2","kind":"switch","label":"SW2","x":4,"y":5},{"id":"PCB","kind":"pc","label":"PC-B","sub":"10.0.10.12/24","x":1,"y":5},{"id":"SW3","kind":"switch","label":"SW3","x":10,"y":3}],"links":[{"from":"PCA","to":"SW1","toLabel":"Fa0/5"},{"from":"SW1","to":"SW2","fromLabel":"Fa0/24","toLabel":"Fa0/24","label":"100 Mbps · cost 19"},{"from":"SW1","to":"SW3","fromLabel":"Gi0/1","toLabel":"Gi0/1","label":"1 Gbps · cost 4"},{"from":"SW2","to":"SW3","fromLabel":"Gi0/1","toLabel":"Gi0/2","label":"1 Gbps · cost 4"},{"from":"PCB","to":"SW2","toLabel":"Fa0/5"}]}
```

| Connection | Port at first end | Port at second end | Cable |
|---|---|---|---|
| PC-A to SW1 | FastEthernet0 | Fa0/5 | Copper straight-through |
| PC-B to SW2 | FastEthernet0 | Fa0/5 | Copper straight-through |
| SW1 to SW2 | Fa0/24 | Fa0/24 | Copper crossover |
| SW1 to SW3 | Gi0/1 | Gi0/1 | Copper crossover |

Both PCs are on one IP subnet and VLAN; they do not need a router. Switch management addresses are unnecessary for a local-console STP exercise. Use the CLI tab on each switch, decline any initial configuration dialog, and press Enter to reach the prompt.

steps.title: Address the PCs and establish connectivity
steps.body:
On each PC, open Desktop → IP Configuration, select Static, and enter the address and mask from the table. Leave gateway and DNS blank. From PC-A's Desktop → Command Prompt, run the following command, allowing initial ARP resolution and STP convergence before judging the result.

```text PC-A
ping 10.0.10.12
```

On SW1, inspect the access port and learned addresses.

```ios SW1
SW1# show vlan brief
SW1# show mac address-table dynamic
SW1# show spanning-tree vlan 10
```

:::expected
Both PCs belong to VLAN 10 through Fa0/5. After convergence and address resolution, repeated pings succeed. MAC addresses are learned along the current forwarding path; a switch does not need an IP address to forward these frames. If pings fail, fix cabling, PC masks, access membership, and trunk VLANs before proceeding.
:::

steps.title: Choose the primary and secondary root
steps.body:
Before configuring root placement, write a prediction row for each switch: chosen root, total cost, root port, designated interswitch ports and alternate ports. Use SW2 priority 24576 and SW3 priority 28672 as the planned values; leave SW1 at 32768. Explain both the received-cost calculation and the designated-end comparison.

With the all-default priorities from Step 1, configure SW2 as primary, then SW3 as secondary. Do not run the primary macro on every switch. Observe the resulting numeric values, since the macro itself is not an ongoing protection mechanism.

```ios SW2
SW2# configure terminal
SW2(config)# spanning-tree vlan 10 root primary
SW2(config)# end
SW2# show spanning-tree vlan 10
```

```ios SW3
SW3# configure terminal
SW3(config)# spanning-tree vlan 10 root secondary
SW3(config)# end
SW3# show spanning-tree vlan 10
```

```ios SW1
SW1# show spanning-tree vlan 10
```

:::expected
SW2 has priority 24576 (displayed 24586), SW3 28672 (28682), SW1 32768 (32778). SW2 is the VLAN 10 root regardless of the actual MAC ordering. The stable roles below assume the complete topology and specified costs:

| Switch | Root path cost / root port | Other interswitch port |
|---|---|---|
| SW2 | 0 / none | Gi0/1 and Fa0/24 designated forwarding |
| SW3 | 4 / Gi0/2 | Gi0/1 designated forwarding |
| SW1 | 8 / Gi0/1 | Fa0/24 alternate discarding |

SW1's direct path costs 19, while the route through SW3 costs 4 + 4 = 8. A representative SW1 row is `Fa0/24 Altn BLK 19 128.24 P2p`. Read the actual output rather than requiring identical spacing or MACs. This is the baseline to which every experiment returns.
:::

steps.title: Prefer the slower physical link with a lower configured cost
steps.body:
Predict the result before changing SW1 Fa0/24 to cost 2. You are changing an STP preference, not increasing that port's 100 Mbps bandwidth.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/24
SW1(config-if)# spanning-tree vlan 10 cost 2
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show spanning-tree vlan 10
```

```ios SW3
SW3# show spanning-tree vlan 10
```

:::expected
SW1 selects Fa0/24 as root port with total cost 2. On the SW1–SW3 segment, SW1 now advertises 2 while SW3 advertises 4, so SW1 Gi0/1 becomes designated and SW3 Gi0/1 becomes alternate. SW3 keeps Gi0/2 as root port: its direct cost 4 beats 4 + 2 = 6 through SW1. The change therefore affects another switch's role as well as SW1's local decision.
:::

steps.title: Restore the cost baseline
steps.body:
Restore the explicit value 19 before testing a physical failure. Confirm the baseline table, then repeat PC-A's ping.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/24
SW1(config-if)# spanning-tree vlan 10 cost 19
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show spanning-tree vlan 10
```

```ios SW3
SW3# show spanning-tree vlan 10
```

:::expected
SW1 returns to cost 8 through Gi0/1, with Fa0/24 alternate. SW3 Gi0/1 returns to designated. Restoring a documented explicit value is preferable here to guessing whether a different platform's automatic cost method matches the worksheet.
:::

steps.title: Fail the SW3-to-root link
steps.body:
Before entering the commands, cross out SW3–SW2 on your diagram and fill a new three-switch prediction table. Include the designated end on SW1–SW3 and whether PC-A still has a physical forwarding path to PC-B.

Keep all cables connected. Administratively shut only SW3 Gi0/2, its link toward SW2. From PC-A, repeat `ping 10.0.10.12` while inspecting the new roles; a Packet Tracer PC ping sends a finite set of probes, so run it again as needed.

```ios SW3
SW3# configure terminal
SW3(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
SW3(config-if)# shutdown
SW3(config-if)# end
SW3# show spanning-tree vlan 10
```

```ios SW1
SW1# show spanning-tree vlan 10
```

:::expected
SW2 stays root because the FastEthernet link still connects it to SW1. SW1 uses Fa0/24 with cost 19 and becomes designated on Gi0/1. SW3 reaches SW2 through SW1: Gi0/1 is root port and total cost is 4 + 19 = 23. Pings may be lost during transition, then recover. Record what you observe; do not infer an exact universal convergence time from simulation animation.
:::

steps.title: Restore the failed link
steps.body:
Re-enable the exact interface you shut, then verify the baseline on both non-root switches.

```ios SW3
SW3# configure terminal
SW3(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
SW3(config-if)# no shutdown
SW3(config-if)# end
SW3# show spanning-tree vlan 10
```

```ios SW1
SW1# show spanning-tree vlan 10
```

:::expected
SW3 again uses Gi0/2 with total cost 4; SW1 uses Gi0/1 with total cost 8. SW1 Fa0/24 is alternate. Confirm ping connectivity before moving to the root-election experiment.
:::

steps.title: Introduce a lower-priority root
steps.body:
Temporarily give SW1 configurable priority 4096. SW2's previous `root primary` command does not prevent this change. Predict the root and both other switches' preferred paths first.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# spanning-tree vlan 10 priority 4096
SW1(config)# end
SW1# show spanning-tree vlan 10
```

```ios SW2
SW2# show spanning-tree vlan 10
```

```ios SW3
SW3# show spanning-tree vlan 10
```

:::expected
SW1 becomes root with displayed priority 4106. SW3's Gi0/1 is root port at cost 4. SW2 reaches SW1 through SW3 using Gi0/1 at total cost 8; SW2 Fa0/24 is alternate because its direct cost is 19. SW2's configured numeric priority remains 24576.
:::

steps.title: Restore, verify, and save
steps.body:
Return SW1 to priority 32768 and verify the Step 3 baseline. Save each device configuration, accepting the default destination filename when prompted. Then use File → Save As to save the entire topology as `stp-baseline.pkt`; saving only the switch configuration does not save the Packet Tracer workspace file.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# spanning-tree vlan 10 priority 32768
SW1(config)# end
SW1# show spanning-tree vlan 10
SW1# copy running-config startup-config
```

```ios SW2
SW2# show spanning-tree vlan 10
SW2# copy running-config startup-config
```

```ios SW3
SW3# show spanning-tree vlan 10
SW3# copy running-config startup-config
```

:::expected
All switches identify SW2 as VLAN 10 root. The root costs are SW1 8, SW2 0, SW3 4, and the only blocked interswitch end for VLAN 10 is SW1 Fa0/24. PC-A reaches PC-B. Keep the worksheet and saved project together so a later result can be compared with a known configuration.

Your evidence record must cover five states: baseline, changed receiving cost, failed link, changed root, and restored baseline. For each, identify the root, root cost/port on both non-root switches, both roles on the redundant segment, and a fresh PC test. Mark predictions separately from observations. A command accepted without the expected operational result is not completion.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- Wrong root: compare the complete Root ID and Bridge ID on all three switches; check the priority for VLAN 10, not VLAN 1 or 999.
- Correct root but unexpected path: compare the local cost with the received neighbor cost. Confirm the port labels and any leftover cost override.
- VLAN 10 missing on a link: inspect `show interfaces trunk` and VLAN existence at both ends. A native-VLAN mismatch is a trunk fault to correct before analyzing STP roles.
- A command is rejected: verify the prompt first. For a rejected optional show command, use the full `show spanning-tree vlan 10` and `show running-config`. Do not replace missing simulation features with guessed observations.
- PC ping fails while the tree matches: verify PC masks and VLAN 10 access ports, allow ARP resolution, and inspect learned MAC addresses. STP does not configure host addressing.
lab.challenge:
Work in a copy of the restored baseline. Keep VLAN 10, its PCs, costs and priorities unchanged. Add a second instance with these requirements before opening the solution:

- Create VLAN 20 on all three switches and add it to every existing interswitch allowed list, preserving VLANs 10 and 999.
- VLAN 20 configurable priorities: SW1 8192, SW2 16384, SW3 24576.
- For VLAN 20 only, use receiving cost 6 on both ends of SW1–SW2 and cost 4 on each end of both Gigabit links.

Set the two new PCs through Desktop → IP Configuration → Static using the supplied addresses and mask 255.255.255.0. From PC-C, ping 10.0.20.12; from PC-D, ping 10.0.20.11. Repeat PC-A to 10.0.10.12. The original baseline file remains your clean starting point; reopen it for later chapters rather than carrying unrecorded challenge changes forward.

questions.prompt: Which two statements accurately describe RSTP port states? (Choose two.)
options: A designated role proves that a port has already reached forwarding.
A discarding port learns user-frame source MACs but sends no BPDUs.
A discarding port forwards broadcasts while holding unicast frames.
A forwarding port learns source MACs and forwards eligible user frames.
A learning port can learn source MACs without forwarding user frames.
questions.explanation: Learning allows MAC learning but does not yet permit user-frame forwarding. Forwarding supports both; role and state must still be considered separately.

whyWrong.0: A designated port can be discarding while a safe transition is established.
whyWrong.1: Discarding does not learn source MACs from user traffic; it can still process control information.
whyWrong.2: Discarding does not permit ordinary broadcast forwarding.

questions.prompt: Which two statements about designated ports are correct? (Choose two.)
options: A segment selects the port advertising the best spanning-tree information.
On ordinary point-to-point links, the root bridge's active ports are designated.
The designated port is selected by the lowest local interface name on each switch.
Every non-root switch must have exactly one designated port per VLAN.
Two links to the same neighbor always make one local port a backup port.
questions.explanation: A designated port wins the comparison for its segment. On ordinary point-to-point links, the root advertises cost zero and supplies the designated end; shared/self-connected arrangements require the more precise segment rule.

whyWrong.2: Advertised root information, cost, BID, and port ID decide the comparison.
whyWrong.3: A switch can have several designated ports or none; one designated port is selected per segment.
whyWrong.4: Separate parallel links commonly produce root/alternate roles downstream, not a backup role.

questions.prompt: Which command provides a table of root bridge IDs, total root costs, and local root ports across VLANs?
options: show spanning-tree summary
show spanning-tree root
show mac address-table
show interfaces trunk
questions.explanation: `show spanning-tree root` summarizes root information per VLAN. It is useful for comparing instances before inspecting a detailed single-VLAN view.

whyWrong.0: Summary emphasizes mode and defaults rather than the requested root-path table.
whyWrong.2: The MAC table describes learned forwarding entries, not spanning-tree root selection.
whyWrong.3: The trunk display describes VLAN carriage and trunk state, not elected root paths.

questions.prompt: Why can an Ethernet loop keep circulating broadcasts through ordinary Layer 2 switches?
options: An STP root port forwards user traffic independently of its state.
Ethernet frames have no hop limit that ordinary bridging decrements.
Learning a source MAC requires a switch to retransmit every frame.
The enclosed IP TTL is decremented by each switch to limit the frame’s lifetime.
questions.explanation: Ordinary bridging does not decrement the enclosed IP TTL, and Ethernet has no equivalent hop counter. STP removes the loop from the forwarding topology.

whyWrong.0: Both the role and current state matter; a discarding port does not forward ordinary user traffic.
whyWrong.2: Source learning records the ingress location; it does not require universal flooding.
whyWrong.3: Ordinary Layer 2 bridging does not decrement the enclosed IP TTL, so it does not provide that loop limit.

questions.prompt: What does Rapid PVST+ maintain for a network carrying several VLANs?
options: One permanent root elected only when the first switch starts.
A root for each IP subnet, selected from the default gateways.
One root for each physical switch, shared by all its VLANs.
A separate spanning-tree instance and elected root for each VLAN.
questions.explanation: Rapid PVST+ applies rapid spanning-tree behavior per VLAN. Two VLANs can therefore have different roots and forwarding topologies.

whyWrong.0: Election can change when better information or topology changes arrive.
whyWrong.1: Bridge information determines this Layer 2 election; IP gateways do not vote.
whyWrong.2: The instance belongs to a VLAN, not to each switch independently.

questions.prompt: What does this representative VLAN 10 interface excerpt establish about SW3?
options: Gi0/1 is administratively shut, so its cost is ignored by the switch.
Both Gigabit ports forward because both are operational point-to-point links.
Gi0/2 is a backup port because another port uses the alternate role.
Gi0/2 is the current root port, while Gi0/1 is a standby path.
questions.explanation: `Root FWD` identifies the current root port and its forwarding state. `Altn BLK` identifies a healthy alternate that discards user frames for this VLAN.

whyWrong.0: An alternate blocked port participates in STP and is not the same as administrative shutdown.
whyWrong.1: Point-to-point link type does not override the blocked state.
whyWrong.2: Backup and alternate are distinct roles; neither changes the Root label on Gi0/2.

Gi0/1               Altn BLK 4         128.25   P2p
Gi0/2               Root FWD 4         128.26   P2p

questions.prompt: Which conclusion about SW1 is supported by this representative excerpt?
options: SW1 reaches the root through Gi0/1 with total path cost 8.
SW1 is the root because the output identifies protocol rstp.
SW1 reaches the root through Gi0/1 with total path cost 4.
SW1 is the root because its Gi0/1 interface is forwarding.
questions.explanation: The Root ID differs from the local Bridge ID, and the root block identifies cost 8 through Gi0/1. The interface cost 4 is only SW1's contribution to that total.

whyWrong.1: The protocol identifies the STP variant, not which bridge won.
whyWrong.2: The interface row reports the local port cost; the root block reports the total path cost.
whyWrong.3: A forwarding root port belongs to a non-root switch, not the root itself.

questions.prompt: For VLAN 20, SW-A has BID 32788.0011.2233.aaaa, SW-B has 28692.0011.2233.ffff, and SW-C has 32788.0011.2233.0001. Which bridge is elected root?
options: SW-B, because its priority field is lower than the others.
SW-A, because its MAC is lower than SW-B's MAC address.
SW-C, because its MAC address is the lowest of the three.
SW-C, because its BID is the last one received by peers.
questions.explanation: SW-B wins because 28692 is lower than 32788. The MAC portion is compared only after the priority/system-ID field ties.

whyWrong.1: SW-A has a higher priority field, so its MAC is not the deciding comparison.
whyWrong.2: The lower MAC cannot override a worse priority field.
whyWrong.3: BPDU arrival order does not replace the best-BID comparison.

questions.prompt: All VLAN 10 switches use default configurable priority 32768. After `spanning-tree vlan 10 root primary` is entered on SW2, which displayed priority should be expected?
options: 32778, because the macro changes only a role label.
24576, because the VLAN ID is omitted from Root ID.
28682, from configurable priority 28672 plus VLAN 10.
24586, from configurable priority 24576 plus VLAN 10.
questions.explanation: With the stated default-priority peers, the macro sets 24576. The per-VLAN displayed field includes the extended system ID, producing 24586 for VLAN 10.

whyWrong.0: The macro changes a numeric priority setting rather than granting a special role.
whyWrong.1: 24576 is the configurable component; the displayed field includes VLAN 10.
whyWrong.2: 28672 is the secondary macro value, not the primary value in this scenario.

questions.prompt: Both candidates advertise the same root. Using the given costs, which interface should SW4 select as its root port?
options: Fa0/24, because the route uses fewer switch links.
Gi0/1, because received cost 4 plus local cost 4 is 8.
Gi0/1, because its local interface number is lower.
Fa0/24, because its neighbor is the root itself.
questions.explanation: The candidate via Gi0/1 costs 4 + 4 = 8; the direct Fa0/24 candidate costs 0 + 19 = 19. Root-port selection prefers the lower total cost, before any port-ID tie-breaker.

whyWrong.0: STP uses path cost rather than a simple hop count.
whyWrong.2: The choice is established by cost before interface IDs are compared.
whyWrong.3: Direct attachment does not beat a lower-cost indirect path.

Gi0/1       4                    4

questions.prompt: SW1 has equal-cost direct links to the same root bridge. Gi0/1 receives sender port ID 128.26; Gi0/2 receives 128.25. Which interface wins?
options: Gi0/2, because its received sending-port identifier is lower.
Neither port, because parallel links require an EtherChannel.
Gi0/1, because SW1's lower local interface number decides first.
Both ports, because equal-cost links share the root-port role.
questions.explanation: Root ID, total cost, and sender BID tie, so the sending port ID decides. Gi0/2 hears 128.25, which is better than 128.26 even though its local interface name is higher.

whyWrong.1: Parallel links can operate under STP without an EtherChannel; one can be alternate.
whyWrong.2: The sender port ID is compared before the local receiving port ID.
whyWrong.3: A non-root bridge selects one root port per instance.

questions.prompt: An interswitch link is using classic interoperability behavior after a replacement switch was installed. Which change aligns the replacement with the intended rapid design?
options: Lower the replacement's VLAN priority to reserve the root role.
Force the replacement's uplink to shared link type for safety.
Configure `spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst` on the replacement.
Enable PortFast on both ends of the interswitch transit link.
questions.explanation: The replacement reports PVST mode, which uses classic behavior. Configuring the intended rapid mode addresses that mismatch; verify the operational peer behavior after protocol negotiation rather than assuming a fixed recovery time.

whyWrong.0: Priority controls root election, not rapid versus classic protocol operation.
whyWrong.1: Shared link type prevents the point-to-point rapid handshake rather than enabling it.
whyWrong.3: PortFast is not the remedy for a transit-link protocol mismatch.
