questions.prompt: An engineer changes SW1 Fa0/24 to `spanning-tree vlan 30 cost 2`. What is the direct effect, and how can it affect other switches?
options: The root bridge changes its BID to include 2; every switch repeats that new BID.
The peer changes its receiving port cost to 2; SW1 keeps its own automatic cost.
SW1 raises the physical link speed; neighboring switches learn the new bandwidth.
SW1 uses cost 2 for that candidate; a changed advertised root cost can affect neighbors.
questions.explanation: The interface command changes SW1's VLAN 30 path-cost contribution on that port. If this changes its selected root cost, updated advertisements can influence downstream root or designated-port decisions.

whyWrong.0: Cost and BID are different fields; this command does not change bridge priority or MAC.
whyWrong.1: The command is local to SW1; it does not configure the peer's interface cost.
whyWrong.2: STP cost is a selection parameter and does not change physical bandwidth.

questions.prompt: The physical link stays up, but an RSTP port misses three consecutive BPDUs with a two-second hello interval. Which interpretation is correct?
options: The bridge must wait exactly 50 seconds before detecting the missing neighbor.
The bridge has proved the fiber transmit strand is physically broken.
The bridge can age the neighbor information after about six seconds.
The bridge guarantees that all application traffic recovers in six seconds.
questions.explanation: Three missed two-second hellos correspond to about six seconds and allow rapid aging of neighbor information. Detection does not identify the physical cause or guarantee a specific end-to-end recovery duration.

whyWrong.0: Classic worst-case timer examples are not the required rapid neighbor-detection behavior.
whyWrong.1: Several faults can stop BPDUs while link status remains up.
whyWrong.3: Neighbor detection and complete traffic recovery are separate events.

questions.prompt: A new switch has VLAN 10 priority 4096. Existing root SW1 was selected using the primary macro and has the shown configured setting. With no guards, what happens?
options: The new switch wins because its configured priority is lower than 24576.
SW1 retains the role because the macro permanently marks it as primary.
SW1 automatically subtracts 4096 from the newcomer's advertised priority.
The new switch waits for SW1 to fail before it may participate in elections.
questions.explanation: The macro left an ordinary priority setting of 24576. The new switch's lower priority gives it the better BID for the same VLAN; the macro does not keep monitoring and reducing SW1's priority.

whyWrong.1: Primary is a configuration convenience, not a permanent protocol privilege.
whyWrong.2: There is no ongoing adjustment process attached to the earlier macro invocation.
whyWrong.3: All participating bridges compare BIDs; no reservation forces the newcomer to wait.

exhibit.text:

spanning-tree vlan 10 priority 24576

questions.prompt: Two ports of the same switch attach to one shared hub segment. One receives the switch's own superior BPDU and provides a redundant attachment to its designated port. Which role describes that port?
options: Backup, because it backs up this bridge's attachment to the same segment.
Designated, because each local interface must advertise onto the hub.
Alternate, because every redundant cable provides a path through another bridge.
Root, because a received BPDU always selects the path toward the root.
questions.explanation: A backup port is associated with a redundant connection to the same segment served by the bridge's own designated port. An alternate instead provides another path toward the root through a different bridge.

whyWrong.1: The segment selects one designated port; redundant local attachments need not both be designated.
whyWrong.2: The stated BPDU comes from the same bridge, not a different bridge on another path.
whyWrong.3: Receiving a BPDU alone does not establish the root-port role.

questions.prompt: SW-A and SW-B advertise the same root with root path cost 8 on their connecting segment. Which end becomes designated based on the worksheet?
options: SW-B, because its sending bridge ID is lower at the tied advertised cost.
SW-A, because its port number is lower than SW-B's port number.
SW-A, because its local interface cost of 4 is lower.
SW-B, because designated-port selection prefers the higher link cost.
questions.explanation: For the designated-port comparison, both advertise cost 8, so the sending BID decides. SW-B has the lower BID; the segment's local receiving cost is not added to the already advertised cost for this comparison.

whyWrong.1: Sender BID is compared before sender port ID.
whyWrong.2: The local cost would matter when evaluating a received root-port candidate, not as a new designated-port tie-breaker here.
whyWrong.3: There is no rule preferring a higher port cost; SW-B wins on BID.

They retain separate roots because both configurable priorities are zero.
SW-A wins because the MAC comparison prefers the higher value.

whyWrong.0: The MAC still breaks a priority tie.
whyWrong.1: Connected participants compare complete BIDs and converge on one root for the instance.
whyWrong.2: The lower MAC wins the tied-priority comparison.

questions.prompt: The candidates advertise the same root and produce equal total cost. Which SW-C port becomes the root port?
options: Gi0/1, because the sender port number is lower.
Gi0/2, because the sending bridge ID is lower.
Both, because equal-cost spanning-tree paths are load shared.
Gi0/1, because the local receiving port number is lower.
questions.explanation: Both totals are 8. Sender BID is compared before either sender port ID or local receiving port ID, so the lower-priority sender on Gi0/2 wins.

whyWrong.0: Sender BID already resolves the tie before sender port ID.
whyWrong.2: A non-root switch chooses one root port per instance; these are not an EtherChannel.
whyWrong.3: The local port is a later tie-breaker and is not reached.

options: C-A for both VLANs because the lower VLAN number wins the election.
C-B for both VLANs because B is a root in one instance.
Both physical links in both VLANs because each VLAN needs two root ports.
C-A in VLAN 10 and C-B in VLAN 20, based on the separate instances.
questions.explanation: Each VLAN compares its own root information. The direct path to its intended root costs 4; crossing the other switch would cost 8. One physical interface can have different roles in different VLANs.

whyWrong.0: VLAN numbers do not compete against each other in a single election.
whyWrong.1: B’s VLAN 20 root role does not make it the VLAN 10 root.
whyWrong.2: C selects one root port in each instance, not both.

questions.prompt: A switch receives these two advertisements. Which root identity is preferred before comparing paths to the same root?

The advertisement on Gi0/1, because advertised cost zero beats cost 100.
The advertisement on Gi0/1, because the receiving port number is lower.
The advertisement on Gi0/2, because it identifies the lower root BID.
questions.explanation: Root identity is compared before cost. A high-cost path to the better root is preferred to information naming a worse root; later comparisons choose the best path to that selected root.

whyWrong.0: Different costs do not authorize two roots in the same connected instance.
whyWrong.1: Cost does not override a better root identity.
whyWrong.2: Port-number comparison is much later in the decision.

questions.explanation: A has the lowest BID. B reaches A at cost 4. C compares 19 directly with 4 + 4 through B and chooses 8. A advertises zero on A-C, so A remains designated there and C discards on its alternate.

whyWrong.0: B has a direct cost-4 path and does not select cost 23.
whyWrong.1: The root advertises cost zero and is designated on both ordinary point-to-point links; the non-root end supplies the alternate.
whyWrong.3: C chooses the cheaper 8 path, not the fewer-hop path costing 19.

A reaches B through C at cost 23; C becomes designated on A-C.

whyWrong.2: B’s new configurable 4096 is lower than A’s 24576.
whyWrong.3: C has a direct cost-4 link to the new root and does not choose 23.

questions.prompt: A remains the root. C changes only its receiving cost on C-A from 19 to 2. Which pair of changes is expected after convergence? Choose two.
options: A loses the root role because C now advertises a smaller cost.
C selects C-A as its root port with total cost 2.

B becomes alternate on B-C, while C is designated there.
B changes its root path to B-C-A with total cost 6.

whyWrong.0: A remains the best BID and advertises root cost zero.

options: Lower SW1’s priority until both interswitch ports have a designated role.
Change PC-B’s mask so frames avoid the blocked SW1 interface.
Reassign PC-A’s port to VLAN 10, then retest through the existing forwarding path.

whyWrong.1: The host masks already match the addressing plan; the demonstrated error is access membership.
whyWrong.3: Forcing redundant paths to forward can reintroduce a loop and does not correct host membership.

questions.prompt: Root A loses both of its interswitch links, but remains powered with PC-A attached. B-C stays up. Which outcome follows for VLAN 10?
options: C becomes root of B-C because its priority is numerically greater.

cards.front: Default configurable bridge priority, and its display in VLAN 10?
cards.back: 32768; the VLAN 10 extended system ID produces displayed priority 32778.

cards.front: How does a VLAN elect its root bridge?
cards.back: Lowest complete BID: priority/system-ID field first, then MAC. Priority zero still has a MAC tie-breaker.

cards.front: What does the root-primary macro configure?
cards.back: 24576 when that wins; for an already lower root, it attempts a value 4096 lower. It is not continuous protection; verify the result, especially near zero.

cards.front: What does the root-secondary macro configure?
cards.back: Priority 28672. This is a useful preference behind 24576 and ahead of default 32768, not a reserved second-place role.

cards.front: Legal configurable bridge priorities?
cards.back: 0 through 61440, in steps of 4096. The VLAN ID is added for the per-VLAN displayed field.

cards.front: Short-method costs at 10 Mbps, 100 Mbps, 1 Gbps, and 10 Gbps?
cards.back: 100, 19, 4, and 2 respectively. Verify the cost method before applying the table.

cards.front: Root-port comparison when candidates advertise the same root?
cards.back: Total root path cost → sender BID → sender port ID → local receiving port ID if still tied.

cards.front: How is a candidate root path cost calculated?
cards.back: Received advertised root cost plus the cost of the local receiving interface. The root advertises zero.

cards.front: How many root and designated ports are selected?
cards.back: One root port per connected non-root bridge per instance; one designated port per segment. The root has no root port.

cards.front: How do alternate and backup roles differ?
cards.back: Alternate: another path toward the root through another bridge. Backup: redundant local attachment to a shared segment served by this bridge's own designated port.

cards.front: Can a healthy alternate remain discarding longer than max age?
cards.back: Yes. It remains discarding while valid superior information keeps the redundant path unnecessary. Max age is not a deadline forcing that port to forward.

cards.front: How does learning differ from forwarding in RSTP?
cards.back: Both learn user-frame source MACs; only forwarding permits eligible user frames to leave through the port. Discarding does neither.

cards.front: Default hello, max-age, and forward-delay timers?
cards.back: 2 seconds, 20 seconds, and 15 seconds. These are distinct timers, not one universal convergence guarantee.

cards.front: Rapid PVST+ command and how to verify the mode?
cards.back: Configure `spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst`; check `show spanning-tree summary` and `protocol rstp` in the VLAN view. Older 2960 defaults use PVST+.

cards.front: What does Prio.Nbr 128.25 represent?
cards.back: Port priority 128 and STP port number 25. The STP number is platform-specific and is not necessarily the interface-name suffix.

cards.front: How does show output identify the local root?
cards.back: Root ID and local Bridge ID match, with `This bridge is the root`; there is no local root port and root cost is zero.

cards.front: How do STP/RSTP relate to PVST+/Rapid PVST+?
cards.back: PVST+ is Cisco's classic per-VLAN version; Rapid PVST+ uses rapid behavior per VLAN. Historical standards are 802.1D and 802.1w.

cards.front: Default and configurable port-priority values?
cards.back: Default 128; values 0–240 in steps of 16. The sending port ID participates before the receiving port ID in root-port ties.

cards.front: How is the designated end chosen on a segment?
cards.back: Compare advertised root ID, root path cost, sender BID, then sender port ID. Do not add the segment's receiving cost to the advertisements.

cards.front: Does an STP cost change increase link bandwidth?
cards.back: No. It changes path selection. A different selected root cost can change the information advertised to neighboring switches.

cards.front: Can one trunk have different Rapid PVST+ roles for two VLANs?
cards.back: Yes. Each VLAN has its own instance, root and path comparison; read the named VLAN rather than treating the physical port as one universal role.

cards.front: Must every switched user frame travel through the root bridge?
cards.back: No. STP supplies a loop-free forwarding topology. Normal destination-MAC forwarding can keep a local exchange away from the root.

commands.task: Configure this switch to run Rapid PVST+.
commands.note: Verify the operational mode rather than relying on a model default.

commands.task: Apply the root-primary macro for VLAN 10.
commands.note: The macro sets a numeric priority; verify the result. An explicit 24576 is not always equivalent when the current root is already lower.

commands.task: Apply the root-secondary macro for VLAN 10.
commands.note: It sets 28672 and does not reserve second place against arbitrary other priorities.

commands.task: Set VLAN 20 priority to the lowest nonzero legal configurable value.
commands.note: Bridge priorities use steps of 4096; the display adds VLAN 20.

commands.task: Display VLAN 10 root ID, local BID, and interface roles/states.

tickets.title: The faster root uplink is not forwarding
tickets.scenario: DSW1 has a direct 10 Gbps link Te1/1 to CORE, the verified root for VLAN 100. DSW1 also has Gi1/1 to DSW2, whose root path cost is 2 through its own 10 Gbps CORE link. The network uses short costs. The following are representative abbreviated teaching exhibits from the stated configuration.

exhibits.title: DSW1# show spanning-tree vlan 100 — excerpt
exhibits.text:
Root path cost: 6 through GigabitEthernet1/1
Te1/1               Altn BLK 19        128.49   P2p
Gi1/1               Root FWD 4         128.25   P2p

exhibits.title: DSW1 running configuration excerpt
exhibits.text:
interface TenGigabitEthernet1/1
 switchport mode trunk
 spanning-tree vlan 100 cost 19

tickets.question: Which cause explains the current path selection?
options: The local port number on Gi1/1 is lower, so it overrides the cost comparison.
The manual direct-link cost 19 loses to the indirect path cost 4 + 2 = 6.
The root is selected by physical interface speed rather than the configured bridge ID.
The root’s sending port ID outweighs any local cost configured on Te1/1.
tickets.explanation: CORE is explicitly established as root, and the worksheet gives DSW2's cost as 2. DSW1 adds its Gi1/1 cost 4 for a total of 6, which beats the manually assigned 19 on Te1/1. The cost comparison is decided before port IDs matter; the port's speed is not increased by changing its STP cost.
tickets.fix:
Remove the unintended per-VLAN override, then verify the displayed automatic cost and root path. With the stated short-cost method, Te1/1 should use cost 2 and become root port.
```ios DSW1
DSW1# configure terminal
DSW1(config)# interface tengigabitethernet1/1
DSW1(config-if)# no spanning-tree vlan 100 cost
DSW1(config-if)# end
DSW1# show spanning-tree vlan 100
```
Retest traffic and save only after confirming the intended root and path. Interface names in this worksheet belong to its example platform; do not paste them into an unrelated 2960 lab.

tickets.title: A replacement restores classic behavior on an interswitch link
tickets.scenario: The intended topology runs Rapid PVST+. After ASW3 is replaced, the transit link from ASW1 toward ASW3 uses legacy behavior during link changes. Host-edge configuration is unchanged. The following representative excerpts show the peer compatibility state and replacement mode.

exhibits.title: ASW1# show spanning-tree vlan 10 — excerpt
exhibits.text:
Spanning tree enabled protocol rstp
Gi0/1               Desg FWD 4         128.25   P2p Peer(STP)

exhibits.title: ASW3# show spanning-tree summary — excerpt
exhibits.text: Switch is in pvst mode

tickets.question: What does the evidence identify as the mismatch?
options: ASW3 uses classic PVST+, causing classic interoperability on the link facing it.
The ASW1 transit port lacks PortFast, so it can never form a rapid handshake.
The replacement’s lower bridge priority requires classic rather than rapid transitions.
The P2p label establishes half-duplex operation and a shared physical segment.
tickets.explanation: ASW3's mode and ASW1's Peer(STP) indication identify the classic neighbor. The effect is on compatibility behavior of the connecting link; this does not prove that every host port in the network now waits 30 seconds. P2p is the point-to-point link type, not shared.
tickets.fix:
Configure the intended mode on ASW3, then verify the local mode and ASW1 peer behavior after negotiation.
```ios ASW3
ASW3# configure terminal
ASW3(config)# spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst
ASW3(config)# end
ASW3# show spanning-tree summary
ASW3# show spanning-tree vlan 10
```
If a peer remains in legacy compatibility, confirm that no legacy bridge remains and consult that platform's protocol-migration procedure. Do not enable PortFast on the transit link as a workaround or promise a fixed number of seconds for the Peer(STP) indication to disappear.

chapters.summary: Choose PortFast, BPDU guard, root guard, and loop guard according to a port's purpose. Read their failure states, correct the cause, and restore service safely; distinguish the two BPDU-filter forms for v1.1.

sections.title: Match protection to the port's purpose
sections.body:
Spanning tree selects a topology from the BPDUs it receives; it does not know your intended administrative boundaries. A newly attached switch with a lower BID can become root even if that switch belongs in a training room. A different fault occurs when an operational uplink stops delivering BPDUs. The receiving switch might discard its previous information and attempt to forward where it should remain blocked.

Protection features address these specific situations. First identify what belongs behind the port: an end device, a downstream switch that must not supply the root, or an uplink expected to receive BPDUs. Then choose a feature whose trigger matches the failure you want to detect. An interface labeled “access” is not necessarily an edge: it can still connect to another switch carrying a single VLAN.

| Intended connection | Appropriate feature | What it accomplishes |
|---|---|---|
| End device with no Layer 2 transit path | PortFast plus BPDU guard | Immediate forwarding; received BPDUs trigger shutdown |
| Downstream switch outside the root-placement boundary | Root guard | Blocks superior information from taking over that boundary |
| Point-to-point root or alternate path | Loop guard | Prevents missing BPDUs from making the port designated |
| A specialized BPDU-suppression requirement | BPDU filter | Suppresses BPDUs; not a replacement for protection |

```diagram
{"type":"topology","title":"Fig 15.1 — Place the policy at the correct boundary","caption":"The access switch expects BPDUs on its uplink, rejects a superior root from the downstream lab, and rejects any BPDU from the host port.","nodes":[{"id":"CORE","kind":"switch","label":"CORE · intended root","x":1,"y":3,"highlight":true},{"id":"ACCESS","kind":"switch","label":"ACCESS","x":5,"y":3},{"id":"PC","kind":"pc","label":"PC","x":10,"y":1},{"id":"LAB","kind":"switch","label":"LAB switch","x":10,"y":5}],"links":[{"from":"CORE","to":"ACCESS","label":"ACCESS: loop guard","toBadge":"RP"},{"from":"ACCESS","to":"PC","label":"PortFast + BPDU guard","fromBadge":"Edge"},{"from":"ACCESS","to":"LAB","label":"ACCESS: root guard","fromBadge":"DP"}]}
```

The lab uses a known three-switch baseline and tests one condition at a time. You will inspect the state before recovery, remove the cause, and verify the restored path. The goal is to explain why traffic stopped and whether the protection behaved as intended, rather than make every blocked interface green.

sections.title: PortFast and operational edge status
sections.body:
:::facts
- PortFast permits immediate forwarding on an end-device port; it does not disable STP.
- Interface BPDU guard reacts to any received BPDU, regardless of PortFast. Global BPDU guard applies to operational PortFast ports.
- Root guard reacts to superior BPDUs; loop guard reacts to missing expected BPDUs on applicable root/alternate ports.
- Root- and loop-inconsistent conditions recover automatically when their triggering condition ends. BPDU-guard errdisable requires manual recovery or an enabled recovery timer.
- On the IOS platforms discussed here, the errdisable recovery interval defaults to `300` seconds; automatic recovery for the cause must be enabled separately.
:::

**PortFast** identifies a port that can safely forward immediately because it connects to an end device rather than a transit bridge. Classic STP otherwise has listening and learning delays, each `15` seconds by default. RSTP can also need timer-based forwarding when no rapid agreement is possible. Marking a genuine edge avoids that wait instead of expecting a PC to participate in a bridge-to-bridge handshake.

Immediate forwarding helps a newly connected host exchange DHCP, ARP, and application traffic without an STP startup delay. It does not guarantee that DHCP has a reachable server or that a host has the right VLAN. A failed first ping can still be address resolution rather than spanning-tree convergence. Verify the port state and the IP configuration independently.

PortFast also affects topology-change handling. In RSTP, ordinary edge-port link transitions do not trigger a topology change; non-edge ports entering forwarding do. Avoid the blanket claim that every RSTP port shutdown generates a topology-change event. The distinction matters because unnecessary topology changes can invalidate learned forwarding information and cause extra flooding while MAC addresses are relearned.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/5
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 10
SW1(config-if)# spanning-tree portfast
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show spanning-tree interface fastethernet0/5 detail
```

The configuration declares an edge, but **operational edge status** is the state actually being used. With PortFast alone, receiving a BPDU causes an RSTP edge port to become an ordinary spanning-tree port; the configured command is not necessarily removed. STP still processes BPDUs and maintains loop-prevention behavior. If BPDU guard is enabled too, its shutdown action is the more visible result.

| IOS configuration | Scope |
|---|---|
| `spanning-tree portfast` | Current interface while operationally nontrunking |
| `spanning-tree portfast trunk` | Current trunk to an appropriate end device |
| `spanning-tree portfast default` | Global default for nontrunking ports |
| `spanning-tree portfast disable` | Interface exception to a global default |

A server or hypervisor may legitimately receive tagged VLANs, but the trunk must still be an edge in the network design. Verify that the host cannot bridge this connection into another path through the LAN. “It is a server” is not sufficient evidence by itself. On current Catalyst IOS XE, the equivalent PortFast syntax may include `edge`, such as `spanning-tree portfast edge trunk`; use interface help for that image. The labs use the 2960-style commands shown above.

sections.title: BPDU guard and errdisable recovery
sections.body:
**BPDU guard** treats a received BPDU as a violation of the port's intended use. The BPDU does not have to advertise a better root. A fully authorized switch with a worse BID will still trigger guard if attached to a guarded host port. This makes BPDU guard suitable where no bridge should participate, rather than where a downstream bridge is allowed but must remain subordinate.

There are two configuration scopes. `spanning-tree bpduguard enable` is an interface command and operates independently of PortFast. `spanning-tree portfast bpduguard default` is a global default applying to interfaces in the operational PortFast state. Therefore a global BPDU-guard line alone does not automatically protect every trunk. Check operational state and interface overrides when interpreting a configuration exhibit.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/5
SW1(config-if)# spanning-tree bpduguard enable
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces status
```

With the conventional Catalyst behavior used here, a violation puts the interface in **err-disabled** state and stops user traffic on the entire port. This differs from a VLAN-specific STP inconsistency on a trunk. Some platforms offer additional recovery/containment options, but do not assume them unless an exhibit explicitly shows their configuration.

First inspect the interface and the log to identify the cause. Errdisable can result from several features; the state alone does not prove BPDU guard. A message containing `bpduguard` alongside the affected port is the useful evidence. Disconnect or correct the BPDU source before resetting the port. Otherwise the same violation can happen as soon as the port is active again.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/5
SW1(config-if)# shutdown
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces status
```

Automatic recovery is an optional policy choice, not the default remedy. `errdisable recovery cause bpduguard` enables attempts for that cause; `errdisable recovery interval 60` changes the shared recovery interval. The documented IOS range is `30`–`86400` seconds, with default `300`. Verify the cause is enabled using `show errdisable recovery`; simply changing the interval does not enable BPDU-guard recovery. Knowing the trigger and corrective workflow matters more than memorizing the maximum timer value.

:::trap Restoring the port is not correcting the cause
Repeatedly issuing `shutdown` and `no shutdown`, or shortening a recovery timer, does not make a prohibited switch acceptable on a host port. Remove the cause or redesign the connection as an authorized interswitch link with the correct VLAN and STP policy.
:::

sections.title: Root guard and root-placement boundaries
sections.body:
**Root guard** allows ordinary spanning-tree participation while preventing a designated boundary port from accepting superior information that would change its intended role. Place it on the managed side of a connection through which the root must not be learned. For example, the access-switch port toward a training-room switch may have root guard. The access switch's uplink toward the intended root should not.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# spanning-tree guard root
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show spanning-tree inconsistentports
```

Consider an intended root at priority `24576` and a downstream training switch accidentally configured at `0`, both for VLAN 10. The guarded boundary hears superior information and enters **root-inconsistent** state for that VLAN. Traffic through the affected instance is blocked, protecting the upstream topology. The training switch may still consider itself root of its isolated portion; root guard is not an instruction that rewrites the training switch's configuration.

In Rapid PVST+, other VLANs on the trunk may continue forwarding if they have no inconsistent condition. Thus “VLAN 10 fails while VLAN 20 works” can be consistent with root guard. Check each VLAN rather than assuming the physical interface is down. Typical output includes `*ROOT_Inc` and a root-inconsistent entry; it is not BPDU-guard errdisable.

Recovery is automatic after superior information ceases and normal STP processing permits forwarding. Correct the downstream priority or cabling rather than removing the protection solely to restore traffic. Do not promise recovery at exactly `20` seconds: protocol state, new BPDUs, and timers affect the observed interval. Root guard also does not solve missing-BPDU faults, because inferior information received by an already legitimate root is not its trigger.

sections.title: Loop guard and missing BPDUs
sections.body:
**Loop guard** protects applicable point-to-point ports that are currently root or alternate ports and should continue receiving BPDUs. If expected information expires, it prevents them from becoming designated and forwarding merely because those BPDUs stopped arriving. The affected instance enters **loop-inconsistent** state. When BPDUs resume, the condition clears automatically and normal STP chooses the role and state again.

A link can remain physically up while its control traffic fails. Possible causes include a one-way transmission fault, a neighbor no longer sending BPDUs, or filtering that prevents delivery. Loop guard detects missing control information; it does not diagnose which of these caused the loss. A `*LOOP_Inc` indication alone cannot prove a broken fiber strand, and an ordinary cable unplug is not the same test because it causes link-down.

```ios SW3
SW3# configure terminal
SW3(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW3(config-if)# spanning-tree guard loop
SW3(config-if)# end
SW3# show spanning-tree inconsistentports
```

The global alternative is `spanning-tree loopguard default`. It enables the feature on applicable point-to-point interfaces; its protective action depends on the port's role and received information. It is not intended to disable a host port because a PC sends no BPDUs. It also cannot reliably detect a failure that existed from first link-up before the port received the information it is meant to monitor. Shared links are outside this mechanism's supported scope.

Root guard and loop guard express different role expectations and cannot operate together on the same interface. One protects a boundary that should remain designated; the other prevents a root/alternate port from becoming designated through missing information. Do not apply every guard to every uplink. A global deployment still requires attention to exceptions and legitimate failover paths.

The guided fault exercise temporarily suppresses BPDUs only in an isolated topology with no redundant physical path. That produces a controlled observation without deliberately constructing a forwarding loop. Packet Tracer may accept some commands but not model the complete failure; the lab provides a paper interpretation fallback. Recognizing an unsupported simulation is preferable to treating a missing reaction as proof that the protocol works differently.

sections.title: BPDU filter: distinguish the two forms
sections.body:
BPDU filter is explicitly listed in the v1.1 protection objective and is not listed in the v2.0 equivalent. Learn it here after the protection features, because suppression changes the evidence on which those features depend. This is a scope distinction, not a claim about Cisco's reason for changing its blueprint.

The interface command `spanning-tree bpdufilter enable` suppresses sending and receiving BPDUs independently of PortFast. Cisco warns that this is effectively disabling spanning-tree participation on that interface and can permit a loop. A physically redundant link can continue carrying user traffic while the switches lack the control exchange needed to block it safely. This is why filter is not a substitute for BPDU guard.

The global command `spanning-tree portfast bpdufilter default` has different behavior on operational PortFast ports. Initial BPDUs are sent at link-up before outgoing filtering takes effect; if a BPDU is received, operational PortFast status and filtering are removed and normal STP operation resumes. Do not extend that fallback behavior to unconditional interface filtering. Avoid memorizing a platform-specific count of initial BPDUs.

Review interface filtering wherever BPDUs appear to be missing. Do not build a host-port template by combining every feature name: suppressing BPDU processing conflicts with a design that relies on received BPDUs to expose a wrong connection. Remove unwanted filtering as the actual repair; adding more guard commands without examining the existing policy can leave the original problem in place.

sections.title: Verify and troubleshoot
sections.body:
The following excerpts are representative IOS-style teaching exhibits. They illustrate distinct states and are not output from one simultaneously running experiment. Actual interface names, timestamps, and detailed formatting vary by device and software.

```output SW1# show interfaces status
Port      Name               Status       Vlan       Duplex  Speed Type
Fa0/5                        err-disabled 10           auto   auto 10/100BaseTX  ← whole interface disabled; inspect the cause
```

```output SW1# show spanning-tree inconsistentports
Name                 Interface                Inconsistency
-------------------- ------------------------ ------------------
VLAN0010             GigabitEthernet0/1        Root Inconsistent  ← superior information at a guarded boundary
Number of inconsistent ports (segments) in the system : 1
```

Start with `show interfaces status` to distinguish link-down, administrative shutdown, and errdisable. Inspect `show logging` for a cause, then use `show spanning-tree vlan 10` and `show spanning-tree inconsistentports` for the affected instance. A protected port may disappear from normal STP output after errdisable; use interface status and running configuration rather than assuming the configuration vanished.

Use `show spanning-tree summary` to inspect global defaults, and `show spanning-tree interface fastethernet0/5 detail` to inspect an active port. Match the configuration scope with the operational state. For root guard, trace where superior information originates. For loop guard, compare BPDU reception and transmission at both ends and check filtering; do not remove the guard until the underlying condition is understood.

After recovery, verify both the expected root/port roles and end-to-end user traffic. A green interface is insufficient if the wrong root now attracts traffic or a VLAN is missing from a trunk. Save only the corrected design, leaving deliberate fault settings out of the startup configuration. Keep a short note of the trigger, evidence, fix, and successful retest.

sections.title: Exam focus
sections.body:
- PortFast enables immediate forwarding for a genuine edge; STP remains active and configured status differs from operational status.
- Interface BPDU guard applies independently of PortFast; the global default applies to operational PortFast ports.
- Any received BPDU triggers BPDU guard; superior information triggers root guard; missing expected BPDUs trigger loop guard.
- Distinguish whole-port errdisable from per-instance root/loop inconsistency in Rapid PVST+.
- Remove the cause before manual or automatic errdisable recovery. A 300-second default interval does not mean recovery is enabled.
- Put root guard at the boundary toward an impermissible root, and loop guard on appropriate root/alternate point-to-point paths.
- Root guard and loop guard are mutually exclusive on one interface.
- For v1.1, distinguish conditional global BPDU filtering from unconditional interface filtering.

lab.intro:
Practice revised September 2026. If you completed an earlier version, repeat the revised exercise and update its checkmarks.

Build a new project with the complete configuration below; no saved file from another chapter is required. You will protect a host port, reject a superior downstream root, and interpret missing-BPDU protection. The base topology is deliberately a line, so the controlled loop-guard demonstration has no redundant physical path that could form a data loop if the feature is unavailable.

These instructions and expected results are authored from Cisco's documented behavior, not a claim of manual Packet Tracer execution. Run the PortFast/BPDU-guard/root-guard exercises where the simulator supports them. Run the BPDU-suppression fault only on an isolated CML/hardware setup after confirming loop guard is operational; Packet Tracer learners use the included prediction and representative evidence. Command acceptance alone does not establish complete simulation support.
