steps.title: Configure PCs and protected edge ports
steps.body:
Enter each PC address and mask using Desktop → IP Configuration → Static; leave gateway and DNS blank. Run `ping 10.0.10.12` and `ping 10.0.10.3` from PC-A after convergence. Then configure PortFast and BPDU guard on SW1's specific host port; on SW2 demonstrate the equivalent global defaults for its nontrunking host ports.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/5
SW1(config-if)# spanning-tree portfast
SW1(config-if)# spanning-tree bpduguard enable
SW1(config-if)# shutdown
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show spanning-tree interface fastethernet0/5 detail
```

```ios SW2
SW2# configure terminal
SW2(config)# spanning-tree portfast default
SW2(config)# spanning-tree portfast bpduguard default
SW2(config)# end
SW2# show spanning-tree summary
SW2# show spanning-tree interface fastethernet0/5 detail
```

:::expected
PC-A can reach PC-B and SW3's SVI. SW1 Fa0/5 becomes forwarding as an edge after the controlled bounce; BPDU guard is configured and no violation exists with PC-A attached. SW2's global defaults apply to Fa0/5 but not its trunk Fa0/24. If an optional detailed show command is unsupported, use `show spanning-tree vlan 10`, `show running-config`, and interface status. Record the actual port behavior instead of assuming an exact delay.
:::

steps.title: Trigger BPDU guard with the third switch
steps.body:
Before changing cables, predict whether the trigger depends on SW3 advertising a better root. Record the expected interface state, affected traffic and evidence that distinguishes this from an alternate port.

Disconnect SW3 Gi0/1 from SW1 Gi0/1 first. Verify that SW3 now has no interswitch cable. Disconnect PC-A from SW1 Fa0/5. Prepare SW3 Fa0/1 as an access port in VLAN 10, then connect it to SW1 Fa0/5 using a crossover cable. This temporary connection has no alternate physical return path.

```ios SW3
SW3# configure terminal
SW3(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
SW3(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW3(config-if)# switchport access vlan 10
SW3(config-if)# no shutdown
SW3(config-if)# end
```

```ios SW1
SW1# show interfaces status
SW1# show logging
```

:::expected
SW3 sends BPDUs; the configured interface BPDU guard causes SW1 Fa0/5 to become err-disabled. SW3 does not need priority zero: any received BPDU is sufficient. Look for the actual `bpduguard` cause in the log. The following shortened lines are representative, not a recorded simulator transcript:

```output Representative SW1 evidence
%SPANTREE-2-BLOCK_BPDUGUARD: Received BPDU on port FastEthernet0/5 with BPDU Guard enabled. Disabling port.
%PM-4-ERR_DISABLE: bpduguard error detected on Fa0/5, putting Fa0/5 in err-disable state
```

If the port stays up, check which physical port received the cable, the SW3 port state, and the presence of BPDU guard. If the simulator does not implement the feature, record that limitation and interpret the evidence above; do not count the exercise as an observed trigger.
:::

steps.title: Remove the BPDU source and recover the host port
steps.body:
Delete the temporary SW3 Fa0/1 cable. Reconnect PC-A to SW1 Fa0/5 with a straight-through cable, and restore SW3 Gi0/1 ↔ SW1 Gi0/1 with a crossover cable. Shut the unused test port on SW3. Only after the wrong connection is removed, reset SW1 Fa0/5.

```ios SW3
SW3# configure terminal
SW3(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
SW3(config-if)# shutdown
SW3(config-if)# end
```

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/5
SW1(config-if)# shutdown
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces status
SW1# show spanning-tree vlan 10
```

:::expected
Fa0/5 returns to connected/forwarding with PC-A attached. Repeat PC-A's pings to 10.0.10.12 and 10.0.10.3. SW2 is still root and SW3's root cost is 23. A repeating violation means a BPDU source is still reaching the protected port; a timer or repeated reset would not correct that source.
:::

steps.title: Guard the downstream boundary and introduce a superior root
steps.body:
Before applying the change, predict which of PC-A→PC-B and PC-A→SW3 should fail, which physical link can remain up, and whether manual errdisable recovery will be appropriate.

SW1 Gi0/1 is a designated boundary toward SW3, so install root guard there. Then change SW3's VLAN 10 priority to zero. Keep all permanent cables exactly as in the topology.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# spanning-tree guard root
SW1(config-if)# end
```

```ios SW3
SW3# configure terminal
SW3(config)# spanning-tree vlan 10 priority 0
SW3(config)# end
SW3# show spanning-tree vlan 10
```

```ios SW1
SW1# show spanning-tree inconsistentports
SW1# show spanning-tree vlan 10
```

:::expected
SW1 Gi0/1 becomes root-inconsistent for VLAN 10, often displayed with `*ROOT_Inc`; it does not become BPDU-guard err-disabled. SW1 still identifies SW2 as root. PC-A can reach PC-B but cannot reach SW3's 10.0.10.3 address across the blocked VLAN. SW3 may identify itself as root in its isolated portion. The objective is to hold the upstream boundary, not change SW3's configuration automatically.
:::

steps.title: Correct the downstream priority
steps.body:
Restore SW3's explicit priority 28672 and allow STP to process the new information. Leave the protective root-guard command on SW1 while observing automatic recovery.

```ios SW3
SW3# configure terminal
SW3(config)# spanning-tree vlan 10 priority 28672
SW3(config)# end
SW3# show spanning-tree vlan 10
```

```ios SW1
SW1# show spanning-tree inconsistentports
SW1# show spanning-tree vlan 10
```

:::expected
The root-inconsistent condition clears without a manual port bounce. SW3 again learns SW2's root ID and uses Gi0/1 at cost 23; PC-A can again ping 10.0.10.3. Record the observed recovery rather than requiring exactly 20 seconds. If it persists, verify that the command changed VLAN 10 and that no other superior source exists.
:::

steps.title: Prepare loop guard and record received BPDUs
steps.body:
For the missing-BPDU exercise, remove root guard from SW1's sending port to keep this experiment focused on one feature. Configure loop guard on SW3's receiving root port. These commands require platform support; if your Packet Tracer image rejects loop guard, use the worksheet exercise in Step 8 and skip the suppression command entirely.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# no spanning-tree guard
SW1(config-if)# end
```

```ios SW3
SW3# configure terminal
SW3(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW3(config-if)# spanning-tree guard loop
SW3(config-if)# end
SW3# show spanning-tree interface gigabitethernet0/1 detail
SW3# show spanning-tree inconsistentports
```

:::expected
SW3 Gi0/1 is still root/forwarding for VLAN 10 and receives BPDUs before the fault. On an implementing image, detail identifies loop guard as enabled; repeated readings show received BPDU activity. The inconsistent-port list is empty. Do not infer enabled loop protection from command acceptance alone, and do not inject the fault if you cannot establish this baseline.
:::

steps.title: Observe a controlled BPDU-loss fault or interpret the exhibit
steps.body:
**CML/hardware only, isolated line topology:** confirm that SW3 has only its Gi0/1 cable and the temporary Fa0/1 test port is shut. On SW1 Gi0/1, temporarily enable interface BPDU filtering. This models lost BPDU delivery while the physical link remains up; it does not reproduce every property of a one-way fiber fault. There is no extra SW2–SW3 link.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# spanning-tree bpdufilter enable
SW1(config-if)# end
```

```ios SW3
SW3# show interfaces status
SW3# show spanning-tree inconsistentports
SW3# show spanning-tree interface gigabitethernet0/1 detail
```

**Packet Tracer/paper path:** do not enter the filter command. From the healthy baseline, predict the result if SW3 stopped receiving BPDUs but the link stayed up. Interpret the representative evidence below and compare it with root guard's trigger.

:::expected
On a supported implementation, expired expected BPDU information causes loop inconsistency on SW3 Gi0/1. Physical link status can remain connected while VLAN 10 cannot forward. A representative abbreviated entry is:

```output Representative loop-guard evidence
Name                 Interface                Inconsistency
-------------------- ------------------------ ------------------
VLAN0010             GigabitEthernet0/1        Loop Inconsistent
```

The reason is missing expected BPDUs, not a received superior BID. VLAN 999 may also be listed depending on its roles and received information. Do not require a fixed role label or six-second trigger from every software version. Root guard would not detect this same absence of control traffic.
:::

steps.title: Remove filtering and restore the boundary
steps.body:
On the CML/hardware path, remove the exact filter introduced in Step 8. On the Packet Tracer/paper path no filter was installed, so simply verify the running configuration and restore root guard. Root guard on SW1 and loop guard on SW3 are on different interfaces at opposite ends and are compatible with this intended design.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# no spanning-tree bpdufilter
SW1(config-if)# spanning-tree guard root
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show running-config
```

```ios SW3
SW3# show spanning-tree inconsistentports
SW3# show spanning-tree vlan 10
```

:::expected
If a fault was executed, BPDUs resume and loop inconsistency clears automatically; SW3 returns to root/forwarding on Gi0/1 with cost 23. PC-A's pings to SW3 and PC-B succeed. No interface BPDU filter remains in the running configuration. On a simulator that rejects the optional removal command, verify that no filter was configured and continue with supported commands.
:::

steps.title: Inspect optional timed recovery without repeating the fault
steps.body:
On an IOS image supporting these commands, enable automatic recovery for BPDU guard and set the interval to 60 seconds. This is a configuration-reading exercise: do not reconnect the prohibited switch. Packet Tracer users whose image rejects the commands should identify the two separate requirements from the lesson and retain manual recovery.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# errdisable recovery cause bpduguard
SW1(config)# errdisable recovery interval 60
SW1(config)# end
SW1# show errdisable recovery
```

:::expected
The output identifies BPDU-guard recovery as enabled and the interval as 60 seconds. No interface is waiting for recovery because the fault was already corrected. Changing only the timer would not enable recovery for the cause. The setting permits future recovery attempts; it does not prevent another violation.
:::

steps.title: Remove the optional timer policy and save the protected baseline
steps.body:
If Step 10 was supported, remove its cause and interval settings to return to manual BPDU-guard recovery. Keep PortFast/BPDU guard on the host ports, root guard on SW1's downstream boundary, and supported loop guard on SW3's uplink. Save each switch and then save the workspace as `stp-protected.pkt` or the equivalent CML lab.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# no errdisable recovery cause bpduguard
SW1(config)# no errdisable recovery interval
SW1(config)# end
SW1# show spanning-tree inconsistentports
SW1# show spanning-tree vlan 10
SW1# copy running-config startup-config
```

```ios SW2
SW2# show spanning-tree vlan 10
SW2# copy running-config startup-config
```

```ios SW3
SW3# show spanning-tree vlan 10
SW3# copy running-config startup-config
```

:::expected
No deliberate fault remains: SW3 priority is 28672, its temporary Fa0/1 is shut, filtering is absent, and SW2 remains root. All three management IPs and both PCs are reachable within VLAN 10. Record any simulator-only omissions in your notes so the saved project does not imply a feature was demonstrated when it was only studied. Accept each device’s save filename prompt and wait for completion before moving to the next device.

Submit one row for each tested or interpreted feature: intended port role; received or missing BPDU trigger; resulting interface/instance state; affected traffic; evidence that identifies the cause; corrective action; and fresh verification. Mark loop-guard worksheet results as supplied, not observed. The optional timer exercise is configuration interpretation, not a timed recovery measurement.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- Fa0/5 stays err-disabled after restoring the PC: remove the BPDU source first, then issue both `shutdown` and `no shutdown`; a lone `no shutdown` is not the complete recovery sequence.
- Root guard does not trigger: confirm it is on SW1 Gi0/1, the SW3 priority change is for VLAN 10, and the correct trunk carries that VLAN.
- SW3 unexpectedly becomes root of the main network: the boundary guard was absent or the switch was attached through a different port. Disconnect the temporary source, correct placement, and restore priority before reconnecting.
- Loop inconsistency does not appear: first determine whether this is the paper/simulator path. On supported equipment verify prior BPDU reception, correct interface, point-to-point status, enabled loop guard, and the exact BPDU-suppression location.
- A management SVI cannot be pinged: check its address and operational line protocol as well as STP. A VLAN without an active forwarding member can make its SVI unavailable.
lab.challenge:
This independent policy worksheet uses a different access switch, ASW4, with all three listed links in VLAN 30. Assume a supported IOS switch, healthy forwarding before the policy change, and no other links. CORE is the intended root. LAB may participate in STP but must not supply the root. The printer must never act as a bridge.

| ASW4 port | Actual neighbor and baseline role | Requirement |
|---|---|---|
| Gi1/0/48 | CORE; root port, point-to-point, receiving BPDUs | Keep expected control information; prevent a silent loss from making this port designated |
| Gi1/0/10 | LAB; designated port | Reject superior root information, while permitting ordinary downstream STP |
| Gi1/0/7 | Printer; static access port | Immediate edge forwarding and errdisable on any received BPDU |

Before opening the answer, select and write the interface commands for each row. Then predict the state, affected traffic and recovery for three separate incidents: LAB advertises a superior VLAN 30 root; the printer is replaced by a BPDU-sending switch; CORE’s expected BPDUs stop arriving while Gi1/0/48 stays physically up. Assume no automatic errdisable recovery.

For the last incident, name two plausible causes and the next evidence needed. Do not claim the state proves one specific cable defect. This is a paper exercise; do not attach new equipment or suppress production BPDUs.

:::solution
The three boundaries require different policies:

```ios ASW4
ASW4# configure terminal
ASW4(config)# interface gigabitethernet1/0/48
ASW4(config-if)# spanning-tree guard loop
ASW4(config-if)# exit
ASW4(config)# interface gigabitethernet1/0/10
ASW4(config-if)# spanning-tree guard root
ASW4(config-if)# exit
ASW4(config)# interface gigabitethernet1/0/7
ASW4(config-if)# switchport mode access
ASW4(config-if)# switchport access vlan 30
ASW4(config-if)# spanning-tree portfast
ASW4(config-if)# spanning-tree bpduguard enable
ASW4(config-if)# end
```

These are additions to the explicitly supplied healthy baseline, not a complete new switch configuration. Some IOS XE images use the `edge` PortFast spelling.

- LAB’s superior information causes root inconsistency on the Gi1/0/10 VLAN 30 instance. Correct LAB’s priority or connection; the inconsistency clears automatically when the triggering information ceases and STP permits recovery. Root guard does not rewrite LAB.
- A BPDU on Gi1/0/7 causes conventional BPDU-guard errdisable for the whole interface. Remove the incorrect switch, then enter `shutdown` and `no shutdown` on Gi1/0/7 and verify a fresh host test. Removing the source alone does not clear the disabled state under the given recovery policy.
- Previously received BPDUs expiring on Gi1/0/48 cause loop inconsistency, keeping the affected instance from unsafe forwarding. Peer BPDU filtering, a peer control-plane problem or a one-way path fault could explain missing delivery. Compare peer transmission/configuration with local reception and physical evidence. Restore delivery; the inconsistency clears automatically when appropriate BPDUs return.

Use `show spanning-tree inconsistentports` for instance inconsistencies and interface status plus a cause-specific log for errdisable. Confirm expected VLAN 30 roles and endpoint traffic after recovery. Installing root guard on Gi1/0/48 would reject the legitimate root path; putting both root and loop guard on one interface is not a valid combined policy.
:::

questions.prompt: What does PortFast change on a correctly designed end-device access port?
options: It makes the port a root port so user traffic avoids the normal tree.
It filters all BPDUs so the host can never influence the bridge election.
It permits immediate forwarding while spanning tree remains active.
It waits for a PC's agreement BPDU before skipping the learning state.
questions.explanation: PortFast permits a genuine edge port to enter forwarding immediately. It does not disable STP; a received BPDU changes operational edge behavior or triggers an enabled guard.

whyWrong.0: PortFast does not elect the port as a root port.
whyWrong.1: BPDU suppression is filtering, not PortFast itself.
whyWrong.3: End hosts do not have to participate in a bridge proposal/agreement handshake.

questions.prompt: On a 2960-style IOS switch, which global command enables PortFast for operationally nontrunking ports?
options: spanning-tree bpduguard enable
spanning-tree portfast default
spanning-tree guard root
spanning-tree portfast trunk
questions.explanation: The global default applies PortFast to nontrunking interfaces. A trunk to a legitimate end device needs the appropriate interface trunk form instead.

whyWrong.0: This enables interface BPDU guard and does not enable global PortFast.
whyWrong.2: Root guard protects a designated boundary and does not create an edge port.
whyWrong.3: This is an interface command for a PortFast trunk, not the global nontrunking default.

questions.prompt: Which event is the intended trigger for loop guard on a point-to-point root port that has been receiving BPDUs?
options: Expected BPDU information expires while the physical link remains up.
The port receives its first BPDU while operational PortFast is enabled.
The local switch learns a host MAC address on the root interface.
The peer advertises a lower root BID while continuing normal BPDU exchange.
questions.explanation: Loop guard handles the loss of expected spanning-tree information on an applicable root or alternate port. It prevents expiry from making that port designated and forwarding on an unsafe assumption.

whyWrong.1: Unexpected BPDU reception on a protected edge is the BPDU-guard case.
whyWrong.2: MAC learning from user frames is not the loop-guard trigger.
whyWrong.3: Superior received information is associated with root-guard policy, not loop guard's silence condition.

questions.prompt: How do the two Cisco IOS BPDU-filter forms differ?
options: The global PortFast form withdraws filtering after a BPDU; the interface form suppresses BPDUs independently.
The global form filters user broadcasts; the interface form filters user multicast without affecting STP.
The global form applies only to trunks; the interface form applies only to nontrunking access ports.
The global form err-disables after a BPDU; the interface form waits for a superior root advertisement.
questions.explanation: The global PortFast default has conditional behavior: received BPDUs remove operational edge/filter status. Interface filtering independently suppresses BPDU participation and does not provide that same fallback.

whyWrong.1: The feature concerns BPDUs, not general user broadcast or multicast filtering.
whyWrong.2: The global form follows operational PortFast status, and the interface form is not limited as stated.
whyWrong.3: These describe guard-like actions, not the two BPDU-filter behaviors.

questions.prompt: Which comparison correctly distinguishes root guard from BPDU guard?
options: Root guard rejects every BPDU; BPDU guard rejects only a lower-priority root.
Root guard rejects superior information; BPDU guard reacts to any received BPDU.
Root guard detects BPDU silence; BPDU guard detects changes in interface speed.
Root guard uses errdisable; BPDU guard uses a per-VLAN root-inconsistent state.
questions.explanation: Root guard enforces a designated boundary against superior spanning-tree information. BPDU guard enforces an expectation that no BPDU should arrive, so it does not need to compare the advertised root first.

whyWrong.0: The trigger comparison is reversed.
whyWrong.2: Missing BPDUs are the loop-guard case, and speed changes do not define BPDU guard.
whyWrong.3: The normal state distinction is root inconsistency versus BPDU-guard errdisable, not the reverse.

questions.prompt: With no configured errdisable recovery timer, which two states can clear automatically when their own triggering conditions end? (Choose two.)
options: Administrative shutdown after the peer link becomes healthy.
Loop inconsistency after expected BPDUs resume.
An administratively disabled SVI after the correct VLAN is created.
Root inconsistency after superior information ceases.
BPDU-guard errdisable after the switch stops sending BPDUs.
questions.explanation: Root and loop inconsistency include automatic return to normal STP processing after their conditions clear. BPDU-guard errdisable needs manual recovery or an enabled recovery policy; administrative shutdown also requires configuration action.

whyWrong.0: A configured shutdown is not cleared by peer health.
whyWrong.2: Creating a VLAN does not remove a configured SVI shutdown.
whyWrong.4: Without enabled automatic recovery, removing the source alone does not reset errdisable.

questions.prompt: A root-facing point-to-point uplink should use loop guard, while a downstream boundary should use root guard. Which implementation principle is correct?
options: Choose the guard by the intended role; root and loop guard cannot coexist on one interface.
Use root guard on every root port because its name identifies where it belongs.
Install both guards on each uplink so either a received or missing BPDU is covered.
Use loop guard on PC access ports because their lack of BPDUs needs protection.
questions.explanation: Root guard preserves a designated boundary, whereas loop guard protects appropriate root/alternate paths from BPDU loss. Their role expectations differ, and IOS does not allow both to operate on the same interface.

whyWrong.1: A root port needs the legitimate superior information that root guard would reject.
whyWrong.2: The two guards are mutually exclusive on a single interface.
whyWrong.3: A genuine edge normally sends no BPDUs and is not the loop-guard monitoring case.

questions.prompt: What caused the outage on Fa0/5, and which recovery sequence fits the evidence?
options: The port is a normal alternate; remove the redundant uplink to make it designated.
A BPDU arrived on the guarded port; remove its source, then shut/no-shut the port.
Expected BPDUs stopped arriving; lower the recovery interval to force learning.
A better root was received; raise SW1's bridge priority to clear the state.
questions.explanation: The log names BPDU guard, and interface status confirms errdisable. Remove the unexpected BPDU source, then perform manual recovery or use an explicitly enabled recovery policy.

whyWrong.0: Err-disabled is not the normal alternate/discarding state.
whyWrong.2: Missing expected BPDUs describe loop guard, not the received-BPDU log.
whyWrong.3: Root guard produces root inconsistency rather than this BPDU-guard error.

exhibit.title: SW1 representative evidence
exhibit.text:
Fa0/5   err-disabled   10
%PM-4-ERR_DISABLE: bpduguard error detected on Fa0/5, putting Fa0/5 in err-disable state

questions.prompt: VLAN 20 is blocked on Gi1/0/10 while another VLAN on the trunk still works. Which diagnosis best fits the representative evidence?
options: Loop guard detected missing expected BPDUs from the intended root neighbor.
BPDU guard disabled the entire physical interface after receiving a BPDU.
Root guard received superior information for VLAN 20 and blocked that instance.
PortFast suppressed the interface's BPDUs until a recovery timer expires.
questions.explanation: The inconsistency explicitly names root guard's condition. In Rapid PVST+, root inconsistency can affect one VLAN while another instance on the physical trunk remains operational.

whyWrong.0: Loop inconsistency is a different indication with a missing-BPDU trigger.
whyWrong.1: Conventional BPDU-guard errdisable affects the interface and is identified by a different state/cause.
whyWrong.3: PortFast does not suppress BPDUs or create this recovery state.

exhibit.title: DSW1# show spanning-tree inconsistentports — excerpt
exhibit.text: VLAN0020             GigabitEthernet1/0/10       Root Inconsistent

questions.prompt: Which two statements about recovery from a BPDU-guard violation are correct? (Choose two.)
options: The source should be corrected before the interface is re-enabled.
Changing the recovery interval alone enables recovery for BPDU guard.
An enabled recovery timer can retry the port but cannot remove the BPDU source.
Root-inconsistent recovery must be enabled before errdisable can clear.
A single received inferior BPDU cannot cause another violation after recovery.
questions.explanation: Recovery restores the interface's ability to operate; it does not correct a wrong connection. Automatic retries must be explicitly enabled for the cause and can fail again if BPDUs continue arriving.

whyWrong.1: The cause must be enabled separately from the interval setting.
whyWrong.3: Root inconsistency and BPDU-guard errdisable are different states with separate recovery behavior.
whyWrong.4: BPDU guard reacts to any received BPDU, including an inferior one.

questions.prompt: CORE must remain the allowed root. A training switch will attach only to ASW1 Gi0/2, currently a designated boundary port. Where should root guard enforce that boundary?
options: On ASW1 Gi0/2, where superior information could enter from the training switch.
On the training switch's own uplink, where its lower-priority BID originates.
On every designated CORE port, including unrelated campus boundaries.
On ASW1's uplink toward CORE, where the best root information is received.
questions.explanation: The controlled side of the boundary is ASW1 Gi0/2. Root guard there prevents the downstream attachment from supplying superior root information into the rest of the topology.

whyWrong.1: Placing policy only on the outside device does not enforce the managed boundary described.
whyWrong.2: Enforce the specified attachment on ASW1 Gi0/2; a blanket CORE policy does not express that local boundary and can affect unrelated paths.
whyWrong.3: That would reject the legitimate root path needed by ASW1.

questions.prompt: Fa0/7 is operationally an access port with no interface overrides. What should happen when a BPDU-sending switch is attached under the shown global configuration?
options: The port remains unprotected because no interface-specific guard line exists.
The port enters root inconsistency only if the attached bridge has a lower BID.
The operational PortFast port is covered by BPDU guard and becomes err-disabled.
The port silently filters the received BPDU and remains an operational edge.
questions.explanation: The PortFast default covers this nontrunking port, and the BPDU-guard default covers its operational edge state. A received BPDU therefore triggers the guard even without an interface-specific enable line.

whyWrong.0: Applicable global defaults do not require duplicate per-interface commands.
whyWrong.1: Any received BPDU triggers BPDU guard, regardless of root superiority.
whyWrong.3: No BPDU-filter command is configured in this exhibit.

exhibit.title: SW1 running-config excerpt
exhibit.text:
spanning-tree portfast default
spanning-tree portfast bpduguard default
interface FastEthernet0/7
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 10

questions.prompt: A non-PortFast trunk to a server must be err-disabled if it receives any BPDU. Which interface command directly configures that behavior?
options: spanning-tree portfast trunk
spanning-tree guard root
spanning-tree loopguard default
spanning-tree bpduguard enable
questions.explanation: Interface BPDU guard operates independently of PortFast state. Its trigger is any received BPDU, which matches the requirement without relying on a global edge default.

whyWrong.0: PortFast controls initial forwarding and does not itself configure errdisable on BPDU reception.
whyWrong.1: Root guard permits ordinary BPDUs and reacts to superior information instead.
whyWrong.2: This is a global loop-guard command for missing expected BPDUs, not interface BPDU guard.

questions.prompt: SW3 Gi0/2 was a root port and had received BPDUs before this event. Which conclusion is supported by these observations?
options: The interface was disabled by BPDU guard, so every VLAN must be physically down.
Expected BPDUs stopped arriving; the output does not by itself prove the physical cause.
The fiber receive strand is conclusively broken because the port is still connected.
A newly received priority-zero BPDU forced SW3 to reject a superior root bridge.
questions.explanation: Loop inconsistency indicates the loss of expected STP information on the applicable port. A one-way fault is one possibility, but filtering or a neighbor control-plane problem can produce the same symptom.

whyWrong.0: The state is loop inconsistency while the physical link remains connected, not BPDU-guard errdisable.
whyWrong.2: The observations identify the symptom but do not distinguish all possible underlying causes.
whyWrong.3: Superior information would fit a root-guard event, which is not the displayed reason.

exhibit.title: SW3 representative observations
exhibit.text:
Gi0/2 physical status: connected
VLAN0010  GigabitEthernet0/2  Loop Inconsistent
VLAN0020  GigabitEthernet0/2  Loop Inconsistent
Received BPDU counter stopped increasing before the event.

questions.prompt: This host-port template is supposed to detect unexpected BPDUs. What is the design problem that should be corrected?
options: Replace BPDU guard with root guard so every BPDU still produces the required errdisable.
Keep the template because interface filtering restores guard visibility after the first BPDU.
Remove PortFast but retain filtering so BPDU guard can inspect normal transit BPDUs.
Remove interface filtering so the intended policy can process received BPDUs.
questions.explanation: Unconditional interface filtering suppresses BPDU participation and conflicts with the goal of using received BPDUs to expose a wrong connection. Remove the unwanted filter and verify a supported PortFast/BPDU-guard policy, rather than relying on mixed-feature precedence assumptions.

whyWrong.0: Root guard reacts to superior information and uses inconsistency, not the required any-BPDU errdisable.
whyWrong.1: The conditional fallback belongs to the global PortFast filter, not unconditional interface filtering.
whyWrong.2: Removing PortFast does not remove unconditional BPDU filtering.

exhibit.title: SW1 host-port configuration
exhibit.text:
interface FastEthernet0/5
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 10
 spanning-tree portfast
 spanning-tree bpduguard enable
 spanning-tree bpdufilter enable

questions.prompt: A port is already err-disabled because of BPDU guard. The BPDU source has been removed. What does the shown recovery configuration establish?
options: The port will be retried after 60 seconds because every cause inherits the interval.
The port must stay disabled until the interval is restored to the default 300 seconds.
The interval is 60 seconds, but BPDU-guard automatic recovery remains disabled.
The port is now root-inconsistent and will recover when a superior BPDU expires.
questions.explanation: The timer interval and the enabled recovery causes are separate settings. The displayed cause remains disabled, so manual recovery or explicitly enabling BPDU-guard recovery is still required.

whyWrong.0: The interval does not enable all causes automatically.
whyWrong.1: The default interval is not a prerequisite for manual or enabled timed recovery.
whyWrong.3: Changing a timer does not convert the port into a different protection state.

exhibit.title: SW1# show errdisable recovery — abbreviated
exhibit.text:
ErrDisable Reason             Timer Status
bpduguard                     Disabled
Timer interval: 60 seconds

exhibit.title: Supplied protection evidence
exhibit.text:
Fa0/8 is an access port.
Configured: spanning-tree portfast
No BPDU guard or BPDU filter at interface or global scope.
After a BPDU arrives: operational edge false; interface remains connected.

questions.prompt: A received BPDU changes an RSTP port from operational edge to non-edge. Which explanation matches the shown configuration and state?
options: The received BPDU is discarded because PortFast disables spanning-tree processing.
The port must be err-disabled because every configured PortFast port has BPDU guard.
The switch must have erased the PortFast command when the first BPDU arrived.
PortFast can remain configured even though the port no longer operates as an edge.
questions.explanation: Configured intent and operational edge status are separate. With PortFast alone, a BPDU removes operational edge status and normal STP participates; BPDU guard is not configured here.

whyWrong.0: PortFast does not disable BPDU processing.
whyWrong.1: PortFast does not imply BPDU guard unless the relevant policy enables it.
whyWrong.2: The operational change does not require removal of the configured command.

exhibit.title: Supplied protection evidence
exhibit.text:
Global: spanning-tree portfast default
Global: spanning-tree portfast bpduguard default
Gi0/1: operational trunk; operational PortFast false
No interface BPDU-guard enable or other overrides.

questions.prompt: A server trunk must reject every received BPDU. Why does the existing global policy not establish that protection for this port?
options: Global BPDU guard suppresses sent BPDUs but never processes received BPDUs.
The root priority must first be lower than the server’s priority before the guard applies.
The trunk is not operationally PortFast, so it is outside this global guard scope.
Global defaults apply only when every VLAN elects this switch as root.
questions.explanation: The global guard follows operational PortFast status. On the stated non-edge trunk, configure the interface guard if the required policy is any-BPDU errdisable, then verify the actual port and design.

whyWrong.0: Suppression is filtering, not the function of BPDU guard.
whyWrong.1: BPDU guard does not require a superior advertised BID.
whyWrong.3: Root identity is not the condition for the global PortFast guard.

exhibit.title: Supplied protection evidence
exhibit.text:
Gi1/0/7: err-disabled
No log cause has yet been collected.
The switch has several different interface security features configured.

questions.prompt: Which additional evidence should be collected before selecting a recovery procedure?
options: The configured VLAN root priority, which identifies every errdisable cause.
The log reason for the affected interface and its relevant configuration.
The lowest MAC address in the switch’s forwarding table.
The STP alternate-port count, which proves BPDU guard caused the outage.
questions.explanation: Errdisable is a resulting interface state shared by several features. A cause-specific log and configuration distinguish a received-BPDU event from other violations before repair.

whyWrong.0: Bridge priority does not identify all interface protection events.
whyWrong.2: A learned host MAC does not identify why the interface was err-disabled.
whyWrong.3: A normal alternate state is separate from errdisable and its cause.

exhibit.title: Supplied protection evidence
exhibit.text:
Only links: CORE—ACCESS—LAB. All carry VLAN 10.
Required root: CORE priority 24576. ACCESS priority 32768. LAB priority 32768.
ACCESS Gi0/1 faces CORE; Gi0/2 faces LAB.
Gi0/1 config: spanning-tree guard root; state Root Inconsistent.
Gi0/2 config: no guard; intended designated boundary.
No other root source or physical failure is present.

questions.prompt: Which correction preserves the intended root boundary and restores the legitimate upstream path?
options: Move both root guard and loop guard to the lab-facing port as one combined policy.
Lower ACCESS’s priority below CORE so its root-facing uplink no longer receives superior information.
Remove root guard from the CORE-facing uplink and place it on the designated LAB-facing boundary.
Disable spanning tree on the uplink and leave both guards in their current places.
questions.explanation: The topology requires ACCESS to learn CORE’s superior information upstream. Root guard was placed on that legitimate path. Put the boundary policy toward LAB and, where supported and intended, use loop guard on the root/alternate uplink instead.

whyWrong.0: The guards cannot coexist on one interface and express different role expectations.
whyWrong.1: Making ACCESS the root violates the stated design instead of correcting guard placement.
whyWrong.3: Disabling the control protocol is not a valid repair of the policy boundary.

exhibit.title: Supplied protection evidence
exhibit.text:
Port policy: access host edge, interface BPDU guard enabled.
Recovery: bpduguard Enabled; interval 60 seconds.
Observed sequence repeated twice: recovery attempts re-enable Fa0/5; a new received-BPDU log appears; Fa0/5 becomes err-disabled again.
Cable audit: a BPDU-sending switch remains attached.

questions.prompt: Which interpretation explains the repeated outage without removing the intended host-port protection?
options: Timed recovery is disabled because the interval is shorter than the default 300 seconds.
Timed recovery is working, but the continuing BPDU source immediately violates the policy again.
Root guard is moving the root bridge at each retry, causing the host’s periodic loss.
The first successful retry proves the BPDU source is gone and later events are stale.
questions.explanation: The cause is enabled and the observed re-enable followed by a fresh BPDU-guard event matches repeated retries. Correct the attached BPDU source before another recovery; a timer does not repair the connection.

whyWrong.0: The cause is explicitly enabled; a supported 60-second interval is valid.
whyWrong.2: The event names BPDU guard, not root guard or a root election.
whyWrong.3: Each new event is fresh evidence that the source persists after the retry.

exhibit.title: Supplied protection evidence
exhibit.text:
Gi0/1: root-facing point-to-point port; BPDUs received before the incident; physical connected; VLAN 10 Loop Inconsistent.
Fa0/8: host port; physical status err-disabled; log names bpduguard.
No automatic errdisable recovery configured.

questions.prompt: Which pair of next actions is justified by these two independent incidents? Choose two.
options: Remove Fa0/8’s BPDU source, then recover that err-disabled interface.
Lower the root priority to resolve both incidents without changing either connection.
Bounce Gi0/1 repeatedly so it forwards without receiving new BPDUs.
Treat both ports as physically disconnected and replace both cables immediately.
Inspect BPDU delivery/filtering toward Gi0/1 while retaining its loop guard.
questions.explanation: Gi0/1’s prior reception and loop inconsistency point to missing expected control information, whose source must be investigated. Fa0/8’s named guard cause requires correction of an unexpected BPDU source and errdisable recovery. The states need different responses.

whyWrong.1: Changing root priority addresses neither the unexpected host BPDU nor missing expected delivery.
whyWrong.2: A reset does not restore missing BPDU delivery and can conceal the protective symptom.
whyWrong.3: One interface stays connected and the other is deliberately disabled; the evidence does not prove two cable failures.

cards.front: What does PortFast change on a genuine edge port?
cards.back: It permits immediate forwarding and avoids topology-change generation from ordinary edge transitions; STP still runs.

cards.front: 2960-style interface command for PortFast on an access port?
cards.back: `spanning-tree portfast`. Use only where the port is a genuine end-device edge.

cards.front: PortFast command for a trunk to a genuine end device?
cards.back: `spanning-tree portfast trunk`; some IOS XE images use `spanning-tree portfast edge trunk`. Verify that the host cannot form a Layer 2 transit loop.

cards.front: Global PortFast command and its scope on 2960-style IOS?
cards.back: `spanning-tree portfast default` applies to operationally nontrunking ports; a trunk is not covered by that default.

cards.front: Does PortFast disable STP or permanently guarantee edge status?
cards.back: No. BPDUs are still processed; with PortFast alone a received BPDU removes operational edge status. The configured command can remain.

cards.front: BPDU guard: trigger and conventional Catalyst result?
cards.back: Any received BPDU, not just a superior one, causes interface errdisable and stops traffic on the port.

cards.front: Interface versus global BPDU-guard scope?
cards.back: `spanning-tree bpduguard enable`: the interface, independently of PortFast. `spanning-tree portfast bpduguard default`: operational PortFast ports.

cards.front: Safe recovery after BPDU-guard errdisable?
cards.back: Remove/correct the BPDU source, then `shutdown` / `no shutdown`, or use an explicitly enabled recovery policy. Verify traffic and roles afterward.

cards.front: Does the default 300-second errdisable interval enable recovery?
cards.back: No. Enable recovery for the specific cause separately; the interval sets retry timing. A retry does not remove an attached BPDU source.

cards.front: Which log evidence distinguishes BPDU guard from other errdisable causes?
cards.back: Look for the affected interface and the `bpduguard` cause, such as `BLOCK_BPDUGUARD` or an `ERR_DISABLE` line naming bpduguard.

cards.front: Root guard: what triggers it and what state results?
cards.back: Superior BPDU information received at the protected boundary creates root inconsistency for the affected STP instance.

cards.front: Where should root guard be placed?
cards.back: On a designated boundary toward a switch through which the root must not be learned; not on the legitimate root-facing uplink.

cards.front: How does root inconsistency recover?
cards.back: Automatically after superior information ceases and STP permits normal forwarding; correct the source rather than removing the guard to hide it.

cards.front: Loop guard: what triggers it and what state results?
cards.back: Expected BPDUs expire on an applicable root or alternate port, causing loop inconsistency. It clears when the required BPDU information resumes.

cards.front: What is the operational scope of loop guard?
cards.back: Applicable point-to-point root/alternate ports with received information to monitor; not ordinary host edges or shared segments.

cards.front: Root guard versus BPDU guard?
cards.back: Root guard reacts to superior information and blocks the affected instance; BPDU guard reacts to any BPDU and conventionally err-disables the port.

cards.front: Can root guard and loop guard operate on one interface together?
cards.back: No. Their designated versus root/alternate expectations differ, and IOS treats them as mutually exclusive.

cards.front: What does *ROOT_Inc in a Rapid PVST+ port row mean?
cards.back: Root inconsistency: a superior BPDU was rejected at a guarded boundary. It is not proof that the physical port is err-disabled.

cards.front: BPDU filter: interface form versus global PortFast form?
cards.back: Interface filtering suppresses BPDUs independently. Global PortFast filtering withdraws filtering/operational edge status on received BPDUs. Filter is explicit v1.1 context.

cards.front: Which command lists STP inconsistent interfaces and affected VLANs?
cards.back: show spanning-tree inconsistentports. Use interface status and the cause-specific log separately for an err-disabled port.

commands.task: On 2960-style IOS, make this genuine end-device access port a PortFast edge.
commands.note: STP remains active. IOS XE may use the explicit edge keyword.

commands.task: Enable PortFast on this trunk to a verified end device with no Layer 2 transit path.
commands.note: A trunk toward another transit switch must not be treated as an edge.

commands.task: Enable the global PortFast default for nontrunking ports.
commands.note: Check exceptions and actual operational trunk state.

commands.task: Configure this interface to err-disable when any BPDU is received, independently of PortFast.
commands.note: Interface scope differs from the global PortFast default.

commands.task: Enable BPDU guard by default on operational PortFast ports.
commands.note: The global default alone does not protect every non-PortFast trunk.

commands.task: Enable automatic errdisable recovery attempts for the BPDU-guard cause.
commands.note: Correct the BPDU source first; a recovery attempt can otherwise trigger another violation.

commands.task: Protect this designated boundary against superior root information from downstream.
commands.note: Do not apply this to the legitimate root-facing uplink.

commands.task: Enable loop guard on this point-to-point uplink expected to receive BPDUs.
commands.note: It cannot operate together with root guard on the same interface.

commands.task: Display STP inconsistent interfaces and their affected instances.
commands.note: Root/loop inconsistency belongs here; use interface status and logs for BPDU-guard errdisable.

commands.task: Display the STP mode and global PortFast and guard/filter defaults.
commands.note: Confirm individual operational ports separately; configured global defaults do not imply every port inherits them.

commands.task: Inspect enabled errdisable recovery causes and their interval before assuming automatic recovery.
commands.note: The cause and interval are separate evidence; neither proves the underlying violation is corrected.

tickets.title: A conference-room port fails again after every reset
tickets.scenario: ASW3 Fa0/12 is a VLAN 30 host port covered by PortFast and BPDU-guard defaults. A desktop switch was recently added under the conference table. The help desk resets Fa0/12, but the room loses connectivity again shortly afterward. These are representative diagnosis exhibits.

exhibits.title: ASW3# show interfaces status — excerpt
exhibits.text: Fa0/12    Conference room     err-disabled 30           auto   auto 10/100BaseTX

exhibits.title: ASW3 log excerpt
exhibits.text:
%SPANTREE-2-BLOCK_BPDUGUARD: Received BPDU on port FastEthernet0/12 with BPDU Guard enabled. Disabling port.
%PM-4-ERR_DISABLE: bpduguard error detected on Fa0/12, putting Fa0/12 in err-disable state

exhibits.title: ASW3# show errdisable recovery — excerpt
exhibits.text:
bpduguard                     Disabled
Timer interval: 300 seconds

tickets.question: What explains the repeated failure after each manual reset?
options: The 300-second interval is too long for a normal Rapid PVST+ handshake.
The attached desktop switch continues supplying the BPDUs that trigger the guard.
The port is an alternate that should remain blocked until the root switch fails.
The absence of automatic recovery itself creates new BPDU-guard violations.
tickets.explanation: The log proves BPDU-guard reception on the same interface that becomes err-disabled. Resetting the interface while the BPDU source remains attached simply exposes it to another violation. Disabled automatic recovery explains why it stays down afterward, not why it repeatedly fails.
tickets.fix:
Remove the unexpected switch and reconnect the authorized end device before recovery.
```ios ASW3
ASW3# configure terminal
ASW3(config)# interface fastethernet0/12
ASW3(config-if)# shutdown
ASW3(config-if)# no shutdown
ASW3(config-if)# end
ASW3# show interfaces status
ASW3# show logging
```
Retest host connectivity and confirm no new bpduguard event. If more ports are required, design an approved interswitch connection with its intended VLAN and STP policy instead of leaving a transit bridge on a protected host edge.

tickets.title: Only one VLAN fails behind the new lab switch
tickets.scenario: LAB1 connects through DSW1 Gi1/0/10, a trunk for VLANs 10 and 20. CORE is the intended VLAN 10 root at configurable priority 24576. LAB1 copied a priority-zero setting for VLAN 10 but uses defaults in VLAN 20. VLAN 20 works; VLAN 10 behind LAB1 fails. These are representative excerpts.

exhibits.title: DSW1# show spanning-tree inconsistentports — excerpt
exhibits.text: VLAN0010             GigabitEthernet1/0/10       Root Inconsistent

exhibits.title: LAB1 running configuration excerpt
exhibits.text:
spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst
spanning-tree vlan 10 priority 0

exhibits.title: DSW1 interface configuration excerpt
exhibits.text:
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/10
 switchport mode trunk
 switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20
 spanning-tree guard root

tickets.question: What is the cause of the VLAN 10 outage?
options: The allowed-VLAN list excludes VLAN 10 and therefore disables only that instance.
BPDU guard err-disabled the trunk after LAB1 sent any spanning-tree control frame.
LAB1 supplies superior root information, triggering root guard for VLAN 10.
Loop guard detected that LAB1 has stopped transmitting expected BPDUs.
tickets.explanation: The displayed root inconsistency and interface root-guard configuration identify the mechanism. LAB1's priority zero is lower than CORE's stated 24576, so the boundary blocks VLAN 10 rather than accept its claim. The differing VLAN 20 result is consistent with separate Rapid PVST+ instances.
tickets.fix:
Restore the intended downstream priority on LAB1; preserve the boundary protection.
```ios LAB1
LAB1# configure terminal
LAB1(config)# spanning-tree vlan 10 priority 32768
LAB1(config)# end
LAB1# show spanning-tree vlan 10
```
Then inspect `show spanning-tree inconsistentports` on DSW1 and verify VLAN 10 traffic. Recovery is automatic after superior information ceases and STP permits forwarding; no exact twenty-second guarantee or manual bounce is required.

tickets.title: The uplink stays connected but STP reports loop inconsistency
tickets.scenario: SW3 Gi0/1 is its VLAN 10 root port toward SW1 in an isolated line topology. It had received BPDUs normally. After a configuration change on SW1, the physical link remains connected but SW3 reports loop inconsistency. Read the supplied configuration and state together; the exhibits are representative.

exhibits.title: SW3 observations
exhibits.text:
Gi0/1 physical status: connected
VLAN0010  GigabitEthernet0/1  Loop Inconsistent

exhibits.title: SW3 interface configuration excerpt
exhibits.text:
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 switchport mode trunk
 spanning-tree guard loop

exhibits.title: SW1 interface configuration excerpt
exhibits.text:
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 description To SW3
 switchport mode trunk
 spanning-tree bpdufilter enable

tickets.question: Which explanation is supported by both the observed state and the peer configuration?
options: A new superior root BID forced BPDU guard to disable the physical uplink.
The configured global recovery interval prevents an otherwise healthy root port from receiving BPDUs.
The physical receive strand is certainly broken despite the filter setting.
Peer interface filtering stopped expected BPDUs, and loop guard blocked the instance.
tickets.explanation: The peer explicitly suppresses BPDUs on the relevant interface. SW3's loop-guard configuration and loop-inconsistent condition fit loss of previously received information. The state alone would not prove a physical fault, and this exhibit supplies a configuration cause to correct first.
tickets.fix:
Remove the unintended filter at the source, then observe recovery without disabling loop guard.
```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# no spanning-tree bpdufilter
SW1(config-if)# end
```
On SW3, check `show spanning-tree inconsistentports` and `show spanning-tree interface gigabitethernet0/1 detail`. Expected BPDUs should resume, inconsistency should clear, and user traffic should recover. Save only the corrected policy.

chapters.title: Layer 2 security
chapters.subtitle: Control endpoint traffic with port security, DHCP snooping, ARP inspection, storm control and RA guard.

Cisco: Catalyst 9300 port security, IOS XE 17.12
Cisco: Catalyst 9300 DHCP and snooping, IOS XE 17.12

chapters.summary: Build an access-port policy from the traffic it must permit. Configure and verify MAC limits, DHCP and ARP trust boundaries, storm thresholds and IPv6 router-advertisement protection, then diagnose failures without disabling every control.

sections.body: VLANs decide which Layer 2 network a port belongs to. Spanning tree manages redundant paths. Neither establishes that a connected endpoint should advertise a router, supply DHCP leases or claim another host's address. This chapter adds controls for those behaviors and shows how to distinguish a blocked policy violation from a legitimate device affected by an incomplete configuration.

sections.title: Protect the access layer
sections.body:
An **access-layer security policy** identifies acceptable traffic at the point where endpoints enter the network. Apply each feature for a specific purpose. A port-security limit does not validate an ARP claim, and a DHCP snooping trust command does not configure IPv6 protection.

:::facts
- Port security is disabled initially. On the documented Catalyst platforms, enabling it gives a maximum of **1** secure MAC address and violation mode **shutdown**; secure-address aging is disabled at time **0**.
- DHCP snooping requires global enablement and a VLAN list. Interfaces are untrusted by default; legitimate server replies must enter through an appropriately trusted path.
- DAI uses a separate trust setting. On the documented Catalyst configuration, untrusted interfaces default to **15 ARP packets/s** over a **1-second** burst interval.
- Sticky addresses enter running configuration; saving is required for startup configuration to retain them.
- Storm thresholds and RA guard are explicit v2.0 configuration topics. v1.1 directly lists port security, DHCP snooping and DAI.
:::

A few protocol definitions are needed before their full chapters. **DHCPv4** leases an IPv4 address and supplies options such as a gateway. The initial Discover–Offer–Request–ACK exchange gives snooping an opportunity to observe a client's address assignment. The server's Offer, ACK and NAK messages must come from an authorized direction. **ARP** maps an IPv4 address to a local link-layer address; forged claims can alter a host's neighbor information. **IPv6 Router Advertisements (RAs)** supply router and link information, including whether a sender can serve as a default router. [IPv6 addressing](#/chapter/ipv6-addressing) and [DHCP](#/chapter/dhcp) develop these protocols fully.

| Problem | Relevant control | Important limit |
|---|---|---|
| Excessive or unexpected source MAC addresses | Port security | A MAC address is not proof of a person's identity |
| Unauthorized DHCP server replies | DHCP snooping trust | Trust is an ingress decision on each switch |
| Excessive DHCP requests | DHCP rate limiting and address checks | Rate limits reduce abuse; they do not guarantee pool availability |
| Forged IPv4-to-MAC claims | Dynamic ARP Inspection | Valid bindings or explicit policy must cover legitimate senders |
| Excess broadcast or multicast traffic | Storm control | Suppression does not remove the underlying loop or fault |
| Unauthorized IPv6 router advertisements | RA guard | It is not a general IPv6 firewall or all-purpose ND validation |

A MAC-flooding attempt can consume learning resources and increase unknown-unicast flooding, but it does not turn every switch into a hub or expose every conversation. Flooding remains subject to VLAN membership, forwarding state and other controls. Similarly, an unauthorized DHCP server or RA can provide misleading settings, but the exact effect depends on which information a host accepts and uses. Diagnose the observed traffic rather than treating every possible outcome as inevitable.

sections.title: Limit source MAC addresses with port security
sections.body:
**Port security** limits accepted source MAC addresses on a switchport. A violation can occur when an additional source appears after the secure-address limit is reached, or when an address secured on one interface appears on another secure interface in the same VLAN. This is distinct from ordinary destination-MAC forwarding.

Use a statically configured access port for the lab. The documented Catalyst implementation also supports secure trunk ports, but rejects dynamic switchport mode and does not support port security on EtherChannel interfaces. Check the platform restrictions before combining features.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 10
SW1(config-if)# switchport port-security
SW1(config-if)# switchport port-security maximum 1
SW1(config-if)# switchport port-security mac-address sticky
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show port-security interface fastethernet0/1
SW1# show port-security address
```

| Address type | How it is established | Persistence |
|---|---|---|
| Static secure | Administrator configures a MAC address | In running configuration; retained after restart when saved |
| Dynamic secure | Switch learns an address within the limit | Operational state; not retained as a configuration entry after restart |
| Sticky secure | Learned or explicitly configured as sticky | In running configuration; retained after restart when saved |

Enable sticky learning while the intended endpoint is connected, then inspect the learned entry. Learning the first sender does not authenticate that sender, and another device can impersonate an approved MAC address. Port security is a useful boundary, not a replacement for identity-based access control.

Choose the maximum from the expected secure address entries, including VLAN context. A documented phone-plus-PC arrangement may need two entries; other endpoint behavior or older phone/switch combinations can require a different allowance. Inspect the data and voice VLAN entries rather than assuming that counting physical devices always gives the exact limit. A trunk to a hypervisor can legitimately carry many source addresses.

Secure-address aging is separate from ordinary MAC-table aging. On the cited Catalyst platform, time `0` disables it; absolute aging uses elapsed time and inactivity aging uses idle time. Static secure entries require static aging to be enabled. Sticky secure aging is not supported on that platform. These differences explain why a normal MAC aging timer does not automatically remove a sticky configuration line.

sections.title: Choose a violation response and recover service
sections.body:
The three core modes share the same security limit but respond differently when a violation occurs.

| Mode | Violating traffic | Traffic from existing secure addresses | Evidence/state |
|---|---|---|---|
| `protect` | Dropped | Continues while the port remains operational | No violation notification or counter increment in this mode |
| `restrict` | Dropped | Continues while the port remains operational | Violation counter and logging/notification behavior |
| `shutdown` | Port stops forwarding | Stops on that interface | Err-disabled; port-security state commonly shows `Secure-shutdown` |

Notification generation does not prove that an external monitoring server received a message. The exact log text, counter behavior after repeated incidents and LED indication should not be assumed from a simplified example. The following is representative, abbreviated output after one shutdown violation:

```output SW1# show port-security interface fastethernet0/1
Port Security              : Enabled
Port Status                : Secure-shutdown  ← the port was disabled by a violation
Violation Mode             : Shutdown
Maximum MAC Addresses      : 1
Total MAC Addresses        : 1                ← the permitted secure-address capacity is occupied
Configured MAC Addresses   : 0
Sticky MAC Addresses       : 1
Security Violation Count   : 1                ← this example shows one incident
```

Identify the offending source and the intended policy before restoring service. If an unapproved device caused the fault, remove it. If an authorized endpoint needs a second source address, correct the policy deliberately. Bouncing a port without correcting the cause can produce another outage.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# shutdown
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces status
SW1# show port-security interface fastethernet0/1
```

Cause-specific automatic recovery can be enabled with `errdisable recovery cause psecure-violation`. The documented default recovery interval is 300 seconds, but recovery is not automatically enabled for every cause. `show errdisable recovery` distinguishes configured recovery from a timer actually pending. Recovery does not remove a conflicting secure address or repair the endpoint.

sections.title: Establish DHCP snooping trust and bindings
sections.body:
**DHCP snooping** inspects DHCP traffic in enabled VLANs. On an untrusted ingress port, server messages such as Offer, ACK and NAK are discarded. Client traffic is subject to the configured validation and rate checks. A trusted port allows the server-side traffic that the design expects to arrive there.

Trace the server-to-client path on each switch. In the topology below, R1 is the only server, connected directly to SW1. SW1 trusts Gi0/1. SW2 trusts its uplink toward SW1. SW1 does **not** automatically trust its downlink toward SW2 merely because that link is a trunk; no authorized server resides behind SW2 in this design.

```diagram
{"type":"topology","title":"Trust follows the permitted server direction","caption":"Snooping trust is applied where authorized replies enter each switch: SW1 Gi0/1 and SW2 Gi0/1. The client-facing downlink on SW1 is not automatically trusted.","nodes":[{"id":"R","kind":"router","label":"R1 · DHCP","x":1,"y":1},{"id":"S1","kind":"switch","label":"SW1","x":5,"y":1},{"id":"S2","kind":"switch","label":"SW2","x":9,"y":1},{"id":"A","kind":"pc","label":"PC-A","x":5,"y":5},{"id":"B","kind":"pc","label":"PC-B","x":9,"y":5}],"links":[{"from":"R","to":"S1","toLabel":"Gi0/1 trusted"},{"from":"S1","to":"S2","fromLabel":"Gi0/2 untrusted","toLabel":"Gi0/1 trusted"},{"from":"S1","to":"A","fromLabel":"Fa0/1 untrusted"},{"from":"S2","to":"B","fromLabel":"Fa0/1 untrusted"}]}
```

This example disables Option 82 insertion on both switches to keep the client-facing interswitch path simple. A deployment that retains Option 82 must also define how upstream devices handle relay information received on an untrusted port. Do not bypass the intended security boundary by trusting every downlink just to make a request pass.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# ip dhcp snooping
SW1(config)# ip dhcp snooping vlan 10
SW1(config)# no ip dhcp snooping information option
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# ip dhcp snooping trust
SW1(config-if)# exit
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# ip dhcp snooping limit rate 15
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show ip dhcp snooping
SW1# show ip dhcp snooping binding
```

The rate of 15 DHCP packets/s is a lab choice, not the default for every access port. Exceeding a configured snooping rate limit can err-disable the interface. An uplink aggregates many clients, so its traffic allowance cannot be copied blindly from a single-PC port. MAC-to-`chaddr` validation can reject mismatched client identity fields; a sender using consistent spoofed values is not necessarily detected by that check alone.

The binding table records learned client IP/MAC information, VLAN, interface and lease information. Enable snooping before obtaining the lab leases. An existing lease is not proof that the switch observed the exchange that created it. A reload can also lose dynamic bindings unless a supported database-persistence mechanism has been configured and verified; saving running configuration alone does not save every operational lease binding.

**Option 82** carries relay-agent information, such as circuit identification. The DHCP `giaddr` field is the relay gateway address used in the ordinary relay design to identify the client network. Some IOS server/relay configurations reject Option 82 with a zero `giaddr` unless their relay-information trust policy permits it. Disabling insertion is an explicit choice in this isolated lab. In a real design, inspect server/relay evidence before changing that policy; snooping trust, relay-information trust and IP routing are separate settings.

sections.title: Validate ARP claims with DAI
sections.body:
:::trap
DHCP snooping trust and DAI trust are separate settings. A correct DHCP reply path does not automatically permit the ARP traffic needed for a working LAN.
:::

**Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI)** checks ARP messages entering untrusted ports in the configured VLANs. DHCP snooping supplies the usual dynamic IP-to-MAC bindings. ARP ACLs can supply policy for static-addressed senders. A DAI-trusted port bypasses these inspections, so assign trust only where the upstream source of ARP claims is controlled.

DHCP trust and DAI trust are independent. A statically addressed router usually has no DHCP-client binding, so this lab deliberately trusts its controlled uplink for DAI. A different design could keep that port inspected and provide suitable ARP policy. An arbitrary switch-to-switch link is not automatically safe to trust.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# ip arp inspection trust
SW1(config-if)# exit
SW1(config)# ip arp inspection vlan 10
SW1(config)# end
SW1# show ip arp inspection interfaces
SW1# show ip arp inspection vlan 10
SW1# show ip arp inspection statistics vlan 10
```

A static printer illustrates a common dependency. Excluding `10.1.10.20` from the DHCP pool prevents its dynamic allocation; it does not create a snooping binding. If the approved printer MAC is `000c.2911.7a3e`, the following ARP ACL permits that pairing while leaving other senders eligible for DHCP-binding validation:

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# arp access-list STATIC-HOSTS
SW1(config-arp-nacl)# permit ip host 10.1.10.20 mac host 000c.2911.7a3e
SW1(config-arp-nacl)# exit
SW1(config)# ip arp inspection filter STATIC-HOSTS vlan 10
SW1(config)# end
```

Without the `static` filter keyword, an implicit ACL nonmatch can fall through to the DHCP binding check; an explicit deny still denies. Adding `static` makes the ACL's implicit deny final and prevents that fallback. It is not a keyword required merely because the printer has a static address.

Optional `ip arp inspection validate src-mac dst-mac ip` adds header/payload checks: source-MAC consistency in requests and replies, destination-MAC consistency in replies, and invalid IP-value checks. A new validate command replaces the selected check set. Understand its effect on legitimate address probes before enabling it indiscriminately.

The cited default untrusted DAI allowance is 15 packets/s with a one-second burst interval; excess can err-disable the port with cause `arp-inspection`. That is independent of the DHCP-packet rate. A legitimate host or aggregated link can exceed an unsuitable ARP limit. A counter increase establishes a rejection category, not the sender's intent.

sections.title: Limit traffic storms
sections.body:
**Storm control** suppresses a selected class of incoming traffic when its configured threshold is reached. Broadcast, multicast and unicast support, accounting and hardware reaction vary by platform. The core example uses broadcast thresholds, avoiding assumptions about a platform's separate known/unknown-unicast implementation.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/2
SW1(config-if)# storm-control broadcast level 1.00 0.50
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show storm-control fastethernet0/2 broadcast
```

The first percentage is the rising suppression threshold; the second is the falling threshold below which forwarding resumes. The falling value cannot exceed the rising value. If omitted, it is set to the rising value in the documented configuration. Thresholds can also use `level bps` or `level pps` on supported platforms. One percent means a nominal 1 Mb/s on a 100 Mb/s port and 10 Mb/s on a 1 Gb/s port; it is not a count of one packet per hundred packets.

Default behavior filters traffic without a configured shutdown or trap action. `storm-control action shutdown` err-disables the interface; `storm-control action trap` requests notification. Suppression can discard the affected traffic class during an interval, not simply trim a precise number of excess bytes. The cited Catalyst documentation describes one-second measurements and also platform-specific hardware policing, so avoid promising an exact universal reaction time.

Read the traffic type as well as `Forwarding` or `Blocking` in the output. A storm-control blocking state is not an STP port role. Do not create a physical loop to test the feature: examine configured limits, use supplied output, or use a controlled traffic source in an isolated supported lab. Find and correct the traffic source or loop after the immediate symptom is contained.

sections.title: Control IPv6 router advertisements
sections.body:
**RA guard** filters Router Advertisements and, on the cited Catalyst implementation, router Redirect messages according to an ingress policy. A host-role policy rejects router messages from endpoint ports. A router-role policy permits the expected router role, subject to any further configured checks. It does not prove the router itself is correctly configured.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# ipv6 nd raguard policy HOSTS
SW1(config-nd-raguard)# device-role host
SW1(config-nd-raguard)# exit
SW1(config)# ipv6 nd raguard policy ROUTERS
SW1(config-nd-raguard)# device-role router
SW1(config-nd-raguard)# exit
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet1/0/1
SW1(config-if)# ipv6 nd raguard attach-policy HOSTS
SW1(config-if)# exit
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet1/0/24
SW1(config-if)# ipv6 nd raguard attach-policy ROUTERS
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show ipv6 nd raguard policy HOSTS
SW1# show ipv6 nd raguard policy ROUTERS
```

These interface names belong to the Catalyst 9300 reference path, not the Packet Tracer 2960. Defining a policy alone does not attach it. On the documented First Hop Security implementation, configure the router-facing role as well as host-facing roles; Router Solicitation forwarding can depend on that classification. A policy that treats the legitimate router as a host can disrupt router discovery while IPv4 still works.

Use a supported platform for the v2.0 configuration exercise. If the simulator does not expose RA guard, complete the supplied policy/evidence worksheet and record that practical configuration still needs a supported environment. Do not substitute an IPv4 ACL or claim that a missing simulator command demonstrates how hardware behaves. Fragment/extension-header handling and other IPv6 First Hop Security features require their own platform documentation; they are not developed here.

sections.title: Verify and troubleshoot
sections.body:
Work from the failing service toward the responsible feature. Keep a valid baseline and change one policy at a time.

| Observation | Check next | Avoid concluding |
|---|---|---|
| Interface is err-disabled | Status, logs, secure addresses and enabled recovery causes | That every outage is port security |
| Client cannot obtain a lease | VLAN, operational snooping list, server-facing trust, rate and Option 82 policy | That an empty binding table identifies one unique fault |
| Client has an address but cannot resolve its gateway | Correct binding, DAI policy/trust and rejection counters | That DHCP success proves ARP is permitted |
| Static sender fails after DAI enablement | Its approved IP/MAC policy and ACL fallback behavior | That a DHCP exclusion supplies an ARP binding |
| Bursts of traffic disappear | Storm type, threshold and filtering state | That STP chose an alternate port |
| IPv4 works but IPv6 router discovery fails | RA policy attachment, host/router roles and received RA evidence | That all neighbor discovery is blocked |

Configuration, operational state and observed packets answer different questions. A policy in running configuration proves intent. A binding or counter provides current state. Successful service tests provide evidence for the tested endpoints and moment. Together they support a diagnosis without requiring you to disable every protection.

sections.title: Exam focus
sections.body:
- Configure and verify static access-port security, address limits, sticky learning and the three violation modes.
- Restore an err-disabled port after correcting the cause; distinguish manual recovery from enabled automatic recovery.
- Enable DHCP snooping globally and on the correct VLAN, trace ingress trust, and read bindings and rate policy.
- Explain why trusted uplinks, Option 82 and DHCP relay trust are different decisions.
- Configure DAI, distinguish its trust from DHCP trust, and admit a static sender with a precise ARP ACL.
- For v2.0, configure storm thresholds/actions and attach host/router RA guard policies on supported interfaces.
- Interpret evidence with its scope. A MAC address, a counter or one successful ping is not a complete security assessment.

lab.title: Verify an access-port security policy
devices: RA guard extension: supported Catalyst switch, two IPv6 routers and test PC
lab.intro:
Practice revised September 2026. If you completed an earlier version, repeat the revised exercise and update its checkmarks.

Build a working IPv4 LAN, apply one control at a time, and diagnose a controlled failure from its evidence. The final exercise covers IPv6 RA guard. Keep the exercises on an isolated lab network.

Record your Packet Tracer version and check the selected switch's command help. It implements a subset of IOS; DHCP snooping, DAI, ARP ACL and storm-control support vary by simulated device and version. If a required command is missing, use a supporting image or switch, or complete that step as an interpretation exercise and record it as **not executed**. For v2.0, return to any unexecuted configuration objective on a supporting platform.

Use four separate study sessions if needed: **A, Steps 1–4: source-MAC policy**; **B, Steps 5–9: DHCP and ARP dependencies**; **C, Step 10: storm-policy interpretation**; **D, Steps 11–13: supported IPv6 RA guard or its worksheet**. Step 14 verifies and saves the results. DHCP server and IPv6 router setup are supplied supporting configuration; their full operation is taught in Chapters 24 and 19. Revisit these controls after those protocol chapters.
lab.topology:
| Connection | SW1 port | Endpoint addressing |
|---|---|---|
| R1 Gi0/0 | Gi0/1 | `10.1.10.1/24`, gateway and DHCP server |
| PC-A FastEthernet0 | Fa0/1 | DHCP |
| PC-B FastEthernet0 | Fa0/2 initially | DHCP; temporarily substitutes for PC-A |
| PRINTER FastEthernet0 | Fa0/3 | `10.1.10.20/24`, gateway `10.1.10.1` |

Use copper straight-through cables. All four switch ports are access ports in VLAN 10. R1 excludes `.1` through `.49`, keeping the static printer outside the allocation range. Record your actual leases and MAC addresses.

```diagram
{"type":"topology","title":"One controlled server path","caption":"Only Gi0/1 receives legitimate DHCP server replies on SW1.","nodes":[{"id":"R1","kind":"router","label":"R1","sub":"10.1.10.1/24","x":6,"y":0.5},{"id":"SW1","kind":"switch","label":"SW1","sub":"VLAN 10","x":6,"y":3,"highlight":true},{"id":"A","kind":"pc","label":"PC-A","sub":"DHCP","x":2,"y":5.5},{"id":"B","kind":"pc","label":"PC-B","sub":"DHCP","x":6,"y":5.5},{"id":"P","kind":"printer","label":"PRINTER","sub":"10.1.10.20/24","x":10,"y":5.5}],"links":[{"from":"R1","to":"SW1","fromLabel":"Gi0/0","toLabel":"Gi0/1","accent":true},{"from":"A","to":"SW1","toLabel":"Fa0/1"},{"from":"B","to":"SW1","toLabel":"Fa0/2"},{"from":"P","to":"SW1","toLabel":"Fa0/3"}]}
```

steps.title: Module A — establish a working LAN
steps.body:
Set the printer's address and gateway in its Config tab. Configure R1 and SW1:

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.1.10.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# ip dhcp excluded-address 10.1.10.1 10.1.10.49
R1(config)# ip dhcp pool USERS
R1(dhcp-config)# network 10.1.10.0 255.255.255.0
R1(dhcp-config)# default-router 10.1.10.1
R1(dhcp-config)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
```

```ios SW1
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW1
SW1(config)# vlan 10
SW1(config-vlan)# name USERS
SW1(config-vlan)# exit
SW1(config)# interface range fastethernet0/1 - 3
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport access vlan 10
SW1(config-if-range)# exit
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 10
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show vlan brief
```

On each PC select Desktop → IP Configuration → DHCP. Record `ipconfig /all`, then ping `10.1.10.1` and `10.1.10.20`. Wait for ports to forward and repeat initial pings if ARP resolution consumed an attempt. Record the printer's MAC from its interface information.

:::expected
R1 Gi0/0 is up/up and the switch ports belong to VLAN 10. The PCs have unique addresses in the pool and gateway `10.1.10.1`; both reach the gateway and printer. Correct this baseline before continuing.
:::

steps.title: Module A — learn the authorized MAC
steps.body:
Predict which MAC should occupy the single entry and whether that learned value will already be in startup configuration. Leave only PC-A attached to Fa0/1. Enable sticky learning and send another PC-A ping.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport port-security
SW1(config-if)# switchport port-security mac-address sticky
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show port-security interface fastethernet0/1
SW1# show port-security address
SW1# show running-config interface fastethernet0/1
```
