If the image rejects the interface-specific running-config command, find the block in `show running-config`. Compare the learned address with PC-A's actual MAC before saving.

:::expected
Fa0/1 is secure-up with maximum 1, shutdown violation mode and PC-A's sticky entry in running configuration. Its presence there does not establish that startup configuration contains it.
:::

steps.title: Module A — trigger a MAC-limit violation
steps.body:
Disconnect PC-B from Fa0/2 and PC-A from Fa0/1. Connect PC-B to Fa0/1 and generate traffic. Keep PC-A's sticky entry and the existing maximum. Inspect `show port-security interface fastethernet0/1` and `show interfaces status`.

:::expected
PC-B presents a different source MAC while the one permitted entry belongs to PC-A. Shutdown mode error-disables the port; the security display indicates secure-shutdown and a violation. The whole port stops forwarding. If it remains up, verify the actual MACs and that PC-B transmitted.
:::

steps.title: Module A — recover the authorized endpoint
steps.body:
Restore PC-A to Fa0/1 and PC-B to Fa0/2, then reset the affected port:

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# shutdown
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show port-security interface fastethernet0/1
```

Ping the gateway from PC-A. Keep maximum 1 because that is the intended policy here. Automatic error recovery cannot correct an unauthorized device that remains attached.

:::expected
Fa0/1 returns to secure-up and PC-A regains service. Historical violation counters may remain; verify current state and a fresh traffic test.
:::

steps.title: Module B — establish snooping and fresh bindings
steps.body:
Before configuration, trace R1’s Offer/ACK back to each client and mark the ingress at SW1. Predict which trust setting admits those server messages and why the client ports do not need it.

This simple design does not use Option 82 for server policy. Disable its insertion explicitly and trust the interface receiving R1's replies. Client ports remain untrusted.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# ip dhcp snooping
SW1(config)# ip dhcp snooping vlan 10
SW1(config)# no ip dhcp snooping information option
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# ip dhcp snooping trust
SW1(config-if)# exit
SW1(config)# interface range fastethernet0/1 - 2
SW1(config-if-range)# ip dhcp snooping limit rate 15
SW1(config-if-range)# end
SW1# show ip dhcp snooping
```

Run `ipconfig /release` and `ipconfig /renew` on each PC. If unavailable, use its IP Configuration controls to request a fresh lease. Compare `show ip dhcp snooping binding` on SW1 with `show ip dhcp binding` on R1. The server lease table and switch binding table are separate records.

:::expected
Snooping covers VLAN 10, Gi0/1 is trusted, and each PC has a binding with its actual IP, MAC, VLAN and access port. No dynamic binding is expected for the static printer. A lease acquired before snooping was enabled does not establish a switch binding.

If the feature is unavailable, use this separate authored binding worksheet: PC-A 10.1.10.50 / 00aa.0000.0001, VLAN 10, Fa0/1; PC-B 10.1.10.51 / 00bb.0000.0002, VLAN 10, Fa0/2. R1 lists those leases and the switch learned matching entries after the exchanges. Identify the fields needed to compare an ARP sender claim; do not substitute these illustrative identities for actual devices.
:::

steps.title: Module B — observe a missing server-trust fault
steps.body:
```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# no ip dhcp snooping trust
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show ip dhcp snooping
```

Release PC-B's lease and request a new one. Where supported, inspect snooping statistics or use Simulation mode filtered to DHCP to follow R1's reply into SW1. Retaining an old lease does not test the new policy.

:::expected
A fresh DHCP exchange cannot complete through the now-untrusted server ingress, even though R1's interface and pool can be operational. The configuration and reply-path evidence identify the cause; a failed lease alone would not.
:::

steps.title: Module B — restore the permitted reply path
steps.body:
```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# ip dhcp snooping trust
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show ip dhcp snooping
```

Renew PC-B's lease, inspect its binding and ping the gateway. Do not make every port trusted as a workaround.

:::expected
The fresh lease completes and PC-B's binding names Fa0/2 and VLAN 10. Only Gi0/1 has server trust.
:::

steps.title: Module B — inspect ARP and observe the static-host failure
steps.body:
Predict which of the two DHCP clients, static router and static printer will have a DHCP-client binding. Name the separate DAI policy that covers each legitimate source, then confirm both PC bindings first. Trust ARP from the controlled router connection separately, then enable inspection.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# ip arp inspection trust
SW1(config-if)# exit
SW1(config)# ip arp inspection vlan 10
SW1(config)# end
SW1# show ip arp inspection vlan 10
SW1# show ip arp inspection interfaces
SW1# show ip arp inspection statistics vlan 10
```

Ping the gateway from both DHCP clients. For a fresh printer ARP exchange, clear PC-B's printer entry with `arp -d 10.1.10.20` if supported, or restart only PC-B and renew its lease. Ping the printer and compare DAI counters before and after. Existing ARP caches can temporarily conceal the missing binding.

:::expected
The DHCP clients' valid ARP claims pass. The printer has no snooping binding, so its fresh ARP claim entering Fa0/3 is rejected by the binding check. A legitimate static host needs an explicit exception; this result does not establish malicious activity.
:::

steps.title: Module B — permit the verified printer pair
steps.body:
Substitute the printer's actual MAC recorded in Step 1. The following example assumes `000c.2911.7a3e`.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# arp access-list STATIC-HOSTS
SW1(config-arp-nacl)# permit ip host 10.1.10.20 mac host 000c.2911.7a3e
SW1(config-arp-nacl)# exit
SW1(config)# ip arp inspection filter STATIC-HOSTS vlan 10
SW1(config)# end
SW1# show arp access-list STATIC-HOSTS
SW1# show ip arp inspection vlan 10
SW1# show ip arp inspection statistics vlan 10
```

Repeat a fresh printer ping and the client gateway tests. Omitting `static` allows ACL nonmatches to continue to DHCP-binding validation. Adding it would make the ACL's implicit denial final, blocking unlisted DHCP clients.

:::expected
The verified printer pair passes and DHCP clients still work. Fa0/3 remains untrusted: the ACL authorizes a specific claim instead of bypassing inspection on the entire port.
:::

steps.title: Module C — interpret storm-control thresholds
steps.body:
```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/2
SW1(config-if)# storm-control broadcast level 1.00 0.50
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show storm-control fastethernet0/2 broadcast
```

Record the configured thresholds. Before opening the worksheet answer, predict the suppression state when broadcast utilization reaches 3.2%, then falls to 0.7%, then to 0.3%. Also calculate the nominal 1% rate on this 100 Mb/s port. These are supplied observations, not captured results; do not create a switching loop.

:::expected
The configured policy should display rising 1.00% and falling 0.50%. Inspect the actual port state and repeat a low-volume client test; do not claim a live threshold event when none was generated.
:::

:::solution
Suppression is active at 3.2% and remains active at 0.7%, which is above the falling 0.50% threshold. It ends below that threshold at 0.3%. One percent of 100 Mb/s is a nominal 1 Mb/s; hardware measurement can differ. Without a shutdown action, the default filters the selected traffic type rather than err-disabling the whole interface.
:::

steps.title: Module D — prepare a separate IPv6 test baseline
steps.body:
Use a separate isolated LAN, two fresh IPv6-capable IOS routers with Gi0/0 (2911 hardware or a verified equivalent), a Windows PC with a capture-capable Ethernet adapter, and a supporting switch; the command reference is Catalyst 9300 with IOS XE 17.12. Connect a test PC to SW-H Gi1/0/1, legitimate R1 Gi0/0 to Gi1/0/24, and test R2 Gi0/0 to Gi1/0/4. Use compatible copper media and substitute verified interface names for your hardware. All three switch ports use access VLAN 10.

Before configuring the feature, run `show version` and `show sdm prefer` on SW-H. Confirm a supported image and an active resource template that accommodates IPv6; the cited 9300 Access template supports IPv6 entries. If this isolated 9300 needs that template selected, enter `sdm prefer access` in global configuration, return to EXEC, save with `copy running-config startup-config`, and `reload` before starting the exercise. Verify the active template after restart. A pending template change is not yet active, and template names on other Catalyst families differ. Do not apply a 2960-specific SDM command to the 9300 by assumption.

The supplied router setup enables advertisements on this LAN. Explicit link-local addresses identify their sources. Chapter 19 explains IPv6 addressing and neighbor discovery in detail.

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# ipv6 unicast-routing
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address fe80::1 link-local
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:16:10::1/64
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
```

```ios R2
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R2
R2(config)# ipv6 unicast-routing
R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R2(config-if)# ipv6 address fe80::2 link-local
R2(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:16:99::1/64
R2(config-if)# shutdown
R2(config-if)# end
```

```ios SW-H
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW-H
SW-H(config)# vlan 10
SW-H(config-vlan)# exit
SW-H(config)# interface range gigabitethernet1/0/1, gigabitethernet1/0/4, gigabitethernet1/0/24
SW-H(config-if-range)# switchport mode access
SW-H(config-if-range)# switchport access vlan 10
SW-H(config-if-range)# exit
SW-H(config)# ipv6 nd raguard policy ENDPOINTS
SW-H(config-nd-raguard)# device-role host
SW-H(config-nd-raguard)# exit
SW-H(config)# ipv6 nd raguard policy ROUTERS
SW-H(config-nd-raguard)# device-role router
SW-H(config-nd-raguard)# exit
SW-H(config)# interface range gigabitethernet1/0/1, gigabitethernet1/0/4
SW-H(config-if-range)# ipv6 nd raguard attach-policy ENDPOINTS
SW-H(config-if-range)# exit
SW-H(config)# interface gigabitethernet1/0/24
SW-H(config-if)# ipv6 nd raguard attach-policy ROUTERS
SW-H(config-if)# end
SW-H# show ipv6 nd raguard policy ENDPOINTS
SW-H# show ipv6 nd raguard policy ROUTERS
SW-H# show running-config interface gigabitethernet1/0/4
```

On the Windows test PC, use the lab adapter’s IPv6 properties to obtain an address and DNS information automatically. This isolated exercise does not require DNS or Internet access. Use a PC with Wireshark installed and permission to capture on the connected Ethernet adapter; its current installer and capture prerequisites are documented by [Wireshark](https://www.wireshark.org/docs/wsug_html_chunked/ChapterIntroduction.html). Record the adapter name so an unrelated Wi-Fi capture is not mistaken for this LAN.

Start a capture on that adapter and apply display filter `icmpv6.type == 134`. With R2 still shut, observe an RA from `fe80::1` and record PC addressing with `ipconfig /all`. Allow for the actual advertisement interval. Verify the two policy definitions and their attachments before the comparison.

:::expected
Fresh legitimate R1 RAs reach the test PC. R2 is still shut; its absence is not evidence of RA guard. The switch has ENDPOINTS on Gi1/0/1 and Gi1/0/4 and ROUTERS on Gi1/0/24. Record unsupported configuration or capture operations as unexecuted.

For the paper path use this labeled supplied baseline: R1 sends from fe80::1 into Gi1/0/24; its RA appears on the PC capture; R2 is administratively shut. Explain which policy/attachment permits the legitimate path. These are authored observations, not simulator measurements.
:::

steps.title: Module D — expose the test advertisement on a permitted comparison path
steps.body:
On supported isolated equipment only, predict the effect of removing ENDPOINTS from the R2 ingress while leaving R1’s policy unchanged. Then enable R2 and temporarily remove that one attachment. Leave the changed state in place long enough to record a fresh R2 advertisement.

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# end
```

```ios SW-H
SW-H# configure terminal
SW-H(config)# interface gigabitethernet1/0/4
SW-H(config-if)# no ipv6 nd raguard attach-policy ENDPOINTS
SW-H(config-if)# end
SW-H# show running-config interface gigabitethernet1/0/4
```

In the same adapter capture, find a fresh RA from fe80::2 and confirm fe80::1 still appears. Record multiple R2 arrivals and their observed intervals. Do not change cables, R2 addressing or VLAN membership between the permitted and guarded tests.

:::expected
R2’s fresh RA reaches the PC when the host-role attachment is absent. This establishes that the test sender and path work, rather than interpreting a negative capture from an inactive router. The PC may learn additional addressing/router information; its exact selection is not the pass criterion.

Paper fallback: supplied capture before protection shows RAs sourced from fe80::1 and fe80::2 arriving on the PC’s lab adapter. The configured interface Gi1/0/4 has no RA guard attachment. State why this is a useful positive control.
:::

steps.title: Module D — restore the boundary and compare fresh evidence
steps.body:
Before restoring the policy, write which RA source should remain visible and which should stop arriving. Keep R2 active for this comparison.

```ios SW-H
SW-H# configure terminal
SW-H(config)# interface gigabitethernet1/0/4
SW-H(config-if)# ipv6 nd raguard attach-policy ENDPOINTS
SW-H(config-if)# end
SW-H# show ipv6 nd raguard policy ENDPOINTS
SW-H# show running-config interface gigabitethernet1/0/4
```

Start a new capture on the same PC adapter and compare several of the R2 advertisement intervals observed in Step 12. Record continued fe80::1 reception and the absence of fresh fe80::2 RAs. If R2 timing changes or neither source is visible, investigate before declaring enforcement. Retained SLAAC addresses/default-router state may remain until advertised lifetimes expire.

:::expected
The restored host-role ingress blocks the test router’s fresh RAs while the legitimate router path continues. This controlled comparison supports the result for the tested traffic and platform; policy text or an old default-router entry alone would not.

Paper fallback: over the supplied repeated comparison, fe80::1 RAs continue, fe80::2 RAs cease, R2 continues sending, and the only change is restoring ENDPOINTS on its actual switch ingress. Explain the bounded conclusion and why immediately clearing all client addresses is unnecessary.
:::

steps.title: Save each verified checkpoint and clean up
steps.body:
Repeat fresh DHCP leases, gateway pings and static-printer communication in the IPv4 lab. Check port-security state, separate DHCP/DAI trust, actual bindings, DAI rejection evidence and the configured storm thresholds. If a feature was unavailable, leave that hands-on result pending rather than claiming its success.

On SW1 and R1 individually, enter `copy running-config startup-config` from privileged EXEC, accept the destination filename with Enter, and wait for completion. Save the Packet Tracer project as `16-ipv4-security-baseline.pkt`. Saving configuration preserves verified sticky entries present in it; it does not automatically persist the operational snooping database.

After the supported RA comparison is complete, stop its test source:

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R2(config-if)# shutdown
R2(config-if)# end
R2# show ipv6 interface brief
```

Verify the ENDPOINTS attachment remains on SW-H Gi1/0/4. Save each extension device separately, accepting its save prompt. Keep this topology isolated.

:::expected
Submit a checkpoint table with each feature’s intended ingress, expected accepted traffic, controlled rejected traffic, cause/state evidence, repair and fresh retest. Mark values as observed or supplied. Preserve the three IPv4 repairs separately: wrong MAC, missing DHCP server trust, and absent static-printer ARP policy. The RA record identifies permitted R1, permitted R2 control, restored R2 rejection, and final R2 shutdown.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
| Symptom | Check |
|---|---|
| PC-A immediately violates again | Correct endpoint, actual MAC and sticky entry; a reset cannot correct a mismatch |
| No fresh lease | VLAN, server reply path, pool and Option 82 policy; a self-assigned address alone does not identify the fault |
| DAI blocks a DHCP client | Current IP/MAC/VLAN/port binding and the relevant counters |
| Printer still blocked | Actual MAC, ACL permit, VLAN application and unintended final implicit denial |
| All ARP on a busy port stops | Error-disable reason and rate policy; individual validation drops differ from a rate-limit shutdown |
| RA policy exists but RAs pass | Attachment on the actual ingress port, role, VLAN path and whether these are fresh advertisements |
| Legitimate IPv6 setup is delayed | Router-facing role, solicitation forwarding and observed advertisements |
lab.challenge:
Use a copy of the restored IPv4 baseline. Add a second Printer-PT, PRINTER-2, to SW1 Fa0/4 using straight-through copper. Set `10.1.10.30/24` and gateway `10.1.10.1`; that address is already inside R1’s excluded range. Record its actual MAC.

Before opening the answer, write the additions needed to permit this verified static IP/MAC pair while keeping both DHCP clients validated by their snooping bindings. Keep the original printer working and leave all client/printer ports untrusted for DAI. Do not replace the existing ARP ACL or add the `static` application keyword. Predict why the DHCP exclusion alone is insufficient.

Verify fresh ARP/communication for both printers and the clients’ gateways. Record the actual added ACL line, binding evidence and test results. If your simulator cannot implement the ARP ACL, use the supplied answer as a configuration worksheet and record the practical check as pending.

Then complete a short paper variation: a new SW2 uplink Gi0/1 connects to SW1 Fa0/5 and serves only DHCP clients. Both switches snoop VLAN 10 and disable Option 82 insertion. Name the server-reply ingress that needs DHCP trust on each switch. Do not actually cable SW2 in the printer exercise.

:::solution
Configure the new endpoint port and add one permit under the existing ACL. Replace `0011.2233.0030` below with PRINTER-2’s recorded MAC; the illustrated MAC is not a measured value.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/4
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 10
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# exit
SW1(config)# arp access-list STATIC-HOSTS
SW1(config-arp-nacl)# permit ip host 10.1.10.30 mac host 0011.2233.0030
SW1(config-arp-nacl)# exit
SW1(config)# ip arp inspection filter STATIC-HOSTS vlan 10
SW1(config)# end
SW1# show arp access-list STATIC-HOSTS
SW1# show ip arp inspection vlan 10
SW1# show ip dhcp snooping binding
```

The original printer permit remains; the new exact pair is permitted. Implicit ACL nonmatches can still use DHCP bindings because the filter lacks `static`. The DHCP exclusion prevents allocation of .30 but does not authorize its ARP. Keep Fa0/4 untrusted.

From PC-B, test .20 and .30. Make the .30 test a fresh resolution by removing that specific ARP entry if supported or using a freshly restarted/released-and-renewed client; verify its new binding before testing. Inspect DAI counters across the test interval. Verify both client gateway pings, then save the separate challenge project.

For the SW2 paper variation, trust SW1 Gi0/1 where R1’s replies enter and SW2 Gi0/1 where upstream replies enter SW2. SW1 Fa0/5 receives client-side traffic, so it does not need server trust merely because it links to a switch. Disabling insertion on both switches avoids an undeclared upstream Option 82 acceptance requirement. DAI still needs its own trust/binding/static-host policy, and IPv6 RA guard requires separate roles and attachments.
:::

questions.prompt: Which mode discards violating frames and records violations while continuing to forward traffic from secure MAC addresses?
options: shutdown
disabled
protect
restrict
questions.explanation: Restrict preserves service for permitted addresses while dropping violating traffic and providing violation reporting.

whyWrong.0: Shutdown error-disables the port, affecting permitted traffic too.
whyWrong.1: Disabling port security removes this enforcement.
whyWrong.2: Protect drops violating traffic without restrict's counter and notification behavior.

questions.prompt: On the documented Catalyst default configuration, which two settings apply after port security is enabled? (Choose two.)
options: The maximum is one secure MAC
The aging interval is five minutes
Sticky learning is enabled
The violation mode is shutdown
The violation mode is restrict
questions.explanation: The documented defaults are maximum 1 and shutdown mode. Port security itself must be enabled; sticky learning and address aging are separate choices.

whyWrong.1: Default aging time is 0, meaning disabled.
whyWrong.2: Enabling port security does not enable sticky learning.
whyWrong.4: Restrict requires an explicit configuration.

questions.prompt: Which two statements correctly describe DAI? (Choose two.)
options: DAI authenticates the user who owns a MAC address
Every inter-switch trunk must bypass ARP inspection
An explicit ARP ACL can permit a verified static host
DHCP snooping trust automatically makes an interface ARP trusted
DHCP bindings can validate a client's sender IP/MAC claim
questions.explanation: DAI can use snooping bindings and configured ARP ACLs. Its interface trust is independent of DHCP snooping trust, and trust placement follows the actual design.

whyWrong.0: Validating an address claim is not user authentication.
whyWrong.1: A trunk's existence does not establish that all ARP arriving on it should bypass inspection.
whyWrong.3: `ip arp inspection trust` is a separate interface setting.

questions.prompt: Which optional DAI validation detects an Ethernet source MAC that differs from the ARP sender hardware address?
options: lease-time
dst-mac
src-mac
ip
questions.explanation: `src-mac` compares the Ethernet source with the sender MAC inside ARP. It supplements the underlying binding or ACL validation.

whyWrong.0: Lease time is binding information, not this validation keyword.
whyWrong.1: The `dst-mac` check compares the Ethernet destination with the ARP target MAC in replies.
whyWrong.3: The `ip` option checks invalid IP-address values in ARP fields, not this MAC comparison.

questions.prompt: No explicit storm-control action is configured. What is the documented default response when broadcast suppression is triggered?
options: Filter the selected controlled traffic type.
Send a notification without suppressing any traffic.
Change the port to an STP alternate role.
Err-disable the entire selected interface.
questions.explanation: The default action filters the storm-controlled traffic. Treat this as suppression, not a guarantee that precisely the excess percentage is discarded; implementation and measurement depend on the platform.

whyWrong.1: A notification action is separate from the default suppression behavior.
whyWrong.2: Storm suppression does not elect an STP port role.
whyWrong.3: Interface shutdown requires the separately configured shutdown action.

questions.prompt: Why can a large number of forged source MAC addresses create a Layer 2 security concern?
options: They can force known unicast to flood across every VLAN regardless of policy.
They can authenticate forged senders by adding more entries to the MAC table.
They can make unknown destinations use only their last learned physical port.
They can pressure learning resources and increase unknown-unicast flooding.
questions.explanation: Excess source addresses can consume MAC-learning resources. If destinations are unknown, frames may be flooded to eligible forwarding ports in that VLAN. The scope and device response depend on the platform and configuration.

whyWrong.0: Known destinations, VLAN boundaries and other forwarding controls still matter.
whyWrong.1: Learning a source MAC is not identity authentication.
whyWrong.2: An unknown destination has no usable learned location to select.

questions.prompt: What does an accepted secure source MAC establish about the sender?
options: It proves the logged-in user owns the physical device.
It establishes that the IP and ARP claims are also authorized.
It proves the device’s application traffic is harmless.
It establishes that the source matches the configured MAC policy.
questions.explanation: Port security evaluates source MAC policy. That match is not user authentication and does not replace DHCP, ARP or application controls.

whyWrong.0: A MAC can be impersonated; this feature does not authenticate a user.
whyWrong.1: Other controls must evaluate the IP/ARP claims.
whyWrong.2: Allowed MAC identity does not classify the safety of every application exchange.

exhibit.title: SW1: port-security status (excerpt)
exhibit.text:
Port Status             : Secure-shutdown
Violation Mode          : Shutdown
Maximum MAC Addresses   : 1
Total MAC Addresses     : 1
Sticky MAC Addresses    : 1
Security Violation Count: 1

questions.prompt: PC-A is the authorized sticky device. After a different PC is connected to Fa0/1, the exhibit is recorded. Which action restores the intended one-device policy?
options: Keep the new PC connected and raise the maximum to two
Reconnect PC-A, then shut and re-enable Fa0/1
Reconnect PC-A and wait for the default automatic recovery
Leave the new PC connected and clear all sticky entries
questions.explanation: Secure-shutdown identifies a shutdown-mode violation. Restore the authorized endpoint before resetting the interface; otherwise the same cause can immediately recur.

whyWrong.0: Increasing the limit authorizes additional addresses instead of restoring the specified one-device policy.
whyWrong.2: Automatic recovery for this cause must be enabled; it is not established by the exhibit.
whyWrong.3: Clearing the approved entry would allow a different device to be learned and changes the intended policy.

exhibit.title: SW1 command result
exhibit.text:
SW1(config-if)# switchport port-security
Command rejected: FastEthernet0/1 is a dynamic port.

questions.prompt: Fa0/1 connects one untagged PC. What should be corrected before retrying port security?
options: Configure a native VLAN on the PC
Enable trunk negotiation on the PC
Enable port security globally
Set the port to static access mode
questions.explanation: The port is still in a dynamic switchport mode. For this endpoint, configure `switchport mode access`, verify its access VLAN, then enable port security.

whyWrong.0: Native-VLAN configuration does not repair the dynamic-mode restriction.
whyWrong.1: A normal untagged PC does not negotiate a trunk.
whyWrong.2: Port security is enabled per interface; a global enable command is not the solution.

questions.prompt: A sticky address was learned after the last configuration save. No later save occurred before power was lost. What should you expect after restart?
options: Startup configuration does not contain that new address
The switch restores it from its ordinary MAC table
The unsaved address becomes a permanent static entry
The address persists because sticky means nonvolatile
questions.explanation: Sticky learning adds a configuration entry to running configuration. Persistence depends on saving that entry to startup configuration before the restart.

whyWrong.1: The ordinary forwarding table is not a backup for unsaved configuration.
whyWrong.2: Learning does not convert the address into an independently persistent static entry.
whyWrong.3: Sticky describes the learning/configuration behavior, not automatic saving.

questions.prompt: R1 serves DHCP. SW1 Gi0/1 connects to R1; SW1 Gi0/2 connects to downstream SW2 Gi0/1. Clients are below SW2. Both switches have snooping enabled and Option 82 insertion disabled. Which server-trust placement fits this reply path?
options: Trust only SW1 Gi0/2 because it is the inter-switch link
Leave both uplinks untrusted and trust only client ports
Trust both ports on SW1 and every client port on SW2
Trust SW1 Gi0/1 and SW2 Gi0/1; leave SW1 Gi0/2 untrusted
questions.explanation: Trust is an ingress decision. R1's replies enter SW1 on Gi0/1 and enter SW2 on its Gi0/1. SW1's downlink receives client traffic and does not need server trust merely because it connects another switch.

whyWrong.0: The server reply actually enters SW1 on Gi0/1; downstream connectivity alone does not identify a trusted ingress.
whyWrong.1: This permits the wrong direction and leaves legitimate server replies blocked.
whyWrong.2: Trusting client ports permits server messages from endpoints and expands the boundary unnecessarily.

exhibit.title: Authored server diagnostic summary
exhibit.text:
Request received: giaddr 0.0.0.0, relay-agent information (Option 82) present
Request rejected by relay-information trust policy

questions.prompt: The server-facing switch port is trusted. The isolated lab does not use relay-agent information for policy, and the server records the exhibit. Which switch change removes the explicitly observed cause?
options: Make all client-facing interfaces trusted
Disable Option 82 insertion on the switch
Configure a new DHCP default gateway
Disable DHCP snooping on every VLAN
questions.explanation: The evidence specifically identifies Option 82 with a zero relay address on a path the server does not trust. In this stated design, `no ip dhcp snooping information option` removes the unused inserted information. Other designs may deliberately retain it and configure an appropriate server/relay trust policy.

whyWrong.0: Client trust does not establish a correct relay-information policy and would permit unauthorized server replies.
whyWrong.2: The gateway option does not repair rejection of the DHCP request.
whyWrong.3: Removing all snooping also removes the required access-layer protection.

questions.prompt: A verified static printer has no snooping binding. Its ARP is rejected on an untrusted port. DHCP clients in the same VLAN must still use their bindings. Which change is appropriate?
options: Add its MAC to the switch's ordinary forwarding table only
Permit its exact IP/MAC in an applied ARP ACL without `static`
Apply an ARP ACL with `static` and list only the printer
Exclude the printer from the DHCP allocation pool only
questions.explanation: An exact ARP ACL permit can admit the static printer. Without the `static` application keyword, an ACL nonmatch can fall back to the snooping database, preserving validation for DHCP clients.

whyWrong.0: A Layer 2 forwarding entry does not establish a valid ARP sender IP/MAC pair.
whyWrong.2: Here `static` makes the ACL's implicit denial final, so unlisted DHCP clients lose the fallback.
whyWrong.3: An exclusion prevents DHCP allocation; it does not create a DAI authorization.

exhibit.title: SW1 interface configuration
exhibit.text: storm-control broadcast level 1.00 0.50

questions.prompt: The broadcast level crossed the rising threshold. It now measures 0.7%. Under the displayed policy, what is the threshold interpretation?
options: All unicast traffic is discarded at the same threshold
Forwarding resumes whenever the rate falls below 1.00%
The port is necessarily error-disabled at 0.7%
Suppression continues until it falls below 0.50%
questions.explanation: After suppression begins, the falling threshold governs recovery. 0.7% is above 0.50%. Exact sampling and counter presentation depend on the hardware.

whyWrong.0: This policy selects broadcast traffic, not all unicast.
whyWrong.1: The separately configured falling threshold prevents immediate recovery at the rising threshold.
whyWrong.2: A threshold alone does not specify a shutdown action; filtering is the documented default.

questions.prompt: An RA guard policy with `device-role host` has been defined, but unwanted router advertisements still enter through an endpoint port with no attached policy. What is missing?
options: Clear the client’s old default route without changing ingress policy.
Redefine the same host policy without applying it to any port.
Attach the host policy to the actual endpoint ingress interface.
Attach a router-role policy to the endpoint to admit its advertisements.
questions.explanation: Defining the policy does not enforce it on an interface. Apply `ipv6 nd raguard attach-policy NAME` to the intended endpoint ingress and verify the policy and attachment.

whyWrong.0: Clearing old state does not block new advertisements entering through an unprotected port.
whyWrong.1: A repeated definition still supplies no interface enforcement.
whyWrong.3: The intended endpoint role rejects unauthorized router messages; a router role does not meet that policy.

questions.prompt: In the documented RA guard design, which two actions support a valid verification? (Choose two.)
options: Judge success from the policy name alone
Assume DHCP snooping also validates IPv6 RAs
Attach the host policy to the endpoint ingress
Require old SLAAC addresses to disappear immediately
Confirm the legitimate router-facing role and fresh permitted RAs
questions.explanation: Verification needs the attachment on the real ingress and evidence that authorized advertisements still pass. Old host state can remain for its advertised lifetime, so fresh packet behavior is the stronger test.

whyWrong.0: A policy can exist without being applied anywhere.
whyWrong.1: These are separate features protecting different traffic.
whyWrong.3: Previously learned addresses and routes need not vanish immediately when future RAs are blocked.

exhibit.title: Supplied access-security evidence
exhibit.text:
Secure maximum: 1; authorized secure MAC: A.
An isolated hub presents frames from A and new source B to this one port.
A’s traffic continues; B’s frames are dropped.
Port remains secure-up; violation counter increases and log records new violations.

questions.prompt: Which violation response matches the recorded behavior?
options: Shutdown: disable the entire port while keeping A’s frames forwarding.
Restrict: reject the additional source while reporting its violations.
Protect: reject the additional source while incrementing the same violation counters.
Disabled: admit both sources after the secure-address total is reached.
questions.explanation: Restrict rejects B and records violations while retaining forwarding for the already secure A. Protect lacks that violation reporting, while shutdown would stop the whole port.

whyWrong.0: A port in shutdown violation state does not continue forwarding A’s user traffic.
whyWrong.2: The documented protect mode does not provide restrict’s violation counting/reporting.
whyWrong.3: The evidence shows B is rejected, so enforcement is active.

exhibit.title: Supplied access-security evidence
exhibit.text:
DAI enabled for VLAN 10; Fa0/2 is untrusted.
Snooping binding: 10.1.10.51, 00aa.0000.0001, VLAN 10, Fa0/2.
Fresh ARP sender: 10.1.10.51 / 00bb.0000.0002; ingress Fa0/2, VLAN 10.
No matching ARP ACL permit or other exception is configured.

questions.prompt: Which comparison explains why the fresh sender claim fails the shown binding validation?
options: The client uses a private IPv4 subnet rather than a public one.
The client’s IP address matches the binding’s IPv4 address.
The ARP sender claims a different MAC from the binding for that IP.
The switch has a client lease binding instead of a router binding.
questions.explanation: The binding maps 10.1.10.51 to 00aa.0000.0001, while the fresh ARP claims that IP with 00bb.0000.0002. That IP/MAC mismatch is sufficient for rejection under this stated binding-only policy. It does not establish whether the cause is spoofing, an approved replacement or stale state.

whyWrong.0: Private IPv4 addressing is normal and does not invalidate the claim.
whyWrong.1: The matching IP identifies the entry to compare; the sender MAC is the mismatch.
whyWrong.3: A DHCP client binding is the intended validation source for this client’s claim.

exhibit.title: Supplied access-security evidence
exhibit.text:
Applied ARP ACL for VLAN 10 has an explicit deny matching client 10.1.10.51 / 00bb.0000.0002.
The filter is applied without the static keyword.
A correct DHCP snooping binding also exists for the same client and ingress.
DAI is enabled; ingress untrusted.

questions.prompt: What happens to the client’s ARP claim under this explicitly supplied policy?
options: The missing static keyword means all ARP ACL entries are ignored.
The explicit ACL deny rejects it even without the static keyword.
The correct binding overrides every configured ACL denial.
The ARP claim is accepted because its Ethernet source is unicast.
questions.explanation: The non-static application permits binding fallback for an implicit nonmatch. An explicit matching deny remains a denial; it is not overridden by the binding.

whyWrong.0: Without static, explicit permit/deny entries still have effect.
whyWrong.2: The matching explicit deny is applied before fallback.
whyWrong.3: A unicast source MAC does not bypass the policy decision.

questions.prompt: A 1% broadcast storm threshold is copied from a 100 Mb/s port to a 1 Gb/s port. What nominal rate comparison is correct?
options: The faster port uses 100 Mb/s because the percentage is a packet count.
The thresholds correspond to 1 Mb/s and 10 Mb/s, before hardware accounting details.
The slower port uses 10 Mb/s while the faster port uses 1 Mb/s.
Both ports use 1 Mb/s because the configured percentage is identical.
questions.explanation: One percent of 100 Mb/s is 1 Mb/s; one percent of 1000 Mb/s is 10 Mb/s. A copied percentage therefore changes the nominal permitted rate. Actual accounting and enforcement depend on the device.

whyWrong.0: The percentage is not one packet per hundred packets or a 100 Mb/s allocation here.
whyWrong.2: The values are reversed.
whyWrong.3: A percentage scales with the stated port bandwidth.

questions.prompt: After verified RA guard enforcement, the client still lists an old IPv6 address and default router. What is the justified conclusion?
options: The policy must have stopped inspecting because the old address is still visible.
The presence of a default router proves its latest advertisement crossed this port.
DAI must erase all IPv6 addresses before RA guard can begin to work.
Old state can remain for its lifetime; inspect fresh RAs to judge current enforcement.
questions.explanation: Existing learned addresses/routes can outlive a policy change. Fresh packet observations distinguish current RA delivery from retained state.

whyWrong.0: Retained state alone does not establish a new policy failure.
whyWrong.1: The router entry can have been learned before the policy change.
whyWrong.2: DAI is an IPv4 ARP feature and does not perform that IPv6 reset.

exhibit.title: Supplied access-security evidence
exhibit.text:
Snooping is correctly enabled globally and for VLAN 10; server ingress trust is correct.
PC-A still uses a lease acquired earlier, before snooping was enabled.
R1 lists that lease; SW1’s binding table is empty.
The intended design will validate PC-A’s ARP through DAI.

questions.prompt: Which action establishes the missing evidence before DAI is enabled?
options: Obtain a fresh DHCP exchange and verify the resulting switch binding.
Add the client’s MAC to the ordinary forwarding table without its IP.
Trust the client port so future ARP never needs a binding.
Save the switch configuration so it copies every client lease automatically.
questions.explanation: The existing server lease was acquired before snooping observed the exchange. Obtain and verify a fresh binding with the actual IP, MAC, VLAN and interface; a lease on the server and a binding on the switch are different records.

whyWrong.1: A MAC forwarding entry does not provide the DHCP-derived IP association.
whyWrong.2: That bypasses the intended client inspection rather than establishing its input.
whyWrong.3: Configuration saving does not automatically persist or synthesize operational DHCP snooping bindings.

exhibit.title: Supplied access-security evidence
exhibit.text:
PC-A MAC 00aa.0000.0001 is still explicitly secured on Fa0/1 in VLAN 10.
An approved move places PC-A on Fa0/2, also a secure VLAN 10 access port.
Fa0/2’s maximum is not full. The old secure entry was not removed.

questions.prompt: The moved endpoint violates the second secure port even though that port has spare capacity. Which evidence explains why?
options: Port security requires the two ports to belong to different STP instances.
The ordinary MAC aging interval has not yet enabled additional secure capacity.
The same address remains secured on another interface in the same VLAN.
A secure source always consumes two entries whenever it sends an ARP request.
questions.explanation: On the documented Catalyst behavior, seeing an address secured on one interface at another secure interface in the same VLAN can itself be a violation. Reconcile the approved move and old secure entry rather than merely raising a limit.

whyWrong.0: STP-instance differences are not the source-address violation rule.
whyWrong.1: Ordinary forwarding-table aging does not remove the shown secure configuration.
whyWrong.3: ARP does not inherently create a second distinct secure source entry.

exhibit.title: SW1 relevant configuration
exhibit.text:
ip dhcp snooping
ip dhcp snooping vlan 20
ip arp inspection vlan 10
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip dhcp snooping trust
 ip arp inspection trust
!
DHCP snooping binding table: 0 entries

questions.prompt: Clients in VLAN 10 have leases, but their fresh ARP requests are dropped after DAI is enabled. Which correction addresses the missing source of bindings shown here?
options: Enable snooping for VLAN 10, then obtain fresh client leases
Enable sticky MAC learning on every client-facing port
Add VLAN 20 to every client access port without changing IPs
Disable the clients' default gateways and renew their leases
questions.explanation: DAI is inspecting VLAN 10, while snooping is configured only for VLAN 20. Enable snooping on VLAN 10 and verify new bindings from fresh leases before retesting ARP.

whyWrong.1: Port-security entries do not replace DHCP snooping bindings for DAI.
whyWrong.2: Moving clients changes the intended LAN and does not correct its missing protection policy.
whyWrong.3: A gateway option does not populate the switch binding table.

exhibit.title: Supplied access-security evidence
exhibit.text:
Approved replacement MAC: 00bb.0000.0002.
Before power loss: running-config sticky entry 00bb.0000.0002; fresh traffic succeeds.
Startup-config sticky entry: 00aa.0000.0001.
No save occurred after replacement. Maximum 1; violation shutdown.

questions.prompt: After a normal restart, why does the approved replacement endpoint fail this saved one-device policy?
options: The normal dynamic MAC-table aging timer immediately deletes every secure address.
The lower source MAC replaces any higher saved sticky address during root election.
A shutdown violation automatically writes the new endpoint into startup configuration.
The running replacement was never saved, so the old saved sticky address is restored.
questions.explanation: The operational replacement was made only in running configuration. Normal boot loads startup configuration, which still reserves the one entry for the old device. Review the approved change and save the corrected identity after verification.

whyWrong.0: The configuration mismatch, not ordinary dynamic aging, is shown.
whyWrong.1: Spanning-tree root election does not choose secure host MACs.
whyWrong.2: Violations do not automatically authorize or save an unknown endpoint.

exhibit.title: Supplied access-security evidence
exhibit.text:
Only R1, an approved static router/server, connects to SW1 Gi0/1.
Gi0/1: DHCP snooping trusted; DAI untrusted.
Client Fa0/1: fresh lease and correct snooping binding.
R1 10.1.10.1 has no DHCP-client binding or ARP ACL permit.
Capture: valid DHCP ACK reaches client; R1’s ARP reply enters Gi0/1 and DAI rejects it.
The approved design explicitly permits an ARP-inspection bypass only on R1’s controlled link.

questions.prompt: Which narrow policy change fits this verified one-router design?
options: Raise the port-security maximum on the client because ARP uses an extra source.
Apply the separate intended DAI trust to the controlled router ingress.
Trust every client port for DHCP so the router can receive their requests.
Remove the client’s lease so DAI stops inspecting its gateway traffic.
questions.explanation: DHCP trust allowed the server replies but did not authorize the static router’s ARP claims. In this deliberately controlled single-router design, the planned separate DAI trust admits that router ingress. A verified ARP ACL is another design option, not shown here.

whyWrong.0: No additional source-MAC limit violation is shown.
whyWrong.2: Client DHCP trust expands server-message permission and does not fix the router ARP rejection.
whyWrong.3: Removing a valid binding would not authorize the static gateway and can break client validation.

exhibit.title: Supplied access-security evidence
exhibit.text:
VLAN 10 DAI enabled; client ports remain untrusted.
STATIC-HOSTS permits only verified printer 10.1.10.20 / 00cc.0000.0020.
ip arp inspection filter STATIC-HOSTS vlan 10 static
All DHCP clients have correct fresh snooping bindings but no ACL permit.
Policy: permit printer’s exact pair and continue binding validation for DHCP clients.

questions.prompt: The printer works, but DHCP clients fail fresh ARP after this change. Which correction preserves the intended checks?
options: Add an ordinary static MAC forwarding entry for each affected DHCP client.
Remove only the static application keyword, retaining the printer permit and binding fallback.
Delete the printer permit because DHCP bindings automatically cover its excluded address.
Keep static and trust every client interface so none needs a binding check.
questions.explanation: The applied static keyword makes the ACL’s implicit deny final. Removing that keyword retains the explicit printer permit and lets implicit nonmatches use correct DHCP bindings.

whyWrong.0: Forwarding-table entries do not supply DAI IP/MAC authorization.
whyWrong.2: A DHCP exclusion does not create a printer binding; removing its permit breaks its authorization.
whyWrong.3: This bypasses the intended client inspection instead of preserving it.

exhibit.title: Supplied access-security evidence
exhibit.text:
Fa0/6 DHCP rate limit: 15 packets/s; observed DHCP traffic below that rate.
Fa0/6 DAI allowance: 15 ARP packets/s, 1-second burst interval.
During a measured ARP burst, log names arp-inspection as the errdisable cause.
No MAC-security violation is recorded.

questions.prompt: Which policy should be investigated first, based on the actual shutdown reason?
options: The sticky MAC limit because every err-disabled port has exceeded it.
The STP root priority because the port is no longer forwarding.
The ARP inspection rate and actual ARP load on this interface.
The DHCP rate because its configured number also happens to be 15.
questions.explanation: The log names arp-inspection after an observed ARP burst. DHCP and DAI packet-rate limits count different protocols even when their numeric settings match. Examine the load and appropriate ARP policy before recovery.

whyWrong.0: No port-security violation is established by the supplied evidence.
whyWrong.1: An STP election does not explain this cause-specific errdisable event.
whyWrong.3: DHCP traffic stayed below its limit and the shutdown reason names the other feature.

exhibit.title: Supplied access-security evidence
exhibit.text:
Supported Catalyst RA guard implementation.
Gi1/0/24 is the only legitimate IPv6 router link.
Running configuration attaches ENDPOINTS, device-role host, on Gi1/0/24.
Fresh RA from fe80::1 is observed before switch ingress but not at the client.
The router sends correctly, VLAN path is verified, and IPv4 still works.
Design calls for a router-role policy on Gi1/0/24.

questions.prompt: Which correction and verification fit the IPv6 evidence?
options: Remove the client’s IPv4 gateway because IPv4 reachability is interfering with router discovery.
Raise the DHCP snooping packet limit until the IPv6 router gains a binding.
Apply the intended router-role policy on the legitimate router ingress, then verify fresh authorized RAs.
Trust all endpoint ports as routers so every advertisement reaches the client.
questions.explanation: The documented router ingress was accidentally classified as a host. Correct that attachment/role and verify fresh authorized RAs while leaving endpoint boundaries protected. Working IPv4 does not validate IPv6 router discovery.

whyWrong.0: The separate working IPv4 gateway is not the demonstrated cause.
whyWrong.1: DHCPv4 snooping does not create RA guard authorization.
whyWrong.3: Allowing every endpoint to act as a router violates the intended policy.

exhibit.title: Supplied access-security evidence
exhibit.text: Isolated supported-switch lab. R1 is the permitted router; R2 is the test router on a host-role ingress. Cables, VLAN and R2 configuration remain unchanged during the comparison.

questions.prompt: Which two observations together provide the strongest bounded evidence that this test enforces the intended RA policy? Choose two.
options: The client retains an address learned before the test began.
The host-policy name appears in the saved configuration.
No R2 RA is seen during one short capture without first proving R2 transmits.
Legitimate R1 RAs continue reaching the client throughout the guarded comparison.
R2 RAs cross the same path when its host policy is removed, then cease after restoration over repeated observed intervals.
questions.explanation: The permitted/blocked comparison controls for R2 being inactive, and continued R1 reception tests the legitimate path. It is evidence for this topology and traffic, not a universal hardware-security certification.

whyWrong.0: Previously learned state does not establish current packet delivery.
whyWrong.1: A name establishes configuration existence but not attachment or enforcement.
whyWrong.2: An unproven sender and a short negative capture cannot distinguish filtering from no transmitted packet.

cards.front: On the documented Catalyst platform, what are the initial port-security settings after enablement?
cards.back: Maximum 1 secure MAC, violation mode shutdown and aging time 0 (disabled). Sticky learning is separate.

cards.front: What switchport mode should precede port security for one untagged PC?
cards.back: Use static access mode and the intended access VLAN. A dynamically negotiated switchport mode can prevent port-security configuration. Supported trunk use is platform dependent.

cards.front: What does protect mode do?
cards.back: Drops violating traffic while leaving permitted traffic forwarding, without restrict-mode violation counting and notifications.

cards.front: What does restrict mode add to protect mode?
cards.back: Violation counting and reporting while the port remains available for permitted source MACs.

cards.front: What does shutdown mode do to a violating port?
cards.back: Error-disables the port, stopping its forwarding. Inspect secure-shutdown/error-disable state and the recorded cause; a fixed counter value is not a universal diagnostic requirement.

cards.front: How does a newly learned sticky MAC survive restart?
cards.back: It appears as a sticky entry in running configuration. Save that configuration to startup configuration after verifying the address.

cards.front: How do static, dynamic and sticky secure addresses differ?
cards.back: Static: explicitly configured. Dynamic: learned operationally without a configuration entry. Sticky: learned into running configuration and retained across restart only if saved.

cards.front: How should a shutdown-mode violation be recovered?
cards.back: Correct the cause, then shut and re-enable the interface. Timed recovery is an optional global policy for the specific cause, not an automatic repair of a persistent violation.

cards.front: Which two settings enable snooping for VLAN 10?
cards.back: Global `ip dhcp snooping` and `ip dhcp snooping vlan 10`. Then establish a correct server-reply trust path.

cards.front: Which interfaces should receive DHCP snooping trust?
cards.back: Interfaces where legitimate server replies enter that switch. Trust is an ingress decision; a trunk or switch-to-switch cable alone is not sufficient justification.

cards.front: What does a DHCP snooping binding associate?
cards.back: A client MAC and IPv4 address with lease information, VLAN and access interface. It is learned from observed DHCP operation, not from every host that happens to have an address.

cards.front: Does DHCP failure after enabling snooping prove an Option 82 problem?
cards.back: No. Check the VLAN, reply ingress, pool and observed exchange. If logs show rejected inserted Option 82 with zero giaddr, choose a supported relay-information policy or disable insertion when the design does not use it.

cards.front: What does `ip dhcp snooping limit rate 15` configure?
cards.back: An interface DHCP-message limit of 15 packets/s on the documented platform. Exceeding it can error-disable the interface. Choose limits for actual traffic; aggregate links can carry many clients.

cards.front: How does DAI validate ARP on an untrusted interface?
cards.back: It checks sender claims against snooping bindings or an applied ARP ACL, with optional additional validation. Its trust setting is independent of DHCP snooping trust.

cards.front: What DAI rate defaults apply on the cited Catalyst configuration?
cards.back: Untrusted ports: 15 ARP packets/s with a 1-second burst interval. Trusted ports: unlimited by default. An exceeded rate can error-disable the interface; verify the actual device policy.

cards.front: What does optional DAI src-mac validation compare?
cards.back: The Ethernet source MAC with the ARP sender hardware address. This header/payload consistency check supplements binding or ACL validation.

cards.front: What does `static` mean when applying a DAI ARP ACL?
cards.back: It makes the ACL's implicit denial final. Without it, an ACL nonmatch can fall back to DHCP bindings. It does not mean that the ACL is required to authorize a static-IP host.

cards.front: How should rising and falling storm thresholds be read?
cards.back: The rising threshold triggers suppression; the falling threshold controls recovery. The default action filters the controlled traffic type. Exact measurement behavior depends on hardware, so do not assume precise excess-only trimming.

cards.front: What is required beyond defining an RA guard host policy?
cards.back: Attach it to the intended endpoint ingress. Establish the legitimate router-facing role too, then verify fresh blocked and permitted advertisements; old host state can outlive the change.

cards.front: Does excluding a static address from DHCP authorize its ARP claims?
cards.back: No. An exclusion prevents allocation; DAI still needs a valid binding or explicit ARP policy for the sender.

cards.front: Does ip dhcp snooping trust also enable DAI trust?
cards.back: No. ip arp inspection trust is separate. Trace and authorize each protocol’s ingress independently.

cards.front: Where do RA guard host and router roles belong in the documented design?
cards.back: Host roles on endpoint ingresses; the appropriate router role on the legitimate router ingress. Verify attachment, not just policy definitions.

cards.front: Does retained IPv6 addressing prove new RAs are passing a guard?
cards.back: No. Old learned state can remain until lifetimes expire. Compare fresh permitted and blocked advertisements.

cards.front: Why is a secure MAC match not proof of user identity?
cards.back: The control checks a source address that another device may impersonate; it does not authenticate the person using it.

commands.task: Enable port security on the interface, which is already a static access port.
commands.note: Verify the endpoint and the default one-address, shutdown policy.

commands.task: The approved design requires exactly two observed secure entries on this port. Set its total maximum.
commands.note: The number follows observed endpoint/VLAN behavior; phone-plus-PC is not a universal two-entry guarantee.

commands.task: Enable learning of secure MAC addresses into running configuration.
commands.note: Verify learned identities before saving to startup configuration.

commands.task: Drop and report violating frames while preserving forwarding for permitted addresses.
commands.note: Shutdown mode instead error-disables the port.

commands.task: Inspect Fa0/1 port-security state, configured maximum and violations.
commands.note: Use current port state and fresh traffic tests alongside historical counters.

commands.task: Snooping is globally enabled. Add VLAN 10 to its inspection list.
commands.note: Both global and VLAN enablement are required.

commands.task: Legitimate DHCP server replies enter on this interface. Configure snooping trust here.
commands.note: Server trust follows reply ingress, not every trunk.

commands.task: This lab does not use Option 82 for server policy. Disable the switch's insertion of it.
commands.answer: no ip dhcp snooping information option
commands.note: This is an explicit design choice, not a universal repair whenever DHCP fails.

commands.task: Bindings and the separate ARP trust policy are verified. Enable DAI for VLAN 10.
commands.note: Plan verified static-host exceptions before enforcing binding checks.

commands.task: Set broadcast storm thresholds to 1% rising and 0.5% falling.
commands.note: Rising controls entry into suppression; falling controls recovery.

commands.task: Attach the existing RA guard policy HOSTS to this endpoint interface.
commands.note: The policy must have the intended host role; inspect both definition and attachment.

commands.task: Display learned DHCP snooping client bindings.
commands.note: Compare IP, MAC, VLAN and interface with the actual client.

commands.task: Display the RA guard policy named HOSTS on a supporting Catalyst.
commands.answer: show ipv6 nd raguard policy HOSTS
commands.note: A correct policy definition alone does not prove attachment or packet enforcement.

commands.task: Apply the separately approved DAI trust to this controlled router-facing interface.
commands.note: DHCP snooping trust does not set this ARP-inspection bypass; client ports remain inspected.

commands.task: Apply existing ARP ACL STATIC-HOSTS to VLAN 10 while retaining DHCP-binding fallback for implicit nonmatches.
commands.answer: ip arp inspection filter STATIC-HOSTS vlan 10
commands.note: Do not add static for this requirement; explicit deny entries still deny.

tickets.title: DHCP fails after snooping is enabled
tickets.scenario: ASW3 has one uplink, Gi0/2, to a distribution switch that relays client requests to DHCP. VLAN 10 clients cannot complete fresh leases after snooping is enabled. The upstream capture confirms a valid server reply reaches ASW3 Gi0/2. Option 82 insertion is disabled in this lab.

exhibits.title: ASW3 relevant configuration
exhibits.text:
ip dhcp snooping
ip dhcp snooping vlan 10
no ip dhcp snooping information option
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/2

 switchport trunk allowed vlan 10
!
interface FastEthernet0/1

exhibits.title: Authored verification observations
exhibits.text:
Gi0/2: up, VLAN 10 forwarding
DHCP snooping: Gi0/2 untrusted
Valid DHCP Offer reaches Gi0/2; snooping records a server-message drop
Client binding table: empty

tickets.question: Which fault is established by the combined evidence?
options: The client-facing port lacks a sticky MAC entry
The DHCP pool must be using the wrong subnet mask
The legitimate reply arrives on an untrusted ingress
Option 82 insertion must be enabled on every client
tickets.explanation: The evidence locates a valid Offer at Gi0/2 and a snooping drop on that untrusted ingress. The necessary repair is server trust on this verified reply path. The exhibit does not establish a pool, port-security or Option 82 requirement.
tickets.fix:
```ios ASW3
ASW3# configure terminal
ASW3(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
ASW3(config-if)# ip dhcp snooping trust
ASW3(config-if)# end
ASW3# show ip dhcp snooping
```
Request a fresh client lease, inspect `show ip dhcp snooping binding`, and test the gateway. Keep client ports untrusted. Save only after the intended path and successful lease are verified.

tickets.title: A phone and PC exceed the permitted MAC total
tickets.scenario: Fa0/7 serves an approved phone and attached PC. Both lose network service when the PC starts transmitting. Inventory and a previous permitted capture establish that this particular phone/PC combination uses exactly two secure entries: the phone in voice VLAN 20 and the PC in data VLAN 10. No additional device is present.

Maximum MAC Addresses   : 1

tickets.question: What explains the repeated error-disable event?
options: The approved PC exceeds the one-entry total already occupied by the phone
The phone's tagged voice traffic requires all data traffic to be trunked
The configured shutdown response permits only voice traffic after the second source arrives.
The existing sticky entry is removed automatically when the data VLAN begins forwarding.
tickets.explanation: The one-entry maximum is already occupied by the phone. The approved PC becomes a second source and triggers shutdown mode. Correct the limit to the verified endpoint requirement before resetting the port; merely bouncing it would leave the cause intact.
tickets.fix:
```ios ASW1
ASW1# configure terminal
ASW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/7
ASW1(config-if)# switchport port-security maximum 2
ASW1(config-if)# shutdown
ASW1(config-if)# no shutdown
ASW1(config-if)# end
ASW1# show port-security interface fastethernet0/7
ASW1# show port-security address
```
Generate phone and PC traffic, verify the two intended address/VLAN entries and restored service, then save. A different phone model or VLAN behavior may need a different total; derive it from the actual design.

chapters.title: The routing table
chapters.subtitle: Read route entries, distinguish route selection from forwarding, and verify the chosen path.

sources.title: Cisco: Route selection in Cisco routers
Cisco: IP routing protocol-independent command reference
Cisco: show ip route output field reference
Cisco: CEF behavior and adjacency on IOS XE
