tickets.title: Only part of the branch subnet is reachable
tickets.scenario: After a route change, a user can reach branch host 10.20.30.50 but not 10.20.30.200. Both hosts share the intended /24, have verified local connectivity, and previously worked from this source. R1's current output and the change record follow.

exhibits.title: R1 destination lookup
exhibits.text:
Routing entry for 10.20.30.128/25
Known via "static", distance 1, metric 0
Routing Descriptor Blocks:
* directly connected, via Null0

exhibits.title: Change record
exhibits.text:
Added: ip route 10.20.30.128 255.255.255.128 Null0
Intended policy: all of 10.20.30.0/24 remains reachable through the branch router

tickets.question: Which change explains the split result?
options: The /24 OSPF metric is compared directly with the static metric.
The new /25 discard overrides the /24 for the .200 destination
The /24 route cannot coexist with a /25 in one routing table
The /25 is less preferred because the /24 was learned first.
tickets.explanation: The .200 address lies inside 10.20.30.128/25; .50 does not. The more-specific static sends .200 to Null0 while the /24 continues to serve .50. This is longest prefix match, not a comparison between static and OSPF distances.
tickets.fix:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# no ip route 10.20.30.128 255.255.255.128 Null0
R1(config)# end
R1# show ip route 10.20.30.200
```
Confirm that the /24 is now selected, then test both .50 and .200 from the affected source. Verify replies and save the corrected configuration after the intended policy is restored.

tickets.title: The intended backup link is preferred
tickets.scenario: Traffic for 10.60.0.0/16 uses the backup path through 10.0.99.2. The intended primary is OSPF. Both next hops are reachable. A protocol inspection confirms a currently eligible OSPF candidate for exactly 10.60.0.0/16 with distance 110 and cost 20; the selected table entry is shown below.

exhibits.title: Verified candidate and next-hop observations
exhibits.text:
OSPF candidate: 10.60.0.0/16, AD 110, cost 20, via 10.0.12.2
10.0.12.2: resolved and reachable
10.0.99.2: resolved and reachable
Required policy: OSPF primary, static backup

tickets.question: What makes the backup preferred?
options: Equal-distance paths are load-sharing, and this flow selected the backup.
OSPF must be absent whenever a static line is configured.
The static command uses default AD 1, which beats OSPF 110
The OSPF cost must be lower than the static metric of zero
tickets.explanation: The candidates describe the same /16, so source preference applies. The static command omits an AD override and uses 1. Its metric is not compared directly with the OSPF metric. The separate exact-prefix candidate evidence establishes that a usable OSPF alternative exists.
tickets.fix:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# no ip route 10.60.0.0 255.255.0.0 10.0.99.2
R1(config)# ip route 10.60.0.0 255.255.0.0 10.0.99.2 130
R1(config)# end
R1# show ip route 10.60.0.0
R1# show running-config | include ^ip route
```
With the stated OSPF candidate still eligible, its AD 110 is preferred over 130. Verify the selected source and traffic in both directions. A planned failure test must separately establish that the backup remains eligible and actually forwards when the primary is withdrawn.

chapters.title: Static routing (IPv4)
chapters.subtitle: Configure a path to a remote network and verify the route back.

sources.title: Cisco: Configure a Next Hop IP Address for Static Routes
Cisco: Route Selection in Cisco Routers
Cisco: Extended Ping and Extended Traceroute

chapters.summary: Configure network, host, default and floating IPv4 routes. Distinguish a configured route from an installed route, choose a suitable next-hop form, and test both directions.

sections.body:
A router can have working interfaces and still be unable to deliver a packet to a remote LAN. Its connected routes describe its own links. A route to another network must come from an additional source. In this chapter you supply it yourself, check that the router can use it, and prove that the destination can send a reply.

The examples use two routers with two separate Ethernet links. Work through the route decisions before entering commands. Understanding why an entry should appear makes the verification much more useful than checking that IOS accepted a line.

sections.title: How static routes become usable
sections.body:
:::facts
- An ordinary IOS static route has administrative distance **1**. A connected route has distance **0**; an OSPF route normally has distance **110**.
- A network route identifies a prefix. A host route uses mask `255.255.255.255`, or **/32**.
- An IPv4 default route identifies `0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0`, or **/0**.
- A floating static route has a higher distance than the preferred route to the **same prefix**. Distance **255** is not usable.
- Forwarding uses the longest matching **installed** prefix. A successful ping also needs a working return path.
:::

A **static route** is an administrator's instruction about where a destination can be reached. It remains in the configuration until changed or removed. That does not mean it remains in the routing table under every condition. IOS must be able to resolve its next hop, the required interface must be usable, and a more preferred route to that same prefix may take its place.

Keep three checks separate. The configuration shows what you requested. The routing table shows the routes currently selected. Packet tests show whether forwarding and the return path actually work. An installed route does not prove that the remote server is available, and a line in the configuration does not prove that the route is installed.

Static routes are useful for a small, stable connection or a deliberate backup. They do not exchange routing-protocol updates, but the network still uses supporting mechanisms such as ARP. Their maintenance cost grows when many routers or prefixes change: an administrator must keep the instructions consistent across the path.

```diagram
{"type":"topology","title":"Two paths between two LANs","caption":"Each router needs a route to the other router's LAN. The two transit networks are separate routed links.","nodes":[{"id":"a","kind":"pc","label":"PC-A","sub":"192.168.10.11/24","x":0.5,"y":3},{"id":"r1","kind":"router","label":"R1","sub":"LAN .10.1","x":3.5,"y":3},{"id":"r2","kind":"router","label":"R2","sub":"LAN .20.1","x":8.5,"y":3},{"id":"b","kind":"pc","label":"PC-B","sub":"192.168.20.12/24","x":11.5,"y":3}],"links":[{"from":"a","to":"r1","label":"192.168.10.0/24"},{"from":"r1","to":"r2","label":"Primary 10.0.12.0/30","fromLabel":"Gi0/0 .1","toLabel":"Gi0/0 .2","accent":true},{"from":"r1","to":"r2","label":"Backup 10.0.13.0/30","fromLabel":"Gi0/1 .1","toLabel":"Gi0/1 .2","style":"dashed"},{"from":"r2","to":"b","label":"192.168.20.0/24"}]}
```

For PC-A to reach PC-B, PC-A first sends the packet to its gateway, `192.168.10.1`. R1 then needs a route covering `192.168.20.12`. R2 already has a connected route to that destination's LAN. For the reply, those roles reverse: R2 needs a route covering PC-A, while R1 can deliver directly onto its connected LAN.

sections.title: Configure network and host routes
sections.body:
The core syntax is `ip route destination mask next-hop` in global configuration mode. The destination is the **network address**, not an arbitrary host inside the network. The next-hop address belongs to the router that should receive the packet next, not to the configuring router.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip route 192.168.20.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.12.2
R1(config)# end
R1# show ip route static
```

Here `192.168.20.0` and `255.255.255.0` describe the remote /24. `10.0.12.2` is R2's primary transit address. It is directly reachable from R1 in this example. The command does not assign an interface address and does not tell R2 how to reach anything.

Representative abbreviated IOS output:

```output R1# show ip route static
S    192.168.20.0/24 [1/0] via 10.0.12.2    ← static, distance 1, metric 0
```

A host route uses all 32 destination bits. For example, `ip route 192.168.20.12 255.255.255.255 10.0.13.2` identifies PC-B alone. It can coexist with the /24 route. When both are installed, PC-B's address matches the /32, while `192.168.20.13` matches only the /24. Host routes are useful for a specific exception; they are not a requirement for every host in a remote LAN.

To remove a route deliberately, read its current configuration and use the corresponding `no ip route ...` line. Including its destination, mask, interface, next hop and nondefault distance as configured makes the intended removal explicit. Verify afterwards; do not infer success merely from an absence of error text.

:::trap
`ip route 192.168.20.12 255.255.255.0 ...` mixes a host address with the /24 network mask. For the whole LAN, use `192.168.20.0`. For that one address, use a /32 mask. A route's mask describes the destination, not the transit link.
:::

sections.title: Choose the next-hop form
sections.body:
IOS accepts different ways to describe the path. They solve the same forwarding problem but make different assumptions.

| Form | Example after the destination and mask | What IOS must determine |
|---|---|---|
| Next hop only | `10.0.12.2` | Resolve that address through the routing table |
| Exit interface only | `serial0/0/0` | Send through the specified interface; suitable for a true point-to-point link |
| Fully specified | `gigabitethernet0/0 10.0.12.2` | Use the named next hop through the named interface |

A next-hop-only route is often called **recursive**: another route determines how to reach the next-hop address. A directly connected transit subnet provides that resolution in the simple example. A next hop can also be reachable through another route, but it must resolve successfully without a routing dependency on itself. You do not need to design multistage recursion to meet this chapter's objective.

An interface-only route on Ethernet has a significant consequence. The router treats destinations covered by that route as reachable directly on that Ethernet link and may ARP for each destination. Remote hosts will not hear those requests across a router. Proxy ARP might hide the mistake on some networks, but its availability is not a sound prerequisite for a remote-LAN route.

Use a next-hop address for the Ethernet examples here. A **fully specified** route additionally fixes the intended exit interface:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip route 192.168.20.0 255.255.255.0 gigabitethernet0/0 10.0.12.2
R1(config)# end
```

This is an alternative to the earlier next-hop-only line, not another line to add blindly. The router still needs the next hop's Ethernet address through ARP. Naming both values does not remove Layer 2 address resolution.

The interface choice also matters during failures. A recursive next hop could remain reachable through an unexpected alternate route. Specifying the intended interface makes the local-link failure exercise more predictable. Neither form, by itself, tests the availability of every device beyond that next hop.

sections.title: Default routes
sections.body:
A **default route** is the least specific destination route: /0 matches every IPv4 address. It is used when no longer installed prefix matches. It is common on a router with one general exit toward the rest of a network.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 gigabitethernet0/0 10.0.12.2
R1(config)# end
R1# show ip route
```

Representative excerpts:

```output R1# show ip route
Gateway of last resort is 10.0.12.2 to network 0.0.0.0
S*   0.0.0.0/0 [1/0] via 10.0.12.2, GigabitEthernet0/0
S    192.168.20.0/24 [1/0] via 10.0.12.2, GigabitEthernet0/0
```

The `S` identifies a static route and the asterisk marks a candidate default. A default does not replace more specific entries. A packet for PC-B still matches /24; a packet for a separately configured R2 loopback at `203.0.113.8` can use /0.

A default is only a forwarding instruction. It does not create Internet access, a destination host, or a return route. If R2 has no way to deliver the packet, sending it to R2 will not solve that problem. Two routers with defaults pointing at each other can also create a loop for unknown destinations. A packet's TTL limits that loop; the sensible repair is to correct the routing design.

Use `show ip route` to inspect the default explicitly. Destination-specific show-command formatting and default lookup behavior vary across IOS implementations. Read the full installed table and calculate the longest match rather than treating one diagnostic message as proof that no default exists.

sections.title: Floating static routes
sections.body:
A **floating static route** is a less preferred candidate that becomes usable when the preferred route to the same destination prefix is withdrawn. In the lab, both primary and backup are static, so distance 5 is greater than the primary's default distance 1.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip route 192.168.20.0 255.255.255.0 gigabitethernet0/1 10.0.13.2 5
R1(config)# end
R1# show running-config
R1# show ip route static
```

The configuration contains both route lines. With the primary working, the routing table normally contains the distance-1 route. When its required interface goes down, the distance-5 route can install if the backup link is usable. When the primary returns, its lower distance makes it preferred again.

Distance is relative to the competing route. A backup intended to follow an OSPF route at distance 110 could use 120. Distance 5 would beat 110 for the same prefix. Distance 255 cannot serve as a working backup. Equal distances can permit multiple installed paths, subject to the platform's multipath behavior; that is not the intended primary/standby design.

:::trap
A distance-200 /32 still wins forwarding over an installed distance-1 /24 for that single destination. Distance selects candidates for the same prefix; longest prefix match selects among the installed destination entries. A mistyped /25 backup can take half a /24's traffic immediately.
:::

The failover trigger must be real. Shutting a directly connected router-to-router link makes both ends lose that link. A remote failure behind an intermediate switch may leave your local interface up. The ordinary static route does not continuously ping the remote LAN. Tracking features can add health checks, but their configuration is outside this introductory chapter.

sections.title: Test the return path
sections.body:
A ping has two routed packets: request and reply. Record both source and destination before concluding which routes it tested.

An ordinary IOS router ping normally chooses the outgoing interface's address as its source. If R1 pings PC-B over the primary link, that source is `10.0.12.1`. R2 already has a connected route back to that transit subnet. The ping may succeed even while R2 lacks any route to PC-A's `192.168.10.0/24` LAN.

Test from PC-A as well. Its source remains `192.168.10.11` in this lab, so the reply requires R2's return route. A router test sourced from R1's LAN address also tests that return prefix. IOS extended ping can select a source address; some simulator images support the inline `source` keyword and others require the interactive extended-ping prompts.

For a working PC-to-PC exchange, check these decisions in order: PC-A's gateway, R1's remote-LAN route, R2's connected delivery to PC-B, PC-B's gateway, R2's return route, and R1's connected delivery to PC-A. ARP must resolve the required local neighbors along the way. A routing fault is one possibility among address, gateway, interface and filtering faults; the observed table and addressing must support your diagnosis.

sections.title: Verify and troubleshoot
sections.body:
Use a repeatable sequence instead of changing several route lines at once.

| Check | Evidence to inspect | What it establishes |
|---|---|---|
| Interfaces | `show ip interface brief` | Correct local addresses and usable link state |
| Configured intent | `show running-config` | Destination, mask, next hop, interface and distance entered |
| Installed routes | `show ip route`; `show ip route static` | Which candidate routes are currently selected |
| Next-hop reachability | Ping the directly attached peer; inspect `show ip arp` | Local transit connectivity and address resolution |
| Destination choice | Inspect covering prefixes; use `show ip route address` where supported | Most specific installed match |
| End-to-end path | PC ping and traceroute; inspect the reverse table | Forwarding and return connectivity for the tested source |

A missing route can mean an unusable interface, unresolved next hop, wrong destination, or a better competing candidate. An installed route with failed traffic can mean the next-hop address is wrong on an otherwise active Ethernet link, a downstream fault, or a missing return route. Read the evidence before choosing between them.

Traceroute can help distinguish primary and backup paths, but response addresses and unanswered probes depend on device behavior. Do not require every hop to print a particular interface address as the sole success test. Use the selected routes, interface state and completed endpoint ping together.

sections.title: Exam focus
sections.body:
Be able to build all four destination types: network, host, default and floating. For each route, identify its destination prefix, exit path and distance before predicting whether it installs. Then perform a separate longest-prefix comparison for the packet.

Finish the lab able to explain why a router ping can succeed while a PC ping fails, why an Ethernet route should identify a next hop, and why a configured backup may be absent from the routing table. Those explanations demonstrate the mechanism behind the commands.

lab.title: Verify primary, backup, host and default IPv4 routes
lab.intro:
Practice revised September 2026. If you completed an earlier version, repeat the revised exercise and update its checkmarks.

Build a new isolated Packet Tracer project. You will first observe a missing return route, then establish a working baseline, test a backup, and compare network, host and default routes. These are guided configuration and reasoning exercises, not a record of an executed simulator session. Output is representative; wording, interface displays and supported diagnostic options can vary by version. If a command is unavailable, use the stated alternative and record the limitation.
lab.topology:
Use two 2911 routers with `GigabitEthernet0/0`, `0/1` and `0/2`. Use two 2960 switches at their default VLAN 1 settings. No trunk, management address, DHCP service, DNS server or Internet connection is required. The switches make the PC-to-router cabling unambiguous.

| Connection | Cable |
|---|---|
| PC-A FastEthernet0 — SW1 FastEthernet0/1 | Copper straight-through |
| SW1 FastEthernet0/24 — R1 GigabitEthernet0/2 | Copper straight-through |
| R1 GigabitEthernet0/0 — R2 GigabitEthernet0/0 | Copper cross-over |
| R1 GigabitEthernet0/1 — R2 GigabitEthernet0/1 | Copper cross-over |
| R2 GigabitEthernet0/2 — SW2 FastEthernet0/24 | Copper straight-through |
| SW2 FastEthernet0/1 — PC-B FastEthernet0 | Copper straight-through |

If a model uses different interface names, record the substitutions before continuing. Do not connect the two switches to one another.

| Device/interface | IPv4 address | Mask | PC gateway |
|---|---|---|---|
| R1 Gi0/0 | `10.0.12.1` | `255.255.255.252` | — |
| R2 Gi0/0 | `10.0.12.2` | `255.255.255.252` | — |
| R1 Gi0/1 | `10.0.13.1` | `255.255.255.252` | — |
| R2 Gi0/1 | `10.0.13.2` | `255.255.255.252` | — |
| R1 Gi0/2 | `192.168.10.1` | `255.255.255.0` | — |
| PC-A | `192.168.10.11` | `255.255.255.0` | `192.168.10.1` |
| R2 Gi0/2 | `192.168.20.1` | `255.255.255.0` | — |
| PC-B | `192.168.20.12` | `255.255.255.0` | `192.168.20.1` |
| R2 Loopback0, added in Step 10 | `203.0.113.8` | `255.255.255.255` | — |

A loopback is a logical router interface used here as a stable test destination. The documentation address does not represent a public Internet service.

steps.title: Cable the project and configure R1
steps.body:
Place and label the devices. Set each PC's static address, mask and gateway under Desktop → IP Configuration. Leave DNS blank. On a new router, decline the initial configuration dialog if offered, then configure R1.

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.0.12.1 255.255.255.252
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.0.13.1 255.255.255.252
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
R1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
```

:::expected
After switch ports finish transitioning, Gi0/2 should be up/up. The transit ports may remain down until R2 is enabled. From PC-A's Desktop → Command Prompt, run `ping 192.168.10.1`. Repeat after address resolution if the first attempt loses a reply. Resolve any local failure before adding routes.
:::

steps.title: Configure R2 and prove the local links
steps.body:
Use R2's console, not R1's.

```ios R2
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R2
R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R2(config-if)# ip address 10.0.12.2 255.255.255.252
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R2(config-if)# ip address 10.0.13.2 255.255.255.252
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
R2(config-if)# ip address 192.168.20.1 255.255.255.0
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# end
R2# show ip interface brief
R2# show ip route
R2# ping 10.0.12.1
R2# ping 10.0.13.1
```

:::expected
Both transit pings should succeed, and PC-B should ping `192.168.20.1`. Each router has connected routes for its three /30 or /24 networks and local routes for its own addresses on images that display L entries. Neither router has a route to the other LAN. PC-A's ping to `192.168.20.12` should fail at this stage. This is a planned baseline, not a reason to change the PC mask.
:::

steps.title: Observe the missing return route
steps.body:
Before configuration, write the expected source of R1’s ordinary ping and PC-A’s ping. For each, identify the reply destination R2 must look up. Add only R1's remote-LAN route.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip route 192.168.20.0 255.255.255.0 gigabitethernet0/0 10.0.12.2
R1(config)# end
R1# show ip route static
R1# ping 192.168.20.12
```

On PC-A, run:

```text
ping 192.168.20.12
```

:::expected
R1 should list the /24 static through Gi0/0 and `10.0.12.2` at distance 1. R1's ordinary ping normally succeeds because its source is `10.0.12.1`, reachable through R2's connected transit route. PC-A's ping fails because R2 has no route back to `192.168.10.11`. Confirm that absence with R2's `show ip route`. In Simulation mode, you can follow the request toward PC-B and the return failure at R2. Do not infer this diagnosis from a failed ping alone outside this controlled configuration.
:::

steps.title: Restore the return path
steps.body:
```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# ip route 192.168.10.0 255.255.255.0 gigabitethernet0/0 10.0.12.1
R2(config)# end
R2# show ip route static
```

:::expected
R2 now has the return /24 at distance 1. Repeat PC-A's ping to PC-B, then ping `192.168.10.11` from PC-B. Both should succeed. Optionally run `tracert 192.168.20.12` from PC-A; response addresses may vary, so use the selected routes and completed ping as the core evidence.
:::

steps.title: Add R1's floating route
steps.body:
Predict which of the two candidates will appear in configuration and which will be selected in the installed table. Use those as separate columns in your evidence record.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip route 192.168.20.0 255.255.255.0 gigabitethernet0/1 10.0.13.2 5
R1(config)# end
R1# show running-config
R1# show ip route static
```

:::expected
The configuration has two routes to `192.168.20.0/24`. The installed table still selects the primary at distance 1. Distance 5 makes the other route a backup; it does not mean five hops. The named interfaces prevent the primary from being resolved through the alternate link.
:::

steps.title: Add R2's floating return route
steps.body:
```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# ip route 192.168.10.0 255.255.255.0 gigabitethernet0/1 10.0.13.1 5
R2(config)# end
R2# show running-config
R2# show ip route static
```

:::expected
R2 likewise keeps the distance-1 primary selected while retaining the distance-5 backup in its configuration. Ping between PCs once more before introducing the next fault.
:::

steps.title: Fail the primary and inspect both tables
steps.body:
Predict the selected prefix, AD and next hop on **both** routers after failure, including the return direction. Shut only R1 Gi0/0. Keep it shut until you have collected the evidence.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
R1# show ip route static
```

Inspect `show ip interface brief` and `show ip route static` on R2 as well. The direct cable should make its primary link lose carrier. Repeat ordinary PC pings; a continuous-ping option is not required.

:::expected
After link and route updates, R1 should select the backup shown below, and R2 should select its return /24 through Gi0/1 and `10.0.13.1` at distance 5. Some probes may fail during the transition; no exact loss count or recovery time is promised.

```output R1# show ip route static
S    192.168.20.0/24 [5/0] via 10.0.13.2, GigabitEthernet0/1
```

PC-to-PC pings should recover over the backup. If they do not, inspect both directions and the backup interface state before restoring the primary.
:::

steps.title: Restore the primary link
steps.body:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip route static
```

:::expected
Allow the physical link to recover. Both routers should again select distance-1 routes through Gi0/0, while their backup lines remain configured. Recheck endpoint pings. Save a separate working project copy now if you want a checkpoint before the next experiment.
:::

steps.title: Make one host use the alternate path
steps.body:
Before entering the supplied host route, predict R1’s choices for PC-B (.12) and R2’s LAN address (.1). Explain whether AD 200 is compared with the /24’s AD 1 during those destination lookups.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip route 192.168.20.12 255.255.255.255 gigabitethernet0/1 10.0.13.2 200
R1(config)# end
R1# show ip route
R1# show ip route 192.168.20.12
```

:::expected
The /32 at distance 200 can coexist with the distance-1 /24. Traffic for PC-B selects /32 through Gi0/1; traffic for `192.168.20.1` selects /24 through Gi0/0. Ping both addresses from PC-A. Use Simulation mode or the installed entries to verify the destination decisions. Replies can return over the primary; an asymmetric path is not itself a failure in this unfiltered lab.
:::

steps.title: Create a real destination for the default route
steps.body:
On R2, add a loopback. It needs no cable.

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# interface loopback0
R2(config-if)# ip address 203.0.113.8 255.255.255.255
R2(config-if)# end
R2# show ip route
```

:::expected
R2 has a connected/local entry covering `203.0.113.8/32`; exact C/L presentation for loopbacks varies. From PC-A, `ping 203.0.113.8` should fail because R1 has no matching route or default. Record R1's current table to establish that reason.
:::

steps.title: Add the default and verify its limits
steps.body:
Predict which entry will serve the loopback and whether the existing PC-B host route will still win for PC-B. Keep the loopback test’s actual PC-A source and R2 return route in your record.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 gigabitethernet0/0 10.0.12.2
R1(config)# end
R1# show ip route
```

:::expected
R1 lists an S* /0 route through R2. PC-A should now ping `203.0.113.8` successfully, using R2's existing return route to the PC LAN. No more specific route at R1 covers that loopback. The /32 for PC-B still takes precedence over the default. This proves a default to a known lab destination; it does not establish Internet connectivity.
:::

steps.title: Remove temporary routes and save the baseline
steps.body:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# no ip route 192.168.20.12 255.255.255.255 gigabitethernet0/1 10.0.13.2 200
R1(config)# no ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 gigabitethernet0/0 10.0.12.2
R1(config)# end
R1# show running-config
R1# copy running-config startup-config
```

At the destination-filename prompt, press Enter and wait for completion. Then use R2's console:

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# no interface loopback0
R2(config)# end
R2# copy running-config startup-config
```

:::expected
Accept R2's filename prompt separately. Each router retains exactly its primary and floating remote-LAN route, and all physical interfaces are enabled. Confirm PC-to-PC ping. Save the project as `18-ipv4-static-baseline.pkt`. A project save and an IOS startup-configuration save are separate actions. Submit a state table for missing return route, repaired baseline, backup configured, primary failed, primary restored, host exception and default test. For each state name the relevant configured candidate, installed prefix/AD/action, tested source/destination and observed result. Distinguish the ordinary router ping from the endpoint test. Do not infer remote outage detection from the direct-cable failure test.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- **Local ping fails:** compare the address table, cable endpoints, switch port state and router `no shutdown`. A remote route cannot fix a local addressing problem.
- **A route is configured but absent:** inspect its distance, destination mask and required interface. Next-hop-only routes also need successful route resolution.
- **A route is installed but traffic fails:** confirm the actual peer address with its interface configuration, then inspect downstream and return routes.
- **Backup does not take over:** check that Gi0/0 really became unusable and Gi0/1 is still up. Compare both backup masks with their primary masks.
- **Two paths have distance 1:** the backup's distance may be omitted. Read the running configuration, remove the incorrect line, and re-enter it with distance 5.
- **A command or display differs:** use IOS `?` to check availability. Record the model/version and verify the same route decision using the full table; do not invent a matching screenshot.
lab.challenge:
Start from a copy of the saved baseline after Step 12: both transits are up; each router has its primary remote-LAN /24 and distance-5 backup; R1 has no host exception or default, and R2 has no Loopback0.

Add a new logical destination on R2: Loopback10 at **198.51.100.65/26**. It needs no cable. Build **network routes for the whole new /26** on R1 using Gi0/0 and 10.0.12.2 as primary, Gi0/1 and 10.0.13.2 as standby with AD 150. Do not add a default or change either existing LAN’s addressing. R2’s existing primary and backup return routes to PC-A remain applicable.

Before opening the answer, write the network identifier and mask, both R1 route commands and the R2 loopback configuration. Predict the installed source/distance and next hop in three states: both transits up, R1 Gi0/0 shut, and Gi0/0 restored. For each state, identify R2’s return route for PC-A’s source.

Implement and test from PC-A to the actual address 198.51.100.65. Keep the failed primary shut while collecting both routers’ interface/table evidence and an endpoint ping, then restore it separately. An ordinary R1 ping alone is insufficient. Explain why the route covering the whole /26 does not create working hosts at its other addresses. Save a separate challenge project with the primary restored.

Finally, on paper, replace only the standby mask with /27 while keeping its written network value 198.51.100.64 and AD 150. Decide which addresses that new prefix would attract while the /26 primary remains installed, and whether it is still a same-prefix floating backup.

:::solution
The new network is 198.51.100.64/26, mask 255.255.255.192, spanning .64–.127. Its loopback address .65 is valid.

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# interface loopback10
R2(config-if)# ip address 198.51.100.65 255.255.255.192
R2(config-if)# end
R2# show ip interface brief
R2# show ip route
```

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip route 198.51.100.64 255.255.255.192 gigabitethernet0/0 10.0.12.2
R1(config)# ip route 198.51.100.64 255.255.255.192 gigabitethernet0/1 10.0.13.2 150
R1(config)# end
R1# show running-config
R1# show ip route static
```

With both links up, R1 installs the /26 at AD 1 through 10.0.12.2; the AD-150 candidate remains configured. R2’s return to 192.168.10.0/24 uses 10.0.12.1 at AD 1. From PC-A run `ping 198.51.100.65` and record the result.

Introduce the independent failure only after that baseline works:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
R1# show ip route static
```

Leave it shut. R1’s new /26 should now use 10.0.13.2 at AD 150. The direct cable makes R2’s Gi0/0 lose carrier; its existing return /24 should use 10.0.13.1 at AD 5. Inspect R2’s interface state and route table and repeat PC-A’s ping before recovery. The two directions do not need equal distances.

Restore the primary in a separate operation:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip route static
```

Verify both routers return to their primary routes and PC-A reaches .65. On each router, save from privileged EXEC with `copy running-config startup-config`, accept the filename with Enter, and wait for completion. Save as `18-ipv4-new-prefix-challenge.pkt`. The original baseline remains available separately.

The /26 route covers possible destinations but does not create hosts. Only .65 was configured as this logical endpoint; another address needs a real responding owner and a usable path.

For the paper mask error, 198.51.100.64/27 spans .64–.95. It is a separate installed prefix, so matching traffic—including .65—can use the supposed standby while the /26 primary works. Addresses .96–.127 use /26. The error cannot be corrected by a higher distance alone; restore the matching /26 mask.
:::

questions.prompt: Which command produces the displayed default route?
options: ip default-gateway 10.0.12.2
questions.explanation: The destination and mask are both zero, identifying /0. The next hop is 10.0.12.2.

whyWrong.0: ip default-gateway serves host-mode management; it does not create this static route on an IP-routing router.
whyWrong.1: A /32 identifies one address, not a default.
whyWrong.2: This names the transit subnet as the destination and does not create a default.

questions.prompt: A floating static is configured but loses to a healthy primary route. Which command directly shows the configured backup line?
options: show ip route static
show interfaces
show running-config
show ip arp
questions.explanation: The running configuration includes configured candidates even when they are not selected into the routing table.

whyWrong.0: This filters installed routes and normally omits the losing floating candidate.
whyWrong.1: Interface details do not list static-route statements.
whyWrong.3: ARP shows address-resolution entries, not configured routes.

exhibit.title: Representative IOS excerpt
exhibit.text: ip route 10.9.0.0 255.255.0.0 GigabitEthernet0/1 10.0.13.2

questions.prompt: A usable fully specified route was entered as shown. Which description is correct?
options: It requires ARP resolution for each host in the remote /16.
It names 10.0.13.2 as the remote destination prefix.
It forwards the /16 through Gi0/1 without using an IP next hop.
It directs the remote /16 to 10.0.13.2 through Gi0/1.
questions.explanation: The destination and mask define 10.9.0.0/16; the interface and next hop jointly define its exit.

whyWrong.0: The Ethernet frame is addressed to the specified next hop, not individually to every remote IP.
whyWrong.1: 10.9.0.0/16 is the destination; 10.0.13.2 is the next router.
whyWrong.2: Both an exit interface and an IP next hop are explicitly supplied.

questions.prompt: A completed traceroute from PC-A lists R1, R2 and PC-B. Which conclusion is justified?
options: The reverse data path must use exactly the same interfaces.
The trace reached PC-B and received its responses.
No route in the network can change.
Every application on PC-B is healthy.
questions.explanation: A successful trace provides evidence about its probes and replies at that time. It is not a general application or symmetric-routing guarantee.

whyWrong.0: Replies can take another valid route.
whyWrong.2: Routes can change after the measurement.
whyWrong.3: Application services require their own tests.

questions.prompt: How does an ordinary configured static route learn that a remote application has failed?
options: It does not provide an application health check by itself
It receives periodic updates from the static next hop
It polls that application whenever the metric is zero
It detects the failure from its configured prefix length
questions.explanation: A static route defines forwarding information. Interface/resolution eligibility can affect installation, but an ordinary route is not an application monitor.

whyWrong.1: Static route statements do not establish a routing-update protocol.
whyWrong.2: Static metric zero does not configure an application probe.
whyWrong.3: A prefix describes destinations, not service health.

questions.prompt: Only server 10.20.30.40 must use neighbor 172.16.1.2. Which route leaves other hosts in 10.20.30.0/24 unaffected?
questions.explanation: The /32 host route matches only 10.20.30.40.

whyWrong.1: The /24 applies to the whole subnet.
whyWrong.2: The default covers all destinations without a more specific match.
whyWrong.3: The host bits are nonzero for that /24 network mask.

exhibit.title: Representative IOS excerpt
exhibit.text: S 192.168.20.0/24 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0

questions.prompt: Gi0/0 is Ethernet. What consequence follows from this interface-only remote-LAN route?
options: R1 treats covered destinations as on-link and may ARP for each destination.
R1 automatically discovers the correct IP next hop using CDP.
The route is a connected interface route with code C.
R1 uses 192.168.20.0 as the next router address.
questions.explanation: Without an explicit next hop, the Ethernet route can cause destination-by-destination ARP. This is unsuitable as the normal design for a remote LAN.

whyWrong.1: CDP does not fill in a missing static-route next hop.
whyWrong.2: The S code remains static; the display wording does not make it an interface-address-derived C route.
whyWrong.3: The prefix identifies destinations, not the next router.

questions.prompt: An OSPF route to 10.5.0.0/16 has distance 110. Which TWO statements correctly describe a static backup to that same prefix?
options: Distance 5 makes the route less preferred than OSPF.
Distance 255 is the safest usable standby value.
The backup's next hop must still be usable when it is needed.
A usable backup can have distance 120.
questions.explanation: The backup must lose the distance comparison while the preferred route exists, and must have a usable path when that route disappears.

whyWrong.0: 5 is lower than 110 and would be preferred for the same prefix.
whyWrong.1: Distance 255 is not installed as a usable route.

exhibit.title: Representative IOS excerpt
exhibit.text:
Configured:
ip route 192.168.20.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.12.2
Gi0/0: administratively down/down
No covering route to 10.0.12.2 in the installed table.

questions.prompt: The only path to 10.0.12.2 was the now-down Gi0/0 connected subnet. No other route resolves it. Why is the configured next-hop-only route absent?
options: The remote network must use the transit link's /30 mask.
IOS cannot resolve the configured next hop.
A static route never installs until its destination answers a ping.
Static routes require a routing-protocol neighbor.
questions.explanation: A recursive route requires a valid route that resolves its next hop. The stated resolving route is gone.

whyWrong.0: The destination mask describes the remote LAN independently of the transit subnet.
whyWrong.2: An ordinary static route does not test the destination with ping.
whyWrong.3: Static routing does not require a dynamic-protocol adjacency.

questions.prompt: R1 and R2 have usable defaults pointing at one another and no other route covering 203.0.113.77. With ordinary forwarding and no filtering, what happens to a packet for that address?
options: The lowest next-hop address breaks the forwarding loop.
It can loop between the routers until its TTL expires.
The router with the lowest static AD becomes the final destination.
The default itself creates an Internet path.
questions.explanation: Each lookup selects a default back to the other router. Each forwarding hop reduces TTL, limiting the loop.

whyWrong.0: Each router independently follows its default; next-hop address magnitude is not a loop-breaking rule.
whyWrong.2: Administrative distance selects sources locally; it does not make a router own the destination.
whyWrong.3: A forwarding instruction cannot create downstream connectivity.

questions.prompt: Both displayed routes are installed. Which next hop handles 10.1.0.77?
options: 10.0.13.2, because /24 is the longer match
10.0.12.2, because distance 1 is lower
Neither, because a /32 is required
Both, because every overlapping route load-shares
questions.explanation: 10.1.0.77 matches both prefixes. Forwarding selects /24, independently of the distances of different prefixes.

whyWrong.1: Distance is not compared between different installed prefix lengths for forwarding.
whyWrong.2: A network route covers all matching addresses.
whyWrong.3: Overlapping prefixes are not equal-cost paths to one identical prefix.

exhibit.title: Representative IOS excerpt
exhibit.text:
R1: LAN 192.168.10.1/24, transit 10.0.12.1/30
R2: LAN 192.168.20.1/24, transit 10.0.12.2/30
R1 ordinary ping to PC-B succeeds; PC-A ping fails.

questions.prompt: In the shown isolated lab, interfaces, host addressing and the outbound route are verified. R2 has no default or other route to 192.168.10.0/24. Which command on R2 fixes the missing return path?
options: ip default-gateway 192.168.10.1
questions.explanation: R2 must route toward the PC-A subnet using R1's adjacent transit address, 10.0.12.1.

whyWrong.0: The host-mode gateway command does not create the required routed entry.
whyWrong.1: R2 already has the PC-B LAN connected; the missing destination is PC-A's LAN.
whyWrong.2: 10.0.12.2 is R2's own transit address, not its next hop.

questions.prompt: Which R1 ping source specifically tests the return route to its LAN 192.168.10.0/24 when pinging remote PC-B?
options: 10.0.12.2, R2's transit address
192.168.20.12, PC-B's address
192.168.10.1, R1's LAN interface address
10.0.12.1, R1's transit address
questions.explanation: A reply to 192.168.10.1 requires a route covering that LAN prefix. Select it through supported extended-ping options.

whyWrong.0: R1 cannot normally use another router's address as its own ping source.
whyWrong.1: The remote destination is not R1's source address.
whyWrong.3: A reply to the transit source tests a different prefix.

questions.prompt: R1's primary interface remains up because it connects to a switch. A remote router beyond that switch fails. No tracking is configured. What should you conclude about the static backup?
options: Raising the backup distance enables remote-failure detection.
The primary may remain installed despite the remote failure.
Static routes exchange updates and will learn the failure.
The backup installs automatically whenever a remote ping fails.
questions.explanation: Ordinary static routing does not provide an end-to-end health check. A local active interface can keep a fully specified route installed even when downstream delivery fails.

whyWrong.0: Distance changes preference rather than adding health monitoring.
whyWrong.2: Static routes do not exchange routing-protocol updates.
whyWrong.3: No probe tracking is configured, so failed pings do not themselves withdraw the primary.

questions.prompt: The remote LAN is 198.51.100.64/26 and peer 10.0.12.2 is directly reachable. Which command names exactly that destination network?
questions.explanation: The /26 mask is 255.255.255.192 and the aligned network starts at .64, covering .64–.127.

whyWrong.0: The /24 mask does not describe the requested /26 and .64 is not its aligned network.
whyWrong.1: That aligned /26 covers .0–.63, a different block.
whyWrong.3: A .65 destination has nonzero host bits for this /26 network route.

questions.prompt: Which command removes the displayed backup while preserving the primary?
questions.explanation: Match the backup’s prefix, mask, exit interface, next hop and explicit distance, then verify configuration.

whyWrong.0: This names a host route that is not the shown /24 backup.
whyWrong.1: This is the primary statement, which the task requires preserving.
whyWrong.3: This targets a different next-hop-only form and does not identify the shown backup.

questions.prompt: R1 must reach the remote LAN through the adjacent R2 interface. Which next hop belongs in R1’s fully specified route?
options: 192.168.20.1, because it is the remote default gateway
192.168.10.11, because it is the requesting client
10.0.12.1, because it is R1’s sending interface
10.0.12.2, because it is R2 on the selected transit
questions.explanation: For this directly adjacent fully specified path, the next hop is the peer on the selected transit link.

whyWrong.0: This is R2’s remote LAN interface, not the stipulated adjacent transit peer.
whyWrong.1: The client is the packet source, not the next routed hop toward the remote LAN.
whyWrong.2: R1’s own address is not the next router.

exhibit.title: Both configured candidates lose eligibility
exhibit.text:
R1 configured:
ip route 192.168.20.0 255.255.255.0 Gi0/0 10.0.12.2
ip route 192.168.20.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.13.2 5
Gi0/0 is down. The only route to 10.0.13.2 is also withdrawn.
No other route or default resolves either next hop.

questions.prompt: The primary route is withdrawn. Which result follows from these complete eligibility observations?
options: The configured backup installs because its distance exceeds 1
The router creates a new next-hop route from the remote prefix
No route to the remote /24 can install from these candidates
Both statics remain installed because their configuration remains
questions.explanation: The primary lost its required interface. The next-hop-only backup also has no valid resolving route. Preference cannot make an ineligible candidate usable.

whyWrong.0: A suitable distance is insufficient without a resolvable next hop.
whyWrong.1: The remote static cannot supply a valid independent path to its own unreachable next hop.
whyWrong.3: Configuration persistence does not establish installation.

exhibit.title: Failover with no reverse route
exhibit.text:
PC-A 192.168.10.11/24 → PC-B 192.168.20.12/24; both gateways correct.
After direct Gi0/0 link failure:
R1 installed S 192.168.20.0/24 [5/0] via 10.0.13.2 Gi0/1.
R2 Gi0/1 and both LANs are up; request delivery is observed.
R2 has no route or default for 192.168.10.0/24 after its Gi0/0 return route is withdrawn.
No filtering.

questions.prompt: PC-A’s request reaches PC-B over the backup after the direct primary link fails. Which interpretation fits the complete evidence?
options: Different ADs in the two directions prevent replies from being forwarded
R1 must use a /32 instead of a /24 before PC-B can reply
R1’s outbound /24 is enough to establish R2’s route back to PC-A
R2 needs its own route to PC-A, and no such route remains installed
questions.explanation: R1 has a working backup for the outbound destination, but R2’s only return route depended on the failed primary. The reverse destination needs its own eligible path.

whyWrong.0: Administrative distances are local preferences; opposite directions do not need matching values.
whyWrong.1: The /24 already delivered the request to PC-B. Its specificity does not create R2’s missing reverse route.
whyWrong.2: Forward and return route tables are independent.

exhibit.title: Equal-preference paths violate the standby policy
exhibit.text:
ip route 192.168.20.0 255.255.255.0 Gi0/0 10.0.12.2
ip route 192.168.20.0 255.255.255.0 Gi0/1 10.0.13.2
Both transits work. The installed /24 shows two static next hops at [1/0].

questions.prompt: The policy requires Gi0/0 as primary and Gi0/1 as standby. What repair follows from the actual table and configuration?
options: Remove both routes and change the LAN mask to /25
Raise the Gi0/1 candidate’s distance above 1 for the same /24
Give Gi0/1 a more-specific /25 so it becomes less preferred
Increase the Gi0/0 route’s distance above the Gi0/1 route
questions.explanation: Both statements omit an override and use AD 1, matching the observed equal-preference installed paths. Reconfigure the intended standby with a higher usable distance while preserving the prefix.

whyWrong.0: No addressing or primary-route failure is shown.
whyWrong.2: A more-specific installed prefix can attract traffic despite a higher AD.
whyWrong.3: That would prefer the intended standby instead of the primary.

exhibit.title: Construct matching primary and standby routes
exhibit.text:
Destination LAN: 198.51.100.64/26
Required primary: R1 Gi0/0 to directly adjacent 10.0.12.2
Required standby: R1 Gi0/1 to directly adjacent 10.0.13.2, AD 150
Both peers and the complete return path work. No other candidate for this /26 exists.

questions.prompt: Which two configured candidates satisfy the stated network policy? (Choose two.)
questions.explanation: The network and backup must describe the same /26. Default static AD 1 supplies primary preference; AD 150 is a usable lower preference and the named exits bind each candidate to its intended link.

whyWrong.1: This is a different /27 and can take traffic while the /26 primary is healthy.
whyWrong.2: AD 255 cannot supply an installed backup.
whyWrong.3: AD 200 would lose to the proposed AD 150 standby, reversing policy.

exhibit.title: Representative IOS excerpt
exhibit.text:
Complete relevant R1 routes:
C 192.168.10.0/24, Gi0/2
C 10.0.12.0/30, Gi0/0
S 192.168.20.0/24 [1/0] via 10.0.12.2
Complete relevant R2 routes (no default):
C 10.0.12.0/30, Gi0/0
C 192.168.20.0/24, Gi0/2

questions.prompt: All shown interfaces and PC gateways are correct, and no filtering is configured. PC-A at 192.168.10.11 pings PC-B at 192.168.20.12. Which result follows?
options: The request fails because R1 needs a /32 for every PC.
The request can reach PC-B, but R2 lacks a route for its reply to PC-A.
R2 learns the return route automatically from the received request.
Both directions work because the transit network is connected.
questions.explanation: R1 has the outbound /24. R2 can deliver to its connected PC-B LAN but has no route covering the source LAN for the reply.

whyWrong.0: The /24 already covers PC-B.
whyWrong.2: Receiving an ordinary packet does not install a reverse static route.
whyWrong.3: The reply destination is the PC-A LAN, not the transit subnet.

exhibit.title: Two transits share one destination-facing interface
exhibit.text:
R1 has /24 primary via R2 on Gi0/0 AD 1 and same-prefix backup via R2 on Gi0/1 AD 5.
Both transits stay up and the peer addresses remain reachable.
R2’s only interface into that destination LAN becomes administratively down.
No tracking or alternate route into that LAN exists.

questions.prompt: Which two conclusions follow after R2’s LAN interface fails? (Choose two.)
options: R1 must withdraw the primary because the final LAN is unavailable
Changing the backup AD alone repairs R2’s failed LAN
R1’s default automatically replaces its still-installed /24
R1 can retain its installed primary even though delivery now fails
R1’s backup through the same R2 does not bypass the failed LAN
questions.explanation: R1’s local primary transit remains eligible without remote tracking. Both paths terminate at the same R2, so neither avoids R2’s failed LAN interface.

whyWrong.0: The explicit local eligibility evidence remains true; no remote tracking is configured.
whyWrong.1: Preference changes cannot restore the destination interface.
whyWrong.2: A less-specific default does not replace a still-selected /24 for matching traffic.

exhibit.title: Alternate recursive next-hop resolution
exhibit.text:
R1 configuration:
ip route 192.168.20.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.12.2
ip route 192.168.20.0 255.255.255.0 Gi0/1 10.0.13.2 5
Independent installed resolver after Gi0/0 failure:
S 10.0.12.2/32 [1/0] via 10.0.13.2, Gi0/1
The Gi0/1 peer is reachable and can reach 10.0.12.2.

questions.prompt: After Gi0/0 fails, why can R1 still display the remote /24 at distance 1 rather than selecting its distance-5 candidate?
options: The primary is automatically converted into a fully specified route.
The next-hop-only primary can resolve through the surviving host route
Both static candidates must be installed whenever their prefixes match.
The backup /24 is more specific than the primary /24.
questions.explanation: The primary is next-hop-only. The supplied independent /32 keeps its next hop recursively reachable through Gi0/1, so it can remain eligible at AD 1. A fully specified primary would bind it to the intended failed exit.

whyWrong.0: The configuration remains next-hop-only; alternate recursive resolution, not automatic conversion, explains the route.
whyWrong.2: For this same prefix the eligible AD-1 candidate remains preferred over AD 5.
whyWrong.3: Both candidates describe the identical /24; only the separate /32 resolves the primary’s next hop.

exhibit.title: Different ping results with incomplete evidence
exhibit.text:
R1’s ordinary ping to PC-B succeeds.
PC-A behind R1 cannot ping PC-B.
The engineer has not yet recorded R1’s ping source, PC-A’s gateway, or R2’s return routes.
No further fault evidence is supplied.

questions.prompt: What is the most defensible next action before changing routing?
options: Compare the two test sources, host configuration and actual return routes
Raise all static distances to force a new path
Change PC-A’s mask so it includes the remote destination
Assume R2 lacks a return route and add a default immediately
questions.explanation: The symptom suggests a source-dependent difference but does not uniquely identify its cause. Obtain the PC configuration and route back to its actual source before proposing a repair.

whyWrong.1: No source-preference defect has been established.
whyWrong.2: Broadening the LAN mask violates the addressing design and can create a new failure.
whyWrong.3: Missing reverse routing is possible, but the stated evidence does not yet establish it.

cards.front: IPv4 static-route core syntax?
cards.back: `ip route destination-network subnet-mask next-hop` in global configuration. Use the destination network and the actual next router's address.

cards.front: Ordinary IOS static and connected distances?
cards.back: Static: 1. Connected: 0. Compare candidate sources for the same prefix.

cards.front: Can distance 255 be a working floating static?
cards.back: No. Distance 255 is unusable. A backup must have a usable path and a distance greater than the primary but below 255.

cards.front: Mask for an IPv4 host route?
cards.back: `255.255.255.255`, or /32. It matches one destination address.

cards.front: How do you write an IPv4 default route?
cards.back: `ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 next-hop`. Substitute the real peer address. A fully specified form also names the exit interface.

cards.front: What does S* identify in an IPv4 route table?
cards.back: S means static; * marks a candidate default. Inspect the /0 entry and gateway-of-last-resort line.
A static route to /24 through 10.0.12.2. Brackets show administrative distance 1 and metric 0.

cards.front: Does 'S ... is directly connected' mean a C route?
cards.back: No. S still means static, commonly with an exit-interface-only form. C is derived from an interface's connected prefix.

cards.front: What makes a static route fully specified?
cards.back: It names both exit interface and next hop. On Ethernet ARP still resolves the next hop's MAC address.

cards.front: How is a recursive next hop resolved?
cards.back: Another usable routing-table entry determines the path to it. A connected transit prefix is the simplest case. Self-dependent resolution is invalid.

cards.front: Why avoid an Ethernet interface-only route to a remote LAN?
cards.back: It treats remote destinations as on-link and may ARP for each. Name the peer next hop; do not rely on proxy ARP hiding a mistake.

cards.front: What makes a route a floating static?
cards.back: A higher distance than the preferred route to the same prefix. It can install after primary withdrawal if the backup path is usable.

cards.front: Example backup distances behind static 1 and OSPF 110?
cards.back: 5 follows static 1; 120 follows OSPF 110. A distance-5 route would beat OSPF 110 for the same prefix.

cards.front: Where can you see an unselected floating static?
cards.back: `show running-config`. The static filter on the route table shows selected entries, not every candidate.

cards.front: Does a /32 at distance 200 lose to a /24 at distance 1?
cards.back: When both are installed, /32 wins forwarding for its one destination. Distance selects candidates for the same prefix.

cards.front: Why select a source address in extended ping?
cards.back: An ordinary router ping normally uses its outgoing interface address. A LAN source tests the return route covering that LAN.

cards.front: Router ping works but a LAN PC ping fails: what next?
cards.back: Compare test sources, reverse routes and PC addressing/gateway. The symptom alone does not uniquely identify a missing return route.

cards.front: Risk of two routers defaulting to one another?
cards.back: Unknown destinations can loop until TTL expires. The default is an instruction, not proof of delivery.

cards.front: How do you verify forwarding when only a default matches?
cards.back: Inspect the installed /0 with `show ip route`, calculate the longest match, and test a real destination. Destination-specific diagnostic behavior can vary.

cards.front: Can a configured static disappear from the routing table?
cards.back: Yes: its interface can fail, its next hop can stop resolving, or a better candidate can win. The configuration may remain unchanged.

cards.front: Can an installed static still fail to deliver traffic?
cards.back: Yes. Installation does not prove Ethernet neighbor resolution, downstream delivery or the reply path.

cards.front: Why can a backup through the same far router fail to restore a LAN?
cards.back: Both paths may share the failed destination-facing router or interface. A second transit is not protection against every failure.

cards.front: Why name the exit interface as well as the next hop in the two-link lab?
cards.back: It binds that static candidate to the intended exit, preventing alternate recursive resolution from keeping the primary eligible through the backup link.
