tickets.title: A backup takes half the LAN traffic
tickets.scenario: R1 should use 10.0.12.2 for branch 192.168.20.0/24 and reserve 10.0.13.2 as standby. Both transit links work. Traffic to .50 uses standby while .150 uses primary. Excerpts are representative.
tickets.question: Which error explains this?
options: The higher backup AD makes it preferred for every destination.
The backup is a separate /25 prefix and wins for .0 through .127.
The two overlapping prefixes form equal-cost paths for all hosts.
The primary must be removed for the backup to float.
tickets.explanation: The /25 covers .50 and wins longest match. .150 does not match it. AD is not compared between different installed prefix lengths; overlapping prefixes are not equal-cost paths, and removing the primary defeats standby operation.
tickets.fix:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# no ip route 192.168.20.0 255.255.255.128 10.0.13.2 5
R1(config)# ip route 192.168.20.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.13.2 5
R1(config)# end
R1# show ip route static
```
Only the distance-1 /24 should remain selected while the primary works. Verify both destination decisions, then test primary-link failure and recovery in the isolated lab before saving.

tickets.title: Router ping works; PC ping fails
tickets.scenario: PC-A is 192.168.10.11/24, gateway 192.168.10.1 on R1. PC-B is 192.168.20.12/24, gateway 192.168.20.1 on R2. Local/transit pings work, with no filtering. R1's ping uses source 10.0.12.1 and succeeds; PC-A's fails.

exhibits.title: Complete relevant R2 routes; no default

tickets.question: Which repair addresses the evidence?
options: Add another outbound route to PC-B on R1.
Change PC-A to /16.
Add R2's route to 192.168.10.0/24 through 10.0.12.1.
Use R2's own 10.0.12.2 as the return next hop.
tickets.explanation: R2's connected /30 covers the router's ping source, but no route covers PC-A. The outbound route exists, /16 violates the plan, and R2's own address is not its next router.
tickets.fix:
```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# ip route 192.168.10.0 255.255.255.0 gigabitethernet0/0 10.0.12.1
R2(config)# end
R2# show ip route static
```
Repeat PC-A-to-PC-B and reverse pings. Both should succeed under the stated conditions. Verify before saving.

chapters.title: IPv6 addressing
chapters.subtitle: Read IPv6 addresses, identify their purpose and verify how a host obtains one.

sources.title: RFC 8106: DNS Options in Router Advertisements
Cisco: IPv6 Addressing and Basic Connectivity
Cisco: Understand the IPv6 Link-Local Address

chapters.summary: Work through IPv6 notation, prefix sizes, address types, modified EUI-64, Neighbor Discovery and SLAAC. Configure interfaces and diagnose address and gateway mistakes.

sections.body:
IPv6 changes more than the length of an address. A host can use several addresses on one interface, discover its router without DHCP, and resolve neighbors without ARP. Start by separating those jobs. Address notation tells you which bits an address contains; its type and scope tell you where it is meaningful; configuration and discovery determine how the host can use it.

All `2001:db8::/32` examples in this course are reserved documentation addresses used in isolated exercises. They are not public Internet destinations. Uppercase and lowercase hexadecimal represent the same bits.

sections.title: Addresses and interfaces
sections.body:
:::facts
- An IPv6 address is **128 bits**, written as eight 16-bit hexadecimal groups.
- One hexadecimal digit represents **4 bits**. Each full group contains **4 digits**.
- `::` can replace a consecutive run of zero groups only **once** in an address.
- An ordinary Ethernet LAN using SLAAC uses a **/64** prefix. That is not a rule that every IPv6 route or link must be /64.
- IPv6 has **unicast, anycast and multicast**; it has no IPv6 broadcast address.
- Neighbor Discovery uses **ICMPv6**, not ARP. Automatic host addressing and default-router discovery are related but separate operations.
:::

A **unicast address** identifies one interface for delivery. A host commonly has a link-local address plus one or more other unicast addresses on the same Ethernet interface. This is normal: the link-local address serves local-link communication, while another address can identify traffic that crosses routers. Some systems also maintain temporary addresses for outbound connections.

Do not assume that all IPv6 addresses are formed from a MAC address. Manual assignment, DHCPv6 and different automatic identifier methods are possible. A host displaying a long, unfamiliar suffix may be correctly configured. Check its prefix, lifetime and assignment method before replacing it with a familiar-looking address.

An IPv6-enabled router can also act as an endpoint. Answering a ping addressed to one of its own interfaces is different from forwarding a packet between two interfaces. The lab first establishes addressing; the next chapter develops the routing-table decisions for remote networks.

sections.title: Read and compress an address
sections.body:
A full example is `2001:0db8:0000:0000:0001:0000:0000:0001`. First remove leading zeros within groups: `2001:db8:0:0:1:0:0:1`. Then compress the longest run of complete zero groups with `::`. There are two equal runs of length two, so the recommended canonical form chooses the first: `2001:db8::1:0:0:1`.

**Canonical** means the consistent spelling recommended by RFC 5952, not the only valid spelling. IPv6 syntax permits several representations of the same bits. Canonical text uses lowercase, removes leading zeros, chooses the longest zero run, chooses the leftmost run on a tie, and does not compress a single zero group.

| Address text | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| `2001:db8:0:1:0:0:0:a` | Valid expanded-short form |
| `2001:db8:0:1::a` | Canonical form of the same address |
| `2001:db8::1:0:0:0:a` | Valid, but compresses only one zero group and is not canonical |
| `2001:db8::1::a` | Invalid: two `::` sequences make expansion ambiguous |
| `2001:db8:1:2:3:4:5:6:7` | Invalid: nine groups exceed 128 bits |

To expand `2001:db8:5::12:3456`, count the five visible groups. Three groups are missing, so expand to `2001:0db8:0005:0000:0000:0000:0012:3456`. Counting visible groups is more reliable than guessing from the number of colons.

Leading and trailing zeros are different. `0a00` becomes `a00`, not `a`. Removing the final zeros would change the value from hexadecimal A00 to A. When checking a configuration, expand both addresses if their short forms look deceptively similar.

sections.title: Work out the prefix
sections.body:
The suffix `/n` means that the first `n` bits identify the prefix. For `2001:db8:10:1::25/64`, the first four full groups identify `2001:db8:10:1::/64`. The final 64 bits identify the interface within the conventional /64 subnet structure.

A /64 is the standard choice for ordinary Ethernet SLAAC because its 64-bit interface identifier and the advertised prefix must total 128 bits. Other prefix lengths are valid for other purposes. A /48 can describe a site's allocation, /128 identifies one address, and /127 is standardized for appropriate router-to-router point-to-point links. This chapter's LANs and the next chapter's training links use /64 for clarity, not because other lengths are invalid.

Calculate the number of equal-size subnets with `2^(new prefix − original prefix)`. Dividing a /56 into /64s uses eight more prefix bits, yielding 256 subnets. A /48 yields 65,536 /64s; a /60 yields 16.

For a worked plan, split `2001:db8:1200:3400::/56` into /64s. The first 56 bits fix the first three groups and the first byte of the fourth. The fourth group therefore ranges from `3400` to `34ff`. The first /64 is `2001:db8:1200:3400::/64`, the next is `2001:db8:1200:3401::/64`, and the last is `2001:db8:1200:34ff::/64`.

A /60 stops after three hexadecimal digits of the fourth group. For `2001:db8:5:c7f2::1/60`, retain `c7f` and zero the remaining prefix-external bits. The network is `2001:db8:5:c7f0::/60`. Do not round it to `2001:db8:5:c700::/60`; that discards four retained bits.

There is no IPv4 broadcast-address subtraction. Nevertheless, avoid claiming every mathematical bit combination is an assignable ordinary host address: IPv6 has reserved addresses and anycast uses. Subnet counting and individual address assignment are distinct questions.

sections.title: Address types and scope
sections.body:
**Scope** describes the region in which an address is meaningful.

| Type or special address | Recognize it | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Global unicast | Common allocated space is `2000::/3` | Routable between networks when allocation, routing and policy permit |
| Documentation unicast | `2001:db8::/32` | Written examples and isolated labs; not public Internet use |
| Unique local | `fc00::/7`; locally generated prefixes use `fd00::/8` | Private routed connectivity within organizations or agreed sites |
| Link-local | Reserved block `fe80::/10` | Communication on one link; routers do not forward it onto another link |
| Multicast | `ff00::/8` | Delivery to members of a group within its scope |
| Loopback | `::1/128` | The local node itself |
| Unspecified | `::/128` | No assigned source address yet, including parts of address initialization |

A conforming link-local address uses `fe80` followed by zero bits before its 64-bit identifier. The /10 identifies the reserved block; it does not mean you should invent arbitrary nonzero bits in the remaining prefix area. You can manually use `fe80::1` on separate links, but two ordinary interfaces on the same link must not claim it as the same unicast identity.

A locally generated **unique local address** uses an `fd` prefix, a pseudorandom 40-bit Global ID, a 16-bit subnet ID and a 64-bit interface ID. The random portion helps independently chosen sites avoid collisions; it is not a guarantee. ULA is not intended for global Internet routing. It can still be routed inside a network with suitable routes and policies.

**Anycast** assigns the same address to multiple interfaces, with routing delivering a packet to one instance according to the selected route. It has no special visible prefix that proves an address is anycast. “Nearest” means reachable through the routing system's preferred path, not necessarily shortest geographic distance. Multicast instead addresses a group and can deliver copies to multiple members.

For local discovery, remember `ff02::1`, all IPv6 nodes on the link, and `ff02::2`, all IPv6 routers on the link. The `2` scope limits these groups to that link. A **solicited-node multicast address** combines `ff02::1:ff00:0/104` with the low 24 bits of a unicast or anycast address. For `2001:db8:10::12:3456`, those bits are `12:3456`, giving `ff02::1:ff12:3456`. Different addresses can share the same last 24 bits and therefore the same group; the complete target address still matters.

sections.title: Modified EUI-64
sections.body:
**Modified EUI-64** is one specific method of creating a 64-bit interface identifier from a 48-bit MAC address. It remains an explicit CCNA topic even though current standards recommend avoiding embedded stable MAC addresses as the default identifier strategy.

Work from MAC `00:1a:2b:3c:4d:5e`:

1. Split after the first three bytes: `00:1a:2b | 3c:4d:5e`.
2. Insert `ff:fe`: `00:1a:2b:ff:fe:3c:4d:5e`.
3. Invert the universal/local bit in the first byte: XOR with `02`. `00` becomes `02`.
4. Regroup the eight bytes into four groups: `021a:2bff:fe3c:4d5e`.
5. Append to `2001:db8:10:1::/64`: `2001:db8:10:1:21a:2bff:fe3c:4d5e`.

:::trap
Invert the bit; do not always add 2. A first byte of `02` becomes `00`, while `00` becomes `02`. The inserted bytes span the second and third groups of the four-group identifier: `xxxx:xxff:fexx:xxxx`. Seeing `fffe` alone is not proof that an address was generated from a MAC.
:::

On IOS, `ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:2::/64 eui-64` requests that method explicitly. For a real lab interface, derive the expected suffix from its displayed MAC. Do not copy a suffix from an example device and expect it to match yours.

sections.title: Neighbor Discovery and automatic addressing
sections.body:
**Neighbor Discovery (ND)** uses ICMPv6 messages for several jobs. Router Solicitation (RS, type 133) asks routers for information; Router Advertisement (RA, 134) supplies it. Neighbor Solicitation (NS, 135) and Neighbor Advertisement (NA, 136) resolve or verify local neighbors. Redirect (137) can inform a host of a better first hop.

```diagram
{"type":"sequence","title":"A host learns how to use its LAN","actors":["Host","Local router","Other nodes on link"],"steps":[{"from":0,"to":1,"label":"RS: request router information"},{"from":1,"to":0,"label":"RA: router lifetime and prefix information"},{"from":0,"to":2,"label":"DAD NS: check tentative address"},{"from":0,"to":1,"label":"NS when the next-hop MAC needs resolution"},{"from":1,"to":0,"label":"NA supplies neighbor information"}]}
```

**SLAAC** lets a host form an address using an advertised prefix and its own interface identifier. A valid RA with a nonzero router lifetime can also identify a default router, using the RA's link-local source address. Learning that router is separate from choosing an address.

The RA header's **M** flag indicates managed address configuration, and **O** indicates other configuration through DHCPv6. The **A** flag belongs to a Prefix Information Option and permits autonomous address formation from that prefix. Its **L** flag supplies on-link information. These are not mutually exclusive address modes: an A-enabled prefix can support SLAAC even when M is set, depending on client capabilities. A prefix's on-link status is not automatically implied merely because a host was assigned an address from it.

DHCPv6 can supply addresses and other settings, but ordinary IPv6 default-router discovery uses RA rather than a DHCPv6 default-gateway option. DNS information can come from DHCPv6, RA DNS options, or manual configuration. Do not promise that SLAAC alone provides DNS unless a supported DNS-information mechanism is also present.

Before normal use, **Duplicate Address Detection (DAD)** checks a tentative unicast address on the link. A DAD NS can use source `::` because the new address is not yet usable. A detected conflict prevents normal use of the duplicate. This is a local-link check, not a global uniqueness service.

For ordinary Ethernet address resolution, an NS targets the destination's solicited-node group and a responding neighbor supplies an NA. Neighbor reachability checks can instead use unicast NS. RAs can be periodic multicast or responses to solicitations; not every RA is necessarily multicast. Blocking essential ICMPv6 discovery messages can break connectivity, even when interface addresses look correct.

sections.title: Configure IPv6 on IOS
sections.body:
Use a complete static address when you want a predictable router address.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ipv6 unicast-routing
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:1::1/64
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address fe80::1 link-local
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ipv6 interface gigabitethernet0/0
```

The global command enables IPv6 forwarding on IOS routers where it is disabled by default. On the ordinary enabled Ethernet interface, with RA transmission not suppressed, the router can advertise its prefix. Interface addressing by itself does not enable inter-interface forwarding.

The address command enables IPv6 processing and the interface has a link-local address, automatically formed unless explicitly configured. `ipv6 enable` enables processing and an automatic link-local address without assigning a global prefix. An `eui-64` command creates an address from a prefix and derived identifier; it does not promise the convenient suffix `::1`.

sections.title: Verify and troubleshoot
sections.body:
Representative abbreviated output, with the configured address from above:

```output R1# show ipv6 interface brief
GigabitEthernet0/0 [up/up]          ← physical and protocol state
    FE80::1                       ← local-link identity
    2001:DB8:ACAD:1::1             ← configured global-form lab address
```

Use `show ipv6 interface` for prefix lengths, multicast groups and ND/RA information. Use `show interfaces` for the MAC used in an EUI-64 calculation. Use `show ipv6 neighbors` after generating local traffic; it shows observed neighbor bindings, not an inventory of every address on every nearby device.

A reachable neighbor has recently confirmed reachability. A stale entry is not automatically broken; it means that recent confirmation is absent. Incomplete means resolution has not completed and can be temporary. Sustained failure with incomplete resolution justifies checking the address, VLAN/link and target availability. Do not interpret every non-reachable state as the same fault.

If automatic hosts have only link-local addresses, inspect the router's forwarding setting, link state, advertised prefix and A flag before assuming DHCP is missing. If a manual gateway fails, confirm that the stated gateway is actually configured on the router. Similar-looking `acad:2::1` and `acad:20::1` are different addresses. Test by numeric address first so DNS does not conceal the addressing problem.

sections.title: Exam focus
sections.body:
Practice expansion and canonical compression, prefix masking and subnet counts without a calculator before checking your work. Identify scope and address purpose from the prefix, while remembering that anycast cannot be identified from text alone.

Then explain how address generation, duplicate detection, neighbor resolution, router discovery and DNS information differ. A correctly configured host needs the appropriate combination for its task; no single command or address pattern proves that all of them work.

lab.title: Configure IPv6 addresses and observe local discovery
lab.intro:
Practice revised September 2026. If you completed an earlier version, repeat the revised exercise and update its checkmarks.

The guided settings are supplied so you can concentrate on how an address is formed and what each test proves. Calculate before opening a solution; copy the actual addresses and observations from your own devices into the worksheet.


Create a fresh isolated file. You will configure one LAN manually, use modified EUI-64 and SLAAC on another, inspect the actual addresses, and test the difference between a router answering for itself and forwarding traffic. No DHCPv6 server, DNS service or static route is required: R1 directly connects both LANs.

This lab has not been executed on your simulator. The examples are representative; Packet Tracer's supported commands, client address-generation method and event detail depend on its version. Compare concepts and actual configuration rather than expecting identical MAC addresses or timings.
lab.topology:
| Connection | Cable |
|---|---|
| PC-A FastEthernet0 — SW1 FastEthernet0/1 | Copper straight-through |
| SW1 FastEthernet0/24 — R1 GigabitEthernet0/0 | Copper straight-through |
| PC-B FastEthernet0 — SW2 FastEthernet0/1 | Copper straight-through |
| SW2 FastEthernet0/24 — R1 GigabitEthernet0/1 | Copper straight-through |

Use fresh 2960 switches with default VLAN 1 access ports. Do not connect the switches together. The two LANs are different links, so R1 can use `fe80::1` on each without a same-link duplicate. Gi0/2 is unused.

| Interface or host | Address/prefix | Gateway |
|---|---|---|
| R1 Gi0/0 | `2001:db8:acad:1::1/64`; link-local `fe80::1` | — |
| R1 Gi0/1 | `2001:db8:acad:2::/64` plus its EUI-64 identifier; link-local `fe80::1` | — |
| PC-A | `2001:db8:acad:1::10/64`, static | `fe80::1` |
| PC-B initially | Automatic IPv6 address from LAN 2's RA | Learned from R1 |
| PC-B later, for a stable fault test | `2001:db8:acad:2::20/64`, static | `fe80::1` |

All documentation addresses stay inside this project.

### Evidence worksheet

Keep this table in your notes. A prediction is written before the corresponding change; an observation comes from your actual device or is explicitly marked as a worksheet fallback.

| Checkpoint | Predict first | Record after testing |
|---|---|---|
| Gi0/1 EUI-64 | Operational MAC, inverted first byte, inserted bytes, complete global address | Actual global address; match or discrepancy |
| PC-B Automatic | Expected prefix and source of the default gateway | Actual address, gateway, and supported assignment behavior |
| New address ending ::99 | NS target and solicited-node destination | Packet fields, or unsupported-event note |
| Forwarding disabled | Local-router ping versus remote-PC ping | Both actual outcomes before repair |
| Forwarding restored | Expected cross-LAN recovery | Both endpoint pings and connected /64s |

The topology table supplies the guided /64 settings. Prefix allocation is tested independently in the challenge; do not copy a subnet from the table into that exercise.

steps.title: Configure R1's first LAN
steps.body:
Place, label and cable the devices. Decline the router setup dialog if offered. Configure the first interface and enable forwarding.

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# ipv6 unicast-routing
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:1::1/64
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address fe80::1 link-local
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ipv6 interface brief
```

:::expected
After the switch port becomes ready, Gi0/0 should show up/up with `fe80::1` and `2001:db8:acad:1::1`. The other interfaces may remain administratively down. A link-local plus another unicast address on one interface is normal.
:::

steps.title: Address PC-A manually and verify its local link
steps.body:
Under PC-A → Desktop → IP Configuration, select IPv6 Static. Enter address `2001:db8:acad:1::10`, prefix length `64` and gateway `fe80::1`. Leave IPv4 and DNS unused. Open Command Prompt:

```text
ipconfig /all
ping 2001:db8:acad:1::1
```

:::expected
Confirm the entered address and a link-local address in the client's display. The ping should succeed after discovery completes. If your version provides different display options, inspect IP Configuration directly. A successful local ping establishes this one link; it does not yet test routing between LANs.
:::

steps.title: Calculate R1's second interface identifier
steps.body:
Read Gi0/1's MAC before configuring its IPv6 address.

```ios R1
R1# show interfaces gigabitethernet0/1
```

Find the hardware-address line. Record the operational MAC shown as `address is`; a separate `bia` field is the burned-in address and can differ if manually overridden. With this fresh router they should normally match.

On paper, split the six MAC bytes after byte three, insert `ff:fe`, and XOR the first byte with hexadecimal `02`. Regroup the resulting eight bytes into four hexadecimal groups.

:::solution
Your calculation produces a 64-bit identifier. As a worked example only, MAC `00:1a:2b:3c:4d:5e` produces `021a:2bff:fe3c:4d5e`. A first byte of `02` would become `00`, not `04`. Keep your own MAC and result; the example is not a prediction of your router's hardware address.
:::

steps.title: Configure and verify modified EUI-64
steps.body:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:2::/64 eui-64
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address fe80::1 link-local
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ipv6 interface gigabitethernet0/1
```

:::expected
Gi0/1 should have a global-form address beginning `2001:db8:acad:2:` followed by the identifier you calculated. Record the entire address as **R1-LAN2** in your notes. The manual link-local stays `fe80::1`; do not assume its suffix matches the EUI-64 global address.

The detailed output should identify the /64 prefix and ND/RA settings on supported images. If the generated suffix differs, recheck the operational MAC, inserted bytes and bit inversion before changing the configuration.
:::

steps.title: Let PC-B obtain an automatic address
steps.body:
Open PC-B → Desktop → IP Configuration and select Automatic in the IPv6 area. Allow router advertisements and duplicate-address checks to complete. Inspect the resulting address and gateway with the GUI and, where supported, `ipconfig /all`.

:::expected
PC-B should acquire an address in `2001:db8:acad:2::/64` and learn R1's link-local address `fe80::1` as a default gateway. Record its complete address as **PC-B-AUTO**. The client may use an EUI-64-derived or another supported identifier; the router's explicit `eui-64` command does not dictate how the PC builds its own identifier.

DNS may remain empty because this lab provides no DNS information. That does not prevent numeric-address pings. If automatic assignment is unavailable in your version, record that limit, use the static values in Step 8 and substitute `2001:db8:acad:2::20` wherever Step 6 refers to **PC-B-AUTO**. Study the representative RA sequence in the lesson rather than claiming a successful SLAAC observation.
:::

steps.title: Test both LANs and inspect neighbors
steps.body:
From PC-B, ping PC-A by its known address.

```text
ping 2001:db8:acad:1::10
```

From PC-A, ping **PC-B-AUTO**, substituting the exact address recorded in Step 5. Do not paste the label itself. Then inspect R1:

```ios R1
R1# show ipv6 route
R1# show ipv6 neighbors
```

:::expected
Both endpoint pings should succeed. R1 has connected /64 routes for both LANs; it needs no static route for either one. Its neighbor table should contain bindings learned while delivering traffic, with the correct interface for each LAN. It need not list every IPv6 address each PC owns.

An entry may be reachable or stale depending on timing. Stale alone is not a failure. An incomplete entry that persists while pings fail calls for checking the target address and local link.
:::

steps.title: Observe a new neighbor-resolution exchange
steps.body:
Before generating traffic, calculate the target's last 24 bits and the solicited-node multicast destination. Keep that prediction next to the captured fields. The configuration below assigns the target; it does not supply your prediction.

First configure a temporary, previously unused **secondary** address on R1 Gi0/0. Do not remove the original.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:1::99/64
R1(config-if)# end
```

Switch Packet Tracer to Simulation mode. Enable ICMPv6/ND events in the event filter if available. From PC-A, ping `2001:db8:acad:1::99` for the first time. Step through the events and inspect the packet details. Because the destination is new to PC-A, this avoids pretending that clearing only R1's neighbor cache also clears the PC's cache.

:::expected
For normal address resolution, PC-A should send an NS for target `2001:db8:acad:1::99` to solicited-node group `ff02::1:ff00:99`. R1's NA supplies neighbor information; echo traffic can then complete. Earlier DAD or other discovery events may also appear. Identify each message by its actual source, destination and target rather than assuming the first envelope is the requested exchange.

If event detail is not modeled, record that limit and draw the expected sequence from the lesson. Return to Realtime mode before continuing.
:::

steps.title: Prepare stable host addresses for the forwarding test
steps.body:
Remove the temporary secondary address.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# no ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:1::99/64
R1(config-if)# end
```

Set PC-B to IPv6 Static: `2001:db8:acad:2::20`, prefix `64`, gateway `fe80::1`. Keep PC-A unchanged. On PC-B, ping the recorded **R1-LAN2** address and `2001:db8:acad:1::10`. From PC-A, ping `2001:db8:acad:2::20`.

:::expected
Local and cross-LAN pings should succeed before the fault. Record both PC configurations. Static host values make the next observation independent of whether an old SLAAC address or RA-learned route remains cached.
:::

steps.title: Disable forwarding and observe the difference
steps.body:
Predict both ping outcomes in the worksheet before making the change. Leave the fault present long enough to collect both results; do not paste the recovery step into the same block.

Only in this isolated lab, remove the forwarding command.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# no ipv6 unicast-routing
R1(config)# end
R1# show ipv6 interface brief
```

Repeat PC-A's ping to its local router address `2001:db8:acad:1::1`, then to remote PC-B `2001:db8:acad:2::20`. On PC-B, separately ping **R1-LAN2**.

:::expected
Each PC can still reach the router address on its own LAN, but PC-to-PC forwarding should fail. Interface addresses remain configured. This distinguishes “the router answers for itself” from “the router forwards between interfaces.”

The router also ceases acting as an advertising IPv6 router in this basic configuration. Do not assume existing automatic host addresses vanish immediately; their lifetimes and simulator handling are separate. The test deliberately uses static PC addresses.
:::

steps.title: Restore forwarding and save
steps.body:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ipv6 unicast-routing
R1(config)# end
R1# show ipv6 route
```

Repeat pings in both directions. When they succeed, save R1:

```ios R1
R1# copy running-config startup-config
```

:::expected
Press Enter at the destination-filename prompt and wait for completion. Both LAN /64s are present and PC-to-PC communication works. Save the project as `19-ipv6-addressing-baseline.pkt`. Record R1-LAN2's exact value so that later work does not mistakenly use `2001:db8:acad:2::1` as though EUI-64 had created it.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- **A numeric local ping fails:** compare every group of the target and interface address, link state and /64 prefix. Do not diagnose DNS when the test uses a literal address.
- **PC-B has only link-local while Automatic:** inspect R1's global forwarding command, Gi0/1 state and RA/prefix information. A DHCPv6 server is not required for SLAAC.
- **The supposed `::1` gateway is absent:** read the complete configured router address. EUI-64 does not create `::1` merely because it is convenient.
- **Neighbor resolution stays incomplete:** verify the target actually exists on the stated link. Clear or refresh caches only as a deliberate isolated-lab action; a correct route cannot resolve a nonexistent target.
- **Local router pings work, cross-LAN fails:** confirm `ipv6 unicast-routing`, both PC gateways and the connected prefixes. Use the controlled Step 9 evidence to distinguish this fault from general routing problems.
- **A source field or output label differs:** record what your simulator actually shows. Do not replace a correct calculated address merely to imitate illustrative output.
lab.challenge:
Use a copy of the restored baseline. First do the following calculations without commands:

1. Derive the modified EUI-64 address for MAC `02:aa:bb:cc:dd:ee` under `2001:db8:44:7::/64`, then derive its solicited-node multicast group.
2. Find the first and last /64 in `2001:db8:44:ab30::/60`. Number the /64s starting at **1** and allocate the **third** to a new LAN C.

Now implement LAN C without copying the solution. Add one blank 2960 switch SW3 and PC-C. Connect R1 Gi0/2 to SW3 Fa0/24 and PC-C FastEthernet0 to SW3 Fa0/1 with straight-through copper. Keep default access VLAN 1; do not connect SW3 to another switch. On the allocated /64 use router identifier `::1`, host identifier `::10`, and router link-local `fe80::3`. Set PC-C manually with the matching /64 and its local link-local gateway. Keep both original LANs unchanged.

Record the calculated prefix, complete router and host addresses, gateway, and commands before revealing the solution. Verify PC-C to its router and to PC-A `2001:db8:acad:1::10`; verify PC-A back to PC-C. Inspect the three connected /64s and the neighbor interfaces. Explain why no static route is needed and why repeating `fe80::1` on the original separate links was valid.

:::solution
The first byte `02` becomes `00`, giving identifier `00aa:bbff:fecc:ddee`. The full address is `2001:db8:44:7:aa:bbff:fecc:ddee`; its solicited-node group is `ff02::1:ffcc:ddee`.

The /60 contains 16 /64s from `2001:db8:44:ab30::/64` through `2001:db8:44:ab3f::/64`. Counting ab30 as first, the third is `2001:db8:44:ab32::/64`.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:44:ab32::1/64
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address fe80::3 link-local
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ipv6 interface brief
R1# show ipv6 route
R1# show ipv6 neighbors
```

PC-C uses `2001:db8:44:ab32::10`, prefix `64`, gateway `fe80::3`. On PC-C:

```text
ping 2001:db8:44:ab32::1
ping 2001:db8:acad:1::10
```

On PC-A:

```text
ping 2001:db8:44:ab32::10
```

After discovery, each test should succeed. R1 directly connects all three prefixes and already has IPv6 forwarding enabled, so extra statics are unnecessary. Its repeated original link-local address is meaningful on two different links, not a same-link duplicate. Save this successful extension under a new project filename after saving R1's running configuration; retain the original two-LAN baseline separately. If a test fails, collect the exact addresses, gateway and interface state before changing them.
:::

questions.prompt: What does /64 describe in an IPv6 address?
options: The first 64 bits identify the prefix.
The final 64 bits identify the prefix.
The subnet contains exactly 64 addresses.
The address contains a total of 64 bits.
questions.explanation: A prefix length counts the retained leading bits; 128 minus that length gives the remaining bits.

whyWrong.1: The prefix consists of the leading bits.
whyWrong.2: A prefix length is a bit count, not an address count.
whyWrong.3: The complete address still contains 128 bits.

questions.prompt: What is true of fd12:3456:789a:1::a1/64?
options: It is multicast because it begins with f.
It is a unique local address for routed private connectivity.
It is link-local and can never cross a router.
It is global unicast intended for normal public Internet allocation.
questions.explanation: fd falls inside the locally generated half of ULA fc00::/7. ULA can be routed within suitable private networks but is not intended for global Internet routing.

whyWrong.0: Multicast begins ff, not fd.
whyWrong.2: Link-local belongs to fe80::/10.
whyWrong.3: The fd prefix identifies locally generated ULA, not globally allocated Internet space.

questions.prompt: Which TWO groups identify all IPv6 nodes and all IPv6 routers, respectively, on the local link?
questions.explanation: ff02::1 is all-nodes and ff02::2 is all-routers, both with link-local multicast scope.

whyWrong.2: ff05::2 has site scope, not the requested link scope.
whyWrong.3: This is a solicited-node group, not the all-nodes group.

questions.prompt: The same unicast-format service address is assigned to instances in several locations and routing sends each packet to one preferred instance. What is this?
options: Broadcast to all locations
Multicast, requiring the address to start ff
Anycast; selection follows the routing system's preferred path
A duplicate that is forbidden even across separate routed links
questions.explanation: Anycast uses one shared address at multiple locations with routing choosing an instance. Its text has no unique anycast prefix.

whyWrong.0: IPv6 has no broadcast addressing type.
whyWrong.1: Multicast is group delivery and uses multicast-format addresses; this scenario is anycast.
whyWrong.3: Deliberate anycast across locations is a defined use, not an ordinary same-link unicast conflict.

questions.prompt: The same MAC is available, but an automatically addressed host does not contain ff:fe in its identifier. Which conclusion is justified?
options: IPv6 cannot operate without a modified EUI-64 identifier.
Another valid identifier method may be in use.
The host must have obtained its address from stateful DHCPv6.
The absence of ff:fe proves Duplicate Address Detection failed.
questions.explanation: SLAAC can use stable opaque or other supported identifiers; not all IIDs embed the MAC. Address appearance alone does not establish a fault.

whyWrong.0: Modified EUI-64 is one method, not a universal requirement.
whyWrong.2: SLAAC can use identifiers that do not embed the MAC, so the suffix does not establish DHCPv6 use.
whyWrong.3: DAD tests local uniqueness; it does not require a particular identifier pattern.

questions.prompt: A host obtains an address and DNS information from stateful DHCPv6. It has no manual routes. What ordinarily supplies its default router?
options: A Router Advertisement with a usable nonzero router lifetime
The DHCPv6 address lease always includes the default-router option.
The host uses its DHCPv6-provided DNS server as the router.
The prefix L flag identifies the router by itself.
questions.explanation: The host learns a default router from RA, independently of how DHCPv6 supplied its address and DNS.

whyWrong.1: Ordinary DHCPv6 address assignment does not supply the IPv6 default router; that normally comes from RA.
whyWrong.2: DNS configuration identifies a name server, not the default router.
whyWrong.3: L provides on-link prefix information; the RA source and router lifetime determine default-router information.

questions.prompt: Which TWO Neighbor Discovery statements are correct?
options: Address-resolution NS messages can target a solicited-node multicast group.
Every NS is broadcast to ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff.
A unicast NS can be used to verify a known neighbor's reachability.
Every stale neighbor entry proves a failed device.
questions.explanation: ND distinguishes initial address resolution from reachability confirmation. NS can be multicast or unicast depending on the operation.

whyWrong.1: IPv6 has no IP broadcast; ordinary IPv6 multicast uses multicast delivery.
whyWrong.3: Stale means reachability is not recently confirmed, not that failure is proven.

questions.prompt: A fresh IOS interface has no configured IPv6 address. Which single interface command enables IPv6 processing and an automatic link-local address without adding a global prefix?
options: ipv6 unicast-routing
ipv6 enable
ipv6 address 2001:db8:1::1/64
questions.explanation: ipv6 enable provides the requested interface behavior without supplying a global prefix.

whyWrong.0: That is a global forwarding command, not this interface-addressing instruction.
whyWrong.2: This also configures a global-form address, contrary to the requested result.
whyWrong.3: This configures IPv4.

questions.prompt: Which is the canonical spelling of 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0001:0000:0000:000a?
questions.explanation: Each zero run has two groups. Canonical spelling compresses the leftmost tied run and removes leading zeros within the remaining groups.

whyWrong.0: Two double-colon sequences make expansion ambiguous.
whyWrong.1: This is valid but compresses the rightmost of two equal zero runs.
whyWrong.2: Moving a zero into the 1 group changes the bits.

questions.prompt: Which is the canonical representation of 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0a00:0000:0001?
questions.explanation: Remove leading zeros and compress the longest run of three zero groups. The trailing zeros in a00 remain significant.

whyWrong.1: Changing a00 to a changes its numeric value.
whyWrong.2: Two double-colon sequences are invalid.
whyWrong.3: This is valid but does not use the canonical compression of the longest zero run.

questions.prompt: An example allocation is 2001:db8:5c00::/56. How many /64s fit, and which is the last?
questions.explanation: 64−56 leaves 8 subnet bits: 256 choices. They occupy the low byte of the fourth group, from 00 through ff.

whyWrong.0: 16 choices correspond to four extra bits, as with /60 to /64.
whyWrong.1: This changes retained bits in the third group.
whyWrong.3: The /56 fixes the upper byte of the fourth group; all 16 bits are not available.

questions.prompt: A site has 2001:db8:1200:3400::/56. Which proposed /64 is outside that allocation?
questions.explanation: The /56 retains 34 in the high byte of the fourth group. The /64 choices run from 3400 through 34ff; 3500 changes a retained bit.

whyWrong.0: This is the last /64 in the allocation.
whyWrong.1: The fixed first byte of the fourth group is 34.
whyWrong.3: This is the first /64 in the allocation.

questions.prompt: What is the prefix containing 2001:db8:5:c7f2::1/60?
questions.explanation: A /60 retains the first three groups and the first three hex digits of the fourth. Zero the last digit and all following bits.

whyWrong.1: c700 discards retained prefix bits.
whyWrong.2: The low fourth-group digit is outside /60 and must be zero in the network address.
whyWrong.3: This removes the entire retained c7f part.

questions.prompt: What /61 prefix contains 2001:db8:7:ab3d::25/61?
questions.explanation: After the first 60 bits, /61 retains one bit of the final hex digit. Hex d is binary 1101: retain its first bit and clear the last three, obtaining 1000, or 8. The block covers ab38 through ab3f.

whyWrong.0: This leaves nonzero bits outside the prefix.
whyWrong.1: A /61 boundary must clear the final three bits of the fourth group.
whyWrong.2: That clears a bit which /61 retains; it covers ab30 through ab37.

questions.prompt: An isolated site needs 20 distinct /64 LANs. Which smallest allocation from this list can contain them?
options: /61, providing 8 distinct /64 prefixes
/64, providing one distinct /64 prefix
/60, providing 16 distinct /64 prefixes
/59, providing 32 distinct /64 prefixes
questions.explanation: Five additional subnet bits provide 2^5 = 32 choices. A /59 is therefore the longest prefix, and smallest block, among these sufficient choices.

whyWrong.0: Eight is fewer than twenty.
whyWrong.1: One LAN prefix cannot meet twenty distinct /64 allocations.
whyWrong.2: Sixteen is fewer than twenty.

questions.prompt: MAC 00:1a:2b:3c:4d:5e uses modified EUI-64 on 2001:db8:10:1::/64. Which address results?
questions.explanation: Insert ff:fe after the first three MAC bytes and invert the first byte's U/L bit, changing 00 to 02. Regrouping yields 021a:2bff:fe3c:4d5e.

whyWrong.0: The first byte's U/L bit was not inverted.
whyWrong.1: The inserted bytes are in the wrong position.
whyWrong.3: EUI-64 does not assign the convenient suffix ::1.

questions.prompt: Derive the modified EUI-64 identifier from MAC 02:aa:bb:cc:dd:ee.
options: 04aa:bbff:fecc:ddee
00aa:bbcc:fffe:ddee
02aa:bbff:fecc:ddee
00aa:bbff:fecc:ddee
questions.explanation: 02 XOR 02 is 00. Insert ff:fe between bb and cc, then regroup the eight bytes into four groups.

whyWrong.0: Invert the U/L bit with XOR 02; do not always add 2.
whyWrong.1: Insert ff:fe after the first three MAC bytes, not after the fourth.
whyWrong.2: This inserts ff:fe but fails to invert the U/L bit.

questions.prompt: Which solicited-node multicast group corresponds to 2001:db8:4::ab12:3456?
questions.explanation: The last 24 bits are 12:3456. Combine those bits with the solicited-node multicast prefix.

whyWrong.0: The low 24 bits belong after the fixed ff02::1:ff00:0/104 prefix.
whyWrong.2: This discards the upper byte of the final 24 bits.
whyWrong.3: This takes the wrong 24 bits.

questions.prompt: R1 has FE80::1 on Gi0/0 and on Gi0/1, which connect to separate isolated LANs. Which two statements are correct? Choose two.
options: A diagnostic targeting FE80::1 must identify the intended link.
DAD on Gi0/0 checks for the duplicate on Gi0/1.
R1 must forward packets addressed to FE80::1 between those LANs.
The two identical address texts can be valid because the links differ.
A link-local address must be globally unique across the whole enterprise.
questions.explanation: Scope includes the link. Text alone cannot distinguish repeated link-local addresses on separate interfaces.

whyWrong.1: DAD checks the local link, not other routed links.
whyWrong.2: Routers do not forward link-local-addressed traffic onto another link.
whyWrong.4: Its required uniqueness is within its link.

questions.prompt: Which interface command explicitly creates an EUI-64-derived address in 2001:db8:acad:2::/64?
options: ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:2::1/64
ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:2::/64 eui-64
ipv6 address fe80::1 link-local
ipv6 enable
questions.explanation: The eui-64 keyword instructs IOS to build the interface identifier from the interface MAC.

whyWrong.0: This manually sets ::1 rather than deriving an identifier.
whyWrong.2: This sets a link-local address.
whyWrong.3: This enables processing and link-local addressing without the requested global prefix.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or observation
exhibit.text:
RA source: fe80::1; Router Lifetime: 1800 seconds
Header: M=0, O=1
Prefix: 2001:db8:acad:1::/64; A=1, L=1
No RA DNS option. A working stateless DHCPv6 server supplies DNS.

questions.prompt: A client supports SLAAC and stateless DHCPv6, with no manual DNS settings. What behavior is supported by the shown RA and available server?
options: DHCPv6 must provide the default router.
A=1 forces the host to derive its identifier from its MAC.
The host cannot form an address without M=1.
SLAAC address, DHCPv6 DNS, and RA-learned default router.
questions.explanation: The A-enabled /64 permits SLAAC. O indicates other DHCPv6 information, supplied here by a server. The nonzero RA lifetime permits the advertised router as default.

whyWrong.0: Ordinary default-router discovery uses RA, not DHCPv6.
whyWrong.1: SLAAC does not require the EUI-64 identifier method.
whyWrong.2: M is not required for SLAAC.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or observation
exhibit.text:
Complete relevant R1 settings:
no ipv6 unicast-routing
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:1::1/64
 no shutdown
Interface up/up; no other advertising router exists.

questions.prompt: Automatic PCs receive only link-local addresses. The router answers a manually addressed PC on the local LAN. What missing prerequisite is directly shown?
options: IPv6 forwarding/router operation has not been enabled globally.
IPv6 processing has not been enabled on the addressed interface.
The manual global address must first be replaced by an EUI-64 address.
The RA managed-address flag must be set for all SLAAC clients.
questions.explanation: The displayed no ipv6 unicast-routing setting leaves the router acting as an IPv6 endpoint instead of the advertising/forwarding router needed here.

whyWrong.1: The configured IPv6 address and successful local ping show interface IPv6 processing is present.
whyWrong.2: The manual /64 address is valid; its derivation method does not enable global router operation.
whyWrong.3: SLAAC does not require the managed-address flag; that flag describes DHCPv6 address configuration.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or observation
exhibit.text:
PC-A: 2001:db8:acad:1::10/64
PC-A gateway: 2001:db8:acad:10::1
R1 Gi0/0 up/up:
 FE80::1
 2001:DB8:ACAD:1::1
No router owns 2001:db8:acad:10::1.

questions.prompt: PC-A's manually configured gateway does not answer. Which evidenced mismatch should be corrected?
options: The PC must obtain its gateway from DHCPv6 instead of using the documented manual address.
The PC should widen its prefix to /48 while retaining the gateway text.
The PC cannot use a manually configured global-form gateway.
The PC names acad:10::1, but the actual router address is acad:1::1.
questions.explanation: The displayed gateway has fourth group 10 rather than 1 and does not match the configured router address. Verify the intended gateway rather than assuming every failure is caused by routing.

whyWrong.0: Ordinary DHCPv6 does not supply the default router, and a correct on-link manual gateway can be valid.
whyWrong.1: Widening a prefix cannot make the router own the mistyped gateway address.
whyWrong.2: A manually configured on-link global unicast gateway can be valid; the fault is the specific incorrect address.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or observation
exhibit.text:
Complete Gi0/1 address configuration:
 ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:2::/64 eui-64
 ipv6 address fe80::1 link-local
Displayed addresses:
 FE80::1
 2001:DB8:ACAD:2:21A:2BFF:FE3C:4D5E

questions.prompt: Hosts use 2001:db8:acad:2::1 as a manual gateway. What does this excerpt establish?
options: The eui-64 keyword guarantees ::1 also exists.
The manual link-local address also creates a global address with the same ::1 suffix.
Clearing the PC neighbor cache will create the missing ::1 address on R1.
The derived address exists, but the expected ::1 is absent.
questions.explanation: The listed global address is not ::1. Repair the addressing plan or gateway expectation; do not assume EUI-64 creates both addresses.

whyWrong.0: EUI-64 supplies the derived suffix, not an additional ::1.
whyWrong.1: A manual link-local address does not assign a matching global address.
whyWrong.2: Cache refresh cannot assign an address absent from the router configuration.

questions.prompt: What action is justified by a duplicate-address indication on a newly assigned host address?
options: Clear the router neighbor cache and assume the address is unique.
Investigate which device on this link already uses that address before assigning it.
Change the address from uppercase to lowercase.
Disable DAD so both hosts can use the planned address.
questions.explanation: DAD is a local uniqueness check. Preserve the evidence and correct the conflicting assignment, rather than hiding it.

whyWrong.0: Clearing cached bindings does not remove another device using the address.
whyWrong.2: Case changes the spelling, not the address bits.
whyWrong.3: Bypassing the conflict check does not resolve the ordinary same-link unicast conflict.

questions.prompt: What explains the host having an address but no automatically learned default router?
options: The prefix can supply an address; router lifetime zero offers no default router.
The host must use the DNS server as its default router.
A=1 means the host must ignore the router-lifetime field.
A /64 address forces the RA sender to be installed as a default router.
questions.explanation: The address may be formed from the autonomous prefix with its usable lifetime. A router lifetime of zero does not offer the RA sender as a default router.

whyWrong.1: DNS server information does not designate the router.
whyWrong.2: A is a prefix option flag and does not override the RA router lifetime.
whyWrong.3: Address assignment and default-router selection use different RA information.

exhibit.title: RA address and router lifetimes (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Fresh host; no static gateway and no other RA sender.
RA source FE80::1, router lifetime 0
Prefix 2001:db8:24::/64, A=1, L=1, usable prefix lifetimes
Host has 2001:db8:24::25/64; default-router list is empty.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion follows from this addressing evidence?
options: L=0 invalidates the /64 and prevents any address from being formed.
SLAAC can form the address, but this PIO does not assert that the prefix is on-link.
A=1 also implies L=1, so the host must resolve every same-prefix destination directly.
The host must replace its prefix length with /128 because L=0.
questions.explanation: Address assignment and on-link determination are separate. Other valid on-link information could exist, but this particular PIO does not supply it.

whyWrong.0: L describes on-link information; A permits autonomous address formation.
whyWrong.2: The autonomous and on-link flags are independent.
whyWrong.3: The flag does not rewrite the autonomous address prefix length.

exhibit.title: Independent A and L flags (exercise)
exhibit.text:
RA source FE80::1, router lifetime 1800
Prefix information: 2001:db8:25::/64, A=1, L=0
Prefix lifetimes are usable; no other on-link information is supplied.

questions.prompt: Which is the smallest addressing repair consistent with the plan and evidence?
options: Change PC-B gateway to R1 LAN 1 global address.
Change both router LANs to /48 to make the mistaken host prefix fit.
Change PC-B to 2001:db8:26:2::20/64 and keep its link-local gateway.
Replace the gateway with ::1 because it always means the local router.
questions.explanation: The link and router gateway are present on LAN 2. The PC global prefix belongs to the other LAN, so correct that field without widening both subnets.

whyWrong.0: That address is not an on-link gateway for PC-B LAN 2.
whyWrong.1: This overlaps the separate routed LANs and abandons the /64 plan.
whyWrong.3: ::1 is the host itself, not its default router.

exhibit.title: Approved and configured LAN prefixes (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Plan: LAN 1 = 2001:db8:26:1::/64; LAN 2 = 2001:db8:26:2::/64
R1 LAN 2: 2001:db8:26:2::1/64, FE80::1, up/up
PC-B on LAN 2: 2001:db8:26:1::20/64, gateway FE80::1
PC-B reaches FE80::1 locally; remote hosts have the intended two LAN prefixes.

questions.prompt: Which two conclusions are supported, without claiming the router knows the cause of every failed test? Choose two.
options: A static route to either directly connected /64 is the missing prerequisite.
Successful local ping proves that R1 forwards between the LANs.
The LAN 1 host can resolve and reach its router as an endpoint.
The failure proves that the LAN 2 host has a duplicate IPv6 address.
IPv6 forwarding is missing even though both connected interfaces have addresses.
questions.explanation: Local success and addressed interfaces establish less than transit success. The complete relevant configuration identifies the disabled forwarding prerequisite; no invented duplicate diagnosis is needed.

whyWrong.0: The prefixes are already connected; the explicit global forwarding setting is the missing prerequisite.
whyWrong.1: An endpoint reply is different from transit forwarding.
whyWrong.3: No DAD or duplicate evidence is supplied.

exhibit.title: Local replies without transit forwarding (exercise)
exhibit.text:
R1 Gi0/0: 2001:db8:28:1::1/64 up/up
R1 Gi0/1: 2001:db8:28:2::1/64 up/up
Global: no ipv6 unicast-routing; no filters
PCs have the matching /64 and their own on-link R1 gateway.
Each PC can ping its own R1 interface; PC-to-PC ping fails.

cards.front: How long is an IPv6 address?
cards.back: 128 bits: eight 16-bit groups. Each full group has four hexadecimal digits.

cards.front: Why may an IPv6 address contain :: only once?
cards.back: It represents omitted zero groups. Two occurrences make the number of zeros in each run ambiguous.

cards.front: Which space is commonly allocated for global unicast?
cards.back: 2000::/3. Having a global-form address does not itself prove Internet reachability; allocation, routes and policy also matter.

cards.front: What is the ULA block and locally generated half?
cards.back: fc00::/7 is ULA. Locally generated prefixes use fd00::/8, with a pseudorandom 40-bit Global ID. They are not intended for global Internet routing.

cards.front: What is link-local scope?
cards.back: The reserved block is fe80::/10; a normal link-local address has fe80 followed by zero prefix bits and its identifier. It is meaningful on one link and is not forwarded onto another.

cards.front: Which multicast groups mean all nodes and all routers on a link?
cards.back: ff02::1 is all IPv6 nodes; ff02::2 is all IPv6 routers. Multicast addresses are in ff00::/8.

cards.front: How do you form a solicited-node multicast address?
cards.back: Append the address's last 24 bits to ff02::1:ff00:0/104. For an address ending 12:3456, the group is ff02::1:ff12:3456.

cards.front: What do ::1 and :: mean?
cards.back: ::1/128 is loopback, the local node itself. ::/128 is the unspecified address, used when no source address is assigned in permitted initialization cases.

cards.front: How is modified EUI-64 derived from a MAC?
cards.back: Split the six MAC bytes after byte three, insert ff:fe, invert the first byte's U/L bit with XOR 02, and regroup into four 16-bit groups.

cards.front: EUI-64 first byte: 00 becomes what, and 02 becomes what?
cards.back: 00 becomes 02; 02 becomes 00. Invert the bit rather than always adding 2.

cards.front: What does the A flag in an RA prefix-information option permit?
cards.back: Autonomous address formation from that prefix when the other SLAAC conditions are met. It does not itself declare the prefix on-link.

cards.front: Where does an automatically learned IPv6 default router come from?
cards.back: A valid RA with a usable nonzero router lifetime. Its link-local source identifies the router; the host's address may separately come from SLAAC or DHCPv6.

cards.front: What does ipv6 unicast-routing enable on a basic IOS router?
cards.back: IPv6 forwarding. With enabled IPv6 interfaces and normal unsuppressed RA settings, it also lets the device operate as an advertising router. Addressing alone is not inter-interface forwarding.

cards.front: ipv6 enable versus ipv6 address prefix/64 eui-64?
cards.back: ipv6 enable supplies IPv6 processing and automatic link-local addressing without a global prefix. The eui-64 form also creates a global-form address using the supplied prefix and derived identifier.

cards.front: How many /64 prefixes fit in a /56?
cards.back: 2^(64 - 56) = 256. This counts subnets; do not subtract IPv4-style network and broadcast addresses.

cards.front: What does a duplicate IPv6 address indication require you to investigate?
cards.back: Another use of that unicast address on the local link. Exact duplicate labels vary by image; do not bypass the conflict check.

cards.front: Is 2001:db8::/32 public Internet address space for deployment?
cards.back: No. It is reserved for documentation. Use it in written examples and isolated labs, not as an assigned public production prefix.

cards.front: Does assigning an IPv6 address automatically prove its prefix is on-link?
cards.back: No. On-link information is separate from address assignment. RA prefix L flags and other explicit on-link configuration supply that information.

cards.front: What does Duplicate Address Detection test?
cards.back: Whether a tentative unicast address conflicts on its local link. A DAD NS can use the unspecified source ::. It does not check uniqueness across the entire Internet.

cards.front: Two equally long zero runs: which does canonical IPv6 text compress?
cards.back: The leftmost run. Canonical text does not compress a single zero group.

cards.front: In a /61, how many low bits of the fourth IPv6 group lie outside the prefix?
cards.back: Three. Clear those bits to calculate the containing prefix; a hex digit contains four bits.

cards.front: What extra information makes FE80::2 a specific neighbor?
cards.back: Its link or local exit interface. The same address text can exist on separate links.

cards.front: What do the RA M and O flags describe?
cards.back: M indicates managed address configuration; O indicates other DHCPv6 configuration. Neither flag supplies a DHCPv6 default-router option.

cards.front: Can an RA provide a usable autonomous prefix but no default router?
cards.back: Yes. A usable A-flagged prefix can remain valid while router lifetime zero excludes the sender as a default router.

cards.front: Does an IPv6 /64 have an IPv4-style broadcast address?
cards.back: No. IPv6 uses multicast for group delivery. Subnet counts do not subtract network and broadcast addresses.

cards.front: Can two router interfaces use FE80::1 on different LANs?
cards.back: Yes, because link-local scope is per link. Reusing an ordinary unicast address on the same link would be a conflict.

commands.note: Use a prefix length, not an IPv4 dotted mask.

commands.note: Calculate the result from the actual operational interface MAC.
