tickets.title: Automatic clients have only link-local addresses
tickets.scenario: A fresh LAN has one R1 router and several SLAAC-capable PCs. All physical links are up. R1 answers a manually configured PC at its global-form interface address. Automatic PCs receive no usable global prefix or default router. There is no other router and no DHCPv6 server. Excerpts are representative.

exhibits.title: Complete relevant R1 configuration
exhibits.text:
no ipv6 unicast-routing
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:1::1/64
 ipv6 address fe80::1 link-local
 no shutdown
No RA-suppression configuration.

exhibits.title: PC observations
exhibits.text:
Manual PC 2001:db8:acad:1::10/64 can ping 2001:db8:acad:1::1.
Automatic PCs show only link-local addresses; no RA is observed.

tickets.question: Which correction addresses the shown missing prerequisite?
options: Enable ipv6 unicast-routing globally on R1.
Add ipv6 enable to the already IPv6-addressed interface.
Replace its manual global address with an EUI-64-derived address.
Set the RA managed flag without changing global forwarding.
tickets.explanation: The complete configuration lacks global IPv6 router operation. Interface addressing already enables local IPv6 processing; EUI-64 is an address-generation choice, and the managed flag describes DHCPv6 behavior. None supplies the missing forwarding/advertising prerequisite.
tickets.fix:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ipv6 unicast-routing
R1(config)# end
R1# show ipv6 interface gigabitethernet0/0
```
Confirm the /64 and RA settings. Allow clients to receive a new RA, or refresh Automatic mode if supported. Verify their actual prefix and learned gateway, then test numeric-address connectivity. A DHCPv6 address server is not required for this SLAAC exercise.

tickets.title: The documented gateway was never assigned
tickets.scenario: On an isolated LAN, PCs use 2001:db8:acad:2::1 as their manual gateway. The router interface is up and its current configuration uses EUI-64. A PC can ping the actual derived address but cannot resolve the documented ::1 address. No other device owns ::1.

exhibits.title: Complete Gi0/1 address settings
exhibits.text:
ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:2::/64 eui-64
ipv6 address fe80::1 link-local

exhibits.title: Representative address display
exhibits.text:
GigabitEthernet0/1 [up/up]
 FE80::1
 2001:DB8:ACAD:2:21A:2BFF:FE3C:4D5E

tickets.question: Which diagnosis matches the evidence?
options: EUI-64 also created ::1; refreshing the neighbor cache is the only required repair.
The PC prefix must be widened until it includes every router address.
The expected manual gateway is absent; the derived address has a different suffix.
The router link-local address must have the same suffix as its derived global address.
tickets.explanation: The complete address display contains the derived address but not ::1. A working ping to the actual address supports local connectivity. Cache refresh or a wider prefix cannot assign the missing address, and manually assigned link-local and derived global suffixes can differ.
tickets.fix:
Choose and document a consistent addressing plan. To retain the intended ::1 gateway in this isolated lab, add it explicitly:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:2::1/64
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ipv6 interface gigabitethernet0/1
```
This adds the manual address alongside the existing derived address; it does not remove it. Verify no duplicate is reported and test the configured gateway. Alternatively, update the manual PC gateway to the correctly scoped fe80::1, then verify that chosen design before saving.

chapters.title: Static routing (IPv6)
chapters.subtitle: Select a remote IPv6 path and scope link-local next hops to the correct interface.

sources.title: Cisco: IPv6 Static Routing, IOS XE 17
Cisco: Understand the IPv6 Link-Local Address
Cisco: IPv6 Addressing and Basic Connectivity
Cisco: Route Selection in Cisco Routers

chapters.summary: Configure network, default, host and floating IPv6 routes. Verify forwarding, neighbor resolution, link-local scope and the return path with a controlled two-link lab.

sections.body:
IPv6 static routing uses the route-selection method you already practiced with IPv4. The destination is still a prefix, a next hop is still the next router, and a reply still needs its own route. The important additions are 128-bit prefix notation, IPv6 forwarding configuration, Neighbor Discovery, and the interface scope of a link-local next hop.

Keep those differences separate. Learning a new address format should not make you abandon the careful sequence of checking the configuration, installed routes and actual traffic.

sections.title: Apply the IPv4 routing method to IPv6
sections.body:
:::facts
- IPv6 static routes use `ipv6 route prefix/length ...` in global configuration mode.
- An ordinary static route has administrative distance **1**. A floating route must have a higher distance than its preferred competitor for the same prefix.
- The default prefix is **::/0**. A single-address host route uses **/128**.
- A link-local next hop requires an **exit interface** in the IOS static-route command.
- Enable `ipv6 unicast-routing` for inter-interface IPv6 forwarding on the basic IOS router used here.
- Ethernet next-hop MAC resolution uses **Neighbor Discovery**, not ARP.
:::

An IPv6 packet matches the longest installed prefix that covers its destination. A packet for `2001:db8:20::12` can match `2001:db8:20::12/128`, `2001:db8:20::/64` and `::/0`. If all three are installed, /128 wins. If that host route is removed, /64 wins. If neither specific prefix exists but a default does, /0 supplies the forwarding instruction.

Administrative distance helps decide which candidate route to an identical prefix enters the routing table. It does not make a less specific installed prefix beat a longer one. Keep installation and packet forwarding as two decisions, just as in the IPv4 chapter.

A router carrying both address families has separate IPv4 and IPv6 routing information. A successful IPv4 ping can support your physical-link investigation, but it does not prove an IPv6 address, next hop, gateway or forwarding setting is correct. Begin a complaint by identifying the destination address family, then inspect that family's configuration and table.

The examples use `2001:db8::/32` documentation space within an isolated lab. The /64 transit links are a teaching choice. They do not contradict the use of other supported prefix lengths, including /127 on appropriate point-to-point router links.

sections.title: Enable addressing and forwarding
sections.body:
Configure a router interface with a predictable global-form address and a chosen link-local address:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ipv6 unicast-routing
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:12::1/64
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address fe80::1 link-local
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ipv6 interface brief
```

Each line has a different job. The global forwarding command allows R1 to move IPv6 packets between interfaces. The address line assigns `2001:db8:12::1` and a /64 prefix. The next line explicitly chooses `fe80::1` for this link. `no shutdown` enables the physical interface administratively; the peer and cable must also be working for a usable link.

An IOS router can have IPv6 addresses and answer traffic addressed to itself while IPv6 forwarding is disabled. Therefore, “I can ping the router” is not enough to establish that it can carry a PC's traffic to another interface. Look for the global command and test through the router.

The interface's local and connected routes are also evidence. A connected /64 describes its attached subnet, while a local /128 identifies an address belonging to the router itself. These are different from a remote /128 **static host route**, which instructs forwarding toward another device.

Router Advertisements can provide attached hosts with prefix and default-router information when IPv6 router operation is enabled and the interface's RA settings permit it. The global command is necessary in this basic lab but does not override an explicit RA suppression or an incorrectly configured prefix.

sections.title: Choose an IPv6 route form
sections.body:
| Form | Example | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| Recursive, next hop only | `ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 2001:db8:12::2` | Resolve the next-hop address through another route |
| Exit interface only | `ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 serial0/0/0` | Direct traffic onto the specified point-to-point interface |
| Fully specified | `ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 gigabitethernet0/0 fe80::2` | Use this neighbor on this exact link |

The **recursive** example works when R1 has a usable resolving route to `2001:db8:12::2`, such as the connected transit /64. The same principle applies to a suitable non-link-local unicast next hop; a link-local address has the additional scope requirement described next.

Recursion must resolve to a usable path without depending on the route being resolved. Also, do not assume that any default automatically resolves every recursive next hop: documented IOS XE behavior excludes default-based IPv6 static recursion unless explicitly enabled. This course uses directly connected resolving prefixes and does not require the advanced override.

An **interface-only** route is reasonable for a true point-to-point interface because only one peer can receive the traffic. Ordinary Ethernet is a multiaccess link type even when the drawing shows only two routers. Without an explicit next hop, an interface-only route treats covered destinations as directly attached and may attempt Neighbor Discovery for those remote destinations on the transit link.

That is the wrong assumption for a LAN behind another router. The remote PC cannot hear a link-local discovery request on the transit segment. Specialized proxy mechanisms exist, but they are not configured or required here. Name the adjacent router as the next hop.

A **fully specified** route states both the exit and the neighbor. It still needs Layer 2 resolution for that neighbor on Ethernet. An active interface and installed static route do not guarantee that the stated neighbor address exists or will answer.

sections.title: Scope a link-local next hop
sections.body:
A link-local address is meaningful only within one link. The text `fe80::2` can legitimately identify interfaces on several different links. IOS cannot infer which link you mean merely from those 128 address bits.

```diagram
{"type":"topology","title":"A link-local next hop includes its link","caption":"The two R2 interfaces deliberately use different link-local values in this lab so a wrong-interface error is visible.","nodes":[{"id":"r1","kind":"router","label":"R1","sub":"fe80::1 on each link","x":3,"y":3},{"id":"r2","kind":"router","label":"R2","sub":"Primary fe80::2; backup fe80::3","x":9,"y":3}],"links":[{"from":"r1","to":"r2","label":"2001:db8:12::/64; peer fe80::2","fromLabel":"Gi0/0","toLabel":"Gi0/0","accent":true},{"from":"r1","to":"r2","label":"2001:db8:13::/64; peer fe80::3","fromLabel":"Gi0/1","toLabel":"Gi0/1","style":"dashed"}]}
```

For R1's primary route, the useful next-hop identity is **fe80::2 on GigabitEthernet0/0**. The correct command is:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 gigabitethernet0/0 fe80::2
R1(config)# end
```

Omitting the interface from a link-local next-hop command is invalid. Supplying an interface makes the syntax complete, but does not prove you supplied the **correct** interface. If `fe80::2` is not present on Gi0/1, a route through that pair cannot deliver to the intended neighbor even if its interface is up and the route is installed.

Read the peer's `show ipv6 interface brief` to establish its actual address on the connected interface. The local neighbor cache can corroborate bindings learned through traffic, but it is not guaranteed to contain every peer address. Pinging a peer's global address alone does not necessarily reveal its link-local address in the cache.

A link-local ping also needs a link selection. Documented IOS interactive behavior asks for `Output Interface:` after a command such as `ping fe80::2`. Enter the local exit interface, not the peer's interface name. Exact prompt support varies in Packet Tracer; the lab also tests the globally unique transit addresses to establish connectivity independently.

:::trap
The next hop can be link-local while the packet's destination is a remote global unicast address. The router resolves the local neighbor and forwards the original packet toward it. It does not replace the packet's destination with `fe80::2`.
:::

sections.title: Network, default, host and floating routes
sections.body:
A **network route** covers the remote LAN. In the diagram, R1's route to `2001:db8:20::/64` points to R2's primary neighbor. R2 needs the corresponding return route for R1's `2001:db8:10::/64`.

A **default route** covers destinations without a more specific installed match:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ipv6 route ::/0 gigabitethernet0/0 fe80::2
R1(config)# end
```

A default does not create downstream connectivity or guarantee a reply. In the lab it reaches a separately configured R2 loopback, `2001:db8:99::8/128`. The destination actually exists and R2 already has a return route to the source LAN, so the test has a complete expected path.

A **host route** uses /128. For `2001:db8:20::12/128` through the backup link, only that address takes the more specific path. Other addresses in `2001:db8:20::/64` keep their /64 path. A distance-200 host route can win that forwarding decision because its prefix is longer; it is not competing for installation with the different /64.

A **floating static route** uses a greater distance than the primary for the same prefix:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 gigabitethernet0/1 fe80::3 5
R1(config)# end
R1# show running-config
R1# show ipv6 route static
```

With the primary working, the distance-1 route is selected and the distance-5 route remains configured. If the primary interface becomes unusable, the backup can install. It still needs a functioning backup link, the correct neighbor on that link and valid downstream/return paths.

Equal distances can allow multiple usable paths to the same prefix, subject to platform support. That is different from standby. A more-specific destination typo is also not standby: it can take matching traffic while the preferred broad route is healthy.

Ordinary floating routes react to changes in route eligibility; they do not continuously test remote applications. A peer failure behind a switch may leave the local interface up. Inspect what actually caused the preferred route to disappear instead of assuming a distance-5 entry proves one particular physical failure.

sections.title: Follow the request and reply
sections.body:
Assume PC-A has `2001:db8:10::11/64` and gateway `fe80::1`. PC-B has `2001:db8:20::12/64` and gateway `fe80::2`. In this lab the /64 LANs are explicitly configured as on-link. In general IPv6, on-link information is separate from simply assigning a host address.

PC-A identifies PC-B as off-link and selects its default router. It resolves R1's local-link address to an Ethernet address if necessary. R1 receives the frame, reads the unchanged destination `2001:db8:20::12` and selects its remote /64 route. It resolves R2's scoped next hop and sends a new Ethernet frame across the transit link.

R2 then uses its connected LAN route and resolves PC-B. The IPv6 source and destination addresses remain PC-A and PC-B through this unfiltered, untranslated lab path. Routers change the link-layer framing and decrement Hop Limit as they forward.

For the reply, PC-B selects its own gateway. R2 must have a route covering `2001:db8:10::11`. R1 finally delivers the reply through its connected LAN. Forward and return routes can legitimately use different links, provided both directions work.

A router-originated ping can use a transit source that the far router already knows as connected. That success does not establish a return route to the PC LAN. Test from the actual PCs or deliberately select an appropriate router source on an image that supports it. Record the source used, not just the destination that answered.

sections.title: Verify and troubleshoot
sections.body:
Representative selected-route output:

```output R1# show ipv6 route static
S   2001:DB8:20::/64 [1/0]             ← destination, distance, metric
     via FE80::2, GigabitEthernet0/0  ← complete scoped next hop
```

After a primary-link failure, the intended backup entry is:

```output R1# show ipv6 route static
S   2001:DB8:20::/64 [5/0]
     via FE80::3, GigabitEthernet0/1  ← different link and neighbor
```

The brackets describe administrative distance and metric, not hop count and packet loss. `show ipv6 route static` filters selected static entries. Use `show running-config` to find unselected backup candidates as well.

| Observation | Next evidence to collect |
|---|---|
| Route command rejected | Prefix syntax, mode, and interface requirement for a link-local next hop |
| Configured route absent | Interface state, resolving route, competing candidate and distance |
| Route installed but ping fails | Actual peer address on the named link, neighbor state, downstream and return routes |
| Local pings work but transit fails | Global IPv6 forwarding and both end-host gateways |
| Unexpected backup path | Exact prefix lengths, distances and the primary route's current eligibility |

In the neighbor cache, a reachable state means recently confirmed reachability. Stale alone is not a fault. Incomplete means address resolution has not completed; sustained incomplete state during repeated failure is useful evidence of a local resolution problem. Compare the address **and interface** before deciding that a similarly named neighbor elsewhere in the table is the correct one.

Do not require an exact route-table entry count. Local multicast entries, formatting and additional implementation-generated routes can vary. The meaningful checks are whether the necessary connected, local and remote prefixes are present with the intended next hops.

sections.title: Exam focus
sections.body:
Configure each static-route type from an address plan, read its selected entry, and explain how its next hop is reached. Practice spotting a correct link-local address paired with the wrong exit interface; valid command syntax does not guarantee valid forwarding.

For every failed endpoint test, walk the request and the reply separately. Combine route-table evidence with interface and neighbor information. You should finish able to justify both the proposed repair and the test that demonstrates it worked.

lab.title: Route IPv6 between two LANs and diagnose a scoped next-hop error
lab.intro:
Practice revised September 2026. If you completed an earlier version, repeat the revised exercise and update its checkmarks.

Use the supplied interface settings as a baseline. The routing work is to predict the selected prefix, scoped neighbor and return path, then compare those predictions with observations before repairing a fault.


Start a new isolated project. This lab reuses the physical layout from the IPv4 static-routing chapter but supplies the complete IPv6 setup here. You will verify a missing return route, fail and restore the primary link, and repair a link-local next hop attached to the wrong link.

No simulator execution is claimed. Output and prompts below are representative of documented IOS behavior. Packet Tracer may omit diagnostic options or detailed neighbor states. Record your version's differences and use the full tables and configuration as alternative evidence.
lab.topology:
Use two 2911 routers with three GigabitEthernet ports each. Use default 2960 switch access ports in VLAN 1, without a connection between SW1 and SW2.

| Connection | Cable |
|---|---|
| PC-A FastEthernet0 — SW1 FastEthernet0/1 | Copper straight-through |
| SW1 FastEthernet0/24 — R1 GigabitEthernet0/2 | Copper straight-through |
| R1 GigabitEthernet0/0 — R2 GigabitEthernet0/0 | Copper cross-over |
| R1 GigabitEthernet0/1 — R2 GigabitEthernet0/1 | Copper cross-over |
| R2 GigabitEthernet0/2 — SW2 FastEthernet0/24 | Copper straight-through |
| SW2 FastEthernet0/1 — PC-B FastEthernet0 | Copper straight-through |

| Interface | IPv6 address/prefix | Link-local |
|---|---|---|
| R1 Gi0/0, primary | `2001:db8:12::1/64` | `fe80::1` |
| R2 Gi0/0, primary | `2001:db8:12::2/64` | `fe80::2` |
| R1 Gi0/1, backup | `2001:db8:13::1/64` | `fe80::1` |
| R2 Gi0/1, backup | `2001:db8:13::2/64` | `fe80::3` |
| R1 Gi0/2, LAN A | `2001:db8:10::1/64` | `fe80::1` |
| R2 Gi0/2, LAN B | `2001:db8:20::1/64` | `fe80::2` |
| PC-A | `2001:db8:10::11/64` | Automatic local-link address |
| PC-B | `2001:db8:20::12/64` | Automatic local-link address |
| R2 Loopback0, added later | `2001:db8:99::8/128` | Not used as a next hop |

PC-A's static IPv6 gateway is `fe80::1`. PC-B's is `fe80::2`. These gateway values belong to the router on each PC's own LAN. R2 intentionally uses `fe80::3` on the backup transit link, so the scope exercise has distinct peers to verify.

### Route and evidence worksheet

Before adding a route, write its destination prefix, next-hop address **and exit interface**, and expected distance. Keep separate rows for R1 and R2; the outbound path is not the return path.

| State | R1 route to PC-B | R2 route to PC-A | Endpoint result and evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Only R1 outbound route | Prediction / actual | Prediction / actual | PC source and observed reply/failure |
| Both primary routes | Prediction / actual | Prediction / actual | Both PC tests |
| Primary physically down | Prediction / actual | Prediction / actual | Installed distances and scoped neighbors |
| Wrong /128 present | PC-B versus R2 LAN address | Unchanged or changed? | Neighbor evidence for the selected next hop |
| /128 repaired | Prediction / actual | Selected return path | Both endpoints; explain any asymmetry |

Do not use a successful router-originated ping as a substitute for a client test unless you have verified the source address and its return lookup.

steps.title: Configure R1
steps.body:
Place and cable the devices. Decline a new router's setup dialog if offered. Configure R1's three interfaces.

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# ipv6 unicast-routing
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:12::1/64
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address fe80::1 link-local
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:13::1/64
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address fe80::1 link-local
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:10::1/64
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address fe80::1 link-local
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ipv6 interface brief
```

:::expected
The assigned addresses appear. Gi0/2 should become up/up after its switch port is ready; the transit ports may remain down until R2 is configured. R1 can use `fe80::1` on separate links without a same-link duplicate.
:::

steps.title: Configure R2
steps.body:
Check that you are on R2's console.

```ios R2
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R2
R2(config)# ipv6 unicast-routing
R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R2(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:12::2/64
R2(config-if)# ipv6 address fe80::2 link-local
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R2(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:13::2/64
R2(config-if)# ipv6 address fe80::3 link-local
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
R2(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:20::1/64
R2(config-if)# ipv6 address fe80::2 link-local
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# end
R2# show ipv6 interface brief
R2# ping 2001:db8:12::1
R2# ping 2001:db8:13::1
```

:::expected
Both transit links should become up/up and both pings should succeed after discovery. Read the actual interface names and peer addresses rather than relying only on green cable indicators. Correct a local-link failure before adding remote routes.
:::

steps.title: Address the PCs and verify link-local scope
steps.body:
Under Desktop → IP Configuration, choose IPv6 Static on each PC. Enter the addresses, prefix length `64` and gateways from the topology table. Leave DNS and IPv4 unused.

From PC-A:

```text
ping 2001:db8:10::1
```

From PC-B:

```text
ping 2001:db8:20::1
```

On R1, run the following command by itself, then answer its interactive prompt:

```ios R1
R1# ping fe80::2
```

:::expected
Both local PC pings should succeed. Documented IOS behavior asks `Output Interface:` for the link-local ping; enter `gigabitethernet0/0` and allow the test to finish. It should reach R2's primary address. Repeat `ping fe80::3` and select `gigabitethernet0/1` for the backup neighbor.

If this prompt is not modeled, use the successful global transit pings from Step 2 and the peer's interface display as evidence, and record the unsupported scoped-ping observation. Do not infer a link's identity from the address text alone.
:::

steps.title: Add only the outbound remote-LAN route
steps.body:
Before adding it, predict which source prefixes R2 can currently return to. Write separate predictions for an explicitly transit-sourced router probe and a PC-A probe; the commands below do not guarantee which source an unsourced router ping chooses.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 gigabitethernet0/0 fe80::2
R1(config)# end
R1# show ipv6 route static
R1# ping 2001:db8:20::12
```

Then ping `2001:db8:20::12` from PC-A. Inspect R2's full IPv6 table before fixing anything.

:::expected
R1 selects the remote /64 through `fe80::2` on Gi0/0. Its router-originated ping may succeed using a transit source that R2 knows as connected; inspect the source if your image displays it. PC-A's ping should fail because R2 has no route covering `2001:db8:10::11`. The missing return prefix in R2's table establishes the fault; router ping source selection alone is not assumed as universal evidence.
:::

steps.title: Add the return route and establish the baseline
steps.body:
```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# ipv6 route 2001:db8:10::/64 gigabitethernet0/0 fe80::1
R2(config)# end
R2# show ipv6 route static
```

:::expected
PC-A-to-PC-B ping and the reverse ping should now succeed. R2 has the return /64 through R1 on the primary link. Record both installed entries before adding standby routes. A successful test in only one direction can still conceal a source-dependent issue, so perform both endpoint tests.
:::

steps.title: Configure both floating routes
steps.body:
Predict which entries belong in the running configuration and which should appear in the installed table while the primary is healthy.

First add R1's standby path.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 gigabitethernet0/1 fe80::3 5
R1(config)# end
R1# show running-config
R1# show ipv6 route static
```

Then add R2's standby return path in its separate console:

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# ipv6 route 2001:db8:10::/64 gigabitethernet0/1 fe80::1 5
R2(config)# end
R2# show ipv6 route static
```

:::expected
Each router retains two configured candidates for its remote /64. With both primary links working, the installed route remains distance 1 through Gi0/0. The distance-5 candidate is not normally displayed by the installed-static filter.
:::

steps.title: Fail the primary and observe the backup
steps.body:
Record both expected interface/address pairs and distances before shutdown. After the change, collect both routing tables and PC tests before opening the recovery step.

Shut R1 Gi0/0 and keep it shut until the checks are complete.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ipv6 interface brief
R1# show ipv6 route static
```

On R2, inspect the same two show commands. Repeat PC pings after allowing link and route updates; no continuous-ping extension is required.

:::expected
Because the primary routers are directly cabled, R2's Gi0/0 should lose carrier as well. The remote /64 on each router should move to Gi0/1 at distance 5. R1 uses `fe80::3`; R2 uses `fe80::1`.

```output R1# show ipv6 route static
S   2001:DB8:20::/64 [5/0]
     via FE80::3, GigabitEthernet0/1
```

Endpoint pings should recover on the backup. No exact loss count or convergence time is promised. If the path fails, inspect the backup neighbor and the reverse route before bringing the primary back.
:::

steps.title: Restore the primary
steps.body:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ipv6 route static
```

:::expected
After link recovery, both routers select their distance-1 primary routes again. Backup candidates remain in the running configuration. Verify both endpoint pings before the next controlled fault.
:::

steps.title: Introduce a host route with the wrong scoped neighbor
steps.body:
Before typing, predict the selected route for PC-B and for R2's LAN address. Explain on paper whether distance 200 prevents a more-specific /128 from being selected.

This deliberately incorrect /128 is syntactically complete. It identifies R2's **primary** link-local address on R1's **backup** interface, where that address does not exist.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::12/128 gigabitethernet0/1 fe80::2 200
R1(config)# end
R1# show ipv6 route
```

From PC-A, ping `2001:db8:20::12`, then separately ping `2001:db8:20::1`. On R1 inspect `show ipv6 neighbors`. On R2 confirm Gi0/1 actually uses `fe80::3`.

:::expected
The host route can install on the active interface and wins for PC-B's address despite distance 200. It cannot resolve the intended next hop on that link, so PC-B's test should fail. The LAN router address `2001:db8:20::1` is not covered by /128 and should still work through the /64 primary.

An unresolved neighbor may appear as incomplete or may disappear between attempts. Compare the interface/address pair rather than requiring one exact state label. If the simulator does not model the expected resolution failure, record that limitation; the peer-address mismatch is still clear in the configuration.
:::

steps.title: Repair the host next hop and verify longest match
steps.body:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# no ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::12/128 gigabitethernet0/1 fe80::2 200
R1(config)# ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::12/128 gigabitethernet0/1 fe80::3 200
R1(config)# end
R1# show ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::12
```

:::expected
PC-A should now reach PC-B through the /128's valid backup next hop. The /64 primary still serves the other LAN addresses. Use the full table if the address-specific query is unsupported. A reply can return over the primary; this asymmetry is valid in the stated lab with no filtering or translation.
:::

steps.title: Add a real destination for a default route
steps.body:
On R2 create the logical test interface:

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# interface loopback0
R2(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:99::8/128
R2(config-if)# end
R2# show ipv6 route
```

From PC-A, ping `2001:db8:99::8` before adding a default to R1.

:::expected
R2 has the loopback destination locally, but R1 has no covering remote route or default. The PC ping should fail. Confirm the absent covering prefix in R1's table. No cable or external service is needed for the loopback.
:::

steps.title: Add and test the default route
steps.body:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ipv6 route ::/0 gigabitethernet0/0 fe80::2
R1(config)# end
R1# show ipv6 route static
```

:::expected
R1 lists the default `::/0` through R2. PC-A's ping to `2001:db8:99::8` should now succeed. R2 already has the return route to the PC-A LAN. PC-B still follows its more specific /128; a default does not override specific routes. This is an isolated routing test, not proof of public IPv6 connectivity.
:::

steps.title: Remove temporary routes and the test loopback
steps.body:
Clean up R1:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# no ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::12/128 gigabitethernet0/1 fe80::3 200
R1(config)# no ipv6 route ::/0 gigabitethernet0/0 fe80::2
R1(config)# end
R1# show running-config
R1# show ipv6 route static
```

Then clean up R2:

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# no interface loopback0
R2(config)# end
R2# show ipv6 route
```

:::expected
R1 retains only its primary and floating remote-LAN candidates; R2 retains its corresponding return candidates. No temporary host route, default or loopback remains. Both physical paths are enabled. Confirm PC-to-PC ping once more.
:::

steps.title: Save the verified baseline
steps.body:
```ios R1
R1# copy running-config startup-config
```

Accept the destination-filename prompt with Enter and wait for completion. Then save R2 separately:

```ios R2
R2# copy running-config startup-config
```

:::expected
Accept R2's prompt separately. Save the Packet Tracer project as `20-ipv6-static-baseline.pkt`. Keep your route and neighbor observations with the file. Project saving and startup-configuration saving are distinct actions.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- **No local transit connectivity:** check the cable endpoints, interface state and exact /64 addresses before adding a route.
- **A link-local route is rejected:** include the local exit interface. Valid syntax still needs the correct neighbor on that link.
- **An installed route does not deliver:** compare the scoped next hop against the peer's interface, generate traffic, and inspect neighbor resolution. Then check downstream and return routes.
- **Router pings work but PC pings fail:** confirm the source used by the router, the return prefix for the PC, both PC gateways and `ipv6 unicast-routing`.
- **The standby never appears:** inspect the preferred route's eligibility and the backup interface. The ordinary route is not an end-to-end health monitor.
- **Both paths have distance 1:** read the backup configuration and restore its intended distance 5. Equal-cost multipath is different from standby.
- **One address fails while the rest of the LAN works:** check for a more specific /128 overriding the working /64.
lab.challenge:
In a copy of the cleaned baseline, add a **new service destination** `2001:db8:77::7/128` on R2 Loopback7. PC-A must reach only that new host prefix using primary R1 Gi0/0, with R1 Gi0/1 as a distance-25 standby. Use link-local next hops. Do not add a default route or widen the host prefix. Preserve all existing LAN routes and R2's primary/floating return routes.

Before configuring anything, write the two R1 routes, their scoped next hops, the selected route while healthy, and the selected route after primary failure. Explain why R2's existing LAN-A routes are sufficient for replies to PC-A. Then perform these separate phases:

1. Add the new loopback and routes. Record the /128 entry and ping the service from PC-A.
2. Shut only R1 Gi0/0. Keep it down while collecting both routers' return/forward entries and another PC-A service test.
3. Restore Gi0/0, verify the primary returns, then remove only the temporary service routes and Loopback7. Recheck PC-to-PC service and preserve the original baseline.

As a separate paper comparison, replace R1's original LAN-B primary with the global-next-hop-only form through `2001:db8:12::2`. Identify its resolving prefix and explain why `fe80::2` cannot omit the interface in the same way.

:::solution
R1's service routes are `2001:db8:77::7/128` through Gi0/0 `fe80::2` at ordinary distance 1 and Gi0/1 `fe80::3` at distance 25. R2 already returns to PC-A's `2001:db8:10::/64` through the appropriate primary or distance-5 backup. The two routers' distances need not match; each makes its own local selection.

Configure the service on R2:

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# interface loopback7
R2(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:77::7/128
R2(config-if)# end
R2# show ipv6 route
```

Configure R1 and inspect before any fault:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ipv6 route 2001:db8:77::7/128 gigabitethernet0/0 fe80::2
R1(config)# ipv6 route 2001:db8:77::7/128 gigabitethernet0/1 fe80::3 25
R1(config)# end
R1# show ipv6 route static
```

On PC-A, at each phase:

```text
ping 2001:db8:77::7
```

The healthy /128 uses distance 1 and Gi0/0. Shut only R1 Gi0/0 using the Step 7 interface procedure. Before recovery, the installed /128 should use distance 25 through Gi0/1 `fe80::3`; R2's return to LAN A should use distance 5 through Gi0/1 `fe80::1`. The PC test should recover after route/neighbor updates. Capture these results while the primary remains down.

Restore R1 Gi0/0 using Step 8 and verify distance 1 returns. Only after the recovery test, clean up:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# no ipv6 route 2001:db8:77::7/128 gigabitethernet0/0 fe80::2
R1(config)# no ipv6 route 2001:db8:77::7/128 gigabitethernet0/1 fe80::3 25
R1(config)# end
R1# show ipv6 route static
```

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# no interface loopback7
R2(config)# end
R2# show ipv6 route
```

The original primary and floating LAN routes remain. Recheck both PC pings, save each router separately, and save the project.

For the paper comparison, `ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 2001:db8:12::2` resolves through connected `2001:db8:12::/64`. In this cleaned topology no default or alternative resolver exists, so primary-link loss removes that resolver and makes the backup eligible. A link-local next hop must include its local exit interface. This paper comparison does not change the saved device configuration.
:::

whyWrong.0: Dotted subnet masks are the IPv4 form here.

cards.front: Which command enables IPv6 forwarding on a basic IOS router?
cards.back: Global `ipv6 unicast-routing`. Addressed interfaces alone can answer local traffic without providing inter-interface forwarding.

cards.front: Why does a link-local next hop need scope?
cards.back: The same address can exist on different links. Its useful neighbor identity includes the local exit interface.

cards.front: Required IPv6 static-route form for a link-local next hop?
cards.back: `ipv6 route destination/prefix-length exit-interface link-local-next-hop`. Substitute the actual prefix, interface and neighbor values.

cards.front: IPv6 default-route prefix?
cards.back: ::/0. It matches all IPv6 addresses but is used only when no longer installed prefix matches.

cards.front: IPv6 host-route prefix length?
cards.back: /128. All address bits are specified, so the route matches one destination.

cards.front: Ordinary static route distance, and unusable distance?
cards.back: Default static distance 1; distance 255 is not usable for installation.

cards.front: How does an IPv6 floating static become selected?
cards.back: It has higher distance than the preferred candidate to the same prefix. It can install after primary withdrawal if the backup path remains usable.

cards.front: Read [5/0] in an IPv6 static route.
cards.back: Administrative distance 5, metric 0. The values do not mean five hops and zero packet loss.

cards.front: What does fully specified mean for an IPv6 static route?
cards.back: Both exit interface and next hop are supplied. Ethernet still needs Neighbor Discovery to resolve the next hop's MAC.

cards.front: Problem with an Ethernet interface-only route to a remote IPv6 LAN?
cards.back: It treats remote destinations as on-link and can attempt ND for them on the transit segment. Name the adjacent router rather than relying on unconfigured proxy behavior.

cards.front: What does a non-link-local next-hop-only route need?
cards.back: A usable resolving route to that next hop without self-dependency. A connected transit prefix provides this in the lab; do not assume default-based recursion is enabled.

cards.front: What do C, L and S mean in the IPv6 route table?
cards.back: C: connected prefix. L: local interface address, usually /128. S: static route. A remote static /128 is different from a local L /128.

cards.front: Which command shows IPv6 neighbor bindings?
cards.back: `show ipv6 neighbors`. Entries include interface scope; the cache is not an inventory of all peer addresses.

cards.front: Does a stale IPv6 neighbor entry prove failure?
cards.back: No. It lacks recent reachability confirmation. Incomplete means resolution has not completed and can be temporary; persistent failures justify further checks.

cards.front: Why can IOS ask for Output Interface during a link-local ping?
cards.back: The destination is meaningful only on one link. Supply the local exit interface. Prompt availability and wording can vary by simulator image.

cards.front: How is an IPv6 route destination written?
cards.back: As prefix/length, such as 2001:db8:20::/64. Do not append an IPv4 dotted mask.

cards.front: Does lower distance make /64 beat an installed /128?
cards.back: No. A matching /128 wins forwarding because it is longer. Distance selects candidates for the same prefix before forwarding compares installed entries.

cards.front: Does an ordinary floating static detect every failure beyond its next hop?
cards.back: No. It takes over when the preferred route becomes ineligible; a remote service failure may leave that route installed.

cards.front: Does failed ND for an installed /128 automatically make a matching /64 the forwarding choice?
cards.back: No. While the /128 remains installed, its longer match still selects it. Investigate its scoped next hop.

cards.front: Why can a router-sourced ping work while a client-sourced ping fails?

chapters.summary: Learn how OSPF forms adjacencies, chooses a designated router, and adds interface costs. Configure area 0, verify both directions of a path, and isolate faults without resetting healthy neighbors.

sections.title: How OSPF learns the topology
sections.body:
:::facts
- OSPFv2 carries IPv4 routes and uses IP protocol number **89**, not a TCP or UDP port.
- On Cisco IOS, the default OSPF administrative distance is **110**.
- This chapter uses one area, **area 0**, throughout.
- For the broadcast and point-to-point interfaces studied here, normal IOS defaults are Hello **10 seconds** and dead **40 seconds**.
- A lower total **cost** is better. A higher OSPF interface **priority** is better for DR/BDR election. These select different things.
:::

A static route records a forwarding decision that you supply. **Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)** lets routers exchange information and calculate paths as the topology changes. It is a **link-state routing protocol**: a router describes its participating links in **link-state advertisements (LSAs)**, and routers in an area synchronize that information in a **link-state database (LSDB)**.

Each router runs the **shortest path first (SPF)** calculation with itself as the starting point. Routers can agree about the topology and still have different next hops: R1 and R3 begin their calculations in different places. The useful output is a set of candidate routes. The routing table then compares these with other route sources, and packet forwarding still uses longest prefix matching as explained in Chapter 17.

Keep three kinds of evidence separate. The neighbor table tells you which routers are communicating. The LSDB contains the information available to the calculation. The routing table tells you which routes were installed. A Full adjacency does not promise an OSPF route to every subnet: the far LAN might not participate, or a connected or static route might already be preferred.

Imagine two branches attached to R1 and R3. Advertising both branch LANs lets each router learn the remote destination and the return path. PCs continue using their ordinary default gateways; they do not become OSPF neighbors. Area 0 is the backbone area and is a straightforward choice for this single-area exercise. Multi-area design, redistribution, and detailed LSA-type memorization are outside this chapter's practical scope.

sections.title: Router ID and process ID
sections.body:
The **router ID (RID)** is a 32-bit identifier displayed in dotted-decimal notation, such as `1.1.1.1`. It identifies the originating router in OSPF information. It must be unique within this routing domain; it need not be a reachable interface address when manually configured.

On the IOS implementation used here, an explicit `router-id` takes precedence. Without one, selection normally uses the highest IPv4 address on an eligible, up loopback interface; if there is no such loopback, it uses the highest eligible active IPv4 interface address. For example, an up loopback at `10.1.1.1` takes precedence over an up physical interface at `192.168.1.1`. The loopback preference is applied before comparing numeric addresses. Use explicit IDs in your labs so startup order and interface state do not obscure the intended result.

The **process ID** in `router ospf 10` selects a local configuration process. It is not the identity announced to neighbors. IOS accepts process IDs from 1 through 65535, and R1's process 10 can form an adjacency with R2's process 20. By contrast, the area assigned to their common link must agree: area `0` and `0.0.0.0` are equivalent notations.

Configure the RID before enabling OSPF interfaces. Changing the configured RID on an already running IOS process may require a process restart to apply; check `show ip ospf` for the active RID. `clear ip ospf process` is disruptive: it drops the local process's adjacencies. It is appropriate only during an authorized lab or maintenance change, not as a first response to a missing route. Restarting one router also does not erase surviving neighbors' DR/BDR history.

sections.title: From neighbor discovery to a full adjacency
sections.body:
A **Hello** discovers and maintains neighbors. On a normal IPv4 Ethernet segment, OSPF Hellos go to `224.0.0.5` (AllSPFRouters). `224.0.0.6` identifies the designated routers for exchanges that use that group. These are local-link control multicasts, not ordinary traffic forwarded between subnets.

For two addressed Ethernet interfaces to establish the intended relationship, first establish Layer 1/2 connectivity and a common IPv4 subnet with matching masks. Enable OSPF on both interfaces in the same area. Compare Hello/dead intervals and ensure neither interface is passive. Router IDs must be different. Compatible network types matter to correct adjacency and route calculation; configure both ends of a two-router point-to-point link consistently.

Authentication, when configured, is another compatibility requirement, but authentication configuration is excluded from v2.0 objective 3.3.a and is not used in this lab. An ACL or other filtering can also prevent protocol 89 from reaching the peer. Ping success alone does not prove OSPF traffic is permitted.

| State | What it establishes | What to investigate if it persists |
|---|---|---|
| Down | No current usable Hello relationship | Link, addressing, process activation, passive setting |
| Init | A Hello arrived, but it does not list the local RID | One-way communication or filtering |
| 2-Way | Each router has seen itself in the other's Hello | May be normal between two DROTHERs |
| ExStart / Exchange | Routers negotiate and exchange database descriptions | Compare MTU and inspect repeated errors |
| Loading | Requested link-state information is being obtained | Missing updates, retransmissions, connectivity |
| Full | Database synchronization for this adjacency completed | Move on to route and forwarding verification |

The five OSPF packet types have jobs, not a rigid one-time sequence: Hello maintains neighbors; **Database Description (DBD)** summarizes database contents; **Link-State Request** asks for missing information; **Link-State Update** carries LSAs; **Link-State Acknowledgment** confirms receipt. Updates and acknowledgments continue after Full when information changes.

Default dead time is documented as four times the Hello interval on this IOS family, but an explicitly configured dead interval can differ. Inspect the effective values with `show ip ospf interface`. When changing timers for a controlled exercise, set both values deliberately on both peers. Do not infer the effective dead timer from a single Hello command or assume every Cisco software family adjusts unspecified timers identically.

sections.title: Broadcast and point-to-point networks
sections.body:
Ethernet uses the OSPF **broadcast network type** by default. A multiaccess segment elects one **designated router (DR)** and one **backup designated router (BDR)**, where enough eligible routers are present. Other routers are **DROTHERs**. Each DROTHER forms Full adjacencies with the DR and BDR; two DROTHERs normally remain 2-Way with each other.

The election ranks eligible routers by interface priority, then RID. IOS priority is 0–255, default 1; priority 0 makes that interface ineligible. Priority is per interface, and the election is per segment, not for the entire area. Existing roles matter: the election is **non-preemptive**. A new router with a higher priority does not displace a healthy existing DR or BDR.

For a clean election in which all candidates know one another before roles are selected, suppose R1 has priority 100, R2 has 50, and R3 has 0. R1 is DR, R2 is BDR, and R3 is DROTHER. If R1 fails, the current BDR R2 takes over as DR. A returning R1 does not automatically reclaim DR. This is why a question must state whether an election is fresh or roles already exist.

:::trap Full is not required between every pair
A stable `2WAY/DROTHER` entry is normal when both local and remote routers are DROTHERs on a broadcast segment. The same state on an intended two-router point-to-point adjacency needs investigation.
:::

On an Ethernet link containing exactly two OSPF routers, configure `ip ospf network point-to-point` on both ends if that is the intended design. The Ethernet framing stays Ethernet; only OSPF's treatment changes. No DR/BDR is needed, and the neighbor state shows `FULL/ -`. Do not use this change as a remedy for an unexplained fault on a shared LAN.

```diagram
{ "type": "topology", "title": "Fig 21.1 — Elections belong to individual segments", "caption": "The shared LAN elects a DR and BDR; the separate two-router link can run as point-to-point.", "nodes": [
{ "id": "R1", "kind": "router", "label": "R1", "sub": "RID 1.1.1.1", "x": 2, "y": 1 },
{ "id": "SW", "kind": "switch", "label": "Shared Ethernet", "x": 6, "y": 1 },

{ "from": "R1", "to": "R3", "label": "point-to-point", "style": "dashed" }

```

sections.title: Cost and the best path
sections.body:
OSPF adds the costs of outgoing interfaces along a path, including the last router's interface toward the destination subnet. This direction matters. Changing R1's outgoing cost changes R1's calculation; it does not automatically change R3's reverse-direction cost.

For IOS automatic calculation, cost is the reference bandwidth divided by the configured interface bandwidth, using integer values with minimum 1. The default reference is 100 Mbps. A 10-Mbps interface therefore has cost 10; 100 Mbps and 1 Gbps both calculate to 1. `auto-cost reference-bandwidth 10000` uses Mbps, so 100-Mbps, 1-Gbps, and 10-Gbps links calculate to 100, 10, and 1. Use a consistent reference across the routing domain. The bandwidth setting is an input to routing metrics; it does not physically change link speed.

An explicit interface command such as `ip ospf cost 25` overrides automatic calculation for that interface. Our lab uses explicit costs to avoid simulator link-speed differences.

Work this example from R1 to R3's LAN. R1 can reach R3 directly with cost 25, or through a shared transit LAN with cost 10. R3's outgoing LAN cost is 1. The choices are **26** and **11**, so the shared path wins. If that shared adjacency fails but the direct one remains Full, R1 should install cost 26. Do not add R3's incoming transit cost a second time.

Cost 11 is not administrative distance 110. In `[110/11]`, 110 ranks OSPF against other route sources for the same prefix, while 11 is the OSPF metric. Equal-cost OSPF paths may be installed together; the supported/default maximum varies by platform. Router ID is not a general replacement for metric comparison when forwarding packets.

sections.title: Configuring single-area OSPFv2
sections.body:
Start with a working addressed interface. Then create the process, set its RID, select participating interfaces, and decide where Hellos are allowed. The following is a configuration pattern for R1, not the complete multi-device lab:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# router ospf 10
R1(config-router)# router-id 1.1.1.1
R1(config-router)# passive-interface default
R1(config-router)# no passive-interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-router)# network 10.0.123.1 0.0.0.0 area 0
R1(config-router)# network 192.168.10.1 0.0.0.0 area 0
R1(config-router)# end
```

The `network` command selects local interfaces by address and wildcard; it is not a command to invent or summarize an advertised route. A wildcard 0 bit must match; a 1 bit is ignored. `0.0.0.0` therefore matches that one interface address. The interface's actual prefix is then advertised. Thus an interface at `172.16.5.33/27` can be selected with `network 172.16.5.33 0.0.0.0 area 0`, and its connected network remains `172.16.5.32/27`.

For a range example, `network 10.0.13.0 0.0.0.3 area 0` ignores the last two address bits and matches local interface addresses from .0 through .3. It includes the lab's .1 and .2 addresses. The /30 subnet mask is `255.255.255.252`; its corresponding contiguous wildcard is `0.0.0.3`. Do not type the subnet mask into the wildcard position. The command still needs a matching local interface; naming a remote network here does not manufacture a route to it.

Alternatively, `ip ospf 10 area 0` in interface mode activates that interface directly. Use one method consistently in an exercise. A **passive interface** does not form OSPF neighbors, but its enabled connected prefix is still advertised through other participating interfaces. Making the PC-facing LAN passive avoids looking for routers where only hosts should exist. Making the transit link passive prevents the very adjacency needed to exchange routes.

sections.title: Verify and troubleshoot
sections.body:
Read this authored, abbreviated example as a set of claims to verify, not a recorded device run:

```output R1# show ip route ospf — representative
O    192.168.30.0/24 [110/11] via 10.0.123.3, 00:00:22, GigabitEthernet0/0  ← AD 110, cost 11, first-hop address
```

Start with `show ip interface brief`, then `show ip ospf interface` and `show ip ospf neighbor`. Check the active RID, area, network type, timers, neighbor role, and Full state where expected. Use `show ip protocols` to inspect process participation/passive configuration and `show ip ospf database` to confirm the router has topology information. Finally inspect the destination route and ping with a source in the actual client network. A router ping sourced from a transit address can succeed while the remote router lacks the client's LAN route.

If the neighbor table is empty, compare both ends before changing either. If ExStart/Exchange repeats, compare interface MTUs and database exchange evidence; MTU mismatch is common, not the only possible cause. Correct the underlying mismatch. `mtu-ignore` bypasses one check and can hide a real packet-size problem.

If neighbors are Full but a LAN route is missing, check that the LAN is up and enabled in OSPF, then look for a preferred connected or static route. If routes look correct but a client still fails, check its mask, gateway, return route, and filtering. Change one variable, observe the result, and restore deliberate faults before saving.

sections.title: Exam focus
sections.body: Explain the relationship among neighbors, the LSDB, SPF, and installed routes. Distinguish a local process ID from the unique RID. Predict DR/BDR results using priority, RID, and existing roles, and recognize normal 2-Way relationships. Calculate outgoing costs in the correct direction, configure area 0 and passive LANs, and verify a client-to-client path in both directions. OSPFv2 is required in both tracks; v2.0 adds OSPFv3 in Chapter 22.

lab.title: Build and troubleshoot a single-area IPv4 network
lab.intro:
Practice revised September 2026. If you completed an earlier version, repeat the revised exercise and update its checkmarks.

The addressing and initial OSPF settings are supplied. Your work is to predict elections and routes, prove them from separate observations, and diagnose a fault before applying its repair. The challenge adds an independently planned LAN and a directional-cost test.

Build from blank devices. You will prove a broadcast election, a point-to-point adjacency, two client routes, and failover between known-cost paths. Keep a table of observations before and after each fault.

Use a new Packet Tracer file with **three 2911 routers**, **one 2960 switch**, and **two PCs**. The 2911 provides Gi0/0, Gi0/1, and Gi0/2. Use straight-through copper for router–switch links, and crossover or the auto-connect tool for router–router and direct PC–router links. On CML/other images, map the interfaces explicitly before typing. All output in this guide is representative, not a recorded run; simulator commands and timing can differ.


| Device/interface | IPv4 address/prefix | Connection or gateway |
|---|---|---|
| R1 Gi0/0 | 10.0.123.1/24 | SW1 Fa0/1 |
| R2 Gi0/0 | 10.0.123.2/24 | SW1 Fa0/2 |

The switch needs no management IP for this lab. There is no simulated Internet destination and no default route is needed: OSPF will carry both specific client prefixes. Shared-interface costs will be 10, direct-link costs 25, and client-LAN costs 1, in both directions.

### Prediction and observation sheet

Before each relevant step, fill the prediction column. Record actual results only after the device has converged; keep the prediction even if it was wrong.

| Checkpoint | Predict | Record actual evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Sequential shared startup | DR, BDR and DROTHER; reason | Each shared interface role and neighbor RID |
| Both paths healthy | R1-to-LAN-30 and R3-to-LAN-10 next hop, interface and cost | Both route entries and PC pings |
| R3 priority raised | Whether existing roles change | Priority and operational role separately |
| R1 shared link shut | Successor DR/BDR and both route costs | Roles, route entries and client result before restoration |
| R1 restored | Existing election versus preferred path | Roles and both route costs |
| Direct timers mismatched | Direct adjacency and client reachability | Both effective timer pairs, neighbors and selected route |

Calculate every path from the router whose route table you are predicting. Add outgoing costs along that path, including the destination LAN; do not add the receiving interface's cost.

steps.title: Cable and address the devices
steps.body:
Cable exactly as shown. Set each PC under Desktop > IP Configuration to the static address, mask 255.255.255.0, and gateway in the table; DNS is not needed. Decline the initial router setup dialog if it appears. Configure SW1 and all router addresses below. The shared interfaces deliberately remain shut until the election steps.

```ios R1
Router> enable
```

```ios R3
Router> enable
```
