:::expected
Each PC can ping its own gateway. R1 and R3 can ping each other on 10.0.13.1/30 and 10.0.13.2/30. Gi0/0 is administratively down on all routers. A PC-to-remote-PC ping is not expected to work yet.
:::

steps.title: Start R1 first and establish its DR role
steps.body:
Configure only R1 now. Wait until its shared interface reports State DR, normally after the initial wait interval (40 seconds with these defaults), before starting R2 or R3. Verify rather than relying on wall-clock timing.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# router ospf 10
R1(config-router)# router-id 1.1.1.1
R1(config-router)# passive-interface default
R1(config-router)# no passive-interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-router)# no passive-interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-router)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip ospf 10 area 0
R1(config-if)# ip ospf cost 10
R1(config-if)# ip ospf priority 100
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip ospf 10 area 0
R1(config-if)# ip ospf network point-to-point
R1(config-if)# ip ospf cost 25
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
R1(config-if)# ip ospf 10 area 0
R1(config-if)# ip ospf cost 1
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# end
R1# show ip ospf interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1# show ip ospf neighbor
```


:::expected
R1 has RID 1.1.1.1 and process 10. Gi0/0 is broadcast, cost 10, priority 100, and DR after the wait. There is no neighbor yet. Gi0/1 is point-to-point; Gi0/2 is OSPF-enabled but passive.
:::

steps.title: Add R2 and R3
steps.body:
Before running the next blocks, write how the startup order and R3 priority zero affect the election. Do not treat the three router IDs as if this were a fresh simultaneous election.

Run R2 first and wait until it is Full with R1 and its interface shows BDR. Then run R3. Different local process numbers are intentional.

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# router ospf 20
R2(config-router)# router-id 2.2.2.2
R2(config-router)# passive-interface default
R2(config-router)# no passive-interface gigabitethernet0/0
R2(config-router)# exit
R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R2(config-if)# ip ospf 20 area 0
R2(config-if)# ip ospf cost 10
R2(config-if)# ip ospf priority 50
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# exit
R2(config)# end
R2# show ip ospf interface gigabitethernet0/0
R2# show ip ospf neighbor
```

```ios R3
R3# configure terminal
R3(config)# router ospf 30
R3(config-router)# router-id 3.3.3.3
R3(config-router)# passive-interface default
R3(config-router)# no passive-interface gigabitethernet0/0
R3(config-router)# no passive-interface gigabitethernet0/1
R3(config-router)# exit
R3(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R3(config-if)# ip ospf 30 area 0
R3(config-if)# ip ospf cost 10
R3(config-if)# ip ospf priority 0
R3(config-if)# no shutdown
R3(config-if)# exit
R3(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R3(config-if)# ip ospf 30 area 0
R3(config-if)# ip ospf network point-to-point
R3(config-if)# ip ospf cost 25
R3(config-if)# exit
R3(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
R3(config-if)# ip ospf 30 area 0
R3(config-if)# ip ospf cost 1
R3(config-if)# exit
R3(config)# end
R3# show ip ospf interface gigabitethernet0/0
R3# show ip ospf neighbor
```


:::expected
R1 remains DR, R2 becomes BDR, and R3 is DROTHER on Gi0/0. R1 sees R2 as FULL/BDR and R3 as FULL/DROTHER on Gi0/0, plus R3 as FULL/ - on Gi0/1. R3 sees R1 as FULL/DR and R2 as FULL/BDR on the shared link. Process 10, 20, and 30 do not have to match.
:::

steps.title: Prove the client routes and their metrics
steps.body:
Calculate both candidate path totals in each direction before running the commands. The solution after the checks lets you compare your arithmetic with the intended result.

On R1 and R3, inspect routes and the database. Then open each PC Desktop > Command Prompt and ping the remote PC. Repeat once if initial ARP resolution causes a lost first echo.

```ios R1
R1# show ip route ospf
R1# show ip ospf database
R1# ping 192.168.30.1 source 192.168.10.1
```

```ios R3
R3# show ip route ospf
R3# ping 192.168.10.1 source 192.168.30.1
```

If the simulator rejects the one-line source option, use the corresponding PC ping below; those packets already have the client-LAN source.
```text
ping 192.168.30.10
```
Run that command on PC-A. On PC-B run:
```text
ping 192.168.10.10
```


:::solution
R1 learns 192.168.30.0/24 [110/11] via 10.0.123.3, Gi0/0. R3 learns 192.168.10.0/24 [110/11] via 10.0.123.1, Gi0/0. Each metric is outgoing shared cost 10 plus remote LAN cost 1. Both PC pings succeed after convergence; connected local LANs appear as C, not O.
:::

steps.title: Test a higher priority without restarting anything
steps.body:
Raise R3 shared-interface priority while R1 and R2 are healthy. Do not clear a process or bounce a link.

```ios R3
R3# configure terminal
R3(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R3(config-if)# ip ospf priority 200
R3(config-if)# end
R3# show ip ospf interface gigabitethernet0/0
```


:::expected
R3 now has configured priority 200 but remains DROTHER. R1 remains DR and R2 BDR. This proves non-preemption; changing priority alone does not reset existing roles.
:::

steps.title: Remove the preferred transit and observe failover
steps.body:
Predict the two route metrics and the surviving election before shutdown. Leave this fault in place while recording all three routers; the following step is a separate recovery.

On R1 only, shut the shared transit. Keep the direct link and both PC LANs up. Observe before restoring it.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip ospf neighbor
R1# show ip route ospf
```

```ios R2
R2# show ip ospf interface gigabitethernet0/0
```

```ios R3
R3# show ip ospf interface gigabitethernet0/0
R3# show ip route ospf
```


:::expected
After loss is detected, R2 is promoted from BDR to DR and R3 becomes BDR. R1 still has a Full point-to-point adjacency to R3. R1 reaches LAN 30 via 10.0.13.2, Gi0/1, at cost 25 + 1 = 26; R3 reaches LAN 10 via 10.0.13.1 at cost 26. PC traffic may lose packets during convergence, then recover. Do not assume an exact duration.
:::

steps.title: Restore transit and inspect the surviving election
steps.body:
Restore R1 Gi0/0. Check both shared interface roles and client routes.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip ospf interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1# show ip route ospf
```

```ios R3
R3# show ip ospf interface gigabitethernet0/0
```


:::expected
R2 remains DR and R3 BDR. Returning R1 is DROTHER; a return does not erase existing roles. R1 and R3 resume the cost-11 shared path after convergence. Save these roles in your notes, not as a promise about roles after a future cold restart.
:::

steps.title: Introduce a timer mismatch on the direct link
steps.body:
Change both timer values on R1 Gi0/1 only, leaving R3 at its defaults. Wait for the adjacency to disappear and compare both ends. The shared link remains available.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip ospf hello-interval 5
R1(config-if)# ip ospf dead-interval 20
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip ospf interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1# show ip ospf neighbor
```

```ios R3
R3# show ip ospf interface gigabitethernet0/1
R3# show ip ospf neighbor
```


:::expected
The direct adjacency cannot remain healthy with R1 at 5/20 and R3 at 10/40. R1 and R3 can still exchange routes over the shared segment, so client ping success alone can hide this failed backup adjacency. No process-ID or priority change would fix the timer mismatch.
:::

steps.title: Restore the timers and save the working network
steps.body:
Remove only the deliberate timer overrides. Verify the direct neighbor returns and both client pings work before saving each device.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# no ip ospf hello-interval
R1(config-if)# no ip ospf dead-interval
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip ospf interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1# show ip ospf neighbor
R1# copy running-config startup-config
```

```ios R2
R2# copy running-config startup-config
```

```ios R3
R3# copy running-config startup-config
```

```ios SW1
SW1# copy running-config startup-config
```

Accept the default destination filename when asked, then save the Packet Tracer project file.

:::expected
Both direct interfaces use 10/40 and the point-to-point adjacency is Full. R2/R3 may retain DR/BDR on the shared segment. The saved priorities are R1 100, R2 50, R3 200; those preferences do not retroactively alter the current election.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- No shared neighbor: check SW1 access VLAN 1, the three /24 addresses, shutdown state, area 0, and passive exceptions.
- Direct neighbor absent: compare /30 addresses, point-to-point settings, timers, and interface activation on both ends.
- Full neighbors but no remote LAN: verify Gi0/2 is up, has its correct /24 address, and is activated in the local OSPF process. Passive is intended there.
- A wrong metric: check explicit interface costs and calculate from the router issuing the command. Incoming interface cost is not added.
- A ping fails: inspect the source PC's mask/gateway and the return route. Initial ARP loss is different from repeated failure after convergence.
lab.challenge:
Work in a copy of the restored lab. Add PC-C using its FastEthernet0 directly to **R2 Gi0/2**, which was unused. Use a copper crossover cable or Packet Tracer's auto-connect. The new LAN must use the **third /26, counting from 1**, inside `192.168.20.0/24`. Assign the router the first usable address and the PC the tenth usable address. Keep this client interface passive, advertise it in R2's existing area-0 process, and set its outgoing OSPF cost to **5**. Do not change any existing interface address, area, or router ID.

Before commands, write the subnet/mask, host/gateway addresses, chosen activation command, and R1/R3 route cost and next hop to the new LAN. Implement your plan and verify PC-C can reach PC-A and PC-B, with replies returning to PC-C. Record routes on all three routers and confirm the client-facing interface is passive.

Then, as an independent directional-cost test, change only R1's shared outgoing cost to **40**. Predict R1's route to LAN 30 and R3's reverse route to LAN 10 before applying the change. Collect both route entries and PC tests while the change is present. Restore R1 shared cost **10** in a separate recovery action and verify again. Save the extended lab as a new file so the original baseline remains available.

:::solution
The /26s begin at .0, .64, .128 and .192. The third is `192.168.20.128/26`, mask `255.255.255.192`; R2 is `.129`, PC-C is `.138`, and PC-C's gateway is `.129`. All are usable in .129 through .190.

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
R2(config-if)# ip address 192.168.20.129 255.255.255.192
R2(config-if)# ip ospf 20 area 0
R2(config-if)# ip ospf cost 5
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# end
R2# show ip ospf interface gigabitethernet0/2
R2# show ip route ospf
```

The process already has `passive-interface default` and only Gi0/0 is an exception, so the new client interface is passive. Both R1 and R3 should learn `192.168.20.128/26` at cost `10 + 5 = 15` through `10.0.123.2`, Gi0/0. R2 reaches LAN 10 and LAN 30 at cost `10 + 1 = 11` through their respective shared neighbors. The new PC must have the planned address and gateway; a router-originated test alone would not verify those fields.

On PC-C:

```text
ping 192.168.20.129
ping 192.168.10.10
ping 192.168.30.10
```

On PC-A and PC-B, separately:

```text
ping 192.168.20.138
```

For the directional test:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip ospf cost 40
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip route ospf
```

R1 chooses direct cost `25 + 1 = 26` to LAN 30 instead of shared cost `40 + 1 = 41`. R3 still chooses shared cost `10 + 1 = 11` to LAN 10. R1 can also reach the new R2 LAN through R3 at `25 + 10 + 5 = 40`, which is cheaper than its now-direct shared choice `40 + 5 = 45`; this is a further reason to read the complete table. R3's path to the new LAN remains 15. Changing one outgoing cost can affect several prefixes, but does not change the reverse direction's configured cost.

Collect both R1 and R3 route displays and endpoint tests before recovery. Then restore only the changed cost:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip ospf cost 10
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip route ospf
```

R1/R3 client routes return to 11 and their new-LAN routes to 15. Verify all three PCs, save each router's configuration, and retain the extended project separately. Election roles may remain those established by the earlier failure; path costs do not reset DR/BDR.
:::

questions.prompt: What does OSPF use to calculate paths within this single area?
options: A link-state database describing the area topology and costs.
The switch MAC table for every remote LAN.
The router with the highest DR priority as the next hop for every prefix.
Only a list of hop counts reported by the last neighbor.
questions.explanation: Each router uses its synchronized topology information to calculate paths from its own position. Different originating routers can choose different outgoing paths.

whyWrong.1: MAC learning supports local Ethernet delivery, not area-wide OSPF path calculation.
whyWrong.2: DR election organizes adjacency and flooding, not every data-plane path.
whyWrong.3: OSPF is a link-state protocol and uses costs, not only distance-vector hop counts.

questions.prompt: How should the same up, OSPF-enabled LAN normally appear in the local and remote route tables?
options: Static on the remote router because the LAN interface is passive.
Connected on its directly attached router; OSPF-learned on a remote router that selects that advertisement.
Local /32 only on every router, regardless of the Ethernet LAN mask.
OSPF-learned on every router, including the router directly attached to the LAN.
questions.explanation: A routing-protocol code identifies how that particular router obtained the installed route. Passive suppresses LAN Hellos but does not change local connected status or remote OSPF advertisement.

whyWrong.0: Passive OSPF advertisement does not turn a learned route into a static.
whyWrong.2: The remote LAN prefix is not replaced by every router own local host route.
whyWrong.3: An enabled local interface still supplies a connected route.

questions.prompt: What does [110/26] mean in this OSPF route?
options: OSPF metric 110 and administrative distance 26.
A /26 prefix learned from router ID 110.
Administrative distance 110 and OSPF metric 26.
A 110-second age and 26-second dead timer.
questions.explanation: The bracket is [administrative distance/metric]. The route uses an OSPF path of cost 26; the /24 prefix and next-hop address are displayed elsewhere.

whyWrong.0: IOS displays administrative distance before metric.
whyWrong.1: The destination prefix is /24, and neither bracket field is a RID.
whyWrong.3: Route age and neighbor timers are separate fields.

questions.prompt: Two routers share an addressed broadcast Ethernet subnet. Which two values must match to form the intended OSPFv2 relationship? Choose two.
options: Local process ID
Area ID on the link
Router ID
Hello and dead intervals
Interface priority
questions.explanation: The area and effective Hello/dead intervals must agree. RIDs must be unique, while process IDs and election priorities may differ.

whyWrong.0: The process ID selects a local process and is not a neighbor matching field.
whyWrong.2: Using the same RID would introduce a duplicate identity.
whyWrong.4: Different priorities are normal when selecting preferred DR/BDR roles.

questions.prompt: R1's Gi0/2 is an up client LAN, activated in area 0 and configured passive. Which two results are expected? Choose two.
options: The LAN prefix can be advertised through other OSPF links.
PCs must establish OSPF neighbors before sending traffic.
The interface sends no OSPF Hellos to discover neighbors.
The LAN connected route disappears from R1.
The interface must be shut to keep it passive.
questions.explanation: Passive OSPF stops neighbor formation on the interface without removing its enabled connected prefix from advertisements. PCs use the router as their gateway and do not run OSPF in this design.

whyWrong.1: PCs do not participate in the routing protocol here.
whyWrong.3: The up addressed interface retains its connected route.
whyWrong.4: Passive is an OSPF setting, not an interface shutdown.

questions.prompt: Which timers are effective on this IOS OSPF interface?
options: Hello 5 seconds and dead 20 seconds.
Hello 10 seconds and dead 40 seconds.
Hello 5 seconds and dead 40 seconds.
Hello 40 seconds and dead 5 seconds.
questions.explanation: Read the configured timer commands separately: Hello is 5 and dead is explicitly 40. A default relationship does not override an explicit dead timer.

whyWrong.0: An explicit dead interval of 40 is present; it is not forced to 4 times Hello.
whyWrong.1: The explicit Hello override replaces the ordinary 10-second value.
whyWrong.3: The commands identify the two intervals in the opposite order.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or output
exhibit.text:
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip ospf hello-interval 5
 ip ospf dead-interval 40

questions.prompt: R1 uses router ospf 10 and R2 uses router ospf 20. Their shared /30 link is in area 0 with matching timers, compatible point-to-point types, and unique RIDs. What should happen?
options: They can form an adjacency despite the different process IDs.
They must change both process IDs to area number 0.
They discover each other but stop at 2-Way because of process IDs.
They require identical RIDs to join the same routing process.
questions.explanation: The process number is locally significant. Shared-link parameters and unique router IDs determine the intended relationship, not equality of the process labels.

whyWrong.1: Process numbers do not have to match area numbers, and IOS process 0 is not the intended valid process.
whyWrong.2: Different local process IDs do not prevent Full synchronization.
whyWrong.3: RIDs must be different.

questions.prompt: When a fresh IOS OSPF process starts, no explicit RID is configured. Loopback0 at 10.1.1.1 and Loopback1 at 10.9.9.9 are both up. Physical interfaces 172.16.1.1 and 192.168.1.1 are also up/up. Which RID is selected?
options: 10.1.1.1 from the lower-addressed loopback
10.9.9.9 from the higher-addressed loopback
192.168.1.1 from the highest physical address
172.16.1.1 from the first listed physical interface
questions.explanation: IOS prefers a loopback address over physical-interface addresses when no RID is explicit. With both loopbacks available, the higher loopback address 10.9.9.9 is selected.

whyWrong.0: Both loopbacks are available, and 10.9.9.9 is numerically higher.
whyWrong.2: Loopback preference is applied before comparing physical-interface addresses.
whyWrong.3: Listing order is not the selection rule.

questions.prompt: Gi0/0 is addressed 172.16.5.33/27. Which router-mode network statement activates only that exact interface address in area 0?
questions.explanation: An all-zero wildcard requires every address bit to match. OSPF then advertises the interface's actual prefix, 172.16.5.32/27; the selector does not turn it into a /32 destination.

whyWrong.0: This matches the entire /27 address range, not only the exact address.
whyWrong.1: This uses a subnet mask where the command expects a wildcard.
whyWrong.2: This exact match selects .32, not the configured .33 address.

questions.prompt: Which prefix is advertised for the selected ordinary Ethernet LAN?
questions.explanation: Retain the interface subnet mask when calculating the advertised connected LAN: .33/27 belongs to .32/27.

whyWrong.1: The mask is /27, not the older classful /24 boundary.
whyWrong.2: A host wildcard selects an interface; it does not change the ordinary Ethernet interface mask.
whyWrong.3: The wildcard is a selection rule, not a default-route advertisement.

exhibit.title: Host wildcard and Ethernet mask (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Gi0/2 up/up: 192.168.21.33/27
router ospf 10
 network 192.168.21.33 0.0.0.0 area 0
 passive-interface Gi0/2

questions.prompt: Which two statements about priority 0 are correct? Choose two.
options: It makes every outgoing route have cost zero.
It forces the current DR to step down in favor of this router.
It makes this interface ineligible for DR and BDR election.
It disables OSPF on the interface.
The router can still become Full with the DR and BDR.
questions.explanation: A DROTHER still exchanges routing information. Priority 0 controls election eligibility, not whether the interface participates.

whyWrong.0: Priority is not OSPF cost.
whyWrong.1: Zero excludes this router from the elected roles.
whyWrong.3: Election eligibility and protocol activation are separate.

questions.prompt: R4 is a DROTHER on a healthy four-router broadcast segment. Which conclusion follows from its neighbor table?
options: The 2WAY relationship with R3 is normal for two DROTHERs.
R3 must be changed to point-to-point on this shared segment.
R4 must have a Full adjacency with every router on the segment.
R3 must receive a different process number to complete synchronization.
questions.explanation: R4 is Full with the DR and BDR and 2-Way with the other DROTHER. That is the expected broadcast adjacency pattern, not evidence of failed database synchronization.

whyWrong.1: All routers should retain the intended common broadcast network type.
whyWrong.2: Two DROTHERs normally stop at 2-Way while each is Full with DR/BDR.
whyWrong.3: Process numbers are local and do not cause this normal state.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or output
exhibit.text:
R4# show ip ospf neighbor
Neighbor ID     Pri State          Address       Interface
1.1.1.1         100 FULL/DR        10.0.123.1    Gi0/0
2.2.2.2          50 FULL/BDR       10.0.123.2    Gi0/0
3.3.3.3           1 2WAY/DROTHER   10.0.123.3    Gi0/0

questions.prompt: A fresh broadcast election occurs after all four candidates are known, with no existing DR or BDR. Who becomes DR and BDR?
options: RB is DR; RD is BDR.
RA is DR; RC is BDR.
RD is DR; RC is BDR.
RD is DR; RA is BDR.
questions.explanation: RD wins by priority 50. Among the remaining eligible candidates, RA and RC tie at 1, so RA wins BDR by RID 4.4.4.4 over 3.3.3.3.

whyWrong.0: Priority 0 makes RB ineligible regardless of its high RID.
whyWrong.1: RD has a higher eligible interface priority than RA and RC.
whyWrong.2: RA and RC tie in priority, and RA has the higher RID.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or output
exhibit.text:
Candidate  Interface priority  RID
RA         1                   4.4.4.4
RB         0                   9.9.9.9
RC         1                   3.3.3.3
RD         50                  1.1.1.1

questions.prompt: R1 is the established DR, R2 is BDR, and R3 joins later with priority 200. After R1 fails, what happens if R2 and R3 remain healthy?
options: R3 becomes DR immediately when it joins.
R2 becomes DR, and R3 can become BDR.
R2 remains BDR while R3 and the remaining DROTHERs run a fresh DR-only comparison.
R3 becomes DR after R1 fails, bypassing R2.
questions.explanation: The non-preemptive election preserves existing roles while healthy. On DR failure, the BDR R2 is promoted and a new BDR can be selected from eligible remaining routers.

whyWrong.0: A later higher priority does not preempt an existing DR.
whyWrong.2: The existing BDR is promoted when the DR is lost; it does not remain reserved as BDR.
whyWrong.3: The existing BDR is promoted before a replacement BDR is chosen.

questions.prompt: R1 reaches a remote LAN through R2 then R3. The outgoing costs along that direction are R1-to-R2 = 10, R2-to-R3 = 20, and R3-to-LAN = 1. What OSPF metric should R1 calculate?
questions.explanation: Add the outgoing costs from the router performing the calculation to the destination network: 10 + 20 + 1 = 31. The receiving interfaces are not added again.

whyWrong.1: This omits the final outgoing interface toward the destination LAN.
whyWrong.2: This omits R1's outgoing cost.
whyWrong.3: 110 is IOS OSPF administrative distance, not this path metric.

questions.prompt: With no explicit interface cost overrides, which command on every OSPF router makes 100-Mbps, 1-Gbps, and 10-Gbps interfaces cost 100, 10, and 1?
options: auto-cost reference-bandwidth 1000
auto-cost reference-bandwidth 10000
ip ospf priority 100
auto-cost reference-bandwidth 100
questions.explanation: The command value is in Mbps: 10000 / 100 = 100, 10000 / 1000 = 10, and 10000 / 10000 = 1. Consistent reference bandwidth prevents inconsistent automatic cost scales.

whyWrong.0: A 1000-Mbps reference gives costs 10, 1, and 1.
whyWrong.2: Priority affects the DR/BDR election, not routing cost.
whyWrong.3: The default 100-Mbps reference gives these links minimum cost 1.

questions.prompt: What cost does OSPF use for this outgoing interface?
questions.explanation: Use the explicit interface cost when it exists. The reference-bandwidth calculation applies to automatic costs.

whyWrong.0: That is the reference bandwidth in Mbps, not the explicit cost.
whyWrong.1: That is the interface bandwidth in Mbps, not the explicit cost.
whyWrong.2: 1000/100 would give 10 automatically, but explicit interface cost overrides it.

exhibit.title: Automatic and explicit cost settings (exercise)
exhibit.text:
OSPF reference bandwidth: 1000 Mbps
Interface configured bandwidth: 100 Mbps
Interface command: ip ospf cost 7

questions.prompt: When R1 sends a packet to R3 client LAN, which next hop is expected on their shared Ethernet?
options: R3 shared-interface address, even if R2 is DR.
The destination PC MAC learned across the routed LAN.
R2 DR address for every packet, regardless of the destination router.
R2 BDR address because only the backup can forward user traffic.
questions.explanation: OSPF flooding roles do not force user packets through the DR. SPF can select a directly reachable router on the shared segment.

whyWrong.1: R1 resolves the adjacent next-hop router on this Ethernet, not the remote PC MAC.
whyWrong.2: The DR is not a mandatory data-plane transit router.
whyWrong.3: BDR is an OSPF control role, not an exclusive user-traffic forwarding role.

exhibit.title: Shared Ethernet forwarding path (exercise)
exhibit.text:
R1, R2 and R3 share 10.0.123.0/24. R2 is DR.
R3 advertises its client LAN.
The shortest path from R1 to that LAN crosses the shared segment directly to R3; there are no filters.

questions.prompt: A router with a configured new RID still displays the old active RID. What should the engineer do before any disruptive action?
options: Assign the same new RID to every router to keep the area consistent.
Verify the active RID and plan a controlled process restart if needed on this image.
Assume the new running-config value already changed every adjacency identity.
Change all neighbor process IDs to the new RID.
questions.explanation: Check operational output rather than inferring live state from the configuration. Restarting OSPF drops local adjacencies, so it must be deliberate.

whyWrong.0: Router IDs must be unique within the OSPF domain.
whyWrong.2: Configuration and the active process identity can differ until restart.
whyWrong.3: Process IDs are local numeric labels, not dotted-decimal router identities.

questions.prompt: R2 has a correctly addressed, up/up transit interface but no neighbor there. Which configuration line explains the absence?
options: passive-interface default without a Gi0/0 exception
router-id 2.2.2.2 in the routing process
router ospf 20 rather than process 10
questions.explanation: The interface is selected into OSPF, but passive-interface default suppresses its Hellos. Add no passive-interface gigabitethernet0/0 under that process after confirming it is the intended transit.

whyWrong.1: A unique explicit RID is appropriate.
whyWrong.2: This statement correctly activates the interface at .2.
whyWrong.3: Neighbors may use different process numbers.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or output
exhibit.text:
router ospf 20

questions.prompt: A cloned router configuration produces the log below. What is the durable identity repair?
options: Give every router a different local process number.
Raise the new router interface election priority.
Put each shared-interface peer in a different area.
Assign unique explicit RIDs and apply any required controlled process restart.
questions.explanation: The log identifies duplicate router ID 10.255.255.1, not a duplicate process number. Configure a unique RID on the affected router, verify the active value, and use a controlled restart only if needed to apply it.

whyWrong.0: Different process numbers do not repair duplicate advertised RIDs.
whyWrong.1: Priority affects DR eligibility, not unique identity.
whyWrong.2: Different areas on the same intended link prevent the required adjacency.

exhibit.title: Representative configuration or output
exhibit.text: %OSPF-4-DUP_RTRID_NBR: OSPF detected duplicate router-id 10.255.255.1 from 10.0.123.3

questions.prompt: Which repair addresses the missing LAN without changing the working transit adjacency?
options: Remove passive status from Gi0/2 but leave it outside OSPF.
Activate Gi0/2 in area 0 and keep it passive toward clients.
Raise the transit DR priority to advertise more LANs.
Change the transit process number to match the neighbor.
questions.explanation: The LAN is connected but never selected by OSPF. Activate it through the intended interface or matching network statement; passive behavior is correct for the client LAN.

whyWrong.0: Removing passive status alone does not activate an interface.
whyWrong.2: DR priority does not enroll a LAN interface in the process.
whyWrong.3: The established adjacency already proves local process-number differences are acceptable.

exhibit.title: Connected LAN outside OSPF (exercise)

Gi0/2 up/up: 192.168.25.1/24; local PC can reach it.
Only Gi0/0 has ip ospf 10 area 0.

Gi0/0 neighbor is Full; no network statements or redistribution.

questions.prompt: Which correction targets the demonstrated OSPF activation mismatch?
options: Widen the actual LAN mask to /24 so the mistaken selector appears to cover it.
Change the LAN selection so that it includes 192.168.31.65, retaining area 0 and the intended /27.
Set the PC default gateway to the neighboring router transit IP.
Lower the reference bandwidth to advertise the missing prefix.
questions.explanation: The wildcard 0.0.0.31 applied at .32 selects .32 through .63. Interface .65 belongs to .64/27 and falls outside that selection.

whyWrong.0: The selector must match the interface address; changing the mask abandons the given subnet plan.
whyWrong.2: That IP is not on the client LAN and does not enable the LAN in OSPF.
whyWrong.3: Cost calculation does not cause an unmatched interface to participate.

Required LAN: 192.168.31.64/27
R1 Gi0/2: 192.168.31.65/27 up/up
Only LAN selector: network 192.168.31.32 0.0.0.31 area 0
Gi0/2 is passive; transit adjacency is Full; remote router lacks this LAN.

questions.prompt: What is the most useful next comparison for this persistent Init state?
options: Increase R1 DR priority so its Hello will include itself as a neighbor.
Check whether R2 receives R1 Hellos and lists R1 RID in its own Hellos.
Assume all Init states are caused by mismatched MTU.
Change both router IDs to the same value so the Hello names match.
questions.explanation: Init means a Hello was heard but bidirectional recognition is not yet established. The supplied repeated evidence identifies the direction to inspect, not a uniquely proven physical cause.

whyWrong.0: Priority does not repair one-way recognition.
whyWrong.2: MTU exchange trouble normally appears later; the evidence points first to missing bidirectional Hello recognition.
whyWrong.3: Router IDs must be unique; duplication is not a repair.

exhibit.title: Persistent one-way Hello recognition (exercise)
exhibit.text:

R1 receives R2 Hellos, but those Hellos do not list R1 RID.
Interfaces are up. No capture or filter inspection at R2 has yet been collected.

questions.prompt: Which routes result from the directed costs?
options: R1 uses the shared path at cost 21; R3 uses the direct path at cost 31.
R1 uses the direct path at cost 6; R3 uses the shared path at cost 11.
Both use the direct path at cost 6 because the physical link is shared.
Both use the shared path because a DR is present there.
questions.explanation: R1 compares 5+1=6 with 20+1=21. R3 compares 30+1=31 with 10+1=11. Costs are calculated from the router originating each path.

whyWrong.0: Each router should select its lower total, not its higher one.
whyWrong.2: Outgoing costs are independently configured in the two directions.
whyWrong.3: DR role does not override path costs.

exhibit.title: Directed OSPF costs (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Area 0, all adjacencies Full, no other paths.
R1 -> shared Ethernet: 20; R3 -> shared Ethernet: 10
R1 -> R3 direct point-to-point: 5; R3 -> R1 direct: 30
LAN-A on R1 cost 1; LAN-B on R3 cost 1
Compare R1 route to LAN-B and R3 route to LAN-A.

questions.prompt: Which result follows when both paths are eligible and the maximum-paths setting permits at least two?
options: The two costs add together and create one cost-32 route.
The lower-bandwidth path must be rejected even when the explicit costs tie.
Both next hops can install at cost 16; equal throughput is not guaranteed.
Only the next hop with the higher router ID is installed.
questions.explanation: Each independent path totals 16. Equal-cost installation is distinct from traffic distribution and application throughput.

whyWrong.0: Each path is evaluated separately; parallel path costs are not summed.
whyWrong.1: The supplied OSPF costs, not a second independent bandwidth comparison, establish the tie.
whyWrong.3: RID election tiebreaking does not choose a sole equal-cost data route here.

exhibit.title: Two eligible paths to one prefix (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Path A: R1 outgoing 5 + R2 outgoing 10 + remote LAN 1
Path B: R1 outgoing 15 + remote LAN 1
Both advertise the same intra-area prefix; no other route source wins.

questions.prompt: Does the installed static route prove OSPF did not learn this prefix?
options: Yes; a prefix cannot exist in both OSPF information and the routing table from another source.
Yes; OSPF administrative distance 110 always beats static distance 1.
No; OSPF must instead install the same prefix as a connected route.
No; the lower-distance static can win installation even when OSPF knows the same prefix.
questions.explanation: For the same prefix, route-source preference can select static distance 1 over OSPF distance 110. Inspect OSPF information separately before diagnosing missing advertisements.

whyWrong.0: OSPF topology knowledge and route installation are distinct.
whyWrong.1: Lower distance wins between eligible candidates for the same prefix.
whyWrong.2: Connected routes represent local connected networks, not alternative learned copies.

exhibit.title: Installed route source (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Installed: S 192.168.26.0/24 [1/0] via 10.0.12.2
OSPF adjacency to R2 is Full.
An engineer claims that the S code alone proves R2 never advertised this LAN.

questions.prompt: R1 and R3 are the only two routers on an Ethernet link. They report Full, but remote LAN routes are missing. Which visible inconsistency should be corrected first?
options: Change R3 process 30 to process 10.
Configure the same intended OSPF network type at both ends.
Change both interfaces to Hello 30 and dead 120.
Replace the /30 addressing with a /24 subnet.
questions.explanation: A Full adjacency is not proof that both routers describe the link consistently. The displayed broadcast/point-to-point mismatch should be corrected on this two-router link, then neighbors and routes rechecked.

whyWrong.0: Different local process IDs do not explain the displayed topology mismatch.
whyWrong.2: The existing effective timer values already agree and are normal here.
whyWrong.3: The two /30 addresses are valid peers; this is not a shortage of host addresses.

    Hello 10, Dead 40

    Hello 10, Dead 40

questions.prompt: This adjacency repeatedly stalls during database exchange. Which evidence best identifies the fault?
options: Point-to-point operation omits the required DR.
The two process numbers are different.
The interface MTU values differ.
The peer uses a unique router ID.
questions.explanation: ExStart/Exchange involves DBD negotiation, including an MTU check. The explicit 1500/1400 mismatch is actionable evidence; fix the intended MTU rather than assuming every ExStart case has the same cause.

whyWrong.0: A point-to-point adjacency does not require a DR.
whyWrong.1: Process IDs are local and can differ.
whyWrong.3: Unique RIDs are required, not a fault.

exhibit.text:

R2 Gi0/1: up/up, MTU 1400, area 0, point-to-point, Hello 10, Dead 40
R1 neighbor 2.2.2.2: repeatedly EXSTART/ -

questions.prompt: What does the successful ping fail to establish?
options: It cannot establish any end-to-end reachability at all.
It does not establish that the direct backup adjacency is healthy.
It proves the direct link is carrying the ping because the routers are neighbors elsewhere.
It proves the two timer settings are compatible.
questions.explanation: Correlate the selected route with the neighbor on each interface. An alternate working path can hide an adjacency failure.

whyWrong.0: The successful endpoint test does establish reachability for that source/destination at that time.
whyWrong.2: The route selects the shared interface, not the direct link.
whyWrong.3: Different Hello/dead values on the intended direct relationship are incompatible.

exhibit.text:

R1 direct Gi0/1: Hello/dead 5/20; no neighbor.

cards.front: Default Cisco IOS OSPF administrative distance?
cards.back: 110. It is separate from the OSPF cost.

cards.front: OSPFv2 protocol number and multicast groups?
cards.back: IP protocol 89; 224.0.0.5 AllSPFRouters, 224.0.0.6 AllDRouters. No TCP/UDP port.

cards.front: How do DBD and LSU packets differ?
cards.back: A DBD summarizes database contents. An LSU carries the actual link-state advertisements being distributed.

cards.front: How does IOS choose a RID when a process starts?
cards.back: Explicit router-id; otherwise highest eligible up IPv4 loopback, then highest eligible active IPv4 interface. Verify the active RID.

cards.front: Normal IOS Hello/dead defaults for broadcast and point-to-point?
cards.back: 10/40 seconds. An explicitly configured dead interval can differ; compare effective values on both ends.

cards.front: What do 2-Way and Full establish?
cards.back: 2-Way confirms bidirectional Hello recognition. Full means database synchronization completed for that adjacency.

cards.front: Which two timer values must agree on the intended OSPF neighbor link?
cards.back: The effective Hello and dead intervals. Compare interface output on both ends; do not infer the effective values from one command alone.

cards.front: Repeated ExStart/Exchange: which common fault should you check?
cards.back: Compare interface MTUs and exchange errors. MTU mismatch is common, not the only cause; correct the mismatch before considering a bypass.

cards.front: When is 2WAY/DROTHER normal?
cards.back: Between two DROTHERs on a broadcast segment, while each is Full with the DR and BDR.

cards.front: What breaks a fresh DR election tie in interface priority?
cards.back: The higher router ID, among eligible routers. Existing DR/BDR roles require separate non-preemption reasoning.

cards.front: Broadcast versus point-to-point OSPF roles?
cards.back: Broadcast elects DR/BDR. Point-to-point has no DR/BDR and normally shows FULL/ -.

cards.front: Configure OSPF point-to-point on a two-router Ethernet link?
cards.back: ip ospf network point-to-point under both interfaces. Ethernet framing stays Ethernet.

cards.front: IOS automatic OSPF cost formula and default reference?
cards.back: Reference bandwidth / configured interface bandwidth, integer cost with minimum 1. Default reference 100 Mbps.

cards.front: Why can Fast Ethernet and Gigabit Ethernet both have automatic OSPF cost 1?
cards.back: With the default 100-Mbps reference, the computed integer cost has a minimum of 1. A higher consistent reference can distinguish faster links.

cards.front: Which interface costs make up a route metric?
cards.back: Outgoing costs from the calculating router to the destination, including the remote LAN interface; do not add receiving costs again.

cards.front: Set an OSPF reference of 1 Gbps?
cards.back: auto-cost reference-bandwidth 1000 in router mode, consistently across the routing domain. Units are Mbps.

cards.front: Two IOS ways to enable OSPFv2 on an interface?
cards.back: A matching network ADDRESS WILDCARD area statement, or ip ospf PROCESS area AREA directly on the interface.

cards.front: What does a passive OSPF interface still advertise?
cards.back: Its enabled, up connected prefix, through other OSPF links. It does not form neighbors on that interface.

cards.front: Must neighboring routers use the same OSPF process number?
cards.back: No. The process number is a local configuration label; the area must agree and router IDs must be unique.

cards.front: What does [110/11] in an IOS OSPF route mean?
cards.back: Administrative distance 110, total OSPF cost 11. Neither number is the prefix length.

cards.front: Does OSPF priority 0 disable adjacency formation?
cards.back: No. It prevents DR/BDR election eligibility; the router can still form Full adjacencies with the elected routers.

cards.front: A higher-priority OSPF router joins a healthy broadcast segment: must it become DR?
cards.back: No. Existing DR/BDR roles are non-preemptive.

cards.front: Which wins: automatic OSPF cost or explicit ip ospf cost?
cards.back: The explicit interface cost overrides the automatic bandwidth calculation.

cards.front: Does a host wildcard in an OSPF network command advertise a /32?
cards.back: No. It selects the interface by address. An ordinary Ethernet LAN is advertised using its actual interface prefix.

cards.front: Does Full prove that every intended client LAN is advertised?
cards.back: No. Verify the remote LAN interface state, activation and its route separately.

cards.front: Can R1 and R3 calculate different costs over the same physical link?
cards.back: Yes. Each uses its own outgoing interface cost; reverse-direction configuration need not be equal.

tickets.title: Database exchange stalls after an MTU change
tickets.scenario: R1 and B2 share a direct point-to-point Ethernet link. The link supports IPv4 MTU 1500, both interfaces are up/up, and small pings work. B2 alone received an accidental ip mtu 1400 command. These excerpts are representative evidence. The compared interface on B2 is GigabitEthernet0/1.

exhibits.title: R1 OSPF neighbor
exhibits.text:
2.2.2.2  EXSTART/ -  10.0.12.2  Gi0/1
State repeatedly returns to EXSTART.

exhibits.title: Interface comparison
exhibits.text:
R1: 10.0.12.1/30, area 0, point-to-point, Hello 10, Dead 40, IP MTU 1500
B2: 10.0.12.2/30, area 0, point-to-point, Hello 10, Dead 40, IP MTU 1400

tickets.question: Which fault is supported by the evidence?
options: No DR exists on the point-to-point link.
B2 has an inconsistent IP MTU during database exchange.
The /30 subnet cannot carry OSPF LSAs.
B2 must use R1's router ID for synchronization.
tickets.explanation: The displayed MTUs differ even though the link supports 1500 and the other intended parameters agree. OSPF database exchange checks MTU; small ping success does not prove a large packet or DBD can be accepted. Restore the intended value and verify Full and the remote LAN route.
tickets.fix:
```ios B2
B2# configure terminal
B2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
B2(config-if)# no ip mtu
B2(config-if)# end
B2# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/1
B2# show ip ospf neighbor
B2# show ip route ospf
```
This scenario explicitly states that 1500 is supported. If the underlying service requires a smaller MTU, agree a consistent supported value instead; do not bypass the check as a routine repair.

tickets.title: A copied timer template prevents shared-LAN neighbors
tickets.scenario: R2 and R3 are in the same Ethernet VLAN. Both /24 interfaces are up/up and bidirectional ping succeeds. R3 received an explicit 30/120 timer template; the intended shared-LAN design is 10/40. Output below is representative.

exhibits.title: R2 Gi0/2 interface
exhibits.text:
10.0.23.2/24, Area 0, Process 10, RID 2.2.2.2
Network Type BROADCAST; Hello 10, Dead 40

exhibits.title: R3 Gi0/2 interface
exhibits.text:
10.0.23.3/24, Area 0, Process 30, RID 3.3.3.3
Network Type BROADCAST; Hello 30, Dead 120

tickets.question: What must be repaired to establish the intended relationship?
options: Make both process IDs 10.
Change one router to a new area for the VLAN.
Restore matching effective Hello/dead intervals.
Replace the /24 with a /30 mask on R3 only.
tickets.explanation: The Hello and dead values differ. The process IDs may differ, the shared area already matches, and changing one mask would introduce another fault. Restore the intended timer defaults and verify rather than promising an exact time to Full.
tickets.fix:
```ios R3
R3# configure terminal
R3(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
R3(config-if)# no ip ospf hello-interval
R3(config-if)# no ip ospf dead-interval
R3(config-if)# end
R3# show ip ospf interface gigabitethernet0/2
R3# show ip ospf neighbor
```
Confirm the effective timer pair is 10/40 and the expected adjacency reaches Full before saving.

chapters.subtitle: Configure IPv6 routing with link-local neighbors, explicit router IDs, and verifiable paths.

sources.title: Cisco IOS: IPv6 Routing with OSPFv3
Cisco IOS XE 17: IPv6 Routing with OSPFv3
Cisco: Implementing OSPFv3 and interface configuration

chapters.summary: Apply single-area OSPF to IPv6. Separate router IDs from IPv6 next hops, configure both supported IOS syntax families, interpret broadcast and point-to-point neighbors, and prove remote prefixes work.

sections.title: OSPF for IPv6
sections.body:
:::facts
- OSPFv3 for IPv6 uses IPv6 **Next Header 89**, without TCP or UDP.
- On ordinary links, OSPFv3 packets use a **link-local source address**. Hellos use **ff02::5**; **ff02::6** identifies the DR/BDR group.
- Router IDs remain **32-bit dotted-decimal identifiers**, even on IPv6-only routers.
- IOS defaults for the broadcast and point-to-point network types studied here are Hello **10 seconds**, dead **40 seconds**, interface priority **1**, and OSPF administrative distance **110**.
- Chapter 22 directly supports v2.0. OSPFv3 is additional practice for the v1.1 track.
:::

**OSPFv3** provides the OSPF mechanisms from Chapter 21 for an IPv6 network: discover neighbors, synchronize link-state information, calculate shortest paths, and install routes. You are learning the address and configuration differences, not a completely different routing algorithm.

Consider an IPv6-only branch. R1 needs a route to R3's LAN, and R3 needs a route back to R1's LAN. Both routers can communicate with adjacent routers using link-local addresses while advertising global unicast prefixes for end-to-end forwarding. The adjacency's address and the final packet destination therefore serve different purposes.

The original OSPFv3 specification supports IPv6. Later address-family extensions also support IPv4; that does not mean an OSPFv2 neighbor becomes an OSPFv3 neighbor automatically. For this course's v2.0 objective, use OSPFv2 for IPv4 and OSPFv3 for IPv6. The two processes do not exchange LSAs with each other.

Before configuration, verify the IPv6 basics from Chapter 19: a /64 LAN prefix, a usable interface address, an IPv6 default gateway on each host, and link-local scope. A successful ping to a directly attached global address proves less than a successful ping between the two client LANs.

sections.title: What changes from OSPFv2
sections.body:
| Feature | OSPFv2 for IPv4 | OSPFv3 for IPv6 |
|---|---|---|
| Neighbor packet source on an ordinary link | IPv4 interface address | IPv6 link-local address |
| AllSPFRouters multicast | `224.0.0.5` | `ff02::5` |
| AllDRouters multicast | `224.0.0.6` | `ff02::6` |
| Router ID | 32-bit dotted decimal | 32-bit dotted decimal |
| Typical IOS route next hop | IPv4 address | Link-local IPv6 address plus interface |

IPv6 link-local addresses identify a neighbor on one link; routers do not forward a packet whose destination is link-local across the network. In a route such as `via FE80::3, GigabitEthernet0/0`, the next hop is reachable through that specific interface. The forwarded packet can still have the remote global destination `2001:db8:30::10`. OSPF is not converting that destination into a link-local address.

An OSPFv3 Hello does not contain the OSPFv2 subnet-mask field. Routers on the same link can establish an adjacency even if their global prefixes differ, provided the actual OSPF and link-local requirements are met. This flexibility is not a reason to misaddress a shared LAN. A Full neighbor entry cannot certify that hosts have the intended global prefix or gateway.

OSPFv3 separates topology descriptions from prefix information. Router and Network LSAs describe connections; other advertisements associate IPv6 prefixes with that topology and supply link information. That distinction explains how a neighbor relationship can work while a destination prefix is absent. You do not need a catalogue of LSA type numbers or multi-area flooding scopes to configure and verify this single-area network.

No authentication is configured in the examples. The v2.0 adjacency objective explicitly excludes authentication. OSPFv3 has security mechanisms beyond its original specification, so avoid the blanket claim that OSPFv3 always uses IPsec or has no other authentication options.

sections.title: Router ID and neighbour requirements
sections.body:
Set the RID explicitly on every router. `router-id 2.2.2.2` is valid on an IPv6-only router because it is an identifier, not an instruction to add an IPv4 interface. Classic IOS automatic selection relies on eligible IPv4 addresses; when none exist, an explicit RID avoids a process that cannot obtain one. Never derive an OSPF RID by truncating an IPv6 address.

Keep three identifiers separate: the local process ID chooses a configuration process, the router ID identifies a router, and the **instance ID** distinguishes OSPFv3 instances on a link. For the classic IPv6-unicast syntax used in the Packet Tracer lab, the default instance ID is 0. Neighbors must use compatible instance IDs on their common link; their locally significant process numbers may differ. Address-family implementations use instance values appropriate to the family, so compare the actual interface output when mixing syntax families.

Both interfaces must be operational, have IPv6 enabled and valid link-local addressing, participate in the same area, and allow OSPF packets. Compare Hello/dead timers and ensure the interface is not passive. Router IDs must be unique, and a duplicated link-local address on the same link is also a fault. Configure matching intended network types; inspect MTUs when database synchronization fails.

A common beginner mistake is entering `ipv6 ospf 10 area 0` without enabling router-wide IPv6 forwarding. `ipv6 unicast-routing` is part of this routed lab's setup. Another is placing the process only on transit links. That can produce perfect neighbors while never advertising either client LAN.

:::trap A dotted-decimal RID is not an IPv4 next hop
In `show ipv6 ospf neighbor`, `2.2.2.2` identifies the neighboring OSPF router. It does not mean IPv4 routing is required or that an IPv6 packet is forwarded to that dotted-decimal address.
:::

sections.title: Broadcast and point-to-point operation
Cost and advertised prefixes
sections.body:
OSPFv3 still chooses a lower total path cost. IOS automatic costs use reference bandwidth divided by interface bandwidth, with minimum 1; the normal default reference is 100 Mbps. For a consistent 10-Gbps reference, configure `auto-cost reference-bandwidth 10000` on every router in the process design. Alternatively set explicit per-interface costs with `ipv6 ospf cost` in classic syntax.

Suppose R1 has two ways to R3. The shared transit's outgoing cost is 10; a direct point-to-point link costs 25. R3's LAN interface costs 1. R1's route to `2001:db8:30::/64` should cost 11 through the shared segment, or 26 through the direct link if the preferred adjacency fails. The next-hop address changes with the selected link. It does not change the destination prefix.

Include the remote LAN's cost once. Do not add the receiving interface's cost, and do not add the local PC-facing interface cost to R1's routing-table metric. The table describes a path beginning at R1. A reverse path is calculated independently at R3 and could be different if costs differ by direction.

An OSPF-enabled physical LAN advertises its configured prefix. A loopback behaves differently on classic IOS: OSPF normally advertises its IPv6 address as a /128 host route even when the address command uses /64. A deliberately chosen point-to-point network type on the loopback can advertise the prefix instead. Verify rather than assuming that every /64 address command creates a learned /64 route. The main lab uses physical LANs to keep client reachability separate from loopback-specific behavior.

Before continuing, work a prefix check without configuration. R3 has `2001:db8:30::1/64` on an up physical client interface, but OSPF runs only on its transit interface. R1 can be Full with R3 and still have no route to `2001:db8:30::/64`. Making the client interface passive does not fix the missing activation. Enable the client interface in the process and retain its passive setting. After convergence, verify the /64 on R1, then test a packet sourced from R1's client LAN. This last test also needs R3 to know R1's client prefix; the forward advertisement is only half of the path.

sections.title: Configuring OSPFv3
sections.body:
Classic IPv6-specific IOS syntax is useful on Packet Tracer router images. This R1 pattern assumes the interfaces have already been addressed:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ipv6 unicast-routing
R1(config)# ipv6 router ospf 10
R1(config-rtr)# router-id 1.1.1.1
R1(config-rtr)# passive-interface default
R1(config-rtr)# no passive-interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-rtr)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ipv6 ospf 10 area 0
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
R1(config-if)# ipv6 ospf 10 area 0
R1(config-if)# end
```

The process settings do not select interfaces by themselves. Each intended interface needs its activation command. There is no IPv4-style `network ADDRESS WILDCARD` statement in this configuration. A passive LAN still needs activation so its prefix is advertised.

Current IOS XE also supports an **address-family syntax**. Recognize this alternative on a clean supported image; do not paste it over a completed classic-syntax lab as an unplanned migration:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ipv6 unicast-routing
R1(config)# router ospfv3 10
R1(config-router)# router-id 1.1.1.1
R1(config-router)# address-family ipv6 unicast
R1(config-router-af)# passive-interface default
R1(config-router-af)# no passive-interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-router-af)# exit-address-family
R1(config-router)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ospfv3 10 ipv6 area 0
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
R1(config-if)# ospfv3 10 ipv6 area 0
R1(config-if)# end
```

Use `show ospfv3 neighbor` and `show ospfv3 interface` for that syntax family. Platform and release determine exact syntax and migration behavior. The guided lab provides a complete classic configuration and a paper translation exercise when the simulator lacks the newer commands.

sections.title: Verify and troubleshoot
sections.body:
These shortened examples are authored representative output, not a recorded simulator run:

```output R1# show ipv6 ospf neighbor — representative
Neighbor ID     Pri   State           Dead Time   Interface ID   Interface
3.3.3.3           0   FULL/DROTHER    00:00:36    3              GigabitEthernet0/0  ← 3 is the neighbor's interface ID
```

The final interface is R1's local interface; the Interface ID column belongs to the neighbor. Use detailed neighbor/interface output when you need its link-local address. The same RID can appear on two rows when routers share two links.

```output R1# show ipv6 route ospf — representative
O   2001:DB8:30::/64 [110/11]  ← administrative distance and total cost
     via FE80::3, GigabitEthernet0/0  ← next hop must be interpreted with its link
```

Verify in layers. `show ipv6 interface brief` checks address and operational state. `show ipv6 ospf interface` checks process, area, RID, network type, timers, cost, and instance. `show ipv6 ospf neighbor` checks relationships. `show ipv6 route ospf` checks installed prefixes, while `show ipv6 route` also reveals competing routes. Finish with client-to-client ping and a route back to the source network.

An empty neighbor table suggests activation, area, instance, timers, passive settings, or link communication. Repeated ExStart/Exchange suggests investigating MTU and database exchange, not immediately disabling the MTU check. Full neighbors with a missing LAN suggest an inactive LAN or missing interface activation. Full neighbors with failed client traffic require checking host parameters and both directions of routing.

After changing an active RID, a controlled classic IOS restart can use `clear ipv6 ospf 10 process`. Check the release's help first, record the active RID, and expect adjacency disruption. A local restart does not guarantee that this router becomes DR: surviving segment roles remain relevant. Restore any deliberate fault before saving configuration.

sections.title: Exam focus
sections.body: Configure a unique RID, IPv6 forwarding, interface activation, area 0, and passive client LANs. Explain why link-local addresses appear as next hops and why a RID still looks like IPv4. Predict broadcast elections using existing roles and priority, recognize a point-to-point adjacency, calculate path cost, and verify both client networks. Detailed multi-area LSA analysis and authentication setup are not needed for this chapter's stated objective.

lab.title: Build IPv6 OSPF neighbors and trace a global prefix
lab.intro:
Practice revised September 2026. If you completed an earlier version, repeat the revised exercise and update its checkmarks.

Use the supplied IPv6 setup to isolate what differs from OSPFv2: explicit router identity, interface activation, scoped link-local neighbors, and global prefix participation. Write the predictions before commands and retain actual evidence before any repair.

Build a separate IPv6-only file from blank devices. This lab uses the classic IPv6-specific IOS syntax; the final step translates the core into address-family syntax without changing the working lab.

Use a new Packet Tracer file with **three 2911 routers**, **one 2960 switch**, and **two PCs**. The 2911 provides Gi0/0, Gi0/1, and Gi0/2. Use straight-through copper for router–switch links, and crossover or the auto-connect tool for router–router and direct PC–router links. On CML/other images, map the interfaces explicitly before typing. All output in this guide is representative, not a recorded run; simulator commands and timing can differ.

The PCs may generate their own unique link-local addresses. No DNS or IPv4 address is required. SW1 is an ordinary Layer 2 switch in VLAN 1, with no management address. Shared costs are 10, direct costs 25, and client-LAN costs 1.

### Prediction and observation sheet

| Checkpoint | Predict before testing | Record actual evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Shared startup | DR/BDR/DROTHER and eligible priorities | Roles, RIDs, local interfaces |
| Normal LAN routes | Prefix, next-hop/interface pair and metric in both directions | Both route entries and PC pings |
| Direct timer fault | Which neighbor disappears and whether clients still work | Both timer pairs and selected route |
| LAN activation removed | Neighbor state versus route to that LAN | Remote route table and local/remote PC tests |
| LAN restored | Required activation, passive behavior | Returned /64 and successful endpoint tests |

Do not treat the router ID, neighbor Interface ID and link-local next hop as interchangeable. Record each in its own field. If Packet Tracer does not support the classic OSPFv3 commands, use a supported IOS/CML image or complete the predictions from these explicitly authored configurations; label a worksheet result as such.

steps.title: Read neighbors and next-hop identities
steps.body:
Inspect R1 and R3. Record the local interface, neighbor RID, neighbor interface ID, link-local next hop, network type, and timers.

```ios R1
R1# show ipv6 ospf neighbor
R1# show ipv6 ospf interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1# show ipv6 route ospf
```

```ios R3
R3# show ipv6 ospf neighbor
R3# show ipv6 route ospf
```


:::expected
R1 sees RID 3.3.3.3 twice: FULL/DROTHER on shared Gi0/0 and FULL/ - on direct Gi0/1. Interface ID is the neighbor interface identifier; it is neither an IPv4 next hop nor necessarily the local process ID. Interface ID values can vary by image.
:::

steps.title: Prove the advertised /64 routes
steps.body:
Calculate the shared and direct path totals first. Predict the global destination prefix separately from the scoped link-local next hop; compare only after recording your calculation.

Use the client PCs so the test requires return routes to the actual client prefixes. On PC-A run:
```text
ping 2001:db8:30::10
```
On PC-B run:
```text
ping 2001:db8:10::10
```
Then inspect the two routers again.

```ios R1
R1# show ipv6 route ospf
```

```ios R3
R3# show ipv6 route ospf
```


:::solution
After Neighbor Discovery and convergence, both pings work. R1 learns 2001:DB8:30::/64 [110/11] via FE80::3, Gi0/0. R3 learns 2001:DB8:10::/64 [110/11] via FE80::1, Gi0/0. The IP destination remains global while the next-hop address is link-local.
:::

steps.title: Break only the direct adjacency
steps.body:
Predict the direct neighbor state and the client ping result separately. A working client test is not a substitute for checking both adjacencies.

Set R1 direct-link timers to 5/20 while R3 remains at 10/40. Wait until the direct neighbor no longer remains Full and compare effective timer output.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ipv6 ospf hello-interval 5
R1(config-if)# ipv6 ospf dead-interval 20
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ipv6 ospf interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1# show ipv6 ospf neighbor
```

```ios R3
R3# show ipv6 ospf interface gigabitethernet0/1
```


:::expected
The direct relationship fails because both timer values disagree. The shared adjacency and cost-11 route remain healthy, so PC traffic can still work. This is an adjacency fault hidden by another usable path.
:::

steps.title: Restore the direct timers
steps.body:
Remove the deliberate overrides from R1 only.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# no ipv6 ospf hello-interval
R1(config-if)# no ipv6 ospf dead-interval
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ipv6 ospf interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1# show ipv6 ospf neighbor
```


:::expected
R1 reports 10/40 again and the direct neighbor reaches FULL/ -. A process clear, RID change, or new IPv4 address is unnecessary.
:::

steps.title: Remove a LAN advertisement while keeping neighbors
steps.body:
Before removing activation, predict the local PC-to-gateway test, the transit neighbor state and R1's remote route. Preserve the failure evidence before Step 8 restores participation.

On R3, disable OSPF activation on Gi0/2 without shutting the interface or changing its address. Inspect R1 after convergence and test PC-A to PC-B.

```ios R3
R3# configure terminal
R3(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
R3(config-if)# no ipv6 ospf 30 area 0
R3(config-if)# end
R3# show ipv6 interface brief
R3# show ipv6 ospf neighbor
```

```ios R1
R1# show ipv6 route ospf
```


:::expected
R3 remains Full with its routers, and PC-B can still ping its local gateway. R1 loses the OSPF route to 2001:db8:30::/64 and PC-A cannot reach PC-B. A Full adjacency proves synchronization, not that every desired LAN participates.
:::

steps.title: Restore LAN participation
steps.body:
Re-enable the intended LAN in area 0. Its process-level passive setting remains correct.

```ios R3
R3# configure terminal
R3(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
R3(config-if)# ipv6 ospf 30 area 0
R3(config-if)# end
R3# show ipv6 ospf interface gigabitethernet0/2
```

```ios R1
R1# show ipv6 route ospf
```


:::expected
R1 relearns the /64 at cost 11 and PC-A/PC-B pings recover. Gi0/2 remains passive: it advertises the LAN through other interfaces while forming no PC-facing adjacency.
:::

steps.body:
In notes, translate R1 process 10 and its three area-0 activations into address-family syntax. Do not paste a migration into this working file. Compare with the answer below, then save each router and switch.

```ios R1
R1# copy running-config startup-config
```

```ios R2

```

```ios R3

```

