exhibit.text:
R1 Gi0/0:
 standby 1 priority 110
 standby 1 preempt
 standby 1 track GigabitEthernet0/1 5
R1 Gi0/1: down/down

questions.prompt: An HSRP standby uses a 10-second active hold timer. It accepted its last active Hello 3 seconds ago, and no further Hello or Resign arrives. How much hold time remains before expiry?
options: Approximately 7 seconds.
Approximately 3 seconds.
Approximately 10 seconds from now.
Exactly three additional Hello transmissions.
questions.explanation: The remaining interval is 10 − 3 = 7 seconds before timer expiry. Actual forwarding recovery also includes state processing and the rest of the network, so this is not an exact application-recovery promise.

whyWrong.1: Three seconds is elapsed time in the question, not the remaining hold time.
whyWrong.2: The timer was already started by the last accepted Hello.
whyWrong.3: The receiver uses a timer; it does not require counting a fixed number of future sends.

questions.prompt: During ordinary same-version HSRP failover, what helps the switch send frames for the virtual MAC toward the new Active router?
options: Changing every PC gateway to the new router real IP.
Updating the PC ARP cache alone while leaving the switch MAC location unchanged.
Keeping the old switch port because the virtual gateway IP did not change.
Frames sourced from the virtual MAC, including gratuitous ARP announcements.
questions.explanation: Switches learn source MAC addresses on incoming ports. The new active router announcements and traffic using the virtual MAC update that location while the host can retain the same IP-to-MAC mapping.

whyWrong.0: The virtual gateway lets hosts retain their configured gateway.
whyWrong.1: The switch must learn which local port leads to the virtual MAC; a host-only cache update does not supply that location.
whyWrong.2: The identity remains but its physical location changes.

questions.prompt: Which two entries should remain unchanged during ordinary same-version failover of this group? Choose two.
options: The switch port learned for the virtual MAC.
The PC configured virtual gateway IP.
The group virtual IP-to-virtual-MAC mapping.
The physical router performing the Active role.
The exact number of application packets lost.
questions.explanation: The virtual identity lets the host keep its gateway. The switch learns the location of that identity toward the replacement router.

whyWrong.0: That location should move toward the new forwarding router.
whyWrong.3: That router changes during the failover.
whyWrong.4: Loss depends on detection, convergence and the rest of the network; it is not a stable identity field.

questions.prompt: Both routers have preemption enabled. R1 uses priority 110 for VLAN 10 and 90 for VLAN 20; R2 uses 90 for VLAN 10 and 110 for VLAN 20. Each VLAN has its own agreed group/VIP. What is the intended steady-state arrangement?
options: R1 forwards for VLAN 10 while R2 forwards for VLAN 20.
R1 and R2 both forward concurrently for each single HSRP group.
R1 becomes Active for both VLANs because it has a 110 somewhere.
R2 becomes Standby for both VLANs because its VLAN 10 priority is lower.
questions.explanation: Different groups can prefer different routers, distributing gateway duties across VLANs. This is per-group sharing, not two routers simultaneously Active for the same group.

whyWrong.1: Ordinary HSRP has one Active per group in steady state.
whyWrong.2: Priority is evaluated within each group rather than router-wide.
whyWrong.3: Its higher VLAN 20 priority makes it preferred in that separate group.

exhibit.title: Representative per-group priority plan
exhibit.text:
VLAN 10 / HSRP group 10: R1 priority 110, R2 priority 90
VLAN 20 / HSRP group 20: R1 priority 90, R2 priority 110
Both routers have preempt enabled in both groups.

questions.prompt: Two intended IPv4 HSRP peers share a VLAN and VIP but each remains Active with unknown Standby. Which two configuration mismatches can create separate groups that do not recognize each other? Choose two.
options: Different HSRP versions on the interfaces
Different configured HSRP priorities
Different real interface IPs in the same subnet
Different HSRP group numbers
Preemption enabled on both peers
questions.explanation: Version and group identity must agree for the intended HSRP relationship. Different real addresses and priorities are normal in a redundant gateway pair.

whyWrong.1: Different priorities intentionally establish preference and do not isolate peers.
whyWrong.2: The routers need different real interface addresses.
whyWrong.4: Preemption on both peers does not by itself create two active routers.

questions.prompt: Why can the virtual gateway still answer while the server test fails?
options: R1 remains a reachable first hop but has no usable route to the server prefix.
The PC must change its gateway to R2 real IP whenever a server stops replying.
R2 Standby proves that its physical LAN interface is shut.
An Active HSRP state guarantees that the complete forward and return path works.
questions.explanation: Read FHRP and routing evidence separately. The active router can answer for the VIP while lacking onward reachability; inspect the remote and reverse paths before claiming application availability.

whyWrong.1: Changing the host gateway bypasses the redundancy design without diagnosing the routed path.
whyWrong.2: Standby is a protocol role; the peer may be fully operational.
whyWrong.3: Active describes the gateway role, not end-to-end path health.

questions.prompt: After the shown tracked failure, what role change is expected, and what must still be verified?
options: R2 can preempt R1; remote service still needs separate verification.
R1 stays preferred because its configured priority is still 135.
R1 changes the VIP to its real address because its effective priority fell.
R2 takes over and this alone proves every server is reachable.
questions.explanation: 135-40=95, below R2 at 110. R2 has preempt, so it can take over from the still-live LAN peer; then verify actual service delivery.

whyWrong.1: Tracking changes effective priority to 95; configured priority is not the current comparison value.
whyWrong.2: Tracking changes priority, not the intended virtual gateway identity.
whyWrong.3: FHRP role transition does not establish all routed or application paths.

questions.prompt: Which next action is supported by the two Active states?
options: Immediately set both real interface addresses to the VIP.
Conclude that preempt must be disabled on both routers.
Compare VLAN reachability, group and version on both peers before naming a specific cause.
Conclude that differing priorities alone caused the split.
questions.explanation: Two Active states are a symptom requiring correlated evidence. Unlike the version-mismatch ticket, this excerpt does not yet identify a single cause.

whyWrong.3: Different priorities are normal and do not prevent recognition.

exhibit.title: Two Active peers with incomplete evidence (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Intended HSRP pair:
R1 State Active, Standby unknown
R2 State Active, Standby unknown
No peer configuration comparison or VLAN/control-traffic test has been collected.

cards.front: HSRP default Hello/hold and what starts the active hold timer?
cards.back: 3/10 seconds. Accepted active Hellos refresh the timer; silent failure is detected at expiry, not by counting exactly three missed packets.

cards.front: Which HSRP priority is preferred?
cards.back: The higher effective priority. The normal configured default is 100; tracking can reduce the effective value.

cards.front: HSRP preemption default and purpose?
cards.back: Disabled. Enabling it lets a higher-priority router take over from a healthy lower-priority Active router.

cards.front: How do Active and Standby differ in an ordinary HSRP group?
cards.back: Active forwards for the virtual gateway. Standby is the selected replacement if the active role is lost.

cards.front: IPv4 HSRP group ranges for versions 1 and 2?
cards.back: v1 0–255; v2 0–4095. Peers must use a compatible version and group.

cards.front: Does VRRPv3 use one shared virtual MAC for both IPv4 and IPv6?
cards.back: No. The address families use different virtual MAC blocks and independent instances; read the family in the status.

cards.front: What VRRP priority identifies the address owner?
cards.back: 255. Ordinary non-owner routers use lower priorities; their normal default is 100.

cards.front: VRRP forwarding role in Cisco output versus the current RFC?
cards.back: Cisco often says Master; RFC 9568 says Active. Backup is the non-forwarding role for that virtual instance.

cards.front: What changes in the switch during ordinary HSRP failover?
cards.back: The learned port for the virtual MAC changes. The virtual IP/MAC identity remains, so hosts need not change their configured gateway.

cards.front: R1's priority 110 minus tracking decrement 20: what else allows R2 takeover?
cards.back: R1 becomes 90; R2 at 100 needs preempt to take over while R1 remains alive on the LAN.

cards.front: Why must an HSRP version change be coordinated across peers?
cards.back: Peers must recognize the same version, and changing versions changes the ordinary IPv4 virtual MAC. It is different from same-version failover.

cards.front: What does unknown in an HSRP peer-role field mean?
cards.back: No peer in that role is currently known. In an intended pair, compare VLAN, version, group, and control traffic.

cards.front: Which VRRP version supports IPv6, and does IPv4 Master prove IPv6 Master?
cards.back: VRRPv3 supports IPv4 and IPv6. Their instances are independent; inspect the address family and virtual address.

cards.front: Which gateway address should the PC use: a peer real IP or the agreed VIP?
cards.back: The agreed virtual IP, so a replacement router can preserve the gateway identity.

cards.front: Does a successful ping to the VIP prove a remote server path works?
cards.back: No. Verify the active router destination route, the return route and the actual remote test.

cards.front: Does tracking an uplink line protocol detect every remote application failure?
cards.back: No. It tracks that local condition. A remote failure can occur while the interface remains up.

cards.front: Which field should be compared with a peer after tracking triggers: configured or effective priority?
cards.back: Effective priority. The configured baseline can stay unchanged while a decrement lowers the value used for preference.

cards.front: Two intended HSRP peers are Active with unknown Standby: is that a unique diagnosis?
cards.back: No. Compare VLAN/control reachability, version, group and other relevant peer settings before choosing a repair.

tickets.title: A responsive virtual gateway has lost its only upstream path
tickets.scenario: R1 and R2 are a healthy IPv4 HSRP pair for 192.168.10.1. R1's priority is 110 and R2 is 100; both have preempt. R1's only upstream link Gi0/1 failed. R2 still has a working path and a verified return route. R1 configuration has no HSRP track command. Representative evidence follows.

exhibits.title: R1 HSRP detail
exhibits.text:
State Active
Active router local; Standby router 192.168.10.3
Preemption enabled
Priority 110 (configured 110)

tickets.question: Which configuration gap explains why the upstream failure has not changed gateway preference?
options: R2 has no preemption configured.
R1's uplink health is not linked to its HSRP priority.
R1 and R2 use the same virtual IP.
R1's configured priority is already below R2.
tickets.explanation: The group still hears a healthy Active router on the LAN, and R1 remains priority 110. Its failed uplink is not tracked, so that failure does not lower its preference. A tracking decrement of 20 makes R1 90 and permits preempt-enabled R2 at 100 to take over.
tickets.fix:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# track 1 interface gigabitethernet0/1 line-protocol
R1(config-track)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# standby 1 track 1 decrement 20
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show standby
```
Use this object form on a supporting IOS image; the legacy interface form is an alternative as explained in the lab. Verify R2 Active and a real remote destination. Restore the physical fault separately, then verify R1 priority returns to 110 and routing works.

tickets.title: Two active routers use different HSRP versions
tickets.scenario: R1 and R2 should share group 1 and VIP 192.168.10.1. Their switch ports are confirmed in VLAN 10, both real addresses can ping, and the condition persists after convergence time. Each device reports Active with unknown Standby. These are representative excerpts.

exhibits.text:
GigabitEthernet0/0 - Group 1 (version 2)
State Active; Priority 110; Preemption enabled
Virtual IP 192.168.10.1
Active virtual MAC 0000.0c9f.f001
Standby router unknown

exhibits.title: R2 show standby excerpt
exhibits.text:
GigabitEthernet0/0 - Group 1 (version 1)
State Active; Priority 100; Preemption enabled
Virtual IP 192.168.10.1
Active virtual MAC 0000.0c07.ac01
Standby router unknown

tickets.question: Which fault is directly established?
options: Both routers must have identical real interface addresses.
Both priorities must be equal before any election can occur.
The peers run incompatible HSRP versions for the intended group.
Preemption must be disabled on both routers to avoid duplicate Active.
tickets.explanation: The version lines and virtual MAC patterns identify v2 on R1 and v1 on R2. They do not exchange compatible group Hellos, so each can consider itself Active. Raising priority will not repair the version mismatch.
tickets.fix:
```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R2(config-if)# standby version 2
R2(config-if)# end
R2# show standby
R2# show standby brief
```
This scenario assumes version 2 is the intended supported design. Verify one Active, one Standby, peer addresses known, and successful client traffic before saving.

chapters.title: DHCP
chapters.subtitle: Obtain, renew, and troubleshoot IPv4 leases across local and routed networks.

sources.title: Cisco IP addressing command reference: DHCP client distance

chapters.summary: Explain DHCPv4 messages and lease state, configure IOS clients and a server, relay requests to a remote subnet, and isolate failures using client, relay, and server evidence.

sections.body:
A DHCP client requests the addressing information it needs to participate in an IPv4 network. A server allocates an address and supplies settings such as the subnet mask, gateway, and DNS resolver. A relay makes the same service available when the client and server are on different subnets.

You will configure all three roles and trace a failed request through them. The current v1.1 objectives emphasize the service role and client/relay configuration. The v2.0 objective explicitly includes troubleshooting the IOS server as well. Understanding the server is also necessary to build a complete client/relay lab.

sections.title: What DHCP provides
sections.body:
:::facts
- **DHCPv4** uses UDP: servers listen on **67**, clients on **68**. Ordinary relay-to-server messages use **67 → 67**.
- The initial selecting exchange is **Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge**, often abbreviated **DORA**.
- The initial Discover and selecting Request are broadcasts from **0.0.0.0** to **255.255.255.255**. This is not the addressing of every later Request.
- Offer/ACK delivery depends on client state, the broadcast flag, and whether a relay is involved.
- Unless the server supplies different valid values, **T1 = 50%** and **T2 = 87.5%** of the lease duration.
- Configure `ip helper-address` on the Layer 3 interface receiving the clients' broadcasts.
:::

**Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol** supplies configuration through a client/server exchange. An address **pool** defines addresses available for allocation. A **lease** permits a client to use an address for an agreed duration. A **binding** records the allocation to a client identifier. A binding is not proof that the client is currently connected or that its applications work.

DHCP reduces repeated manual configuration and lets administrators manage address use centrally. Static addressing remains useful for selected infrastructure; reservations or manual bindings can also provide predictable assignments. Do not mix unmanaged static addresses into a dynamic range. Exclude infrastructure addresses, and verify that gateways, servers, and pools follow the same subnet plan.

The server sends configuration in numbered **options**. Option **1** supplies the mask, **3** the default router, **6** DNS server addresses, **15** a domain name, and **51** the lease duration. The values are separate: a correct address with a wrong gateway can reach local neighbors but fail off subnet. A correct gateway with an unavailable DNS resolver can permit IP traffic while name-based access fails.

DHCP does not create a VLAN, configure a switch access port, or install all the network's routing. Those paths must already exist. This chapter concerns DHCPv4; IPv6 uses different assignment mechanisms and messages, covered in the IPv6 addressing chapter.

sections.title: Understand the initial exchange
sections.body:
Consider a new client with no usable address. It broadcasts DHCPDISCOVER on its local Ethernet network. The IP source is `0.0.0.0`, destination `255.255.255.255`, and UDP ports are 68 to 67. On Ethernet the destination MAC is `ffff.ffff.ffff`. A transaction identifier helps associate messages with this exchange; the client also identifies itself in the DHCP payload.

A server with a suitable available address can send DHCPOFFER. The **yiaddr** field contains the offered address. An offer is a proposal, not permission for the client to start using that address. Multiple servers may answer, and client selection policy is implementation dependent. Do not assume that the first reply must always be selected.

The client broadcasts a selecting DHCPREQUEST naming its chosen server and requested address. The server identifier is option **54**; the requested address is option **50**. Other offering servers can observe that another server was selected. DHCPACK then confirms the accepted lease and parameters. The client must also handle duplicate-address detection; if it detects a conflict, it can decline the address rather than use it.

| Initial message | Sender | Important observation |
|---|---|---|
| Discover | Client | Local broadcast seeking service |
| Offer | Server | Proposed address and parameters; delivery may be broadcast or unicast |
| Selecting Request | Client | Broadcast identifies the selected server and address |
| ACK | Server | Confirms the lease; delivery follows state and message fields |

A client that cannot receive an IP unicast before configuration sets the **broadcast flag**. With no relay and no already-configured client address, the server broadcasts its Offer/ACK when that flag is set. When it is clear, the server can send directly to the offered IP and client's hardware address. If a relay address is present, the server instead sends its response to the relay. A capture must therefore be interpreted at the point where it was taken.

```diagram
{"type":"sequence","title":"Initial allocation on one LAN","caption":"This example assumes a client requesting broadcast replies; other permitted reply delivery is explained in the text.","actors":["New client","DHCP server"],"steps":[{"from":0,"to":1,"label":"Discover","note":"0.0.0.0 → 255.255.255.255; UDP 68 → 67","accent":true},{"from":1,"to":0,"label":"Offer","note":"Proposed address; broadcast in this example"},{"from":0,"to":1,"label":"Selecting Request","note":"Broadcast; requested address and selected server","accent":true},{"from":1,"to":0,"label":"ACK","note":"Accepted lease and configuration options"}]}
```

:::trap Identify which DHCPREQUEST you are reading
A selecting Request broadcasts before the client uses the offered address. A renewal Request normally unicasts from an address already in use. The message name alone does not determine its source address, destination, or meaning.
:::

sections.title: Follow renewal and lease expiry
sections.body:
A bound client does not repeat all four initial messages each time it extends a lease. At **T1**, it enters renewing state and normally unicasts DHCPREQUEST to the leasing server. It continues using its valid address while seeking renewal. The request carries the current address in **ciaddr**, the client-address field. A successful ACK supplies an updated lease.

If renewal has not succeeded by **T2**, the client enters rebinding state and broadcasts DHCPREQUEST so another suitable server can respond. It still has its current leased address until expiry. With no successful extension before expiry, the client must stop using that lease. A valid DHCPNAK can also require it to discard an invalid requested configuration and restart acquisition.

The server can supply T1 and T2 through options **58** and **59**. The familiar fractions are defaults, not unconditional deadlines. For an eight-hour lease using those defaults, T1 is four hours and T2 is seven hours. That leaves three hours between T1 and T2 and one hour between T2 and expiry. Read the actual lease if an exercise specifies other timers.

| Message outside initial DORA | Purpose |
|---|---|
| DHCPNAK, server to client | Reject an address/configuration the server can determine is invalid |
| DHCPDECLINE, client to server | Report that the proposed address appears to be in use |
| DHCPRELEASE, client to server | Give up an allocation early |
| DHCPINFORM, client to server | Request other parameters when the client already has an address |

A working lease can conceal a broken relay: normal unicast renewal may still reach the server through ordinary routing. A new client needing broadcast discovery can fail immediately, while another device continues using its lease. This is why a fault test must specify whether the client is new, renewing, or rebinding.

Some clients, including Windows when automatic private addressing applies, can self-configure an IPv4 link-local address after DHCP acquisition fails. An automatically assigned `169.254.x.x` address with no useful gateway is evidence to investigate acquisition; it does not prove that no Offer ever arrived or identify one failed component. Link-local traffic stays on the local link and is not routed. Retry schedules and fallback behavior vary by client.

sections.title: Configure an IOS DHCP server
sections.body:
The referenced Cisco server normally uses a one-day lease unless configured otherwise. Our explicit eight-hour example serves `10.10.10.0/24`. Addresses `.1` through `.49` are excluded; the potential dynamic range is `.50` through `.254`, or **205 addresses**, before other bindings, exclusions, or conflicts are considered. The network and broadcast addresses are not host allocations.

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# service dhcp
R2(config)# ip dhcp excluded-address 10.10.10.1 10.10.10.49
R2(config)# ip dhcp pool USERS
R2(dhcp-config)# network 10.10.10.0 255.255.255.0
R2(dhcp-config)# default-router 10.10.10.1
R2(dhcp-config)# dns-server 10.10.20.53
R2(dhcp-config)# domain-name dhcp.example
R2(dhcp-config)# lease 0 8 0
R2(dhcp-config)# end
R2# show ip dhcp pool
R2# show ip dhcp binding
```

The exclusion is a global command. The `network` statement selects the client subnet, not necessarily a subnet directly attached to this server. `default-router` is the gateway that clients must use; it is not automatically the DHCP server. `dns-server` advertises a resolver address but does not start a DNS service there. The full lab supplies the interfaces, route, and actual resolver device.

For a locally attached client, ordinary pool selection uses the server's receiving subnet. For a relayed client, it uses the client-subnet information discussed below. The allocation algorithm and prior bindings can affect which address appears first; do not require the lowest eligible address as the only passing result. Verify that the assigned address belongs to the intended available range.

Cisco can withhold addresses detected as conflicts. Read `show ip dhcp conflict` and investigate the actual device or stale record before clearing an entry. Clearing a binding or conflict does not remove an address already configured on another host. Also distinguish an exclusion from a reservation: an excluded address is withheld from dynamic allocation; it is not automatically assigned to a particular client.

sections.title: Configure an IOS DHCP client
sections.body:
A router can request an address on an Ethernet interface while serving or relaying a different LAN. Configure the intended interface explicitly:

```ios R3
R3# configure terminal
R3(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R3(config-if)# ip address dhcp
R3(config-if)# no shutdown
R3(config-if)# end
R3# show ip interface brief
R3# show ip route
R3# show dhcp lease
```

Confirm the learned address and mask, lease state where supported, and the corresponding server binding. Client identifiers need not be a plain printed MAC address, so compare actual identifiers rather than reconstructing a universal `01 + MAC` rule. `show dhcp lease` and release/renew commands are not equally implemented by every simulator image; the lab gives a specific fallback.

When a usable router option is supplied, the referenced IOS DHCP client can install a default route. Cisco documents default administrative distance **254** when no interface/global distance override is configured. That is a platform behavior, not a DHCP protocol field or proof that every image installs an identical route. A lower-distance alternative wins between eligible routes to the same prefix; longest-prefix matching still applies to forwarding.

An address alone does not establish off-subnet service. Verify the route and return path separately. Releasing a client lease affects that client; it is different from clearing all server bindings. Avoid broadly clearing leases just to make a troubleshooting display look empty.

sections.title: Relay requests to another subnet
sections.body:
A router does not normally route the client's limited broadcast to a different subnet. A **DHCP relay agent** receives the local message and forwards a DHCP message toward a configured server. In this design R1 Gi0/0 is `10.10.10.1/24`, R1 Gi0/1 is `10.10.20.1/24`, and server R2 is `10.10.20.2/24`.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# service dhcp
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip helper-address 10.10.20.2
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/0
```

R1's client-facing interface is where the helper belongs. In this ordinary relay design it inserts `10.10.10.1` into **giaddr**, the gateway-address field. R2 uses that field to select the `10.10.10.0/24` pool and sends its response back toward the relay on UDP 67. R2 therefore needs a route to the relay's client-side address, even though R1 and R2 share the server subnet.

R1 then delivers the response on the client link according to the message state and broadcast flag. The relay does not replace the client identifier with its own identity, and it does not make every packet broadcast. The helper is also a Cisco UDP broadcast-forwarding feature with behavior beyond DHCP on some platforms; review the configured forwarding policy rather than enabling it indiscriminately.

The referenced IOS `service dhcp` controls server and relay functionality. An explicit `no service dhcp` can therefore stop otherwise correct helpers. The absence of that negative command alone is not proof of a complete working relay; verify interface configuration and traffic.

**Option 82** adds relay-agent information, commonly identifying the circuit and remote device. It is distinct from giaddr. In chapter 16, DHCP snooping may insert it while giaddr remains zero. Cisco's IOS server can reject that combination unless its receiving interface is configured to trust relay information. Snooping trust on a switch, relay-information trust on a router, and an IP return route are different controls. Use the earlier lab's deliberate Option 82 policy; this lab starts without snooping or added Option 82 policy. Advanced classes and relay-source overrides are outside this exercise.

sections.title: Verify and troubleshoot
sections.body:
Start at the client: link, access VLAN, DHCP mode, assigned address/mask, gateway, DNS, and lease state. Next inspect the receiving Layer 3 interface and helper. Finally inspect server pool selection, free candidates, exclusions, bindings, conflicts, and routes. Test one stage at a time instead of assigning the same cause to every self-assigned address.

This is a representative, abbreviated server binding display. The actual identifier, lease expiry, and formatting come from your device:

```output R2# show ip dhcp binding
IP address       Client-ID/              Lease expiration        Type
                 Hardware address/
                 User name
10.10.10.50       0100.1122.3344.55       Sep 20 2026 08:00 AM     Automatic  ← One recorded allocation, not proof of current reachability
```

`show ip dhcp pool` helps compare capacity and use; `show ip dhcp server statistics` shows cumulative message counts. Increasing Discover counts with no Requests narrows the investigation, but does not uniquely prove a return-route fault: the server may have no available offer, the reply may be dropped, or the client may not accept it. Compare before/after counts for one controlled attempt.

Use packet observations or brief supported debugging only when the show evidence leaves a specific question unanswered. Record the actual interface, message type, client state, and giaddr. Stop debugging with `undebug all`. The exercise does not depend on a particular debug sentence, and a simulator lacking a display is not evidence of a broken protocol.

sections.title: Exam focus
sections.body:
- Distinguish client, server, and relay roles and UDP ports.
- Interpret selecting, renewing, and rebinding Requests in their correct state.
- Explain conditional Offer/ACK delivery and default versus supplied lease timers.
- Configure pools/options, an IOS client, and a client-facing helper.
- Use giaddr, server pool selection, and a valid return route together.
- Separate allocation failure, wrong options, exhaustion, conflicts, and security drops.
- Verify a recovered lease and actual connectivity without assuming a particular address or output string.

lab.title: Trace DHCP clients through a relay, then diagnose two allocation failures
devices: 3 × Cisco 2911 routers (R1 relay, R2 server, R3 client)
lab.intro:
Practice revised September 2026. If you completed an earlier version, repeat the revised exercise and update its checkmarks.

Build a remote DHCP service, obtain leases on a PC and an IOS router, and test a misplaced helper separately from an exhausted pool. Start with new devices and use console CLI tabs throughout. Answer `no` if the initial configuration dialog appears. These configurations were reviewed against Cisco documentation; they have not been executed in Packet Tracer during this audit. Output formatting, supported show commands, and retry timing can differ. For an unavailable show command, combine supported client/interface fields, server configuration and bindings. For unavailable packet details, draw the four message stages from the topology and label them predicted. If the model rejects DHCP server, relay or client configuration itself, complete that portion as a configuration-and-packet worksheet or use a licensed supporting lab image. Do not report an allocation you did not observe.
lab.topology:
```diagram
{"type":"topology","title":"Client subnet and remote server subnet","caption":"R1 relays from VLAN 10 toward R2 in VLAN 20; R2 needs a return route to the client subnet.","nodes":[{"id":"PC","kind":"pc","label":"PC-A","sub":"DHCP","x":1,"y":2},{"id":"SW1","kind":"switch","label":"SW1","sub":"VLAN 10","x":3,"y":3},{"id":"R1","kind":"router","label":"R1","sub":"Relay","x":6,"y":3},{"id":"SW2","kind":"switch","label":"SW2","sub":"VLAN 20","x":9,"y":3},{"id":"R2","kind":"router","label":"R2","sub":"10.10.20.2","x":11,"y":1},{"id":"DNS","kind":"server","label":"DNS1","sub":"10.10.20.53","x":11,"y":5}],"links":[{"from":"PC","to":"SW1","toLabel":"Fa0/1"},{"from":"SW1","to":"R1","fromLabel":"Gi0/1","toLabel":"Gi0/0"},{"from":"R1","to":"SW2","fromLabel":"Gi0/1","toLabel":"Gi0/1"},{"from":"SW2","to":"R2","fromLabel":"Gi0/2","toLabel":"Gi0/0"},{"from":"SW2","to":"DNS","fromLabel":"Fa0/1"}]}
```

| Local device/port | Peer device/port | Role |
|---|---|---|
| PC-A FastEthernet0 | SW1 Fa0/1 | First DHCP client |
| R3 Gi0/0 | SW1 Fa0/2 | IOS DHCP client, enabled in step 5 |
| PC-B FastEthernet0 | SW1 Fa0/3 | Fresh client for helper fault; connect in step 6 |

All listed cables are copper straight-through because each connects an end device/router to a switch. These are access links, not trunks. Leave PC-B and PC-C uncabled initially. Do not enable DHCP on R3 before step 5.

| Interface/device | Address and mask | Gateway/DNS |
|---|---|---|
| R1 Gi0/0 | 10.10.10.1 / 255.255.255.0 | Client gateway |
| R1 Gi0/1 | 10.10.20.1 / 255.255.255.0 | Server-subnet router |
