The three-address initial range is deliberate, so a fourth new client exposes exhaustion without generating hundreds of clients. The precise address assigned to each client is not predetermined.

steps.title: Build the two subnets
steps.body:
Cable the initially listed devices and explicitly prepare the access VLANs.

```ios SW1
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW1
SW1(config)# vlan 10
SW1(config-vlan)# name CLIENTS
SW1(config-vlan)# exit
SW1(config)# interface range fastethernet0/1 - 4
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport access vlan 10
SW1(config-if-range)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if-range)# exit
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 10
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# end
```

```ios SW2
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW2
SW2(config)# vlan 20
SW2(config-vlan)# name SERVICES
SW2(config-vlan)# exit
SW2(config)# interface range gigabitethernet0/1 - 2
SW2(config-if-range)# switchport mode access
SW2(config-if-range)# switchport access vlan 20
SW2(config-if-range)# no shutdown
SW2(config-if-range)# exit
SW2(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
SW2(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW2(config-if)# switchport access vlan 20
SW2(config-if)# no shutdown
SW2(config-if)# end
```

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# service dhcp
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.10.10.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.10.20.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
```

```ios R2
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R2
R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R2(config-if)# ip address 10.10.20.2 255.255.255.0
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# end
```

On DNS1, use Desktop → IP Configuration to enter the address, mask, gateway, and DNS value in the table. Under Services → DNS, turn the service On and add an A record named `portal.dhcp.example` with address `10.10.20.53`. Under Services → HTTP, turn HTTP On. This single record supplies a controlled service test; chapter 25 teaches DNS diagnosis in depth.

:::expected
R1's two interfaces and R2 Gi0/0 become operational. SW1's connected client ports belong to VLAN 10; SW2's service ports belong to VLAN 20. DNS1 has the stated static configuration. No helper is configured yet, and no client lease is expected.
:::

steps.title: Configure the server, small pool, and return route
steps.body:
Before entering commands, calculate the remaining candidates after both inclusive exclusions. Write which relay address the server must reach when answering a remote client. Compare those predictions with the pool and routing checks below.

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# service dhcp
R2(config)# ip dhcp excluded-address 10.10.10.1 10.10.10.49
R2(config)# ip dhcp excluded-address 10.10.10.53 10.10.10.254
R2(config)# ip dhcp pool USERS
R2(dhcp-config)# network 10.10.10.0 255.255.255.0
R2(dhcp-config)# default-router 10.10.10.1
R2(dhcp-config)# dns-server 10.10.20.53
R2(dhcp-config)# domain-name dhcp.example
R2(dhcp-config)# lease 0 8 0
R2(dhcp-config)# exit
R2(config)# ip route 10.10.10.0 255.255.255.0 10.10.20.1
R2(config)# end
R2# show ip dhcp pool
R2# show ip dhcp binding
R2# show ip route
R2# ping 10.10.10.1
```

On R1 verify server reachability:

```ios R1
R1# ping 10.10.20.2
R1# ping 10.10.20.53
```

:::expected
Both subnets and the return path are correct. A /24 has 254 ordinary host addresses. The exclusions cover 49 plus 202 addresses, leaving three candidates: .50, .51, .52. Bindings should be empty on these fresh devices. Pool counters and their headings vary; derive eligibility from the actual network and exclusions rather than demanding one exact display.
:::

steps.title: Observe acquisition before the relay exists
steps.body:
Predict whether R1 forwards the initial broadcast without a helper. Record R2's current bindings and supported message counters before the attempt, then compare afterward; counters need not start at zero.

On PC-A, open Desktop → IP Configuration and select DHCP. In Simulation mode, filter for DHCP (some versions group this under DHCP/BOOTP), advance the events, and inspect the client's initial request. Use Realtime afterward. Do not configure a static client address to conceal the missing service.

```ios R1
R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1# show running-config
```

```ios R2
R2# show ip dhcp binding
R2# show ip dhcp server statistics
```

:::expected
PC-A cannot complete remote allocation because its local broadcast has no relay on R1 Gi0/0. The server receives no corresponding relayed attempt. The PC may report DHCP failure or assign a link-local address; record what this image actually does. The expected fact is no valid pool lease, not a particular message or timeout length.
:::

steps.title: Enable the client-facing helper and obtain the first lease
steps.body:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip helper-address 10.10.20.2
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/0
```

Retry DHCP on PC-A. If necessary, select Static and then DHCP in its IP Configuration to start another acquisition attempt. Inspect its address, mask, gateway, and DNS fields. In its Command Prompt, ping `10.10.10.1` and `10.10.20.53`. Open Web Browser and test `http://10.10.20.53`, then `http://portal.dhcp.example`. This supplied one-record service checks whether the received gateway and resolver settings support the intended application; chapter 25 teaches record diagnosis.

```ios R2
R2# show ip dhcp binding
R2# show ip dhcp pool
R2# show ip dhcp server statistics
```

:::expected
PC-A receives one address in .50–.52, mask /24, gateway 10.10.10.1, and DNS 10.10.20.53. The server binding matches its actual client identity. In a supported packet-detail view, the relayed request carries giaddr 10.10.10.1; reply delivery on the client link may be broadcast or unicast according to the flag/state. A packet on the server subnet is not expected to look identical to the client's original broadcast. If the simulator omits a field, use the lesson's protocol explanation as a paper observation, not a captured result.
:::

steps.title: Obtain the second lease on an IOS client
steps.body:
R3 Gi0/0 is already cabled to SW1 Fa0/2. Configure it now. First calculate T1 and T2 for the explicit eight-hour lease if the server supplies no alternate timers; you do not need to wait for those events.

```ios R3
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R3
R3(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R3(config-if)# ip address dhcp
R3(config-if)# no shutdown
R3(config-if)# end
R3# show ip interface brief
R3# show ip route
R3# show dhcp lease
R3# ping 10.10.10.1
```

```ios R2
R2# show ip dhcp binding
R2# show ip dhcp pool
```

:::expected
R3 receives a second distinct address in the range and reaches R1's local gateway. The Method field commonly identifies DHCP. If the image implements `show dhcp lease`, inspect the actual state and timers; if it does not, use the interface, server binding, and traffic evidence. Inspect any default route instead of assuming it exists with a fixed distance on every image. Save a working Packet Tracer checkpoint.
:::

:::solution Timer check
Eight hours × 0.5 gives T1 at four hours; eight hours × 0.875 gives T2 at seven hours. T1 attempts unicast renewal; T2 broadens to broadcast rebinding if needed. Expiry is the later stop condition. Observed timers can reflect supplied options or implementation behavior.
:::

steps.title: Move the helper to the wrong interface and observe a fresh client
steps.body:
Use Save As to create an experiment copy. Verify PC-A's controlled page and unexpired lease first. Predict separately what happens to its ordinary traffic and to fresh PC-B's acquisition. Move the helper from the client interface to the server-facing interface on R1. Keep existing clients' leases; they are useful evidence that old connectivity can conceal a new-allocation failure.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# no ip helper-address 10.10.20.2
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip helper-address 10.10.20.2
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/1
```

Connect fresh PC-B to SW1 Fa0/3 with a straight-through cable, select DHCP, and let it attempt acquisition. Repeat PC-A's gateway ping and controlled HTTP-by-address test while its lease remains valid. Leave the fault installed until you record both old-client and fresh-client results, R1's helper placement and R2's binding count.

:::expected
PC-B gets no valid pool lease even though one candidate remains. Its broadcasts arrive on Gi0/0, which no longer has the helper. Previously configured PC-A and R3 may still use their unexpired addresses; this does not prove the relay works. Record the incorrect helper placement and the fresh-client failure before recovery.
:::

steps.title: Restore the helper and obtain the third lease
steps.body:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# no ip helper-address 10.10.20.2
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip helper-address 10.10.20.2
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/0
```

Retry PC-B's DHCP acquisition and test its gateway and DNS1 address. Then inspect R2:

```ios R2
R2# show ip dhcp binding
R2# show ip dhcp pool
```

:::expected
There are now three distinct active allocations in the only three eligible addresses. Do not continue to the exhaustion test until PC-A, R3, and PC-B all have valid leases and the server records them. If a prior lease expired during a long interruption, reacquire and verify this baseline first.
:::

steps.title: Observe genuine pool exhaustion
steps.body:
First calculate the free count from the exclusions and three active bindings, and record R2's available counters. Connect fresh PC-C to SW1 Fa0/4 using straight-through copper and select DHCP. Do not clear any existing client's binding or change exclusions yet.

```ios R2
R2# show ip dhcp pool
R2# show ip dhcp binding
R2# show ip dhcp conflict
R2# show ip dhcp server statistics
```

:::expected
The fourth client cannot obtain a new address because the three eligible candidates are already allocated. The working relay alone cannot solve that capacity problem. Existing leases need not lose immediate connectivity. Confirm the three bindings and the exclusion arithmetic; do not diagnose exhaustion solely from a link-local client address or a Discover counter.
:::

steps.title: Expand the lab range and recover PC-C
steps.body:
Before reading the command, choose the single exclusion that can be removed while preserving .1–.49 for infrastructure. Predict the expanded range and count. This recovery removes only the temporary upper exclusion.

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# no ip dhcp excluded-address 10.10.10.53 10.10.10.254
R2(config)# end
R2# show ip dhcp pool
R2# show running-config
```

Retry DHCP on PC-C and verify its parameters and pings to 10.10.10.1 and 10.10.20.53. Recheck server bindings.

:::expected
The potential dynamic range is now .50–.254, or 205 addresses before existing bindings/conflicts. PC-C receives a distinct available address. The existing clients keep their current valid addresses. No broad binding clear or address duplication was needed to demonstrate recovery.
:::

steps.title: Save and document the recovered configuration
steps.body:
On R1, R2, R3, SW1, and SW2, individually enter `copy running-config startup-config` from privileged EXEC. Complete each `Destination filename [startup-config]?` prompt with Enter before moving to the next device. Save the Packet Tracer project as `24-dhcp-complete.pkt`.

Record each client's actual leased address, R1's client-facing helper, R2's network/exclusions/options, and R2's return route. Record any unavailable simulator commands separately from successful observations.

Your evidence must show: (1) client settings correlated with a server binding, (2) wrong-helper failure while capacity remains, (3) correct-helper failure while capacity is exhausted, and (4) fresh allocation plus the controlled HTTP service after recovery. Identify the exact client and current request for each. Configuration alone does not establish these outcomes.

:::expected
The final state has the helper only on R1 Gi0/0, the wider intended dynamic range, four valid client allocations, and reachable DNS1. The project contains the server GUI configuration as well as the device configurations. Your record can explain why the two fault tests failed for different reasons.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- No local link: inspect cable, port, power, and administrative state before DHCP settings.
- Wrong or absent lease: check access VLAN, fresh versus renewing state, client-facing helper, and service dhcp.
- Server sees the attempt but offers nothing: inspect pool selection, exclusions, bindings, conflicts, and security policy.
- Server offers but client does not complete: verify the route to giaddr, reply delivery, snooping trust, and client state; counters alone do not select one cause.
- Correct address but wrong gateway/DNS: inspect the corresponding pool option and the client's actual refreshed settings.
- A snooping-enabled topology differs from this lab: inspect Option 82/giaddr and the deliberate trust policy taught in chapter 16. This fresh topology adds neither snooping nor Option 82 policy.
lab.challenge:
Use Save As for a separate challenge copy. Add a Catalyst 2960-24TT named SW3 and a fresh PC-PT named PC-D behind unused R1 Gi0/2. Connect R1 Gi0/2 to SW3 Gi0/1 and PC-D FastEthernet0 to SW3 Fa0/1 using straight-through copper. Create VLAN 30 on SW3 and put both connected ports in that access VLAN.

Design and implement the remaining configuration. The new gateway is 10.10.30.1/24; only .50–.59 may be allocated in this subnet. Use an eight-hour lease and the existing DNS1 service at 10.10.20.53. Preserve USERS and the original clients.

Before requesting PC-D's first lease, write its eligible range, expected giaddr and the server's required return route. Then prove the client's settings, matching binding and controlled page by address and name. Recheck an original client's page. If a needed feature is absent, submit both the per-device configuration and predicted evidence labeled unexecuted.

:::solution
The new subnet needs its access VLAN, client-facing helper, matching pool and server return route. These commands preserve USERS.

```ios SW3
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW3
SW3(config)# vlan 30
SW3(config-vlan)# name GREEN
SW3(config-vlan)# exit
SW3(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
SW3(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW3(config-if)# switchport access vlan 30
SW3(config-if)# no shutdown
SW3(config-if)# exit
SW3(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW3(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW3(config-if)# switchport access vlan 30
SW3(config-if)# no shutdown
SW3(config-if)# end
SW3# show vlan brief
```

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.10.30.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# ip helper-address 10.10.20.2
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/2
```

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# ip dhcp excluded-address 10.10.30.1 10.10.30.49
R2(config)# ip dhcp excluded-address 10.10.30.60 10.10.30.254
R2(config)# ip dhcp pool GREEN
R2(dhcp-config)# network 10.10.30.0 255.255.255.0
R2(dhcp-config)# default-router 10.10.30.1
R2(dhcp-config)# dns-server 10.10.20.53
R2(dhcp-config)# lease 0 8 0
R2(dhcp-config)# exit
R2(config)# ip route 10.10.30.0 255.255.255.0 10.10.20.1
R2(config)# end
R2# show ip dhcp pool
R2# show ip dhcp binding
R2# show ip route 10.10.30.1
```

On PC-D choose Desktop → IP Configuration → DHCP. Exclusions remove 49 + 195 = 244 of 254 host addresses, leaving ten candidates .50–.59. The client should receive /24, gateway 10.10.30.1 and DNS 10.10.20.53. The relayed request's expected giaddr is 10.10.30.1.

Correlate PC-D's identity with its binding, ping 10.10.30.1 and 10.10.20.53, then browse to `http://portal.dhcp.example`. Original PC-A should still use its 10.10.10.x lease and load that page. Save the challenge copy after verification; the original completed project remains your recovery point.
:::

questions.prompt: In the initial Discover–Offer–Request–ACK exchange, which two messages are sent by the client? Select two.
options: DHCPDISCOVER
DHCPOFFER
DHCPREQUEST
DHCPACK
questions.explanation: The client discovers available service and then requests the selected offer. The server offers configuration and acknowledges the accepted allocation.

whyWrong.1: An Offer is a server response proposing configuration.
whyWrong.3: An ACK is a server response confirming configuration.

questions.prompt: A client receives a DHCPOFFER during initial allocation. What has that message established?
options: The client may use the address until the advertised lease expires.
A server has proposed configuration for the client.
The client has completed its duplicate-address check.
Every other server has withdrawn its offer.
questions.explanation: An Offer proposes configuration. The client still selects a server, requests the offer, and processes the acknowledgment before normal use; an Offer alone does not complete allocation.

whyWrong.0: The proposed lease is not yet an acknowledged allocation.
whyWrong.2: Receipt of an Offer does not establish the client's later checks.
whyWrong.3: Other servers learn selection through the client's Request; receipt alone does not withdraw their proposals.

questions.prompt: A DHCPv4 client has no usable address and starts its initial allocation on Ethernet. Which IPv4 source and destination normally carry its DHCPDISCOVER?
options: 0.0.0.0 to the known default gateway
The proposed lease address to the offering server
The current lease address to 255.255.255.255
questions.explanation: The initial client cannot use an assigned source address or assume that it knows a DHCP server. It sends an IPv4 broadcast from 0.0.0.0, normally UDP source 68 to destination 67.

whyWrong.1: The initial client has no configured gateway and discovers service by broadcast.
whyWrong.2: The proposed address is not yet an acknowledged lease.
whyWrong.3: A client starting without a usable address cannot use a current leased source.

questions.prompt: A leased IPv4 address reaches its expiry time without a successful renewal or rebinding. What must the client do?
options: Keep using it while the default gateway responds.
Stop using that lease and restart address acquisition.
Extend it locally for another original lease interval.
Keep using it until another client reports a duplicate.
questions.explanation: Lease expiry ends the client's permission to use that address. A working data path or silence from other clients does not extend the lease.

whyWrong.0: Gateway reachability is not lease authorization.
whyWrong.2: The client cannot grant itself a server lease extension.
whyWrong.3: Duplicate detection does not replace the lease lifetime.

exhibit.title: Representative client settings
exhibit.text:
Autoconfiguration IPv4 Address : 169.254.87.14
Subnet Mask                  : 255.255.0.0
Default Gateway              :

questions.prompt: A Windows client was set to obtain IPv4 settings automatically. What conclusion is supported by this output?
options: A normal routed DHCP lease is present, but its gateway is optional.
The relay failed; no server or client checks are necessary.
IPv4 link-local is in use; the intended DHCP configuration is absent.
The pool is exhausted; available-address checks are unnecessary.
questions.explanation: The 169.254/16 address is link-local, and no gateway is shown. This is evidence that the intended DHCP configuration was not obtained or retained. It does not identify where the exchange failed; check link/VLAN, client settings, relay, server, and return delivery.

whyWrong.0: This link-local address and absent gateway do not demonstrate the planned routed DHCP lease.
whyWrong.1: The display does not locate the failure at the relay.
whyWrong.3: Exhaustion requires pool and allocation evidence, which is not supplied.

questions.prompt: Which explicit global configuration disables the documented IOS DHCP server and relay service?
options: no ip dhcp pool USERS
no ip domain-lookup
no ip dhcp excluded-address 10.10.10.1
no service dhcp
questions.explanation: The global no service dhcp command disables the documented IOS server and relay functions. service dhcp enables them; do not diagnose disabled DHCP merely because a default command is absent from an abbreviated configuration.

whyWrong.0: Removing one server pool does not disable the global relay service.
whyWrong.1: This disables the router's DNS client lookup function.
whyWrong.2: Removing an exclusion changes availability, not global service enablement.

questions.prompt: R1 receives client broadcasts on Gi0/0. Its DHCP server is reachable at 10.10.20.2 through Gi0/1. Where should the ordinary relay helper be configured?
options: Under the DHCP pool on the remote server
On the server-facing Gi0/1 interface only
On every interface, including unused interfaces
On the client-facing Gi0/0 interface
questions.explanation: The helper belongs on the Layer 3 interface that receives the client subnet broadcast. R1 then sends a relayed request toward the configured server using normal IP forwarding.

whyWrong.0: Pool settings select the configuration to offer; they do not receive and relay R1’s local broadcast.
whyWrong.1: The initial client broadcast arrives on Gi0/0, not Gi0/1.
whyWrong.2: Configure the required client subnet interface deliberately; unused or server-facing helpers do not replace it.

exhibit.title: Representative R1 configuration
exhibit.text:
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.10.10.1 255.255.255.0
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip address 10.10.20.1 255.255.255.0
 ip helper-address 10.10.20.2

questions.prompt: A fresh client on 10.10.10.0/24 cannot obtain a lease. R2 has an available matching pool; both R1 interfaces are up and routing between them works. Which correction addresses the shown relay mistake?
options: Move the helper from Gi0/1 to Gi0/0.
Set the client gateway option to 10.10.20.2.
Change Gi0/1's helper target to 10.10.10.1.
Change the pool network to 10.10.20.0/24.
questions.explanation: The helper is on the server-facing interface. The fresh client’s broadcast reaches Gi0/0, where no helper is configured. Place it there and test a new request.

whyWrong.1: The server is not the clients' reachable local default gateway.
whyWrong.2: The helper target must be the server, and the receiving client interface is still missing its helper.
whyWrong.3: That would select the server subnet rather than the clients' subnet.

questions.prompt: An ordinary relayed request arrives at an IOS server with giaddr 10.10.30.1. The server has matching /24 pools for 10.10.20.0 and 10.10.30.0 and no special class/link-selection policy. Which pool should supply the client?
options: Either pool, chosen only by its free-address count.
The 10.10.20.0/24 pool, matching the server interface.
The 10.10.30.0/24 pool, matching the relay's giaddr.
Neither pool, because giaddr must be zero.
questions.explanation: The relay gateway field identifies the subnet on whose behalf the relay is requesting service. In this ordinary case, 10.10.30.1 matches the 10.10.30.0/24 pool.

whyWrong.0: Capacity matters after selecting a suitable subnet; it does not make an unrelated subnet valid.
whyWrong.1: The receiving server subnet does not identify this remote client's subnet.
whyWrong.3: An ordinary relay supplies a nonzero gateway address.

questions.prompt: A client has a 12-hour lease. The server supplies no alternate renewal or rebinding timers. What does the standard default T1 behavior call for?
options: Broadcast a Discover immediately after three hours.
Stop using the address after six hours even if renewal succeeds.
Wait until all twelve hours have elapsed before contacting a server.
Attempt renewal with the leasing server by unicast after six hours.
questions.explanation: Default T1 is half the lease: 12 × 0.5 = 6 hours. A renewing client still has a valid address and attempts a DHCPREQUEST to its leasing server. Failure at T1 does not immediately invalidate the lease.

whyWrong.0: T1 is not one quarter of the lease, and renewal is not a new initial Discover.
whyWrong.1: The address remains leased while the client seeks renewal before expiry.
whyWrong.2: Waiting until expiry would omit the renewal and rebinding opportunities.

questions.prompt: The server has no conflicts or reservations beyond those shown. A fourth fresh client’s Discover reaches it. Why can the server not supply another address from this pool?
options: One candidate remains because the upper exclusion ends before .254.
No candidate remains because all three permitted host addresses are leased.
Two candidates remain because both exclusion endpoints are usable.
Three candidates remain because active bindings do not consume the pool.
questions.explanation: A /24 has 254 ordinary host addresses. Excluding 10.10.10.1–49 and 53–254 excludes 49 + 202 = 251. The remaining .50, .51, and .52 are already leased, leaving none for a fourth client.

whyWrong.0: The exclusion includes .254, and .255 is the subnet broadcast.
whyWrong.2: Both ends of each configured exclusion are included.
whyWrong.3: Active bindings occupy the three unexcluded addresses.

questions.prompt: An IOS DHCP server records 10.10.10.60 as a Ping-detected conflict. What should you do before clearing the conflict entry?
options: Clear .60 immediately because conflict entries cannot represent live hosts.
Clear every binding so the server can allocate a new address set.
Investigate who is using .60 and resolve the duplicate or stale condition.
Shorten the pool lease so the responding static host releases .60.
questions.explanation: A conflict entry means the server is withholding an address because it detected evidence of a collision. Identify the responding device or stale condition, correct the address plan, and clear only an appropriately resolved entry. The display alone does not identify the owner.

whyWrong.0: The conflict may represent a device still using .60.
whyWrong.1: Clearing healthy bindings risks reallocation while existing clients continue using them.
whyWrong.3: Changing a DHCP lease does not release an independently configured static address.

exhibit.title: Representative request and configuration
exhibit.text:
Relayed DHCPDISCOVER: giaddr = 10.10.30.1
Configured dynamic pool networks:
 USERS  10.10.10.0 255.255.255.0
 SERVER 10.10.20.0 255.255.255.0

questions.prompt: The relay and server paths work. No special subnet-selection policy is configured. Why does the request fail to find a suitable dynamic pool?
options: The server has no pool matching client subnet 10.10.30.0/24.
The server must use the pool with the greatest free capacity.
The relay must advertise its server-facing address as the client subnet.
The server must use its own connected subnet despite nonzero giaddr.
questions.explanation: The ordinary pool selection uses the nonzero giaddr to identify the client subnet. A request relayed for 10.10.30.1 needs a matching 10.10.30.0/24 pool; the two shown networks do not match.

whyWrong.1: Free capacity in an unrelated subnet does not supply valid client configuration.
whyWrong.2: Changing giaddr to the server-facing subnet would misidentify where the client lives.
whyWrong.3: The nonzero giaddr identifies the client subnet in this ordinary relayed case.

questions.prompt: A client moves to another subnet and requests reuse of its previous address. A DHCP server determines from authoritative subnet information that the requested address is invalid on the new subnet. Which response tells the client to abandon that configuration?
options: DHCPRELEASE
DHCPDECLINE
DHCPNAK
DHCPINFORM
questions.explanation: A server uses DHCPNAK to reject a configuration it determines is invalid. The client must stop using the rejected address and restart appropriate acquisition. This does not mean every server must NAK every request it cannot satisfy; a server without the necessary knowledge can remain silent.

whyWrong.0: RELEASE is a client message relinquishing a lease.
whyWrong.1: DECLINE is sent by a client reporting that the offered address appears to be in use.
whyWrong.3: INFORM is a client request for additional configuration when it already has an address.

questions.prompt: A client receives the intended address, mask, and gateway, and reaches a lab web server by its IPv4 address. Its current DNS setting is 10.10.20.99; the design specifies 10.10.20.53. Which repair directly addresses the demonstrated DHCP option mistake?
options: Correct the pool DNS option, then refresh the client's settings.
Correct only the router's ip name-server setting.
Clear only the client's cached DNS answers.
Reacquire the lease without correcting the pool option.
questions.explanation: DHCP option 6 supplies resolver addresses. Correct dns-server to 10.10.20.53, then renew or reacquire settings as appropriate and verify the actual client configuration. An edited pool does not instantly rewrite an existing client’s settings.

whyWrong.1: The router's own resolver setting does not repair the DNS option supplied to PCs.
whyWrong.2: Clearing answers does not correct the client's configured resolver address.
whyWrong.3: An unchanged pool can supply the same wrong setting again.

questions.prompt: A server answers an initial client directly on the same subnet: giaddr and ciaddr are zero, and the client sets the BROADCAST flag. How should the server deliver its Offer or ACK under the RFC 2131 rule for this case?
options: Unicast to the offered client IPv4 address.
Broadcast the Offer or ACK.
Unicast to the relay gateway address.
Unicast to the client's current IPv4 address.
questions.explanation: With no relay gateway or current client address and the broadcast flag set, the server broadcasts the Offer/ACK. Other cases can use unicast to a current address, to the relay, or to the offered address/client hardware address. “Offer and ACK are always broadcast” is therefore inaccurate.

whyWrong.0: The set broadcast flag selects broadcast delivery in the stated zero-giaddr/ciaddr case.
whyWrong.2: giaddr is zero; this directly attached case has no relay destination.
whyWrong.3: ciaddr is zero; there is no current client address for this delivery branch.

questions.prompt: The only intended dynamic candidates are 10.8.0.10–10.8.0.29 in 10.8.0.0/27. Which pair of inclusive exclusions produces that range?
questions.explanation: The /27 has ordinary host addresses .1 through .30. Excluding .1–.9 and .30 leaves exactly .10–.29, twenty candidates; network .0 and broadcast .31 are not host candidates.

whyWrong.0: This excludes .29, reducing the intended range to .10–.28.
whyWrong.1: This also excludes both desired endpoints .10 and .29.
whyWrong.2: This leaves .9 available and excludes .29, so it does not match the requested range.

questions.prompt: A client has passed T2 without receiving renewal replies, but its lease has not expired. Which DHCP behavior matches this rebinding stage?
options: Broadcast Request while retaining the still-valid leased address.
Send Request only to the original server and ignore other servers.
Use Discover with source 0.0.0.0 and immediately discard the lease.
Use Release to ask all available servers to extend the lease.
questions.explanation: At rebinding the client broadcasts DHCPREQUEST so a suitable server may respond. The client can continue using its unexpired lease; expiry is the later stop condition.

whyWrong.1: Restricting requests to the original server describes renewal before rebinding.
whyWrong.2: This describes abandoning configuration, not the stated unexpired rebinding stage.
whyWrong.3: Release relinquishes an address rather than requesting an extension.

questions.prompt: An IOS server excludes 10.8.0.20 from a dynamic pool. A printer is intended to always use .20. What does the exclusion accomplish by itself?
options: It reserves .20 for whichever printer requests first.
It creates a manual binding for the printer's client identifier.
It configures .20 directly on the printer's interface.
It prevents this server's dynamic pool from offering .20.
questions.explanation: An exclusion withholds the address from dynamic allocation. Assigning the printer a static address or a supported manual binding is a separate configuration decision.

whyWrong.0: An exclusion does not identify a particular client.
whyWrong.1: No client identifier or manual binding is configured by an exclusion.
whyWrong.2: The server command does not configure the printer interface.

questions.prompt: A server table lists an active binding for the test client's identifier. Which additional check best establishes that the client actually received and is using the intended configuration?
options: Inspect only the total server allocation counter.
Treat the binding alone as proof that the client received the ACK.
Verify its actual address/options and test the required service.
Compare only the configured lease duration with the design.
questions.explanation: Server state and client state are separate evidence. Inspect the affected client's settings, correlate its identity with the binding, and test the service those settings should support.

whyWrong.0: An aggregate counter is not the affected client's configuration.
whyWrong.1: The table does not by itself establish successful delivery and client use.
whyWrong.3: A configured duration does not demonstrate delivery of this allocation.

questions.prompt: A new client receives 10.50.0.60/24, gateway 10.50.0.99 and the intended DNS resolver. The approved gateway is 10.50.0.1; .99 is unused. Local-subnet tests work but routed services fail. What is the narrow repair?
options: Change the DHCP pool network to the DNS resolver's subnet.
Correct default-router to .1, refresh the client, and retest routed service.
Remove the client-subnet exclusion protecting the router's address.
Correct only the DNS option and repeat a name lookup.
questions.explanation: The client has the correct subnet but an unusable default gateway. Correct the gateway option and verify the refreshed client settings before repeating an off-subnet service test.

whyWrong.0: The client belongs to 10.50.0.0/24; moving its pool would create a new fault.
whyWrong.2: The router address should remain protected from dynamic allocation.
whyWrong.3: The resolver setting is already correct; a DNS-only edit does not repair the gateway.

questions.prompt: A packet capture shows the server receiving a Discover and sending an Offer to relay giaddr 10.10.10.1. The client capture contains repeated Discovers and no received Offer. Which two faults are consistent with that evidence? Select two.
options: The path from server to relay drops the reply.
The server has no matching pool and therefore never sent an Offer.
The relay-to-client delivery path drops the Offer.
The client successfully received and accepted this Offer.
questions.explanation: The server demonstrably sent a reply, but the client did not observe it. Investigate the return path to the relay and delivery from the relay to the client. These captures narrow the failure stage without proving which of those paths failed.

whyWrong.1: The captured outgoing Offer contradicts the claim that none was sent.
whyWrong.3: The supplied client capture has no received Offer and no accepted allocation.

exhibit.title: Representative teaching evidence
exhibit.text:
R1: Gi0/0 10.30.0.1/24, helper 10.20.0.2; Gi0/1 10.20.0.1/24
R2: 10.20.0.2/24; service dhcp enabled; pool 10.30.0.0/24 has free addresses
R2 routes: connected 10.20.0.0/24; no default or other route
Current request at R2: giaddr 10.30.0.1; Offer prepared for relay
R1 ping 10.20.0.2: success

questions.prompt: Which missing dependency explains the fresh client's failure after the server prepares an Offer?
options: The relay needs another helper on its server-facing interface.
The server needs a route toward the nonzero giaddr.
The client needs a static address before sending Discover.
The pool must match the server's connected subnet.
questions.explanation: The server prepares its relayed reply toward giaddr 10.30.0.1, but its supplied routing table has no route there. Add the client-subnet return route through R1; a successful ping between service-side addresses never tested that destination.

whyWrong.0: The client-side helper already delivered the Discover; adding a server-side helper does not create the server's return route.
whyWrong.2: Initial DHCP is specifically designed for a client without a usable address.
whyWrong.3: The pool already matches the remote client subnet identified by giaddr.

exhibit.title: Representative teaching evidence
exhibit.text:
R1 guest Gi0/2: 10.40.0.1/24, helper 10.20.0.2
R1 users Gi0/0: 10.30.0.1/24, helper 10.20.0.2
R2 service-side address 10.20.0.2/24; peer R1 10.20.0.1
R2 only pool: USERS 10.30.0.0/24, free candidates available
R2 only remote route: 10.30.0.0/24 via 10.20.0.1
Guest Discover reaches R2 with giaddr 10.40.0.1

questions.prompt: The new guest VLAN must receive leases while the existing users continue working. Which two changes address the missing dependencies? Select two.
options: Add a 10.40.0.0/24 pool with guest gateway 10.40.0.1.
Move the existing USERS pool from 10.30.0.0/24 to 10.40.0.0/24.
Add a server return route for 10.40.0.0/24 via 10.20.0.1.
Replace the guest helper target with 10.40.0.1.
Remove exclusions from the already working USERS pool.
questions.explanation: The new subnet requires its own matching pool and a server route back toward its relay address. Preserve USERS and the verified helper rather than moving existing service or changing unrelated exclusions.

whyWrong.1: Moving USERS would remove allocation service from the existing subnet.
whyWrong.3: The helper must target the DHCP server, not the relay itself.
whyWrong.4: Capacity in the old subnet cannot serve the guest subnet.

exhibit.title: Representative teaching evidence
exhibit.text:
Five clients retain unexpired leases and reach the remote application.
After a relay change, one newly connected PC has no valid lease.
No current server or packet evidence has yet been collected.

questions.prompt: Which next test best separates a current DHCP allocation failure from continued use of earlier configuration?
options: Clear every lease and infer success if existing clients reconnect.
Ping the default gateway only from a client with an unexpired lease.
Request a lease from a fresh client while correlating relay/server evidence.
Shorten every lease and wait until users report a new outage.
questions.explanation: An unexpired lease can keep ordinary traffic working after the acquisition path fails. A controlled fresh-client test, correlated at relay and server, tests that path without unnecessarily disrupting healthy clients.

whyWrong.0: Broad clearing disrupts healthy leases and removes useful before-state evidence.
whyWrong.1: This repeats the already-known data-path test without testing a new allocation.
whyWrong.3: Changing all timers is disruptive and provides less specific evidence than a controlled fresh request.

cards.front: What is the purpose of each message in initial DORA?
cards.back: Discover: client seeks service. Offer: server proposes configuration. Request: client selects an offer. ACK: server confirms allocation. This initial sequence does not describe every later renewal exchange.

cards.front: What IP addresses do an initial Discover and a selecting client’s Request normally use?
cards.back: Source 0.0.0.0 to destination 255.255.255.255. Scope this to initial acquisition before the client has a usable lease; a renewing Request can instead use the current address and unicast to the server.

cards.front: Which UDP ports belong to DHCPv4 clients and servers?
cards.back: Client port 68; server port 67. Initial client messages normally travel 68→67. A server replies to a relay’s giaddr on server port 67, and the relay then delivers toward client port 68.

cards.front: Why is the selecting DHCPREQUEST broadcast?
cards.back: It identifies the chosen server and requested address while allowing other offering servers to learn that their proposals were not selected. Do not extend that broadcast rule to renewal Requests.

cards.front: How do default T1 and T2 differ?
cards.back: T1 is normally 50% of the lease: unicast renewal with the leasing server. T2 is normally 87.5%: broadcast rebinding if renewal has not succeeded; server-supplied timers can differ.

cards.front: What does a Windows 169.254/16 address tell you after an attempted DHCP setup?
cards.back: The client is using IPv4 link-local configuration rather than the planned DHCP assignment. It does not identify a unique cause such as a bad helper or exhausted pool. Check actual settings and trace the acquisition path.

cards.front: How do you exclude 10.10.10.1 through 10.10.10.49 on IOS?
cards.back: In global configuration: ip dhcp excluded-address 10.10.10.1 10.10.10.49. Exclusions protect addresses from dynamic allocation; both endpoints are included.

cards.front: How do default-router and dns-server pool options differ?
cards.back: default-router supplies the client's local gateway; dns-server supplies resolver addresses. Neither value is automatically the DHCP server's own address.

cards.front: How do you make an IOS routed Ethernet interface a DHCPv4 client?
cards.back: Enter interface configuration and use ip address dhcp, then no shutdown. Verify the learned interface address, lease where supported, and actual routing table. Do not assume a default route’s presence or distance without checking it.

cards.front: Where is ip helper-address placed for ordinary DHCP relay?
cards.back: On the Layer 3 interface receiving the client subnet’s broadcasts, such as its gateway SVI or routed interface. Its value is the reachable DHCP server address. A helper only on the server-facing interface misses that initial broadcast.

cards.front: What does nonzero giaddr do in an ordinary relayed DHCP request?
cards.back: It identifies the relay gateway for the client subnet, allowing normal server pool selection and return delivery to the relay. The server also needs a route to that address. Specialized policies can add selection rules.

cards.front: What does no service dhcp disable on the documented IOS implementation?
cards.back: The IOS DHCP server and relay agent. service dhcp enables them. Absence of a displayed service dhcp line does not prove disabled service because an enabled default can be omitted from running configuration.

cards.front: What does show ip dhcp binding establish?
cards.back: The server's recorded address-to-client bindings. Correlate the client identity and verify the client's actual settings; a binding alone does not prove that the client received the ACK.

cards.front: How do you verify which interface carries a helper?
cards.back: Inspect the relevant interface in show running-config and show ip interface interface-name. Confirm the helper’s address, the client-facing interface, and its operational state; exact display text varies by image.

cards.front: What should happen before clearing a DHCP conflict entry?
cards.back: Identify and correct the underlying duplicate address or stale evidence. Clearing an entry does not evict the host that might already use the address. Preserve infrastructure exclusions and healthy active bindings.

cards.front: Do increasing Discover counters with no successful allocation identify one exact DHCP fault?
cards.back: No. Check matching pools, capacity, server policy, outgoing replies, relay return routing, and delivery to the client. Counters establish stages only when correlated with the current attempt and other evidence.

cards.front: Who sends DHCPNAK and DHCPDECLINE, and why?
cards.back: A server sends NAK for configuration it determines is invalid. A client sends DECLINE when an offered address appears already in use.

cards.front: Are initial DHCP Offers and ACKs always broadcasts?
cards.back: No. Delivery depends on giaddr, ciaddr, and the BROADCAST flag. A relay receives a server reply at nonzero giaddr; an already-addressed client can receive unicast. A directly attached initial client that requests broadcast gets broadcast delivery under RFC 2131.

cards.front: How do giaddr and Option 82 differ?
cards.back: giaddr is the relay gateway address used in ordinary subnet selection and return delivery. Option 82 is additional relay information; it is not another name for giaddr.

cards.front: What must a client do when its DHCP lease expires?
cards.back: Stop using that leased address and restart acquisition if renewal or rebinding has not succeeded.

cards.front: Does an old client's working connection prove new DHCP allocation works?
cards.back: No. An unexpired lease can sustain traffic while the current acquisition path is broken. Test a fresh client and correlate relay/server evidence.

cards.front: Does a DHCP exclusion assign an address to a particular device?
cards.back: No. It withholds the address from dynamic allocation. A static endpoint configuration or manual binding is a separate operation.

cards.front: Does editing a pool option instantly change existing clients?
cards.back: No. Refresh configuration appropriately, then verify the affected client's actual option values before retesting service.

commands.task: Exclude 10.10.10.1 through 10.10.10.49 from dynamic allocation.
commands.note: Both endpoints are excluded: 49 addresses, preserving the client gateway and planned static infrastructure.

commands.task: Create or enter the DHCP pool named USERS.
commands.note: The prompt becomes R2(dhcp-config)#. A pool name alone does not define an address range.

commands.task: Set the USERS pool network to 10.10.10.0/24, using dotted-decimal mask syntax.
commands.note: The network identifies the client subnet, even when the server is on 10.10.20.0/24.

commands.task: Supply 10.10.10.1 as the clients’ default gateway.
commands.note: The gateway belongs to the clients’ local subnet, not necessarily to the DHCP server subnet.

commands.task: Supply 10.10.20.53 as the resolver for this pool.
commands.note: This supplies DHCP option 6; it does not configure the router’s own DNS client.

commands.task: Set a lease of zero days, eight hours, zero minutes.
commands.note: This is an eight-hour lease. Without alternate T1/T2 values, default renewal starts at four hours and rebinding at seven hours.

commands.task: Relay DHCP for clients arriving on this client-facing interface to 10.10.20.2.
commands.note: First confirm this is the interface with the client subnet gateway. The server must be reachable and have a route back to giaddr.

commands.task: Make this routed Ethernet interface obtain its IPv4 configuration with DHCP.
commands.note: Enable the interface with no shutdown if needed; then inspect its actual learned address and routes.

commands.task: Display the server’s current DHCP address bindings.
commands.note: Correlate an address and client identifier with the current test client. A displayed binding does not alone prove the client received the ACK.

commands.task: Display DHCP pools and their address usage.
commands.note: Compare the network, exclusions, active allocations, and available capacity; do not infer exhaustion from a client timeout alone.

commands.task: Display addresses withheld because of detected DHCP conflicts.
commands.note: Investigate a conflict before clearing it. An empty table does not by itself prove every address on the LAN is unused.

commands.task: Display the IOS DHCP server's message statistics before and after one controlled fresh-client request.
commands.note: Compare the interval's changes with client and relay evidence. Aggregate counters do not identify one unique cause; use the image's supported output.

tickets.title: Fresh branch clients cannot obtain a lease
tickets.scenario: R1 connects clients on Gi0/0, 10.10.10.1/24, to R2 through Gi0/1, 10.10.20.1/24. R2 is the server at 10.10.20.2/24. DHCP service is enabled on both routers. A new PC has no prior lease; an older PC still has a valid lease and can reach a server. Links and VLAN membership are verified. The following abbreviated records are representative teaching evidence.

exhibits.title: R1 relevant interface configuration
exhibits.text:
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.10.10.1 255.255.255.0
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip address 10.10.20.1 255.255.255.0
 ip helper-address 10.10.20.2

exhibits.title: R2 pool and return-path checks
exhibits.text:
Pool USERS network: 10.10.10.0/24
Ordinary host addresses: 254
Excluded: 10.10.10.1–10.10.10.49 (49)
Active bindings: 2
Conflicts: none
Route: 10.10.10.0/24 via 10.10.20.1
Ping to 10.10.10.1: successful

exhibits.title: Current attempt capture
exhibits.text:
Client-side capture: DHCPDISCOVER arrives at R1 Gi0/0.
Server-side capture: no matching forwarded Discover reaches R2.

tickets.question: Which demonstrated configuration mistake should be corrected first?
options: The matching DHCP pool is exhausted by its active bindings.
The server lacks a return route toward the client subnet.
The helper is configured on the server-facing interface.
The server has no pool matching the relayed client subnet.
tickets.explanation: The client broadcast arrives on Gi0/0, but only Gi0/1 has the helper. Move it to the receiving client interface. Capacity is not exhausted: 254 − 49 − 2 = 203 addresses are available under the stated conditions. The return route is supplied. An old client can keep working with a valid lease; its later unicast renewal might also work without this helper, so it does not validate initial relay acquisition.
tickets.fix:
Move the helper, then repeat the fresh client request.

```ios
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# no ip helper-address 10.10.20.2
R1(config-if)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip helper-address 10.10.20.2
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/0
```

Verify a new R2 binding and the client’s actual address, mask, gateway, and DNS setting. Test the gateway and intended remote service. Save the corrected configuration after verification.

tickets.title: The fourth training-room client receives no lease
tickets.scenario: An isolated training room uses R1 as a verified relay and R2 as an IOS DHCP server. The first three clients still have valid leases and are powered on. A fourth fresh client receives no allocation. Its Discover reaches R2. The reserved infrastructure range is .1–.49; the upper exclusion was temporary for this exercise. These are representative records, not simulator captures.

exhibits.title: R2 pool configuration
exhibits.text:
ip dhcp excluded-address 10.10.10.1 10.10.10.49
ip dhcp excluded-address 10.10.10.53 10.10.10.254
ip dhcp pool USERS
 network 10.10.10.0 255.255.255.0
 default-router 10.10.10.1
 dns-server 10.10.20.53
 lease 0 8 0

exhibits.title: Current allocation and conflict checks
exhibits.text:
Active leases: 10.10.10.50, 10.10.10.51, 10.10.10.52
Conflict entries: none
Fourth client's Discover received; no new binding recorded.

tickets.question: Which repair restores capacity while preserving the intended static-address range and healthy leases?
options: Clear all three active bindings and retry the fourth client.
Remove the temporary .53–.254 exclusion and retry the fourth client.
Reconfigure the verified helper to point to the local gateway.
Remove only the .1–.49 exclusion and retry the fourth client.
tickets.explanation: The two exclusions leave only .50–.52, all of which are occupied. Removing the temporary upper exclusion expands the candidate range to .50–.254, 205 addresses, while preserving static infrastructure. Broadly deleting bindings risks allocating an address still in use. Changing a working helper does not add capacity; removing gateway protection is unsafe. Existing eight-hour leases can expire or be released; they are not permanent.
tickets.fix:
Remove only the temporary exclusion.

```ios
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# no ip dhcp excluded-address 10.10.10.53 10.10.10.254
R2(config)# end
R2# show ip dhcp pool
R2# show ip dhcp binding
```

Retry DHCP on the fourth client, confirm its new address is outside .1–.49 and distinct from active clients, and test the gateway. Verify all original clients retain service. Save after the check.

chapters.title: DNS
chapters.subtitle: Resolve names, interpret records, and isolate the cause of a failed lookup.

sources.title: RFC 2181: DNS clarification and alias rules
Cisco IOS: clear host command reference

chapters.summary: Explain DNS client, resolver, and authoritative roles; diagnose A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, NS, and PTR records; configure an IOS DNS client and distinguish resolution from application reachability.

sections.body:
DNS lets applications use names while IP forwarding uses addresses. When a user cannot reach an application by name, your job is to establish which name was queried, which server answered, what record was returned, and whether that result matches the intended service.

The v1.1 objective asks you to explain DNS's network role. The v2.0 objective specifically asks you to diagnose A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, NS, and PTR records. The examples therefore emphasize these six types and evidence-based troubleshooting. The IOS client configuration supports that work; building a production recursive resolver or authoritative service is not the scope of this chapter.

sections.title: What names and DNS records provide
sections.body:
:::facts
- **DNS**, the Domain Name System, stores different types of information under names; it does more than return IPv4 addresses.
- **A** identifies IPv4 addresses; **AAAA** identifies IPv6 addresses; **CNAME** identifies an alias target.
- **MX** identifies mail exchangers; **NS** identifies authoritative name servers; **PTR** supports reverse name lookup.
- Conventional DNS uses **UDP 53 and TCP 53**. TCP is not limited to one special kind of query.
- A record's **TTL** is a cache lifetime in **seconds**, not an IP hop limit.
- A DNS answer does not prove that the destination application is reachable or healthy.
:::

A **domain name** consists of labels separated by dots, such as `app.lab.example`. The hierarchy is interpreted from the right: the root, a top-level domain, and the labels below it. An **FQDN**, or fully qualified domain name, identifies the complete name. A trailing dot makes that absolute meaning explicit in DNS tools and zone notation. Applications often accept an apparently complete name without a trailing dot; search behavior depends on the client, so avoid universal rules based only on punctuation.

A **zone** is an administratively served portion of the namespace. An **authoritative server** answers from the zone data for which it is responsible. A zone can delegate a subdomain to other authoritative servers. A server does not need to contain every organization's records to participate in DNS.

The client normally uses a **stub resolver**, part of its operating-system or application environment, to ask a configured DNS service. A **recursive resolver** does the necessary lookup work on the client's behalf and may cache results. One device can perform more than one DNS role; the roles describe what it is doing for a particular query.

DHCP option 6 can supply resolver addresses, but DHCP and DNS remain separate services. A host may receive a correct address and gateway while being given an incorrect resolver. Changing a DHCP pool's DNS option does not immediately update all already-configured clients; check their actual settings and obtain refreshed configuration through the appropriate renewal process.

sections.title: Follow a lookup and its cached answer
sections.body:
Suppose a resolver has no relevant cached information, is allowed to perform recursion, and is not forwarding the request to another resolver. For `www.example.com`, it can ask a root server, follow a referral to a `.com` server, and follow the domain's delegation to an authoritative server. A **referral** directs the resolver toward servers that may know the next portion of the name. The root need not know the application's final address.

```diagram
{"type":"sequence","title":"A simplified uncached recursive lookup","caption":"This example has no forwarding resolver or useful cached delegation; real lookups can omit stages because of caching or local policy.","actors":["Client","Recursive resolver","Root","TLD server","Authoritative server"],"steps":[{"from":0,"to":1,"label":"Ask for www.example.com A","accent":true},{"from":1,"to":2,"label":"Find the next authority"},{"from":2,"to":1,"label":"Referral toward .com"},{"from":1,"to":3,"label":"Find example.com authority"},{"from":3,"to":1,"label":"Referral for example.com"},{"from":1,"to":4,"label":"Query the required name/type"},{"from":4,"to":1,"label":"Address answer and TTL"},{"from":1,"to":0,"label":"Return the result","accent":true}]}
```

The resolver can reuse cached information instead of repeating the entire process. A **recursive query** asks the receiving service to complete resolution if it supports and permits that work. An **iterative query** can receive an answer or a referral, which the querying resolver follows itself. A client configured with an authoritative-only server may not receive general recursive service; reachability of port 53 alone does not establish that server's permitted role.

A TTL of 3,600 seconds allows ordinary caching for up to one hour from receipt, subject to resolver policy. If a resolver obtained an answer 15 minutes ago, a simple unrefreshed cache has 2,700 seconds remaining. Changing the authoritative record does not push the change instantly into every cache. Lowering a TTL is useful before a planned change only after earlier cached copies have had time to expire; it cannot retroactively shorten a copy already held elsewhere.

Negative answers can be cached too. A name created after a negative lookup may remain unavailable through a resolver holding the earlier result. RFC 2308 derives the negative-cache lifetime from the smaller of the SOA record's TTL and its MINIMUM field. You need the operational implication here, not a complete lesson in zone-maintenance timers: query the relevant server and inspect the actual remaining lifetime before deciding an edit failed.

Small queries commonly use UDP. A truncated reply, indicated by **TC**, may require retry over TCP; DNS implementations must support TCP as described by RFC 7766. TCP can also carry ordinary queries by choice and full zone transfers. The traditional unextended DNS UDP limit is 512 bytes, while EDNS allows a larger advertised size. Do not assume every answer above 512 bytes requires TCP today, or that UDP-only reachability proves complete DNS connectivity.

sections.title: Choose and verify the correct record type
sections.body:
A **resource record** associates a name and type with data. Record types matter because a correct answer of the wrong type may not help the application. Ask which address family or service the client actually needs.

| Type | Example data | What to verify |
|---|---|---|
| A | `app.lab.example → 10.1.1.80` | Correct IPv4 address and reachable IPv4 service |
| AAAA | `app.lab.example → 2001:db8:25::80` | Correct IPv6 address and usable IPv6 path |
| CNAME | `www.lab.example → app.lab.example` | Correct alias target and resolution of the requested type |
| MX | `lab.example → preference 10, mail.lab.example` | Exchanger hostname, preference, and address records |
| NS | `lab.example → ns1.lab.example` | Correct authority/delegation and reachable name-server addresses |
| PTR | `80.1.1.10.in-addr.arpa → app.lab.example` | Reverse data for the particular address |

An **A record** and an **AAAA record** are separate data. An IPv4 answer does not establish an IPv6 address. A name can have several records of a type, so compare all returned addresses with the intended design. Multiple addresses do not by themselves prove that every backend works or that a particular client will choose the same one each time.

A **CNAME** makes its owner name an alias of another name. `www.lab.example` can point to `app.lab.example`, whose address records identify the server. For a web lookup, follow the alias until a usable requested address record is found. A target may itself be an alias; a loop or missing final address prevents completion. An alias is not inherently invalid just because its target has no address record, but it cannot then provide the address-based service being requested.

Ordinary CNAME data cannot coexist with other ordinary record data at that same owner name. Thus a conventional zone apex, which already has SOA and NS data, cannot also be an ordinary CNAME. Provider-specific alias conveniences are not evidence that standard CNAME rules changed. Correct the data according to the actual record type rather than adding contradictory records to make a symptom disappear.

An **MX record** has a preference value and an exchanger hostname. Smaller preferences are preferred; equal values can distribute attempts according to sender behavior. The exchanger needs appropriate address records and must not itself be a CNAME alias. For `lab.example MX 10 mail.lab.example`, query the domain's MX record, then resolve `mail.lab.example`, then test the intended mail service. Website success establishes none of those mail dependencies.

An **NS record** identifies an authoritative server. It is not the DNS-resolver IP address entered in a PC's settings. If a domain delegates to a wrong or unreachable server, the records behind that delegation may become unavailable. Compare parent delegation and the intended authoritative service. The name-server hostname must also be resolvable; necessary parent-supplied address information is called **glue**. Detailed delegation administration belongs to DNS operations, but you must recognize the dependency when diagnosing an unreachable authority.

A **PTR record** maps a reverse-lookup name to a hostname. IPv4 reverses its octets under `in-addr.arpa`: `10.1.1.80` becomes `80.1.1.10.in-addr.arpa`. IPv6 reverse lookup uses hexadecimal digits in reverse order under `ip6.arpa`; ordinary tools construct this for you. Forward A/AAAA and reverse PTR data are managed separately. A correct forward record does not automatically prove a matching PTR exists.

SOA describes a zone's authority and maintenance information; TXT carries text used by various applications and verification systems. Recognize their purpose when they appear, but the six record types above are the explicit v2 diagnosis focus.

sections.title: Configure the router as a DNS client
sections.body:
A router can forward users' DNS packets, advertise resolver addresses through DHCP, and resolve names for its own commands. These are three different functions. Configuring `ip name-server` affects the router's own lookups; it does not change every attached PC's settings or make the router an authoritative DNS server.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip domain-lookup
R1(config)# ip name-server 10.1.1.53
R1(config)# ip domain name lab.example
R1(config)# ip host localweb 10.1.1.80
R1(config)# end
R1# show hosts
R1# ping app.lab.example
```

`ip domain-lookup` enables the documented IOS DNS client function. Some releases display or accept the spelling `ip domain lookup`; use the supported syntax. `ip name-server` selects the resolver, and `ip domain name` supplies a default suffix for unqualified names such as `app`. `ip host` creates a local static mapping. Static/cached name information can satisfy a lookup before a new DNS query occurs.

If an IOS **domain list** is configured, Cisco's referenced procedure uses that list instead of the single default domain name. It is not an extra suffix appended after `ip domain name`. This matters when a short name fails but its full name works. Verify the complete name being queried, not only that a resolver address is present.

`show hosts` reports name-service settings and the host table. Permanent entries represent static mappings; temporary entries can be cached answers. On the documented IOS implementation, `clear host app.lab.example` clears the named hostname-cache entry; `clear host *` selects all entries in the applicable cache. Removing an intentional static mapping from configuration uses `no ip host name`. Inspect the resulting table instead of assuming identical cache handling on every image. Do not assume a cached name will still be present for a later test—inspect the actual table.

Disabling lookup with `no ip domain-lookup` prevents the router from making ordinary DNS lookups for its own command names. It does not block forwarded UDP/TCP 53 traffic for users. A console typo can otherwise trigger hostname lookup depending on IOS command handling and settings. Configure or disable the client deliberately; do not promise that every spelling error, resolver, or image produces the same delay or error text.

:::trap A cached answer is still an answer
A successful name-based ping can use a local mapping or an earlier cached result. It does not prove that a new DNS query reached a server. Conversely, a cached negative answer can remain after the authoritative record is fixed. Inspect the name table or query the chosen server explicitly before deciding which stage works.
:::

sections.title: Diagnose the failing stage
sections.body:
Use a specific name, requested type, resolver, and expected result. Compare the client's actual DNS setting with the design. Query that resolver explicitly when the tool permits it. Then determine whether you received a reply, whether it contains usable data, and whether the returned data is correct.

| Observed result | Meaning | Next useful check |
|---|---|---|
| Query timeout | No usable response arrived within the tool's wait | Resolver address, service, path, UDP/TCP policy |
| NXDOMAIN | Reply reports the queried name, or final alias target, absent | Spelling, intended zone, negative cache, server/view queried |
| Completed NODATA response | No data of the requested type at the name | Requested type and corresponding record |
| SERVFAIL | DNS service replied that it could not complete the lookup | Resolver/authority/delegation or validation evidence |
| Usable but wrong address | Resolution returned data inconsistent with the design | Record, alias chain, cache, split views or local override |
| Correct address, failed application | Resolution succeeded for the tested type | Address reachability, application port, server behavior |

**NXDOMAIN** is not proof that your PC directly reached an authoritative server; a recursive resolver can return a cached negative answer. **NODATA** is a completed no-data result, commonly represented by `NOERROR` without the requested answer. An arbitrary `NOERROR` response with zero answers can instead be a referral, so inspect the response context. **SERVFAIL** does not uniquely identify a missing record or one failed upstream device.

Testing by IP is useful but should match the service. A successful ping tests ICMP reachability, not HTTP or mail. A browser may require a particular hostname for virtual hosting or certificates, so failure of an IP-literal URL is not automatically a network failure. In the controlled Packet Tracer lab, one HTTP server serves the same simple page by address and name, making that comparison valid.

Applications can use local host files or caches, while a diagnostic query can contact the configured DNS server directly. If `ping` and `nslookup` disagree, compare the exact name, address family, selected server, and local overrides before changing authoritative data. Windows `ipconfig /displaydns` and `/flushdns` inspect and clear its client cache; clearing that cache does not edit a hosts file or purge a remote resolver.

sections.title: Reading the output
sections.body:
These are representative, abbreviated teaching records, not captured simulator runs. A real tool's labels and formatting may differ.

```output Client query: nslookup www.lab.example 10.1.1.53
Server:  ns1.lab.example
Address: 10.1.1.53  ← Server queried, not the web server

Non-authoritative answer:
Name:    app.lab.example
Address: 10.1.1.80  ← Returned application address
Aliases: www.lab.example  ← The alias points to the canonical name
```

`Non-authoritative answer` normally means the response was not marked authoritative for this data; it is common when asking a recursive resolver and is not a failure indication. Likewise, `Server: UnKnown` can indicate no reverse name for the queried resolver. Inspect the actual answer before calling the lookup unsuccessful.

```output Representative dig response excerpts
;; ->>HEADER<<- opcode: QUERY, status: NXDOMAIN, id: 1001  ← A negative name result was received
;; ->>HEADER<<- opcode: QUERY, status: SERVFAIL, id: 1002  ← Failure response, not silence
```

With `nslookup`, request a type and server explicitly: `nslookup -type=MX lab.example 10.1.1.53`. With `dig`, the equivalent form is `dig @10.1.1.53 lab.example MX`; `dig -x 10.1.1.80` constructs the reverse lookup. These tools are not equally available in Packet Tracer, so record-based MX, NS, PTR, and IPv6 exercises have a paper path. Do not install a DNS service or alter a public zone just to reproduce an example.

Finish by retesting the corrected record chain and the actual service from the affected client. A working query from a different network can use another resolver or view. Keep the before/after evidence so the repair explains the user's original failure.

sections.title: Exam focus
sections.body:
- Distinguish client resolver settings, recursive service, and authoritative data.
- Diagnose A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, NS, and PTR dependencies.
- Explain ordinary caching and why record edits may not be visible immediately.
- Recognize both UDP and TCP 53 and a truncated response.
- Separate timeout, NXDOMAIN, NODATA, SERVFAIL, and a wrong answer.
- Configure and inspect the router's own DNS client without confusing it with user forwarding.
- Verify the corrected name/type/server result and then the required application.

lab.title: Build DNS records, compare lookup failures, and diagnose all six record types
devices: Optional: another Server-PT for the challenge
lab.intro:
Practice revised September 2026. If you completed an earlier version, repeat the revised exercise and update its checkmarks.

Use Packet Tracer for the address/name comparison and IOS client configuration. Use the supplied paper records for types and response details that the simulator may not implement. The paper cases are required practice for record diagnosis, not claims of a working recursive or authoritative DNS deployment in Packet Tracer.

Start with new devices. Use their console CLI tabs, answer `no` to any initial configuration dialog, and inspect the named ports before cabling. This exact lab has not been executed in Packet Tracer during this review. Its GUI labels, cache behavior, and supported record/query types may vary; where a feature is absent, use the explicit paper alternative.
lab.topology:
```diagram

```

| Device/port | Peer | Address / mask | Gateway; DNS |
|---|---|---|---|
| PC-A FastEthernet0 | SW1 Fa0/1 | 10.1.1.10 / 255.255.255.0 | 10.1.1.1; 10.1.1.53 |
| DNS1 FastEthernet0 | SW1 Fa0/2 | 10.1.1.53 / 255.255.255.0 | 10.1.1.1; 10.1.1.53 |

This is a simple isolated addressing exercise, not a recommendation to use VLAN 1 for production management. No real Internet connection or public DNS change is required. Reserve unused 10.1.1.54 and 10.1.1.81 for the stated fault tests; do not add devices at those addresses until the optional challenge.

steps.title: Configure and prove the IP path
steps.body:
Set PC-A, DNS1, and WEB1 in Desktop → IP Configuration using the complete table. Configure the router and switch explicitly.

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.1.1.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
```

```ios SW1
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW1
SW1(config)# interface range fastethernet0/1 - 3
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport access vlan 1
SW1(config-if-range)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if-range)# exit
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 1
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show vlan brief
```

From PC-A's Command Prompt, ping 10.1.1.1, 10.1.1.53, and 10.1.1.80. Repeat after link startup and ARP resolution if necessary.

:::expected
All three addresses respond once the links forward. This is local-subnet connectivity, so no route to another network is involved. An IP ping is not yet a DNS or HTTP test. Correct any addressing/cabling fault before proceeding.
:::

steps.title: Add controlled DNS records and a web service
steps.body:
Before enabling DNS, predict which test can already work with HTTP enabled: the literal address, the app name or the alias. Record why the alias requires more than an address on WEB1.

On DNS1, open Services → DNS, turn it On, and add the following records with the Name, Type, and Address/target fields. Use Add or the equivalent save action for each entry.

| Name | Type | Data |
|---|---|---|
| app.lab.example | A | 10.1.1.80 |
| fresh.lab.example | A | 10.1.1.80 |
| ns1.lab.example | A | 10.1.1.53 |
| www.lab.example | CNAME | app.lab.example |

If the selected simulator does not offer CNAME or does not follow it in a query, retain the A-record exercises and use this explicit paper result for the alias: `www.lab.example CNAME app.lab.example`, followed by `app.lab.example A 10.1.1.80`. Do not silently replace the alias with an A record and call that a CNAME test. Record the available type list; no fixed list of unsupported simulator types is assumed.

On WEB1, enable Services → HTTP. Keep its default simple page or replace its title with `CCNA DNS lab`. From PC-A, open Web Browser and request `http://10.1.1.80`.

:::expected
The stored records match the table, and WEB1 serves the controlled HTTP page by address. This page is intentionally suitable for both IP-literal and hostname access. These local records do not simulate the public root/TLD delegation process.
:::

steps.title: Configure and verify R1's DNS client
steps.body:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip domain-lookup
R1(config)# ip name-server 10.1.1.53
R1(config)# ip domain name lab.example
R1(config)# end
R1# ping app.lab.example
R1# ping app
R1# show hosts
```

The hyphenated lookup command and two-word form `ip domain lookup` are accepted/displayed differently by IOS releases. Use the image's supported spelling. If short-name completion is absent in the simulator, retain the successful full-name test and inspect the configured domain as a paper explanation of the documented IOS behavior.

:::expected
The full name resolves to 10.1.1.80 and reaches WEB1. On the documented IOS behavior, `app` is completed with the default domain. `show hosts` identifies DNS1 and the configured suffix and may show a temporary cached mapping. Record what is actually present; no exact cache lifetime or formatting is required. Do not query `fresh.lab.example` yet.
:::

steps.title: Distinguish static mapping from disabled DNS lookup
steps.body:
Predict the result for each of the two names before running its ping. Identify which one needs a new server query and which one can use local configuration.

Create a local static name and disable the router's DNS client. Test the static name, then the deliberately unused fresh name so an earlier successful cache entry cannot hide the difference.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip host localweb 10.1.1.80
R1(config)# no ip domain-lookup
R1(config)# end
R1# show hosts
R1# ping localweb
R1# ping fresh.lab.example
```

:::expected
`localweb` is available through the static host table. The router cannot obtain a new DNS answer for `fresh.lab.example` while lookup is disabled, even though that name exists on DNS1. Existing cached entries may behave differently and are not the test target. Record the actual failure rather than requiring a particular error string. Leave the router disabled until the next recovery step.
:::

steps.title: Restore router lookup and compare PC resolution
steps.body:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip domain-lookup
R1(config)# end
R1# ping fresh.lab.example
R1# show hosts
```

On PC-A, run `nslookup app.lab.example` and, where supported, `nslookup www.lab.example`. Then request `http://www.lab.example` in its browser, or use `http://app.lab.example` for the stated alias fallback. In Simulation mode, filter for DNS and inspect a new query/reply; return to Realtime afterward.

:::expected
The router's previously unavailable fresh name now resolves. PC-A asks 10.1.1.53 and receives the application address 10.1.1.80. For an observed UDP exchange, the query destination port is 53 and the reply source port is 53; the client's other port is not required to be 53. A cache or alias implementation can change the number of visible messages. If `nslookup` is missing, use the browser name test and available packet details, and interpret the lesson's supplied query output on paper.
:::

steps.title: Use an unreachable resolver and observe the difference
steps.body:
Predict whether this client-only DNS change alters the stored record on DNS1, the IP-literal page, or the ability to receive a new DNS answer. Write your predictions before the test.

Save a working checkpoint. Change only PC-A's DNS setting to unused 10.1.1.54. Ask for `app.lab.example` with nslookup; the command sends a direct query rather than relying on an application's prior result. Also request `http://10.1.1.80` by address. Do not restore the setting until you have recorded the evidence.

If the simulator lacks direct lookup, compare its current DNS configuration with the unused-address plan and attempt an uncached name. Use the paper observation “no usable DNS reply arrived” instead of claiming a specific on-wire query was seen: local ARP failure can stop the UDP packet before transmission.

:::expected
The direct lookup cannot obtain a response from the selected unused resolver, while the simple IP-literal HTTP page remains reachable. This isolates the resolver selection in this controlled setup. A timeout does not mean that DNS1's app record has disappeared.
:::

steps.title: Restore the resolver and test a negative name response
steps.body:
Set PC-A's DNS address back to 10.1.1.53. Query `app.lab.example` to reestablish success, then query absent `nosuch.lab.example`. Keep WEB1's HTTP service unchanged.

:::expected
