On SRV1 Desktop → IP Configuration, set the static address, mask `255.255.255.0` and gateway from the topology above. Leave DNS blank. On R1, decline the initial setup dialog if presented:

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# description ISOLATED_FILE_LAB
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.29.0.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
R1# ping 10.29.0.100
```

Wait for SW1's ports to forward. Save the project as `files-baseline.pkt` and continue in `files-working.pkt`.

:::expected
Gi0/0 is up/up and ping replies arrive after address resolution. No router default route is needed for a server on the same subnet. Repair connectivity before starting file operations.
:::

steps.title: — Predict and inspect the correct stores
steps.body:
Before executing anything, write which store `copy running-config startup-config` changes, and whether it creates an off-device backup.

:::solution
The active configuration is the source; the saved startup file is the destination. This saves locally for startup and creates no off-device copy.
:::

Run the save command alone:

```ios R1
R1# copy running-config startup-config
```

Accept the destination filename with Enter. After the copy completes, inspect:

```ios R1
R1# show startup-config
R1# show file systems
R1# dir flash:
R1# show version
```

:::expected
The startup configuration includes hostname R1 and the lab interface address. Record actual local prefixes, available bytes and the running image filename. Do not expect an exact capacity or image version from a screenshot. If `flash:` is not listed, use the actual persistent-storage prefix in subsequent local-file commands.
:::

steps.title: — Send a named TFTP backup
steps.body:
In SRV1 → Services → TFTP, enable the service. On R1:

```ios R1
R1# copy running-config tftp:
```

At the prompts, provide server `10.29.0.100` and destination `R1-before.cfg`. Wait until the copy completes; do not paste the prompt answers as IOS commands.

:::expected
The router reports completion and SRV1's TFTP file list contains `R1-before.cfg`. Record the actual file size if shown. This operation did not also save startup-config. TFTP offers no encrypted transport; use only this isolated, nonsensitive lab.
:::

steps.title: — Retrieve to a staged file
steps.body:
Your requirement is to retrieve `R1-before.cfg` as `flash:R1-received.cfg` for inspection while leaving both configuration stores unchanged. Write the source and destination before opening the supplied command.

:::solution
The source is remote TFTP and the destination is a new named local flash file. Use `copy tftp: flash:R1-received.cfg`, host `10.29.0.100` and source `R1-before.cfg`. A running-config destination would apply commands; startup-config would overwrite the saved configuration.
:::

Execute your chosen operation, using the answer above only after attempting the direction yourself. Enter `10.29.0.100` for the remote host and `R1-before.cfg` for the source. Accept the specified destination. Once complete:

```ios R1
R1# dir flash:
R1# more flash:R1-received.cfg
```

:::expected
The staged file contains the R1 baseline. Its presence does not mean a configuration has been applied. If the simulator omits `more`, inspect the file through the server/GUI where supported and mark local content inspection unavailable. Do not substitute `copy ... running-config` merely to read a file.
:::

steps.title: — Predict a merge, then observe it
steps.body:
The staged baseline contains `hostname R1` and does not mention Loopback29. You will change the hostname and add that unused interface, then merge the baseline. Write whether each change will remain before running the block.

:::solution
The hostname command in the file restores R1. An extra interface absent from the file can remain because the operation merges commands instead of removing every setting missing from the source.
:::

Make two harmless isolated changes. Loopback29 has no address and is not used by the topology.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# hostname R1-TEMP
R1-TEMP(config)# interface loopback29
R1-TEMP(config-if)# description TEMPORARY_MERGE_TEST
R1-TEMP(config-if)# end
R1-TEMP# copy flash:R1-received.cfg running-config
```

Accept the destination prompt, wait for completion, then inspect:

```ios R1
R1# show running-config
R1# show ip interface brief
```

:::expected
The hostname returns to R1 because the file contains `hostname R1`. Loopback29 remains because the earlier backup did not contain a command to remove it. Transfer completion and hostname restoration do not prove exact replacement.
:::

steps.title: — Recover the baseline explicitly
steps.body:
After recording the merge result, remove the temporary interface:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# no interface loopback29
R1(config)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
R1# ping 10.29.0.100
```

Then save separately:

```ios R1
R1# copy running-config startup-config
```

Accept Enter when asked for the destination.

:::expected
Loopback29 is absent, the server remains reachable, and startup-config again represents the intended lab state. A carefully reviewed explicit removal repaired this one known change; no reload or complete replacement was necessary.
:::

steps.title: — Compare FTP and introduce an authentication fault
steps.body:
In SRV1 → Services → FTP, enable FTP and create account `filelab` with fictional lab password `FileLab2026!`. Grant that account Read, Write and List permissions in the simulator; additional Delete/Rename permissions are unnecessary. Save/add the account before testing.

Configure an intentionally wrong router FTP client password:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip ftp username filelab
R1(config)# ip ftp password WrongLabPassword
R1(config)# end
R1# copy running-config ftp:
```

Supply server `10.29.0.100` and destination `R1-ftp.cfg` when prompted.

:::expected
The server should reject authentication; exact error text depends on the simulator. No successful backup should appear under that name. The IP baseline can still work. These `ip ftp` commands configure the router's client credentials, not an FTP server on R1.
:::

steps.title: — Repair FTP and verify the destination
steps.body:
Set the matching fictional password:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip ftp password FileLab2026!
R1(config)# end
R1# copy running-config ftp:
```

Use the same server and filename. After completion, inspect SRV1's FTP file list and retrieve `R1-ftp.cfg` with `copy ftp: flash:R1-ftp-received.cfg` if supported, answering its prompts individually. Inspect the staged text.

:::expected
The repaired credentials permit the authorized transfer. FTP control and data use separate TCP connections; a login alone would not prove the data transfer succeeded. The backup may include the stored lab FTP password, demonstrating why configuration files need access protection. Save `files-complete.pkt`. Do not use this cleartext method for real secrets.
:::

steps.title: — Supplied preparation: Linux transfer server
steps.body:
Create an Ubuntu 24.04 VM with a console and a dedicated isolated lab NIC. Before isolating it, install OpenSSH using the official Ubuntu procedure:

```bash
sudo apt update
sudo apt install openssh-server
sudo systemctl enable --now ssh
sudo adduser ccnafile
```

This lab uses password authentication on the isolated VM so the IOS client can authenticate. Read `sudo sshd -T` and find `passwordauthentication yes`. If a fresh VM template disables it, use its console to create `/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-ccna-lab.conf` with the single line `PasswordAuthentication yes`. Run `sudo sshd -t` before `sudo systemctl restart ssh`, then confirm the effective result again. Existing Match blocks or earlier settings may require the template's documented correction. Do not change a shared server. A failed syntax check is a stop condition.

Choose a unique password for the new `ccnafile` account; it need not have sudo rights. Record it privately. At the VM console, identify the lab NIC:

```bash
ip -br link
```

Use a dedicated lab NIC with no existing address or DHCP profile on this isolated segment. The following example assumes its name is `ens3`. Replace that name with the actual dedicated lab NIC. Do not run these commands on the host computer's working network adapter.

```bash
sudo ip link set ens3 up
sudo ip address add 10.29.0.100/24 dev ens3
ip -br address
sudo sshd -t
sudo ss -lntp
sudo ufw status
sudo -iu ccnafile
```

The address command is temporary and does not require a gateway. As `ccnafile`, create the working directory and test file:

```bash
mkdir -p ~/ccna-files
chmod 700 ~/ccna-files
printf 'CCNA secure transfer practice\n' > ~/ccna-files/probe.txt
chmod 600 ~/ccna-files/probe.txt
sha512sum ~/ccna-files/probe.txt
exit
```

:::expected
The dedicated NIC has `10.29.0.100/24`. SSH configuration validation produces no error, and a TCP 22 listener exists. The file is 30 bytes including its final newline. If Ubuntu UFW reports active, from the administrator shell permit only the lab client with `sudo ufw allow in on ens3 from 10.29.0.1 to 10.29.0.100 port 22 proto tcp`, substituting the actual lab NIC. For another active firewall, apply its equivalent scoped rule. Do not disable the firewall globally. Keep the VM console open and verify the account can log in locally.
:::

steps.title: — Supplied preparation: IOS XE identity and SCP
steps.body:
This block is for a fresh, isolated Catalyst 9300 S1. A virtual router uses its actual Layer 3 port name and omits `no switchport`. Do not apply it over an existing production AAA policy.

```ios S1
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname S1
S1(config)# interface gigabitethernet1/0/1
S1(config-if)# no switchport
S1(config-if)# ip address 10.29.0.1 255.255.255.0
S1(config-if)# no shutdown
S1(config-if)# exit
S1(config)# username labbackup privilege 15 secret RouterLab2026!
S1(config)# ip domain name ccna.example
S1(config)# aaa new-model
S1(config)# aaa authentication login default local
S1(config)# aaa authorization exec default local
S1(config)# line console 0
S1(config-line)# login authentication default
S1(config-line)# exit
S1(config)# line vty 0 15
S1(config-line)# login authentication default
S1(config-line)# transport input ssh
S1(config-line)# exit
S1(config)# crypto key generate rsa modulus 2048
S1(config)# ip ssh version 2
S1(config)# ip ssh source-interface gigabitethernet1/0/1
S1(config)# ip scp server enable
S1(config)# end
S1# show ip interface brief
S1# show ip ssh
S1# ping 10.29.0.100
```

Generate keys only on this new device; if it already has keys, inspect and retain the intended key rather than replacing it. Keep the current console session open. Before the first Linux login, read `show ip ssh` **through that trusted console**. In its SECSH public-key section, locate the actual `ssh-rsa` key used by this SSH server. Copy the key into `~/S1-console-key.pub` on Linux using a text editor: one line containing `ssh-rsa`, one space, and the complete base64 key. Join wrapped key lines without inserting spaces into the base64 data. Do not copy the label, modulus line, terminal prompt or an example key.

Calculate its fingerprint on Linux:

```bash
ssh-keygen -lf ~/S1-console-key.pub -E sha256
```

The result identifies an RSA public key and a SHA256 fingerprint. `show crypto key mypubkey rsa` alone may display ASN.1 hexadecimal data; that is not directly comparable with OpenSSH's fingerprint. If this release cannot display/export the active SSH public key in a supported comparable format, stop this checkpoint and use its documented trusted key-export procedure.

Now test a separate login:

```bash
ssh labbackup@10.29.0.1
```

Compare the offered **RSA** fingerprint with the locally calculated value before accepting it. An unexpected key type, mismatch or changed-key warning requires investigation through the console; do not bypass the check. Enter the fictional router password only after identity verification.

:::expected
The second session reaches S1 and has the intended privilege. Run `show privilege` there, then `exit`. The verified login records the server key in Linux's known-hosts file for the later SCP connection. If algorithms are incompatible, use a supported current image and inspect both ends' SSH logs; do not globally enable obsolete algorithms or disable host-key checks. If SFTP/SCP commands are unavailable, this environment cannot complete the secure-transfer part.
:::

steps.title: — Pull a configuration backup with classic SCP
steps.body:
On S1, inventory local storage and create a snapshot:

```ios S1
S1# show file systems
S1# copy running-config flash:S1-before.cfg
```

Accept the destination prompt and wait. If this device uses `bootflash:` instead of `flash:`, consistently substitute it. Before using Linux, identify which device is the listening server and whether this pull will write startup-config. Then create a protected local destination and pull the staged file:

```bash
mkdir -p ~/ccna-received
chmod 700 ~/ccna-received
scp -O labbackup@10.29.0.1:flash:S1-before.cfg ~/ccna-received/S1-before.cfg
chmod 600 ~/ccna-received/S1-before.cfg
ls -l ~/ccna-received/S1-before.cfg
```

Inspect the received file privately; do not paste secrets into a shared transcript.

:::expected
The workstation initiates SCP and the Cisco device acts as server. `-O` is deliberate because the cited Cisco server supports classic SCP and OpenSSH 9+ defaults to SFTP. A successful file transfer and readable configuration confirm more than a successful SSH login. The local snapshot and remote backup do not automatically update startup-config.
:::

steps.title: — Observe rejection of an untrusted SFTP server identity
steps.body:
S1 is now the client; Ubuntu's SSH/SFTP service is the server. Client authentication by password and verification of the **server's identity** are different checks. The documented IOS XE procedure uses a trusted server public key and `ip ssh stricthostkeycheck`; do not assume it offers OpenSSH's interactive acceptance prompt.

On the trusted Ubuntu console, inspect its existing **server** RSA public key, not a user's login key:

```bash
ssh-keygen -lf /etc/ssh/ssh_host_rsa_key.pub -E sha256
awk '{print $1" "$2}' /etc/ssh/ssh_host_rsa_key.pub | fold -w 70
```

Record the fingerprint and retain the complete wrapped public-key text. These are public-key data; never copy the file without the `.pub` suffix.

First verify enforcement on this fresh S1, which has no server public-key entry yet:

```ios S1
S1# configure terminal
S1(config)# ip ssh stricthostkeycheck
S1(config)# end
S1# copy sftp://ccnafile@10.29.0.100//home/ccnafile/ccna-files/probe.txt flash:probe-sftp.txt
```

An initial destination-filename prompt may appear. The SSH connection must then fail server authentication before requesting the account password or transferring a file. If it instead reaches a password prompt, cancel with Ctrl+C: do not enter credentials or count this image as demonstrating authenticated SFTP. Check the exact release's supported client/server-authentication procedure or use a compatible image.

:::expected
Record whether the missing-key attempt was rejected before the account password was sent. No file should be accepted. If the client bypasses the configured check, stop this path and investigate image support; do not label the operation authenticated.
:::

steps.title: — Pin the verified identity and perform the secure copy
steps.body:
Keep the Ubuntu public key and fingerprint collected through its trusted console. Enter that trusted key on S1:

```ios S1
S1# configure terminal
S1(config)# ip ssh pubkey-chain
S1(conf-ssh-pubkey)# server 10.29.0.100
S1(conf-ssh-pubkey-server)# key-string
```

At the `conf-ssh-pubkey-data` prompt, paste **all** of Ubuntu's wrapped `ssh-rsa` public-key text from above, with no shell prompts. Wait for the key text to be entered before continuing:

```ios S1
S1(conf-ssh-pubkey-data)# exit
S1(conf-ssh-pubkey-server)# end
S1# show running-config | section ip ssh
```

Confirm the server-address entry and strict checking. IOS may store the entered key as a hash. Repeat the file operation:

```ios S1
S1# copy sftp://ccnafile@10.29.0.100//home/ccnafile/ccna-files/probe.txt flash:probe-sftp.txt
```

Answer the account-password and destination prompts individually. If server authentication still fails, inspect the trusted key, exact server address and negotiated key type; keep strict checking enabled. Use the matching server public key and documented support for that release, rather than substituting an unverified key.

After completion:

```ios S1
S1# dir flash:probe-sftp.txt
S1# more flash:probe-sftp.txt
S1# verify /sha512 flash:probe-sftp.txt
```

:::expected
The missing-key attempt was rejected before account authentication; the trusted-key attempt succeeds. Record both outcomes. This checks the actual SFTP implementation's enforcement instead of inferring it from a configured command alone.

The file contains `CCNA secure transfer practice` and its SHA-512 matches the server's Step 9 value. On an image without SHA-512 verification, compare MD5 at both ends (`md5sum` on Linux and `verify /md5` on IOS) for this benign transfer exercise and record the limitation. Do not treat MD5 as proof of software authenticity. If the specific release requires interactive `copy sftp: flash:`, supply the same host, user, absolute source path and destination when prompted. An unsupported identity check is a documented lab limitation, not a successful secure-transfer result.
:::

steps.title: — Observe a source-path failure
steps.body:
Attempt a source filename that does not exist:

```ios S1
S1# copy sftp://ccnafile@10.29.0.100//home/ccnafile/ccna-files/missing.txt flash:missing-test.txt
```

Record the error. Check the source directory from Linux's console with `sudo -u ccnafile ls -l /home/ccnafile/ccna-files` before changing any network settings.

:::expected
Authentication may succeed while the file operation fails. The trusted directory contains `probe.txt`, not `missing.txt`, so the source path is the demonstrated fault. Record the actual stage and error before moving on.
:::

steps.title: — Repair only the path and repeat the file operation
steps.body:
Use the existing source and a new destination:

```ios S1
S1# copy sftp://ccnafile@10.29.0.100//home/ccnafile/ccna-files/probe.txt flash:probe-recovered.txt
```

Wait for completion, then inspect `dir flash:probe-recovered.txt` and compute its supported hash.

:::expected
The received file matches the trusted source content and hash. Connectivity, user credentials and the enforced host key did not need changing. The retest is the actual file operation that failed, not just a ping or SSH login.
:::

steps.title: — Apply the checks to approved software or the worksheet
steps.body:
If you have an authorized Cisco software download for this exact lab platform, place it in `/home/ccnafile/ccna-files` with owner `ccnafile` and read permission for that account. Record its exact filename, size, release compatibility and Cisco-published SHA-512. Check available Cisco storage and keep the working image and package files intact.

Use the Step 13 SFTP operation with the **actual approved filename** as source and destination, or push it from Linux with `scp -O` to the named local Cisco file. Replace only the filename and path, not the protocol's security checks. Compute the stored file's hash and compare with Cisco's published value.

:::expected
A file with the expected size and matching trusted hash is staged, not activated. `show version` still reports the original running software. If no licensed suitable image is available, use the benign file from Step 13 to demonstrate the mechanics and produce the software preflight worksheet; explicitly mark actual software staging as unperformed. Never rename the text file to `.bin` or attempt to boot it.
:::

steps.title: — Submit separate backup, staging and recovery evidence
steps.body:
Submit this evidence checklist with actual results or an explicit unperformed/paper label for each part:

- Backup: identify current active versus saved source, remote filename, restricted destination access and readable contents.
- Staging: identify client/server roles, trusted server key, source/destination filename, received size/content and source/destination hash comparison.
- Configuration state: show that a staged file did not apply itself; record the merge prediction, observed extra interface and explicit cleanup.
- Recovery: retain the failed source-path evidence and the successful repeat of that operation after the narrow correction.
- Software decision: identify exact model/release, trusted metadata, stored-file verification, current active software and the separate activation boundary.

Record image/version, successful operations, errors and unsupported features. Preserve the secure backup in a restricted directory. Keep the original lab checkpoint and working software. If the lab will be retained, save only the verified intended device configuration:

```ios S1
S1# copy running-config startup-config
```

Accept the destination prompt before doing anything else. Keep the isolated lab available for the independent challenge, then stop it when finished.

:::expected
The record distinguishes a transferred file, a verified file, an applied configuration and active software. No boot setting or image activation was changed by this exercise.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- Timeout with successful ping: inspect the particular transfer service, transport ports, source interface, return path and server logs. ICMP success does not uniquely identify a firewall or service fault.
- FTP login works but file transfer stalls: investigate the separate active/passive data connection and permissions.
- SCP subsystem error with OpenSSH 9+: confirm the Cisco server supports classic SCP, then use `-O`. Authentication and authorization must still work.
- SSH authentication succeeds but file access is denied: check EXEC authorization, device privilege and file/directory permissions.
- SFTP file not found: compare case and absolute path at the server; a working login does not prove the named path exists.
- Hash mismatch: stop before applying or activating anything. Recheck the source identity, expected hash, filename and actual destination bytes.
lab.challenge:
Use the secure lab's completed baseline. This is a new handover requirement, not another restoration of Loopback29. If the supported environment is unavailable, write the command/verification plan and complete the supplied acceptance worksheet; mark secure execution pending.

**Supplied source preparation:** at the Ubuntu console, become `ccnafile` with `sudo -iu ccnafile` and create a second benign file. This is preparation; it does not answer which copy direction to choose.

```bash
printf 'CCNA handover checkpoint\n' > ~/ccna-files/handover.txt
chmod 600 ~/ccna-files/handover.txt
sha512sum ~/ccna-files/handover.txt
exit
```

Independently complete these requirements before opening the answer:

1. Preserve S1's **current active** configuration off-device as Linux `~/ccna-received/S1-handover.cfg`, using the verified classic SCP service. Do not overwrite startup-config or the earlier backup.
2. Retrieve Ubuntu's `/home/ccnafile/ccna-files/handover.txt` into S1 as `flash:handover-review.txt` through SFTP. Keep existing host-key enforcement. Inspect the destination and compare its complete hash.
3. A draft request incorrectly names `Handover.txt`. Predict which stage will fail on this case-sensitive server and the narrow correction. If trying it live, record failure before retrying.
4. Evaluate these **supplied software candidates**. The plan requires a compatible release for the inventoried model, trusted matching SHA-512 and a separate approved activation:
   - Candidate A is the exact compatible release; its stored hash differs from Cisco's trusted value.
   - Candidate B matches Cisco's trusted hash, but its release documentation targets a different device family.
   State whether either can be accepted for this device. Do not change boot settings.

Submit command choices, destination evidence, file-error/retest results and both acceptance decisions. Passwords and configuration secrets do not belong in a shared submission.

:::solution
For the current configuration, create a new snapshot on S1:

```ios S1
S1# copy running-config flash:S1-handover.cfg
```

Finish its filename prompt first. Then, from Linux, retrieve the named source:

```bash
scp -O labbackup@10.29.0.1:flash:S1-handover.cfg ~/ccna-received/S1-handover.cfg
chmod 600 ~/ccna-received/S1-handover.cfg
ls -l ~/ccna-received/S1-handover.cfg
```

Inspect the received configuration privately and compare it with the intended current snapshot. Neither operation targets startup-config. The distinct filename preserves the earlier backup.

For the benign file, S1 initiates an SFTP download from Ubuntu:

```ios S1
S1# copy sftp://ccnafile@10.29.0.100//home/ccnafile/ccna-files/handover.txt flash:handover-review.txt
```

Complete prompts, then inspect:

```ios S1
S1# dir flash:handover-review.txt
S1# more flash:handover-review.txt
S1# verify /sha512 flash:handover-review.txt
```

The text is `CCNA handover checkpoint` followed by a newline. Compare the whole hash with the trusted Ubuntu result; if the platform supports only the benign MD5 comparison, state that limitation. The file is staged and has not changed active configuration or running software.

The uppercase `Handover.txt` is a file-path error after a working authenticated connection, assuming the earlier service remains healthy. Correct source case to `handover.txt`; do not change the password or disable host-key verification.

Neither software candidate meets all requirements. A fails integrity comparison; B is the wrong platform despite an intact trusted file. Preserve working software, obtain the exact approved compatible candidate and verify it. Even an accepted staged candidate needs a separate approved activation procedure. No reload, replacement or image activation belongs to this challenge.
:::

exhibit.title: Representative show file systems excerpt
exhibit.text:
Size(b)      Free(b)     Type  Flags  Prefixes
*   256000000     180000000     disk     rw  flash0: flash:
       262144        240000    nvram     rw  nvram:
            -             -  network    rw  tftp:

questions.prompt: Which statement is supported by this file-system inventory?
options: The two flash prefixes refer to the same listed local storage
The TFTP prefix is a local disk containing 180 MB of free space
The 256,000,000-byte value is the free capacity available now
The startup configuration occupies the complete flash file system
questions.explanation: The prefixes flash0: and flash: share one row, identifying aliases in this example. The Free column, not Size, reports available bytes.

whyWrong.1: Type network describes remote transfer access, not local storage capacity.
whyWrong.2: Size reports total capacity; Free is 180,000,000 bytes.
whyWrong.3: The inventory distinguishes flash storage from nvram; it does not show configuration contents.

questions.prompt: How does base TFTP start a file transfer?
options: A UDP request targets port 69, which also carries every server data reply
A UDP request targets server port 69, then selected UDP transfer ports are used
A TCP control session targets port 21, followed by a separate data session
An SSH session targets port 22, then requests the file-transfer subsystem
questions.explanation: The initial TFTP request targets UDP 69. The server selects a transfer identifier/UDP port for the exchange; retransmitted requests can again target 69.

whyWrong.0: The server normally selects another transfer port; filtering only the initial service port can miss the actual exchange.
whyWrong.2: This is FTP’s control/data model, not TFTP.
whyWrong.3: This describes an SSH-based protocol such as SFTP, not TFTP.

questions.prompt: Which two statements describe classic FTP? Choose two.
options: The server initiates the active-mode data connection toward the client
Passive mode sends file contents inside the control connection
The normal control connection uses server TCP port 21
A username/password login encrypts the subsequent file contents
Passive mode requires every data connection to use server port 20
questions.explanation: FTP has a control connection and a separate data connection. Active/passive describes who initiates the data connection. Classic FTP does not provide encryption.

whyWrong.1: Directory listings and files use the separate data connection in passive mode too.
whyWrong.3: Authentication and encryption are different; classic FTP sends credentials/data in cleartext.
whyWrong.4: In passive mode the server advertises a data endpoint; it is not fixed to port 20.

questions.prompt: SSH already works on the cited IOS XE device. Which two additional conditions belong to its classic SCP server setup? Choose two.
options: The VTY transport must accept Telnet instead of SSH
FTP client credentials are stored with `ip ftp username`
The SFTP server subsystem must be enabled on this device
SCP server functionality is enabled with `ip scp server enable`
AAA EXEC authorization permits the user's required access
questions.explanation: The Cisco SCP server requires its server feature and appropriate authentication/authorization. The lab uses local AAA and an authorized privilege-15 account; successful SSH authentication alone does not prove all file access is permitted.

whyWrong.0: SCP relies on SSH, not Telnet.
whyWrong.1: These credentials apply to the router acting as an FTP client.
whyWrong.2: Classic SCP does not require an SFTP server; the cited implementation is SFTP-client-only.

questions.prompt: What do `ip ftp username filelab` and `ip ftp password ...` configure on the IOS device?
options: The username and password needed by a TFTP transfer
An encrypted login service for incoming FTP users
Credentials used by the device's FTP client operations
A local authorization list for access to every stored file
questions.explanation: The device uses these settings when acting as an FTP client. Stored credentials may appear in configuration backups; keeping them out of a URL does not make those backups nonsensitive.

whyWrong.0: Base TFTP has no username/password exchange.
whyWrong.1: These commands do not create an encrypted FTP server.
whyWrong.3: Remote client credentials are not a local file authorization policy.

questions.prompt: After `copy running-config tftp:` completes, what does it establish about startup-config?
options: Startup-config must be read first because running-config cannot be transferred
Startup-config now holds the active configuration because every backup saves it
Startup-config now holds the file received from the remote TFTP server
Startup-config is unchanged by this copy because it is neither destination nor source
questions.explanation: The source is running-config and the destination is the remote TFTP file. Updating startup-config requires its own explicit operation.

whyWrong.0: IOS can transfer running-config directly; a startup copy is not required first.
whyWrong.1: An off-device backup does not also save the local startup file.
whyWrong.2: This direction sends a file to the server; it does not download into startup-config.

exhibit.title: Representative console extract
exhibit.text:
R1-TEMP# copy flash:R1-before.cfg running-config
Destination filename [running-config]?
[OK]
R1# show ip interface brief
Loopback29       unassigned      YES unset  up  up

questions.prompt: R1-before.cfg contains `hostname R1` but no reference to Loopback29. The shown copy restored the hostname but left that interface. Why?
options: The active hostname changed, but interface changes require a reload
The copy merged its commands without removing the extra interface
The file was staged in flash but none of its commands were applied
The copy replaced startup-config while preserving the current session
questions.explanation: Copying into running-config merges the file’s commands. Its hostname command takes effect, but the older file contains no command removing Loopback29. Explicit no commands could remove settings during a merge.

whyWrong.0: The issue is the absence of a removal command, not a requirement to reload for interface changes.
whyWrong.2: The returned hostname demonstrates that a command was applied, and the destination is running-config.
whyWrong.3: The explicit destination is running-config, not startup-config.

questions.prompt: A verified backup is copied into startup-config. No other operation is performed. What changes immediately?
options: The booted IOS image changes to the one named in the backup
The active configuration becomes identical to the backup
The device erases all extra interfaces from running-config
The saved startup file changes; the active configuration does not
questions.explanation: The destination is the saved startup configuration. Applying it to the running system is a separate decision. A later normal startup may load it, subject to platform boot settings.

whyWrong.0: Copying a configuration file does not load a new running image.
whyWrong.1: The active configuration is not applied by this copy alone.
whyWrong.2: This destination is not running-config.

questions.prompt: An OpenSSH 9 client authenticates successfully to a verified classic-SCP-only IOS server, but its default `scp` command fails at SFTP subsystem negotiation. Which client option addresses that known mismatch?
options: `-O`, to select classic SCP instead of the SFTP default
`-P 21`, to move the secure operation to FTP's control port
`-p`, to preserve timestamps while changing the protocol
`-r`, to recursively copy the configuration directory
questions.explanation: OpenSSH 9 changed scp's default transfer protocol to SFTP. Uppercase -O selects classic SCP, still over SSH. The premise establishes a protocol mismatch rather than an unknown login fault.

whyWrong.1: The server is an SSH/SCP service, not an FTP control service.
whyWrong.2: Preserving file times does not select the SCP protocol.
whyWrong.3: Recursive copying does not change the transfer protocol.

exhibit.title: Verification worksheet
exhibit.text:
Cisco download metadata: SHA-512 value A
Local staged candidate: SHA-512 value B
A and B differ
Current running image remains unchanged

questions.prompt: The computed SHA-512 for a staged image differs from the value recorded from Cisco's trusted download page. What is the appropriate next action?
options: Retry activation to let the boot process settle the conflicting hashes
Stop and recheck the exact file, trusted metadata and stored bytes
Compare the saved configuration because it controls the file hash
Accept the file if its byte count and advertised release are correct
questions.explanation: The differing hashes prevent acceptance as the intended candidate. Preserve the running software while checking the expected filename, trusted comparison and transferred bytes.

whyWrong.0: Activation is not an appropriate validation test for an unverified file.
whyWrong.2: The candidate’s stored bytes, not the running configuration, determine this file hash.
whyWrong.3: Matching size and name do not override a mismatch with the trusted hash.

exhibit.title: Two tests
exhibit.text:
R1# ping 10.29.0.100
Success rate is 100 percent (5/5)

R1# copy running-config tftp:
%Error opening tftp://10.29.0.100/R1-before.cfg (Timed out)

questions.prompt: R1 can ping its TFTP server, but a write request times out. What is the best next investigation supported by those results?
options: Repeat ICMP with larger payloads before checking whether the file was created
Change the gateway before inspecting a service that uses a different transport
Save startup-config again because TFTP reads only the saved configuration
Check TFTP requests, replies, service state and write permission at the server
questions.explanation: A successful ICMP test does not establish that the TFTP service accepts a write or that its UDP exchange completes. Inspect the failed operation and the destination evidence before changing working network settings.

whyWrong.0: Larger ICMP probes may be useful for a demonstrated size problem, but none is established here; first inspect this transfer.
whyWrong.1: The result does not demonstrate a wrong gateway; the service-specific traffic supplies a more discriminating next check.
whyWrong.2: The command explicitly reads running-config. Saving another store does not enable server writes.

exhibit.title: Platform capability sheet — supplied facts
exhibit.text:
S1 on the cited IOS XE release:
SSH server: supported
SCP server: supported after configuration
SFTP client: supported
SFTP server: not supported

questions.prompt: A Linux workstation needs to retrieve a named file from S1. Which plan is consistent with this capability sheet?
options: Enable SFTP client on S1, then use Linux SFTP to request its file
Use passive FTP over TCP 22 because the SSH server is supported
Use Linux classic SCP to S1 after its SCP server prerequisites are met
Request SFTP first; an SSH server must accept every SSH subsystem
questions.explanation: The requested operation is initiated by Linux against a listening Cisco service. S1 supports the required classic SCP server role. SFTP client support on S1 does not supply an SFTP server for Linux to contact.

whyWrong.0: SFTP client capability permits S1 to initiate transfers to another server; it does not reverse the role.
whyWrong.1: FTP and SSH-based transfer protocols are different; moving a port does not convert one into another.
whyWrong.3: SSH transport support does not imply every application subsystem is implemented.

exhibit.title: Candidate acceptance record
exhibit.text:
Download: third-party file mirror
SHA-512: matches the value posted by that same mirror
Filename: matches the desired release
Cisco download metadata: not yet compared

questions.prompt: The transfer is intact relative to the mirror’s value. What evidence is still needed before accepting it as the intended Cisco software?
options: Compare against trusted Cisco metadata for the exact compatible image
Run the same local hash twice to establish the publisher’s identity
Copy the file through SSH again so its contents become Cisco-approved
Compare only its filename with the release named in the change plan
questions.explanation: A matching value from the same untrusted source establishes agreement with that source, not trusted provenance. Compare the exact image against Cisco’s authenticated download/release information and applicable authenticity checks; a secure transport does not certify the publisher.

whyWrong.1: Repeated local results demonstrate consistency, not the trustworthiness of the comparison source.
whyWrong.2: SSH protects this transport and authenticates its endpoint; it does not turn an untrusted file into an approved release.
whyWrong.3: Filenames can be copied or changed and do not establish trusted origin or byte integrity.

questions.prompt: A device reports 180,000,000 free bytes. The approved file is 70,000,000 bytes. What conclusion is justified from these two numbers alone?
options: It meets the upgrade requirements because file size is below free capacity
It leaves 110,000,000 bytes of RAM available for the installation process
It fits in reported storage, but compatibility and installation needs remain separate
It will become the boot candidate because the transfer destination has enough room
questions.explanation: The subtraction gives 110,000,000 bytes of storage headroom. It does not describe RAM, expanded packages, compatibility, saved boot intent or activation.

whyWrong.0: Fitting the compressed/staged file does not establish all installation or compatibility requirements.
whyWrong.1: These values concern persistent storage, not RAM.
whyWrong.3: Storage availability does not set the boot candidate.

questions.prompt: A verified remote backup must be downloaded for inspection without changing either active or startup configuration. The device lists flash: as writable. Which destination serves that requirement?
options: flash:R1-review.cfg, a new named file on local storage
running-config, because inspection requires merging the file
tftp:, because the remote source must also be the destination
startup-config, because the active system remains unchanged
questions.explanation: A new named local file stages the bytes for inspection. Neither running-config nor startup-config is the destination.

whyWrong.1: Merging applies commands; reading a file does not require that change.
whyWrong.2: The requirement is to retrieve the remote file into local storage, not write back to the remote service.
whyWrong.3: Although running-config would remain unchanged, this would overwrite the saved configuration, contrary to the requirement.

questions.prompt: An SSH client reports that S1’s host key differs from its previously verified key. No approved replacement is recorded. What should precede sending credentials or configuration files?
options: Remove the known-host entry and accept the new key as the current value
Verify the current key through trusted console/change records and reconcile the mismatch
Retry with a longer timeout because key comparison depends on link latency
Select a different filename because only the destination file changed
questions.explanation: A key mismatch could follow a legitimate replacement or an unintended endpoint. Resolve identity through a trusted independent path before proceeding; it is not evidence that the password is wrong.

whyWrong.0: Deleting the trusted comparison without verification discards the protection that detected the change.
whyWrong.2: A completed key comparison is not repaired by waiting longer.
whyWrong.3: The warning concerns the SSH server identity before file-path handling.

questions.prompt: The SSH server accepted the account, and its SFTP log reports “No such file” for /home/ccnafile/ccna-files/Probe.txt. The trusted directory listing shows only probe.txt. What is the narrow next correction?
options: Change the SSH user password, then repeat the same case-sensitive path
Use the existing source path with matching case, then verify the received file
Enable an FTP data port to carry the SFTP file after authentication
Replace the client’s gateway because a remote filename was not found
questions.explanation: Authentication and access to the server worked. The supplied source name differs in case from the actual file; use the verified path and retest.

whyWrong.0: The account was accepted; changing its password does not correct a path.
whyWrong.2: SFTP does not use FTP’s separate data connection.
whyWrong.3: The server processed the request and returned a file-path error; no gateway error is demonstrated.

exhibit.title: Linux shell
exhibit.text: scp -O labbackup@10.29.0.1:flash:S1-before.cfg ~/ccna-received/S1-before.cfg

questions.prompt: Which two interpretations of the command are correct? Choose two.
options: The -O option disables SSH encryption for this transfer
S1 downloads the named file from a Linux SCP server
The final path overwrites S1’s active running configuration
The remote source is S1’s flash:S1-before.cfg file
Linux initiates the connection to S1 as an SCP client
questions.explanation: OpenSSH scp reads source then destination. The remote user@host:path source is on S1; the local ~/ccna-received path is on Linux. -O selects classic SCP while keeping SSH.

whyWrong.0: The protocol changes from SFTP to classic SCP; the SSH protection remains.
whyWrong.1: The command is executed on Linux and contacts S1; the source is remote, not local.
whyWrong.2: The destination is a local workstation file, not a Cisco configuration store.

exhibit.title: Change requirements
exhibit.text:
running-config: approved new routing changes
startup-config: older recovery checkpoint to retain
Server: separate protected storage; SCP verified
Do not apply or activate anything

questions.prompt: The engineer needs a protected off-device copy of the current active configuration and must preserve the older startup checkpoint. Which completion record satisfies the whole requirement?
options: Copied running-config by SCP; verified remote contents; left startup-config unchanged
Copied running-config to local flash; verified it; left startup-config unchanged
Copied running-config by FTP; verified contents; left startup-config unchanged
Copied startup-config by SCP; verified contents; then saved running-config locally
questions.explanation: Only the last record uses the requested current source, protected transport, off-device destination and preservation of the older startup checkpoint.

whyWrong.1: The copy is still on the device and therefore does not meet the off-device requirement.
whyWrong.2: Classic FTP does not provide the required encrypted transport.
whyWrong.3: This backs up the older saved source and then overwrites that recovery point; both conflict with the requirements.

exhibit.title: Authored FTP client/capture observations
exhibit.text:
Control: TCP 21 connected; login accepted
PASV reply: data endpoint 10.29.0.100:50010
LIST requested
Client sends repeated SYNs to 10.29.0.100:50010; no SYN-ACK observed
Directory listing times out

questions.prompt: Which failure stage is demonstrated most directly by these FTP observations?
options: The username was rejected before the control session became usable
The transferred file was rejected because its SHA-512 differed
The client successfully received the complete requested directory listing
The separate passive data connection is not completing its TCP handshake
questions.explanation: Login and PASV responses demonstrate a working control exchange. The captured SYN retries toward the advertised passive endpoint show the data connection has not established. They do not uniquely identify which device or rule caused the absence of a reply.

whyWrong.0: The successful login and PASV reply contradict a rejected control-session login.
whyWrong.1: No completed file or hash comparison is shown.
whyWrong.2: The data connection required for the listing has not established.

exhibit.title: Supplied isolated IOS XE/server evidence
exhibit.text:
Gi1/0/1: 10.29.0.1/24, up/up
Loopback29: 10.29.29.2/32, up/up
ip ssh source-interface Loopback29
Routing is working bidirectionally for both addresses.
Server policy permits SSH only from 10.29.0.1.
Server log: denied TCP 22 connection from 10.29.29.2.

questions.prompt: What best explains why this SFTP transfer is refused even though S1 can ping the server?
options: The saved configuration lacks an IP address because the ping was local
The source file is missing because authentication has not yet occurred
The client selected a source address not allowed by the server’s stated policy
The server requires an FTP data port for files larger than the probe
questions.explanation: The SSH source-interface selection and the server log agree on 10.29.29.2, while the policy permits only 10.29.0.1. Correct the source to the intended authorized interface and retest server identity, login and transfer. ICMP success does not override an SSH access rule.

whyWrong.0: The actual source is present in both current configuration and the server’s received connection.
whyWrong.1: The connection is refused before the file request; no filename result is available.
whyWrong.3: This is an SSH/SFTP connection, not FTP with a separate data port.

cards.front: What does copy running-config startup-config do?
cards.back: It writes the active configuration to the saved startup store. This is separate from creating an off-device backup.

cards.front: What changes when a file is copied into startup-config?
cards.back: The saved startup file is replaced; the active configuration does not change immediately. A later configuration application/startup is separate, and saving running-config over it would overwrite it.

cards.front: Copying a saved file into running-config: merge or replace?
cards.back: Merge. The file's commands are applied to current configuration. Extra settings absent from the file can remain; explicit commands, including `no`, can change or remove settings.

cards.front: Does copying a software image activate it?
cards.back: No. Transfer, integrity/compatibility verification and activation are separate stages. Confirm active software with the platform's operational displays.

cards.front: What makes a backup filename useful?
cards.back: It identifies the device and a known checkpoint, with a date/change label when appropriate. Verify the destination file and restrict access to its sensitive contents.

cards.front: How does a TFTP transfer use UDP ports?
cards.back: Requests target server UDP 69. The server selects a transfer ID/port for the exchange with the client's selected port; retransmitted requests can still use 69.

cards.front: What protection does base TFTP provide for users and file contents?
cards.back: No built-in user login authentication or encryption. Server file permissions still matter, but they do not turn TFTP into a secure transport.

cards.front: Which FTP connection normally targets server TCP 21?
cards.back: The control connection for login and commands. Files and directory listings use a separate data connection.

cards.front: Active versus passive FTP data connections?
cards.back: Active: server initiates toward client. Passive: client initiates toward the server's advertised data endpoint. Both use a separate control connection; defaults depend on implementation.

cards.front: Common transport for SCP and SFTP?
cards.back: SSH, normally TCP 22. Both protect data in transit; permissions and protection of files at rest remain separate responsibilities.

cards.front: IOS FTP client credential commands?
cards.back: `ip ftp username` and `ip ftp password` supply client credentials. They do not create a server, and saved configuration may contain sensitive credential information.

cards.front: What does a Cisco SCP server require?
cards.back: Working SSH, suitable authentication and EXEC authorization, adequate user privilege and `ip scp server enable`. Successful login alone does not prove permission for a file operation.

cards.front: Can SFTP client support on a Cisco device prove that it accepts incoming SFTP requests?
cards.back: No. Client and server are separate roles. The cited Catalyst 9300 release supplies an SFTP client; consult the actual device’s server capabilities before choosing the transfer direction.

cards.front: Why might OpenSSH 9+ scp need `-O` for an IOS server?
cards.back: Its default transfer protocol is SFTP. Uppercase `-O` selects classic SCP for a verified SCP-only server; it does not repair passwords or file permissions.

cards.front: Does an SSH password authenticate the server’s identity?
cards.back: No. Verify the SSH host key through a trusted path. User authentication and server-identity verification are separate checks.

cards.front: What does `configure replace` require?
cards.back: A complete compatible replacement configuration and a supporting platform. It applies differences, including removals; use validated recovery access and inspect errors/results.

cards.front: How should a staged image hash be verified?
cards.back: Compute a supported strong hash, such as `verify /sha512 flash:filename`, and compare with trusted Cisco metadata for that exact image. MD5 can detect transfer errors but is not modern proof of authenticity.

cards.front: A file matches a hash from the same untrusted mirror. Is its publisher established?
cards.back: No. The match shows agreement with that value; compare with trusted metadata for the exact intended software and applicable authenticity checks.

cards.front: SFTP login succeeds, then “No such file” names the requested path. What should you check?
cards.back: Compare the exact server-side path, filename case and account access with a trusted directory listing before changing the network.

cards.front: Does an SCP transfer encrypt the backup file stored at its destination?
cards.back: SSH protects the bytes in transit. Restrict access and apply appropriate storage protection separately; configuration backups may contain secrets.

commands.task: List file-system types and prefixes, including the default file system.
commands.note: Network protocol prefixes refer to remote access, not local disk capacity.

commands.task: List the files and capacity in the explicitly verified flash: file system.
commands.note: Use the actual prefix reported on the device; an unqualified dir may target a different default.

commands.task: Read the running software identity and platform details before planning any image change.
commands.note: A directory listing alone does not identify the active software.

commands.task: Create a named local snapshot of the active configuration as flash:S1-before.cfg, without overwriting startup-config.
commands.note: Complete any destination prompt, then inspect the file. This local snapshot still needs an off-device copy to survive loss of the device.

commands.task: Back up running-config to TFTP, prompting for the remote host and filename.
commands.note: Complete each interactive prompt before entering another IOS command. This does not save startup-config.

commands.task: Stage a file from TFTP into the device's verified flash: storage, prompting for filenames.
commands.note: Check free space and choose a new destination filename. A software transfer does not activate it.

commands.task: Replace only the saved startup file from a TFTP server, prompting for the source details.
commands.note: This does not immediately apply the configuration. Do not append reload; first inspect and validate the intended result.

commands.task: Enable the Cisco SCP server after SSH and appropriate AAA authorization have been verified.
commands.note: Server access still depends on user authentication, privilege and file permissions.

commands.task: From Linux, pull flash:S1-before.cfg from the verified classic-SCP-only server 10.29.0.1 as labbackup into ~/ccna-received/S1-before.cfg. The local directory already exists.
commands.note: Source precedes destination. -O selects classic SCP; keep host-key verification enabled and inspect the resulting protected local file.

commands.task: On a supporting IOS XE image with server identity and credentials verified, stage /home/ccnafile/ccna-files/probe.txt from SFTP user ccnafile at 10.29.0.100 as flash:probe-sftp.txt. Do not put the password in the URL.
commands.note: Complete the password/destination prompts individually; verify the server identity and resulting file.

commands.task: On a supporting IOS XE release, compute SHA-512 for the staged flash:approved-image.bin.
commands.note: Compare the complete result with trusted metadata for that exact compatible image. Computing a hash is not activation.

tickets.title: The old hostname returned but a temporary interface remains
tickets.scenario: In an isolated lab, R1-before.cfg was saved before an unused, unnumbered Loopback29 was created. The file contains hostname R1 and no reference to Loopback29. A learner changed the hostname and added the loopback, then applied the backup. No other changes are intended.

exhibits.title: Console history
exhibits.text:
R1-TEMP# copy flash:R1-before.cfg running-config
Destination filename [running-config]?
[OK]
R1#

exhibits.title: Active configuration excerpt
exhibits.text:
hostname R1
interface Loopback29
 description TEMPORARY_MERGE_TEST

tickets.question: What explains the remaining interface?
options: The file merged into running-config without removing the extra interface
The file was staged locally and none of its commands reached running-config
The active configuration exactly matches the old file; the interface is only cached
The copy replaced startup-config while the current configuration stayed unchanged
tickets.explanation: The explicit running-config destination and changed hostname show that commands were applied. A merge does not remove an extra interface merely because the source omits it. Staging, exact replacement and a startup-only copy do not explain all the observations.
tickets.fix:
Compare the active result with the intended lab baseline, then remove only the known unused interface:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# no interface loopback29
R1(config)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
```
Retest the actual lab connectivity. Save the verified result with a separate `copy running-config startup-config` operation, completing its prompt. A full configuration replacement would require a complete validated file and an appropriate recovery procedure; it is unnecessary for this demonstrated harmless change.

tickets.title: SSH works, but the protected source file cannot be read
tickets.scenario: In an isolated IOS XE/Ubuntu transfer lab, S1 has already verified the server host key. The ccnafile account can read another test file through SFTP. The engineer now requests probe.txt at the exact path below. Destination space is sufficient. These are authored diagnostic observations, not a captured device session.

exhibits.title: Transfer stages
exhibits.text:
Server host-key verification: passed
SSH account ccnafile: accepted
SFTP subsystem: started
OPEN /home/ccnafile/ccna-files/probe.txt: Permission denied

exhibits.title: Trusted Ubuntu console inspection
exhibits.text:
Parent directories allow ccnafile to traverse them.
ls -l /home/ccnafile/ccna-files/probe.txt
-rw------- 1 root root 30 probe.txt
sudo -u ccnafile test -r /home/ccnafile/ccna-files/probe.txt
Exit status: 1

tickets.question: Which correction addresses the demonstrated source-file problem?
options: Repeat the request with the FTP control port instead of SSH
Replace the verified host key to permit the current SFTP account
Make the intended ccnafile account the owner, retaining private file permissions
Reset the login password before retrying the unchanged file permissions
tickets.explanation: Authentication and the SFTP subsystem succeeded. The exact file exists but mode 600 permits only its root owner to read it. The negative account-specific read test confirms the source-file access fault. Port, key and password changes do not address that evidence.
tickets.fix:
At the trusted Ubuntu console, first confirm this is the intended benign lab file. Grant access only to its intended lab owner:

```bash
sudo chown ccnafile:ccnafile /home/ccnafile/ccna-files/probe.txt
sudo chmod 600 /home/ccnafile/ccna-files/probe.txt
sudo -u ccnafile test -r /home/ccnafile/ccna-files/probe.txt
```

The last command should exit successfully without output. Repeat the original SFTP request from S1 to a new named flash file, completing each prompt. Inspect its size/content and compare its hash with the trusted source. Do not relax the whole directory to world-writable access or change the SSH identity policy.

chapters.title: Client OS troubleshooting
chapters.subtitle: Read the endpoint, test a specific path, and separate symptoms from causes.

sources.title: Apple: DHCP or manual IP settings
RFC 5416: SSID length in the 802.11 binding
Cisco: WLAN authentication and key exchange

chapters.summary: Verify IP configuration on Windows, macOS and Linux, diagnose address, mask, gateway and DNS faults, and check wireless connection and security evidence without overclaiming what a ping or connection icon proves.

sections.body:
“The network is down” can mean a disconnected adapter, an address from the wrong subnet, an unreachable DNS service or a single application failure. Start by turning that report into a testable statement: which client, which connection, which destination, which application and when?

A useful diagnosis preserves the evidence before making changes. Read the current settings, compare them with the intended network, and test one part of the path at a time. A familiar symptom should suggest the next test, not replace it.

sections.title: Start with the active adapter and its parameters
sections.body:
An endpoint may have Ethernet, Wi-Fi, a VPN and virtual-machine adapters simultaneously. First identify the adapter that should carry the affected traffic. Its name is not necessarily `Ethernet`, `en0` or `eth0`; discover the real name before interpreting output or running a change.

For a conventional IPv4 LAN, examine the address, subnet mask, default gateway and DNS server. The address identifies the interface. The mask helps establish the directly connected subnet. A gateway provides a next hop for routes through a router; the default gateway is used when no more specific route matches. DNS resolves names independently of the forwarding decision.

:::facts
- An on-subnet numeric-IP test can work without a default gateway or DNS.
- A default gateway alone does not prove that every remote destination is reachable.
- DHCP can supply correct or incorrect values; manual settings can override selected values.
- A host can have several routes, DNS resolvers and IPv4/IPv6 addresses.
- Read the intended adapter, route and address family for the failing destination.
:::

These four IPv4 parameters are a starting point, not the whole network. A VPN may install a more specific route. An application may use a proxy or its own encrypted DNS. A certificate or clock error may prevent HTTPS even while the network delivers packets correctly.

Also inspect IPv6. A link-local `fe80::` address is normal on an IPv6-enabled interface; it does not by itself show that global IPv6 routing works. Identify any global/unique-local address, its prefix, the default route and the scope of a link-local next hop. Keep IPv4 and IPv6 results separate: success over one does not prove the other is healthy.

sections.title: Ask the same questions on three operating systems
sections.body:
The commands differ, but the investigation is consistent:

| Question | Windows | macOS | Linux |
|---|---|---|---|
| Addresses, masks and adapter details? | `ipconfig /all` | `ifconfig`; Network settings | `ip -br address` |
| Default route and other routes? | `route print -4` / `route print -6` | `route -n get default`; `netstat -rn` | `ip route` / `ip -6 route` |
| DNS configuration? | `ipconfig /all` | `scutil --dns` | `resolvectl status` or `nmcli device show` |
| Cached IPv4 neighbors? | `arp -a` | `arp -a` | `ip neigh` |
| DNS query to a specified server? | `nslookup name server` | `nslookup name server`, where installed | `nslookup name server`, where installed |

Linux distributions choose different network managers; `nmcli` applies to NetworkManager and `resolvectl` to systemd-resolved. If neither manages the machine, use that distribution's documented tools. Legacy `ifconfig` may be absent on Linux, so do not begin by installing old tools simply to match a screenshot.

A neighbor cache shows a recorded IP-to-link-layer mapping. An entry can be stale, static or incorrect; it is not independent proof that the current path is good. Combine it with a fresh test and interface evidence.

sections.title: Read Windows configuration and routes
sections.body:
Use `ipconfig /all` to identify the intended adapter and its configured values. Compare the MAC address with inventory if necessary, while allowing for private/randomized wireless MAC settings. A disconnected unused adapter is not automatically the cause of a fault on another connection.

Representative excerpt:

```output Windows: ipconfig /all
Ethernet adapter Ethernet:
   DHCP Enabled. . . . . . . . . . . : Yes              ← address configuration uses DHCP
   IPv4 Address. . . . . . . . . . . : 10.1.20.57
   Subnet Mask . . . . . . . . . . . : 255.255.255.0    ← expected /24
   Default Gateway . . . . . . . . . : 10.1.20.1
   DHCP Server . . . . . . . . . . . : 10.1.10.5        ← can be remote through a relay
   DNS Servers . . . . . . . . . . . : 10.1.10.5
```

`DHCP Enabled: Yes` does not establish that every displayed value came from the lease: manually specified DNS can coexist with automatic addressing. A remote DHCP server address is also not an error by itself; a relay can serve the LAN.

A Windows **Autoconfiguration IPv4 Address** in `169.254.0.0/16`, with DHCP enabled and no usable lease, indicates IPv4 link-local fallback, commonly called APIPA. It suggests DHCP acquisition failed, but does not identify which message or device failed. The server could be unreachable, a pool could be exhausted, or replies could fail to reach the client.

RFC 3927's dynamic selection range excludes the first and last /24 within that /16. The important operational point is link scope: these addresses are not a substitute for routed IPv4 service. Existing IPv6 or another adapter may still provide connectivity. A number starting `169.254` alone is weaker evidence than the autoconfiguration label plus the configuration context.

Read `route print -4` when multiple adapters are active. Longest matching prefix comes before metric. With two usable default routes and no more specific match, the lower effective metric is preferred. Do not assume Ethernet always wins simply because it is wired.

To request a lease update, use `ipconfig /renew "Ethernet"` with the actual adapter name. `/release` deliberately discards the lease and can interrupt the current session, so use release/renew only where that disruption is intended. The exact exchange depends on client state; do not infer a captured four-message DHCP sequence from the command alone.

sections.title: Read macOS and Linux configuration
sections.body:
On macOS, Network settings shows each network service's details. TCP/IP shows the address, subnet mask, router and configuration method. DNS settings shows resolver choices. `networksetup -listallhardwareports` helps map a friendly service to an interface; `networksetup -getinfo "Wi-Fi"` reads that named service's IP settings.

In `ifconfig en0`, a mask such as `0xffffff00` is hexadecimal. Each `f` represents four one-bits: six of them give 24 one-bits, so the mask is `255.255.255.0` or /24. `0xffffff80` is /25 because `0x80` adds one further one-bit. Use the actual interface, which may differ from en0.

`route -n get default` identifies the default IPv4 route. `scutil --dns` shows resolver configuration, including supplemental domain-specific resolvers used by some VPNs. Do not assume the first displayed server answers every query: domain and interface scope can affect selection. A configured “reachable” status is not equivalent to a completed DNS query.

On Linux, `ip -br address` provides a compact interface/address view. `ip route` shows IPv4 routes. Representative excerpt:

```output Linux: ip -br address and ip route
enp0s3  UP  10.1.20.59/24 fe80::a00:27ff:fe4e:66a1/64
default via 10.1.20.1 dev enp0s3 proto dhcp src 10.1.20.59 metric 100
10.1.20.0/24 dev enp0s3 proto kernel scope link src 10.1.20.59
```

Here `via 10.1.20.1` is the next hop and `src 10.1.20.59` is the preferred source address, not another gateway. `proto dhcp` labels the route's origin; confirm the address acquisition method through the network manager or lease information rather than assuming that one route label proves every address's origin.

For systemd-resolved, `resolvectl status` displays per-link DNS configuration. A `127.0.0.53` entry in `/etc/resolv.conf` can identify a local DNS stub, not the upstream server. With NetworkManager, `nmcli device show` includes addresses, gateway and DNS information.

Failed DHCP on Linux does not have one universal visual result. Depending on the manager and profile, an interface may have no usable IPv4 address, retain another configuration, or obtain a link-local address. NetworkManager's link-local behavior is configurable. Its `device reapply` operation reapplies supported connection changes; it is not a universal “force a fresh DHCP lease” command.

sections.title: Recognize fault patterns and their limits
sections.body:
Use a simple network to reason precisely. PC-A is intended to be `192.168.40.100/24`, gateway `192.168.40.1`. A local server is `192.168.40.20`; a remote PC is `192.168.50.10/24` behind the router.

| Suspected fault | Useful observation | Confirmation needed |
|---|---|---|
| No usable DHCP lease | Autoconfiguration/link-local or no expected IPv4 address | Manager status, DHCP requests/replies and server state |
| Wrong gateway | Local tests work; intended routed test fails | Compare configured next hop with the actual router |
| Wrong mask | Failure differs by destination subnet | Compute the client's on-link decision |
| Wrong DNS choice | Numeric access works; direct DNS query fails | Server selected, query response and record correctness |
| Duplicate address | Conflict indication or inconsistent neighbor evidence | Compare leases/static assignments and packet observations |

A wrong gateway of `192.168.40.254` can prevent off-link traffic if that address is unused and no other matching route exists. It need not break direct communication with `192.168.40.20`. The failure is in selecting or reaching the next hop, not in DNS merely because a website name was involved.

A /16 mask on PC-A creates a different problem. The client now considers `192.168.50.10` on-link and tries to resolve that destination directly instead of using `192.168.40.1`. In the lab, proxy ARP is explicitly disabled, so no router answers on behalf of the remote PC. Yet a destination outside `192.168.0.0/16` would still be sent toward the configured gateway. This explains why one successful remote test cannot validate the mask for all destinations.

```diagram
{"type":"topology","title":"Test the local and routed paths separately","nodes":[{"id":"pc","kind":"pc","label":"PC-A","sub":"192.168.40.100/24","x":1,"y":1},{"id":"server","kind":"server","label":"Local server","sub":"192.168.40.20/24","x":1,"y":5},{"id":"sw","kind":"switch","label":"SW1","x":4,"y":3},{"id":"r","kind":"router","label":"R1","sub":".40.1 / .50.1","x":8,"y":3},{"id":"remote","kind":"pc","label":"PC-B","sub":"192.168.50.10/24","x":11,"y":3}],"links":[{"from":"pc","to":"sw"},{"from":"server","to":"sw"},{"from":"sw","to":"r"},{"from":"r","to":"remote"}],"caption":"A /16 error changes PC-A's decision about PC-B; a local server test does not exercise the gateway."}
```

A DNS timeout means the query did not obtain the expected timely response. It does not distinguish a wrong server address, filtering, a stopped service or a return-path failure. NXDOMAIN is different: a responding server reported that the queried name does not exist. Use an explicit query and read the response rather than calling every name failure “DNS down.”

:::trap A ping result has a limited scope
A reply proves an ICMP exchange worked for that test. A timeout does not prove a firewall blocked it, and it does not prove the packet left the client. A local “destination unreachable” is a useful clue, but inspect the route and neighbor state before assigning the exact cause.
:::

sections.title: Verify wireless connection and security settings
sections.body:
Wireless adds association and security checks before useful protected data exchange. Compare the intended **SSID**, security mode and required credentials with the client's profile. SSIDs are case-sensitive and have a maximum length of 32 octets; displayed characters need not always occupy one byte.

WPA2-Personal commonly uses an 8–63 ASCII-character passphrase, or a directly entered 64-hexadecimal-digit PSK where supported. WPA3-Personal uses SAE, and Enterprise security uses 802.1X/EAP methods whose credentials may involve certificates, passwords or both. Do not apply the WPA2 passphrase rule to every wireless authentication method.

In WPA2-Personal, initial 802.11 association can occur before the four-way key handshake finishes. A wrong shared key can therefore produce an association followed by a key-exchange failure. Useful protected client data, including DHCP, requires the security process to succeed. Exact operating-system messages vary; one error phrase does not establish the cause for every client.

On Windows, `netsh wlan show interfaces` reports current connection information, including SSID and authentication/cipher details where available. `netsh wlan show profiles` lists saved profiles; `netsh wlan show profile name="CCNA-LAB"` reads a chosen profile without requesting its cleartext key. There is no need to expose a password to compare the security mode.

On macOS, use the Wi-Fi details and Option-click the menu-bar Wi-Fi icon to open Wireless Diagnostics. It analyzes the connection without changing network settings. On Linux with NetworkManager, `nmcli device wifi list` shows nearby networks and `nmcli connection show` identifies profiles. Inspect the active profile's `802-11-wireless-security.key-mgmt` to distinguish its authentication method. Privacy permissions, driver support and OS release can limit displayed radio details; document missing fields.

A “connected” indication with an APIPA address calls for checking DHCP acquisition **and** the intended WLAN/VLAN/data path. It is not proof that every wireless parameter or infrastructure mapping is correct. A strong signal does not establish correct credentials, DHCP service or DNS operation. Likewise, a valid lease can be stale or obtained on the wrong network.

sections.title: Test a path and verify the repair
sections.body:
Record the intended adapter and compare its actual address, prefix, route and DNS values with the network plan. For wireless, establish which SSID/security method is in use. Then test a known local peer, the intended gateway, a known routed destination, a direct DNS query and the required application.

A loopback ping or ping to the client's own address can test local processing, but does not exercise the cable, AP or gateway. A gateway may also be configured not to answer ICMP, so combine that result with neighbor state and another appropriate test instead of stopping every investigation at a failed ping.

On Windows PowerShell, `Test-NetConnection 192.168.50.20 -Port 443` tests a TCP connection to that address and port. A successful TCP connection still does not prove TLS negotiation, certificate validation or application authorization. `-TraceRoute` is a different diagnostic mode; do not combine incompatible parameter sets as though one command universally performs every test.

Change one demonstrated cause at a time and repeat the previously failing test. After repairing a wrong client DNS address, verify the server selected and the expected answer, then try the application. A cached result can conceal the effect of a changed resolver, so direct queries to a specified server are valuable.

If DHCP settings were wrong, repair the correct server/profile and renew through the operating system's supported method. On macOS, the selected network service's TCP/IP pane provides Renew DHCP Lease. On Linux, use its actual network manager; disconnecting and reconnecting a profile interrupts traffic and belongs in an isolated or approved maintenance context.

sections.title: Exam focus
sections.body:
For v1.1, read and verify client IP parameters on Windows, macOS and Linux. For v2.0, extend that work to wired/wireless reachability and wireless security settings. Be able to explain the next useful test and what its result would establish.

Keep configuration evidence, packet evidence and inference separate. A correct answer identifies the supported cause or next investigation without claiming that a single ping, neighbor entry or Wi-Fi icon proves the whole network.

lab.title: Isolate client address, gateway, DNS and wireless faults
lab.intro:
Practice revised September 2026. If you completed an earlier version, repeat the revised exercise and update its checkmarks.

Work from a small test matrix: **active adapter/parameters → local peer → gateway → remote numeric destination → fresh DNS answer → application**. Write a prediction before each controlled fault, retain its actual observations, and repair it in a later step. A familiar symptom suggests a test; it does not prove the cause.

Use Packet Tracer for deliberate changes. Inspect **one actual OS you have**, then interpret the supplied evidence for the others; three OS installations are not required. The wireless module is optional where the simulator lacks a working supported AP/client combination, but its evidence worksheet still needs an answer. None of the output here is presented as an executed simulator capture.
lab.topology:
Build a new isolated Packet Tracer project. Use an ISR 2911 R1, a 2960 SW1, two PC-PT endpoints and Server-PT. The optional wireless extension uses WRT300N and a Laptop-PT with a compatible wireless adapter.

| Connection | Cable | Address / gateway |
|---|---|---|
| PC-A Fa0 — SW1 Fa0/1 | Copper straight-through | DHCP |
| Server-A Fa0 — SW1 Fa0/2 | Copper straight-through | 192.168.40.20/24, GW 192.168.40.1 |
| R1 Gi0/0 — SW1 Fa0/3 | Copper straight-through | R1 192.168.40.1/24 |
| R1 Gi0/1 — PC-B Fa0 | Copper crossover | R1 192.168.50.1/24; PC-B 192.168.50.10/24, GW 192.168.50.1 |
| Optional WRT1 Ethernet 1 — SW1 Fa0/4 | Copper straight-through | WRT1 LAN 192.168.40.2/24; its DHCP service disabled |

Server-A provides DHCP, DNS and HTTP. Its DHCP range is **192.168.40.100–149**, safely excluding the router, wireless device and static server. There is no Internet connection. R1 needs only its connected routes.

These are documented, reviewed procedures with expected results, not a record of an executed Packet Tracer run. Packet Tracer's PC shell and wireless controls differ by version. Use its IP Configuration GUI if a PC command is absent, and record unsupported observations honestly. The final OS inspection is read-only on a real Windows, Mac or Linux machine; all deliberate faults stay in the isolated simulator.

steps.title: — Configure router and static endpoints
steps.body:
Set Server-A and PC-B in Desktop → IP Configuration → Static from the topology table, mask `255.255.255.0`. Server-A's DNS field is `192.168.40.20`; PC-B's is also `192.168.40.20`.

On a new router, decline the setup dialog if presented:

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.40.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no ip proxy-arp
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.50.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
R1# show ip route connected
```

:::expected
Both router interfaces become up/up and both /24 networks are connected. Proxy ARP is explicitly disabled on Gi0/0 so the later mask error will not be concealed by the router answering for a remote host. If the filtered route command is unavailable, use `show ip route` and identify the connected routes. If `no ip proxy-arp` is rejected or its state cannot be verified, complete the wrong-mask steps as an address-decision worksheet: predict the on-link ARP request and explain why proxy ARP could conceal the fault. Do not record the predicted timeout as an observed result. The DNS, gateway and wireless exercises can still proceed.
:::

steps.title: — Configure DHCP, DNS and HTTP explicitly
steps.body:
On Server-A → Services:

1. **DHCP:** turn the service On.
