Create a pool named `CLIENTS` with default gateway `192.168.40.1`, DNS `192.168.40.20`, starting address `192.168.40.100`, mask `255.255.255.0` and maximum users `50`. Add/save the pool. Remove or correct any default pool that could serve this same interface with conflicting values.
2. **DNS:** turn the service On. Add A records `lab.example` and `fresh.example`, each resolving to `192.168.40.20`.
3. **HTTP:** explicitly turn HTTP On. The default page is adequate; its content is not part of the diagnosis.

On PC-A → Desktop → IP Configuration, select DHCP.

:::expected
PC-A receives an address in .100–.149, /24 mask, gateway .40.1 and DNS .40.20. Do not assume which exact address it receives. If the fields are wrong, fix the server pool before continuing; the static server at .20 is outside the lease range.
:::

steps.title: — Record a known working baseline
steps.body:
Before testing, make a six-row worksheet for the active adapter/parameters, local server, gateway, remote PC, fresh DNS and web service. Write what each test exercises; a local HTTP page cannot establish routed connectivity. On PC-A inspect its actual address with `ipconfig` or the GUI. Then use its command prompt:

```text
ping 192.168.40.20
ping 192.168.40.1
ping 192.168.50.10
nslookup lab.example
```

Open Desktop → Web Browser and visit `http://192.168.40.20`, then `http://lab.example`. If `nslookup` is absent, record that limitation and use the DNS request/response in Simulation mode as the query observation.

:::expected
After any initial ARP delay, local server, gateway and remote PC respond. The query resolves lab.example to .40.20 and both browser tests show the server page. The remote PC ping exercises routing; browsing the local server alone does not. Save `clients-baseline.pkt` and continue in `clients-faults.pkt`.
:::

steps.title: — Introduce only a DNS-selection fault
steps.body:
Predict which worksheet rows should change when only the DNS selection changes. Write down PC-A's leased address. Change PC-A to Static, retaining that exact address, /24 mask and gateway .40.1, but change DNS to unused `192.168.40.99`. No other device uses .99 in this topology.

Repeat numeric pings and try `nslookup fresh.example`. Read which DNS server the query uses; do not rely solely on a previously cached browser result.

:::solution
Numeric local and routed tests should still work. The DNS request to .99 has no configured server to answer it. Cached lab.example data might still work in an application, so it is not a reliable test of the new resolver setting. The demonstration identifies the wrong configured resolver by comparison with the known server address.
:::

steps.title: — Restore DNS and verify its response
steps.body:
Keep the same static address, mask and gateway, and restore DNS to `192.168.40.20`. Repeat `nslookup fresh.example` or inspect the DNS exchange in Simulation mode, then open `http://fresh.example`.

:::expected
The configured resolver is .40.20 and returns .40.20 for the name. The page opens. Record this recovery before creating the next fault.
:::

steps.title: — Introduce only a gateway fault
steps.body:
Predict local delivery, remote delivery and the local DNS query separately. In PC-A's static IP settings, change gateway to unused `192.168.40.254`. Keep its address, /24 mask and correct local DNS. Test:

```text
ping 192.168.40.20
ping 192.168.50.10
arp -a
```

If the neighbor command is absent, watch ARP in Simulation mode.

:::solution
The local server remains reachable; the intended remote PC should fail because the configured next hop is unused. Observe the attempted resolution for .40.254 where the simulator exposes it. A local DNS server can still answer, so this fault need not make every name lookup fail. Exact ping error wording is platform-dependent.
:::

steps.title: — Restore the gateway
steps.body:
Return PC-A's gateway to `192.168.40.1` without changing its other values. Repeat the local and remote pings.

:::expected
Both tests work after necessary address resolution. Successful recovery agrees with the demonstrated wrong next hop. Keep the known configuration rather than making unrelated DNS or router changes.
:::

steps.title: — Introduce only a subnet-mask fault
steps.body:
Before testing, compute whether .40.20 and .50.10 appear on-link under the new mask, and name the ARP target for .50.10. Change PC-A's mask to `255.255.0.0`. Retain its address, gateway and DNS. Test the local server and remote `192.168.50.10`. In Simulation mode, filter ARP/ICMP, clear the event list, send a new PC-A-to-PC-B simple PDU and inspect PC-A's decision. Do not interpret an old event as a new test.

:::solution
The local .40.20 server remains within the client's perceived /16. The client incorrectly treats .50.10 as on-link and tries to resolve it directly. With proxy ARP disabled on R1 Gi0/0, that remote endpoint is not resolved on this LAN. The failure concerns the mask's local/remote decision, even though the displayed gateway value is correct.
:::

steps.title: — Restore the mask and repeat the same destination test
steps.body:
Return PC-A's mask to `255.255.255.0`. Repeat the remote ping and inspect a new simulation event if available.

:::expected
PC-A now recognizes .50.10 as outside its /24 and sends toward .40.1. The remote ping succeeds. Save a separate checkpoint `clients-recovered.pkt`.
:::

steps.title: — Observe a DHCP acquisition failure
steps.body:
Predict why leaving a still-valid lease in place would be a poor test of fresh DHCP acquisition. First return PC-A to DHCP and verify it again receives the correct settings. Turn **Server-A's DHCP service Off**, leaving DNS and HTTP On. On this isolated PC-A only, discard the existing lease and request another:

```text
ipconfig /release
ipconfig /renew
```

If those commands are unsupported, toggle PC-A's IP Configuration to Static, then back to DHCP after the server is Off. In Simulation mode, observe the client's DHCP attempts.

:::solution
PC-A cannot acquire a new lease from the disabled server. Depending on simulator timing, it may report a failed request, show no usable IPv4 configuration or display an autoconfiguration address. Record the actual result; do not require an invented exact APIPA address. The absence of a lease alone would not prove which DHCP message failed, but this controlled service-off change supplies the known cause.
:::

steps.title: — Restore DHCP without changing unrelated services
steps.body:
Turn Server-A's DHCP service On. Confirm the CLIENTS pool still contains .100–.149, gateway .40.1 and DNS .40.20. Renew on PC-A or click DHCP in its GUI. Repeat the baseline tests after a valid lease appears.

:::expected
The client again obtains intended settings, resolves lab.example and reaches PC-B. The numeric address may differ from its earlier lease. Server-A's static .20 address has not entered the pool, and DNS/HTTP did not need restarting.
:::

steps.title: — Build the optional wireless client path
steps.body:
Add a WRT300N named WRT1. Connect **Ethernet 1, a LAN port**, to SW1 Fa0/4; leave its Internet/WAN port disconnected. Through WRT1's GUI:

- Set Local IP Address to `192.168.40.2` with mask `255.255.255.0`.
- Disable its DHCP server; Server-A remains the only intended DHCP server.
- Set the SSID to `CCNA-LAB`.
- Set wireless security to **WPA2-Personal**, encryption **AES**, and fictional lab passphrase `StudyNet2026!`.
- Save each relevant page. If changing the LAN address interrupts a management page, reopen the GUI at the new address.

For Laptop-PT, use an available compatible wireless module. If the model lacks one, open Physical, power it off, replace its removable Ethernet module with the listed WPC300N wireless module where supported, then power it on. In Desktop → PC Wireless, select/connect to CCNA-LAB with matching WPA2-Personal/AES settings and the lab passphrase. In IP Configuration, select DHCP for the wireless interface.

:::expected
The laptop joins the intended WLAN and obtains a .100–.149 address from Server-A, gateway .40.1 and DNS .40.20. Test its local server and PC-B, then browse lab.example. An address in the WRT's former default subnet means its DHCP service or cabling is wrong. If the installed version lacks the named model/security controls, use an available equivalent documented WPA2-Personal AP or use the supplied evidence in Step 13. Complete the real-OS inspection in Step 15 and record simulated wireless execution as unperformed.
:::

steps.title: — Observe a wireless credential fault
steps.body:
Predict whether a retained IP address alone can demonstrate a successful new protected connection. On the simulated laptop, disconnect from CCNA-LAB and change only its saved profile passphrase to `WrongStudyKey!`. Reconnect with that profile. Do not change the AP, DHCP pool or router.

If this simulator path is unavailable, use this **authored evidence worksheet** instead: an earlier successful connection leased .40.120; after the client profile edit a fresh connection reports key-exchange failure; that old address remains displayed; a wired control client still opens the lab web page; the approved credential comparison confirms the edited value differs. Identify which observation describes the current failure, what the retained address does not prove, and what must be retested after the correction.

:::solution
The client should fail to establish usable protected access with the mismatched key. UI wording and whether an old IP address remains displayed vary. An old lease is not proof of a currently functioning wireless data path. Compare the failed new connection attempt and intended security settings instead of asserting a particular DHCP packet sequence without observing it.
:::

steps.title: — Repair wireless access and save the complete lab
steps.body:
Correct the laptop's profile to `StudyNet2026!`, reconnect and request DHCP if needed. Retest the server, remote PC and name-based page. Confirm PC-A is also using correct DHCP settings. Save `clients-complete.pkt`. Save R1 separately:

```ios R1
R1# copy running-config startup-config
```

Complete the destination prompt with Enter.

:::expected
Both clients have intended addresses and can use the lab services. WRT1's DHCP service remains disabled, its LAN port provides the bridge to SW1, and every introduced fault is repaired.
:::

steps.title: — Inspect the operating systems without creating real faults
steps.body:
Choose one actual OS environment you have. For the other two, interpret this chapter's representative Windows/macOS/Linux outputs and record the commands you would use to obtain the missing route or resolver evidence. Do not install three operating systems to complete this exercise. These are **read-only inspections**: do not release a working lease, alter DNS, disconnect Wi-Fi or disable security on a personal/work machine. Its addresses will not match the simulator unless it is intentionally part of that isolated network. For an unavailable OS, interpret the chapter's representative output and mark direct practice pending.

**Windows:** open Command Prompt and run:

```text
ipconfig /all
route print -4
route print -6
arp -a
netsh wlan show interfaces
netsh wlan show profiles
```

Record the intended adapter, IPv4/IPv6 addresses, prefixes, gateway/route and resolver choices. If a wireless adapter is active, record its displayed SSID, authentication and cipher. To inspect a chosen saved profile without displaying its cleartext password, use `netsh wlan show profile name="PROFILE-NAME"` after replacing the name with one from the list. If location/privacy permission restricts radio fields, note the restriction; an absent field is not proof of a network fault.

**macOS:** in System Settings → Network, inspect the active service → Details → TCP/IP and DNS. In Terminal:

```text
networksetup -listallhardwareports
ifconfig
route -n get default
netstat -rn
scutil --dns
```

Map the active service to its actual interface. For Wi-Fi, Option-click its menu-bar icon and open Wireless Diagnostics. Read current connection/security details available in that release; the analysis does not change settings. Keep generated diagnostic archives private because they contain network details.

**Linux:** use:

```bash
ip -br address
ip route
ip -6 route
ip neigh
```

On NetworkManager systems, add:

```bash
nmcli device status
nmcli device show
nmcli connection show --active
nmcli -f IN-USE,SSID,SECURITY,SIGNAL device wifi list
```

For an active wireless profile, use `nmcli -f 802-11-wireless-security.key-mgmt connection show "PROFILE-NAME"` with its actual profile name. On systemd-resolved systems, inspect `resolvectl status`. Missing NetworkManager or resolved tools can simply mean a different network manager is in use.

:::expected
For the chosen real OS and the other supplied examples, produce a small private worksheet mapping the active adapter to its address/prefix, usable routes, DNS configuration and wireless security evidence. Identify which observations came from saved configuration and which describe the current connection. A VPN-specific resolver or route may explain a path different from the default. Do not record passwords or claim direct practice on operating systems you did not access.

Your completion record must include:
- The intended adapter and actual address/prefix, selected route and resolver for the tested destination.
- A baseline matrix and one observed failure matrix, with fresh tests distinguished from cached/saved information.
- The narrow correction and the repeated failing test plus actual application outcome.
- Current wireless security/data-path evidence, or a clearly labeled unsupported-environment worksheet.
- One actual OS inspection and interpretations for unavailable systems, with direct practice honestly marked pending.

A successful answer explains the evidence; it is not the number of commands typed.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- Initial link failure: check the exact ports, crossover for the direct router-to-PC link, interface shutdown state and switch forwarding.
- DHCP serves .20 or the wrong subnet: repair/remove conflicting simulator pools; reserve .1, .2 and .20 outside .100–.149.
- Local web access works but remote PC fails: that local application test did not exercise routing; inspect the client mask and selected next hop.
- DNS change appears ineffective: query a fresh name and inspect the actual resolver; caches or another adapter may hide the change.
- Wrong mask still reaches a remote endpoint: confirm proxy ARP is disabled in this controlled exercise and inspect actual packet decisions.
- Wireless laptop receives a different subnet: check WRT DHCP is disabled and the switch cable is in a LAN port, not the WAN port.
- Wi-Fi says connected but no lease: inspect current authentication/data-path evidence, WLAN-to-LAN mapping and DHCP exchange; the icon does not identify one unique cause.
lab.challenge:
A new routed application must work from a new wired client. This variation uses a different destination network and two independently testable client/service settings. Keep the recovered baseline and save a copy as `clients-challenge.pkt`.

### Supplied setup and service plan

Add **PC-PT PC-C** to SW1 Fa0/5 using copper straight-through. Add **Server-PT Server-B** directly to R1 Gi0/2 using copper crossover or the auto-connect tool. These named ports exist on the selected 2911/2960 models.

| Device | Intended address | Intended gateway / DNS |
|---|---|---|
| PC-C | 192.168.40.60/24 | GW 192.168.40.1; DNS 192.168.40.20 |
| R1 Gi0/2 | 192.168.60.1/27 | Connected route; no new static route |
| Server-B | 192.168.60.10/27 | GW 192.168.60.1; DNS 192.168.40.20 |

PC-C's .60 address is outside the DHCP pool. Server-B's mask is `255.255.255.224`. Set its static fields from the plan and explicitly turn its **HTTP** service On. Use this supplied router preparation:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
R1(config-if)# description CHALLENGE_WEB_LAN
R1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.60.1 255.255.255.224
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
R1# show ip route connected
```

The service plan says `challenge.example` must resolve to Server-B at `192.168.60.10`. Establish these initial incident settings rather than immediately correcting them:

- On PC-C, enter static `192.168.40.60/24`, gateway `192.168.40.254` and DNS `192.168.40.20`.
- On Server-A's DNS service, add the A record `challenge.example → 192.168.60.30`. Address .60.30 is unused; it is not the broadcast address.
- Keep every other recovered baseline field unchanged.

### Independent investigation

Do not open the solution yet. First use healthy PC-A as a control to verify numeric HTTP at `http://192.168.60.10`. If that control fails, fix the supplied physical/server/router setup before diagnosing PC-C.

From PC-C, record: actual parameters, local `.40.20` reachability, intended gateway `.40.1` reachability, numeric `.60.10` reachability/HTTP, a fresh `challenge.example` query, and the named web result. Choose the next test rather than changing both suspicious fields at once.

Explain why pinging the real gateway can succeed even when the configured default next hop is wrong. Make one demonstrated correction, repeat its numeric/applicable tests, then investigate the remaining named-service failure. Record the actual resolver and answer; a DNS response is not automatically the right answer.

Submit the two causes, the evidence distinguishing them, each narrow repair, and a fresh successful `http://challenge.example` test. Keep the base clients working. If Packet Tracer cannot expose a query field, use Simulation-mode DNS evidence or the supplied initial record and clearly label your worksheet inference.

:::solution
The new /27 is `192.168.60.0/27`: ordinary host range .1–.30, broadcast .31. Server-B .10 and router .1 are valid. PC-C .40.60 is on the existing /24 and outside .100–.149.

The initial evidence should distinguish these outcomes:

| Test from PC-C | Expected result and reason |
|---|---|
| Local Server-A .40.20 | Works on the local link |
| Intended gateway .40.1 | Can work directly; ping does not use the incorrect default next hop |
| Remote .60.10 / numeric HTTP | Fails through unused configured gateway .40.254 |
| Fresh DNS query to .40.20 | Can answer locally, but returns the wrong .60.30 address |
| Named challenge application | Fails; both the wrong next hop and wrong record must be addressed |

First set only PC-C's gateway to `192.168.40.1`, retaining .40.60/24 and DNS .40.20. Check a fresh remote ping and `http://192.168.60.10`. The successful numeric page demonstrates the routed application path. The name can still fail because the record points to unused .60.30.

Next correct only Server-A's `challenge.example` A record to `192.168.60.10`. Query that same resolver again and read the answer. Use `nslookup challenge.example 192.168.40.20` if supported; otherwise inspect a fresh DNS exchange in Simulation mode. An old cached answer is not the new result: refresh the client/browser using supported simulator controls or reopen the client test after the record correction.

Open `http://challenge.example` and verify Server-B's page. Compare with the healthy PC-A numeric control; do not change its working configuration. Record the two repaired values and keep the new topology if desired. Save `clients-challenge-complete.pkt`. Save verified R1 configuration with a separate `copy running-config startup-config` and finish its destination prompt. No router static route, DHCP-pool change or wider client mask was needed.
:::

questions.prompt: What does this Windows adapter output most directly indicate?
options: The output identifies a failed wireless passphrase as the specific cause
The adapter’s DNS lookup failed after a normal office lease was accepted
The adapter is using the intended routed office DHCP configuration
The adapter is using IPv4 link-local fallback, not the intended LAN lease
questions.explanation: The DHCP-enabled autoconfiguration context identifies link-local fallback. It does not establish which DHCP message, server condition or path failed.

whyWrong.0: No current wireless authentication evidence is supplied.
whyWrong.1: DNS query state is not reported; the evidence concerns address acquisition.
whyWrong.2: The autoconfiguration address and absent gateway do not show the intended office lease.

questions.prompt: On a Linux machine using NetworkManager, which two commands can display IPv4 default-gateway information? Choose two.
options: ip route
resolvectl status
ip -br address
ip link
nmcli device show
questions.explanation: The routing table can contain a default via entry, and NetworkManager's device details can include IP4.GATEWAY. These reports serve different views of the active configuration.

whyWrong.1: resolvectl reports resolver information, not default forwarding routes.
whyWrong.2: The brief address view lists addresses/prefixes rather than gateways.
whyWrong.3: ip link reports link attributes, not the IP routing table.

exhibit.title: ip route excerpt
exhibit.text: default via 10.1.20.1 dev enp0s3 proto dhcp src 10.1.20.59 metric 100

questions.prompt: Which interpretation of this Linux default route is supported?
options: The route applies only to destinations inside 10.1.20.0/24
The default next hop is 10.1.20.59 because it follows src
The route proves every interface address was assigned by DHCP
The default next hop is 10.1.20.1, reached through enp0s3
questions.explanation: The next hop follows via; dev identifies the interface. proto dhcp labels this route's origin, while src identifies the preferred source. Other routes must also be considered for a particular destination.

whyWrong.0: default is the fallback route, not a connected /24 route.
whyWrong.1: src names a preferred local source address, not the next hop.
whyWrong.2: A route-origin label does not prove the origin of every address.

questions.prompt: On an isolated Windows lab PC, which sequence deliberately discards the current DHCP lease and requests configuration again?
options: ipconfig /release then ipconfig /renew
route print -4 then arp -a
netsh wlan show profiles then ipconfig /all
ipconfig /displaydns then ipconfig /flushdns
questions.explanation: Release discards DHCP configuration and renew requests configuration. This can interrupt connectivity, so it belongs in the isolated exercise or an approved change; the command alone is not proof of a captured four-message exchange.

whyWrong.1: These are read-only route and neighbor displays.
whyWrong.2: These inspect profiles and configuration rather than discarding a lease.
whyWrong.3: These commands inspect/clear DNS cache rather than releasing an address lease.

questions.prompt: The security mode is already correctly set to WPA2-Personal. Which two values must match the intended WLAN for the normal shared-passphrase connection? Choose two.
options: The intended case-sensitive SSID
The client’s current DHCP hostname
The configured shared passphrase
The AP’s management IPv4 address
The preferred DNS search suffix
questions.explanation: The client must select the intended SSID and use the matching WPA2-Personal credential. Security mode is stipulated correct; these two values address network selection and key agreement.

whyWrong.1: A DHCP hostname does not select the SSID or establish the shared key.
whyWrong.3: The AP management address is not the network name or key used by the client profile.
whyWrong.4: A DNS suffix affects name processing after useful connectivity, not WPA2 key agreement.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes IPv4 link-local addressing?
options: It uses 169.254.0.0/16 for local-link communication rather than routed fallback
It is a private routed prefix that can replace an office address without new routes
It proves a DHCP DISCOVER never left the adapter that displays the address
It supplies an alternate default gateway when a DHCP server does not answer
questions.explanation: IPv4 link-local is link-scoped. OS/profile behavior varies, and other adapters or IPv6 may still provide service; the address alone does not reconstruct the DHCP exchange.

whyWrong.1: This is link-local scope, not an ordinary RFC 1918 routed LAN substitute.
whyWrong.2: Failure can occur after different exchange stages; inspect the actual transaction.
whyWrong.3: Link-local selection does not create a usable routed default gateway.

questions.prompt: Which macOS command reports current DNS resolver configuration, including supplemental domain-specific resolvers?
options: scutil --dns
route -n get default
networksetup -listallhardwareports
ifconfig -a
questions.explanation: scutil --dns reports resolver configuration. Supplemental domain-specific resolvers can affect VPN queries, so do not assume a single displayed nameserver handles every name.

whyWrong.1: This reports a default route, not resolver selection.
whyWrong.2: This maps hardware ports/services to interface names.
whyWrong.3: The interface-address display does not provide the complete resolver configuration.

questions.prompt: A single-homed host has 10.1.20.57/24 and gateway 10.1.20.254. The actual router is 10.1.20.1; .254 is unused. With no alternate routes, what pattern is expected from this gateway error?
options: Numeric off-link traffic works, but local peers require a working gateway
DNS alone fails because the default gateway selects the resolver for each query
Local peer traffic also fails because it must pass through the unused gateway
Local peers can work while destinations requiring the default route fail
questions.explanation: A correct connected-subnet decision permits direct local delivery. Traffic requiring the only default route cannot resolve its unused next hop; this does not identify the state of unrelated services.

whyWrong.0: This reverses local delivery and default-route dependence.
whyWrong.1: The configured DNS resolver and IP next-hop selection serve different functions; off-link numeric traffic is affected too.
whyWrong.2: On-link peer delivery normally uses the local link directly, not the default gateway.

questions.prompt: PC-A is 192.168.40.100/16 on a real /24 LAN. Its gateway is .40.1, proxy ARP is disabled, and remote 192.168.50.10 sits behind another router interface. Which destination does this mask error incorrectly classify as on-link?
questions.explanation: The configured /16 is 192.168.0.0/16, so .50.10 is mistakenly treated as a direct neighbor. The other remote examples remain outside the /16; this says how they are forwarded, not that their entire paths work.

whyWrong.1: 172.16.5.5 is outside the wrong /16 too.
whyWrong.3: The gateway is correctly on-link under both the intended /24 and wrong /16.

exhibit.title: Representative ifconfig en0 extract
exhibit.text:
inet 10.1.20.58 netmask 0xffffff00 broadcast 10.1.20.255
status: active

questions.prompt: What mask and prefix correspond to this macOS netmask?
questions.explanation: 0xffffff00 has six f digits, each contributing four one-bits: 24 one-bits followed by eight zeros. The displayed address and broadcast are consistent with that /24.

whyWrong.0: A /20 mask would be 0xfffff000.
whyWrong.2: A /16 mask would be 0xffff0000.
whyWrong.3: A /32 mask would be 0xffffffff.

questions.prompt: A client can ping its gateway and one remote IPv4 address, but a fresh nslookup query times out. Which client setting is the most relevant next check?
options: The configured default gateway
The configured DNS server
The configured DHCP server identity
The configured subnet mask
questions.explanation: Inspect the DNS server actually queried, then test its service/path and the name. The successful numeric test does not certify all masks, routes or applications; it simply makes DNS-specific evidence the useful next step.

whyWrong.0: The tested numeric route worked; inspect the resolver selected for the failing query before changing that working path.
whyWrong.2: The DHCP server identity can explain where settings originated, but it is not the server that must answer this DNS query.
whyWrong.3: One remote ping does not prove the mask universally correct, but the fresh query failure makes the resolver choice the direct next check.

exhibit.title: Representative client details
exhibit.text:
Wireless state: connected
SSID: CCNA-LAB
Authentication: WPA2-Personal
IPv4: 169.254.201.44/16 (Autoconfiguration)
Default gateway: none

questions.prompt: The laptop reports a connection to the intended SSID but has no usable DHCP lease. Which next investigation is justified?
options: Replace the DNS resolver first so the client can locate an address for itself
Treat the connection icon as sufficient proof and investigate only the DHCP server
Inspect fresh DHCP acquisition and the current protected WLAN-to-LAN path
Request a wider client subnet mask before checking the observed DHCP exchange
questions.explanation: The client lacks the intended lease. Compare current security/data-path evidence with fresh DHCP requests and replies; the icon alone neither proves all WLAN mapping is correct nor identifies a specific failure.

whyWrong.0: Ordinary DHCP address acquisition does not depend on first resolving a name through DNS.
whyWrong.1: The server is one possibility, but current wireless data delivery and VLAN mapping still need evidence.
whyWrong.3: A guessed static mask does not repair acquisition and can conceal the actual fault.

questions.prompt: Which observation most directly supports investigating a WPA2-Personal key mismatch rather than starting with DNS?
options: The client reaches its gateway but a fresh query to the intended resolver times out
A new key-exchange failure appears after the saved profile credential was changed
The client reaches a remote IP while the approved name returns the wrong address
A successful Wi-Fi reconnection is followed by DHCP replies with a wrong gateway
questions.explanation: A fresh key-exchange failure after a credential change supports checking that key and security profile first. Confirm the current event; a generic connection icon is less specific.

whyWrong.0: These observations concern name-resolution service/path after tested connectivity.
whyWrong.2: A wrong DNS answer points toward name data rather than a key-exchange failure.
whyWrong.3: Usable data delivery and a received DHCP reply instead point toward the supplied client parameters.

questions.prompt: These are the complete relevant IPv4 routes. Which gateway is selected for 8.8.8.8?
options: 192.168.1.1 because the first displayed matching route wins before metrics
192.168.1.1 because its interface address has the higher numerical value
Both gateways because every installed default receives a copy of each packet
10.1.20.1 because both relevant matches are /0 and its effective metric is lower
questions.explanation: Both matching routes are defaults. With the stated usable-route conditions, effective metric 25 is preferred to 50; neither connected /24 matches 8.8.8.8.

whyWrong.0: Displayed row order does not override a lower metric for an equal-length match.
whyWrong.1: Interface-address size is not the stated route-selection rule.
whyWrong.2: Different metrics do not create an equal-cost choice, and default routes do not imply duplication of every packet.

questions.prompt: Only the DNS server selection differs from the intended client plan. Server-A has a verified A record for intranet.example → 192.168.50.20. Numeric HTTP works, but a fresh query is sent to unused 192.168.40.99 and times out. Which correction addresses the shown fault?
options: Set the client's default gateway to the unused .40.99 address
Change the client's mask from /24 to /16 for wider local reach
Set the client's DNS server to Server-A at 192.168.40.20
Replace the verified A record with the router's gateway address
questions.explanation: The intended resolver is .40.20, while the failed query targets unused .40.99. Correcting that selection addresses the demonstrated fault; the numeric HTTP result only establishes that tested IP/application path.

whyWrong.0: The unused address is not the intended next hop.
whyWrong.1: A broader mask does not select the proper DNS service and can introduce an on-link error.
whyWrong.3: The record is stipulated correct and should remain pointed at the web server.

questions.prompt: On Windows, `Test-NetConnection 192.168.50.20 -Port 443` reports TCP success. Which conclusion stays within that evidence?
options: The web certificate must be trusted because TCP used the HTTPS port
The IPv6 route must work because the same server supports both address families
The tested TCP connection succeeded; TLS and the application still need verification
The client's DNS configuration is correct because the destination was numeric
questions.explanation: A successful TCP connection tests transport reachability to that address/port. A numeric IPv4 test does not validate DNS, IPv6, TLS certificates or application authorization.

whyWrong.0: Certificate verification occurs in TLS, after the underlying TCP connection.
whyWrong.1: IPv4 success is not proof of IPv6 reachability.
whyWrong.3: A numeric target does not require name resolution for that target.

exhibit.title: Windows relevant IPv4 routes — effective metrics

questions.prompt: Both interfaces and next hops are usable. Which route carries a packet to 10.70.8.25?
options: The Wi-Fi default because private destinations must use the wireless adapter
Both default routes because the /24 VPN route has a metric above 100
The Ethernet default because its metric is smaller than the VPN metric
The /24 VPN route despite its larger metric, because it is the longest match
questions.explanation: The /24 matches 10.70.8.25 more specifically than either /0. Metrics compare matching routes of equal prefix length; they do not let a /0 defeat this /24.

whyWrong.0: Private addressing does not prescribe a physical adapter.
whyWrong.1: A metric above 100 does not make a valid /24 ineligible.
whyWrong.2: The lower metric on a less-specific route does not override longest-prefix matching.

exhibit.title: Client, query and service plan
exhibit.text:
Client: 192.168.40.120/24, GW 192.168.40.1, DNS 192.168.40.20
Plan: intranet.example must point to 192.168.50.20
Fresh explicit query to 192.168.40.20: intranet.example A 192.168.50.99
HTTP to numeric 192.168.50.20 succeeds; .50.99 is unused.

questions.prompt: What should be corrected first based on this supplied plan and fresh answer?
options: The intranet.example record on the intended resolver, then retest the application
The client’s resolver choice, because a responding server cannot have bad data
The client’s subnet mask, because a DNS answer changes the local subnet
The default gateway, because the DNS server returned a reachable address
questions.explanation: The query reaches the intended resolver, but its fresh answer disagrees with the verified service plan. Correct the relevant record and verify a new response, then test the named service.

whyWrong.1: The resolver selection is correct, but a correctly selected server can hold an incorrect record.
whyWrong.2: DNS answer data does not change the adapter prefix.
whyWrong.3: No next-hop mismatch is shown; the response identifies wrong name data.

exhibit.title: Authored dual-stack tests
exhibit.text:
portal.example: A 192.0.2.40; AAAA 2001:db8:40::40
TCP 443 to 192.0.2.40: succeeds
TCP 443 to 2001:db8:40::40: times out
Client IPv6 routes have not yet been inspected.

questions.prompt: Which two conclusions follow without assuming one address family proves the other? Choose two.
options: The failed IPv6 test needs separate IPv6 route and path investigation
The IPv4 test demonstrates TCP reachability to its stated IPv4 endpoint
The IPv4 success proves the server’s AAAA answer is usable from this client
The failed IPv6 test proves the client’s IPv4 default gateway is wrong
Removing the AAAA record is justified before checking the IPv6 path
questions.explanation: The two tests use different destination addresses and address families. A succeeded IPv4 TCP connection does not validate IPv6 routing, and an IPv6 timeout alone does not determine the faulty component.

whyWrong.2: The IPv4 test did not exercise the AAAA destination or its route.
whyWrong.3: The successful IPv4 test contradicts treating the IPv6 result as proof of an IPv4 next-hop error.
whyWrong.4: Removing valid service data is not justified by a timeout with the path still unexamined.

questions.prompt: A client cannot ping an approved server, but a fresh TCP 443 connection and the required HTTPS page both work from that same client. What is justified?
options: The application has recovered for that tested path; ICMP behavior can be investigated separately
The web response must be cached because ICMP is required before TCP can connect
The unsuccessful ping proves the client must still have an unusable default route
The working HTTPS result proves all traffic and all other clients are unaffected
questions.explanation: The fresh TCP and application results demonstrate the required service path. Ping is a different exchange; ICMP filtering or response policy may explain its result, but that cause still needs evidence.

whyWrong.1: TCP and HTTPS do not require a successful ICMP echo exchange first.
whyWrong.2: Fresh successful off-link application traffic, where applicable, cannot be dismissed solely because ICMP times out.
whyWrong.3: One client, destination and service test does not establish universal health.

exhibit.title: Windows DHCP and adapter evidence
exhibit.text:
Plan: automatic address and DNS, intended resolver 192.168.40.20
Fresh DHCP ACK: address .40.120/24, router .40.1, DNS .40.20
Adapter DNS setting: manually selected 192.168.40.99
Fresh query is sent to .40.99; .99 is unused.
Renewing the lease repeats the same ACK but leaves the manual DNS choice.

questions.prompt: Which correction and retest follow from all three observations?
options: Repair the DHCP pool’s DNS option because the captured ACK proves it is wrong
Return this client’s resolver selection to the approved automatic setting, then query afresh
Restart the DHCP server because every displayed setting must have come from its ACK
Remove the valid client lease because manual DNS requires a static IPv4 address
questions.explanation: The captured lease supplies the intended resolver, but the adapter’s manual DNS override wins for actual queries. Correct that override according to the plan, inspect the active result and issue a fresh name query before the application test.

whyWrong.0: The ACK carries the intended DNS option; the client override accounts for the mismatch.
whyWrong.2: DHCP address configuration can coexist with manually selected DNS.
whyWrong.3: A manual DNS choice can coexist with a DHCP address; discarding that valid lease is not the demonstrated repair.

exhibit.title: Authored client incident timeline
exhibit.text:
09:00 Laptop joined CCNA-LAB and obtained 192.168.40.120/24.
09:10 Saved WPA2-Personal passphrase was edited; laptop disconnected.
09:11 New connection attempt: key exchange failed; old IPv4 address still displayed.
09:12 Wired control PC reaches the gateway and lab web service.

questions.prompt: Which evidence should drive the next correction?
options: The profile change and fresh key failure support checking the intended WLAN credential
The wired control client proves every wireless exchange is also functioning
The old gateway value proves R1 has lost its currently working interface address
The retained address proves Wi-Fi data works; investigate the DNS server first
questions.explanation: The retained address is older than the failed new connection. The new key-exchange evidence plus the profile change focus the next check on matching the approved credential and security mode; the wired result is a control for the service, not proof of wireless access.

whyWrong.1: A wired path does not exercise the wireless security exchange.
whyWrong.2: A previously valid stored gateway does not demonstrate a router interface failure.
whyWrong.3: A retained lease is not proof of current protected data delivery.

exhibit.title: Authored macOS investigation
exhibit.text:
Active en0 address and intended default route are correct.
Resolver configuration: corp.example uses VPN DNS 10.8.0.53.
Explicit query: host.corp.example at LAN DNS 192.168.40.20 returns expected 10.70.8.25.
Observed fresh application lookup instead goes to 10.8.0.53 and returns NXDOMAIN.
The VPN is required for approved access to this internal domain.

questions.prompt: Which next investigation explains the difference without changing the working adapter configuration?
options: Replace the active address because a direct DNS response proves duplicate addressing
Clear only the Ethernet ARP entry, because it controls domain-specific resolver choice
Inspect the VPN resolver’s answer and approved split-DNS policy for this domain
Remove the default gateway because the VPN resolver is an IPv4 destination
questions.explanation: The application’s fresh request uses the domain-specific VPN resolver, while the successful manual test explicitly queried another server. Compare the actual selected resolver’s answer with the intended split-DNS policy; the manual result did not test the failing path.

whyWrong.0: The responses identify different resolver paths, not duplicate IP use.
whyWrong.1: ARP mappings do not choose domain-specific DNS resolvers.
whyWrong.3: Removing forwarding configuration does not repair inconsistent DNS data.

exhibit.title: Client configuration and fresh observations
exhibit.text:
Plan: 192.168.40.120/24; gateway .40.1; DNS .40.20
Actual: 192.168.40.120/16; gateway .40.1; DNS .40.99
Local HTTP at .40.20 succeeds.
Numeric test to .50.10: client ARPs directly for .50.10, no reply; proxy ARP is disabled.
Fresh DNS query: sent to unused .40.99, no reply.

questions.prompt: Which explanation accounts for both failed tests while preserving the demonstrated working local service?
options: A DNS failure alone changes the next hop selected for the numeric remote test
Two client fields are wrong: the mask changes next-hop choice and the resolver points elsewhere
The local web server must be down because the remote PC cannot be reached
A wrong default gateway alone explains both numeric routing and a local DNS query
questions.explanation: The intended /24 differs from the configured /16: the client attempts direct ARP for the remote PC. Its query also targets unused .99 rather than the local .20 resolver. These are distinct client faults; repair one and retest its path before repairing the other.

whyWrong.0: The remote test is numeric; DNS does not control the mask-based on-link decision.
whyWrong.2: The numeric local HTTP success demonstrates that service worked for this test.
whyWrong.3: The gateway value matches the plan, and a local resolver query would not require it under either shown mask.

cards.front: A disciplined client troubleshooting sequence?
cards.back: Identify the adapter/address family; compare address/prefix/routes/DNS/security; test local, routed, DNS and application paths; repair one demonstrated fault and repeat its test.

cards.front: Windows command for detailed adapter IP, DHCP and DNS settings?
cards.back: `ipconfig /all`. Identify the intended adapter; DHCP-enabled addressing does not prove every DNS value came from DHCP.

cards.front: Linux command for compact addresses and prefixes?
cards.back: `ip -br address`. Use full address output and network-manager/lease information when investigating acquisition; one route label does not prove every address came from DHCP.

cards.front: macOS command for the default IPv4 route?
cards.back: `route -n get default`; `netstat -rn` gives broader route information. Check the actual interface and any more specific route for the destination.

cards.front: In `default via 10.1.20.1 ... src 10.1.20.59`, which is the gateway?
cards.back: The next hop is 10.1.20.1 after `via`. `src` is the preferred local source address. Inspect other routes before applying the default to a destination.

cards.front: How are competing Windows routes selected?
cards.back: Inspect `route print -4` or `-6`. Longest matching prefix comes first; for matching routes of equal prefix length, the lower effective metric is preferred.

cards.front: What does scutil --dns add beyond a single macOS service’s settings?
cards.back: It reports current resolver configuration, including supplemental/domain-specific resolvers. Check which resolver actually handles the failing name.

cards.front: Linux: why might resolv.conf show only 127.0.0.53?
cards.back: It can point to systemd-resolved's local DNS stub. Inspect `resolvectl status` for per-link upstream information, or the actual manager's tools such as `nmcli device show`.

cards.front: Must Linux DHCP failure look the same on every distribution?
cards.back: No. Manager/profile settings can leave no usable IPv4 address, retain other configuration, or provide link-local fallback. Inspect actual configuration and manager evidence.

cards.front: What does DHCP-enabled Windows autoconfiguration suggest?
cards.back: An Autoconfiguration IPv4 Address in 169.254/16 indicates link-local fallback rather than a usable intended lease. It does not identify the exact failed DHCP stage or device.

cards.front: Does ipconfig /flushdns renew a Windows DHCP lease?
cards.back: No. It clears the DNS resolver cache. Lease renewal is a different operation; releasing a working lease can interrupt connectivity.

cards.front: Does a gateway entry in the ARP cache prove the current path works?
cards.back: No. `arp -a` shows a stored mapping that may be stale/static/incorrect. Combine it with fresh traffic and link/route evidence.

cards.front: Expected effect of an unused default gateway on a simple single-homed LAN?
cards.back: Local peers can remain reachable while traffic needing the default route fails. This assumes no alternate routes; verify the configured next hop and neighbor resolution.

cards.front: How can a mask that is too wide break selected destinations?
cards.back: The client may consider a remote destination on-link and try direct ARP instead of its gateway. Proxy ARP can conceal this under some conditions; compute the actual prefix decision.

cards.front: Numeric access works but a fresh name lookup times out: next check?
cards.back: Read the actual resolver choice and query result, then test its service/path and the record. Numeric success does not prove that every mask, route or application is correct.

cards.front: The intended DNS resolver answers with an address that disagrees with the service plan. What comes next?
cards.back: Check the queried name/type and correct the relevant record or approved DNS view. Verify a fresh answer, then the actual application.

cards.front: Does successful numeric IPv4 access verify an IPv6 path to the same named service?
cards.back: No. Identify the address family and destination actually tested, then inspect and test the other family separately.

cards.front: Which WLAN profile values should you compare with the intended network?
cards.back: The intended case-sensitive SSID, security/authentication mode and required credential. A saved profile does not prove that the current connection uses it.

cards.front: Why can WPA2 association exist before a wrong-key failure?
cards.back: Initial 802.11 association can precede the four-way key handshake. Failed key agreement prevents usable protected data; OS connection/error displays vary.

cards.front: Connected Wi-Fi plus no usable DHCP lease: what should be checked?
cards.back: The current wireless/security state, intended WLAN-to-LAN/VLAN path, and DHCP request/reply evidence. A connection icon alone does not isolate a unique cause.

cards.front: Why is a retained IPv4 address weak proof of a new Wi-Fi connection?
cards.back: It can belong to an earlier lease. Check the current connection/security event and fresh protected data traffic before treating the address as usable.

commands.task: Display Windows adapter IP settings, DHCP details and DNS configuration.
commands.note: Read the intended adapter; disconnected unused adapters need not be the active fault.

commands.task: On an isolated Windows DHCP lab PC, request renewal on the adapter named Ethernet.
commands.note: Renewal may change configuration. Do not release a working remote-session adapter without an intended maintenance action.

commands.task: Display the Windows IPv4 routing table explicitly.
commands.note: Compare longest matching prefixes before metrics; use -6 separately for IPv6.

commands.task: Display current Windows wireless interface connection details.
commands.note: SSID/security fields may be restricted by permissions or OS release. A connected indication does not validate the whole data path.

commands.task: On macOS, display the default IPv4 route and its interface.
commands.note: Use netstat -rn separately for the broader route table.

commands.task: On macOS, report current DNS resolvers including supplemental domain-specific configuration.
commands.note: A single service's manually configured DNS list is not an equivalent complete resolver view.

commands.task: On Linux, show each interface and its addresses in the brief form.
commands.note: Full ip address output is useful too, but it is not the brief format requested.

commands.task: On Linux, show the IPv4 routing table.
commands.note: The default via entry is a fallback; more specific destination routes take precedence.

commands.task: On a Linux machine using systemd-resolved, display resolver status.
commands.note: The local stub address alone is not the upstream server configuration.

commands.task: On NetworkManager Linux, show detailed current device configuration including IP gateway and DNS information.
commands.note: This reads device information; device reapply is not a universal DHCP renewal operation.

commands.task: On Windows, query fresh.example directly at the intended DNS server 192.168.40.20, independent of the configured default resolver choice.
commands.note: Read the server used and its actual answer or error. This explicit query does not prove an application uses the same resolver.

commands.task: In Windows PowerShell, test a TCP connection to the numeric server 192.168.50.20 on port 443.
commands.note: TCP success does not verify DNS, TLS certificates or the application response. Retest the actual service separately.

tickets.title: Local files work, but remote services time out
tickets.scenario: A single-homed sales PC has no VPN or alternate routes. The verified network plan assigns 10.1.20.57/24 to this PC and 10.1.20.1 to its router. Address 10.1.20.254 is unused. A local file server at .20 responds. Other clients can reach the approved remote test server at 10.1.50.20. These are representative diagnostic observations.

exhibits.title: PC configuration
exhibits.text:
DHCP Enabled: No
IPv4 Address: 10.1.20.57
Subnet Mask: 255.255.255.0
Default Gateway: 10.1.20.254
DNS Server: 10.1.10.5

exhibits.title: Packet/route worksheet
exhibits.text:
Only default route: 0.0.0.0/0 via 10.1.20.254
Remote numeric test: 10.1.50.20
Observed ARP: Who has 10.1.20.254? Tell 10.1.20.57
No reply to these ARP requests is observed.

tickets.question: Which configuration fault is directly supported?
options: A local DNS record is missing, so numeric off-link traffic has no destination
The default route selects unused .254 instead of the intended router .1
The client’s correct /24 forces .1 outside its directly connected network
The remote application listener is down, causing ARP for the wrong local next hop
tickets.explanation: The plan, default route and fresh ARP requests agree: the client attempts to resolve the wrong next hop. The numeric test does not require DNS. A remote listener failure would not explain selecting an unused local gateway, and the shown /24 includes .1.
tickets.fix:
On this approved isolated/static client, open its adapter's IPv4 settings and retain 10.1.20.57 with mask 255.255.255.0 and DNS 10.1.10.5; correct only the default gateway to 10.1.20.1. Then test:

```text
ping 10.1.20.1
arp -a
ping 10.1.50.20
```
Inspect the fresh neighbor/route evidence and then test the intended DNS/application operation. A ping timeout alone would not have proven this cause; the configuration plan and ARP evidence support it.

tickets.title: The intranet name fails while numeric web access works
tickets.scenario: A single-homed client cannot open intranet.example. The approved plan names Server-A at 192.168.40.20 as its DNS resolver and 192.168.50.20 as the intranet server. There is no VPN, hosts-file override, browser DNS override or proxy in this isolated case. The observations below are authored and fresh.

exhibits.title: Client and numeric path
exhibits.text:
Client: 192.168.40.120/24, gateway 192.168.40.1, DNS 192.168.40.20
Local peer: replies
Gateway: replies
HTTP to 192.168.50.20: expected intranet page

exhibits.title: Fresh query and server-side check
exhibits.text:
Query: intranet.example A, explicitly sent to 192.168.40.20
Answer: 192.168.50.99
DNS administrator confirms the current A record is .50.99; this address is unused.
Approved service address remains 192.168.50.20.

tickets.question: Which narrow correction is supported by the combined evidence?
options: Select a public DNS resolver so the internal service name uses another namespace
Correct the client’s gateway even though the tested routed HTTP service works
Change the local DNS server’s intranet A record to the approved .50.20 address
Renew the client’s address because the DNS response proves a failed lease
tickets.explanation: The selected resolver matches the plan and responds, but its current record disagrees with the approved working service address. The numeric HTTP test supplies a control for the application path. Public DNS, gateway changes and DHCP renewal do not correct the demonstrated record.
tickets.fix: In the isolated DNS service or through its authorized administrator, correct only intranet.example’s A record to 192.168.50.20. Query the same resolver again and confirm the new answer. If a client/application still uses cached data, use its supported refresh procedure or wait for expiration rather than changing routes. Then reopen the named intranet page and compare it with the known numeric service response. Keep the correct address, prefix, gateway and resolver selection.

tickets.title: An old wireless address survives a failed new connection
tickets.scenario: A laptop previously worked on the isolated WPA2-Personal WLAN CCNA-LAB. Someone edited its saved passphrase and disconnected it. The intended AP profile and DHCP service have not changed. The current events below matter more than the old address still displayed by the client.

exhibits.title: Timeline and current status
exhibits.text:
10:00 successful protected connection; DHCP address 192.168.40.120/24
10:10 saved profile passphrase edited, then disconnected
10:11 fresh attempt to CCNA-LAB fails key exchange
10:12 old address .40.120 remains displayed; fresh gateway/application traffic fails

exhibits.title: Control and configuration check
exhibits.text:
Wired control PC reaches the same DNS and web service.
AP security: WPA2-Personal/AES; intended SSID CCNA-LAB.
Approved credential comparison: the laptop’s edited passphrase differs.
No password values are included in this record.

tickets.question: Which correction addresses the demonstrated cause?
options: Restore the approved client credential, reconnect, then verify fresh network and application traffic
Keep the changed credential and widen the client prefix so its old lease remains on-link
Change the DHCP server’s default gateway because the laptop retains a valid-looking address
Replace the DNS A record because wired access excludes any wireless security failure
tickets.explanation: The profile change, current key-exchange failure and approved credential mismatch identify the client security fault. A retained lease and a working wired control do not prove the current WLAN data path works.
tickets.fix: On this isolated laptop, restore the approved WPA2-Personal profile credential without changing the AP or DHCP pool. Reconnect to the intended SSID and check the current security/connection state. If necessary, request a lease with the client’s supported procedure; inspect the actual address/prefix/gateway/DNS. Repeat the previously failing gateway and routed numeric tests, issue a fresh name query and open the required application. Record current observations, not just the old displayed address.

chapters.title: Troubleshooting toolkit
chapters.subtitle: Use tests, tables, logs, and captures to distinguish evidence from a diagnosis.

sources.title: Cisco: Extended ping and extended traceroute
Cisco: IOS XE system message logging

chapters.summary: Investigate a two-way network path, compare ordinary and sourced tests, interpret interface and capture evidence, and verify a repair from the affected client.

sections.title: Define the problem and preserve evidence
sections.body:
:::facts
- A successful ping demonstrates a completed ICMP exchange for that source, destination, size, and time. It does not test every application.
- IOS `!` means an echo reply arrived; `.` means the wait expired; `U` reports destination-unreachable evidence. Read the response source and details before choosing a cause.
- A router-originated test can use a different source and policy path from a client's traffic.
- A traceroute `*` means no usable response arrived for that probe within the wait; it does not locate a definite forwarding failure.
- Save current counters, relevant configuration, logs, and timestamps before clearing or changing them.
:::

**Troubleshooting** is the process of testing explanations against evidence until you can restore and verify the intended service. Start by defining the symptom precisely. “The network is down” might mean one name fails, one application port is closed, a client has no address, or an entire building has lost power. Ask which users, addresses, protocols, and times are affected, what still works, and what changed. An observed change is a useful lead, not proof of responsibility.

Write down a baseline and a **hypothesis**: a proposed cause that a test could support or disprove. For example, “PC-A is in the wrong access VLAN” predicts that its learned MAC will appear in an unexpected VLAN and that the gateway will not receive its local broadcasts. “R2 lacks a return route” predicts different results when R1 uses its transit address versus its LAN address as the source.

Use a repeatable sequence: define the problem, gather evidence, choose a hypothesis, make a focused test, apply a justified correction, verify service, and document the outcome. There is no mandatory exam ritual with one uniquely correct number of steps. Avoid several simultaneous changes: if you change an address, a route, and a VLAN together, a successful retest will not tell you which was wrong.

Keep original evidence in your notes. Record the device, command, source/destination, time, and whether the clock is trustworthy. Capture sensitive configuration only in an appropriate private location. Restarting a device can erase volatile evidence; shutting an interface does not inherently clear every counter or its logging buffer. Check what a proposed action actually changes.

sections.title: Choose the next test
sections.body:
A **bottom-up** approach starts with power, media, and interface state. **Top-down** starts with the application. **Divide-and-conquer** chooses a useful middle test, such as an IP-address ping, and uses the result to narrow the next investigation. **Follow-the-path** checks forwarding and return delivery across the actual topology. Comparing an affected host with a working peer is useful when their intended policies match.

| Evidence wanted | Useful check | What it does not establish |
|---|---|---|
| Client configuration | Windows `ipconfig /all`; the appropriate macOS/Linux address and route displays | Whether an assigned gateway is reachable |
| Physical and link state | `show ip interface brief`, `show interfaces`, switch `show interfaces status` | Correct VLAN, subnet, or application policy |
| Layer 2 membership | VLAN, trunk, STP, and MAC-table displays | Correct host IP configuration |
| Forwarding decision | Route lookup for the destination, then the return destination | Whether every forwarding policy permits the flow |
| Application dependency | Exact-name DNS query, then the intended service test | Health of unrelated names or services |

A useful test answers a specific question. If an IP ping works but a browser fails, inspect the name, returned address, transport connection, and service. If a gateway ping fails, also check whether that gateway permits ICMP: a router can forward client traffic while declining to answer its own echo requests. Keep packet forwarding and responses generated by the device separate.

```diagram
{"type":"sequence","title":"Request and reply need separate paths","caption":"These are logical endpoints; each direction must have usable forwarding and permitted traffic.","actors":["PC-A 10.0.10.50","R1","R2","SRV 10.0.20.10"],"steps":[{"from":0,"to":1,"label":"Request to remote server","accent":true},{"from":1,"to":2,"label":"Route toward 10.0.20.0/24"},{"from":2,"to":3,"label":"Deliver on server LAN"},{"from":3,"to":2,"label":"Reply to 10.0.10.50","accent":true},{"from":2,"to":1,"label":"Need route toward 10.0.10.0/24"},{"from":1,"to":0,"label":"Deliver reply to client"}]}
```

sections.title: Ping and extended ping
sections.body:
For IPv4, ICMP echo request is type **8**, echo reply type **0**. The referenced IOS basic ping defaults to **five 100-byte datagrams** with a **two-second wait**; read the actual command output because tools and options differ. Windows `ping` normally sends four requests with 32 bytes of ICMP data. IOS datagram size and a host tool's payload-size argument are different scopes: an ordinary IPv4 packet adds 20 bytes of IP header and 8 bytes of ICMP header to an echo payload.

This is representative output, not a recorded run:

```output R1# ping 10.0.20.10
Sending 5, 100-byte ICMP Echos to 10.0.20.10, timeout is 2 seconds:
.!!!!  ← one reply was not received within its wait; four were
Success rate is 80 percent (4/5)
```

An initial delay can occur during address resolution, but the period alone does not prove ARP caused it. Repeat the test and inspect the relevant ARP entry or capture. Persistent loss needs investigation even if small pings sometimes succeed. A `U` identifies an unreachable response rather than an echo reply. Its ICMP code can distinguish a reported network/host delivery problem, port unreachable, fragmentation needed, or administrative prohibition; those are reports to investigate, not a substitute for configuration evidence.

**Extended ping** lets you choose a source address owned by the router. Suppose R1's transit address is `10.0.99.1`, its client LAN address is `10.0.10.1`, and the remote server is `10.0.20.10`. The ordinary IOS test normally uses the outgoing interface address. A sourced test makes the reply destination different:

```ios
R1# ping 10.0.20.10 source 10.0.99.1
R1# ping 10.0.20.10 source 10.0.10.1
```

If only the first succeeds, inspect return routing and source-dependent policy. You have narrowed the difference; you have not yet proved a missing route. The sourced request is still router-originated and does not exercise the PC's access port or every ingress policy applied to the PC. Confirm the diagnosis with routes, captures, and a final client test.

On an image without the one-line source syntax, enter `ping` at privileged EXEC, supply the target, choose `y` for extended commands, and enter the source when prompted. Retain defaults for unrelated fields. Increasing repeat count samples more exchanges; it does not guarantee that an intermittent fault will appear. Use bounded tests.

**MTU** testing compares sizes while holding other variables steady. In IPv4, setting **DF**, Don't Fragment, prevents routers from fragmenting that packet. A received fragmentation-needed message is positive evidence of a size constraint; large-probe silence alone could also be filtering or loss. On supporting IOS, `ping 10.0.20.10 repeat 5 size 1500 df-bit` requests a 1500-byte IP datagram. Windows `ping -n 4 -l 1472 -f 10.0.20.10` requests 1472 data bytes, making 1500 with ordinary headers. Do not transfer these IPv4 arithmetic rules blindly to IPv6.

sections.title: Interpret traceroute
sections.body:
Traceroute sends probes with increasing **TTL**. A transit router that expires an IPv4 TTL can return ICMP **time exceeded**, type **11**, code **0**. Conventional IOS traceroute uses UDP probes toward high destination ports beginning at **33434**; reaching a closed destination port normally yields ICMP destination unreachable, type **3**, code **3**. Windows `tracert` uses echo requests and expects an echo reply from the destination. Common Linux traceroute implementations support UDP, ICMP, and TCP methods; check the installed tool and selected options.

The responding address identifies the source of an ICMP response; it is not guaranteed to be the interface that received your probe. Each reported time is a round trip for that probe. It includes processing and the reply path, which can differ from the outward path. Different probes can also follow different equal-cost routes.

```output Representative trace toward 203.0.113.10
1  10.0.99.2      1 ms  1 ms  2 ms
2  * * *  ← no usable replies for these probes
3  203.0.113.10   4 ms  4 ms  5 ms  ← later probes received destination replies
```

The middle stars do not prove a broken link. Filtering, response rate limits, return-path behavior, and load sharing can affect what appears. Nor do the later replies certify application performance. If all later hops are silent, inspect the last known path and both directions, but do not label that last responding device as the culprit without further evidence. Compare the trace's actual source and probe protocol with the affected application.

:::trap A received TTL is not a hop count
A reply with TTL 126 has an unknown initial TTL unless you have independent evidence of the sender's setting. You cannot infer “two routers” merely by assuming it started at 128. Even a known difference describes that packet's return path, not necessarily the request path.
:::

sections.title: Interfaces, counters, MAC and ARP tables
sections.body:
Read interface state before interpreting counters. On routed Ethernet, `administratively down` identifies the local administrative shutdown state; `down/down` directs attention toward link and peer availability. `up/up` confirms those operational states but does not certify configuration or service. `up/down` requires interface-type-specific investigation rather than one universal explanation. On switches, `err-disabled` calls for the recorded protection/error cause; `inactive` can indicate an unavailable access VLAN. Consult the VLAN state and intended design before enabling or moving a port.

Compare counters over a known interval. If CRC increases from 120 to 145 during one minute, **25 new errors** occurred; 145 old errors over months is different evidence. CRC/FCS errors indicate received corruption, not its unique cause. Inspect cables, optics where applicable, both endpoints, and negotiated settings. On a 100-Mb/s link, displayed half duplex at one end and full at the other directly establishes a duplex mismatch. Late collisions support that diagnosis on the half-duplex side but can have other causes. A few clean input counters do not certify the cable.

Runts and giants refer to sizes outside what the interface accepts; exact giant thresholds and tagged-frame counting depend on platform and configuration. Output drops indicate discarded outgoing traffic, often queue pressure; compare traffic and queue evidence. Do not diagnose every drop as a bad cable. Correct the demonstrated cause, then compare fresh counter increments. Preserve the original snapshot before an approved `clear counters`.

The **MAC address table** maps a VLAN/MAC to a learned switch port. The **ARP table** maps an IPv4 neighbor to a link-layer address. They answer different questions. A learned MAC proves source frames were observed, not that the host has the right IP address. A missing entry can reflect aging, a reset, filtering, or lack of recent relevant traffic. Use the configured aging policy rather than memorizing one global timer. An incomplete ARP entry means resolution is not complete at this observation; it does not prove the neighbor never replied in the past.

sections.title: Logs and device operations
sections.body:
Use `show logging` to inspect enabled destinations, thresholds, and buffered events. A message commonly contains `%FACILITY-SEVERITY-MNEMONIC: text`. Lower severity numbers are more severe: **0 emergency, 1 alert, 2 critical, 3 error, 4 warning, 5 notification, 6 informational, 7 debugging**. A threshold of warnings selects levels 0–4 for that destination; selection does not prove delivery to the remote collector.

```output Representative relevant log lines
Sep 20 10:15:01: %LINK-3-UPDOWN: Interface GigabitEthernet0/1, changed state to down  ← link event, severity 3
Sep 20 10:15:02: %LINEPROTO-5-UPDOWN: Line protocol on Interface GigabitEthernet0/1, changed state to down  ← separate severity-5 event
```

A log can correlate a symptom with an event, but a down message does not uniquely identify a cable pull. Check both ends and current configuration. A timestamp with `*` on documented IOS displays indicates an unauthoritative clock; it does not establish one specific missing NTP command. Compare synchronization and clock adjustments before ordering events across devices.

`show version` helps identify software, uptime, and reported reload information. CPU and memory displays help assess device load; compare a sustained trend with a baseline instead of treating one busy instant as the cause. Exact environmental commands depend on the model. A historical CDP neighbor may remain until aging, and a reboot can remove evidence.

For a controlled lab, configure a bounded log buffer with `logging buffered 16384 informational`. `terminal monitor` requests eligible log/debug output in the current remote terminal; logging destination settings still matter. Debugging can affect device resources and expose sensitive details. Use a focused supported debug only when needed, then stop it with `undebug all`. Capture existing evidence before clearing logs.

sections.title: Reading packet captures
sections.body:
A **packet capture** records traffic visible at its collection point. First identify the interface, direction, filter, time range, and whether packets were dropped by the capture mechanism. Absence from one capture is not proof of absence everywhere. Packet Tracer Simulation mode displays simulated PDUs; a real capture may come from a switch mirror port or a router capture facility. Their setup syntax is platform-specific and is not the core recall task here.

For ARP, ask which next-hop IP is being resolved and whether its request and reply are visible. For a remote destination, a host normally resolves its gateway, not the remote server. For DHCP, follow the transaction between the client subnet, relay, and server; a missing Offer narrows the failed stage but does not uniquely prove exhaustion. For DNS, a received NXDOMAIN is a negative name result; SERVFAIL reports inability to complete resolution. A timeout contains no such answer. A completed NODATA result lacks the requested type. Consult Chapter 25 for aliases, caching, and authoritative dependencies.

For TCP, distinguish a successful handshake, a reset, and unanswered requests. SYN/SYN-ACK/ACK establishes the connection; it does not prove HTTP or another application subsequently succeeds. A matching RST reports an active rejection/reset, possibly generated by the endpoint or an intermediary. Use a server-side capture and service status before asserting which device generated it. Repeated SYNs without replies leave both forward and return delivery uncertain.

Wireshark's retransmission and duplicate-ACK labels are analysis based on captured sequence history. Loss is a common explanation, but reordering, incomplete captures, and duplicated capture paths can affect labels. Compare both directions and the same flow. Avoid turning a label into an unsupported accusation against one link.

sections.title: Work through a complete diagnosis
sections.body:
PC-A can ping `10.0.10.1` but cannot reach server `10.0.20.10`. R1's transit-source test succeeds; its `10.0.10.1` source test fails. First record those different sources. Then inspect R2's route lookup for `10.0.10.1` and `10.0.10.50`, its default route, and any more-specific entry.

Suppose R2 has only connected `10.0.99.0/30` and `10.0.20.0/24` routes, no default, and no policy routing. Now the route evidence establishes the missing return path. R1's successful ordinary ping was consistent with R2's connected transit route. Restore the intended route on R2:

```ios
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# ip route 10.0.10.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.99.1
R2(config)# end
R2# show ip route 10.0.10.50
```

Repeat the sourced test, then test from PC-A by address, exact name, and actual application. If the name returns a wrong address, that is an additional problem; a successful route repair should not hide it. Record the missing route, the evidence, the command applied, and the client verification. Save only the verified intended configuration.

sections.title: Exam focus
sections.body:
- Match a test to the question it can answer; do not certify every layer from one successful ping.
- Compare source addresses and return destinations when a router works but its clients fail.
- Read ping/traceroute responses as evidence with scope and limitations.
- Combine interface state, current configuration, counter changes, MAC/ARP entries, and relevant logs.
- Interpret capture flows and distinguish a received error from silence.
- Verify the repaired application from the affected client and retain useful notes.

lab.title: Diagnose four faults on a two-router path
lab.intro:
Practice revised September 2026. If you completed an earlier version, repeat the revised exercise and update its checkmarks.

Build a working network, collect its baseline, and break one feature at a time. For each fault, record the symptom, evidence, proposed cause, repair, and client retest. All outputs described below are expected or representative teaching evidence; this lab has not been manually executed in Packet Tracer or CML. Simulator support and response wording vary.

The configuration blocks are supplied preparation. Your assessed work is choosing useful observations, separating facts from remaining explanations, and proving recovery from PC-A. Use one row per test: source, destination/name, protocol, prediction, observed result, and what that result still leaves uncertain. A predicted result is not an observation; mark any unsupported capture or command as a worksheet instead.
lab.topology:
```diagram
{"type":"topology","title":"Two LANs with a routed transit","caption":"The server and client each need their local gateway; R2 also needs a route back to the client LAN.","nodes":[{"id":"PC","kind":"pc","label":"PC-A","sub":"10.0.10.50/24","x":1,"y":1},{"id":"S1","kind":"switch","label":"SW1","sub":"VLAN 10","x":4,"y":1},{"id":"R1","kind":"router","label":"R1","x":8,"y":1},{"id":"R2","kind":"router","label":"R2","x":8,"y":5},{"id":"S2","kind":"switch","label":"SW2","sub":"VLAN 20","x":4,"y":5},{"id":"SRV","kind":"server","label":"SRV","sub":"10.0.20.10/24","x":1,"y":5}],"links":[{"from":"PC","to":"S1","toLabel":"Fa0/1"},{"from":"S1","to":"R1","fromLabel":"Fa0/24","toLabel":"Gi0/0"},{"from":"R1","to":"R2","fromLabel":"Gi0/1","toLabel":"Gi0/1","label":"10.0.99.0/30","accent":true},{"from":"R2","to":"S2","fromLabel":"Gi0/0","toLabel":"Fa0/24"},{"from":"S2","to":"SRV","fromLabel":"Fa0/1"}]}
```

| Device/interface | Address and mask | Connection/cable |
|---|---|---|
| PC-A FastEthernet0 | 10.0.10.50, 255.255.255.0; gateway 10.0.10.1; DNS 10.0.20.10 | SW1 Fa0/1, straight-through |
| R1 Gi0/0 | 10.0.10.1, 255.255.255.0 | SW1 Fa0/24, straight-through |
| R1 Gi0/1 | 10.0.99.1, 255.255.255.252 | R2 Gi0/1, crossover or Auto-Connect |
| R2 Gi0/1 | 10.0.99.2, 255.255.255.252 | R1 Gi0/1, same transit cable |
| R2 Gi0/0 | 10.0.20.1, 255.255.255.0 | SW2 Fa0/24, straight-through |
| SRV FastEthernet0 | 10.0.20.10, 255.255.255.0; gateway 10.0.20.1; DNS 10.0.20.10 | SW2 Fa0/1, straight-through |

All devices are fresh lab devices. Switch ports are access ports, with no trunks required. Leave 10.0.20.99 unused for a later DNS fault. This is an isolated simulated network; no Internet connection or NAT is required.

steps.title: Build the complete baseline
steps.body:
Cable the listed ports. Set PC-A and SRV under Desktop → IP Configuration. Open each Cisco CLI, decline the initial setup dialog if offered, and configure the following. If a logging command is unsupported, record that limitation and use current interface state plus Simulation observations for the log portion.

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.0.10.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.0.99.1 255.255.255.252
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# ip route 10.0.20.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.99.2
R1(config)# service timestamps log datetime msec
R1(config)# logging buffered 16384 informational
R1(config)# end
```

```ios R2
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R2
R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R2(config-if)# ip address 10.0.99.2 255.255.255.252
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R2(config-if)# ip address 10.0.20.1 255.255.255.0
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# exit
R2(config)# ip route 10.0.10.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.99.1
R2(config)# service timestamps log datetime msec
R2(config)# logging buffered 16384 informational
R2(config)# end
```

```ios SW1
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW1
SW1(config)# vlan 10
SW1(config-vlan)# name USERS
SW1(config-vlan)# vlan 20
SW1(config-vlan)# name FAULT-TEST
SW1(config-vlan)# exit
SW1(config)# interface range fastethernet0/1, fastethernet0/24
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport access vlan 10
SW1(config-if-range)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if-range)# end
```

```ios SW2
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW2
SW2(config)# vlan 20
SW2(config-vlan)# name SERVERS
SW2(config-vlan)# exit
SW2(config)# interface range fastethernet0/1, fastethernet0/24
SW2(config-if-range)# switchport mode access
SW2(config-if-range)# switchport access vlan 20
SW2(config-if-range)# no shutdown
SW2(config-if-range)# end
```

On SRV → Services, turn HTTP and DNS On. Add A record `app.lab.example` with address `10.0.20.10`, and a second A record `fresh.lab.example` with the same address. Leave DHCP Off on SRV; R2 will supply an optional DHCP demonstration later. Wait for switch ports to reach forwarding before testing.

:::expected
