The router interfaces become up/up with the table's addresses. SW1 VLAN 10 contains Fa0/1 and Fa0/24; SW2 VLAN 20 contains its two used ports. Both static routes are installed. Server records use the intended address; neither .99 nor a public resolver is involved.
:::

steps.title: Record a healthy path and a sourced test
steps.body:
Before testing, fill the prediction column for PC-A to its gateway, PC-A to the server, R1 using its transit source, and R1 using its LAN source. Identify the reply destination in each case. For the browser, record both the intended name and the numeric address separately.

On PC-A run these commands, then open Web Browser to `http://10.0.20.10` and `http://app.lab.example`.

```text
ipconfig /all
ping 10.0.10.1
ping 10.0.20.10
nslookup app.lab.example
tracert 10.0.20.10
```

If PC `nslookup` is absent, use a fresh name-based ping and inspect the DNS PDU in Simulation. On R1, compare two source addresses. If one-line `source` syntax is unavailable, enter `ping`, supply the target, choose extended commands `y`, and enter the required source; accept unrelated defaults. Use that same alternative throughout the lab.

```ios R1
R1# show ip interface brief
R1# show ip route
R1# show arp
R1# show cdp neighbors
R1# ping 10.0.20.10 source 10.0.99.1
R1# ping 10.0.20.10 source 10.0.10.1
R1# copy running-config startup-config
```

```ios R2
R2# show ip route
R2# show logging
R2# copy running-config startup-config
```

```ios SW1
SW1# show interfaces status
SW1# show mac address-table
SW1# copy running-config startup-config
```

```ios SW2
SW2# copy running-config startup-config
```

Accept the destination filename prompt with Enter. Save the project as `toolkit-baseline.pkt`, then use Save As `toolkit-work.pkt` before injecting faults. Record PC-A's actual MAC address from its configuration/PC output.

:::expected
Both source tests and the client tests succeed after any transient startup delays. The name resolves to .20.10 and HTTP works. A conventional PC trace can show R1, R2, and SRV; exact interface addresses and response timing may differ. Do not require an initial ping loss. The next-hop ARP entries and PC MAC appear after relevant traffic; a successful test is stronger evidence than assuming an entry must already exist.
:::

steps.title: Remove and diagnose the return route
steps.body:
Keep all client settings unchanged. Before removing the route, predict which of your four source/destination pairs should still work and which route each reply would need. Then remove only R2's return route:

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# no ip route 10.0.10.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.99.1
R2(config)# end
R2# show ip route
```

```ios R1
R1# ping 10.0.20.10 source 10.0.99.1
R1# ping 10.0.20.10 source 10.0.10.1
```

Repeat PC-A's server-address ping and trace. In Simulation mode, clear old events, filter ICMP and ARP, generate one test, and inspect the forward request and return attempt. If the simulator does not expose a particular drop reason, record the available route and PDU evidence instead.

:::expected
The transit-source ping works because R2 knows 10.0.99.0/30. The LAN-source and PC tests fail because R2 now lacks a route to 10.0.10.0/24 and has no default. A trace may lose later responses even while forward probes progress. The route table establishes the cause here; source-test failure alone would also be compatible with source-based filtering.
:::

steps.title: Restore the return route and verify the client
steps.body:
```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# ip route 10.0.10.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.99.1
R2(config)# end
R2# show ip route 10.0.10.50
```

```ios R1
R1# ping 10.0.20.10 source 10.0.10.1
```

Return Simulation to Realtime after observation. Repeat PC-A's ping and HTTP-by-name test. Write the cause and recovery evidence before continuing.

:::expected
R2 selects the static return route through 10.0.99.1; the LAN-source ping and client HTTP work. The earlier failure is resolved before another fault is introduced.
:::

steps.title: Diagnose a shutdown at the far endpoint
steps.body:
Predict the local administrative state, the far-end link state, and whether PC-A's local gateway should remain reachable. Shut only R2's transit interface, then inspect both ends. Keep the predicted cause separate from the actual displayed evidence.

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R2(config-if)# shutdown
R2(config-if)# end
R2# show ip interface brief
R2# show logging
```

```ios R1
R1# show ip interface brief
R1# show ip route
R1# show cdp neighbors
R1# show logging
```

Repeat PC-A's gateway and server pings. Keep current evidence; do not clear logs.

:::expected
R2 reports Gi0/1 administratively down. R1's peer link normally reports down/down, and its static route loses usable next-hop resolution. PC-A can still reach R1's LAN address but not SRV. A cached CDP entry may persist until it ages; its presence does not override current link state. Log messages and timing vary, but R2's administrative state directly identifies the deliberate shutdown.
:::

steps.title: Restore the transit interface
steps.body:
```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# end
R2# show ip interface brief
```

```ios R1
R1# show ip route
R1# ping 10.0.20.10 source 10.0.10.1
```

Repeat the client's server ping and HTTP test after convergence.

:::expected
The transit becomes up/up, the intended routes are installed, and both sourced and client tests work. Record restoration separately from the earlier fault evidence.
:::

steps.title: Move the client into the wrong access VLAN
steps.body:
Predict the physical link state, VLAN used for new source-MAC learning, and gateway reachability before applying this one change. Do not change the PC address or clear tables to make the display match a prediction.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 20
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces status
SW1# show vlan brief
```

Keep PC-A's 10.0.10.50/24 settings unchanged. Ping its gateway, then inspect the MAC table. On R1, ping 10.0.10.50 and inspect ARP. Existing cached entries can persist; use the current VLAN configuration and newly generated frames rather than demanding instantaneous table erasure.

```ios SW1
SW1# show mac address-table
```

```ios R1
R1# ping 10.0.10.50
R1# show arp
```

:::expected
The physical PC link remains connected, but its port is now in VLAN 20 while R1's port remains in VLAN 10. New source frames from PC-A are learned in VLAN 20. Gateway communication fails despite link-up status. ARP may be incomplete, absent, or temporarily stale depending on timing; the mismatched VLAN membership supplies the decisive evidence.
:::

steps.title: Restore the client VLAN
steps.body:
```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 10
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show vlan brief
```

Repeat gateway and server pings from PC-A, then inspect the MAC table again.

:::expected
PC-A's new source frames appear in VLAN 10 on Fa0/1, and the intended service works. Old entries in another VLAN may age independently; judge current forwarding from the test and intended configuration.
:::

steps.title: Introduce a valid but wrong DNS answer
steps.body:
Predict whether the direct-IP HTTP test, the new DNS answer, and the name-based HTTP test should agree. Choose a check that distinguishes a wrong received answer from a DNS timeout before changing the record.

On SRV → Services → DNS, edit only `app.lab.example` to `10.0.20.99`, the unused address. Keep `fresh.lab.example` unchanged. From PC-A, explicitly query `app.lab.example` with `nslookup` if supported and compare the answer with a ping to `10.0.20.10`. Inspect the DNS response in Simulation. If the client uses cached data or lacks the direct-query tool, add a new fault-test name `wrong.lab.example` → .20.99 and query that new name.

:::expected
The controlled IP-address service remains reachable. The fresh/direct DNS result points to unused .20.99, so a name-based connection cannot reach the intended server. This is a received positive answer containing wrong design data, distinct from NXDOMAIN or silence. Record what was actually queried and returned.
:::

steps.title: Restore DNS and verify the complete service
steps.body:
Restore `app.lab.example` → `10.0.20.10` and delete optional `wrong.lab.example`. Repeat a direct query and browser test. If an application retains stale data, close and reopen it or use a new correctly configured test name, recording the cache limitation instead of changing unrelated routing.

:::expected
The responsible DNS service returns .20.10 and the client's intended HTTP test works. Verify the returned address as well as the page. All four injected faults have now been restored.
:::

steps.title: Trace a fresh DHCP transaction through the same path
steps.body:
This optional integration exercise uses R2 as the DHCP server and R1 as relay; it reinforces the transaction evidence already taught in Chapter 24. Keep SRV DHCP Off. Before the client requests a lease, identify the relay address that should select the pool, the permitted address range, and the required reply path. Then use the supplied setup below. If omitting this extension, retain PC-A's verified static settings and record that choice in Step 12.

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# service dhcp
R2(config)# ip dhcp excluded-address 10.0.10.1 10.0.10.99
R2(config)# ip dhcp pool USERS
R2(dhcp-config)# network 10.0.10.0 255.255.255.0
R2(dhcp-config)# default-router 10.0.10.1
R2(dhcp-config)# dns-server 10.0.20.10
R2(dhcp-config)# end
```

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# service dhcp
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip helper-address 10.0.99.2
R1(config-if)# end
```

In Simulation, filter DHCP and ARP and clear previous events. Change PC-A → Desktop → IP Configuration to DHCP, then use Capture/Forward until allocation completes. Inspect the original request on the LAN, the relayed request toward R2, and delivery back to PC-A. Return to Realtime before subsequent pings. Inspect `show ip dhcp binding` on R2 and actual client settings.

:::expected
PC-A receives an available .100–.254 address, /24 mask, gateway .10.1, and DNS .20.10; do not assume allocation of the numerically first address. The relay's giaddr identifies 10.0.10.1. Offer/ACK delivery can be broadcast or unicast depending on client state and flags. A simulated event may appear at several devices, so the event count is not a protocol message count. Client HTTP still works with the new source.
:::

steps.title: Save the verified final state
steps.body:
Keep the verified DHCP client/relay/server configuration if you completed the optional extension; otherwise retain the static baseline addressing. Record PC-A's actual address and every intended difference from the initial baseline. Verify both router interfaces, routes, switch membership, DNS response, and HTTP. Save each Cisco device from privileged EXEC with `copy running-config startup-config`, completing its destination prompt before moving to the next device, then save the project as `toolkit-complete.pkt`. Preserve `toolkit-baseline.pkt` separately.

:::expected
The final network has no outstanding injected fault. Four device startup configurations and the Packet Tracer project are saved; notes contain the original symptoms and the evidence supporting each repair. No debug or experimental capture is left running.
:::

### Evidence to keep

For each of the four faults, keep the prediction and the observation before the repair, the decisive configuration/state or packet evidence, a plausible explanation the test ruled out, the exact narrow correction, and the repeated client service test. Include source addresses for paired router tests and capture location/filter when using Simulation. Record which counters or logs you could not observe; do not convert that absence into a passed check. Finish with one paragraph explaining why a router ping, a route entry, a DNS answer and an HTTP response each establish different things.

lab.troubleshooting:
- If the first baseline fails, inspect exact masks, both host gateways, switch membership, and both static routes before injecting any fault.
- A failed ping with stars or periods does not identify a unique failure; compare source, route lookup, current link state, and capture point.
- If pipe filters or `show running-config interface` are unsupported, use the complete `show running-config` and locate the intended interface manually.
- Empty logs can reflect destination configuration, buffer history, or simulator limits. Use current configuration/state and record the missing evidence.
- A missing DNS event can mean cached resolution, a different test name, an incorrect resolver, or capture filtering; inspect these before blaming the server.
lab.challenge:
Use this fresh, independent incident as a paper diagnosis; it is not an assertion about the state of your saved project. The topology has the same roles as above but these addresses: client LAN `10.31.10.0/24`, R1 `.10.1`, PC-A `.10.50`, PC-B `.10.60`; transit `10.31.99.0/30`, R1 `.99.1`, R2 `.99.2`; server LAN `10.31.20.0/24`, R2 `.20.1`, SRV `.20.10`. Both clients and the server have their correct local gateways. Both client ports are verified in the intended active VLAN. The two routers' links are up, and there is no policy routing or traffic filter in this supplied case.

SRV has HTTP and DNS enabled, with `app.lab.example A 10.31.20.10`. Both clients use DNS `10.31.20.10`. The original complaint is that PC-A cannot open `http://app.lab.example`, while PC-B can load that page. These service settings and the following ICMP checks are supplied evidence for the paper case.

```output Supplied observations from the same interval
PC-A to its local gateway: success
PC-B to its local gateway and SRV by address: success
R1 LAN-source 10.31.10.1 to SRV: success
PC-A to SRV by address: failure
Server-side capture: PC-A's echo request arrives; matching reply leaves toward R2
R2: 10.31.10.0/24 via 10.31.99.1
R2: 10.31.10.50/32 via Null0 — confirmed obsolete test route
```

Before opening the solution, state the selected reply route for `.50`, `.60` and `.1`; explain why R1's successful sourced test did not certify PC-A; write the smallest justified repair; and choose the original-service and unaffected-service retests. Include the command that would inspect each return destination. Do not remove the working /24 route.

:::solution Check the client-specific diagnosis
The `.50/32` is a longer match than the client `/24`, so R2 discards PC-A's return traffic through Null0. PC-B `.60` and R1 `.1` use the working /24 via `10.31.99.1`. The server capture rules out a claim that this particular request never reached SRV; the supplied exact route and obsolete-test confirmation support a narrow removal rather than a speculative change to the server gateway.

```ios R2
R2# show ip route 10.31.10.50
R2# show ip route 10.31.10.60
R2# show ip route 10.31.10.1
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# no ip route 10.31.10.50 255.255.255.255 Null0
R2(config)# end
R2# show ip route 10.31.10.50
```

After removal, `.50` should select the intended /24. Verify PC-A's numeric ping, fresh name answer and original application; repeat PC-B's working application and R1's sourced check to preserve evidence of unaffected service. Save only after actual tests in a separately built implementation pass. For this paper submission, distinguish the reasoned result from an executed configuration. This variation tests a more-specific exception that a successful router-source check misses.
:::

exhibit.title: Bounded ping result
exhibit.text:
Sending 5, 100-byte ICMP Echos; timeout 2 seconds:
.!!!!
Success rate: 80 percent (4/5)

questions.prompt: What does this ping result establish?
options: The destination enforced a four-reply ICMP limit for this source.
One request did not receive a reply within its wait; the cause needs more evidence.
A routing update installed the route immediately after the first request.
The first request was definitely discarded during ARP resolution.
questions.explanation: The period reports a timeout and the four exclamation marks report replies. ARP startup delay is one possible explanation; repeat the test and correlate a current ARP/capture observation before assigning that cause.

whyWrong.0: Four replies do not establish a configured response limit.
whyWrong.2: No routing change is shown.
whyWrong.3: The output contains no ARP observation.

exhibit.title: Ping response characters
exhibit.text:
R1# ping 10.0.50.1
U.U.U
Success rate: 0 percent

questions.prompt: What conclusion follows from the U characters?
options: Destination-unreachable responses were reported for some probes.
The source router had no usable interface for every probe.
The destination application accepted and then closed its connections.
Each period proves a fixed 500-ms ICMP response limiter on R2.
questions.explanation: U indicates unreachable evidence, unlike a period indicating a wait expired. Inspect the ICMP source and code, then routing/policy, rather than infer one device or a fixed rate limiter from the pattern.

whyWrong.1: The display does not establish all interfaces were unusable.
whyWrong.2: Echo testing does not create an application connection.
whyWrong.3: The pattern alone supplies neither the timer nor its location.

questions.prompt: Which two statements correctly compare conventional IOS traceroute and Windows tracert? Select two.
options: IOS normally uses ICMP echo while Windows normally uses UDP.
Windows tracert normally uses ICMP echo requests.
IOS normally uses UDP probes toward high destination ports.
Both tools must use the same probe transport to discover any hops.
questions.explanation: Both use increasing TTL to obtain transit time-exceeded responses. Their probe protocols differ, which matters when comparing source and policy paths.

whyWrong.0: This reverses the conventional implementations described here.
whyWrong.3: Different probe transports can elicit TTL-expiry responses; their policies may differ.

questions.prompt: Which two statements about these tables are accurate? Select two.
options: An absent ARP entry proves the host has never received a neighbor reply.
A dynamic MAC entry identifies a VLAN/port that learned that source MAC.
An incomplete ARP entry shows resolution is incomplete at this observation.
A learned MAC establishes the host has the correct mask and gateway.
questions.explanation: The tables describe different current mappings. Aging, clearing, and recent traffic affect their contents; neither alone certifies host addressing or all historical communication.

whyWrong.0: Entries can age or be cleared after earlier successful communication.
whyWrong.3: MAC learning does not inspect the host mask/gateway as proof of correctness.

exhibit.title: Routed Ethernet state
exhibit.text: Gi0/1 10.0.99.1 YES manual down down

questions.prompt: On this routed Ethernet interface, what should be investigated first?
options: Remove a local shutdown command, which this status explicitly proves.
Change the IP mask before checking whether either end has carrier.
Replace the cable immediately because down/down uniquely proves its failure.
Inspect local media and the connected peer's current link state.
questions.explanation: Down/down directs attention to physical/link availability and the peer. It does not uniquely identify a cable defect; a local shutdown normally has the distinct administratively-down status.

whyWrong.0: A local shutdown normally has the distinct administratively-down state.
whyWrong.1: The IP mask does not restore physical link detection.
whyWrong.2: The peer may be disabled or unpowered; this display does not isolate the cable.

exhibit.title: Both-end duplex and current counters
exhibit.text:
SW1 Fa0/24: 100 Mb/s, half duplex; late collisions rose 40→65
R1 Gi0/0: speed 100; duplex full

questions.prompt: Which demonstrated problem should be corrected before further performance testing?
options: Late collisions establish damaged copper regardless of the peer settings.
The displayed half/full settings establish a duplex mismatch.
The rising late collisions measure output-queue congestion.
The two 100-Mb/s values establish a negotiated speed mismatch.
questions.explanation: Half duplex at SW1 and full duplex at R1 establishes a mismatch. Coordinate matching supported settings at both ends, then compare new error increments; clean CRC alone does not certify media.

whyWrong.0: The configuration directly establishes duplex disagreement; the counter alone cannot isolate copper damage.
whyWrong.2: Late collisions are not output-queue drops.
whyWrong.3: Both displayed speeds match at 100 Mb/s.

exhibit.title: Trace with a silent intermediate hop

questions.prompt: A web application is slow. Which interpretation of this trace is justified?
options: The destination replies certify that HTTP performance is normal.
The three stars establish three seconds of forwarding delay for each user packet.
The third router dropped every packet and caused the slow application.
Later probes received replies, so the middle stars alone do not prove a forwarding break.
questions.explanation: A star is a missing probe response within the wait. Later replies weaken the claim of a complete path break, but load sharing, response policy, and application behavior still require investigation.

whyWrong.0: Traceroute does not test the HTTP transaction.
whyWrong.1: A response timeout is not a measurement of per-packet forwarding delay.
whyWrong.2: Later responses contradict an assertion that all traffic necessarily stops there.

exhibit.title: Logging threshold and two messages
exhibit.text:
logging trap warnings
%LINK-3-UPDOWN: Gi0/1 changed state to down
%LINEPROTO-5-UPDOWN: Gi0/1 line protocol changed state to down

questions.prompt: Which shown message is eligible for remote syslog at the configured threshold?
options: Neither message is selected because warnings means exactly severity 4.
Only the severity-5 LINEPROTO message is selected by this threshold.
Both messages are selected because both concern the same interface.
Only the severity-3 LINK message is selected by this threshold.
questions.explanation: Warnings admits severity 4 and lower-numbered, more severe messages. This selects the severity-3 message; actual receipt still requires a working logging path.

whyWrong.0: The threshold includes more severe levels, not just exact level 4.
whyWrong.1: Severity 5 is less severe than the configured level 4 threshold.
whyWrong.2: Each message is filtered by its own severity.

questions.prompt: What does this client-side TCP observation support?
options: A matching reset was received; identify the generating endpoint or intermediary before attributing the refusal.
The reset proves the client cannot receive any packet from that direction.
The SYN was silently discarded and no response reached the client.
The capture alone proves the application server itself generated the reset.
questions.explanation: The reset is an active response, unlike silence. A firewall or intermediary can generate resets using the endpoint address, so correlate server-side capture and service status before declaring the server process at fault.

whyWrong.1: The reset itself arrived from that direction.
whyWrong.2: The matching RST is an observed response.
whyWrong.3: The observed source address alone does not exclude an intermediary.

exhibit.title: Received ICMP error
exhibit.text:
10.0.99.2 → 10.0.10.50
ICMP Destination Unreachable: communication administratively prohibited (type 3, code 13)

questions.prompt: Which next check is supported by the received ICMP error?
options: Replace the missing default route that this code uniquely identifies.
Correct the expired TTL that is explicitly reported in this message.
Inspect administrative forwarding policy at the reporting device and the matching flow.
Repair ARP for the destination because this is a host-unreachable code.
questions.explanation: Type 3 code 13 reports administrative prohibition. It supports investigating policy, but does not identify one exact ACL line without further configuration/counter evidence.

whyWrong.0: No-route evidence would be a different unreachable reason.
whyWrong.1: TTL expiry uses time-exceeded rather than this administrative prohibition.
whyWrong.3: Host unreachable is a different code.

questions.prompt: On supporting IOS, which bounded command compares a 1500-byte IPv4 datagram with the path MTU?
options: ping 10.0.20.10 source 10.0.10.1 repeat 5 size 1500 df-bit
ping 10.0.20.10 source 10.0.10.1 repeat 5 size 1472
ping 10.0.20.10 source 10.0.10.1 repeat 5 size 100 df-bit
ping 10.0.20.10 source 10.0.10.1 repeat 5 size 1500
questions.explanation: IOS size specifies the datagram size in this command and df-bit prevents fragmentation. A received fragmentation-needed error is informative; a timeout alone does not prove the MTU value.

whyWrong.1: That requests a different IOS datagram size, not 1500.
whyWrong.2: A 100-byte datagram does not perform the requested large-size comparison.
whyWrong.3: Without DF, IPv4 fragmentation can occur.

exhibit.title: Two independent switch-port conditions
exhibit.text:
Fa0/3: err-disabled
Fa0/4: inactive, configured access VLAN 30
show vlan brief: VLAN 30 absent

questions.prompt: The design requires VLAN 30 on Fa0/4. Which action pair follows the supplied evidence?
options: Move both ports to an existing VLAN without checking their intended subnets.
Replace both cables before inspecting the recorded state and VLAN database.
Inspect Fa0/3's protection cause and restore the intended VLAN 30 for Fa0/4.
Enable Fa0/3 without checking why its protection acted.
questions.explanation: Err-disabled requires its recorded cause and corrective action before controlled recovery. The explicit VLAN inventory identifies the missing intended VLAN for Fa0/4; do not move clients into an unrelated network.

whyWrong.0: That changes the documented VLAN design without repairing its missing object.
whyWrong.1: The two displayed conditions do not establish physical cable damage.
whyWrong.3: Recovery without resolving the triggering cause can repeat the failure.

questions.prompt: Which statement describes errors during the measured interval?
options: There were 900 new CRC errors during this transfer.
The retained total proves that the present cable must be replaced.
The 2,000,000 packets prove that no loss occurred elsewhere.
No new CRC errors were counted on this interface during the interval.
questions.explanation: The CRC counter remained 900, so its delta is zero. Preserve that distinction between history and this test; a clean delta on one interface is not an end-to-end certification.

whyWrong.0: Nine hundred is the retained total, not the difference.
whyWrong.1: The retained count lacks evidence of a current cable fault.
whyWrong.2: One receive count cannot prove delivery across the whole path.

exhibit.title: Counters bracketing one controlled transfer
exhibit.text:
Same interface; no counter clear or reboot.
Before: 1,000,000 input packets; 900 CRC
After: 3,000,000 input packets; 900 CRC

questions.prompt: What should the investigation focus on next for this transaction?
options: Inspect the responding application and its dependencies for the reported failure.
Change the client resolver and repeat the same lookup before examining the service.
Add a host route to the approved server to repair the unsuccessful request.
Raise the TCP connection timeout and retry before checking the service response.
questions.explanation: The completed connection and received application response prove more than a ping. The service reports temporary unavailability for this request; investigate that service and its dependencies without declaring unrelated traffic healthy.

whyWrong.1: The observed lookup already returned the approved address.
whyWrong.2: A complete TCP exchange and HTTP response do not justify this route change.
whyWrong.3: The request received an explicit response; this is not an uncompleted TCP connection attempt.

exhibit.title: One captured application transaction
exhibit.text:
Intended name resolves to the approved IPv4 address.
TCP SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK complete for that address.
HTTP response to the request: 503 Service Unavailable.

questions.prompt: Which evidence is still required before closing the incident?
options: A repeat of R1's successful directly connected peer ping.
A screenshot showing the exact intended configuration line.
A fresh original-service test from the affected client.
An updated uptime display after restarting the router.
questions.explanation: A route change and router test do not cover the affected client's whole path or application. Retest its original service and record the source, destination/name, result and any remaining limitation.

whyWrong.0: The local router test exercises a narrower path.
whyWrong.1: Configuration shows intent, not successful delivery.
whyWrong.3: A restart is not an acceptance test and may erase useful evidence.

exhibit.title: Repair acceptance record
exhibit.text:
Original complaint: PC-A cannot load the named application.
A missing route was restored.
R1 can ping the server.
No PC-A application test has been repeated.

exhibit.title: Same DHCP attempt at two capture points
exhibit.text:
Server-side: relayed Discover received; Offer sent to giaddr 10.0.10.1
Client-side: Discover transmitted; no Offer observed in the same interval

questions.prompt: Which conclusion is justified by these captures from the same fresh DHCP attempt?
options: Investigate delivery of the Offer from the server through the relay to the client.
The client certainly received the ACK but lost its default gateway setting.
The helper must be absent because no server reply can exist without it.
The server certainly had no matching pool and never constructed an Offer.
questions.explanation: The server-side observation shows an outgoing Offer while the client-side view does not show receipt. Narrow the investigation to return and relay delivery, including capture coverage; do not assert a unique fault yet.

whyWrong.1: No ACK receipt is shown.
whyWrong.2: A forwarded Discover and outgoing reply have already been observed.
whyWrong.3: An outgoing Offer contradicts the claim that none was constructed.

questions.prompt: Which follow-up preserves the useful distinction between the two probe results?
options: Treat the error as evidence of a size constraint; inspect the reported MTU and a smaller DF probe.
Treat both tests as proof that the server is down at every packet size.
Replace DNS settings because a larger numeric-address probe cannot resolve the name.
Remove DF and call the original unfragmented-size requirement verified if a reply arrives.
questions.explanation: A received fragmentation-needed error positively reports a constraint for that DF packet. Correlate its source and any next-hop MTU value, then compare a smaller packet with the same source and destination; fragmentation-permitted success answers a different question.

whyWrong.1: The smaller probe already received replies.
whyWrong.2: The test already uses a numeric address.
whyWrong.3: Fragmented delivery does not verify the original unfragmented requirement.

exhibit.title: Controlled IPv4 size comparison
exhibit.text:
Same source and destination, ordinary 20-byte IPv4 header.
100-byte DF datagrams receive replies.
1500-byte DF datagrams receive ICMP fragmentation-needed errors.
No numeric next-hop MTU has yet been read.

questions.prompt: Which incident note is defensible before comparing these event times?
options: R2 must have caused R1's event because its printed time is earlier.
Record each clock's uncertainty and correlate a shared observation before ordering the events.
Use the collector's arrival order as proof of the devices' event order.
Subtract the displayed times and report a measured propagation delay.
questions.explanation: Different unverified clocks do not provide a reliable cross-device timeline. Preserve their original text and obtain synchronization/offset or a shared observation before asserting which event preceded the other.

whyWrong.0: Printed times on unverified clocks do not establish causality.
whyWrong.2: Collection paths and buffering can change arrival order.
whyWrong.3: The difference includes unknown clock offsets.

exhibit.title: Log times from two devices
exhibit.text:
R1: *10:15:01 link event; clock not authoritative
R2: 10:14:58 neighbor event; synchronization not checked
Collector receives R1's message first.

questions.prompt: Which narrow next action fits the remaining failure?
options: Undo the route repair and return to investigating the original missing route.
Correct the stale DNS record, then test a fresh answer and the named application.
Clear only the client DNS cache and close the incident after a numeric-address test.
Assign the server the stale address .99 to avoid changing the DNS service.
questions.explanation: The restored numeric-address service and fresh wrong answer identify a separate DNS-data problem. Preserve both findings and validate the original name-based service after correcting the record.

whyWrong.0: The repaired path now carries the numeric-address service, and the DNS data shows a separate fault.
whyWrong.2: A fresh direct response from the resolver is already wrong; a client cache clear does not repair that configured record.
whyWrong.3: The approved server remains .10, so renumbering it to match stale DNS changes the design unnecessarily.

exhibit.title: Checks after a routing repair
exhibit.text:
Approved server: 10.31.20.10.
PC-A HTTP to 10.31.20.10 now succeeds.
Fresh direct query to its intended resolver: app.lab.example A = 10.31.20.99.
The DNS configuration confirms that stale address; .99 is unused.

questions.prompt: Which two conclusions are supported before a repair is chosen? Choose two.
options: This interface has counted new outgoing drops during the interval.
The clean CRC count certifies every cable in the network.
Raising a buffer limit would guarantee recovery without any further evidence.
The switch must have a duplex mismatch despite both endpoints showing full.
The displayed queue evidence is relevant to local egress congestion.
questions.explanation: Current outgoing drops and a full egress queue point toward congestion at this observation point. They do not uniquely identify its source, prescribe one fix, or certify the rest of the path.

whyWrong.1: A clean receive counter on one interface does not certify all media.
whyWrong.2: Traffic demand, scheduling and downstream capacity still matter.
whyWrong.3: The stated duplex settings agree.

exhibit.title: Current egress observations
exhibit.text:
During one test: output drops 50→150.
Receive CRC unchanged at 0.
Both endpoints operate full duplex.
The egress queue reaches its configured limit during the test.

exhibit.title: Tests with different source addresses
exhibit.text:
R1 source 10.0.99.1 → 10.0.20.10: success
R1 source 10.0.10.1 → 10.0.20.10: failure
PC-A 10.0.10.50/24: local gateway ping succeeds

questions.prompt: R1 can ping the server from its transit source, but not from its LAN source. What should the engineer check next?
options: Retest from the transit source and close the issue if it succeeds again.
Add another R1 route to the server subnet before checking the reply destination.
Inspect the server return routes and source-dependent policy for the LAN source.
Replace the PC access cable, then repeat only the router-source test.
questions.explanation: Changing the source changes the return destination and may change policy handling. The failed sourced test supports investigating those differences; it does not alone prove a missing route.

whyWrong.0: The transit source does not test replies toward the failed LAN source.
whyWrong.1: The successful transit-source test and changed reply destination call for return/policy investigation before another forward-route change.
whyWrong.3: The failed router-originated LAN-source test does not traverse the PC access cable.

questions.prompt: Which next measurement best tests whether the observed capture gap is actual path loss?
options: Count the analyzer warnings and report that count as packets lost on the server link.
Run a short ping after the transfer and use its loss percentage as the TCP loss rate.
Capture a different successful flow and use that result to dismiss the original gaps.
Compare a complete capture at a second point for the same flow and interval.
questions.explanation: The analyzer reports what its captured sequence history lacks. The capture itself dropped packets, so corroborate the same flow elsewhere before attributing loss to a network link.

whyWrong.0: The capture dropped packets itself, so missing sequence history does not count losses on an identified network link.
whyWrong.1: A later ICMP sample is not the same TCP flow or observation interval.
whyWrong.2: A different flow may take different treatment and does not corroborate the missing sequence history.

exhibit.title: Capture coverage and application evidence
exhibit.text:
Client transfer completes, but intermittently slowly.
Capture tool reports dropped capture packets.
Wireshark labels a gap: Previous segment not captured.
No second capture or current interface counter interval is available.

questions.prompt: Which next check most directly separates a wrong server return next hop from a forward-path failure?
options: Install another R2 route to the client subnet before examining the server route.
Inspect the server's selected route and neighbor resolution for the client reply.
Ping the server from R2 and treat that reply as proof of the client return path.
Capture the client gateway ARP exchange again before examining reply forwarding.
questions.explanation: The server-side capture confirms the tested request arrived. Its route and selected next-hop resolution are now useful discriminators for the missing reply; the capture alone does not establish whether the application generated one.

whyWrong.0: A matching R2 return route is already supplied; the server next-hop choice is the missing dependency under investigation.
whyWrong.2: A reply to R2 uses a different destination and does not settle how the server returns to the client.
whyWrong.3: The request reached the server, so the unresolved return next hop is more directly discriminating here.

exhibit.title: Matched observations for one attempt
exhibit.text:
Client 10.31.10.50 sends to server 10.31.20.10.
Server capture sees that request. Client capture sees no reply.
Server is /24; its route/default-gateway configuration has not been inspected.
R2 route to 10.31.10.0/24 is present.

questions.prompt: What is the most useful next test for the original client failure?
options: Capture only R1-originated replies and use them to clear the client access path.
Repeat the router-source service test until five successive attempts pass.
Compare client-source policy and the client-facing ingress path.
Increase the client's retry timeout before comparing how its flow is handled.
questions.explanation: The router-source test does not traverse the client-facing ingress path and uses a different source address. Compare the actual client flow and both policy directions before concluding the paths are equivalent.

whyWrong.0: Router-originated replies do not establish treatment of the actual client source or ingress.
whyWrong.1: Repeated router tests still omit client ingress and use a different source.
whyWrong.3: The supplied source/path difference deserves investigation before changing a client timer.

exhibit.title: Different-origin test paths
exhibit.text:
PC-A reaches its gateway but cannot reach a remote service.
R1 reaches that service with source set to its LAN interface address.
PC-A's address, mask and gateway match the plan.
Client-source policy and ingress handling have not been checked.

cards.front: Does an initial .!!!! prove an ARP delay?
cards.back: No. ARP delay is possible, but the timeout itself does not identify a cause. Repeat and correlate current ARP/capture evidence.

cards.front: How is a period different from an unreachable result?
cards.back: A period reports no timely usable reply. An unreachable result reports an error; inspect its source/code rather than assume one missing route.

cards.front: What changes when you select a router ping source?
cards.back: The reply destination and possibly policy handling change. It helps test return reachability but does not reproduce the PC’s full ingress path.

cards.front: Why can IOS traceroute and Windows tracert encounter different policies?
cards.back: Conventional IOS uses UDP probes; Windows uses ICMP echo. Both use increasing TTL, but their source and transport treatment can differ.

cards.front: What does a traceroute star report?
cards.back: No usable response for that probe within its wait. It does not prove the probe stopped at the last responding router.

cards.front: What do routed Ethernet administrative down and down/down suggest?
cards.back: Administrative down identifies local shutdown state. Down/down directs investigation toward link/media/peer availability; it is not a unique cable diagnosis.

cards.front: How do err-disabled and inactive guide switch diagnosis?
cards.back: Find the recorded error/protection cause for err-disabled. Inspect intended VLAN availability for inactive; recover only after correcting the demonstrated cause.

cards.front: What directly establishes a duplex mismatch?
cards.back: Different operational duplex settings at the two ends. Late collisions can support the diagnosis; compare both ends and fresh increments.

cards.front: Does a rising CRC counter identify one exact physical fault?
cards.back: No. It reports new received corruption; compare both endpoints and the medium before selecting a cause.

cards.front: Does a matching TCP reset prove the server application sent it?
cards.back: No. It is an active response, potentially from an endpoint or intermediary. Correlate server-side evidence; unanswered SYNs leave both directions uncertain.

cards.front: What should a useful troubleshooting note preserve?
cards.back: Affected flow/source, time and clock confidence, original evidence, hypothesis, focused change, and the final client/application retest.

cards.front: What context must accompany a packet capture?
cards.back: Capture point, direction, filter, time interval and capture loss. Missing traffic there is not proof it was absent everywhere.

cards.front: How do two counter snapshots distinguish current activity from history?
cards.back: Compare their delta over a known interval, checking for a clear, wrap or restart. Preserve the original observations.

cards.front: Can two device timestamps alone establish event order?
cards.back: Only with adequate clock confidence. Unknown offsets, adjustments and collector delays can make apparent order misleading.

commands.task: Ping server 10.0.20.10 from this router’s owned Gi0/0 address 10.0.10.1.
commands.note: Use supported one-line syntax or the interactive extended-ping source prompt. Check return routing and policy.

commands.task: On supporting IOS, send five 1500-byte IPv4 datagrams to 10.0.20.10 with fragmentation prohibited.
commands.note: A received fragmentation-needed message supports an MTU constraint; a timeout alone does not.

commands.task: Trace the route toward 10.0.20.10 using this IOS router’s conventional command.
commands.note: Compare the actual source and probe protocol with the affected client traffic.

commands.task: Display Gi0/1 speed, duplex, and interface counters.
commands.note: Compare counters across a known observation interval and inspect the other endpoint.

commands.task: Filter buffered log output to lines containing the literal text LINK.
commands.note: The literal LINK filter selects matching LINK events; inspect LINEPROTO separately or use a supported combined expression. Read timestamps with current state.

commands.task: Find the VLAN and port associated with MAC 0001.9612.0a11.
commands.note: A current learned MAC does not establish the host’s IP mask or gateway.

commands.task: Display this router’s IPv4 ARP mappings.
commands.note: Incomplete or absent entries are current observations, not proof the neighbor never replied.

commands.task: Inspect the installed route selected for return destination 10.0.10.50.
commands.note: Check the actual selected prefix and next hop, including any more-specific route or default.

tickets.title: The transit link is down at both ends
tickets.scenario: R1 Gi0/1 at 10.0.99.1/30 connects directly to R2 Gi0/1 at .2/30. Users behind R1 cannot reach R2’s server LAN. Both routers are available through independent console access. These are representative current records.

exhibits.text: Gi0/1 down/down

exhibits.title: R2 current configuration/state
exhibits.text:
interface GigabitEthernet0/1

State: administratively down/down

exhibits.title: R2 relevant event

tickets.question: Which correction addresses the demonstrated configuration fault?
options: Apply no shutdown to R1 without checking the already enabled local interface.
Replace the transit cable before addressing the displayed far-end shutdown.
Restore the intended no-shutdown state on R2 Gi0/1.
Change both transit masks to /24 while leaving R2 shut.
tickets.explanation: R2's current shutdown configuration and administrative state identify the disabling of the transit. Enabling only R1 or changing masks cannot override R2's shutdown; the evidence does not yet justify replacing the cable. Restore the approved far-end state, then verify both ends, routes and the original client service.
tickets.fix:
```ios
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# end
R2# show ip interface brief
```

Check R1’s state and routes separately, test from the affected PC, and save after verification.

tickets.title: The transit-source test works while client traffic fails
tickets.scenario: PC-A is 10.0.10.50/24, gateway R1 10.0.10.1. R1/R2 transit is 10.0.99.1/.2 on /30. SRV is 10.0.20.10/24 with gateway R2 .20.1. R1 has the intended route to the server; no policy routing is configured.

exhibits.title: R1 paired tests
exhibits.text:
Source 10.0.99.1 to SRV succeeds
Source 10.0.10.1 to SRV fails

exhibits.title: R2 complete installed forwarding prefixes
exhibits.text:
10.0.99.0/30 connected Gi0/1
10.0.20.0/24 connected Gi0/0
Local /32 interface routes only; no other route or default

tickets.question: Which demonstrated missing dependency explains the source difference?
options: R1 has no route toward the server network.
R2 has no route to the client-source subnet.
SRV has no local gateway configured.
PC-A’s access cable is disconnected.
tickets.explanation: R2 can return toward the transit-source .99.1 over a connected route, but no listed prefix matches .10.1 or .10.50. Unlike the source-test result alone, the complete route evidence establishes this missing return route.
tickets.fix:
```ios
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# ip route 10.0.10.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.99.1
R2(config)# end
R2# show ip route 10.0.10.50
```

On R1 separately:
```ios
R1# ping 10.0.20.10 source 10.0.10.1
```
Then verify PC-A by address, name, and actual service before saving.

tickets.title: Transfers slow on a 100-Mb/s link
tickets.scenario: SW1 Fa0/24 connects to R1 Gi0/0. The approved lab design pins both endpoints to 100 Mb/s full duplex. Transfer performance declined after a change. Counters below cover the same current observation interval.

exhibits.title: SW1
exhibits.text:
Fa0/24: 100 Mb/s, half duplex
Late collisions: 100→135

exhibits.title: R1
exhibits.text: Gi0/0: speed 100; duplex full

exhibits.title: Neighbor evidence
exhibits.text: CDP reports local not-full duplex and peer full duplex

tickets.question: Which correction follows the stated design and evidence?
options: Set SW1 Fa0/24 to the intended matching 100/full settings.
Change R1 to 1000/full while retaining SW1 at 100/half.
Clear counters without changing either operational duplex.
Restart both devices before saving the mismatch evidence.
tickets.explanation: The displayed settings directly establish a duplex mismatch. Correct the one deviating endpoint in this explicitly fixed-speed design, then compare fresh increments under a controlled transfer. This does not establish that every other aspect of the link is fault-free.
tickets.fix:
```ios
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/24
SW1(config-if)# speed 100
SW1(config-if)# duplex full
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces fastethernet0/24
```
Preserve previous counters, verify both endpoints, repeat a bounded transfer, and compare new errors before saving.

chapters.title: Security concepts
chapters.subtitle: Connect threats and weaknesses to practical controls, policy, and authentication choices.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-50 Rev. 1: Cybersecurity and privacy learning program
Cisco: Protecting secrets on network devices
RFC 4987: TCP SYN flooding and mitigations

chapters.summary: Distinguish security risks and attack mechanisms, explain security-program and password-policy elements, and evaluate local management controls without mistaking a lab feature for a complete security policy.

sections.title: Protect confidentiality, integrity, and availability
sections.body:
:::facts
- **Confidentiality** protects information from unauthorized disclosure; **integrity** protects against improper modification; **availability** supports timely, reliable access.
- A vulnerability is a weakness; a threat is a potential adverse event or circumstance; an exploit uses a weakness; a mitigation reduces risk.
- Authentication factors are knowledge, possession, and inherence. Two knowledge secrets do not make multifactor authentication.
- Cisco type 7 password storage is reversible obfuscation, not a strong password hash. Protect configuration backups even when they contain hashes.
- A password policy includes how credentials are chosen, used, stored, recovered, replaced, and removed, not just a character count.
:::

Security decisions begin with what a service must protect. A branch router connects staff to an accounting application. If someone reads salary records without permission, confidentiality is affected. If a payment destination is changed, integrity is affected. If staff cannot reach the application during business hours, availability is affected. One incident can affect all three; choose the property described by the specific evidence.

| Objective | Example control | Limitation to remember |
|---|---|---|
| Confidentiality | Authenticated encryption and restricted access | Encryption does not fix excessive permissions at an endpoint |
| Integrity | Authenticated messages, signatures, controlled changes | An untrusted replacement checksum does not prove authenticity |
| Availability | Redundant paths, capacity planning, recovery procedures | Redundancy does not prevent every shared failure |

A **control** is a measure intended to manage risk. Preventive controls try to stop an event; detective controls help identify it; corrective and recovery controls limit harm afterward. A door lock, access log, and tested restoration procedure do different jobs. Their effectiveness depends on operation and maintenance, not merely their presence on a checklist.

These foundations directly support v1.1 objectives 5.1, 5.2, and 5.4. They remain useful background for v2.0 security configuration, but this conceptual chapter does not claim to complete those configuration objectives. Local SSH is taught in Chapter 8, Layer 2 enforcement in Chapter 16, and AAA follows in Chapter 33.

sections.title: Threats, weaknesses, and risk
sections.body:
Consider an administrator account left active after its owner leaves. The account and unnecessary permissions are a **vulnerability**. Unauthorized use is a **threat**. Using a retained credential to log in is one way to **exploit** the weakness. Disabling the account, reviewing active sessions, and correcting account-removal procedures are **mitigations**.

A threat need not be a malicious person: fire, power loss, accidental deletion, or equipment failure can also harm a service. A **threat actor** is a person or organization associated with an intentional threat; do not call the attacker a software vulnerability. An open service port is not automatically a vulnerability either. Ask whether it is required, appropriately protected, correctly configured, and maintained.

**Risk** combines the likelihood of an adverse event with its impact. Multiplying two scores can be one organization's assessment method, but it is not a universal scientific formula for all risks. Prioritize with the asset's importance, exposure, existing controls, and plausible consequences. A small probability of losing a critical service may justify more effort than frequent failures of an unused test device.

| Situation | Weakness or exposure | Appropriate first action |
|---|---|---|
| Default management credential is still accepted | Predictable authentication secret | Replace it and test legitimate access |
| Configuration backups are broadly readable | Unauthorized disclosure of secrets and network details | Restrict access, assess exposure, rotate affected credentials |
| Unnecessary remote service is reachable | Extra attack surface | Disable or restrict it after confirming dependencies |
| A vendor fixes an exploitable defect | Vulnerable installed software | Assess the advisory and plan a supported update |

:::trap A log is evidence, not the attacker's biography
A successful login from an unexpected address deserves investigation. It does not prove who used the account or how the credential was obtained. A weak leaked backup demonstrates exposure even before you can attribute the login. State those two findings separately.
:::

sections.title: Reconnaissance, spoofing and denial of service
sections.body:
**Reconnaissance** gathers information about a target: public documentation, address ranges, reachable services, or software versions. Authorized inventory and troubleshooting can use similar observations, so a scan alone does not establish intent. Some active probes can affect fragile services. Limit tests to the scope of the lab or the approved operational task.

**Spoofing** presents a false identity, such as a forged source IP or a false ARP mapping. An IP address is routing information, not strong proof of a user's identity. A source filter helps enforce an address plan, while authenticated protocols establish stronger identity claims. The correct control depends on which trust decision is being abused.

A **denial-of-service** attack impairs legitimate service. A distributed attack uses multiple sources; it need not consist of compromised endpoints in every case. A **SYN flood** targets the resources used while a TCP server awaits completion of handshakes. Spoofed source addresses are common but not required. Backlog management, SYN cookies, rate controls, and upstream defenses can reduce impact; implementation and load determine which resource becomes limiting.

**Reflection** makes third-party services reply to a forged victim address. **Amplification** means responses are larger than the triggering requests. These are separate properties: reflection need not produce a large size increase. DNS and other UDP services have been abused this way, but no particular query type guarantees one fixed response size or multiplier.

```diagram
{"type":"sequence","title":"Reflection and amplification are different effects","caption":"The sizes are a hypothetical measured example, not a DNS default or a recommended test.","actors":["Sender forging victim source","UDP service","Victim"],"steps":[{"from":0,"to":1,"label":"Request: 80 bytes","note":"Source address claims to be the victim","accent":true},{"from":1,"to":2,"label":"Response: 800 bytes","note":"Reply follows the forged source address"},{"from":0,"to":1,"label":"Further forged requests"},{"from":1,"to":2,"label":"Further replies","note":"10× response/request byte ratio in this example"}]}
```

The example's ratio is 800/80 = **10**, assuming both measurements count the same protocol layers. It illustrates arithmetic, not a universal amplification factor. Source-address validation reduces spoofed traffic at its origin. Service operators restrict unnecessary open services and apply supported controls. A victim whose access link is saturated may need upstream assistance because filtering after that link does not recover its capacity.

sections.title: Interception, malware, and social engineering
sections.body:
An **on-path attack**, also called man-in-the-middle, allows an intermediary to observe or alter a communication. ARP poisoning can redirect LAN traffic by associating a gateway IP with an attacker's MAC. Rogue DHCP information or a deceptive wireless access point can create other interception opportunities. The exact behavior depends on endpoints, filters, and existing neighbor state; not every unsolicited ARP is malicious.

Authenticated SSH, TLS, or IPsec can protect a session even over an untrusted path, provided the endpoints validate the expected identity and the implementation is secure. Blindly accepting a changed host key or invalid certificate weakens that protection. Encryption alone does not guarantee availability: an intermediary can still discard traffic.

**Malware** is software intended to perform harmful or unauthorized actions. A virus attaches to other content and runs when that content executes; a worm can propagate without needing a user to manually copy and launch each new infection. A Trojan presents itself as useful or legitimate while performing another action. Ransomware may encrypt data, steal it for extortion, or both. These categories can overlap within one incident.

Patching, reduced privileges, endpoint defenses, segmentation, and tested backups address different parts of the problem. Backups help restoration but do not undo theft or guarantee rapid recovery. Likewise, an installed patch does not prove an already compromised system is clean.

**Social engineering** manipulates people into granting access or revealing information. Phishing can arrive through several channels; spear phishing is targeted, whaling targets senior personnel, vishing uses voice, and smishing uses text messages. Pretexting uses a fabricated situation. Tailgating follows someone into a controlled area. These labels can overlap: a targeted voice call can be both spear phishing and vishing.

A believable message can use correct names, good grammar, and current projects. Teach a trusted verification route rather than a checklist of superficial “bad email” clues. For example, verify an unexpected password-reset request through an independently known helpdesk contact, report the message, and never give a caller an authentication code merely because the caller knows your name.

sections.title: Password attacks and Layer 2 attacks
sections.body:
Password guessing can be online, through a login service, or offline against stolen verifier data. **Brute force** tries candidate combinations; a **dictionary attack** uses likely words or patterns. **Password spraying** tries a small set of candidates across many accounts. **Credential stuffing** reuses exposed account/password pairs from another service. Stuffed credentials can fail because they are outdated or the user did not reuse them.

A log with many usernames does not reveal the attempted passwords. It can be consistent with spraying, but account enumeration or other guessing could produce similar records. Rate limits and lockouts address online attempts, while a slow salted password hash raises the cost of offline guessing. Salt defeats efficient reuse of one precomputed table across many accounts; it does not make weak passwords unguessable.

| LAN misuse | Relevant control | Important boundary |
|---|---|---|
| Rogue DHCP server replies | DHCP snooping with deliberate trust placement | Trust the legitimate server path, not every uplink automatically |
| Forged ARP bindings | DAI with valid bindings or authorized static policy | Check both dynamic and static endpoint requirements |
| Excess source MAC identities | Port security or suitable access policy | One permitted MAC can still be spoofed; it is not user authentication |
| Unwanted trunk negotiation | Explicit access mode and negotiation policy | Match the design and protect native-VLAN use |
| Unexpected BPDUs/root claims | BPDU guard or root guard in their intended roles | These do not inspect arbitrary user traffic |

A full MAC table does not turn every switch into an unrestricted hub; unknown-unicast behavior remains VLAN- and platform-dependent. Becoming a spanning-tree root does not automatically place every traffic flow through that switch. Use the earlier switching chapters' mechanisms to assess what an attack could actually change.

sections.title: Password policy and its alternatives
sections.body:
A password policy covers account ownership, credential selection, storage, sharing, recovery, replacement after exposure, and removal when access is no longer needed. **Complexity** describes composition requirements such as character classes; **history** prevents configured reuse; **expiry** is a maximum age; **lockout** or throttling limits failed attempts. Know these terms without treating every traditional value as a current recommendation.

Current NIST SP 800-63B-4, for its digital-authentication scope, requires at least **15 characters** for a single-factor password, allowing a minimum of **8** when the password is used only as part of MFA. It calls for blocklisting common/compromised choices, permits password managers, rejects mandatory character-class composition rules, and rejects routine forced changes without evidence of compromise. This is guidance for the covered authentication system, not a claim that every Cisco image implements those controls. An organization's approved policy and platform capabilities still need to be reconciled.

A **password manager** helps produce and retain distinct credentials. Do not reuse the public demonstration passwords in this course on real devices. Longer passwords do not stop keylogging or phishing; controls must also protect the endpoint, transport, and recovery process. A recovery workflow that gives an attacker a replacement credential can defeat an otherwise strong login.

**Multifactor authentication** combines distinct factor categories: something you know, such as a password; something you have, such as a cryptographic authenticator; and something you are, such as a biometric characteristic. A username is an identifier. Password plus PIN is still knowledge alone. A hardware key activated with a PIN can implement possession and knowledge within one authenticator. MFA methods also differ in phishing resistance; manually relayed one-time codes are not equivalent to origin-bound cryptographic authentication.

A **certificate** binds identity information to a public key under a signed trust framework. Authentication requires proof of the matching private key and validation of the certificate's chain, intended identity, usage, and validity, with revocation handling as appropriate. Copying the public certificate is not proof of private-key possession. Private keys must be protected; do not promise that every product makes them non-exportable.

**Biometrics** involve measurement and comparison, so false matches and false non-matches are possible. A biometric is not a secret that can simply be replaced like a password. NIST treats it as part of MFA with a physical authenticator, with an alternative available. In a device-unlock design, a fingerprint can activate a locally protected key rather than be sent to every remote service.

sections.title: The security program: awareness, training, physical access
sections.body:
**Awareness** helps people recognize situations and know where to report them. **Training** develops role-specific skills through instruction and practice. A reminder about suspicious requests emphasizes awareness; a workshop in which staff verify a caller and follow a recovery procedure emphasizes training. A phishing simulation with feedback can contribute to both, depending on its purpose and design. Avoid making the delivery format alone a rigid classification rule.

Physical controls restrict access to rooms, racks, cabling, consoles, and storage. Locks and badge-controlled entrances help prevent entry; cameras and access records help detect and investigate it. Visitor procedures, escorts, and staff practice address tailgating. An unlocked rack or unattended console can undermine remote access controls, but physical access does not guarantee instant privilege on every protected platform.

Programs need owners and follow-through. Record who approves access, how leavers are removed, who reviews alerts, how incidents are reported, and whether restoration is tested. Measure useful outcomes such as reporting speed and correct procedure execution, not only attendance. A banner explains acceptable use; it does not authenticate users, filter packets, or replace consent and policy requirements.

sections.title: Apply and verify device controls
sections.body:
The lab begins with a required policy and evidence worksheet. Its complete SSH setup and bounded quiet-mode test are an optional device extension; learning the security concepts does not require repeating every management configuration drill.

The practical exercise reviews local IOS controls introduced earlier. It separates protection of a stored credential from protection of a management session. SSH protects the session; a supported slow password hash protects a verifier in a stolen configuration; neither replaces access restrictions or account lifecycle management.

| Cisco storage type | Meaning | Treatment |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Cleartext | Protect and replace exposed credentials |
| 7 | Reversible obfuscation | Treat the configuration as revealing the secret |
| 5 | Salted MD5-based hash | Legacy; prefer supported stronger options |
| 8 | PBKDF2-SHA256 | Supported stronger password-verifier format |
| 9 | scrypt | Supported stronger password-verifier format |

Do not infer the type solely from the word `secret`; inspect the result and the software's supported syntax. Modern IOS XE may support `username admin algorithm-type scrypt secret ...`; older simulator images may support only basic secret syntax. Such a fallback teaches the command relationship, not a recommendation to deploy obsolete storage. Some protocol shared keys must be recoverable by the device; their storage requirements differ from a login password verifier.

```ios
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# username admin privilege 15 secret Lab-Admin-Only-2026!
R1(config)# line vty 0 4
R1(config-line)# login local
R1(config-line)# transport input ssh
R1(config-line)# exec-timeout 5 0
R1(config-line)# end
```

This excerpt assumes SSH keys already exist and covers the shown VTY range. Inspect all ranges on the actual device. Privilege 15 is broad administrative access, not least privilege for every user. A production design should grant only the required role.

The following representative state describes a configured remote-login block:

```output Representative show login excerpt
Router presently in Quiet-Mode.
Will remain in Quiet-Mode for 87 seconds.  ← remaining block interval
No Quiet-Mode access list has been configured.  ← no configured source exception
```

`login block-for 120 attempts 3 within 60` defines a remote login failure threshold and a 120-second quiet period. On the documented IOS feature, quiet mode restricts new Telnet/SSH logins; console access remains available. A quiet-mode ACL is a source exception, not a grant of password-free access and not an override of other access controls. It is separate from per-account AAA lockout. Validate behavior on the image and retain a working console before testing. A login delay alone does not identify the control involved.

sections.title: Exam focus
sections.body:
- Distinguish threat, vulnerability, exploit, mitigation, and the impact on CIA.
- Explain attack mechanisms and select controls according to the trust or resource affected.
- Know password-policy terminology, authentication factors, certificate/private-key proof, and biometric limitations.
- Distinguish awareness, training, and physical access control without artificial boundaries.
- Recognize reversible storage, protect backups, and separate legacy lab capability from current security guidance.

lab.title: Evaluate security controls and observe an optional login block
lab.intro:
Evaluate risks, authentication choices, and security-program actions in a required 35-minute paper exercise. An optional device extension takes about 45 additional minutes and demonstrates one remote-login control using a complete supplied setup. It is not a second SSH configuration exam. No Packet Tracer, CML, or hardware execution is claimed; use the paper evidence when the chosen image lacks the feature.

Practice revised September 2026. If you completed an earlier version, repeat the revised exercise and update its checkmarks.

For each decision, write the asset at risk, the evidence, a suitable control, how you would verify it, and what the control would not prove. Complete your answer before opening each solution. Public example passwords in the optional exercise belong only in this disposable lab.
lab.topology:
The following topology is needed only for the optional device extension, Steps 4–9. The required paper exercise needs no simulator.
