
| Device/interface | IPv4 settings | Cable/port |
|---|---|---|
| R1 Gi0/0 | 10.0.0.1 / 255.255.255.0 | Straight-through to SW1 Fa0/24 |
| Admin-PC FastEthernet0 | 10.0.0.10 / 255.255.255.0; gateway .1 | Straight-through to SW1 Fa0/1 |
| Test-PC FastEthernet0 | 10.0.0.66 / 255.255.255.0; gateway .1 | Straight-through to SW1 Fa0/2 |
| Admin-PC RS-232 | Terminal defaults: 9600 baud, 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit, no flow control | Console cable to R1 Console |

No DNS service, Internet connection, or AAA server is required. All Ethernet ports use VLAN 1. Both PCs and all login attempts belong to this isolated exercise.

steps.title: Prioritize a documented exposure
steps.body:
A branch uses a router to reach its payroll service. The current configuration backup is readable by every employee. It contains a reversible type-7 management password that is still accepted. An unsuccessful login was logged from an unexpected address yesterday; its source has not been attributed. The backup is also needed for legitimate recovery.

Write four findings: the asset and security property at risk; the confirmed weakness; an appropriate immediate response; and a claim the login record does not support. Do not treat deletion of all backups as the only way to protect them. Explain why setting a new storage type without changing the exposed credential would be incomplete.

:::solution
The configuration and management credential require confidentiality, while continued legitimate recovery supports availability. Broad access to the backup and the still-valid reversible credential are confirmed exposures. Restrict backup access, preserve relevant evidence, replace the affected credential through an approved change, and verify legitimate access and recovery. Secure the retained backups as well as future copies.

The unsuccessful login does not identify a person or establish that this backup was used. Re-encoding or hashing the same exposed password does not make that password unknown again. Keep the confirmed exposure separate from the unproven explanation of the login.
:::

steps.title: Review a password and authentication policy
steps.body:
The proposed policy for a password-only administration portal is: “Use one shared administrator account, at least eight characters with three character classes, and change the password every 60 days. Anyone who forgets it can ask a colleague for the current value.” The portal can support named accounts, common/compromised-password screening, managed recovery, and an additional possession factor.

Write a replacement policy summary using the lesson's current NIST guidance. Separate password selection, accountability, recovery, and multifactor authentication. Identify one requirement that a router minimum-length command alone cannot implement. Then explain why a password plus a second secret question remains the same factor category.

:::solution
Use named accounts and unique secrets with managed recovery. For the stated password-only use under NIST SP 800-63B-4, require at least 15 characters and screen proposed values against an appropriate blocklist. Do not impose mandatory composition rules or routine expiry in the absence of evidence of compromise; require a change when compromise is indicated. An additional possession factor can make the authentication multifactor, depending on its implementation.

A length command does not implement screening, account lifecycle, secure recovery, or the whole MFA process. Passwords and secret-question answers are both knowledge factors. A longer shared password still fails to provide individual accountability, and colleagues should not distribute the active credential as a recovery process.
:::

steps.title: Choose program actions and interpret a login control
steps.body:
Design three different actions for the branch: a brief reporting reminder for all staff, practice for help-desk staff who recover accounts, and protection of unattended console access. For each, specify one observable sign that it was implemented. A reminder being sent is evidence of delivery, not proof that every recipient can perform the recovery procedure.

Next, read the representative device evidence below. Predict whether a new SSH attempt with the correct password should succeed during the displayed state, whether the already tested console remains available, and what to verify after the remaining interval expires. The output is supplied for reasoning; it is not a recorded simulator run.

```output Representative IOS login state
Configured remote-login block: 120 seconds
Failure threshold: 3 attempts within 60 seconds
Current state: Quiet-Mode
Remaining quiet interval: 87 seconds
Quiet-mode access exception: none
Console local authentication: configured and previously verified
```

:::solution
A reporting reminder develops awareness; role-specific recovery practice develops the ability to perform the task; restricted physical access protects the console. Suitable evidence includes delivery records, a supervised recovery exercise, and an inspected access-control process. Each check has limits, and attendance alone does not prove practical competence.

On the documented IOS feature, the displayed quiet state restricts new remote logins even when the password is correct. Console access remains available. After expiry, inspect `show login` and test a fresh valid SSH session. Do not change a known-correct password to repair a temporary remote-login block. This output establishes a device state, not the identity or intent of whoever generated the failed attempts.
:::

At this point the required guided exercise is complete. Keep your findings and attempt the independent Challenge below. Steps 4–9 are optional device observation; leave their checkmarks incomplete if you did not execute them, and label any substituted worksheet results as predictions.

steps.title: Optional — prepare the supplied management LAN
steps.body:
Use fresh devices and the table's exact cables. Set the two PCs under Desktop → IP Configuration. Open Admin-PC → Desktop → Terminal for R1; decline the initial configuration dialog if offered.

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.0.0.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
```

```ios SW1
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW1
SW1(config)# interface range fastethernet0/1 - 2, fastethernet0/24
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport access vlan 1
SW1(config-if-range)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if-range)# end
```

If this image rejects the combined interface range, apply the same three interface commands separately to Fa0/1, Fa0/2, and Fa0/24. Wait for forwarding, then ping 10.0.0.1 from both PCs.

:::expected
R1 Gi0/0 is up/up at .1/24 and both PC pings work. A successful ping tests addressing and ICMP reachability; it does not yet prove that remote management is configured.
:::

steps.title: Optional — establish and test local management access
steps.body:
The commands below are supplied preparation. Predict what a successful ping, a successful fresh SSH login, and a successful fresh console login each demonstrate before running them.

Keep the console open. Configure length, local secrets, and SSH. If `security passwords min-length 15` is unsupported, record the missing enforcement and continue with the supplied longer lab secrets. This fallback does not claim enforcement. Use the basic `secret` form for simulator compatibility; inspect the actual resulting storage type and record if the image provides only a legacy hash.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# security passwords min-length 15
R1(config)# enable secret Lab-Enable-Only-2026!
R1(config)# username admin privilege 15 secret Lab-Admin-Only-2026!
R1(config)# ip domain-name lab.example
R1(config)# crypto key generate rsa general-keys modulus 2048
R1(config)# ip ssh version 2
R1(config)# line console 0
R1(config-line)# login local
R1(config-line)# exec-timeout 10 0
R1(config-line)# exit
R1(config)# line vty 0 4
R1(config-line)# login local
R1(config-line)# transport input ssh
R1(config-line)# exec-timeout 5 0
R1(config-line)# end
R1# show running-config
R1# show ip ssh
```

If the RSA one-line form is rejected, enter `crypto key generate rsa` from global configuration and supply 2048 at the modulus prompt. Inspect the full running configuration. If a `line vty 5 15` block exists, apply its controls too:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# line vty 5 15
R1(config-line)# login local
R1(config-line)# transport input ssh
R1(config-line)# exec-timeout 5 0
R1(config-line)# end
```

Use this second block only when those lines exist on the selected image. Do not create a different range based on guesswork.

:::expected
A named privilege-15 account and enable secret exist, SSH version 2 is enabled, and every available VTY uses local login, SSH-only transport, and the five-minute timeout. The shown console timeout is ten minutes so you can complete the exercise without accidentally leaving an unattended session indefinitely. Record any unsupported feature instead of treating it as configured.
:::

From Admin-PC Command Prompt:

```text
ssh -l admin 10.0.0.1
```

Enter `Lab-Admin-Only-2026!`. Verify the privilege with `show privilege`. Keep this tested SSH session open while you exit and reopen the console Terminal, authenticate as admin, and return to privileged EXEC. Then close the SSH session with `exit`; the console remains your control path.

On the console inspect `show running-config`, without posting the full secrets elsewhere. Interpret this separate paper excerpt:

```output Representative storage labels, values deliberately omitted
username olduser password 7 [omitted]  ← reversible credential exposure
username neweruser secret 9 [omitted]  ← scrypt verifier; still sensitive
```

The bracketed omissions are not valid configurations to paste. Try Telnet from a PC only as a transport check using `telnet 10.0.0.1`; do not supply a credential if any unexpected Telnet prompt appears. Inspect all VTY ranges if Telnet remains available.

:::expected
A fresh SSH login succeeds and reports privilege 15. Console reauthentication also works. Telnet is unavailable through the configured VTY transport. The paper type-7 entry is reversible; type 9 is a slow verifier but still warrants backup access control and a strong secret. Your simulator's actual type is recorded rather than assumed.
:::

steps.title: Optional — configure remote-login observation
steps.body:
Enable the documented IOS login block and logging features from the console. If `login block-for` or `show login` is absent, perform Steps 6–8 as a paper state exercise using the stated configuration and outcomes; do not repeatedly attempt to trigger an unsupported feature. If only login event logging is absent, use `show login` plus the controlled session results and record the logging limitation.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# login block-for 120 attempts 3 within 60
R1(config)# login on-failure log
R1(config)# login on-success log
R1(config)# logging buffered 16384 informational
R1(config)# banner motd #Authorized lab access only. Activity may be logged.#
R1(config)# end
R1# show login
```

Before testing, predict the effect on a new valid remote login and on console access. Record the configured threshold, watch window, block interval, and whether a quiet-mode exception is shown. Save the working state to a separate project file `security-before-test.pkt` before inducing failures.

:::expected
On a supporting image, login monitoring is enabled with the intended values and starts in normal mode. The banner communicates policy but does not enforce authentication. Existing console access remains available during the later remote block on the documented IOS feature.
:::

steps.title: Optional — observe the bounded login block
steps.body:
From Test-PC, make a small bounded set of new SSH attempts to `admin` using an intentionally wrong lab password. Use at most four failed attempts within the 60-second window and inspect `show login` on the console after each. Stop as soon as Quiet-Mode appears. If the image does not reproduce the documented behavior, stop testing and record its output; use the paper expectation rather than launching a guessing loop.

While Quiet-Mode is displayed, try one fresh SSH login from Admin-PC with the correct password. Keep using the established console to collect `show login` and `show logging`. Do not claim a precise message sequence if the simulator prints different text.

:::expected
With no quiet-mode exception, documented IOS restricts new remote Telnet/SSH logins during the quiet interval, including the correct Admin-PC attempt. The existing console is usable. This demonstrates a remote block, not a per-user lockout, and not permanent failure of the password. A paper result can state “87 seconds remain,” but no actual remaining value is guaranteed.
:::

steps.title: Optional — recover and verify separately
steps.body:
Allow the remaining block interval shown by `show login` to expire while retaining console access. Then run `show login` again and open a fresh successful Admin-PC SSH session. If an unexpectedly persistent experimental block requires rollback, use the console to remove the experimental policy:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# no login block-for
R1(config)# end
R1# show login
```

Reapply the Step 6 `login block-for 120 attempts 3 within 60` command only after normal access is verified and the selected image supports the exercise. Do not change an otherwise correct password to repair quiet mode.

:::expected
Normal mode permits the valid SSH login again. Your notes distinguish waiting for the defined interval from removal of the experimental feature. No wrong credential was promoted to a valid one. Record whether the final configuration retains the supported block or uses the documented paper fallback.
:::

steps.title: Optional — record the final device state
steps.body:
Inspect all VTY ranges, actual secret types, SSH status, and login state. Verify a new admin session, then close unused remote sessions. On R1 and SW1 separately, save from privileged EXEC with `copy running-config startup-config`. Complete each `Destination filename [startup-config]?` prompt with Enter before moving to the next device, then save the project as `security-controls-complete.pkt`.

Add to the required worksheet two gaps this exercise does not implement, such as enterprise MFA, breached-password screening, protected centralized backup storage, or central command accounting. Assign each a suitable control or later chapter rather than declaring the router “fully secure.”

:::expected
The configuration matches the intended local lab design and no induced lockout remains. SSH and console have been tested with fresh sessions. The report distinguishes implemented controls from policy goals and simulator limits; no broad security guarantee is made.
:::

### Evidence to keep

- Your exposure assessment distinguishes confirmed facts, possible consequences, and unsupported attribution.
- Your policy review addresses named access, password selection, recovery, and authentication factors without claiming that one IOS command implements them all.
- Your program plan connects awareness, practice, and physical control to observable evidence.
- If you executed the optional extension, retain before/during/after login state, one fresh successful SSH result after recovery, a verified console result, and any unsupported features. Keep credentials out of shared evidence.

lab.troubleshooting:
- A broad proposal such as “make it secure” is not a control: name the asset, action, verification, and limitation.
- Do not infer credential theft or attacker identity from an unexplained login source. Preserve the observation and investigate attribution separately.
- In the optional lab, an SSH failure before a password prompt requires reachability, SSH status, keys, and VTY transport checks before an authentication diagnosis.
- A previously open console session does not prove future console authentication. Retest it while another verified access path remains open.
- If `login block-for` or `show login` is unsupported, stop the induced attempts and use Step 3's representative evidence. Do not invent an observed quiet interval.
lab.challenge:
A different branch has named administrators with unique passwords and a second-factor authenticator. Its approved help-desk procedure never asks a user to reveal a password or one-time code. An employee receives a call from someone who knows their supervisor's name and requests the current one-time code to “complete a security update.” Meanwhile, a former employee's administrator account remains enabled, and the only recent configuration backup is stored on a routinely lost, unencrypted USB drive. The branch needs both reliable recovery and restricted access.

Write a short response plan that covers the suspicious request, the stale account, and the backup. For each, state one immediate action, one follow-up check, and one limit on what the evidence proves. Choose a relevant awareness or training action without replacing technical access controls with a reminder. This is an independent policy exercise; no devices or attack simulation are needed.

:::solution
Do not reveal the code. End the unverified contact and report or verify the request through the established help-desk channel obtained independently. Knowing a supervisor's name does not establish authorization, and the request conflicts with the approved procedure. A report supports investigation; the call alone does not identify the caller.

Disable the departed user's account through the approved process and review remaining sessions and access assignments. Confirm that fresh access with that account is denied and that legitimate administrators still have access. Account disablement limits future use; it does not establish whether the account was previously abused.

Protect and relocate the usable backup to approved access-controlled, protected storage, assess whether credentials or other sensitive data were exposed, and replace affected secrets where required. Verify that authorized staff can restore a suitable configuration and that unauthorized readers cannot retrieve it. Do not solve the confidentiality problem by destroying the only recovery copy before a protected replacement is verified.

Use an awareness reminder for recognizing and reporting code requests, and role-specific practice for help-desk recovery and administrator offboarding. These support, rather than replace, the account and backup controls. MFA is valuable but does not make a disclosed live code harmless.
:::

questions.prompt: An unnecessary management service still accepts its publicly known default credential. Which term best describes that condition?
options: A vulnerability that exposes the service to unauthorized use.
A completed mitigation because the service requires a password.
A confirmed exploit showing the credential was already used.
A threat actor identified by the default account name.
questions.explanation: The condition is a weakness, not evidence that an attack already occurred. Unauthorized use is a potential threat; using the credential would be a way to exploit the weakness.

whyWrong.1: A publicly known credential does not provide the intended protection.
whyWrong.2: The weakness does not prove that anyone has exploited it.
whyWrong.3: The account name does not identify a person or group.

questions.prompt: An unauthorized change replaces a supplier's bank-account number while the record remains readable and the service stays available. Which security property is directly affected by that change?
options: Integrity of the payment data.
Availability of the application.
Authentication of the person reading the record.
Confidentiality of the stored record.
questions.explanation: The demonstrated harm is improper modification of the record. The scenario does not establish that reading was blocked or that the record was disclosed to an unauthorized reader.

whyWrong.1: The service remains available in the stated facts.
whyWrong.2: The demonstrated action is unauthorized data modification, not a failed reader identity check.
whyWrong.3: The specific evidence concerns modification rather than disclosure.

questions.prompt: Which server behavior is targeted by a conventional TCP SYN-flood mechanism?
options: A receiver's advertised window for already established data transfers.
Application resources used only after the requested file transfer finishes.
Resources retained while incomplete handshakes await their final ACK.
The client's TIME-WAIT state after a normally completed connection.
questions.explanation: A SYN flood can pressure resources associated with incomplete handshakes. Source spoofing is common but not mandatory, and the first exhausted resource depends on implementation and load.

whyWrong.0: An established-flow receive window is different from half-open connection state.
whyWrong.1: The mechanism targets incomplete connection establishment, before that transfer.
whyWrong.3: The described server pressure is not the client's normal closed-connection state.

questions.prompt: Malware spreads automatically from one file server to twelve others through an unpatched service, without anyone opening an infected file. Which propagation category best fits?
options: A Trojan identified solely by its useful-looking installer.
A file-infecting virus requiring the infected host file to execute.
A credential-stuffing campaign using exposed username/password pairs.
A worm propagating through the vulnerable service.
questions.explanation: A worm can replicate and spread between systems without a user running a host file. The scenario identifies automated propagation through a service; this example does not mean every worm uses the same vulnerability.

whyWrong.0: The evidence describes replication through a service, not a disguised installer.
whyWrong.1: The supplied propagation does not depend on opening an infected host file.
whyWrong.2: No reused credential pairs are described.

questions.prompt: Which combination uses two distinct authentication-factor categories?
options: A password and a code generated by a separate possessed authenticator.
A password and a memorized PIN entered into the same login.
A password and a memorized answer to a personal question.
A username and a longer memorized passphrase.
questions.explanation: The password is knowledge and the authenticator provides possession evidence. Distinct categories matter; a username identifies an account and is not itself an authenticator.

whyWrong.1: Both are knowledge factors.
whyWrong.2: Both are knowledge-based evidence.
whyWrong.3: The username is an identifier; only the passphrase is an authentication factor.

questions.prompt: A client authenticates with a certificate and the server validates the expected trust and identity. What additional proof must the client supply?
options: Possession of any copy of the certificate without its private key.
Knowledge of the issuing certificate authority’s private key.
Control of the private key matching the certified public key.
A secret password embedded in the public certificate.
questions.explanation: The public certificate supplies a signed binding; authentication also requires proof of its matching private key. Private-key protection and certificate validation are both necessary.

whyWrong.0: A public certificate copy alone does not prove private-key possession.
whyWrong.1: The client must not possess the CA’s signing key.
whyWrong.3: A public certificate is not a container for the user password.

questions.prompt: Which two definitions of traditional password-policy terms are correct? Select two.
options: History restricts reuse of a configured set of previous passwords.
Expiry sets a maximum age after which change is required.
Lockout sets the minimum password character count.
Complexity sets the number of seconds in a login failure window.
questions.explanation: These are definitions of history and expiry, not a recommendation to impose routine expiry. Current NIST guidance in its scope rejects periodic forced changes without compromise evidence.

whyWrong.2: Lockout concerns failed attempts/access restriction, not length.
whyWrong.3: Complexity concerns composition rules, not the watch window.

questions.prompt: A short monthly reminder tells staff how to recognize unexpected credential requests and where to report them. Which program element is its primary purpose?
options: An audit proving that every recipient followed the required process.
User awareness through recognition and reporting guidance.
Role-specific training demonstrated by observed procedure practice.
Physical admission control enforced at the office entrance.
questions.explanation: The reminder maintains attention and a reporting route. Formal practice can add training; program activities can overlap, so classify the stated primary purpose rather than a rigid delivery format.

whyWrong.0: Sending a reminder is not evidence that each person performed the procedure.
whyWrong.2: The stated reminder does not include a practiced role-specific task.
whyWrong.3: The message does not enforce entry.

questions.prompt: Staff practise verifying a caller through the approved directory and an instructor checks each person's execution of the account-recovery procedure. What is the primary program outcome?
options: Replacing the technical authentication service.
Enforcing physical admission through a badge reader.
Developing and checking a role-specific skill through training.
Proving that future phishing attempts cannot succeed.
questions.explanation: The activity provides practice and checks procedure execution, so training is its primary outcome. It may also improve awareness without proving immunity to future deception.

whyWrong.0: The exercise does not replace authentication controls.
whyWrong.1: No physical entry control is being enforced.
whyWrong.3: A completed exercise cannot guarantee every future response.

questions.prompt: An office wants to reduce visitors following staff through a controlled door. Which control most directly addresses that entry behavior?
options: Retain camera footage without changing how people enter.
Review room-entry records monthly without enforcing individual entry.
Increase the number of signs while allowing shared admission.
Require individual admission and verify visitor authorization.
questions.explanation: Individual admission and visitor procedures address tailgating prevention. Detection and recovery controls remain useful but do not replace the entry control itself.

whyWrong.0: A recording helps detection but does not prevent following through the door.
whyWrong.1: Review can identify incidents later but does not directly prevent this entry behavior.
whyWrong.2: Signs do not enforce one-person admission.

exhibit.title: Supplied security scenario evidence
exhibit.text:
Controlled worksheet: attacker sends an 80-byte UDP request using victim source IP.
A third-party service sends an 800-byte response to the victim.

questions.prompt: Which explanation distinguishes reflection from amplification in this example?
options: Reflection requires TCP; the supplied UDP exchange can demonstrate only amplification.
Reflection redirects the reply to the forged source; amplification describes the larger response.
Both terms mean that a server has cached an incorrect DNS record.
Reflection is the size increase; amplification is the forged reply destination.
questions.explanation: The forged source makes the third-party reply target the victim, which is reflection. The larger response is amplification; neither property requires one universal DNS multiplier.

whyWrong.0: UDP services can be used for reflection.
whyWrong.2: The exhibit does not describe a cache change.
whyWrong.3: This reverses the two mechanisms.

exhibit.title: Supplied security scenario evidence
exhibit.text:
Configured: login block-for 120 attempts 3 within 60
Times shown as HH:MM:SS
02:00:00 admin failed
02:15:00 operator failed
02:30:00 support failed

questions.prompt: The investigation also confirms that the same candidate password was tried against each listed account. Which attack pattern and threshold result fit?
options: Credential stuffing; the successful pairs must therefore have bypassed failure logging.
Password spraying; the shown attempts do not meet three failures within 60 seconds.
An account lockout; every different username shares one expired password.
Single-account brute force; all shown failures belong to one identity.
questions.explanation: Trying one candidate across many accounts is spraying. The stated times keep the failures outside the configured watch window. Usernames alone would not reveal the candidate passwords; the investigation supplies that missing evidence.

whyWrong.0: The records are failures, and the scenario identifies one shared candidate rather than exposed pairs.
whyWrong.2: No account expiry is demonstrated.
whyWrong.3: Several distinct usernames are listed.

exhibit.title: Supplied security scenario evidence
exhibit.text:
Approved gateway: 10.0.10.1 at 0011.2233.4455
Unauthorized laptop claim: 10.0.10.1 at aaaa.bbbb.cccc

questions.prompt: An unauthorized laptop sends the shown gateway claim. Which intended control validates the ARP binding?
options: DAI using approved dynamic bindings or static ARP policy.
An SSH banner stating authorized use.
Root guard selecting the spanning-tree root.
Port security allowing that laptop’s one observed source MAC.
questions.explanation: DAI addresses ARP validation on its inspected ports. The legitimate gateway binding must be covered by the approved trust/static policy; a one-MAC allowance alone does not establish the claimed IP ownership.

whyWrong.1: A banner does not inspect ARP.
whyWrong.2: Root guard handles BPDUs, not ARP bindings.
whyWrong.3: One MAC can make a false IP claim without exceeding its allowed count.

exhibit.title: Supplied security scenario evidence
exhibit.text:
Representative labels; values omitted:
enable password 7 [value]
username admin password 7 [value]
line password 7 [value]

questions.prompt: What exposure is established if the following configuration is broadly readable?
options: The type-7 values are strong one-way password verifiers.
The type-7 credentials are recoverable from their reversible representation.
Readers must obtain a separate per-device decryption key for type 7.
Only the line credential is recoverable; the username uses a different type.
questions.explanation: Type 7 is reversible obfuscation. Restrict the exposed file and rotate affected secrets under the incident process; conversion to a hash alone does not undo disclosure.

whyWrong.0: Type 7 is not a one-way verifier.
whyWrong.2: Type-7 recovery does not require a unique device-held key.
whyWrong.3: All shown credentials have the same type label.

exhibit.title: Supplied security scenario evidence
exhibit.text:
show login:
Router presently in Quiet-Mode.
Will remain in Quiet-Mode for 87 seconds.
No Quiet-Mode access list has been configured.

questions.prompt: On the documented IOS login-block feature, why can a correct new SSH attempt be refused in this state?
options: The console must also be unavailable for the same interval.
The SSH RSA key pair must be expired.
The remote quiet-mode control is active and no source exception is configured.
The displayed state proves a permanent per-user AAA lockout.
questions.explanation: Quiet mode restricts new remote login attempts under this feature. The console remains a separate recovery path; the output does not identify account lockout or a cryptographic key problem.

whyWrong.0: The documented feature retains console access.
whyWrong.1: No key expiry is shown.
whyWrong.3: Remote quiet mode is distinct from per-user AAA lockout.

questions.prompt: A covered password service already meets its approved length requirement. Which response to a confirmed exposed password matches the current NIST guidance described here?
options: Retain the exposed value and require one extra character class only at the next routine change.
Disable blocked-password screening because a longer replacement makes screening redundant.
Wait for the normal expiry date because changing early would weaken history.
Change the exposed password, screen its replacement against the blocklist, and review the recovery process.
questions.explanation: Compromise evidence calls for a change, even though arbitrary periodic changes are not recommended in this guidance. Length alone does not replace blocked-value screening, safe recovery or investigation of the exposure.

whyWrong.0: A later composition rule does not revoke the exposed password.
whyWrong.1: Long passwords can still be known or compromised values.
whyWrong.2: A routine schedule is not a reason to leave a compromised authenticator active.

questions.prompt: A caller knows your manager's name and asks for your one-time login code to fix an urgent account problem. What is the best response?
options: Decline the code request and verify through the independently known helpdesk channel.
Share only the newest code because older codes may already have expired.
Ask the caller for a callback number and trust that number alone.
Provide the code if the caller correctly names the current project.
questions.explanation: Correct personal details do not authenticate the caller. Use an independently established contact path and the reporting process without handing over an authenticator.

whyWrong.1: A fresh code may be exactly what the claimant needs.
whyWrong.2: A contact route supplied by the same claimant is not independent verification.
whyWrong.3: Public or leaked context can make impersonation convincing.

questions.prompt: Which priority best follows the combined exposure and business-impact evidence?
options: Treat both as equal because each row contains exactly one weakness.
Defer both because neither record proves that an attack already succeeded.
Patch the isolated test device first solely because its issue was reported more recently.
Address the exposed privileged credential first while planning the lower-impact patch.
questions.explanation: Risk assessment uses exposure, likelihood and impact, not simply issue count or age. The reachable privileged credential on a business-critical service warrants prompt containment; that does not make the test-device weakness irrelevant.

whyWrong.0: One weakness can have very different likelihood and impact from another.
whyWrong.1: Controls should reduce risk before confirmed exploitation, not only after harm.
whyWrong.2: Report recency alone does not outweigh the stated exposure and consequence.

exhibit.title: Two documented risks in a small branch
exhibit.text:
A: public default administrator credential on a reachable business-critical router.
B: an unpatched unused feature on an isolated, powered-off disposable test device.
No exploitation is confirmed. Both have an assigned owner.

cards.front: What is a vulnerability?
cards.back: A weakness that can contribute to harm, such as an exposed default credential or excessive permissions. A required, protected open service is not automatically a vulnerability.

cards.front: What is an exploit?
cards.back: A method or action that takes advantage of a weakness. Distinguish the method from the weakness and from evidence of actual successful use.

cards.front: How do threat and threat actor differ?
cards.back: A threat is a potential adverse event/circumstance; a threat actor is a person or organization associated with intentional harm. Threats can also be accidental or environmental.

cards.front: What is mitigation?
cards.back: A measure that reduces likelihood or impact. It may prevent, detect, correct, or support recovery; no single control removes every risk.

cards.front: What does the CIA triad protect?
cards.back: Confidentiality protects against unauthorized disclosure; integrity against improper modification. Availability supports timely, reliable use. One incident can affect all three.

cards.front: What does a conventional SYN flood target?
cards.back: Resources associated with incomplete TCP handshakes. Spoofing is common but not required; actual exhaustion and effective mitigation depend on the implementation.

cards.front: How do reflection and amplification differ?
cards.back: Reflection sends replies toward a forged victim source. Amplification is a larger response/request ratio measured at the same layer; neither implies one fixed DNS multiplier.

cards.front: How does a worm's propagation differ from a file-infecting virus?
cards.back: A worm can spread between systems without someone launching a host file for each copy. A file-infecting virus attaches to content that executes.

cards.front: How do spraying and credential stuffing differ?
cards.back: Spraying tries few candidate passwords across many accounts. Stuffing reuses exposed account/password pairs, which can succeed or fail. Logs of usernames alone do not reveal the candidates.

cards.front: How does ARP poisoning support an on-path attack?
cards.back: A false IP-to-MAC association can redirect frames. Validated ARP policy and authenticated end-to-end protocols address different parts of the risk.

cards.front: What belongs in a password policy beyond complexity?
cards.back: Ownership, length, blocked choices, uniqueness, storage, recovery, compromise response, and account removal. Traditional history/expiry terms describe controls, not universal recommended values.

cards.front: What are the three authentication-factor categories?
cards.back: Knowledge, possession, and inherence. A certificate file alone is public; proof of a protected private key is the relevant possession mechanism.

cards.front: Is password plus PIN multifactor authentication?
cards.back: Not when both are simply knowledge secrets. A possessed cryptographic authenticator activated by a PIN can combine possession and knowledge.

cards.front: What does certificate authentication require?
cards.back: Proof of the matching private key plus appropriate chain, identity, usage, validity, and revocation checks. Copying a public certificate alone proves no private-key control.

cards.front: Why are biometrics not treated like replaceable passwords?
cards.back: They involve probabilistic comparison and sensitive characteristics that cannot simply be changed. NIST uses them with a physical authenticator as part of MFA and requires an alternative.

cards.front: How do awareness and training differ?
cards.back: Awareness supports recognition and reporting; training develops a task-specific skill through instruction and practice. One activity can contribute to both.

cards.front: What does type 7 in a Cisco backup imply for credential exposure?
cards.back: It is reversible obfuscation. Restrict the backup and replace exposed credentials; changing the stored format alone does not undo disclosure.

cards.front: What does login block-for 120 attempts 3 within 60 configure?
cards.back: A remote-login failure threshold/watch window and 120-second quiet interval. Documented IOS retains console access; a quiet-mode source exception does not bypass normal authentication.

cards.front: What determines security risk beyond the existence of a weakness?
cards.back: The likelihood of harm and its impact, considering exposure, asset importance and existing controls. A score is a chosen assessment method, not a universal law.

commands.task: Inspect login-block configuration and current quiet/normal state.
commands.note: A current state and timer are evidence; a login delay by itself does not identify this control.

tickets.title: Valid remote management sign-ins are refused
tickets.scenario: In this isolated representative case, authorized administrators use 10.0.99.0/24. The console remains accessible. Remote SSH tests with the correct password fail intermittently after unrelated failed login attempts.

exhibits.title: Configuration
exhibits.text:
login block-for 120 attempts 3 within 60
No quiet-mode exception configured

exhibits.title: Current state
exhibits.text:
Router presently in Quiet-Mode
Will remain in Quiet-Mode for 64 seconds

exhibits.title: Events
exhibits.text: Remote failed-login threshold reached, followed by QUIET_MODE_ON

tickets.question: Which explanation follows from the current evidence?
options: A permanent account lockout must persist after the displayed quiet interval.
The active remote quiet interval is restricting new remote login attempts.
A quiet-mode source exception would accept users without their passwords.
A current SSH session proves every new remote attempt must be accepted.
tickets.explanation: The displayed quiet state explains why a correct new remote login can be refused. It is not proof of permanent account lockout, and an established session does not test new authentication. A source exception bypasses only this block, not normal credentials or other access restrictions; preserve the console and test a new session after normal mode returns.
tickets.fix: First use the existing console, observe the remaining interval, and retest a fresh valid SSH login after Normal-Mode returns. If the approved policy calls for a management exception, create its narrowly scoped ACL before applying login quiet-mode access-class. ACL design/configuration is developed in Chapter 34. An exception still requires authentication and does not override other restrictions; preserve evidence and save only the verified policy.

tickets.title: An unexpected login and a broadly readable backup
tickets.scenario: An audit finds an old R2 backup readable by unauthorized users. A separate alert shows one unexpected successful admin login. Investigation has not established which person logged in or how the credential was obtained.

exhibits.title: Backup excerpt
exhibits.text:
enable password 7 [value omitted]
username admin privilege 15 password 7 [value omitted]

exhibits.title: Authentication evidence
exhibits.text: One unexpected successful admin login; no attributable credential-acquisition evidence

tickets.question: Which conclusion and response are justified now?
options: The successful login proves the backup was the only possible credential source.
The backup exposes reversible credentials; treat them as compromised and investigate the login separately.
The type-7 label proves the backup is protected by a one-way hash.
The absence of earlier failures proves the login was authorized.
tickets.explanation: Type 7 establishes recoverable-secret exposure regardless of whether it caused this particular login. Restrict the backup and rotate affected credentials through the approved process while preserving evidence and examining active sessions/configuration changes. Do not claim attribution from an account name alone.
tickets.fix: From an authorized working recovery session, protect the exposed backup, replace all affected credentials with new unique values and supported stronger storage, and verify intended access before retiring old access. Review the unexpected session and changes using the incident process. Do not paste public training passwords into a real repair or assume changing one enable secret covers every leaked shared key.

chapters.summary: Compare authentication, authorization, and accounting; configure IOS TACACS+ and RADIUS management clients; and distinguish a rejected login from an unavailable authentication method.

sections.title: Separate identity, permission, and records
sections.body:
:::facts
- **Authentication** verifies an identity claim; **authorization** determines allowed access or actions; **accounting** records selected activity.
- Classic **TACACS+** uses TCP **49** for separate authentication, authorization, and accounting exchanges.
- Conventional **RADIUS** uses UDP **1812** for authentication/authorization and **1813** for accounting. Legacy **1645/1646** deployments exist; configure matching ports explicitly.
- The router is an SSH server to the administrator and an AAA client to the central service.
- In a login method list, an authentication **FAIL** stops the attempt. An **ERROR**, meaning the method could not complete authentication, can advance to the next method.
- Establish local recovery, bind the intended lists, and test new sessions before saving a management-access change.
:::

Morgan's SSH credentials are accepted by a router, but `configure terminal` is denied by central policy. Authentication succeeded; authorization denied the requested action. An accounting record describing that attempt serves a third purpose. These operations are related, but they are not interchangeable. Logging an action does not authorize it, and successful authentication does not promise privilege 15.

The v1.1 objective compares these concepts. The v2.0 objective additionally requires configuring devices with local usernames and as TACACS+/RADIUS management clients. That requires understanding the complete dependency chain: management transport, server reachability, client identity and shared key, server definition/group, login list, and line binding. Detailed enterprise policy design and a full identity-server deployment are beyond this chapter's scope.

sections.title: Local accounts versus a central server
sections.body:
A local `username` entry can contain both a secret and a privilege level. It is therefore inaccurate to say that local accounts can express no authorization information. Local accounts are useful on a small lab and for controlled recovery. At scale, however, distributing account changes across many devices is difficult, and shared accounts reduce individual accountability.

A **central AAA server** provides a place to maintain identities and policies and receive supported records. Cisco ISE is one example with RADIUS and TACACS+ capabilities; features and licensing depend on the deployed product. The device still needs explicit configuration to request and record the intended operations. Installing a server does not automatically record every command or close every unused local account.

The network device is often called the **NAS**, network access server, in AAA terminology. The NAS sends the AAA request using its own IP source. That address can differ from the administrator's address in the SSH connection. A server's client definition must recognize the NAS source and use the matching shared key. This key protects the client/server relationship; it is different from the user's login password.

```diagram
{"type":"sequence","title":"Two client/server relationships","caption":"The administrator authenticates through R1; the AAA server recognizes R1 as its client.","actors":["Admin-PC 10.0.0.50","R1 10.0.0.1","AAA 10.0.0.100"],"steps":[{"from":0,"to":1,"label":"SSH management connection","note":"PC is SSH client; R1 is SSH server","accent":true},{"from":1,"to":2,"label":"AAA authentication request","note":"R1 is AAA client; server checks its source/key"},{"from":2,"to":1,"label":"Authentication result or challenge"},{"from":1,"to":0,"label":"Continue or reject this login"}]}
```

Plan for outages as well as normal service. A local recovery account needs a protected secret, deliberate privilege, tested console access, and an owner responsible for its lifecycle. Its existence does not mean central rejection should be bypassed. Record when recovery access is used and restore the intended management policy afterward.

sections.title: TACACS+ versus RADIUS
sections.body:
| Property | Classic TACACS+ | Conventional RADIUS/UDP |
|---|---|---|
| Transport | TCP 49 | UDP 1812 and 1813; legacy pairs exist |
| AAA organization | Separate exchanges | Access-Accept can carry authorization attributes; accounting is separate |
| Common role | Device administration | Network access; can also authenticate device management |
| Command control on referenced IOS | Supports per-command authorization/accounting | Does not supply TACACS+-style per-command authorization |
| Protection scope | Body obfuscation; header remains visible | User-Password hiding in the ordinary password case; much other data is visible |

**TACACS+** supports an authentication dialogue, followed by separate requests for authorization or accounting where configured. That separation permits a device to ask whether a particular administrator may issue a command. TCP provides reliable byte-stream delivery, but a working TCP connection is not proof that the shared key, account, or policy is correct.

Older comparisons call TACACS+ body protection “encryption.” RFC 8907 deliberately calls the classic MD5-based mechanism **obfuscation**, because it does not meet modern cryptographic protection expectations. The header is not hidden, and the protocol must be deployed on a protected management path. This distinction improves the familiar exam comparison without suggesting that TACACS+ is a replacement for SSH or a secure transport design. RFC 8907 is a published protocol specification on the Informational track, not a reason to label all TACACS+ protection modern encryption.

RADIUS sends **Access-Request**, followed by **Access-Accept**, **Access-Reject**, or **Access-Challenge**. An Accept can carry attributes such as session restrictions; a Challenge continues the authentication exchange. RADIUS accounting uses Accounting-Request and Accounting-Response. Network access examples include 802.1X and VPN services, but the v2.0 task here is configuring a management client.

For the classic User-Password case, RADIUS hides that attribute using the shared secret; it does not encrypt the whole packet. Avoid “every other attribute is always clear” as a universal rule: other authentication methods, protected attributes, and secure-transport extensions exist. The practical comparison concerns the conventional versions used in this lab, not every later RADIUS deployment.

Explicitly match the server's listening ports. The legacy IOS `radius-server host` form has documented historical defaults that can differ from a current service. A lab or appliance might use 1645/1646; another uses 1812/1813. Inspect and configure the values rather than using a delay as proof of a wrong port. A timeout is also compatible with routing, filtering, client-definition, or key problems.

sections.title: Enable AAA with a tested recovery path
sections.body:
`aaa new-model` enables the IOS AAA framework and changes the authentication behavior available to lines. Cisco documents local authentication for non-console access with just this command on the referenced IOS behavior, but relying on implicit defaults is a poor rollout plan. Define exactly what the console and VTY lines should use. Do not assume console authentication and console authorization are the same setting.

Before enabling AAA, create a local administrative recovery account and enable secret, configure and test SSH, preserve a known working configuration, and keep a privileged console session open. The complete lab supplies these steps. Once AAA is enabled, make an explicit local default and a separate console list:

```ios
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# aaa new-model
R1(config)# aaa authentication login default local
R1(config)# aaa authentication login CONSOLE local
R1(config)# aaa authentication login VTY-AUTH local
R1(config)# line console 0
R1(config-line)# login authentication CONSOLE
R1(config-line)# exit
R1(config)# line vty 0 4
R1(config-line)# login authentication VTY-AUTH
R1(config-line)# transport input ssh
R1(config-line)# end
```

A **named method list** applies where it is explicitly bound. `default` is used where the corresponding default applies and no overriding named list is selected. Inspect every existing VTY range; many devices show additional lines beyond 0–4. Apply the same intended binding and SSH transport to those lines too.

Test a fresh local SSH login. To verify console reauthentication, keep the tested privileged SSH session open while closing and reopening the console session. This gives you a way to correct a mistyped console credential or binding. Merely leaving a preexisting console session open does not prove the next console login will work.

Do not use a scheduled reload as a universal recovery guarantee. It can interrupt a network and restores only the actual saved state after a successful reboot. In this isolated exercise, a separately saved baseline and tested local console are the deliberate recovery mechanisms.

sections.title: Servers and server groups
sections.body:
A **server definition** specifies the address, shared key, and applicable protocol options. A **server group** identifies which definitions a method can use. On supporting IOS/IOS XE, the named TACACS+ form is:

```ios
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# tacacs server TAC1
R1(config-server-tacacs)# address ipv4 10.0.0.100
R1(config-server-tacacs)# key Lab-Tacacs-Key-2026!
R1(config-server-tacacs)# exit
R1(config)# aaa group server tacacs+ MGMT-TAC
R1(config-sg-tacacs+)# server name TAC1
R1(config-sg-tacacs+)# exit
R1(config)# end
```

A RADIUS definition and group use their corresponding modes:

```ios
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# radius server RAD1
R1(config-radius-server)# address ipv4 10.0.0.100 auth-port 1812 acct-port 1813
R1(config-radius-server)# key Lab-Radius-Key-2026!
R1(config-radius-server)# exit
R1(config)# aaa group server radius MGMT-RAD
R1(config-sg-radius)# server name RAD1
R1(config-sg-radius)# exit
R1(config)# end
```

These blocks illustrate two alternatives; they do not make a line use either server by themselves. The legacy forms include `tacacs-server host 10.0.0.100 key ...` or `radius-server host 10.0.0.100 auth-port 1812 acct-port 1813 key ...`. The built-in groups `tacacs+` and `radius` select configured servers of that protocol. The lab uses one server per protocol to avoid ambiguous membership, then provides a modern syntax translation.

With multiple interfaces, a supported `ip tacacs source-interface` or `ip radius source-interface` can make the client source predictable. That interface must exist, have the intended address, and be reachable from the service. The flat lab naturally uses R1's sole active LAN interface. In a routed deployment, explicitly check the source, routing instance, return route, firewall policy, and server client entry.

Group behavior can include server availability state, timers, retries, and selection policy. If one server cannot complete the exchange, another eligible group member may be tried. An authoritative rejection is not a request to search for a server with a more permissive policy. Do not promise a fixed five-second login delay for all configurations.

sections.title: Build and apply method lists
sections.body:
Change only the already-bound VTY list when the server is ready:

```ios
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# aaa authentication login VTY-AUTH group MGMT-TAC local
R1(config)# end
```

The **method order** expresses a policy. `group MGMT-TAC local` asks the group first and allows the local method when the group returns ERROR. A bad password or disabled account that produces FAIL ends authentication. ERROR means the method could not complete the decision; unreachable servers and exhausted timeouts are common examples, but a reachable service can also report an error. Thus ERROR is not simply another word for “the server is offline.”

| Current method result | Next action in this login list |
|---|---|
| PASS | Authentication succeeds; other configured stages still apply |
| FAIL | Deny this attempt; do not try `local` |
| ERROR | Try the next method if one is configured |
| No successful method remains | Deny authentication |

:::trap The recovery account is not a rejection override
Suppose `recovery` exists only locally. A healthy central server that rejects this username prevents the VTY list from reaching local authentication. The separately bound `CONSOLE local` list can still authenticate it. That is the intended distinction, not a broken fallback.
:::

`aaa authorization exec` controls shell access and associated attributes when configured. A login may succeed yet EXEC authorization fail. If the approved outage policy permits specified local accounts and privileges, a corresponding local authorization method can be appropriate. Do not append `if-authenticated` as an interchangeable repair: it accepts an already authenticated user without the same local-user policy check and changes the access policy.

On supporting IOS, TACACS+ command authorization and command accounting can be configured for particular privilege levels and command contexts. “Commands 15” is not a promise that every possible command at every level is checked. Verify the intended policy rather than expanding this introductory management lab into an untested command-authorization rollout. Console authorization is a separate deliberate feature; it is not enabled in this lab.

**Accounting** records selected events. `aaa accounting exec default start-stop group MGMT-TAC` requests session start and stop records; `stop-only` requests a stop record. It does not configure per-command records. Delivery still depends on the server path and accounting configuration, and abrupt failures can leave incomplete records. Authentication success does not prove accounting worked.

sections.title: Verify and troubleshoot
sections.body:
Read the configured chain from the line backward: which login list is bound, which methods it contains, which group and server are referenced, and which source/key/port the server expects. Then correlate a fresh test with the client's and server's evidence. Historical counters or a displayed UP state are not proof that the next username will be accepted.

```output Representative authentication evidence
VTY login list: VTY-AUTH
Methods: group MGMT-TAC, local
Current attempt: central authentication rejected  ← a completed denial, not a timeout
Local method selected: no  ← expected after FAIL
```

A supported `show aaa servers`, `show tacacs`, or `show radius statistics` can reveal requests, responses, failures, and timeouts. Simulator output may be less detailed. `test aaa group` can issue an actual authentication test on supporting software; its syntax and supported protocols vary. Cisco demonstrates a named TACACS+ group with the `legacy` form on CML IOL, while some IOS command references explicitly limit the command to RADIUS. Do not assume the CML example works on a Packet Tracer 2911. It also places a test password in command input, so use only a dedicated lab account and avoid exposing real secrets in notes. A successful direct test does not prove that VTY lines select that group.

If login succeeds but the shell is denied, inspect EXEC authorization separately. If local VTY login works immediately and no server requests occur, a local-only list or wrong binding is a strong candidate; cached availability policy can also affect delay, so verify the configuration. If the server reports a rejection, correct the account/policy rather than changing routing without evidence.

A focused authentication debug can help on supporting images, but stop it with `undebug all` after the observation. Preserve useful evidence without publishing credentials. The final proof is a fresh successful intended login, a demonstrated denial, tested outage behavior, and a working recovery path. Save only after those checks match the design.

sections.title: Exam focus
sections.body:
- Compare the three AAA functions and the roles of client, server, user secret, and shared key.
- Know conventional protocol ports and qualified protection differences.
- Build server definitions/groups, method lists, and VTY bindings; local accounts also need deliberate privileges.
- Distinguish FAIL from ERROR and authentication from EXEC authorization.
- Test TACACS+ and RADIUS management access, console recovery, and the actual selected method.

lab.title: Configure and test TACACS+ and RADIUS management clients
lab.intro:
Build local SSH and a tested console recovery path, then configure TACACS+ and RADIUS in separate saved copies of the same lab. Test success, rejection, and service unavailability. The main simulator configurations use classic server syntax; the final worksheet translates them to named server objects and groups. No Packet Tracer, CML, or hardware execution is claimed. Feature and server-policy support vary, so record unsupported behavior and use the specified paper fallback.

Practice revised September 2026. If you completed an earlier version, repeat the revised exercise and update its checkmarks.

The LAN and SSH commands are supplied preparation. Your main task is to trace the selected line, method list, group, server, and result for a **new session**. Before each login test, record a prediction. Afterward, record the username, server state, list selected, available server/device evidence, outcome, and whether the result was measured or supplied on paper. Never put the actual secret in the evidence table.
