steps.title: Cable and address the fresh devices
steps.body:
Create the listed models, use the exact table, and set PC/server IP values in Desktop → IP Configuration. Open the router through Admin-PC Terminal and keep that console available throughout. Decline the setup dialog if offered.

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.0.0.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
```

```ios SW1
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW1
SW1(config)# interface range fastethernet0/1 - 2
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport access vlan 1
SW1(config-if-range)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if-range)# exit
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 1
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# end
```

After forwarding begins, ping .1 and .100 from Admin-PC and ping .100 from R1.

:::expected
All intended local addresses are reachable and R1 Gi0/0 is up/up. These tests establish IP/ICMP reachability; the AAA service and accounts have not yet been tested.
:::

steps.title: Build and verify local SSH before AAA
steps.body:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# username recovery privilege 15 secret Lab-Recovery-2026!
R1(config)# enable secret Lab-Enable-2026!
R1(config)# ip domain-name lab.example
R1(config)# crypto key generate rsa general-keys modulus 2048
R1(config)# ip ssh version 2
R1(config)# line console 0
R1(config-line)# login local
R1(config-line)# exec-timeout 10 0
R1(config-line)# exit
R1(config)# line vty 0 4
R1(config-line)# login local
R1(config-line)# transport input ssh
R1(config-line)# exec-timeout 5 0
R1(config-line)# end
R1# show running-config
R1# show ip ssh
```

If the RSA one-line form is unsupported, use `crypto key generate rsa` in global configuration and answer 2048 at its modulus prompt. Inspect the complete VTY configuration. If the image also has `line vty 5 15`, apply `login local`, `transport input ssh`, and `exec-timeout 5 0` to that existing range in line configuration mode too.

From Admin-PC Command Prompt run:

```text
ssh -l recovery 10.0.0.1
```

Enter the recovery password and run `show privilege`. Keep that tested SSH session open while exiting and reopening the console and verifying its local login. Return to privileged EXEC on the console, then close the SSH session with `exit`.

:::expected
Both fresh access paths authenticate recovery. `show privilege` reports 15. A legacy secret-storage type is a simulator limitation, not a modern password-storage recommendation. Record any unsupported SSH setup instead of proceeding to remote AAA with no tested recovery.
:::

steps.title: Enable explicit local AAA lists and save recovery
steps.body:
Before applying this block, identify which list will protect the console, which list the VTY lines will select, and which database each currently uses. Predict whether enabling a central server later should change the CONSOLE list automatically.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# aaa new-model
R1(config)# aaa authentication login default local
R1(config)# aaa authentication login CONSOLE local
R1(config)# aaa authentication login VTY-AUTH local
R1(config)# line console 0
R1(config-line)# login authentication CONSOLE
R1(config-line)# exit
R1(config)# line vty 0 4
R1(config-line)# login authentication VTY-AUTH
R1(config-line)# transport input ssh
R1(config-line)# end
```

If an additional VTY range was found, bind it to the same named list now:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# line vty 5 15
R1(config-line)# login authentication VTY-AUTH
R1(config-line)# transport input ssh
R1(config-line)# end
```

Use the second block only for an existing range. Repeat a fresh recovery SSH login, keep it open while verifying a new console login again, and return to the console. Inspect the lists and line bindings in `show running-config`. Do not add EXEC or command authorization in this baseline.

Save R1 and SW1 with `copy running-config startup-config` and save the project as `aaa-local-baseline.pkt`. Use Save As `aaa-tacacs-work.pkt` before the next step.

:::expected
Both local-only lists work through their actual line bindings. Recovery remains available independently of the future central server. The separately saved baseline contains no remote-server dependency.
:::

steps.title: Configure the TACACS+ server and client
steps.body:
First fill in the prediction column below for a VTY list that tries the central group and then local. A displayed FAIL and ERROR are different supplied method results; do not treat every unsuccessful connection as one or the other. Keep these predictions for Steps 5–7 and use a separate copy for the RADIUS tests.

| New login case | Predicted next method/outcome | Later observed result and evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Morgan, correct central secret, central method PASS | Write before testing | Record after testing |
| Recovery exists locally; central method explicitly FAIL | Write before testing | Record the actual result or paper substitution |
| Recovery exists locally; central method ERROR | Write before testing | Record after the controlled outage |
| Morgan is absent locally; central method ERROR | Write before testing | Record after the controlled outage |
| Recovery on the separately bound console | Write before testing | Verify a fresh console session |

On AAA → Services → AAA, set Service On. Add a network client named R1 with Client IP `10.0.0.1`, Secret `Lab-Tacacs-Key-2026!`, and TACACS/TACACS+ server type as named by the GUI. Add central user `morgan` with password `Lab-Morgan-2026!`. Do not add `recovery` to the central service. Inspect the resulting client/user rows before configuring R1.

The following uses classic IOS server syntax, commonly available in simulator images:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# tacacs-server host 10.0.0.100 key Lab-Tacacs-Key-2026!
R1(config)# aaa authentication login VTY-AUTH group tacacs+ local
R1(config)# end
R1# show running-config
```

If the classic server command is rejected but named TACACS+ objects are available, use the complete TACACS+ translation in Step 12 and substitute group `MGMT-TAC` in this list. Do not configure both alternatives. If the image has no usable server-client syntax, keep the local baseline and perform the central tests as a paper exercise with the lesson's documented method results.

:::expected
The VTY list now selects the one defined TACACS+ server before local. The default and CONSOLE lists remain local-only. R1 is the server's client at .1; .50 is the SSH user endpoint and would be the wrong client IP for the AAA server entry.
:::

steps.title: Verify central success and an explicit rejection
steps.body:
Open a new SSH session as `morgan` and enter the central password. Inspect the resulting prompt and `show privilege` where allowed, then close the session. This lab configures login authentication only; do not require privilege 15 from the server. On a simple server that returns no privilege attributes, user EXEC is the expected starting point; the enable secret permits the deliberately configured lab elevation.

With the server On, attempt one Morgan login with a wrong password and one recovery login with its correct local password. Inspect server records or supported device evidence for a rejection. If the simulator handles unknown users differently, record it and use the explicit paper FAIL case; service reachability alone is not proof of the returned result.

:::expected
Morgan's intended authentication succeeds. An explicit central FAIL rejects the wrong password and stops the list. If the server explicitly rejects local-only recovery, R1 must not use local as a second chance. The console still uses CONSOLE local. A central ERROR would be a different case even if the service is reachable.
:::

steps.title: Observe TACACS+ service unavailability
steps.body:
Close remote test sessions. On AAA → Services → AAA, set Service Off. Start a fresh recovery SSH login. Then try Morgan, who does not exist locally. From the console inspect supported `show aaa servers` or `show tacacs` output; use Simulation to inspect the request path if available. A disabled TCP service might refuse a connection promptly or produce a timeout; do not require a fixed delay.

:::expected
When the TACACS+ group cannot complete authentication and returns ERROR, the local method can accept recovery. Morgan fails because the local database contains no Morgan account. A delay alone is not proof of this branch; correlate the controlled service state, selected list, and available evidence. Keep the service Off only for this step.
:::

steps.title: Restore TACACS+ service and save its working copy
steps.body:
Turn the AAA service On. Verify a new successful Morgan login and a new console recovery login while preserving a tested active session during the console check. Confirm `VTY-AUTH group tacacs+ local` or the chosen named-group equivalent and CONSOLE local. If a debug was used on supported software, stop it:

```ios R1
R1# undebug all
R1# show running-config
R1# copy running-config startup-config
```

Save as `aaa-tacacs-complete.pkt`. If remote policy must be rolled back, use the tested console and change only the VTY list to `aaa authentication login VTY-AUTH local`, test recovery SSH, and preserve the faulty evidence separately. Do not use `no aaa new-model` as a blind reset recipe.

:::expected
The service is restored and central authentication works. The working TACACS+ copy and independent local baseline remain saved. No debug is intentionally left running.
:::

steps.title: Open a clean copy for RADIUS and match its ports
steps.body:
Predict whether changing from TACACS+ to RADIUS changes the FAIL-versus-ERROR rule. Before configuring a port, record the server's actual authentication listener and the corresponding router setting; do not use a successful ping as evidence that these match.

Open `aaa-local-baseline.pkt`, then Save As `aaa-radius-work.pkt`. This avoids mixing two protocol exercises. Configure AAA → Services → AAA with Service On, client R1 at .1, RADIUS type, key `Lab-Radius-Key-2026!`, and central user Morgan with the table's password.

Inspect the server's displayed or documented RADIUS port. If configurable, select standard authentication 1812 and accounting 1813. If the simulator fixes the authentication port at 1645, use the explicit legacy pair 1645/1646 in the alternative below and record it. Do not assume every Packet Tracer release has the same GUI or port defaults. If no reliable port setting/evidence is available, use the standard pair as a paper configuration and do not claim a successful central test.

For a service at 1812/1813:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# radius-server host 10.0.0.100 auth-port 1812 acct-port 1813 key Lab-Radius-Key-2026!
R1(config)# aaa authentication login VTY-AUTH group radius local
R1(config)# end
```

For the documented/observed legacy 1645 service, use this block instead:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# radius-server host 10.0.0.100 auth-port 1645 acct-port 1646 key Lab-Radius-Key-2026!
R1(config)# aaa authentication login VTY-AUTH group radius local
R1(config)# end
```

Choose exactly one. If the classic form is unsupported, use Step 12's named RADIUS block with the verified port pair and group `MGMT-RAD` instead. Accounting is not enabled merely by defining its destination port.

:::expected
R1's server address, client source, shared key, and selected authentication port match the service. VTY-AUTH uses RADIUS before local; CONSOLE remains local-only. The standard and legacy examples differ in explicit port values, not in fallback policy.
:::

steps.title: Verify RADIUS success and rejection
steps.body:
Repeat fresh Morgan authentication, then a wrong Morgan password. Test local-only recovery while central service is On and inspect the actual result. Use `show radius statistics` or `show aaa servers` where supported; otherwise use the controlled accounts, service configuration, and Simulation evidence with a stated limit. A direct `test aaa` command, if available, does not replace the SSH binding test.

:::expected
A valid central account can authenticate. An Access-Reject is a completed denial and does not allow local fallback. An Access-Challenge continues authentication rather than meaning either success or server failure. No per-command authorization or accounting outcome is asserted by these login-only tests.
:::

steps.title: Observe RADIUS unavailability
steps.body:
Set the AAA service Off, close prior test sessions, and attempt a new recovery login. Try the central-only Morgan account separately. Observe the supported request/timeout evidence from the console or Simulation.

:::expected
An unavailable RADIUS method can return ERROR and advance to local, where recovery succeeds and Morgan fails. Retries, dead-server state, and timers affect timing; do not require a five-second pause or infer the selected method from delay alone.
:::

steps.title: Restore RADIUS and save its working copy
steps.body:
Turn the service On, verify a new Morgan session, and confirm the console recovery path. Stop any optional debug, inspect the selected list and complete VTY bindings, and save R1 with `copy running-config startup-config`. Save the project as `aaa-radius-complete.pkt`.

:::expected
RADIUS service is restored, its configured authentication port is documented, and the final copy has no induced outage. The TACACS+ complete copy and local baseline remain separate. An unsuccessful simulator branch is recorded as incomplete execution, not passed from paper expectations alone.
:::

steps.title: Translate both clients to named server objects
steps.body:
Complete a paper configuration from the requirements below before opening the solution. On supporting IOS/IOS XE software, you may then apply one translation to a fresh copy of the local baseline and repeat the fresh-session checks. Do not paste it over existing classic server definitions. If you reached this step because the earlier classic form was unsupported, use the solution directly as the supplied setup for that branch, then return to its tests.

| Configuration component | TACACS+ copy | RADIUS copy |
|---|---|---|
| Named server object | TAC1 | RAD1 |
| Server IPv4 address | 10.0.0.100 | 10.0.0.100 |
| Shared key | Lab-Tacacs-Key-2026! | Lab-Radius-Key-2026! |
| Named group containing the object | MGMT-TAC | MGMT-RAD |
| Login list | VTY-AUTH: selected group, then local | VTY-AUTH: selected group, then local |
| Existing VTY binding | login authentication VTY-AUTH | login authentication VTY-AUTH |
| RADIUS ports | Not applicable | Verified server pair from Step 8 |

Write the object, group membership, method list, and line-binding relationship. Explain why an object can exist without a login ever using it, and why defining an accounting destination does not prove that accounting records are being sent.

:::solution
These alternatives assume the already verified local baseline, including CONSOLE local and the VTY-AUTH line bindings. Choose one protocol per saved copy.

```ios R1 TACACS+ alternative
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# tacacs server TAC1
R1(config-server-tacacs)# address ipv4 10.0.0.100
R1(config-server-tacacs)# key Lab-Tacacs-Key-2026!
R1(config-server-tacacs)# exit
R1(config)# aaa group server tacacs+ MGMT-TAC
R1(config-sg-tacacs+)# server name TAC1
R1(config-sg-tacacs+)# exit
R1(config)# aaa authentication login VTY-AUTH group MGMT-TAC local
R1(config)# end
```

```ios R1 RADIUS alternative
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# radius server RAD1
R1(config-radius-server)# address ipv4 10.0.0.100 auth-port 1812 acct-port 1813
R1(config-radius-server)# key Lab-Radius-Key-2026!
R1(config-radius-server)# exit
R1(config)# aaa group server radius MGMT-RAD
R1(config-sg-radius)# server name RAD1
R1(config-sg-radius)# exit
R1(config)# aaa authentication login VTY-AUTH group MGMT-RAD local
R1(config)# end
```

Use the RADIUS server's actual verified pair: the shown block uses 1812/1813; replace it with 1645/1646 only for the verified legacy service. TAC1 belongs to MGMT-TAC, and RAD1 belongs to MGMT-RAD. The line selects VTY-AUTH, that list selects the named group, and the group contains the server. A missing group member or a different line binding breaks that selection chain even if the object is correctly defined.

CONSOLE remains local-only. These blocks configure login authentication, not EXEC/command authorization or accounting policy. On a supporting image, verify new successful, rejected, and unavailable-server logins through the selected VTY list; restore service afterward. A paper translation is not a measured successful login.
:::

### Evidence to keep

- The saved local baseline and a freshly tested console recovery path, not just an old open session.
- Separate TACACS+ and RADIUS records tracing line → list → group → server; server address, NAS/client address, and actual authentication port must agree.
- Predictions and actual new-session results for success, explicit rejection, and service unavailability, including the account that exists only locally and the one that exists only centrally.
- Supported rejection/error counters, server records, or capture evidence, with unavailable evidence and simulator limitations stated. A delay alone is not a method result.
- Service restored and a new central login verified after each induced outage. Record login authentication separately from untested authorization/accounting features.

lab.troubleshooting:
- New SSH session fails before authentication → check LAN reachability, SSH keys/status, VTY transport and restrictions before diagnosing a password.
- Central FAIL → inspect account and policy; local is not a rejection override.
- Group ERROR → inspect address, source/client entry, key, transport port, path, and service; a ping proves none of the AAA-specific settings.
- No central requests during a fresh login → inspect the selected list and binding; do not infer method selection only from login speed.
- Authentication succeeds but shell fails on an extended setup → inspect EXEC authorization independently and apply only the approved fallback policy.
- If remote access is lost, use tested CONSOLE local and restore VTY-AUTH local. If that recovery was not verified, return to the separately saved baseline rather than guessing through a live management change.
lab.challenge:
Diagnose this independent **paper** management design without modifying the working projects. R3 Gi0/0 is 10.33.0.1/24, the AAA server is 10.33.0.100/24, and Admin-PC is 10.33.0.50/24. The server and PC share the management LAN. R3 also owns Loopback0 at 10.255.33.1/32, and a supported TACACS+ source-interface setting deliberately uses that loopback. The chosen group, key, central account `avery`, and local recovery account have been checked. CONSOLE local has been tested with a fresh session.

The following are supplied findings from two stages of the investigation, not measurements from your simulator:

```output Selected R3 configuration — initial state
aaa authentication login default local
aaa authentication login CONSOLE local
aaa authentication login VTY-REMOTE group MGMT-B local
!
tacacs server TAC-B
 address ipv4 10.33.0.100
 key [agreed lab value omitted]
!
aaa group server tacacs+ MGMT-B
 server name TAC-B
!
line console 0
 login authentication CONSOLE
line vty 0 4
 login authentication default
 transport input ssh
```

```output Investigation findings
Initial fresh Avery SSH attempt: no TACACS+ request leaves R3.
After correcting the VTY list selection:
  server capture sees request source 10.255.33.1
  server client registry recognizes only 10.33.0.1
  server route table has 10.33.0.0/24 connected; no default or host route
Approved design: register the loopback NAS address;
                use R3 at 10.33.0.1 as the server's default gateway.
No additional VTY ranges or path filters exist in this paper case.
```

Identify the initial selection fault and the two independent server-side corrections required by the approved design. Supply the exact R3 line-binding correction and the server client/gateway values. Explain why changing Avery's password, adding the SSH PC to the server's network-client registry, or retaining an old working SSH session does not verify the repair. Finish with a fresh-session validation plan covering rejection and server unavailability as distinct cases.

:::solution
The initial VTY selects `default local`, so the otherwise valid VTY-REMOTE list is unused. Correct the binding from the tested console:

```ios R3
R3# configure terminal
R3(config)# line vty 0 4
R3(config-line)# login authentication VTY-REMOTE
R3(config-line)# end
R3# show running-config
```

Register **10.255.33.1** as the permitted TACACS+ network client with the agreed device/server key. Set the AAA server's default gateway to **10.33.0.1**, as approved, so it can return traffic to the off-link loopback source. The request reaching the server proves neither recognition of that NAS nor a working reply path. Admin-PC .50 is the SSH endpoint, not the source of R3's TACACS+ requests.

The supplied account/key checks do not repair method selection, NAS registration, or routing, so changing Avery's password is unsupported. Inspect the actual VTY binding and server settings, then start a new Avery SSH login and correlate new request/response evidence with its result. An existing session can survive configuration changes and is not that test.

With the service available, verify an explicit central rejection stops the list. In a separately controlled outage, verify that a group ERROR can reach local recovery while the central-only Avery account cannot authenticate locally. Restore service, verify a new central login, and retain a fresh console recovery check before saving the intended configuration. These paper corrections do not assert that authorization or accounting was configured or tested.
:::

questions.prompt: A valid SSH login succeeds, but the server denies configure terminal through a command policy. Which AAA function made that denial?
options: Authentication.
Session accounting.
Authorization.
Command accounting.
questions.explanation: Authentication accepted the identity claim. Authorization decides permitted actions; accounting can record the result without being the permission decision.

whyWrong.0: The identity check already succeeded.
whyWrong.1: Session records do not decide this command permission.
whyWrong.3: Command accounting records an action; command authorization decides permission.

questions.prompt: What role does the separately deployed central AAA service perform in this device-management design?
options: It evaluates the configured central identity and policy requests from R1.
It is R1's local username database and exists only inside that router.
It forwards every user data packet after the administrator logs in.
It is the administrator's SSH client and supplies the laptop's transport connection.
questions.explanation: R1 is the AAA client and sends requests to the central service. That role is separate from the administrator's SSH client, R1's local account database and ordinary packet forwarding.

whyWrong.1: A separate service is not the router's local username table.
whyWrong.2: An AAA decision does not make the service a mandatory data-plane next hop.
whyWrong.3: The administrator's client initiates SSH to R1, not the central AAA exchange.

questions.prompt: Which conventional transport and service port does TACACS+ use?
options: TCP 22.
TCP 49.
questions.explanation: TACACS+ carries its separate AAA exchanges over TCP port 49. SSH to the router is a different client/server relationship.

whyWrong.0: TCP 22 is SSH rather than the router-to-TACACS+ exchange.
whyWrong.2: UDP 1812 is conventional RADIUS authentication.
whyWrong.3: UDP 1813 is conventional RADIUS accounting.

questions.prompt: Which two statements correctly describe conventional RADIUS/UDP? Select two.
options: Its ordinary User-Password protection encrypts the entire IP packet.
An Access-Accept can carry authorization attributes with its successful result.
It uses the TACACS+ TCP-49 per-command authorization exchange.
Authentication normally uses UDP 1812 and accounting UDP 1813.
questions.explanation: Conventional RADIUS combines the successful access decision with associated attributes, while accounting has separate messages/port. The ordinary password-hiding comparison does not mean whole-packet encryption.

whyWrong.0: The conventional User-Password hiding mechanism does not protect the entire packet.
whyWrong.2: RADIUS is not the TACACS+ command protocol.

questions.prompt: Which two statements explain the documented classic TACACS+ device-administration model accurately? Select two.
options: It has separate authorization exchanges that support command policy.
Its UDP transport is what supplies per-command authorization.
Its cleartext header means no shared key is needed.
Its body obfuscation is not a substitute for a protected management path.
questions.explanation: Separate exchanges support TACACS+ command control on relevant IOS configurations. RFC 8907 calls the classic body mechanism obfuscation and requires a secure deployment; do not equate it with modern authenticated transport encryption.

whyWrong.1: TACACS+ uses TCP, and the command policy comes from its protocol/application model.
whyWrong.2: A shared key is still required for the documented protected client/server exchange.

questions.prompt: Which configuration pair must share the same device/server key?
options: R1's SSH host key and Morgan's account password on the AAA server.
R1's local recovery secret and the AAA server's own administrator password.
Morgan's user password and the shared key in R1's server definition.
R1's AAA server definition and the server's client entry for R1.
questions.explanation: The shared key belongs to the NAS-to-server relationship. User credentials and enable access are separate decisions; forcing them to equal the shared key would conflate independent secrets.

whyWrong.0: The SSH host identity belongs to a different connection.
whyWrong.1: These administrative login secrets are unrelated to the NAS-to-server key.
whyWrong.2: The user password and the device/server shared secret serve different checks.

questions.prompt: Which line-configuration command binds the named login list VTY-AUTH?
options: login authentication VTY-AUTH
authorization exec VTY-AUTH
aaa authentication VTY-AUTH
accounting exec VTY-AUTH
questions.explanation: The login authentication line command selects a login list. Authorization and accounting are separate list types and do not bind login authentication.

whyWrong.1: This selects an EXEC authorization list, not login authentication.
whyWrong.2: AAA list definition commands belong to global configuration and use different syntax.
whyWrong.3: This selects accounting rather than the login check.

exhibit.title: Supplied AAA state and configuration
exhibit.text: radius-server host 10.0.0.100 auth-port 1645 acct-port 1646 key [omitted]

questions.prompt: Which listening ports must the server match for the shown classic RADIUS client definition?
options: TCP 22 for authentication and UDP 1646 for accounting.
UDP 1645 for authentication and UDP 1646 for accounting.
TCP 49 for both authentication and accounting.
UDP 1812 for authentication and UDP 1813 for accounting.
questions.explanation: The explicitly configured port keywords select the legacy pair. Do not infer standard ports from the RADIUS name or rely on an image default when the configuration gives the values.

whyWrong.0: SSH is a different management transport.
whyWrong.2: TCP 49 is TACACS+, not this RADIUS definition.
whyWrong.3: Those are the standard pair but not the shown explicit values.

questions.prompt: Which command requests records at EXEC session start and stop on supporting IOS?
options: aaa accounting exec default start-stop group MGMT-TAC
aaa accounting exec default stop-only group MGMT-TAC
aaa authentication login default group MGMT-TAC local
aaa authorization exec default group MGMT-TAC local
questions.explanation: EXEC start-stop accounting requests session lifecycle records. Verify delivery at the server; this does not automatically record every command.

whyWrong.1: Stop-only requests a stop record rather than both lifecycle points.
whyWrong.2: Login authentication checks identity rather than recording the session lifecycle.
whyWrong.3: Authorization decides permitted shell access, not the requested accounting events.

questions.prompt: No local usernames exist in the complete relevant configuration. Why do these VTY logins fail?
options: The VTY line password automatically replaces the absent username database.
A central server definition must precede any local AAA account.

whyWrong.3: A named VTY list can use local accounts without becoming the console list.

questions.prompt: The central method returns an explicit authentication FAIL. What does this login list do?
options: Accept the enable secret even though enable is not a listed method.
Try the local password because every first-method failure means fallback.
Reject this attempt without trying the local method.
Bypass authentication because the server was reachable.
questions.explanation: FAIL is a completed denial and stops authentication. ERROR is the result that can advance to the next method; reachability is not itself permission.

whyWrong.0: The enable method is not part of this list.
whyWrong.1: A rejection is different from a method that cannot complete its decision.

Group result: ERROR
Local recovery account exists and credentials are valid

questions.prompt: All eligible group methods return ERROR and the supplied recovery credentials match a local account. What happens next?
options: The next local method can authenticate the recovery account.
An ERROR is always an explicit credential rejection, so the attempt must stop there.
AAA grants access without checking any remaining method.
The console list replaces VTY-AUTH automatically.
questions.explanation: ERROR permits advancement to the next method. Local still must accept valid account credentials; the line does not inherit the console list and does not become unauthenticated.

whyWrong.1: FAIL is the explicit-denial branch; ERROR means this method could not complete authentication.
whyWrong.2: The remaining local method still makes a real check.
whyWrong.3: A console binding does not automatically replace a VTY binding.

line con 0

questions.prompt: While the central group returns ERROR, which access behavior follows from these explicit bindings?
options: Both paths allow access without validating credentials.
Console waits on MGMT-TAC; VTY ignores its bound list and uses CONSOLE.
Both paths require a central PASS before any local check.
Console uses local immediately; VTY can reach local after the central method cannot complete.
questions.explanation: The console is explicitly bound to a local-only list. VTY-AUTH contains a central group followed by local, so the ERROR branch can select local there; both still require accepted credentials.

whyWrong.0: Local is an authentication method, not no authentication.

10.0.0.50, because it initiates the SSH connection.

Add another central server while leaving the local-only binding.
Bind login authentication VTY-AUTH to the intended VTY lines.
Change only the console binding to VTY-AUTH.

Change the server's client IP to Admin-PC while retaining auth-port 1645.

The selected central method could not complete the exchange, allowing its configured local fallback.

questions.prompt: The approved outage policy allows defined local accounts with their local privilege levels. Which correction meets that policy?
options: Add local as the fallback to the EXEC authorization list.
Enable console authorization to make the remote server reachable.
Remove local from login authentication so authorization no longer matters.
Add if-authenticated and treat it as exactly the same local-account check.
questions.explanation: Authentication and EXEC authorization have separate method lists. A local EXEC fallback can enforce the stated local-account policy after central ERROR; if-authenticated is a different, broader decision and is not interchangeable.

whyWrong.1: Console authorization does not fix server reachability.
whyWrong.2: Removing recovery authentication does not meet the required outage access policy.
whyWrong.3: It does not perform the same local-user authorization policy check.

questions.prompt: Which explanation fits a successful identity check followed by a denied shell?
options: A central authentication PASS automatically overrides every later policy.
EXEC authorization is a separate permission decision that can deny shell access.
The console list must have replaced the VTY list after the password prompt.
A received accounting record must have changed the user's password.
questions.explanation: Authentication and authorization are distinct stages. Inspect the configured EXEC policy and current authorization result rather than repeatedly changing a password the authentication method accepted.

whyWrong.0: Successful authentication does not promise shell permission.
whyWrong.2: Bindings do not switch to the console list automatically.
whyWrong.3: Accounting records do not change passwords.

exhibit.title: Two explicit results for one new SSH session
exhibit.text:
Authentication result: PASS.
EXEC authorization result: FAIL by central policy.
Shell not granted.
The intended login and EXEC lists are bound to this VTY.

questions.prompt: What should happen after the RADIUS Access-Challenge?
options: Treat it as final success and open the shell without the requested response.
Treat it as ERROR and try the local password immediately.
Treat it as Access-Reject and delete the central account.
Continue the supported authentication dialogue; no final acceptance has been shown.
questions.explanation: Access-Challenge asks for further authentication information. It is neither final acceptance nor evidence that the method is unavailable; the client must support the requested exchange.

whyWrong.0: The challenge is not an Access-Accept.
whyWrong.1: A challenge is an ongoing authentication exchange, not method ERROR.
whyWrong.2: It is not an explicit rejection or a reason to remove the account.

exhibit.title: Conventional RADIUS exchange
exhibit.text:
NAS sends Access-Request.
Server returns Access-Challenge with a prompt for further information.
No Access-Accept or Access-Reject has yet been received.

questions.prompt: Which configuration should be compared with the server's observed source before changing credentials?
options: The user's shell-command policy and requested privilege level.
The NAS source selection and its server-side client registration.
The VTY idle timeout and the time of the last interactive command.
The SSH client address and the administrator's browser settings.
questions.explanation: The server receives an unregistered NAS source even though a different client entry has the intended key. Verify how R1 selected that source and register the approved actual source with return reachability; do not substitute the administrator's SSH address.

whyWrong.0: The service cannot yet associate the request with the approved device client.
whyWrong.2: Idle timeout does not change the AAA source identity.
whyWrong.3: The browser profile does not select the router's AAA source.

exhibit.title: Observed request and registered NAS identity
exhibit.text:
Admin-PC SSH source: 10.0.0.50.
Server received the AAA request from R1 address 10.255.33.1.
Approved server client row currently recognizes only 10.0.0.1.
Server reports unknown network client; user policy is not evaluated.

questions.prompt: Which two separate checks are required before claiming the change meets the stated acceptance criteria? Choose two.
options: Remove the local console list to make both paths use the new central method.
Treat the preexisting session as proof that the new method accepted it.
Verify actual receipt of the selected accounting records at the service.
Establish a new login through the changed VTY binding.
Assume authentication success records every command automatically.
questions.explanation: A session established before the edit does not exercise the new login path. Accounting has its own configured scope and delivery, so inspect the required records independently while preserving recovery.

whyWrong.0: That removes the independent recovery path without establishing either criterion.
whyWrong.1: The session's original authentication predates the change.
whyWrong.4: EXEC start/stop accounting is not per-command accounting.

exhibit.title: Incomplete change acceptance
exhibit.text:
Policy requires central authentication and EXEC start/stop records.
The VTY method list was edited while one SSH session stayed open.
That old session still accepts commands.
No new login or server accounting records have been checked.

questions.prompt: Which next investigation is justified without replacing the user password yet?
options: Assume the configured local fallback means the server sent Access-Reject.
Replace the SSH host key because the AAA response is missing.
Trace reply delivery to the NAS and verify the received response can be validated.
Clear every local account because a server-side reply was recorded.
questions.explanation: The server reports a response, but the NAS did not record a usable one for this attempt. Follow the reverse path and client/key/protocol validation rather than equating a sent response with a completed NAS decision.

whyWrong.0: Fallback after ERROR is not evidence of a completed reject.
whyWrong.1: The SSH transport already reached the separate AAA stage.
whyWrong.3: Local account removal does not deliver or validate the central response.

exhibit.title: Correlated fresh authentication attempt
exhibit.text:
R1 selected MGMT-RAD; one request counter increment.
Server capture: matching Access-Request arrives; Access-Accept sent.
R1: no usable response recorded, timeout increases; group result ERROR.
An existing console remains local and available.

cards.front: What are authentication, authorization, and accounting?
cards.back: Identity verification, permission decisions, and selected activity records. Success in one function does not establish success in the others.

cards.front: What conventional transport/port does TACACS+ use?
cards.back: TCP 49 for its separate authentication, authorization, and accounting exchanges.

cards.front: Which service ports must a RADIUS client and server agree on?
cards.back: The explicitly configured authentication and accounting ports. Conventional UDP uses 1812/1813; legacy pairs exist, so verify the service rather than assume defaults.

cards.front: How do classic TACACS+ and RADIUS protection scopes compare?
cards.back: TACACS+ obscures the body, not header; RFC 8907 calls it obfuscation. Conventional RADIUS hides User-Password, not the whole packet. Protect the management path; extensions can differ.

cards.front: Where can RADIUS provide authorization attributes?
cards.back: In the Access-Accept associated with successful access authentication. Accounting uses separate messages. This differs from TACACS+ separate authorization exchanges.

cards.front: Which model supplies TACACS+-style per-command authorization?
cards.back: TACACS+ on supporting device configurations. Configure the intended privilege/context coverage; an EXEC login alone does not enable every command check.

cards.front: What are common TACACS+ and RADIUS uses?
cards.back: TACACS+ for device administration; RADIUS for network access and also supported management authentication. Typical use is not an exclusivity rule.

cards.front: Who is the AAA client during an administrator’s SSH login?
cards.back: The router/NAS is the AAA client of the central service, while it is the SSH server for the administrator. The two source identities differ.

cards.front: What should accompany enabling aaa new-model?
cards.back: A precreated recovery account, tested SSH and console, explicit lists/bindings, and a saved baseline. Verify fresh sessions instead of relying on implicit line behavior.

cards.front: When does a login method list advance to the next method?
cards.back: On ERROR, when the method cannot complete authentication. Explicit FAIL denies the attempt. ERROR can include more than an offline server.

cards.front: How do you define a central-first named VTY list with local fallback?
cards.back: aaa authentication login VTY-AUTH group MGMT-TAC local. Local is a fallback for method ERROR, not a second password chance after rejection.

cards.front: How is a named login list bound to a VTY line?
cards.back: In that line’s configuration: login authentication VTY-AUTH. Inspect and configure every existing VTY range intentionally.

cards.front: What belongs in a named AAA server definition?
cards.back: Its reachable address, matching device/server key and protocol options such as RADIUS ports. Group membership and VTY binding are separate.

cards.front: How is a named server added to its protocol group?
cards.back: aaa group server tacacs+ MGMT-TAC, then server name TAC1; use the radius group type for a named RADIUS definition.

cards.front: What do EXEC start-stop and stop-only accounting request?
cards.back: Session start and stop records, or only the stop record. They do not automatically record each command; verify collection and failure behavior.

cards.front: How should AAA verification combine tests and evidence?
cards.back: Inspect line→list→group→server configuration, correlate a fresh login with supported counters/server records, and test rejection/outage separately. A direct test aaa result does not prove VTY binding.

cards.front: Why does a continuing old SSH session not verify an AAA change?
cards.back: Its authentication occurred before the edit. Test a new session through the intended line and correlate its actual method result.

cards.front: Can authentication succeed while EXEC authorization fails?
cards.back: Yes. Check the separate lists and permission result; a valid password alone does not grant a shell or privilege level.

cards.front: Does a central AAA response shown as sent prove that the NAS accepted it?
cards.back: No. Return delivery and response validation must also work. Correlate the same fresh exchange at both ends.

commands.task: Enable the AAA framework after creating and testing the local recovery path.
commands.note: Immediately follow with deliberate lists and line bindings; do not rely on undocumented defaults.

commands.task: Enter a modern TACACS+ server definition named TAC1.
commands.note: Configure its reachable address and shared key in the server submode.

commands.task: Set this TACACS+ definition’s server address to 10.0.0.100.
commands.note: The AAA server must recognize the NAS source and matching shared key.

commands.task: Set this RADIUS server to 10.0.0.100 with standard authentication and accounting UDP ports explicitly.
commands.note: The actual service must listen on the same ports; defining accounting’s port does not enable accounting.

commands.task: Create the named TACACS+ group MGMT-TAC.
commands.note: Add the intended named server definitions to this protocol group.

commands.task: Add the already-defined TAC1 server to this TACACS+ group.
commands.note: The referenced definition must exist; a group name is distinct from a login-list name.

commands.task: Make VTY-AUTH try MGMT-TAC first and local only after method ERROR.
commands.answer: aaa authentication login VTY-AUTH group MGMT-TAC local
commands.note: An explicit central rejection stops authentication and does not invoke local.

commands.task: Create a local-only login list named CONSOLE.
commands.note: Bind it deliberately to line console 0 and verify a fresh console login.

commands.task: Bind this console line to the named CONSOLE login list.
commands.note: This is login authentication, not EXEC authorization or a password-free exception.

commands.task: Set the default EXEC authorization list to group MGMT-TAC, then local as the approved outage fallback.
commands.answer: aaa authorization exec default group MGMT-TAC local
commands.note: if-authenticated is not an equivalent local-user policy check. Test remote authorization without extending it to the console blindly.

commands.task: Define the default EXEC accounting list to request start/stop records through MGMT-TAC.
commands.answer: aaa accounting exec default start-stop group MGMT-TAC
commands.note: Verify actual server receipt; this is session accounting rather than automatic per-command accounting.

tickets.title: New SSH sign-ins fail after an authentication change
tickets.scenario: BR1 is reachable by SSH and a privileged console session remains open. A change selected local AAA for the VTY lines, but the complete relevant configuration contains no local username. These are representative records.

exhibits.title: Current authentication
exhibits.text:
aaa new-model
aaa authentication login default local
line vty 0 4
 login authentication default
 transport input ssh
No username entries

exhibits.title: Observed test
exhibits.text: Fresh SSH reaches authentication and no submitted local account is accepted.

tickets.question: Which missing dependency explains the selected method’s failure?
options: Add a central server even though the selected method is local.
Create a valid account for the explicitly selected local method.
Change only the line password while continuing to select local usernames.
Add EXEC accounting and expect it to supply the missing login identity.
tickets.explanation: The line selects the local username method and the complete configuration contains no such account. A server definition, line password or accounting list does not populate that database. Correct the local identity through the retained console, then test a new VTY session and console recovery before saving.
tickets.fix:
In the disposable lab, from the retained privileged console:
```ios
BR1# configure terminal
BR1(config)# username recovery privilege 15 secret Lab-Recovery-2026!
BR1(config)# aaa authentication login CONSOLE local
BR1(config)# line console 0
BR1(config-line)# login authentication CONSOLE
BR1(config-line)# end
```
Test a fresh recovery SSH login. Keep it open while verifying a fresh console login, then inspect every VTY range and save the intended configuration. Replace public examples with approved unique secrets outside a disposable lab.

tickets.title: The central service sees no requests during SSH sign-ins
tickets.scenario: R2 has one TACACS+ server TAC1 in MGMT-TAC. A controlled new SSH login uses a local account instantly. The central service sees no request and the device’s request counter does not increase. The complete VTY configuration for this test is shown.

exhibits.text:
tacacs server TAC1

aaa group server tacacs+ MGMT-TAC

aaa authentication login default local
aaa authentication login VTY-AUTH group MGMT-TAC local

exhibits.title: Actual selected VTY configuration
exhibits.text:
line vty 0 4
 login authentication default
 transport input ssh

exhibits.title: Fresh-attempt counter comparison
exhibits.text: TACACS+ authentication requests before: 0; after: 0

tickets.question: Which configuration change selects the intended central-first login policy?
options: Bind login authentication VTY-AUTH to the intended VTY range.
Change the central account password before selecting its method list.
Add the same reachable server to a second unused group.
Change only the default list while assuming the explicitly named VTY list is already selected.
tickets.explanation: The VTY explicitly selects default, which is local-only. The central-first VTY-AUTH list exists but does not participate. Binding that intended list preserves the separate local default and console policy; changing credentials or an unused group would not select it. Replacing the default list would change the scope of other users of default rather than implement the specified named binding.
tickets.fix:
Keep the tested local console session open:
```ios
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# line vty 0 4
R2(config-line)# login authentication VTY-AUTH
R2(config-line)# end
```
Apply the intended binding to any additional existing VTY ranges. Test a fresh central success, explicit rejection, and controlled ERROR fallback while keeping console recovery. Save only after those results match policy.

chapters.title: Access control lists
chapters.subtitle: Turn an access policy into IPv4 rules, then test the packet path in both directions.

sources.title: Cisco: IP Access List Overview, IOS 15M&T
Cisco: Creating an IP Access List and Applying It to an Interface
Cisco: IP Access List Entry Sequence Numbering
Cisco: Harden IOS Devices, management access controls
Cisco: Commonly Used IP ACLs, TCP flag matching
Cisco: Classic IOS locally generated packet behavior
Cisco: Clear access-list counters command reference
Cisco: Catalyst 9000 Access Control Lists Configuration Guide

chapters.summary: Configure standard and extended IPv4 ACLs, calculate wildcard matches, edit named and numbered lists, choose interface direction, restrict VTY access, and verify the intended policy without mistaking TCP flags or counters for session tracking.

sections.body: An access control list makes a traffic policy precise. Instead of saying “protect the server,” you identify the clients, destination, protocol and permitted service. You then choose where the router should check those fields. An ACL can be syntactically correct and still enforce the wrong policy because its entries are out of order or it is attached to the wrong interface direction.

sections.title: Start with the access policy
sections.body:
:::facts
- An access control entry (ACE) contains matching conditions and a `permit` or `deny` action. An ACL is a list of those entries.
- For an IPv4 interface filter, the first matching entry decides; traffic matching no entry is implicitly denied.
- Standard IPv4 ACLs match source addresses. Extended IPv4 ACLs can also match destinations, IP protocols and relevant protocol fields.
- Standard numbered ranges: `1–99`, `1300–1999`. Extended numbered ranges: `100–199`, `2000–2699`.
- Wildcard bit `0` means compare; bit `1` means ignore. `host` compares all 32 address bits; `any` ignores all 32.
- `ip access-group NAME in|out` attaches an interface filter. `access-class NAME in` restricts incoming VTY management access.
- Ordinary interface ACLs do not keep a connection table. TCP `established` tests ACK or RST, not a remembered session.
:::

Consider clients `10.100.10.0/24`, a web server `10.100.20.20`, and a file server `10.100.20.30`. The policy is: allow clients to use HTTP on the web server, deny their other traffic to that server, and leave other destinations available. This needs an extended ACL because source addresses alone cannot distinguish HTTP from ping or one server from another.

Write down what must remain available before configuring: application requests, their replies, DNS if names are used, and your management connection. Also identify the default policy. “Permit listed services, deny everything else” requires no final broad permit. “Block these exceptions, allow the rest” does. Neither is universally correct; the requirement decides.

ACLs are also used as selectors by NAT, QoS and VPN features. In those contexts an ACL match identifies traffic for another action. A `deny` in a NAT selection ACL normally excludes traffic from that translation rule; it does **not** by itself mean an interface discarded the packet. Always identify the command referencing the ACL before interpreting its effect.

sections.title: First match and implicit deny
sections.body:
For an interface filter, evaluate entries from the top of the effective list and stop at the first match. A matching permit lets the packet continue through processing; it does not supply a missing route or override a later filter. A matching deny discards it. A nonempty list also has an implicit deny at its end, even when no deny appears in the displayed configuration.

```output Representative CLIENTS-IN rules
10 permit tcp 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.100.20.20 eq 80
20 deny ip 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.100.20.20
30 permit ip any any
```

A TCP request from `10.100.10.11:51000` to `10.100.20.20:80` matches entry 10. An ICMP echo from the same client to the same server misses 10 because ICMP is not TCP, then matches deny 20. A packet to `10.100.20.30` misses both destination tests and reaches permit 30. All fields on an entry must match; matching the destination alone is insufficient.

Move permit 30 to the top and the deny becomes unreachable. The router does not search for the most specific ACL entry as it searches for the longest matching route. Specific exceptions therefore normally precede broader rules. Likewise, a list containing only denies blocks all IPv4 traffic evaluated by that filter: an unmatched packet reaches the implicit deny.

On the classic IOS interface behavior documented for these labs, a referenced list that is absent or empty does not provide a deny-all filter. Once entries exist, implicit deny becomes relevant. Do not use an empty list as a security policy or build a restrictive list one line at a time while it is live. Prepare the complete list before attachment. Platform-specific ACL features can have different behavior, so use the documentation for the device being configured.

sections.title: Wildcard masks
sections.body:
An IPv4 address is 32 bits. The wildcard chooses which of those bits the ACL compares. For the pair `10.100.10.64 0.0.0.31`, the first three octets must match exactly. In the final octet, `64` is `01000000` and `31` is `00011111`. The first three bits must therefore be `010`; the remaining five may vary. That matches `.64` through `.95`.

For a subnet, subtract its mask from `255.255.255.255`, octet by octet. A /27 mask is `255.255.255.224`; its wildcard is `0.0.0.31`. Write the subnet's network address as the base for clarity. The ACL compares addresses, including the network and broadcast values; it does not automatically remove values that cannot be ordinary host assignments.

| Intended set | Address and wildcard | Matching address range |
|---|---|---|
| One server | `host 10.100.20.20` | Only `10.100.20.20` |
| /24 | `10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255` | `10.100.10.0–10.100.10.255` |
| /27 | `10.100.10.64 0.0.0.31` | `10.100.10.64–10.100.10.95` |
| /30 | `10.100.10.4 0.0.0.3` | `10.100.10.4–10.100.10.7` |
| /20 | `172.16.32.0 0.0.15.255` | `172.16.32.0–172.16.47.255` |
| /21 | `192.168.16.0 0.0.7.255` | `192.168.16.0–192.168.23.255` |

The shortcuts are `host A` = `A 0.0.0.0`, and `any` = `0.0.0.0 255.255.255.255`. Ignored bits in the base do not affect the match: `.77` with wildcard `0.0.0.31` describes the same last-octet set as `.64`, because both begin `010`. Network-aligned notation is easier to review, but alignment is not an additional wildcard matching rule.

A wildcard need not be the inverse of a valid subnet mask. For example, `10.1.1.0 0.0.254.255` compares only the lowest bit of the third octet. That bit is `1`, so it matches odd third octets, including `10.1.1.0/24`, `10.1.3.0/24` and `10.1.255.0/24`. It does not describe one contiguous subnet. The general test is `(packet XOR base) AND (NOT wildcard) = 0`; the simpler block-range shortcut works only for the corresponding contiguous pattern.

:::trap Using a subnet mask as a wildcard
`10.100.10.0 255.255.255.0` ignores the first three octets and compares the last octet to zero. It matches `192.0.2.0` and excludes `10.100.10.25`. IOS can accept a logically wrong wildcard because noncontiguous wildcards are legitimate syntax.
:::

sections.title: Standard ACLs
sections.body:
A standard ACL can permit PC-A while denying other sources, but it cannot select a particular destination or service. This numbered example allows only PC-A through whichever filter references it:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# access-list 10 permit host 10.100.10.10
R1(config)# access-list 10 deny any
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip access-group 10 out
R1(config-if)# end
```

Here G0/1 faces the entire server LAN. PC-A can reach both servers; PC-B can reach neither. The explicit deny documents the policy and provides an observable entry. Omitting it gives the same forwarding decision through implicit deny, but usually less useful counter evidence.

The usual placement guideline is to put a standard ACL near the destination. Denying PC-B inbound on the client LAN would also block its traffic to other destinations. Filtering outbound toward the protected LAN confines the effect to that path. A standard list still cannot distinguish two hosts on that same destination LAN: use an extended ACL if one must remain available while the other is blocked.

Named standard ACLs express the same source-only conditions under `ip access-list standard NAME`. Naming does not make an ACL extended. Standard and extended describe matching capability; numbered and named describe how you identify the list. Recognize all four combinations required by the IPv4 ACL objective.

sections.title: Extended ACLs and return traffic
sections.body:
Read an extended ACE in this order: action, protocol, source, optional source-port test, destination, optional destination-port test, additional options. Use `ip` for all IPv4 protocols, `tcp` or `udp` when ports matter, and `icmp` when matching messages such as `echo` or `echo-reply`.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# access-list 101 permit tcp 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.100.20.20 eq 80
R1(config)# access-list 101 deny ip 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.100.20.20
R1(config)# access-list 101 permit ip any any
R1(config)# end
```

The `eq 80` follows the destination and matches the service port on the server. Moving it after the source would require the client to use source port 80, which ordinary web requests do not. For the reply, the addresses reverse and TCP source port is 80; its destination is the client's chosen port. Treat it as a separate packet through a separate interface direction.

| Operator | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `eq` | Equal | `eq 443` |
| `neq` | Not equal | `neq 23` |
| `lt` | Less than | `lt 1024` |
| `gt` | Greater than | `gt 1023` |
| `range` | Inclusive range | `range 10000 10010` |

Port numbers are unambiguous; IOS may display familiar aliases such as `www` for 80 or `domain` for 53. Use TCP 22 for SSH, TCP 80 for HTTP, TCP 443 for HTTPS, and both UDP and TCP 53 when a DNS policy must support both transports. A permit for one transport does not permit the other.

The TCP option `established` matches when **ACK or RST is set**. A normal initial SYN lacks both and misses that entry. A SYN-ACK response matches. However, a packet with a forged ACK also matches, even when no client opened a session. An ordinary ACL does not validate that a packet belongs to a connection. A stateful firewall maintains connection state and applies additional checks; this keyword does not turn the ACL into one.

ICMP echo and echo-reply also need separate consideration. Their meaning does not determine interface direction: a server can send an echo request too. UDP has no TCP flags, so `established` cannot help its replies. If filtering both directions, write the necessary reverse rules explicitly and test them with the intended application.

sections.title: Names, sequence numbers and safe edits
sections.body:
Use meaningful names and short remarks. A named extended ACL is easier to edit when you assign sequence numbers explicitly:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip access-list extended CLIENTS-IN
R1(config-ext-nacl)# 10 permit tcp 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.100.20.20 eq 80
R1(config-ext-nacl)# 20 deny ip 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.100.20.20
R1(config-ext-nacl)# 30 permit ip any any
R1(config-ext-nacl)# end
```

On IOS supporting ACL sequence editing, `15 permit icmp host 10.100.10.10 host 10.100.20.20 echo` inserts an exception before deny 20. `no 20` in this ACL's configuration mode removes that entry. `ip access-list resequence CLIENTS-IN 100 10` in global configuration renumbers entries starting at 100 in increments of 10, preserving their relative order. It is housekeeping, not a policy change. Without explicit numbers, IOS commonly assigns increments of ten; always inspect the actual list before editing.

Numbered ACLs can also be edited through named-list configuration mode on supported IOS: `ip access-list extended 101`. In contrast, the legacy global command `no access-list 101` deletes the whole ACL. Cisco also documents legacy syntax that deletes the entire numbered list even when the rest of an ACE follows that command. Use the sequence in the correct submode instead of guessing how a global `no access-list` line behaves.

For a substantial change, build a complete replacement under a new name, review it, then change the interface reference. Keep console access while changing management rules. Do not delete the live list first and create an unfiltered interval. Simulator support for individual editing commands varies; if resequencing is unavailable, keep the existing numbers or build a replacement list offline.

sections.title: Interfaces, direction and VTY access
sections.body:
“In” and “out” are relative to the interface on the device doing the filtering. Follow the packet, not the location of the user. The request enters R1 G0/0 and leaves G0/1. Its reply enters G0/1 and leaves G0/0.

```diagram
{ "type": "topology", "title": "Request and reply use opposite directions", "caption": "CLIENTS-IN on G0/0 inbound checks the request. It is not automatically evaluated for the return packet leaving G0/0.", "nodes": [ { "id": "C", "kind": "pc", "label": "Client", "sub": "10.100.10.10", "x": 1, "y": 3 }, { "id": "R", "kind": "router", "label": "R1", "x": 6, "y": 3 }, { "id": "S", "kind": "server", "label": "WEB", "sub": "10.100.20.20", "x": 11, "y": 3 } ], "links": [ { "from": "C", "to": "R", "toLabel": "G0/0 in", "accent": true }, { "from": "R", "to": "S", "fromLabel": "G0/1 out", "accent": true } ] }
```

For ordinary routed IPv4 interface ACLs, there is one inbound and one outbound list per interface. Another IPv4 `ip access-group` in the same direction replaces that reference; it does not append a second independent list. In the normal forwarding path, inbound filtering precedes the route lookup and outbound filtering follows selection of the egress interface. Place extended filters near the source when that enforces the intended policy efficiently; placement is a guideline, not a syntax restriction.

A VTY access class protects sessions terminating on the router. The following allows only PC-A as a source; SSH and authentication must also be configured, as the lab demonstrates:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip access-list standard VTY-ADMINS
R1(config-std-nacl)# permit host 10.100.10.10
R1(config-std-nacl)# exit
R1(config)# line vty 0 4
R1(config-line)# access-class VTY-ADMINS in
R1(config-line)# end
```

Apply the restriction to every VTY range present on the device; check `show line` and the running configuration. `in` here means incoming management connections. It is not an interface direction and does not filter transit web traffic. An interface ACL can still reject the SSH packet before it reaches the VTY control.

sections.title: Verify and troubleshoot
sections.body:
Check both definition and attachment. `show access-lists CLIENTS-IN` shows entries and supported counters; `show ip interface gigabitethernet0/0` identifies its inbound and outbound lists. An ACL's existence alone proves no attachment.

```output Representative excerpt after controlled tests
Extended IP access list CLIENTS-IN
    10 permit tcp 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.100.20.20 eq www (12 matches)
    15 permit icmp host 10.100.10.10 host 10.100.20.20 echo (4 matches)
    20 deny ip 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.100.20.20 (4 matches)
    30 permit ip any any (8 matches)
```

Record counters before a test and compare afterward. These illustrative totals are not a required Packet Tracer result. A web connection sends multiple packets and may reuse cached content; hardware platforms may update counters differently. A counter increase means the entry matched observed traffic, not that the application completed. A zero counter may mean no matching traffic arrived, the list is attached elsewhere, or an earlier rule matched.

Test from a host whose packet traverses the intended interface. Router-originated probes can have a different source address and processing path; classic IOS outbound filters commonly exclude locally generated traffic. Never use a successful router ping alone to prove a host's ACL path is permitted. For a failure, check links, addressing, routes and application service as well as the forward and return filters. An ICMP error may help localize a rejection, but a timeout does not prove a request passed: loss or filtering anywhere can produce silence.

sections.title: Exam focus
sections.body: Be able to translate a short policy into standard or extended IPv4 ACEs, using both names and numbers. Calculate a wildcard, trace the first match, identify implicit deny, distinguish source and destination ports, and attach the list in the correct direction. Explain why a return packet needs its own evaluation and why `established` is not stateful inspection. V1.1 requires configuring and verifying ACLs; v2.0 explicitly names IPv4 standard, extended, numbered and named lists. IPv6 ACL configuration and advanced firewall design are outside this chapter's required exercise.

lab.title: Build and verify an IPv4 access policy in both directions
lab.intro:
Practice revised September 2026. If you completed an earlier version, repeat the revised exercise and update its checkmarks.

Use a new Packet Tracer file and devices with default configurations. You will establish connectivity before filtering, compare standard and extended lists, insert an exception, restrict management, and diagnose a missing return rule. Work through R1's local CLI tab so a management restriction cannot disconnect your configuration session.

All output below is representative teaching evidence, not a capture from an executed simulator. Exact port aliases, counters and failure messages vary. If output filters such as `| section` are unavailable, read the full running configuration. Sequence editing and resequencing vary by image; a complete replacement-list fallback is provided. The finished lab demonstrates a limited policy, not a stateful firewall.
