steps.title: Address the devices and establish a working baseline
steps.body:
Before configuring, sketch the request and reply across R1: record each ingress/egress interface, original source/destination IP, and the server/client port roles for HTTP. This is supplied addressing setup; the assessed work starts with predicting and enforcing the policies.

Set every PC/server address under Desktop → IP Configuration → Static. On WEB, choose Services → HTTP and explicitly turn HTTP On. FILES is an addressable test host; no file-transfer or SSH server is required.

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.100.10.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.100.20.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
R1# show ip route
```

From both PCs, ping `10.100.20.20` and `10.100.20.30`. From PC-A only, open Desktop → Web Browser and load `http://10.100.20.20`. Leave PC-B's browser unused until the deliberate fault in Step 7. Wait for links and initial ARP resolution before repeating an initially unsuccessful ping.

:::expected
Both routed interfaces are up/up. R1 has connected routes for both /24 LANs; no static route is needed. Both PCs reach both servers, and PC-A loads WEB over HTTP. Correct any baseline failure now. An ACL cannot fix a wrong host gateway or a stopped HTTP service.
:::

steps.title: Permit one source with a standard ACL
steps.body:
Allow only PC-A toward the entire server LAN. Before entering the supplied reference, choose standard or extended matching and predict the results for both PCs reaching both servers. Explain why an inbound source-only deny on G0/0 would affect more destinations. The intended attachment here is outbound on the destination-facing interface.

Keep a test record with columns **stage, source, destination/service, predicted first match, observed result, and counter delta**. Record every required permit as well as every required denial. A failed service without packet-path evidence is not automatically an ACL success.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# access-list 10 permit host 10.100.10.10
R1(config)# access-list 10 deny any
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip access-group 10 out
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show access-lists 10
R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/1
```

Record the displayed permit and deny counters. Repeat pings to both servers from both PCs, then read the counters again.

:::expected
PC-A still reaches both servers. PC-B reaches neither. The explicit deny gives a visible entry for rejected requests on images that report counters. A timeout or unreachable response is possible; neither exact wording nor exactly four matches is required. The outgoing list on G0/1 is 10. This placement restricts the whole server LAN, not an individual server.
:::

steps.title: Apply a service-specific extended policy
steps.body:
The new requirement allows both clients to use HTTP on WEB, denies their other traffic to WEB, and permits other destinations. First draft the three ordered entries yourself. Complete this packet worksheet before comparing your work with the reference. All requests arrive on G0/0.

| Packet | First matching rule/action to predict |
|---|---|
| PC-A TCP source 51000 → WEB TCP destination 80 | Record the matching protocol, addresses and service port |
| PC-A ICMP echo → WEB | Explain which earlier condition fails |
| PC-B ICMP echo → FILES | Explain why the WEB exception does not apply |
| WEB TCP source 80 → PC-A destination 51000 | State whether this G0/0 inbound attachment is traversed |

Build CLIENTS-IN completely, attach it inbound on the client interface, then remove the old standard attachment. Until removal, the old source-only rule is temporarily more restrictive; there is no interval with neither policy attached. The following is a guided reference, not evidence that you independently wrote the policy.

:::solution Compare the ordered policy

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip access-list extended CLIENTS-IN
R1(config-ext-nacl)# 10 permit tcp 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.100.20.20 eq 80
R1(config-ext-nacl)# 20 deny ip 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.100.20.20
R1(config-ext-nacl)# 30 permit ip any any
R1(config-ext-nacl)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip access-group CLIENTS-IN in
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# no ip access-group 10 out
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show access-lists CLIENTS-IN
R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/1
```

:::

If the image rejects explicit entry numbers, enter the three ACEs without them in the displayed order, then inspect their assigned numbers. For the following exercise use the complete replacement fallback if insertion is also unavailable.

From PC-A, reload HTTP on WEB, ping WEB, and ping FILES. From PC-B, ping FILES. Predict the first matching entry before each test.

:::solution Check the packet worksheet after attempting it
TCP/80 to WEB matches permit 10; ICMP echo to WEB misses the TCP entry and matches deny 20; the packet to FILES reaches permit 30. The reply enters G0/1 and leaves G0/0, so it does not traverse CLIENTS-IN inbound.

HTTP to WEB and pings to FILES succeed. Ping to WEB fails because it matches deny 20. R1 shows CLIENTS-IN inbound on G0/0 and no outbound ACL on G0/1. No server reply crosses CLIENTS-IN in its applied direction.
:::

steps.title: Add an exception and inspect the order
steps.body:
PC-A must be allowed to ping WEB; PC-B must still be denied. Before entering the reference, write the protocol, exact source/destination, ICMP message and insertion position. Predict what would happen if you appended the exception after deny 20. Then insert it before that deny.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip access-list extended CLIENTS-IN
R1(config-ext-nacl)# 15 permit icmp host 10.100.10.10 host 10.100.20.20 echo
R1(config-ext-nacl)# end
R1# show access-lists CLIENTS-IN
```

If insertion is unsupported, build CLIENTS-V2 without sequence numbers, in order: the HTTP permit, the PC-A echo permit, the deny to WEB, and the final permit. The following is the complete fallback; use it only instead of insertion, and use CLIENTS-V2 wherever later instructions refer to the active client list.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip access-list extended CLIENTS-V2
R1(config-ext-nacl)# permit tcp 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.100.20.20 eq 80
R1(config-ext-nacl)# permit icmp host 10.100.10.10 host 10.100.20.20 echo
R1(config-ext-nacl)# deny ip 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.100.20.20
R1(config-ext-nacl)# permit ip any any
R1(config-ext-nacl)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip access-group CLIENTS-V2 in
R1(config-if)# end
```

Ping WEB from each PC. On supported IOS, optionally run `ip access-list resequence CLIENTS-IN 100 10` in global configuration and inspect the resulting sequence order. It changes numbering, not the intended policy. If rejected, keep the existing numbers; subsequent steps do not depend on them. Do not assume resequencing preserves counter values on every image.

:::expected
PC-A's echo matches its exception before the deny and succeeds. PC-B's echo still reaches the deny. The HTTP policy is unchanged. An exception below the deny would have no effect.
:::

steps.title: Filter return traffic and recognize the limit of established
steps.body:
Before applying this limited inbound filter on G0/1, classify three packets on paper: WEB → PC-A TCP SYN-ACK, WEB → PC-A ICMP echo-reply, and WEB → PC-A ICMP echo request. Add a fourth invented TCP ACK that has no prior client session. Predict each first match before testing.

Apply this filter on G0/1. It allows TCP segments with ACK or RST set and ICMP echo replies from the server LAN to the client LAN. It blocks other server-to-client packets. It does not verify whether clients really initiated those packets.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip access-list extended SERVERS-IN
R1(config-ext-nacl)# 10 permit tcp 10.100.20.0 0.0.0.255 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 established
R1(config-ext-nacl)# 20 permit icmp 10.100.20.0 0.0.0.255 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 echo-reply
R1(config-ext-nacl)# 30 deny ip any any
R1(config-ext-nacl)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip access-group SERVERS-IN in
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show access-lists SERVERS-IN
```

If explicit sequence syntax was unavailable earlier, omit the numbers here and inspect the assigned numbers. From PC-A, test HTTP and ping to WEB again. From WEB's Desktop → Command Prompt, ping `10.100.10.10`. Then explain the result for an invented TCP packet from WEB to PC-A with ACK set, even though no matching client connection exists.

:::solution Compare the return-packet predictions
PC-A's HTTP responses and echo replies are permitted. WEB's own echo requests are denied. The invented ACK packet would match the TCP permit: that is the important limitation. The observed application behavior is consistent with normal replies, but the ACL has no connection table.
:::

steps.title: Restrict incoming SSH management to PC-A
steps.body:
Create the SSH service first. These credentials are for this isolated exercise. Use the local CLI tab throughout. When the RSA command asks for a modulus, enter `2048`, then continue with the next block. If your image cannot create that key, complete the VTY policy as a configuration review and use a supported IOS image for live SSH; do not silently substitute an insecure production setting.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip domain-name ccna.test
R1(config)# username labadmin secret LabAdmin34!
R1(config)# crypto key generate rsa
```

```ios R1
R1(config)# ip ssh version 2
R1(config)# ip access-list standard VTY-ADMINS
R1(config-std-nacl)# permit host 10.100.10.10
R1(config-std-nacl)# exit
R1(config)# line vty 0 4
R1(config-line)# login local
R1(config-line)# transport input ssh
R1(config-line)# access-class VTY-ADMINS in
R1(config-line)# end
R1# show line
R1# show running-config
R1# show ip ssh
```

The 0–4 range is the baseline used here. If the running configuration also has `line vty 5 15`, enter that range and apply the same three line commands; every available VTY must have the restriction. Without the output filter, inspect the full configuration directly.

From PC-A, run `ssh -l labadmin 10.100.10.1`, enter `LabAdmin34!`, then `exit`. Repeat from PC-B. Also repeat PC-B's ping to FILES to distinguish management control from transit filtering.

:::expected
PC-A can authenticate to R1. PC-B cannot open an allowed SSH management session, but its ping to FILES still works. The client interface ACL permits traffic addressed to R1 through its final permit; the VTY access class supplies the source restriction. Exact refusal wording and VTY ACL counter totals are not required evidence.
:::

steps.title: Introduce a missing return rule and observe the failure
steps.body:
Predict which previously permitted service will fail and which PC-A test should continue working. Then remove only the TCP permit from SERVERS-IN. Use the sequence displayed for that permit; it is 10 in the explicit configuration above.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip access-list extended SERVERS-IN
R1(config-ext-nacl)# no 10
R1(config-ext-nacl)# end
R1# show access-lists SERVERS-IN
```

If sequence deletion is unsupported, remove the exact permit with `no permit tcp 10.100.20.0 0.0.0.255 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 established` inside the named ACL and verify the result. Now open PC-B's browser for the first time and request `http://10.100.20.20`. From PC-A, ping WEB. Read both ACLs before making a repair. In Simulation mode, include TCP/HTTP if needed to confirm that a fresh HTTP connection was attempted rather than relying on a cached page.

:::expected
The HTTP request is allowed into R1 by the client list, but WEB's TCP response reaches the explicit deny in SERVERS-IN. The connection fails. PC-A's ICMP ping still succeeds because echo-reply remains permitted. A working ping therefore does not prove the web application's return traffic is allowed. Stop and record this fault state before Step 8.
:::

steps.title: Restore the rule, retest and save
steps.body:
On an image supporting sequence insertion, restore the missing permit before the deny:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip access-list extended SERVERS-IN
R1(config-ext-nacl)# 10 permit tcp 10.100.20.0 0.0.0.255 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 established
R1(config-ext-nacl)# end
```

If insertion is unsupported, create SERVERS-V2 with the TCP permit, echo-reply permit and deny in that order, then replace the G0/1 inbound attachment. Do not append the restored permit below the existing deny.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip access-list extended SERVERS-V2
R1(config-ext-nacl)# permit tcp 10.100.20.0 0.0.0.255 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 established
R1(config-ext-nacl)# permit icmp 10.100.20.0 0.0.0.255 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 echo-reply
R1(config-ext-nacl)# deny ip any any
R1(config-ext-nacl)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip access-group SERVERS-V2 in
R1(config-if)# end
```

Use only the recovery appropriate to your image. Retry PC-B's HTTP request, both PCs' pings to FILES, PC-A's ping to WEB, and PC-B's ping to WEB. Repeat fresh SSH from PC-A and a denied attempt from PC-B. Confirm both interface attachments and every VTY range, then save:

```ios R1
R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1# show access-lists
R1# copy running-config startup-config
```

:::expected
HTTP works again. Both clients reach FILES. PC-A can ping WEB; PC-B cannot. The SSH restriction remains in place. Press Enter to accept the startup-config filename, then save the Packet Tracer file as `acl-baseline.pkt`. Unattached demonstration ACLs do not filter traffic; document which names are active rather than assuming all displayed lists are applied.
:::

### Evidence to keep

- Your preconfiguration packet worksheet and first-match predictions, including the reversed HTTP endpoints.
- Definition and attachment evidence for the active standard/extended stages; unsupported counters or syntax explicitly noted.
- Successful required services and required denials from the actual clients, including fresh SSH sessions.
- Separate observations of the missing TCP return rule and its recovery; ping success is not the HTTP result.
- Saved startup configuration and project, plus the independent challenge policy and test record.

lab.troubleshooting:
- If both PCs fail before filtering, verify full addresses, /24 masks, gateways, cabling and R1's up/up interfaces. Repeat after ARP resolution.
- If PC-B loses FILES after Step 3, check whether ACL 10 is still attached outbound on G0/1. A second filter can deny a packet the first one permitted.
- If HTTP never matches its permit, inspect whether port 80 follows the destination and whether the server HTTP service is On.
- If an exception has no effect, locate the first matching entry. An earlier deny can prevent a later permit from being considered.
- If an ACL counter does not change, check its attachment, direction, the actual packet fields, and earlier rules. Counters alone do not prove the route or application is healthy.
- If SSH fails for PC-A, confirm SSH is enabled, local authentication is configured, the username is correct, the VTY source matches, and the interface list permits traffic to R1.
- If a command is unsupported, use the stated replacement-list or paper fallback. Do not erase the live ACL in an attempt to reproduce a screenshot.
lab.challenge:
Build a **new** project with the same device models and six-link physical port table, using these fresh addresses. Add one Server-PT DNS connected by straight-through cable from Fa0 to SW2 Fa0/3. The switch ports remain default access VLAN 1. Work from these requirements before opening the answer.

| Role | IPv4 address/mask | Gateway or service |
|---|---|---|
| R1 G0/0 | 10.34.16.1 / 255.255.255.224 | Client /27 |
| PC-A, PC-B | 10.34.16.10 and 10.34.16.11 / 255.255.255.224 | Gateway 10.34.16.1; DNS 10.34.20.53 |
| R1 G0/1 | 10.34.20.1 / 255.255.255.0 | Server /24 |
| WEB | 10.34.20.20 / 255.255.255.0 | Gateway 10.34.20.1; HTTP On |
| FILES | 10.34.20.30 / 255.255.255.0 | Gateway 10.34.20.1; HTTP On for this challenge |
| DNS | 10.34.20.53 / 255.255.255.0 | Gateway 10.34.20.1; DNS On |

Set the PC/server addresses in Desktop → IP Configuration. On DNS create A records `web.challenge.test` → 10.34.20.20 and `files.challenge.test` → 10.34.20.30. The name FILES is a role label; this challenge uses its HTTP service and does not assume a Packet Tracer SSH server. No Internet, NAT, static route or remote management setup is needed.

Write and apply complete named extended lists with these requirements:

1. Both clients may use HTTP on WEB and query DNS with UDP or TCP destination port 53.
2. Only PC-A may use HTTP on FILES. All other traffic from the client /27 to the server /24 is denied. Other client destinations remain permitted.
3. At the server-facing inbound boundary, permit the described HTTP replies from WEB/FILES and DNS replies from DNS; deny other server-side traffic. Use source service ports, and the taught ACK/RST test for TCP. Explain why this is still not session tracking.

Before applying filters, establish the new HTTP-by-address baseline from both PCs to both web services. Calculate the /27 wildcard and predict at least eight flows: both clients to WEB HTTP, both to FILES HTTP, UDP and TCP DNS, client ICMP to a server, and a server-initiated initial TCP SYN toward a client. After attachment, test fresh named HTTP from both PCs, an allowed and a denied destination, and a server-originated ping. Record the first match and actual result. Use a closed/reopened browser or Simulation evidence to avoid treating cached content as a new transaction. If TCP DNS is unsupported in the simulator, evaluate its request/reply tuples on paper and label that row unexecuted.

:::solution One complete policy and verification key
The /27 uses wildcard `0.0.0.31`. On R1, configure the supplied interfaces first; perform the unfiltered baseline tests before adding the lists below.

```ios R1 — supplied addressing setup
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.34.16.1 255.255.255.224
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.34.20.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
R1# show ip route
```

```ios R1 — complete policy
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip access-list extended CLIENTS-CHALLENGE
R1(config-ext-nacl)# permit tcp 10.34.16.0 0.0.0.31 host 10.34.20.20 eq 80
R1(config-ext-nacl)# permit tcp host 10.34.16.10 host 10.34.20.30 eq 80
R1(config-ext-nacl)# permit udp 10.34.16.0 0.0.0.31 host 10.34.20.53 eq 53
R1(config-ext-nacl)# permit tcp 10.34.16.0 0.0.0.31 host 10.34.20.53 eq 53
R1(config-ext-nacl)# deny ip 10.34.16.0 0.0.0.31 10.34.20.0 0.0.0.255
R1(config-ext-nacl)# permit ip any any
R1(config-ext-nacl)# exit
R1(config)# ip access-list extended SERVERS-CHALLENGE
R1(config-ext-nacl)# permit tcp host 10.34.20.20 eq 80 10.34.16.0 0.0.0.31 established
R1(config-ext-nacl)# permit tcp host 10.34.20.30 eq 80 10.34.16.0 0.0.0.31 established
R1(config-ext-nacl)# permit udp host 10.34.20.53 eq 53 10.34.16.0 0.0.0.31
R1(config-ext-nacl)# permit tcp host 10.34.20.53 eq 53 10.34.16.0 0.0.0.31 established
R1(config-ext-nacl)# deny ip any any
R1(config-ext-nacl)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip access-group CLIENTS-CHALLENGE in
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip access-group SERVERS-CHALLENGE in
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show access-lists
R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/1
```

Both clients can resolve and open `http://web.challenge.test`. Only PC-A can open `http://files.challenge.test`; PC-B may resolve that name successfully while its HTTP connection is denied. Client ICMP to a server reaches the client-side deny. A server-originated ping or initial TCP SYN to a client reaches the server-side deny. A TCP ACK with the allowed source port can still pass without a remembered session; a UDP packet from DNS source port 53 can pass without a remembered query.

A router permit or one counter increment is not an application result. Retain the named-page observations and denied-flow evidence together with both attachments. Save R1 with `copy running-config startup-config`, accept its destination filename, and save the new project as `acl-independent.pkt`. Keep the original guided baseline separately.
:::

questions.prompt: What happens to a packet that matches no entry in a nonempty ordinary IPv4 interface ACL?
options: It is denied by the implicit final rule
It uses the action of the preceding matching flow
It is permitted when the route is directly connected
It is evaluated only against the opposite direction
questions.explanation: A nonempty interface ACL implicitly denies unmatched packets. A connected route or a previous permitted flow does not create an exception.

whyWrong.1: An ordinary ACL makes a per-packet decision rather than inheriting a flow's action.
whyWrong.2: Routing does not override an ACL deny.
whyWrong.3: The packet is evaluated in the direction it actually traverses.

questions.prompt: Which two numbers identify standard IPv4 ACLs on IOS? Choose two.
questions.explanation: Standard IPv4 ranges are 1–99 and 1300–1999. Thus 99 and 1400 are standard; the other values belong to extended ranges.

whyWrong.1: 150 belongs to 100–199, an extended range.
whyWrong.3: 2300 belongs to 2000–2699, an extended range.
whyWrong.4: 199 is an extended ACL number.

questions.prompt: On the classic IOS interface ACL behavior used in this chapter, CLIENTS-IN has not been created. What filtering is provided by referencing that absent list with ip access-group CLIENTS-IN in?
options: Implicit deny applies before any entry is created
The last previously attached list remains selected
An absent reference leaves this IPv4 path unfiltered
The empty list inherits the opposite direction's rules
questions.explanation: The documented classic IOS behavior permits traffic through an absent or empty referenced list. A misspelled name can therefore leave the intended filtering absent. Create and review the complete ACL before applying it.

whyWrong.0: The stated classic IOS behavior does not apply implicit deny to the absent list.
whyWrong.1: The reference selects the supplied name; it does not retain a previous list as a fallback.
whyWrong.3: Inbound and outbound attachments do not inherit one another's entries.

exhibit.title: Representative interface and ACL excerpts
exhibit.text:
R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/0
  Outgoing access list is not set
  Inbound access list is not set
R1# show access-lists CLIENTS-IN
  10 permit tcp 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.100.20.20 eq 80
  20 deny ip 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.100.20.20
  30 permit ip any any

questions.prompt: The list was intended to filter traffic arriving from clients on G0/0. Which fault is directly established by this output?
options: No IPv4 interface ACL is attached to G0/0
A broad permit is ahead of the specific deny
The ACL is attached outbound on G0/0
Counters must be cleared before the list can filter
questions.explanation: The interface reports no list in either direction. Defining the list does not attach it to this interface. Its use elsewhere is not established by this excerpt.

whyWrong.1: The displayed list places specific entries before the broad permit.
whyWrong.2: Outgoing also says not set.
whyWrong.3: Clearing counters is optional measurement housekeeping; it does not activate filtering.

questions.prompt: Which two statements are correct for ordinary routed IPv4 interface ACLs? Choose two.
options: One IPv4 list can be attached in each interface direction
Two inbound list names form a combined ordered filter
An inbound attachment also checks replies leaving that interface
A host transit test avoids assuming a router ping follows that path
An outbound permit overrides an inbound deny on the same router
questions.explanation: The ordinary IPv4 attachment provides one list per interface direction. Router-originated traffic can follow different processing and source-address choices, so test from the affected host when checking a transit policy.

whyWrong.1: A second ordinary inbound reference replaces the first; it does not append another list.
whyWrong.2: Inbound and outbound are separate packet directions.
whyWrong.4: A packet denied on ingress does not reach an outbound permit.

questions.prompt: Which two statements describe the TCP established keyword accurately? Choose two.
options: It checks that the segment belongs to a stored connection
It accepts a TCP segment carrying ACK or RST
It requires the initial client SYN to have been observed
It can match a forged ACK without a previous connection
It applies the same return-session test to UDP replies
questions.explanation: Established is a per-packet TCP flag test. It allows typical SYN-ACK and later reply segments, but does not remember or validate that an inside host opened the connection.

whyWrong.0: Ordinary ACLs do not retain a TCP connection table.
whyWrong.2: The decision uses the current flags rather than prior packets.
whyWrong.4: UDP has no TCP ACK/RST flags and requires separate rules.

questions.prompt: R1 has only VTY lines 0–4. Which command, entered under those lines, restricts incoming management connections to sources permitted by standard ACL 10?
options: ip access-group 10 in
transport input 10
access-class 10 out
access-class 10 in
questions.explanation: Access-class 10 in restricts incoming VTY connections by the list. Configure SSH and authentication as well; the access class neither enables SSH nor verifies a password.

whyWrong.0: Ip access-group is an interface attachment command, not a VTY line command.
whyWrong.1: Transport input selects protocols such as ssh, not an ACL number.
whyWrong.2: Out applies to outgoing connections from the line, not the incoming sessions in the requirement.

questions.prompt: CLIENTS-IN is applied inbound on R1 G0/0, facing 10.100.10.0/24. Which entry first matches an ICMP echo request from 10.100.10.11 to 10.100.20.20?
options: 10: the destination is the web server
15: this entry matches the ICMP protocol
20: neither earlier entry matches every field
30: the final permit overrides earlier denies
questions.explanation: Entry 10 requires TCP. Entry 15 requires source .10, not .11. The request therefore first matches deny 20; evaluation ends there.

whyWrong.0: A destination match is insufficient when the protocol differs.
whyWrong.1: All conditions must match, including the source address.
whyWrong.3: Later permits cannot override an earlier match.

questions.prompt: With base address 172.16.32.0, which wildcard matches exactly the /20 subnet?
questions.explanation: The /20 subnet mask is 255.255.240.0. Subtracting each octet from 255 produces 0.0.15.255, covering third octets 32 through 47.

whyWrong.0: This ignores five third-octet bits and matches a /19, twice the intended set.
whyWrong.1: 16 is the block size, not its wildcard. Binary 00010000 ignores only one third-octet bit.
whyWrong.3: This ignores all of the last two octets and matches the whole /16.

exhibit.title: Numbered standard ACL
exhibit.text: access-list 20 permit 192.168.16.0 0.0.7.255

questions.prompt: Which source range matches the displayed entry?
questions.explanation: Wildcard 7 is binary 00000111. It permits the third octet to vary from 16 to 23 while wildcard 255 ignores the last octet. ACL matching includes every address in that set.

whyWrong.0: That would use wildcard 0.0.0.255.
whyWrong.2: The compared high bits require the third octet to remain in the 16–23 block.
whyWrong.3: That /20-sized set would use wildcard 0.0.15.255.

exhibit.title: Representative effective ACL order
exhibit.text:
access-list 101 permit ip any any
access-list 101 deny tcp any host 10.100.20.30 eq 22

questions.prompt: ACL 101 is applied inbound where client requests arrive. The goal is to block SSH to 10.100.20.30 and permit other IPv4 traffic. Why does SSH remain permitted?
options: The final deny overrides the permit only after counters are cleared
Adding established to the deny will catch the initial SYN
The more specific deny should win regardless of sequence
The broad permit accepts SSH before the deny is evaluated
questions.explanation: The first entry matches all IPv4 packets, including TCP destination port 22. Place the specific deny above the general permit.

whyWrong.0: Counter clearing changes measurements, not evaluation order.
whyWrong.1: A normal initial SYN has neither ACK nor RST and would miss established.
whyWrong.2: ACL evaluation uses the first match, not the most specific match.

exhibit.title: Topology and port roles
exhibit.text:
PC1 10.1.1.10/24 -> R1 G0/0
R1 G0/1 -> R2 -> R3 G0/0
R3 G0/1 -> LAN C 10.3.3.0/24
R3 G0/2 -> LAN D 10.4.4.0/24
All routes and baseline connectivity are working.

questions.prompt: A standard ACL denies source 10.1.1.10 and permits other sources. It must restrict PC1 only when reaching LAN C, leaving its traffic to R3 itself and LAN D available. Where should it be applied?
options: R1 G0/0 inbound
R1 G0/1 outbound
R3 G0/1 outbound
R3 G0/0 inbound
questions.explanation: G0/1 outbound on R3 is the path specifically into LAN C. A standard ACL cannot select a destination, so its attachment supplies the destination boundary.

whyWrong.0: This would reject PC1 traffic to every routed destination reached through R1.
whyWrong.1: This would also reject PC1 traffic continuing toward R3 and LAN D.
whyWrong.3: This would reject PC1 traffic arriving for R3 itself and for LAN D.

questions.prompt: An extended ACL must block only TCP destination port 23 from PC1 to SRV. Following the usual placement guideline, where should it first filter those requests?
options: R2 inbound on the transit link
R3 G0/1 outbound
R1 G0/0 inbound
R1 G0/1 inbound
questions.explanation: An extended list can identify this exact source, destination and service. R1 G0/0 inbound rejects the unwanted requests nearest their source, before they cross the transit network.

whyWrong.0: This is farther from the source and does not automatically filter the reverse direction.
whyWrong.1: This could filter the requests, but carries them across the network before rejection and is not the requested placement guideline.
whyWrong.3: Requests leave R1 G0/1; they do not enter it.

exhibit.title: Representative named ACL
exhibit.text:
10 permit tcp any host 10.100.20.20 eq 80
20 deny ip any host 10.100.20.20
30 permit ip any any

questions.prompt: On IOS supporting sequence editing, which action removes only sequence 20 from named extended ACL CLIENTS-IN?
options: Use no access-list CLIENTS-IN 20 in global mode
Enter CLIENTS-IN configuration mode and use no 20
Enter CLIENTS-IN configuration mode and use delete 20
Use ip access-list resequence CLIENTS-IN 20 10
questions.explanation: Enter ip access-list extended CLIENTS-IN, then no 20. Verify the resulting entries; the operation removes the selected ACE rather than deleting the whole list.

whyWrong.0: That is not the named-ACL sequence deletion syntax.
whyWrong.2: Sequence deletion uses no, not delete.
whyWrong.3: Resequencing renumbers remaining entries; it does not delete an entry.

exhibit.title: Representative WEB-ONLY ACL
exhibit.text:
10 permit tcp 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 eq www host 10.100.20.20
20 deny ip any any

questions.prompt: The displayed ACL is inbound on the client-facing interface. A client uses source TCP port 51000 to request WEB port 80. Why is the request denied?
options: The permit tests source port 80 rather than destination port 80
The server's reply requires source port 51000 instead of 80
The final deny overrides a permit even when all fields match
The www alias matches a different service than numeric port 80
questions.explanation: Eq www follows the source address pair. The packet has source port 51000, so it misses the permit and reaches deny 20. Place eq 80 after host 10.100.20.20. The shown rule does not automatically match replies either: the source and destination address conditions would still need to match.

whyWrong.1: The question is about the request; its source is 51000 and destination is 80.
whyWrong.2: A matching earlier permit ends evaluation; the deny does not override it.
whyWrong.3: www is the TCP port 80 alias on the stated IOS syntax.

questions.prompt: What sources match access-list 1 permit 10.100.10.0 255.255.255.0?
options: Any IPv4 source whose fourth octet is zero
Only source address 10.100.10.0
Exactly the addresses in 10.100.10.0/24
No sources because noncontiguous wildcards are invalid
questions.explanation: The wildcard ignores the first three octets and compares the fourth to zero. For example, 192.0.2.0 matches, whereas 10.100.10.25 does not.

whyWrong.1: Matching a single host requires wildcard 0.0.0.0 or host.
whyWrong.2: IOS interprets the supplied value as a wildcard; it does not infer the intended subnet mask.
whyWrong.3: The wildcard bit pattern need not be contiguous.

questions.prompt: Which single ACE matches a UDP DNS query from a client using source port 51000 to server 10.1.1.53 on destination port 53?
options: permit tcp any host 10.1.1.53 eq 53
permit udp any host 10.1.1.53 eq 67
permit udp any host 10.1.1.53 eq 53
permit udp any eq 53 host 10.1.1.53
questions.explanation: This packet is UDP and its service port is the destination port. The correct ACE puts eq 53 after the destination host. A complete DNS policy may also need TCP 53 and separate reverse-path permissions.

whyWrong.0: DNS can use TCP, but a TCP entry does not match the UDP packet specified.
whyWrong.1: UDP 67 is a DHCP server port, not this DNS destination.
whyWrong.3: This tests source port 53; the query source port is 51000.

questions.prompt: Which pair correctly predicts the first match for both packets?
options: A matches 10; B matches 30
A matches 20; B matches 30
A matches 20; B matches 40
A matches 10; B matches 20
questions.explanation: Packet A misses the HTTPS permit and matches the deny for the first /26. Packet B is outside that /26 but inside the /24 HTTP permit. The /26 boundary is .0 through .63.

whyWrong.0: Destination port 80 does not match entry 10's port 443.
whyWrong.2: Packet B matches entry 30, so it never reaches 40.
whyWrong.3: A misses HTTPS and B is outside the deny's /26.

exhibit.title: DNS request and reply endpoints (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Query: 10.34.0.10 UDP/51000 -> 10.34.8.53 UDP/53
Reply: 10.34.8.53 UDP/53 -> 10.34.0.10 UDP/51000
Filter: R1 server-facing interface inbound

questions.prompt: Which ACE narrowly permits the displayed UDP reply?
options: permit udp host 10.34.8.53 host 10.34.0.10 eq 53
permit udp host 10.34.8.53 eq 53 host 10.34.0.10 eq 51000
permit udp host 10.34.0.10 eq 51000 host 10.34.8.53 eq 53
permit tcp host 10.34.8.53 eq 53 host 10.34.0.10 eq 51000
questions.explanation: The reply reverses the query's endpoint roles. Its source service port is 53 and its destination is the client's port 51000. This matches one described packet; it is not a stateful DNS policy.

whyWrong.0: This incorrectly requires destination port 53 on the client.
whyWrong.2: This describes the query direction.
whyWrong.3: The described reply is UDP, not TCP.

questions.prompt: An inbound ACL permit counter rises for a new HTTP request, but R1 has no usable route to its destination. What does that permit establish?
options: The permit creates a temporary route to the destination
The request passed this filter; forwarding still needs a route
The HTTP session completed because the entry matched
The permit bypasses subsequent forwarding and filtering checks
questions.explanation: A permit means that this ACL did not discard the matched packet. Routing, other filters and the application must still work. An ACL does not supply a missing route.

whyWrong.0: ACL permission does not install a forwarding route.
whyWrong.2: A matching request does not prove receipt of an HTTP response.
whyWrong.3: Other processing stages still apply.

questions.prompt: Which addresses match the source pair 10.34.0.77 0.0.0.31? Choose two.
questions.explanation: The low five bits of the fourth octet are ignored. The compared high bits of 77 select the .64–.95 block. Ignored bits in an unaligned base do not create a new .77–.108 range.

whyWrong.0: 63 belongs to the preceding block.
whyWrong.3: 96 begins the next block.
whyWrong.4: The third octet is compared exactly and must be zero.

questions.prompt: A policy must permit client DNS queries to 10.34.8.53 over both supported transports and deny other traffic. Which two request entries are required? Choose two.
options: permit tcp 10.34.0.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.34.8.53 established
questions.explanation: TCP and UDP are separate protocol matches, and a query uses the server's destination port 53. The broad IP permit would exceed the DNS-only policy. Evaluate return filters separately.

whyWrong.2: This incorrectly matches the query's source port.
whyWrong.3: A new TCP DNS connection begins with a SYN that lacks ACK/RST.
whyWrong.4: This admits other protocols and services to the DNS host.

questions.prompt: Two hosts with correct /24 masks share VLAN 10 and communicate directly through a Layer 2 switch. An ACL is inbound on the router's VLAN 10 gateway interface. Why does it not block their direct host-to-host packets?
options: A standard ACL automatically permits all same-subnet addresses
ARP removes the ACL attachment after resolving a local neighbor
Inbound lists inspect only packets destined for the router itself
The hosts exchange those frames without traversing the router interface
questions.explanation: With the stated local addressing, each host resolves the other host directly and the switch forwards within the VLAN. The ordinary routed interface ACL only evaluates traffic that crosses its attachment. A different enforcement point is required for that local path.

whyWrong.0: The path bypasses this attachment; standard ACLs do not have a universal same-subnet permit.
whyWrong.1: ARP supplies a neighbor mapping and does not change ACL configuration.
whyWrong.2: An inbound interface list can inspect transit traffic as well as router-destined traffic.

exhibit.title: ACL counter comparison (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Same ACL, same attachment, no counter reset or reload:
HTTP permit: before 70, after 80
Explicit deny: before 12, after 12
Only the controlled client generated matching test traffic.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion follows from this controlled before/after comparison?
options: The permit increase establishes receipt of the server response
Exactly ten HTTP transactions completed during the test
The unchanged deny proves the whole path permits traffic
Ten new packets matched; application success remains unverified
questions.explanation: The permit increased by ten and the deny did not change during the stated interval. Those are match observations, not a count of web transactions or proof of delivery. Confirm the requested page separately.

whyWrong.0: A request-side match does not establish receipt of a response.
whyWrong.1: One application transaction can produce several matching packets.
whyWrong.2: These counters do not describe other interfaces or filters.

exhibit.title: Forward and return evidence (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Clients: 10.34.0.0/24; DNS: 10.34.8.53
Client-facing inbound ACL permits UDP and TCP queries to DNS port 53.
Server-facing inbound ACL:
 10 permit tcp 10.34.8.0 0.0.0.255 10.34.0.0 0.0.0.255 established
 20 deny ip any any
Capture: fresh UDP query reaches DNS; DNS sends reply to client port 51000.
R1 sees that reply on its server interface; deny 20 increases.
Policy: allow those DNS replies; retain the denial of other server-initiated traffic.

questions.prompt: Which narrow change restores the required service while preserving the stated limits?
options: Permit UDP replies from DNS source port 53 before the server-side deny
Replace the client-side deny with permit ip any any
Permit TCP destination port 53 on the server-side inbound list
Remove the server-side list because the client list is restrictive
questions.explanation: The allowed UDP query reaches DNS, and the response is observed entering the router. That response misses the TCP-only return permit and reaches the deny. Add the required reverse UDP match while retaining the restrictions; then test a fresh query and the denied server-initiated traffic.

whyWrong.1: The request already passes; this would broaden the wrong side of the policy.
whyWrong.2: The missing packet is a UDP reply with source port 53, not a TCP request to destination 53.
whyWrong.3: Removing that filter would abandon the stated server-to-client restriction.

exhibit.title: A constrained policy change (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Active CLIENTS-IN:
10 permit tcp 10.34.0.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.34.8.20 eq 80
20 deny ip 10.34.0.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.34.8.20
30 permit ip any any
Change requirements: retain HTTP for all clients; add HTTPS only for admin 10.34.0.10; continue denying other client traffic to WEB.

questions.prompt: Which proposed insertion meets all three access requirements?
options: Insert permit ip host 10.34.0.10 any at sequence 5
Insert permit tcp host 10.34.0.10 host 10.34.8.20 eq 443 at sequence 15
Append permit tcp host 10.34.0.10 host 10.34.8.20 eq 443 at sequence 40
Replace deny 20 with permit ip 10.34.0.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.34.8.20
questions.explanation: The admin-specific HTTPS permit belongs before the deny and after, or before, the unrelated HTTP permit. It adds the approved exception without granting other clients HTTPS or granting the admin other services to WEB.

whyWrong.0: This permits the admin's other protocols to WEB, contrary to the requirement.
whyWrong.2: The packet would reach deny 20 before the appended exception.
whyWrong.3: This grants all client traffic to WEB rather than the single exception.

exhibit.title: Safe replacement requirements (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Change constraints:
- Classic IOS interface behavior from this chapter
- Working console session retained
- Existing LIVE ACL ends with deny ip any any
- Add one approved management source while preserving other restrictions
- No deliberate unfiltered interval; fresh-session acceptance required

questions.prompt: Which change procedure preserves the filtering policy and the console recovery path?
options: Delete LIVE first, then recreate it while its interface reference remains
Detach LIVE, verify management from the console, then construct NEXT
Append the new exception after LIVE's final deny and test only an existing session
Build and inspect NEXT in full, replace the reference, then test approved and denied flows
questions.explanation: The requirement rules out an unfiltered interval and demands fresh policy evidence. Build the complete replacement before attachment, keep the console open, replace the reference, and test both desired access and required denials. Retain the old definition for rollback until the change is accepted.

whyWrong.0: The absent or partly built live list would not preserve the intended policy.
whyWrong.1: Removing the attachment creates the prohibited unfiltered interval.
whyWrong.2: The final deny prevents the appended exception from matching; an existing session is also insufficient evidence.

exhibit.title: Two interface filters on one request path (exercise)
exhibit.text:
PC 10.34.0.10 -> WEB 10.34.8.20 TCP/80.
Approved policy permits this HTTP service and blocks other client traffic to WEB.
R1 G0/0 inbound CLIENTS-IN: HTTP permit increases during a fresh test.
R1 G0/1 outbound OLD-SERVERS: deny ip host 10.34.0.10 any increases during that test.
WEB HTTP was verified locally; connected routes and both links remain working.

questions.prompt: Which next action is supported without broadening a policy that is already correct?
options: Inspect and reconcile the remaining outbound ACL with the approved HTTP policy
Change only the inbound permit to permit ip any any
Remove both ACLs because ping works from R1
Reset the HTTP server because an inbound permit proves end-to-end delivery
questions.explanation: The request passes the correct inbound filter but also encounters the outbound list, where an explicit deny matches it. Reconcile that second attachment with the approved policy, then retest the original client and retained restrictions. A permit in one filter cannot override a later deny.

whyWrong.1: The request already matches the inbound permit; widening it does not repair the outbound deny.
whyWrong.2: Router-originated ping does not validate this host TCP path, and removing both lists discards required policy.
whyWrong.3: The egress evidence identifies a filter rejection before application delivery.

cards.front: Which numbered ranges identify standard IPv4 ACLs?
cards.back: 1–99 and 1300–1999. These lists match source IPv4 addresses.

cards.front: Which numbered ranges identify extended IPv4 ACLs?
cards.back: 100–199 and 2000–2699. Extended lists can match protocol, source, destination and relevant transport fields.

cards.front: How does an ordinary nonempty IPv4 interface ACL decide a packet?
cards.back: Use the first matching entry. If none matches, the nonempty list implicitly denies the packet; later entries do not override an earlier match.

cards.front: How do you calculate the wildcard for a CIDR subnet?
cards.back: Subtract each mask octet from 255. For /20, 255.255.240.0 becomes 0.0.15.255.

cards.front: What do wildcard bits 0 and 1 mean?
cards.back: 0: compare the corresponding address bit. 1: ignore it. This is independent of whether the base address is a usable host.

cards.front: What wildcard represents a /27 subnet?
cards.back: 0.0.0.31: compare the first 27 bits and ignore the final five. Use the network address as a clear base.

cards.front: What do host and any replace in an IPv4 ACL?
cards.back: host A replaces A 0.0.0.0. any replaces 0.0.0.0 255.255.255.255.

cards.front: Which packet address does a standard IPv4 ACL match?
cards.back: The source. It cannot distinguish destination hosts, TCP from UDP, or one destination service from another.

cards.front: What additional fields can an extended IPv4 ACL use?
cards.back: Destination address and IP protocol, plus applicable fields such as TCP/UDP ports, ICMP type or TCP ACK/RST flag tests. All specified conditions must match.

cards.front: What are the usual placement guidelines for standard and extended ACLs?
cards.back: Standard: near the destination, to limit a source-only rule’s effect. Extended: near the source, when it can precisely identify unwanted traffic. Trace the actual path before choosing a direction.

cards.front: How is named ACL CLIENTS-IN attached inbound on an interface?
cards.back: Enter the interface configuration mode and use ip access-group CLIENTS-IN in. Verify the attachment with show ip interface for that interface.

cards.front: How does a standard ACL restrict incoming VTY management access?
cards.back: Apply access-class NAME in under every VTY range present. This restricts permitted source addresses; SSH transport and authentication are separate settings.

cards.front: How many ordinary IPv4 interface ACL references are available per interface?
cards.back: One inbound and one outbound. Applying another IPv4 ip access-group in the same direction replaces that reference. Other platform-specific ACL features are separate.

cards.front: What does TCP established actually check?
cards.back: ACK or RST set on the current segment. It does not validate a remembered connection and can match a forged ACK without a preceding client session.

cards.front: How do you remove only sequence 20 from a named ACL on supported IOS?
cards.back: Enter ip access-list extended NAME (or standard as appropriate), then no 20. Verify the resulting list rather than deleting the whole ACL.

cards.front: Which two checks establish ACL contents and interface attachment?
cards.back: show access-lists NAME for entries and supported counters; show ip interface INTERFACE for inbound and outbound references. An ACL can exist without filtering that interface.

cards.front: Why is a successful router-originated ping insufficient to validate a transit ACL?
cards.back: Its source and processing path can differ from the host’s packet. Classic IOS outbound ACL behavior commonly bypasses locally generated traffic. Test the affected host’s actual path.

cards.front: What is the classic IOS behavior for an absent or empty referenced interface ACL?
cards.back: It provides no restriction in the documented classic behavior. Build and review the complete list before attachment; do not assume a misspelled or empty list supplies implicit deny.

cards.front: How do TCP/UDP port roles change in a reply?
cards.back: The server's service port becomes the source port; the client's chosen port becomes the destination. Reverse the addresses too.

cards.front: What does an increasing ACL permit counter prove?
cards.back: More packets matched that entry during the interval. It does not by itself prove routing, reply delivery or application success.

commands.task: Permit sources in 10.100.10.0/24 using numbered standard ACL 10.
commands.note: This defines an entry, not its attachment. A standard list cannot select destination services.

commands.task: In numbered extended ACL 101, permit TCP from 10.100.10.0/24 to host 10.100.20.20 destination port 443.
commands.note: The service-port condition follows the destination. Other requirements, including return traffic, need separate evaluation.

commands.task: Attach IPv4 ACL 101 to packets entering the current interface.
commands.note: In is relative to this interface. A second inbound IPv4 attachment replaces the current one.

commands.task: Enter configuration mode for the named extended ACL CLIENTS-IN.
commands.note: The extended keyword chooses the matching capabilities. The name does not determine standard versus extended.

commands.task: Add sequence 15 permitting ICMP echo requests from 10.100.10.10 to 10.100.20.20 in the current extended ACL.
commands.note: Use an image supporting sequence insertion. The exception must appear before a broader matching deny.

commands.task: Delete only sequence 20 from the current named ACL on IOS supporting sequence editing.
commands.note: This removes one entry in ACL submode. Global no access-list N can remove the whole numbered list.

commands.task: Permit TCP from any source to 10.100.10.0/24 when ACK or RST is set.
commands.note: This checks flags only; it does not prove the packet belongs to an established session.

commands.task: Restrict incoming sessions on the current VTY range using standard ACL VTY-ADMINS.
commands.note: Apply to every available VTY range. This does not filter unrelated transit packets.

commands.task: Display configured access lists and the match counters supported by this IOS image.
commands.note: Counter changes are evidence of matches, not proof of end-to-end application success.

commands.task: Display detailed IPv4 information, including ACL attachments, for GigabitEthernet0/0.
commands.note: Read both incoming and outgoing list names. show ip interface brief does not provide these ACL references.

tickets.title: WEB loads but new management connections fail
tickets.scenario: PC-A is 10.100.10.10/24 and connects through R1 G0/0 at 10.100.10.1. WEB is 10.100.20.20 behind G0/1. Before the change, PC-A could SSH to R1 and browse WEB. SSH, credentials and VTY-ADMINS remain unchanged; VTY-ADMINS permits PC-A. After CLIENTS-IN is attached inbound on G0/0, WEB still loads but a fresh SSH connection to R1 fails.

exhibits.title: Representative interface and ACL excerpts
exhibits.text:
GigabitEthernet0/0: Inbound access list is CLIENTS-IN
10 permit tcp 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.100.20.20 eq 80
20 deny ip any any

exhibits.title: Controlled test observations
exhibits.text:
PC-A -> 10.100.20.20 TCP destination 80: succeeds
PC-A -> 10.100.10.1 TCP destination 22: fails
Entry 20 increments during fresh SSH attempts.

tickets.question: Which missing permission explains the management failure?
options: Permit the same host under an outbound VTY access class
Permit PC-A TCP/22 to R1 before the interface deny
Move the HTTP permit below the interface deny
Add established to the incoming SSH permission
tickets.explanation: The interface list checks the incoming SSH request even though its destination is R1 itself. It misses the WEB-only permit and reaches deny 20 before the VTY access class can allow the source. An outbound VTY rule does not admit an incoming session; moving HTTP below the deny would break its working service; established would miss a normal initial SSH SYN because ACK/RST is not yet set.
tickets.fix:
Use the local console and a supported sequence-editing image.

```ios
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip access-list extended CLIENTS-IN
R1(config-ext-nacl)# 15 permit tcp host 10.100.10.10 host 10.100.10.1 eq 22
R1(config-ext-nacl)# end
R1# show access-lists CLIENTS-IN
```
Retry a new SSH session from PC-A, confirm WEB still loads, and confirm an unapproved client remains blocked. If insertion is unsupported, build an equivalent complete replacement ACL under a new name and replace the interface reference.

tickets.title: New SSH sessions still succeed after the policy change
tickets.scenario: A branch policy must deny TCP destination port 22 from 10.100.10.0/24 to FILES at 10.100.20.30, while permitting other IPv4 traffic. The list is correctly attached inbound on the branch LAN interface. There is no other filter in the path. Fresh SSH connections still succeed.

exhibits.title: Representative show access-lists BRANCH-IN
exhibits.text:
10 permit ip any any (64 matches)
20 deny tcp 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.100.20.30 eq 22 (0 matches)

exhibits.title: Interface attachment
exhibits.text: GigabitEthernet0/0: Inbound access list is BRANCH-IN

tickets.question: What change enforces the stated policy?
options: Move the list outbound on the same client interface
Add a second permit after sequence 20
Put the SSH deny before the general permit
Replace destination port 22 with UDP port 22
tickets.explanation: Every IPv4 packet matches sequence 10, so the router never reaches deny 20. Placing the specific deny first implements the intended exception. Reversing direction on the client interface would miss requests; another permit does not repair order; SSH uses TCP.
tickets.fix:
Build a complete replacement before changing the reference.

```ios
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip access-list extended BRANCH-FIXED
R1(config-ext-nacl)# deny tcp 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.100.20.30 eq 22
R1(config-ext-nacl)# permit ip any any
R1(config-ext-nacl)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip access-group BRANCH-FIXED in
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show access-lists BRANCH-FIXED
```
Start a new SSH connection and verify denial. Test a separately permitted service and compare counter changes. Existing application sessions and cached displays are not sufficient fresh tests.

tickets.title: One client loses access to two destination networks
tickets.scenario: PC-B is 10.100.10.11 on R1 G0/0. R1 G0/1 faces the protected server LAN 10.100.20.0/24. R1 G0/2 faces another reachable network 10.100.30.0/24. PC-B should be blocked only from the server LAN. The new standard ACL instead prevents PC-B from reaching either network; other clients still work.

exhibits.title: Representative relevant configuration
exhibits.text:
access-list 10 deny host 10.100.10.11
access-list 10 permit any
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip access-group 10 in
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 no shutdown
interface GigabitEthernet0/2
 no shutdown

exhibits.title: Baseline
exhibits.text:
Both /24 destination networks were reachable before applying ACL 10.
There are no other ACL attachments on these interfaces.

tickets.question: How can the same standard ACL enforce the intended destination boundary?
options: Move ACL 10 to G0/1 outbound
Move ACL 10 to G0/0 outbound
Delete the permit any entry
Apply ACL 10 inbound on all three interfaces
tickets.explanation: ACL 10 matches only the source. Inbound on G0/0 it rejects PC-B before any destination is selected. Outbound on G0/1 confines that rejection to traffic entering the server LAN. Outbound on G0/0 tests replies with different sources; deleting permit any would deny everyone evaluated by the list; applying it everywhere would broaden the error.
tickets.fix:
Configure through the console. First attach the unchanged list at the correct destination boundary; retain the original ingress restriction until this attachment is confirmed.

```ios
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip access-group 10 out
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/1
```
Confirm that G0/1 names ACL 10 as its outgoing list. Then remove the incorrect ingress attachment.

```ios
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# no ip access-group 10 in
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/1
```
Verify that PC-B remains denied toward the tested server in 10.100.20.0/24 and can again reach the tested host in 10.100.30.0/24, while another client retains its permitted access. Attaching the correct restriction before removing the old one avoids an interval of unintended server access. If the policy later distinguishes two servers in the same LAN, use an extended ACL.

chapters.summary: Describe site-to-site and remote-access IPsec, compare ESP and AH, distinguish tunnel and transport modes, explain IKEv2 and NAT traversal, and separate successful negotiation from working application traffic.

sections.body: A branch can reach headquarters over the Internet without trusting every network between them to protect its traffic. IPsec lets the endpoints authenticate each other and protect selected IP packets. To understand a VPN, start by identifying those endpoints, the traffic selected for protection, and where that protection ends. A successful login or an “up” status is only one part of that assessment.

sections.title: What an IPsec VPN protects
sections.body:
:::facts
- A site-to-site IPsec VPN normally terminates on two gateways acting for their networks. A remote-access IPsec VPN terminates on a user's device and a VPN gateway.
- ESP is IP protocol `50`; AH is IP protocol `51`. These are IP protocol numbers, not TCP or UDP ports.
- IKE commonly starts on UDP `500`. Standard UDP NAT traversal carries IKE and UDP-encapsulated ESP on UDP `4500`.
- ESP can provide encryption, integrity, data-origin authentication and anti-replay protection according to its negotiated services. AH provides integrity/authentication and anti-replay, but no confidentiality.
- ESP tunnel mode protects the complete original IP packet inside a new outer IP header. Transport mode retains the original IP header for routing and protects the carried payload.
- IKEv2 establishes authenticated negotiation and IPsec security associations. IKEv1 is legacy and deprecated; its phase names still appear in older material and simulator examples.
- The CCNA verb is **describe**. Full VPN configuration is optional implementation practice, not a requirement to memorize a long crypto template.
:::

A VPN is a logical connection across another network. “Private” does not automatically mean encrypted: a provider MPLS VPN separates customer forwarding but does not, by that fact alone, encrypt customer packets. An IPsec VPN adds cryptographic protection where it is configured. Nor does a leased or logically private service imply that no other customer's traffic shares any physical infrastructure.

Consider branch PC `10.1.1.10` sending to headquarters server `10.2.2.20`. The branch gateway encrypts the selected packet; the headquarters gateway decrypts it. If the application itself is unencrypted, the packet can be readable on the LAN before encryption and after decryption. HTTPS can provide separate application protection across those segments. IPsec does not remove the need for access policy, endpoint security or application authentication.

The transport network must still carry the outer packets between gateways. Encryption does not create reachability, guarantee availability, or prevent an attacker from disrupting the path. It prevents an observer without the relevant keys from reading the protected plaintext and allows the receiving peer to reject packets that fail the negotiated authenticity and integrity checks.

sections.title: Site-to-site and remote access
sections.body:
In a **site-to-site VPN**, a router or firewall at each location handles IPsec for hosts behind it. A branch PC uses its ordinary default gateway; it does not need its own VPN client for the gateway-to-gateway connection. Protection applies to selected traffic, not automatically to every packet from every device. The connection may be maintained or established when traffic requires it, depending on the design.

In a **remote-access VPN**, the user's device participates as a VPN endpoint. A laptop can authenticate to a corporate gateway from a home or hotel network and receive policy such as an internal address, routes and DNS settings. The gateway may authenticate a device certificate, user credentials, or both, and the deployment may require multifactor authentication. Successful authentication does not itself mean the user is authorized to reach every internal network.

| Question | Site-to-site IPsec | Remote-access IPsec |
|---|---|---|
| Where does IPsec terminate? | At the two gateways | At the user device and gateway |
| Who sends the original traffic? | Hosts behind the gateways | Applications on the connected device |
| Is a host VPN client required? | Normally no | A client or supported built-in VPN implementation is required |
| Typical identity | Gateway identity | Device and/or user identity |
| Typical purpose | Connect branch and headquarters networks | Give a remote user approved network access |

**Full tunneling** sends the traffic covered by the full-tunnel policy through the VPN gateway, including Internet access in a typical enterprise full-tunnel design. **Split tunneling** sends selected destinations through the VPN while other traffic follows the local connection. A split-tunnel connection is not protecting traffic that bypasses it. DNS treatment is also a policy decision; do not assume every query follows the same path merely because the VPN is connected.

Cisco Secure Client can use IKEv2/IPsec or a TLS-based VPN, depending on configuration. A client application's name therefore does not prove the underlying protocol. TLS/DTLS remote access is useful comparison context, but the published objective specifically names IPsec remote access. A browser portal giving access to selected applications is also different from assuming every application on that computer has a network-layer IPsec tunnel.

```diagram
{ "type": "topology", "title": "Identify the VPN endpoints", "caption": "The branch path is gateway to gateway. The remote user's device is itself an endpoint. Plaintext can exist beyond the IPsec termination unless another layer protects it.", "nodes": [ { "id": "P", "kind": "pc", "label": "Branch PC", "x": 1, "y": 1 }, { "id": "B", "kind": "router", "label": "R-BR", "sub": "198.51.100.1", "x": 3, "y": 1 }, { "id": "I", "kind": "cloud", "label": "Internet", "x": 6, "y": 3 }, { "id": "H", "kind": "router", "label": "R-HQ", "sub": "203.0.113.1", "x": 9, "y": 1 }, { "id": "S", "kind": "server", "label": "HQ server", "x": 11, "y": 1 }, { "id": "L", "kind": "laptop", "label": "Remote user", "sub": "VPN client", "x": 3, "y": 5 } ], "links": [ { "from": "P", "to": "B" }, { "from": "B", "to": "I", "label": "site-to-site IPsec", "accent": true }, { "from": "I", "to": "H", "accent": true }, { "from": "H", "to": "S" }, { "from": "L", "to": "I", "label": "remote-access IPsec", "style": "dashed" } ] }
```

sections.title: IPsec services, ESP and AH
sections.body:
**Confidentiality** prevents an observer from reading protected content. IPsec commonly uses symmetric encryption such as AES for this purpose. Both peers obtain suitable traffic keys; the user does not type a new encryption key for every packet.

**Integrity** detects unauthorized changes to protected information. **Data-origin authentication** establishes that the packet came from an entity holding the appropriate key. These are related but different from authenticating a person to an application. An authenticated VPN gateway may be forwarding traffic from many internal users.

**Anti-replay** helps the receiver reject a duplicate protected packet captured and sent again. Sequence numbers and a receive window distinguish acceptable packets from duplicates or packets too old for the window. This is not a promise that IPsec prevents every attack or that every dropped packet was malicious. Window sizes and extended sequence-number features vary; memorizing a universal default is unnecessary here.

**ESP**, Encapsulating Security Payload, provides the commonly used IPsec data protection. The negotiated transform determines the services. Secure VPN examples normally combine confidentiality and integrity/authentication, using an authenticated-encryption algorithm or encryption plus an integrity mechanism. ESP also permits configurations without encryption, so the label ESP alone is not proof that a particular capture contains encrypted user data. Inspect the negotiated algorithms when that conclusion matters.

**AH**, Authentication Header, authenticates protected packet content and selected IP-header fields but does not encrypt the payload. Ordinary NAT changes addresses included in AH's integrity calculation, making that combination problematic. ESP is the usual choice for encrypted VPN traffic; AH is principally important here for recognizing that authentication is not confidentiality.

| Function | Relevant mechanism |
|---|---|
| Protect user packets | ESP, or AH for its specified services |
| Authenticate peers and negotiate keying material | IKE |
| Let ordinary NAT/PAT carry ESP using UDP | NAT traversal |
| Identify the receiving IPsec SA | Security Parameter Index (SPI) and associated SA context |

With **NAT traversal**, ESP is encapsulated in UDP so a NAT/PAT device can handle a UDP flow. IKE includes NAT detection; UDP 4500 carries the subsequent NAT-T exchange and protected packets in the normal UDP-based design. The ESP content remains protected inside the UDP wrapper. UDP 4500 alone is not proof of a fault or of a specific NAT location.

:::trap Protocol 50 is not port 50
An IPv4 rule permitting `udp ... eq 50` does not permit native ESP. Native ESP uses IP protocol 50. UDP-encapsulated ESP uses UDP 4500 in the NAT-T arrangement described here. A perimeter policy must permit the transport actually in use; it does not necessarily need native ESP when all protected data uses UDP encapsulation.
:::

sections.title: Tunnel mode and transport mode
sections.body:
In **ESP tunnel mode with encryption**, the original IP header, transport header and application data become protected content. A new outer IP header identifies the VPN endpoints. For the branch example, the outer packet goes from `198.51.100.1` to `203.0.113.1`; the inner packet still goes from `10.1.1.10` to `10.2.2.20`. An intermediate router uses the outer destination. It does not need a route to the inner server subnet to forward that encapsulated packet.

The observer can still see the outer addresses, packet lengths, timing, and the visible ESP header. Encryption does not conceal all traffic metadata. In particular, the ESP SPI and sequence fields are not the encrypted application payload.

In **transport mode**, ESP is inserted after the original IP header. That header remains available for routing while the carried upper-layer content is protected. A straightforward example is two IPsec-capable hosts protecting their own communication. Another valid arrangement is ESP transport mode protecting a GRE packet already addressed between two routers. In that case GRE has already supplied an outer router-to-router IP header, and its inner user packet is inside the protected payload.

| ESP with encryption | Tunnel mode | Transport mode |
|---|---|---|
| Additional outer IP header supplied by IPsec | Yes | No |
| Original IP header | Inside encrypted content | Remains outside ESP encryption |
| Typical simple example | Gateway-to-gateway protection for LAN hosts | Host-to-host protection |
| Can transport-network routers read the original host header? | Not from the encrypted inner packet | Yes, for the ordinary host-to-host example |

```output Simplified ESP packet layouts; not a readable ciphertext capture
Tunnel:
Outer IP (gateway A -> gateway B) | ESP header | encrypted {original IP + transport + data + ESP trailer} | authentication data

Transport:
Original IP (IPsec endpoint A -> B) | ESP header | encrypted {transport + data + ESP trailer} | authentication data
```

These are explanatory layouts. A normal capture on the untrusted path cannot display the encrypted original header in plaintext without appropriate decryption material. AH can also use tunnel or transport mode, but AH never acquires encryption merely by using tunnel mode. The comparison above explicitly assumes ESP with confidentiality enabled.

sections.title: IKE and security associations
sections.body:
A **security association (SA)** records agreed parameters such as protocol, algorithms, keys, lifetime and traffic scope. An IPsec SA is unidirectional: the outbound SA used to protect a packet corresponds to an inbound SA at the receiver. Bidirectional user traffic needs SAs for both directions. An SPI helps the receiver select the appropriate SA; it is an identifier, not an encryption key or a GRE tunnel number.

IKE's protected negotiation is separate from the IPsec data SAs. In **IKEv2**, the initial `IKE_SA_INIT` exchange agrees parameters and exchanges material for key derivation. `IKE_AUTH` authenticates the peers and normally establishes the first CHILD_SA, which provides the IPsec SA pair. The basic initial exchange has four messages, but authentication methods and later exchanges can add more. Do not treat four as the lifetime packet count of an IKEv2 session.

Diffie-Hellman allows peers to derive shared secret material without sending that secret directly across the network. DH alone does not establish whom the peer is; authentication supplies that assurance. A pre-shared key is a secret configured for authentication. A certificate associates a public key with an identity under a trust system. Certificates can support larger deployments, but require correct identity checks, trusted issuers, time validity and an effective revocation policy. Revocation is not an instant universal result just because a certificate exists.

IKEv2 can create and rekey additional SAs. The negotiation SA is bidirectional; one negotiation relationship may support multiple protected data flows. A data SA's lifetime and the IKE SA's lifetime are not interchangeable. Rekeying replaces keying material and should be considered separately from a fresh user login.

Older IOS material calls **IKEv1** negotiation “phase 1” and “phase 2.” Phase 1 establishes the authenticated ISAKMP/IKE SA; phase 2 negotiates the IPsec data SAs. The legacy command `show crypto isakmp sa` reports that IKEv1 state. IKEv2 uses different exchanges and commands; it is not a backward-compatible setting of IKEv1. RFC 9395 deprecates IKEv1. Recognize it when interpreting older examples, but use current IKEv2 guidance for a new supported implementation.

sections.title: Traffic selection and tunnel interfaces
sections.body:
A **policy-based VPN** commonly uses a crypto map referencing a crypto ACL. A permit in that selection ACL identifies traffic to protect for the configured peer. Traffic excluded from that selection is not automatically discarded as it would be by an interface filter; another policy or routing decision controls its fate. If there is an unencrypted route and no separate restriction, unselected traffic may leave unprotected.

For branch-to-HQ traffic, a simple selector is source `10.1.1.0/24`, destination `10.2.2.0/24`. The opposite gateway uses the reverse perspective. A test ping sourced from a public router interface may not match either protected LAN selector. Test from the protected host or explicitly choose a source inside the protected subnet before concluding that selection failed.

A **route-based VPN** represents the protected path with a logical interface, such as an IPsec virtual tunnel interface. Routes direct selected destinations toward that interface. This changes how the forwarding configuration is expressed; it does not eliminate authentication, IPsec SAs, return routes or access policy.

**GRE** is separate encapsulation, identified by IP protocol 47. It can carry traffic such as multicast between routers and can be protected by IPsec. Plain GRE supplies no encryption. This explains GRE-over-IPsec references in older designs, but GRE/OSPF tunnel construction, DMVPN components and platform MTU defaults are not required by these VPN describe objectives. A tunnel interface showing up/up is not evidence that its content is encrypted or that a remote application responds.

sections.title: Verify the path, negotiation and data
sections.body:
Check the evidence in layers. First confirm usable interfaces and an underlay route to the peer's public address. A successful public-address ping tests IP/ICMP reachability, not permission for IKE, ESP or UDP 4500. Then inspect IKE status with the command appropriate to the configured version. On supported IOS XE, `show crypto ikev2 sa` may show READY; legacy IKEv1 examples often show QM_IDLE. Neither is a substitute for inspecting data SAs and testing the application.

```ios R-BR
R-BR# show ip interface brief
R-BR# show ip route 203.0.113.1
R-BR# show crypto ikev2 sa
R-BR# show crypto ipsec sa
```

The following simplified excerpt is representative, not a simulator capture. The counts are cumulative, so compare observations during a controlled test rather than interpreting a lone historical total.

```output Representative IPsec counters for the same SA before and after a test
                         Before        After
#pkts encaps                100          104
#pkts decaps                100          100
```

This router protected four additional outbound packets but recorded no additional successful inbound decapsulation for that SA. It does not identify a unique cause. Inspect the far peer, WAN transport, remote LAN delivery, return route, selectors, filtering and receive errors. Encrypted traffic might have been lost before reaching the peer or rejected on receipt; the application may also have produced no reply.

If both directions increase, the selected SA has carried protected traffic in both directions during that interval. It still does not prove that a particular website, user permission or DNS lookup works. Test the actual application and correlate its timing and addresses. A small successful ping also does not prove that larger packets fit the path; encapsulation adds overhead and MTU problems need separate evidence.

An empty IKE table can result from no triggering traffic, configuration not being used, expired negotiation, or failure. A single intermediate or deleted IKE state is not a unique diagnosis of a wrong key. Check matching proposals, peer identities, authentication and transport evidence before changing settings. Unsupported simulator commands call for the supplied evidence worksheet or a suitable IOS XE environment, not invented output.

sections.title: Exam focus
sections.body: Explain where site-to-site and remote-access VPNs terminate and what traffic is protected. Distinguish encryption from authentication, ESP from AH, IP protocol numbers from UDP ports, and IKE negotiation from data protection. Draw tunnel and transport layouts and describe NAT-T's purpose. V1.1 asks you to describe IPsec remote access and site-to-site VPNs; v2.0 additionally names protocols and transport modes. The optional implementation reference and two status-command drills make those concepts concrete on supported IOS XE. They are supplementary observation practice, not additional published exam verbs or a requirement to memorize advanced VPN design.

lab.title: Trace an IPsec VPN and distinguish transport, negotiation and application faults
devices: Optional encryption: 2 × ISR 4351 with supported IOS XE and IPsec capability, replacing the two edge routers
lab.intro:
Practice revised September 2026. If you completed an earlier version, repeat the revised exercise and update its checkmarks.

The required exercise combines a reproducible Packet Tracer IP baseline with an IPsec evidence worksheet. Both exam versions ask you to **describe** these VPNs. You can complete the packet-path, protection, fault and recovery reasoning without an emulator that supports modern IPsec.

Step 4 is an optional complete IKEv2 configuration reference for two supported IOS XE routers. It is **not a Packet Tracer instruction**. Cisco documents this crypto-map/IKEv2 configuration family on ISR 4351 with IOS XE 16.12; use a suitable supported image with the necessary IPsec capability and confirm its command support. The explicit optional hardware target is two physical ISR 4351 routers with that configuration family available; virtual-platform names and interface numbering require their own image documentation. An arbitrary CML node or Packet Tracer router is not assumed to emulate these features. Do not substitute an obsolete IKEv1 or weak-algorithm configuration merely to make a simulator accept the commands.

The required path is Steps 1–3, the supplied-evidence parts of Steps 5–8, and the summary in Step 9. Allow about 60 minutes. Step 4 and every block marked optional live VPN are additional implementation practice, not prerequisites for completing the conceptual outcomes. Keep two columns in your notes: **predicted from the model** and **actually observed in your own environment**.

No lab was executed in Packet Tracer or on IOS XE during this content review. All VPN status, counter and capture examples are representative teaching evidence. Keep the required baseline and worksheet separate from any claim that Packet Tracer encrypted a packet.
