```ios R-HQ
R-HQ(config-if)# no shutdown
R-HQ(config-if)# exit
R-HQ(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R-HQ(config-if)# ip address 10.2.2.1 255.255.255.0
R-HQ(config-if)# no shutdown
R-HQ(config-if)# exit
R-HQ(config)# ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 203.0.113.2
R-HQ(config)# end
```

:::expected
Each PC and its local router share a /24. Each WAN link has the two usable addresses of its /30. ISP needs only its connected WAN routes to reach either edge's public address. These documentation WAN addresses model a transit network; this lab is not connected to the public Internet.
:::

steps.title: Verify what works before IPsec
steps.body:
On each router, inspect `show ip interface brief` and `show ip route`. From PC-BR ping `10.1.1.1`; from PC-HQ ping `10.2.2.1`. From the edge routers test the opposite public address:

```ios R-BR
R-BR# ping 203.0.113.1
R-BR# show ip route 203.0.113.1
```

```ios R-HQ
R-HQ# ping 198.51.100.1
R-HQ# show ip route 198.51.100.1
```

Before that final test, predict whether ISP can forward an ordinary packet to the private destination using its displayed table. Then, from PC-BR, ping `10.2.2.20`. Record the result without adding a private route to ISP.

:::expected
Local gateway pings and edge-to-edge public-address pings should succeed after links and ARP settle. The private host-to-host ping fails: ISP has no route for the inner LAN destinations. A timeout or an unreachable may be displayed. This establishes underlay IP/ICMP reachability, not working IPsec. Save this required Packet Tracer baseline as `vpn-underlay.pkt`.
:::

steps.title: Draw the protected packet on paper
steps.body:
For an ESP tunnel-mode VPN with encryption between R-BR and R-HQ, write the source and destination at three points: PC-BR to R-BR, R-BR to ISP, and R-HQ to PC-HQ. Identify where the original IP header is encrypted and which destination ISP uses. Then describe what plain GRE would change.

:::solution Check the packet drawing
Before R-BR: original IP `10.1.1.10 -> 10.2.2.20`. Across ISP: outer IP `198.51.100.1 -> 203.0.113.1`, followed by ESP and protected inner content. After R-HQ decrypts: original IP `10.1.1.10 -> 10.2.2.20` again. ISP forwards using `203.0.113.1`, not the encrypted inner destination. Plain GRE would provide encapsulation but no encryption; its inner content would remain readable to a suitable observer.
:::

steps.title: Optional supported IOS XE IKEv2 configuration
steps.body:
Worksheet-only learners should skip this optional implementation and continue to Step 5. **Do not paste this into the Packet Tracer baseline.** For live optional practice, use the supported edge devices and interface mapping specified in Topology; complete Steps 1–2 on that environment first. Confirm `show version`, feature availability and the `crypto ikev2` command family. Use a fresh isolated configuration with no other crypto policy, NAT or ACL attachment.

The complete reference below is optional. Worksheet-only learners may leave it closed and continue to Step 5; the endpoint and selector values they need are supplied there.

:::solution Optional IOS XE implementation reference
The proposal specifies IKE algorithms; the policy references that proposal. The profile matches the peer's identity and configures authentication. The transform set specifies ESP data protection. The selector identifies the two LANs; the crypto map combines the peer, profile, transform and selector, then attaches to the WAN interface. The demonstration pre-shared key is the same at both ends and is intended only for this isolated exercise.

```ios R-BR — optional IOS XE
R-BR# configure terminal
R-BR(config)# crypto ikev2 proposal CCNA-PROPOSAL
R-BR(config-ikev2-proposal)# encryption aes-cbc-256
R-BR(config-ikev2-proposal)# integrity sha256
R-BR(config-ikev2-proposal)# prf sha256
R-BR(config-ikev2-proposal)# group 14
R-BR(config-ikev2-proposal)# exit
R-BR(config)# crypto ikev2 policy CCNA-POLICY
R-BR(config-ikev2-policy)# proposal CCNA-PROPOSAL
R-BR(config-ikev2-policy)# exit
R-BR(config)# crypto ikev2 profile CCNA-PROFILE
R-BR(config-ikev2-profile)# match identity remote address 203.0.113.1 255.255.255.255
R-BR(config-ikev2-profile)# identity local address 198.51.100.1
R-BR(config-ikev2-profile)# authentication remote pre-share key 0 CCNA-Only-35-Lab!
R-BR(config-ikev2-profile)# authentication local pre-share key 0 CCNA-Only-35-Lab!
R-BR(config-ikev2-profile)# exit
R-BR(config)# crypto ipsec transform-set CCNA-ESP esp-aes 256 esp-sha256-hmac
R-BR(cfg-crypto-trans)# mode tunnel
R-BR(cfg-crypto-trans)# exit
R-BR(config)# ip access-list extended VPN-SELECT
R-BR(config-ext-nacl)# permit ip 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 10.2.2.0 0.0.0.255
R-BR(config-ext-nacl)# exit
R-BR(config)# crypto map CCNA-MAP 10 ipsec-isakmp
R-BR(config-crypto-map)# set peer 203.0.113.1
R-BR(config-crypto-map)# set transform-set CCNA-ESP
R-BR(config-crypto-map)# set ikev2-profile CCNA-PROFILE
R-BR(config-crypto-map)# match address VPN-SELECT
R-BR(config-crypto-map)# exit
R-BR(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0/0
R-BR(config-if)# crypto map CCNA-MAP
R-BR(config-if)# end
```

```ios R-HQ — optional IOS XE
R-HQ# configure terminal
R-HQ(config)# crypto ikev2 proposal CCNA-PROPOSAL
R-HQ(config-ikev2-proposal)# encryption aes-cbc-256
R-HQ(config-ikev2-proposal)# integrity sha256
R-HQ(config-ikev2-proposal)# prf sha256
R-HQ(config-ikev2-proposal)# group 14
R-HQ(config-ikev2-proposal)# exit
R-HQ(config)# crypto ikev2 policy CCNA-POLICY
R-HQ(config-ikev2-policy)# proposal CCNA-PROPOSAL
R-HQ(config-ikev2-policy)# exit
R-HQ(config)# crypto ikev2 profile CCNA-PROFILE
R-HQ(config-ikev2-profile)# match identity remote address 198.51.100.1 255.255.255.255
R-HQ(config-ikev2-profile)# identity local address 203.0.113.1
R-HQ(config-ikev2-profile)# authentication remote pre-share key 0 CCNA-Only-35-Lab!
R-HQ(config-ikev2-profile)# authentication local pre-share key 0 CCNA-Only-35-Lab!
R-HQ(config-ikev2-profile)# exit
R-HQ(config)# crypto ipsec transform-set CCNA-ESP esp-aes 256 esp-sha256-hmac
R-HQ(cfg-crypto-trans)# mode tunnel
R-HQ(cfg-crypto-trans)# exit
R-HQ(config)# ip access-list extended VPN-SELECT
R-HQ(config-ext-nacl)# permit ip 10.2.2.0 0.0.0.255 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255
R-HQ(config-ext-nacl)# exit
R-HQ(config)# crypto map CCNA-MAP 10 ipsec-isakmp
R-HQ(config-crypto-map)# set peer 198.51.100.1
R-HQ(config-crypto-map)# set transform-set CCNA-ESP
R-HQ(config-crypto-map)# set ikev2-profile CCNA-PROFILE
R-HQ(config-crypto-map)# match address VPN-SELECT
R-HQ(config-crypto-map)# exit
R-HQ(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0/0
R-HQ(config-if)# crypto map CCNA-MAP
R-HQ(config-if)# end
```

The selector on each router is the reverse of the other's. The default routes send packets toward the WAN; the crypto map protects matching packets before they cross ISP. `ipsec-isakmp` in the crypto-map command is not evidence of IKEv1 here: the `set ikev2-profile` reference selects this IKEv2 implementation. No private route is added to ISP, and no GRE tunnel is required for these unicast host tests. If the required feature or algorithm is unavailable, use the evidence worksheet rather than assuming an equivalent command exists.
:::

steps.title: Read negotiation and data evidence separately
steps.body:
In the optional environment, send a fresh ping from PC-BR to PC-HQ. Initial requests may be lost while negotiation occurs; repeat after inspecting the status. Use the protected host as the source, not a router's public interface. The following commands are for supported IOS XE:

```ios R-BR
R-BR# show crypto ikev2 sa
R-BR# show crypto ipsec sa
R-BR# show crypto map
R-BR# show access-lists VPN-SELECT
```

Run the IKEv2 and IPsec checks on R-HQ as well. Worksheet learners should interpret this supplied evidence instead. Before opening the answer, list what the IKE state, each counter direction and the host result separately establish. It assumes no NAT, native ESP and the selector pair from Step 4; fields are simplified and totals illustrative.

```output Representative evidence for one controlled test interval
R-BR IKEv2: local 198.51.100.1/500, remote 203.0.113.1/500, READY
R-BR IPsec selectors: local 10.1.1.0/24, remote 10.2.2.0/24
R-HQ IPsec selectors: local 10.2.2.0/24, remote 10.1.1.0/24
Negotiated data protection: ESP AES-256 with SHA-256 integrity, tunnel mode
WAN packet type for protected data: native ESP, IP protocol 50

Counter deltas during fresh PC-BR -> PC-HQ echo tests:
R-BR: encaps +4, decaps +4
R-HQ: encaps +4, decaps +4
Host observation: echo replies received
```

:::solution Compare negotiation, data and host evidence
The IKE state shows a completed negotiation relationship. The selected IPsec SAs carried traffic in both directions during the interval, and the host test received replies. These conclusions rely on the combination of evidence, not on READY alone. Four is an illustrative test count, not an invariant command result. ISP can still have no route to either private LAN because it forwards the protected outer packets.
:::

steps.title: Introduce a native-ESP filter fault and observe
steps.body:
For the worksheet, assume the displayed native-ESP transport from Step 5. In the live optional lab, first verify that protected traffic actually uses native ESP; if it uses UDP encapsulation, this particular fault will not block that transport, so use the worksheet for this case.

Before reading the fault evidence, predict which of public ICMP, IKE UDP and native ESP this filter can pass. On ISP, apply an outbound ACL toward R-HQ that denies native ESP from R-BR but leaves IKE and other IPv4 packets permitted. This configuration is a real interface filter, unlike the VPN-SELECT crypto selector.

```ios ISP — optional live VPN environment
ISP# configure terminal
ISP(config)# ip access-list extended VPN-FAULT
ISP(config-ext-nacl)# deny esp host 198.51.100.1 host 203.0.113.1
ISP(config-ext-nacl)# permit ip any any
ISP(config-ext-nacl)# exit
ISP(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
ISP(config-if)# ip access-group VPN-FAULT out
ISP(config-if)# end
ISP# show access-lists VPN-FAULT
ISP# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/1
```

Send new host-to-host pings and compare both peers' counters. Also test a public-address ping from R-BR. Do not remove the fault until you have explained the following representative observations.

```output Representative fault evidence
Public-address ping R-BR -> 203.0.113.1: succeeds
Fresh PC-BR -> PC-HQ ping: fails
R-BR IKEv2 relationship: still present
During the fresh host test:
  R-BR encaps increases; R-BR decaps does not increase
  ISP VPN-FAULT ESP deny counter increases
  R-HQ decaps does not increase
```

:::solution Explain the supplied fault evidence
The public ping uses ICMP, and IKE uses UDP; both can pass the final permit. The selected data packets use native ESP and hit the specific deny. This is why an underlay ping and an established IKE SA can coexist with failed user traffic. The ACL and controlled counter changes supply the fault evidence; the one-sided IPsec counters alone would not uniquely identify the cause. In the required Packet Tracer baseline no ESP is generated, so applying this ACL there would not reproduce an IPsec failure.
:::

steps.title: Remove the fault and verify recovery
steps.body:
In the live optional environment, remove the attachment through ISP's local console. Worksheet learners should predict the next observations before reading the expected result.

```ios ISP
ISP# configure terminal
ISP(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
ISP(config-if)# no ip access-group VPN-FAULT out
ISP(config-if)# end
ISP# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/1
```

Retry host-to-host traffic and recheck both IPsec counters. Existing SAs can carry the restored traffic; if negotiation expired, fresh matching traffic can establish it again. No broad clear-crypto reset is required merely to remove this filter fault.

:::solution Check the separate recovery prediction
ISP reports no outbound ACL on G0/1. With the rest of the baseline unchanged, host replies resume and the appropriate encapsulation/decapsulation counters increase at both ends. Record new deltas instead of comparing cumulative counters with an earlier screenshot. Leave the now-unattached VPN-FAULT list as documentation or remove it only after confirming it has no other references.
:::

steps.title: Compare a remote-access user and NAT-T
steps.body:
This is a paper exercise; the topology does not include a configured remote-access headend. A laptop on hotel Wi-Fi authenticates to the corporate gateway using an IKEv2/IPsec client. The hotel translates the laptop's private source address with PAT. The gateway assigns VPN address `10.250.0.10` and a split-tunnel route for `10.2.2.0/24`.

Explain: which device is the remote IPsec endpoint; how the translated path can carry ESP; whether a public website outside the split route is protected by this tunnel; and whether a successful VPN login guarantees access to PC-HQ. Then contrast the arrangement with the site-to-site branch.

:::solution Check the remote-access comparison
The laptop, not the hotel's router, is the remote VPN endpoint. UDP NAT-T can carry ESP through PAT using UDP 4500. Traffic outside the split route follows the local connection in this stated policy and is not protected by this VPN. The client still needs an appropriate route, gateway policy, return route and working application service. In the site-to-site branch, R-BR protects traffic on behalf of its LAN hosts. DNS settings and DNS query routing require their own policy review.
:::

steps.title: Save the environment and write the evidence summary
steps.body:
Keep the required Packet Tracer file labeled as an underlay exercise. If you completed the optional live VPN, save the recovered configurations on all three routers and retain the actual show output separately from this worksheet.

```ios R-BR
R-BR# copy running-config startup-config
```

```ios R-HQ
R-HQ# copy running-config startup-config
```

```ios ISP
ISP# copy running-config startup-config
```

:::expected
Accept each default startup-config filename. Your written summary identifies the two protected LANs, both public peer addresses, IKE version, ESP mode and algorithms, whether data is native ESP or UDP-encapsulated, the exact tested service (ICMP echo in this setup), and the separate fault/recovery observations. A successful echo is not a claim that an unconfigured HTTP or file service worked. If you used the worksheet only, label those observations as supplied representative evidence rather than live measurements.
:::

### Evidence to keep

- Working local/WAN baseline observations and the expected private-path failure before protection.
- Inner/outer endpoint drawings, the point where confidentiality begins/ends, and a transport-mode comparison.
- Separate conclusions from peer reachability, negotiation state, protected-data deltas and the actual host test.
- A bounded explanation for the supplied native-ESP fault, followed by the separate recovery prediction.
- Remote-access endpoint, NAT-T and split-policy reasoning, plus the independent challenge. Label supplied evidence and unsupported actions clearly.

lab.troubleshooting:
- **Public-address ping fails:** check interfaces, /30 masks, connected routes and both edge default routes. Restore underlay reachability before investigating IKE.
- **Public ping works but IKE does not:** inspect the configured IKE version, UDP transport policy, peer identity, matching proposals and authentication. A ping does not test those requirements.
- **No data counters change:** confirm the actual source and destination match the selector and the correct map is attached. A public-interface-sourced ping is not the LAN-to-LAN test.
- **Only outbound protection increases:** check the far peer's received traffic, access policy, host reply generation, return route and return protection. Do not infer a unique wrong key or selector from that counter pattern alone.
- **Counter totals exist but current traffic fails:** they may be historical. Measure new deltas for the relevant SA while running a fresh test.
- **Both data directions work but an application fails:** test the service, host firewall, DNS if names are used, user authorization and packet-size behavior.
- **A crypto command is rejected:** confirm the exact model, release and supported features. Packet Tracer and a generic CML node are not substitutes for the optional IOS XE platform.
lab.challenge:
Complete this independent paper case without using the guided topology's addresses. No remote-access server or client deployment is assumed.

A laptop behind hotel PAT establishes a remote-access IKEv2/IPsec VPN. Its hotel address is `192.168.50.10`; the PAT public address is `198.51.100.50`. The corporate gateway is `203.0.113.5`. The VPN assigns inner address `10.250.35.10` and protects only destinations in `10.35.8.0/23`; other destinations follow the local Internet route. The negotiated mode is ESP tunnel with encryption and integrity, carried using UDP NAT-T. Server `10.35.9.80` serves a controlled HTTP application. A public website is at `192.0.2.80` and uses HTTPS.

1. Identify the IPsec endpoints, inner HTTP request addresses, and outer addresses visible on the hotel uplink after PAT. State the encapsulation's destination port.
2. Decide which of the two destinations is covered by the split route. Explain whether the public website may still have protection outside this VPN.
3. Draw what remains visible to the transit network and what is encrypted. Contrast a simple host-to-host ESP transport-mode packet.
4. During a fresh request to `10.35.9.80`, the relevant client SA changes from encaps 900/decaps 300 to encaps 906/decaps 306. The application returns its normal login page, then displays “This account is not authorized” after login. State what the combined evidence supports, what it does not prove about other flows, and the next responsible owner/check.
5. A later screenshot contains the same totals but no new test. Does it demonstrate that the application works at that later time? Define the evidence needed for closure.

:::solution Check the new remote-access case
The laptop and corporate gateway terminate IPsec; the hotel PAT device does not. The original HTTP request uses inner `10.250.35.10 → 10.35.9.80`. The hotel uplink sees outer `198.51.100.50 → 203.0.113.5` with UDP destination port 4500 in the stated NAT-T arrangement. PAT may also translate the UDP source port; there is no need to assume one source-port mapping.

The /23 covers `10.35.8.0–10.35.9.255`, so the internal server is included. `192.0.2.80` is outside that VPN selection; its HTTPS connection can have separate application-layer protection. The VPN icon does not make that local route part of the split tunnel.

Transit observers can see outer addresses, UDP/ESP wrapper information, lengths and timing. The original host packet is inside encrypted ESP content. In the simple ESP transport-mode comparison, the original endpoint IP header remains the routing header rather than being enclosed in a new IPsec outer header.

The measured interval adds six encapsulations and six successful decapsulations, and the returned page establishes a working application transaction for that selected test. The subsequent account denial calls for checking the application's identity/authorization policy with its owner. It does not justify rebuilding IKE or declaring every destination and user permitted. It also does not prove an exact six HTTP transactions: packets and application transactions are different units.

Unchanged cumulative totals without a fresh test do not establish present service. Record the intended source, destination, service and authorization requirement; inspect relevant new deltas; then repeat the authorized user's actual application action. Document whether the evidence was supplied on paper or measured on a supported implementation.
:::

questions.prompt: Which two pairings correctly describe IPsec protection services? Choose two.
options: Confidentiality: prevent unauthorized reading of protected content
Integrity: guarantee delivery of every packet
Anti-replay: reject duplicate protected packets using receive sequence processing
Data-origin authentication: grant every authenticated peer unlimited application rights
Encryption: hide all outer addresses and traffic timing
questions.explanation: Confidentiality protects the content from unauthorized reading. Anti-replay processing helps reject duplicates and packets outside the acceptable receive window. These services do not imply availability, authorization or the concealment of all metadata.

whyWrong.1: Integrity detects unauthorized modification; it does not guarantee delivery.
whyWrong.3: Origin authentication and application authorization are different functions.
whyWrong.4: Outer routing information and timing remain observable.

questions.prompt: Which two statements describe remote-access IPsec correctly? Choose two.
options: The user device can be an IPsec endpoint
The hotel router must terminate the corporate IPsec tunnel
Successful VPN authentication also grants all application permissions
The configured policy may authenticate the device, user, or both
A VPN client product name identifies the negotiated transport
questions.explanation: Remote access protects a connection involving the remote device and a gateway. Authentication and authorization are policy-dependent; the client product name alone does not determine whether it uses IPsec or TLS.

whyWrong.1: In remote access the user device can terminate IPsec through the hotel NAT/PAT device.
whyWrong.2: Network and application authorization remain separate policy decisions.
whyWrong.4: The same client product can support different configured VPN transports.

questions.prompt: Which service is absent from AH even when AH uses tunnel mode?
options: Integrity checking of protected content
Confidentiality through payload encryption
Data-origin authentication using the agreed key
Anti-replay support through sequence processing
questions.explanation: AH authenticates protected information and supports replay checking, but it does not encrypt. Adding a tunnel-mode outer header does not turn AH into an encryption protocol.

whyWrong.0: Integrity is an AH service.
whyWrong.2: AH supports data-origin authentication.
whyWrong.3: AH includes sequence-number mechanisms for anti-replay processing.

questions.prompt: Which two protocol identifiers are correct for the ordinary IPsec arrangements in this chapter? Choose two.
options: AH is UDP destination port 51
Native ESP is IP protocol 50
IKE commonly starts on UDP destination port 500
UDP NAT-T encapsulates ESP using TCP port 4500
Plain GRE is IP protocol 50
questions.explanation: Native ESP is identified in the IP Protocol field by 50. IKE commonly begins over UDP 500. AH is protocol 51; standard UDP NAT-T uses UDP 4500.

whyWrong.0: 51 is an IP protocol number for AH, not a UDP port.
whyWrong.3: The UDP encapsulation specified here uses UDP 4500, not TCP.
whyWrong.4: GRE is IP protocol 47 and does not itself provide encryption.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly separates IKEv2 from IPsec user-data protection?
options: IKEv2 status alone verifies the protected application's response
IKEv2 encrypts application packets within the negotiation messages
IKEv2 installs the same bidirectional SA for negotiation and user data
IKEv2 authenticates and negotiates; CHILD_SAs supply the IPsec data SAs
questions.explanation: IKEv2 establishes an authenticated negotiation relationship and negotiates CHILD_SAs for IPsec data protection. That control-plane result must be checked separately from data forwarding and application access.

whyWrong.0: Application verification requires its own traffic and result.
whyWrong.1: Protected user packets normally use ESP data SAs rather than IKE messages.
whyWrong.2: The negotiation relationship and directional data SAs are distinct.

questions.prompt: A branch needs protected access to headquarters for its LAN hosts, without installing VPN software on each host. Which arrangement fits?
options: A site-to-site IPsec VPN between the two gateways
A remote-access VPN client installed on every computer
An HTTPS application portal used separately by each person
A plain GRE tunnel with no cryptographic protection
questions.explanation: A site-to-site VPN lets the gateways protect selected traffic on behalf of their LANs. Hosts send ordinary traffic to their default gateways; they need no client for this gateway-to-gateway protection.

whyWrong.1: This makes each user device a VPN endpoint and violates the stated setup requirement.
whyWrong.2: An application portal is not the requested LAN-to-LAN IPsec arrangement.
whyWrong.3: Plain GRE encapsulates but does not encrypt.

exhibit.title: Representative counter comparison
exhibit.text:
Before: #pkts encaps 1180, #pkts decaps 100
After:  #pkts encaps 1184, #pkts decaps 100
Fresh client test: no reply received

questions.prompt: These deltas were measured for the same IPsec SA during a fresh host test. Which conclusion is supported?
options: No packet matched the local selector during the interval
Outbound protection increased; successful inbound decapsulation did not
The pre-shared keys are definitely different at the peers
The remote LAN default gateway is definitely missing
questions.explanation: The outgoing counter increased while incoming decapsulation did not. Check the far peer, WAN path, receive errors, remote host delivery and return path. The counters do not uniquely distinguish those possible causes.

whyWrong.0: An increase in encapsulation shows additional traffic was selected and protected locally.
whyWrong.2: The counter pattern does not prove an authentication mismatch; existing data SAs can also outlive a separate IKE event.
whyWrong.3: A missing return gateway is one possible fault, but no host configuration evidence identifies it here.

questions.prompt: An IKEv2/IPsec client connects through a hotel PAT device using UDP encapsulation. What carries the protected ESP data through PAT?
options: NAT-T changes native ESP into TCP using port 50
The PAT device decrypts ESP before translating each inner flow
NAT-T carries ESP inside UDP using port 4500
AH supplies UDP ports while retaining the same encryption
questions.explanation: UDP NAT traversal supplies a UDP flow that the NAT/PAT device can handle while the ESP protection remains inside. IKEv2 includes NAT detection and supports this encapsulation.

whyWrong.0: Native ESP is protocol 50, and the described NAT-T wrapper is UDP 4500.
whyWrong.1: The intermediate PAT device does not need the VPN traffic keys; it translates the outer UDP flow.
whyWrong.3: AH neither supplies UDP encapsulation nor payload encryption.

exhibit.title: Simplified layout, not readable captured ciphertext
exhibit.text:
Outer IP: 198.51.100.1 -> 203.0.113.1
ESP header: SPI and sequence
Encrypted: original IP 10.1.1.10 -> 10.2.2.20, TCP header, data, ESP trailer
Authentication data

questions.prompt: The packet layout is a teaching diagram of an ESP VPN with confidentiality enabled. Which mode is shown?
options: Transport mode, because ESP follows an IP header
Transport mode, because the inner packet uses TCP
Tunnel mode: the gateways use a newly added outer IP header
Tunnel mode, because the SPI specifies a GRE tunnel
questions.explanation: IPsec has added an outer header for the gateways and protected the original host-to-host packet inside it. That is ESP tunnel mode. A normal WAN capture cannot read the inner plaintext without decryption material.

whyWrong.0: ESP can follow an IP header in either mode; the new outer header is decisive here.
whyWrong.1: TCP versus UDP does not choose IPsec tunnel or transport mode.
whyWrong.3: An SPI identifies an SA, not a GRE tunnel, and no GRE header is shown.

questions.prompt: Which example directly fits ESP transport mode without another encapsulating tunnel?
options: Two gateways adding a new outer header for hosts behind them
A gateway hiding an entire original host-to-host IP header inside ESP
A VPN whose packet uses two IP headers because IPsec added an outer one
Two IPsec-capable hosts protecting their own payload while retaining the original IP header
questions.explanation: In the straightforward host-to-host transport-mode case, the original IP header remains the routing header and ESP protects the carried upper-layer content. Tunnel mode supplies an additional outer header.

whyWrong.0: Adding an outer header for other hosts describes tunnel mode.
whyWrong.1: Putting the complete original packet inside ESP describes tunnel mode.
whyWrong.2: The added IPsec outer header identifies tunnel mode.

questions.prompt: Which comparison of certificates and pre-shared keys is accurate for gateway authentication?
options: Certificates bind identity to a key but still need validation
A reused PSK contains each peer's compromise within one tunnel
A CA distributes the traffic keys instead of an IKE exchange
Certificates replace the need to check the intended peer identity
questions.explanation: Certificates can make identities easier to manage across many peers, but the peers must validate those identities and their trust and validity conditions. Revocation also requires an effective checking policy. IKE still negotiates and derives traffic keying material.

whyWrong.1: A shared secret reused across peers broadens the impact of disclosure.
whyWrong.2: The CA certifies an identity/key relationship; IKE derives session keying material.
whyWrong.3: The intended identity and trust/validity conditions must still be checked.

exhibit.title: Relevant crypto-map reference
exhibit.text:
ip access-list extended VPN-SELECT
 permit ip 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 10.2.2.0 0.0.0.255
crypto map CCNA-MAP 10 ipsec-isakmp
 match address VPN-SELECT
 set peer 203.0.113.1

questions.prompt: VPN-SELECT is referenced only by a crypto map, not by ip access-group. What does its implicit deny mean for a packet outside the selected LAN pair?
options: The packet is denied by the crypto ACL as if it were an interface filter
The packet inherits the last successfully negotiated peer
The packet is outside this rule's protected traffic selection
The packet is protected whenever its route uses the WAN interface
questions.explanation: A crypto selector identifies traffic for protection. Exclusion from that selector does not itself impose an interface drop. If another route and policy permit it, unselected traffic can leave unprotected.

whyWrong.0: This list selects protection; it is not attached as an interface drop policy.
whyWrong.1: An unmatched packet does not inherit a previous flow's crypto selection.
whyWrong.3: Egress through the mapped interface is not sufficient; the selection also matters.

questions.prompt: ISP has routes to both public gateway addresses but no route to either private LAN. Why can it still forward the encrypted tunnel-mode packet?
options: ISP forwards on the unencrypted outer destination 203.0.113.1
IKE distributes every protected subnet to ISP
ISP decrypts the inner destination and uses a default private route
The ESP SPI tells ISP the private subnet route
questions.explanation: The intermediate router forwards the outer packet toward the receiving VPN gateway. Only that gateway needs to recover the inner packet and route it onward to the local LAN.

whyWrong.1: IKE between the gateways does not distribute those routes to ISP.
whyWrong.2: ISP has no IPsec keying role in this topology and does not decrypt the payload.
whyWrong.3: ISP does not use the ESP SPI as a route to the private destination.

questions.prompt: A laptop has an IPsec split-tunnel policy for only 10.2.2.0/24. A public website is reached through the local Internet route. Which conclusion is correct?
options: Every laptop packet is protected because the VPN icon is connected
The local website traffic uses this VPN even without a matching route
The laptop has become a site-to-site gateway for all hotel devices
The public website traffic is outside this VPN protection; it may have separate HTTPS protection
questions.explanation: Only traffic selected by the stated split policy follows this VPN. A website using HTTPS can have independent application-layer encryption, but the VPN connection does not automatically protect the local Internet path.

whyWrong.0: Connection status does not change the stated split selection.
whyWrong.1: The scenario explicitly routes that destination outside the VPN.
whyWrong.2: A remote-access client does not automatically provide a gateway-to-gateway service for other hotel devices.

exhibit.title: Protection boundary (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Branch browser -> branch LAN -> VPN gateway A -> transit network -> VPN gateway B -> HQ LAN -> HTTP server
ESP tunnel mode with encryption between gateways only.
The application uses plain HTTP; hosts do not run their own IPsec.

questions.prompt: Where can a suitable observer see the unencrypted HTTP content in this stated site-to-site design?
options: On the branch and HQ LAN segments outside IPsec termination
Only on the transit segment between the two public gateways
On no segment because the gateway VPN protects it end to end
Only inside IKE messages during the initial authentication
questions.explanation: The gateways protect the segment between them. Plain HTTP exists before the branch gateway encrypts it and after the HQ gateway decrypts it. Application TLS would be separate protection and is explicitly absent here.

whyWrong.1: ESP confidentiality protects the carried content on the stated transit segment.
whyWrong.2: Gateway termination leaves the stated LAN segments outside that IPsec protection.
whyWrong.3: IKE negotiates protection; it does not carry the web page as its user data.

exhibit.title: What a transit capture exposes (exercise)
exhibit.text:
ESP tunnel mode with confidentiality enabled.
Outer IPv4: gateway A -> gateway B
Protected content: complete original IP packet carrying HTTP
Observer: authorized capture on the transit link; no decryption material.

questions.prompt: Which two facts remain visible to a transit observer without decryption keys in the described packet? Choose two.
options: The outer gateway IP addresses
The original encrypted HTTP request body
The packet lengths and arrival times
The encrypted inner host IP addresses
The plaintext TCP destination port inside ESP
questions.explanation: ESP tunnel confidentiality protects the inner packet, while outer routing fields and traffic timing/length remain observable. Encryption is not the concealment of all network metadata.

whyWrong.1: The request body is inside the protected inner payload.
whyWrong.3: The stated encrypted tunnel contains the original header inside ESP.
whyWrong.4: The TCP header is part of the protected inner packet.

exhibit.title: Application and VPN observations (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Same remote-access client and intended server 10.35.20.80:
- A fresh HTTP request to http://10.35.20.80 returns the expected page.
- Matching protected-data counters increase in both directions during that request.
- The isolated service accepts both numeric and named URLs.
- http://portal.branch.example fails on a fresh attempt.
- The application's resolved address and DNS response have not been inspected.

questions.prompt: Which next check best separates the remaining explanations for the failed named request?
options: Rebuild the IKE relationship because every application fault starts there
Capture or query the fresh hostname through the intended resolver and compare the application's chosen address
Add native ESP permission without checking the currently used transport
Replace the VPN route with a public default because both counter directions changed
questions.explanation: The controlled IP-literal HTTP test establishes a working protected application path to the stated server at that time. The failing name lookup may involve DNS data, a local override or a different selected address. Inspect that exact name and application resolution path before changing functioning crypto or routing.

whyWrong.0: The supplied successful protected HTTP transaction does not support resetting negotiation first.
whyWrong.2: The already successful transaction gives no basis for assuming missing ESP permission.
whyWrong.3: Changing the route would not diagnose name resolution and could bypass required protection.

cards.front: Is native ESP identified by a transport port or an IP protocol number?
cards.back: IP protocol 50. It does not have TCP or UDP ports unless an outer transport such as UDP NAT-T encapsulates it.

cards.front: What identifies AH, and what does it not provide?
cards.back: AH is IP protocol 51. It provides integrity/authentication and anti-replay support, but no confidentiality. Tunnel mode does not add encryption to AH.

cards.front: Which port commonly carries the initial IKE exchange?
cards.back: UDP 500. IKE negotiates and authenticates; it is separate from ESP user-data protection.

cards.front: What is the purpose of standard UDP NAT-T?
cards.back: Encapsulate ESP in UDP, normally using port 4500, so NAT/PAT can handle a UDP flow. The protected ESP content remains inside the wrapper.

cards.front: Does permit udp any any eq 50 permit native ESP?
cards.back: No. Native ESP is IP protocol 50, not UDP port 50. Standard UDP-encapsulated ESP uses UDP 4500 in the NAT-T arrangement described here.

cards.front: How do confidentiality and integrity differ?
cards.back: Confidentiality protects against unauthorized reading; integrity detects unauthorized modification. Neither guarantees packet delivery.

cards.front: How do ESP tunnel and transport mode differ when encryption is enabled?
cards.back: Tunnel mode adds an outer IP header and protects the entire original packet. Transport mode retains the original routing header and protects the carried upper-layer content.

cards.front: What does IKEv2 establish for IPsec traffic?
cards.back: An authenticated negotiation relationship and CHILD_SAs providing directional data SAs. IKE status and protected application success are separate checks.

cards.front: What does Diffie-Hellman provide, and what is still needed?
cards.back: It helps peers derive shared secret material without sending the secret directly. Authentication is still required to establish the peer identity. DH alone does not authenticate a person or encrypt application data.

cards.front: How do pre-shared keys and certificates differ for peer authentication?
cards.back: A PSK is a configured shared secret. A certificate links an identity and public key through a trust system. Certificate use still requires identity, trust, time-validity and revocation-policy checks; IKE still derives session keying material.

cards.front: Where do site-to-site and remote-access IPsec terminate?
cards.back: Site-to-site normally terminates at two gateways acting for their networks. Remote access terminates at a user device and a VPN gateway.

cards.front: What does split tunneling change about VPN protection?
cards.back: Only selected traffic follows the VPN. Other traffic uses the local connection and is outside that VPN’s protection, though it may use separate HTTPS or other application security. DNS path policy must also be checked.

cards.front: Does a READY IKEv2 relationship establish application success?
cards.back: No. Check the relevant IPsec data SAs, fresh packet delivery and the actual service separately; negotiation is only one stage.

cards.front: Encapsulation rises during a test but decapsulation does not. What is established?
cards.back: The observed SA protected more outbound packets but recorded no additional successful inbound decapsulation. Check both peers and the forward/return paths; the pattern alone does not prove a specific key, route or selector fault.

cards.front: Does a plain GRE tunnel protect its contents from reading?
cards.back: No. GRE supplies encapsulation, including support for carrying multicast between routers, but not encryption. IPsec can protect GRE; a tunnel interface being up does not prove that protection.

cards.front: What does IPsec anti-replay processing help reject?
cards.back: Duplicate protected packets and packets outside the acceptable receive sequence window. It is not a guarantee of availability.

cards.front: Where does gateway-to-gateway IPsec protection end?
cards.back: At the receiving VPN gateway. Traffic beyond that endpoint needs any separately required link or application protection.

commands.task: On supported IOS XE, display IPsec SAs and encapsulation/decapsulation counters.
commands.note: Compare before/after counters for the relevant SA during a controlled test. Historical totals do not prove current application success.

commands.task: On supported IOS XE, display IKEv2 security associations.
commands.note: Inspect the expected peer and negotiated relationship. Continue with data-SA and application checks.

tickets.title: Public reachability remains but protected host tests fail
tickets.scenario: R-BR 198.51.100.1 and R-HQ 203.0.113.1 protect LANs 10.1.1.0/24 and 10.2.2.0/24. ISP G0/0 faces R-BR and G0/1 faces R-HQ. The VPN previously worked. There is no NAT and a capture confirms native ESP, not UDP-encapsulated ESP. After a filter change on ISP G0/1 outbound, fresh branch-to-HQ pings fail although public-address ping and IKEv2 negotiation still work.

exhibits.title: Representative current IKE and controlled-test evidence
exhibits.text:
R-BR: IKEv2 peer 203.0.113.1 READY
Fresh host test counter deltas:
R-BR encaps +4, decaps +0
R-HQ decaps +0
ISP general deny +4; other traffic quiet during the test.

exhibits.title: ISP attachment and effective OUTSIDE-OUT list
exhibits.text:
GigabitEthernet0/1: Outgoing access list is OUTSIDE-OUT
10 permit udp host 198.51.100.1 host 203.0.113.1 eq 500
20 permit udp host 198.51.100.1 host 203.0.113.1 eq 4500
30 permit icmp any any
40 deny ip any any

exhibits.title: Representative capture immediately before ISP filtering
exhibits.text:
Source 198.51.100.1, destination 203.0.113.1
IPv4 Protocol: 50 (ESP)
No UDP encapsulation

tickets.question: Which policy omission explains this controlled test?
options: Missing UDP source-port 50 permission before the deny
Missing native ESP permission before the final deny
Missing UDP destination-port 4500 permission before the deny
Missing private HQ-subnet route on the transit router
tickets.explanation: The capture explicitly identifies native ESP, IP protocol 50. It matches neither UDP permit nor ICMP and therefore reaches deny 40, while IKE can remain healthy. A UDP source-port 50 rule would not match this native-ESP packet, and the existing UDP-4500 permit is for a different encapsulation. ISP forwards the outer gateway addresses and does not need a route to the encrypted private destination.
tickets.fix:
On the isolated ISP device, add a specific native-ESP permit before deny 40.

```ios
ISP# configure terminal
ISP(config)# ip access-list extended OUTSIDE-OUT
ISP(config-ext-nacl)# 25 permit esp host 198.51.100.1 host 203.0.113.1
ISP(config-ext-nacl)# end
ISP# show access-lists OUTSIDE-OUT
```
Generate fresh host traffic and compare both peers’ counter deltas and application results. The filter is only on ISP G0/1 outbound in this scenario; it does not filter the reverse direction. A different deployment using UDP NAT-T needs permission for its actual UDP transport rather than assuming native ESP is always required.

tickets.title: The new gateway pair does not establish an IKE relationship
tickets.scenario: A new IKEv2 VPN uses R-BR 198.51.100.1 and R-HQ 203.0.113.1. Public routing is working and a capture confirms IKE request and response traffic. A support log reports NO_PROPOSAL_CHOSEN. The listed policies are the only matching IKEv2 policies; there are no other proposals offered. Peer identities and configured authentication are correct. No data SA is installed.

exhibits.title: R-BR active proposal and policy
exhibits.text:
crypto ikev2 proposal BR-PROP
 encryption aes-cbc-256
 integrity sha256
 prf sha256
 group 14
crypto ikev2 policy BR-POLICY
 proposal BR-PROP

exhibits.title: R-HQ active proposal and policy
exhibits.text:
crypto ikev2 proposal HQ-PROP
 encryption aes-cbc-128
 integrity sha256

 group 14
crypto ikev2 policy HQ-POLICY

exhibits.title: Deployment requirement
exhibits.text:
Both peers are approved to use IKE AES-CBC-256, SHA-256 integrity/PRF and DH group 14.
The HQ configuration should match that requirement.

tickets.question: Which mismatch is established by the shown configuration?
options: The local proposal names differ across the two routers
The only offered encryption choices have no common value
The data selectors contain different local source networks
The IKE source and destination addresses are reversed at HQ
tickets.explanation: The only matching proposal at one peer offers AES-CBC-256 and the other only AES-CBC-128, so the encryption choices do not intersect. Local names need not match. Reversed endpoint perspectives are normal, and no supplied evidence identifies a data-selector problem as this IKE proposal failure. Correct the approved mismatch, then verify later stages separately.
tickets.fix:
Correct the HQ proposal to the agreed deployment requirement on supported IOS XE. Clear the old encryption choice before setting the single agreed choice.

```ios
R-HQ# configure terminal
R-HQ(config)# crypto ikev2 proposal HQ-PROP
R-HQ(config-ikev2-proposal)# no encryption
R-HQ(config-ikev2-proposal)# encryption aes-cbc-256
R-HQ(config-ikev2-proposal)# end
R-HQ# show crypto ikev2 proposal HQ-PROP
```
Allow the failed negotiation to retry and generate fresh matching host traffic. Verify the negotiated IKEv2 relationship, IPsec SAs and actual host result. Proposal compatibility is necessary but does not by itself prove correct selectors, return routes or application permissions.

chapters.title: Wireless principles
chapters.subtitle: Understand shared airtime, signal measurements, channel selection and the network name a client joins.

sources.title: Cisco: Radio resource management and RF measurements
RFC 5416: IEEE 802.11 binding and SSID fields
Cisco Networking Academy: Packet Tracer wireless security workflow

chapters.summary: Explain RF and interference, choose sensible band and channel plans, distinguish SSID from BSSID, and read wireless evidence without confusing signal strength with successful connectivity.

sections.body:
A wireless client must do more than detect a network name. It needs a usable radio link, compatible security settings, and working IP configuration. A strong signal solves only part of that problem. This chapter explains the radio and identification terms so you can tell what a wireless report establishes and what still needs testing.

The examples use ordinary infrastructure Wi-Fi. The next chapter explains where APs and controllers forward traffic; chapter 38 develops security and the controller GUI. Product generations and regulatory rules change, so use the actual country setting and device capabilities when implementing a channel plan.

sections.title: How stations share a radio channel
sections.body:
:::facts
- Wi-Fi uses shared airtime. Ordinary radio operation is half duplex; a station does not transmit and receive on the same radio channel simultaneously.
- **CSMA/CA** means carrier sense multiple access with collision avoidance.
- A strong received signal does not establish free airtime, correct security, or IP reachability.
- **SSID** names the WLAN; **BSSID** identifies a particular basic service set.
- Use the allowed channel list for the device and regulatory domain, not a universal channel-count table.
:::

On a full-duplex switched Ethernet link, the two ends can send in both directions at once. An ordinary Wi-Fi radio must listen and transmit at different times. Other APs and clients within radio range may use the same channel even though they belong to different organizations.

With CSMA/CA, a station checks whether the medium is busy and follows waiting and random-backoff rules before transmitting. A receiver normally acknowledges individually addressed data; if the expected acknowledgment does not arrive, the sender may retry. This reduces collisions but does not eliminate them. Some frame types, including ordinary broadcast/multicast delivery, do not use the same individual acknowledgment behavior.

**Airtime** is the time used on the radio channel. It includes useful data, management frames, acknowledgments, waiting and retries. A slow transmission occupies more airtime for the same payload than a fast one. That is why a busy cell can perform poorly while every client shows a strong signal.

Modern Wi-Fi can coordinate multiple users with features such as OFDMA and multi-user MIMO. Do not turn the basic shared-medium explanation into an absolute claim that only one user can ever exchange data at a time. These features improve scheduling and efficiency; they do not make interference or airtime limits disappear.

The IEEE defines the 802.11 MAC and physical-layer specifications. The Wi-Fi Alliance certifies interoperability and security programs. National regulators determine permitted spectrum and power. A Wi-Fi generation name is therefore different from both a legal channel authorization and a security mode.

sections.title: Read frequency, power and noise
sections.body:
**Frequency**, measured in hertz, describes the rate of a radio wave's cycles. The familiar Wi-Fi band names are 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz. **Wavelength** decreases as frequency increases: in free space it is about 12.5 cm at 2.4 GHz, 6 cm at 5 GHz and 5 cm at 6 GHz. These are explanatory examples, not a channel-planning formula.

Signals weaken with distance and interact with materials. Walls can absorb energy; metal can reflect it; several reflected paths may reach a receiver at different times. This is **multipath**. Multiple-antenna systems can use suitably different paths to improve reception or carry multiple spatial streams, but they cannot guarantee a usable link through every obstruction.

| Measurement | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| dB | A ratio or difference on a logarithmic scale | A 10 dB power increase is tenfold |
| dBm | Power referenced to 1 milliwatt | 0 dBm = 1 mW; 20 dBm = 100 mW |
| dBi | Antenna gain relative to an isotropic reference | Directional gain concentrates radiation |
| Received level | Power arriving at the receiver | −55 dBm is stronger than −75 dBm |
| SNR | Signal-to-noise ratio | Signal −65 dBm minus noise −92 dBm = 27 dB |

A 3 dB change is approximately a factor of two in power; 10 dB is a factor of ten. Thus raising a transmitter from 20 to 23 dBm changes approximately 100 mW to 200 mW. This does not mean twice the distance or twice the throughput.

**RSSI**, received signal strength indicator, is reported differently by different radios and tools. Many Cisco displays express a received level in dBm; a client may instead show a percentage. Normal received Wi-Fi levels are often negative dBm because they are below 1 mW. Negative is not an intrinsic requirement of the dBm unit, and a percentage is not universally convertible using one formula.

Subtract comparable signal and noise measurements from the **same receiver, band and observation period** to obtain SNR. If a laptop receives −65 dBm over a −92 dBm noise floor, its SNR is 27 dB. Combining the laptop's signal reading with noise measured at a distant AP would not establish the laptop's SNR.

An antenna directs available energy; it does not create transmitter power. An omnidirectional pattern covers directions around an axis, while a directional pattern concentrates coverage toward a chosen area. Actual patterns are three-dimensional and depend on mounting and antenna design. Directional antennas suit a planned building-to-building link, but distance alone cannot establish the required antenna, legal power or clear path.

A useful optional calculation is **EIRP**: transmitter power in dBm plus antenna gain in dBi minus cable/connector loss in dB. A 17 dBm radio with 6 dBi gain and 1 dB loss has 22 dBm EIRP. Check the applicable regulatory rules rather than assuming this is legal everywhere.

:::trap Signal strength and SNR answer different questions
A client receiving −55 dBm over −60 dBm noise has only 5 dB SNR. Another receiving −65 dBm over −92 dBm noise has 27 dB SNR. The stronger signal is not automatically the more usable link.
:::

sections.title: Choose bands and channels
sections.body:
A **channel** occupies a range of frequencies, not a single frequency point. Its center frequency and width determine whether it overlaps another transmission. Selecting different channel numbers is insufficient if their occupied spectrum overlaps.

In the usual North American 2.4 GHz plan, channels 1–11 are available and adjacent channel centers are 5 MHz apart. Common 20 MHz deployments use **1, 6 and 11** as the nonoverlapping reuse plan. Their centers are 2412, 2437 and 2462 MHz. Other regulatory domains have different permitted channels; do not describe 1, 6 and 11 as the only legal Wi-Fi channels.

Suppose three nearby APs all use 20 MHz channel 1. Where their coverage overlaps, they contend for the same airtime. Assigning 1, 6 and 11 separates their channel use. A fourth AP requires a survey-based reuse decision: it may reuse channel 1 if sufficiently separated, but its position in a numbered row alone does not prove adequate isolation.

```diagram
{"type":"topology","title":"Fig 36.1 — Separate neighboring cells","caption":"The APs share an SSID and wired LAN, while different 20 MHz channels reduce overlap between neighboring 2.4 GHz cells.","nodes":[{"id":"A","kind":"ap","label":"AP-A","sub":"STAFF · channel 1","x":2,"y":1},{"id":"B","kind":"ap","label":"AP-B","sub":"STAFF · channel 6","x":6,"y":1},{"id":"C","kind":"ap","label":"AP-C","sub":"STAFF · channel 11","x":10,"y":1},{"id":"S","kind":"switch","label":"LAN switch","x":6,"y":5}],"links":[{"from":"A","to":"S"},{"from":"B","to":"S"},{"from":"C","to":"S"}]}
```

| Band | Useful planning distinction | What to verify |
|---|---|---|
| 2.4 GHz | Limited nonoverlapping choices; many other devices use the band | 20 MHz width, allowed channels and nearby reuse |
| 5 GHz | More channel choices; wider channels may be available | Client support, width and any DFS requirements |
| 6 GHz | Additional spectrum for compatible newer equipment | Local authorization, AP/client support and security requirements |

**Channel bonding** combines spectrum for a wider channel. At similar radio capabilities and conditions, wider channels can support a higher PHY rate. They also consume more spectrum, leave fewer independent channel choices, and can encounter more interference. An 80 MHz channel overlaps its component 20 MHz channels. Increasing width is not an automatic fix for a crowded office; 20 MHz is the conservative planning choice in the limited 2.4 GHz band.

Some 5 GHz channels require **dynamic frequency selection (DFS)** to protect radar users. An AP may need to check a channel before using it and leave it when radar is detected. Exact channels and timing depend on the country, channel and implementation. Learn why a radio may wait or change channels; do not treat a single worldwide timer as the explanation for every interruption.

6 GHz is a separate radio capability. A 5 GHz-only client cannot gain it from an SSID setting. Modern 6 GHz Wi-Fi security uses WPA3 or Enhanced Open as applicable; ordinary WPA2-only or unencrypted-open operation is not the appropriate 6 GHz design. Spectrum, indoor/outdoor use and power rules must be checked for the actual deployment.

sections.title: Recognize Wi-Fi generations
sections.body:
Generation names help you compare capabilities, but a client and AP use only features both support. Product labels do not establish the negotiated channel width, number of streams or application throughput.

| Technology | Relevant bands | Recognition point |
|---|---|---|
| 802.11b / 802.11g | 2.4 GHz | Older generations; 11 and 54 Mb/s maximum PHY rates respectively |
| 802.11a | 5 GHz | Older OFDM generation; 54 Mb/s maximum PHY rate |
| 802.11n / Wi-Fi 4 | 2.4 and 5 GHz | Multiple spatial streams and optional 40 MHz channels |
| 802.11ac / Wi-Fi 5 | 5 GHz | Wider channels, including 80 MHz |
| 802.11ax / Wi-Fi 6 | 2.4 and 5 GHz; 6 GHz as Wi-Fi 6E | Efficiency improvements including OFDMA |
| 802.11be / Wi-Fi 7 | 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz, subject to product support | Newer features include multi-link operation and 320 MHz in 6 GHz |

Wi-Fi 6E refers to 802.11ax equipment extended into 6 GHz; it is not a security protocol. A dual-band Wi-Fi 5 AP still needs another supported technology on its 2.4 GHz radio because 802.11ac itself uses 5 GHz.

The **PHY rate** is the radio transmission rate for the connection. Application throughput is lower because of protocol overhead, shared airtime, retries and other bottlenecks. There is no fixed rule that useful throughput is exactly half the PHY rate. A displayed 866 Mb/s receive rate is neither a measured file-transfer result nor proof of an 866 Mb/s Internet service.

The full theoretical maximum of each amendment and its publication year are optional reference material. Focus on band compatibility, shared airtime and the difference between capability, negotiated rate and achieved performance.

sections.title: Identify the WLAN and its cells
sections.body:
An **SSID** is the WLAN identifier presented as a network name. Its field supports up to **32 octets**, which are bytes; a displayed character can require more than one byte in some encodings. Treat names as case sensitive. The SSID is not a password.

A **basic service set (BSS)** in an infrastructure WLAN consists of an AP's service and the stations associated with it. Its **BSSID** is a 48-bit identifier, commonly shown in MAC-address form. One physical AP can advertise multiple BSSIDs across several SSIDs and radios. Similar BSSIDs are not sufficient evidence that two cells belong to the same physical chassis.

An **extended service set (ESS)** joins infrastructure BSSs through a distribution system so clients can move between coverage areas. In a typical campus, APs advertise the same SSID and compatible security, with a consistent network design behind them. The distribution system need not be assumed to be one particular wire or switch.

**Roaming** changes the serving BSS. Keeping an IP address and active sessions depends on VLAN/subnet placement or an appropriate mobility design. Matching the SSID alone does not guarantee uninterrupted sessions, identical security or even the same organization.

Clients discover WLANs by listening for beacons and, when permitted, sending probe requests. They then perform the required authentication/association and security exchanges. For WPA2-Personal, an association can exist before the four-way key handshake has successfully completed. DHCP requires a working data path after the required security steps. A dotted simulator line or a “connected” label must be interpreted with the tool's actual state information.

An **IBSS**, also called ad hoc mode, allows stations to communicate without an infrastructure AP. Recognize the distinction; ordinary enterprise WLAN design and this course's labs use infrastructure mode.

sections.title: Investigate interference and coverage
sections.body:
Start by separating three possibilities: a weak desired signal, competing Wi-Fi traffic, and other energy in the band. They can occur together.

**Co-channel contention** occurs when nearby Wi-Fi transmitters share a channel. They may defer to one another and share airtime. Hidden stations, collisions and retries can still occur; “same channel” does not guarantee error-free traffic or an exact 50% throughput reduction.

**Adjacent-channel interference** occurs when occupied spectra overlap. For example, 2.4 GHz channels 1 and 3 at ordinary widths overlap. The effect depends on strength, timing, receiver behavior and spacing. Do not assume every overlapping frame must fail or that stations can never sense one another.

**Non-Wi-Fi interference** can come from equipment such as microwave ovens, Bluetooth devices or other transmitters sharing the band. A lunchtime symptom near a break room suggests an investigation, not proof of a microwave cause. Correlate the affected band, time, spectrum measurements and a controlled change before identifying the source.

Coverage problems also arise from placement, obstacles and an unbalanced link. Increasing AP transmit power may improve what the client hears without improving the client's weaker transmission back to the AP. A site survey considers both directions, coverage, capacity, retry rates and application needs. **Radio resource management (RRM)** can adjust channels and power, but it does not replace that assessment.

A basic investigation records SSID/BSSID, band, channel, width, received level, noise where available, utilization and retries. Change one justified setting, then compare the same tests and locations. Packet Tracer can illustrate settings and connectivity; it is not evidence of actual RF coverage, interference or application capacity.

sections.title: Recognize the security choices
sections.body:
Encryption protects data on the wireless link. Authentication decides which party or user may participate; integrity mechanisms help detect unauthorized alteration. None of these automatically protects data after it leaves the secured link.

| Choice | Main recognition point |
|---|---|
| WEP | Obsolete, insecure protection; do not select it for a new deployment |
| Original WPA/TKIP | Legacy protection based on RC4; not a modern replacement for WPA2/WPA3 |
| WPA2-Personal with AES-CCMP | Shared passphrase; the GUI configuration required by the v1.1 objective |
| WPA2/WPA3 Enterprise | Individual authentication through 802.1X/EAP, commonly using RADIUS |
| WPA3-Personal | SAE password authentication and protected management frames |
| Enhanced Open / OWE | Encryption for an open-style network without authenticating its identity |

WPA3 does not mean one universal cipher. The security suite and product support matter; the optional Enterprise 192-bit mode is not required for every WPA3 WLAN. SAE improves resistance to passive offline password guessing compared with WPA2-PSK, but weak credentials, implementation defects and malicious endpoints remain concerns.

Protected management frames protect specified robust management exchanges once the required keys and protection are established. They do not prevent all radio disruption or encrypt every management frame. Chapter 38 explains these boundaries and the configuration fields.

sections.title: Read a wireless connection report
sections.body:
The following Windows-style excerpt is representative, not a captured run. Fields and permissions vary with OS and adapter versions.

```output netsh wlan show interfaces — representative excerpt
State                  : connected
SSID                   : STAFF                  ← WLAN name
BSSID                  : 02:11:22:33:44:55       ← current service-set identifier
Radio type             : 802.11ac               ← Wi-Fi 5 on this connection
Authentication         : WPA2-Personal
Cipher                 : CCMP                   ← negotiated protection
Band                   : 5 GHz
Channel                : 44
Receive rate (Mbps)    : 866.7                   ← link rate, not a throughput test
Signal                 : 82%                    ← tool-specific quality indication
```

This establishes reported association parameters. It does not establish a DHCP lease, a reachable gateway, free airtime or successful DNS. Follow it with IP configuration and reachability tests from chapter 30.

`netsh wlan show networks mode=bssid` can show multiple visible BSSIDs under the same name. Scanning results are limited to what the adapter and OS report at that time; “not listed” is not proof that an AP does not exist. Use device inventory to map BSSIDs to physical APs instead of guessing from their addresses.

As an optional controller preview, Catalyst 9800 commands `show wlan summary`, `show ap summary` and `show wireless client summary` list WLAN objects, registered APs and clients respectively. They answer different inventory questions; a configured WLAN is not a connected client. The next two chapters explain the controller and client-policy context. These commands are not expected to run on a Packet Tracer home wireless router.

sections.title: Exam focus
sections.body: Explain channel overlap and sensible reuse, read dBm and SNR correctly, distinguish band support from negotiated rate, and separate SSID, BSSID, BSS and ESS. Identify plausible RF causes without claiming that one symptom proves them. Compare the security families and recognize that successful wireless access also requires compatible security and a functioning IP path.

lab.title: Build a WLAN and interpret channel, signal and service evidence
lab.intro:
Practice revised September 2026. If you completed an earlier version, repeat the revised exercise and update its checkmarks.

Build a fresh, isolated project. The supplied WLAN setup gives you a working application path; the assessed work is interpreting identity, channel use and comparable RF evidence. Steps 7–8 are an optional security refresher, and the second cell in Step 10 and real-computer queries in Step 12 are optional. Complete the required RF worksheet and fresh planning challenge even if your simulator cannot report physical measurements.

Keep a table with **question/prediction, source of evidence, actual observation, conclusion and remaining uncertainty**. Simulator graphics are not RF measurements. Supplied paper readings are clearly separate from the values your tool actually reports.

| Device/connection | Setting |

| WRT300N LAN | 192.168.80.1, mask 255.255.255.0 |
| Server-PT Fa0 to WRT Ethernet 1 | Copper straight-through; 192.168.80.20/24, gateway 192.168.80.1 |
