Packet Tracer controls vary by version. Check the actual device dialog. Do not substitute WEP or an open network if the selected model lacks the required WPA2/AES option. Use a compatible model/activity or complete the affected fields as a worksheet and record the limitation. No simulator run was executed during authoring.

steps.title: — Place, power and cable the equipment
steps.body:
Place WRT300N, Laptop-PT and Server-PT. If the laptop lacks a wireless interface, power it off in Physical, remove its Ethernet module, insert the compatible WPC300N module when offered, and power it on. If that module name differs, use the device's compatible wireless option rather than forcing an incompatible module.

Cable Server-PT Fa0 to WRT Ethernet 1 with copper straight-through. Leave the WRT Internet/WAN port disconnected. Set the server's static address, mask and gateway from the table. Under Services → HTTP, turn HTTP On. This isolated server is the application destination; no DNS or Internet service is required.

:::expected
The laptop exposes a wireless interface; the server's Ethernet link becomes active. Record actual interface labels. A default wireless association, if one appears, is not the configured secure baseline.
:::

steps.title: — Configure the LAN and DHCP
steps.body:
Open WRT300N → GUI → Setup → Basic Setup. Set Router IP to 192.168.80.1 and mask to 255.255.255.0. Enable the LAN DHCP service, set the starting host to 100 and maximum users to 50, then Save Settings. A field that accepts a full address uses 192.168.80.100.

From the server's command prompt:

```text
ping 192.168.80.1
```

:::expected
The saved page shows the intended LAN subnet and DHCP settings. After link/ARP convergence, the server can reach .1. The server's .20 address is outside .100–.149, so it cannot collide with this pool. This is a local LAN test; Internet service is not part of the topology.
:::

steps.title: — Set the WLAN name and channel
steps.body:
Under Wireless → Basic Wireless Settings, set SSID to CCNA-LAB, select a compatible mixed radio mode, choose Standard/20 MHz when exposed, channel 1 and SSID Broadcast Enabled. Save Settings. Record which width options your model actually exposes.

:::expected
A fresh client scan should list CCNA-LAB when the radio is enabled and the client is within simulated range. The configured channel is 1. If the model does not report width or signal numerically, do not invent those measurements.
:::

steps.title: — Apply WPA2-Personal security
steps.body:
Under Wireless → Wireless Security, select WPA2 Personal, AES, and Cedar-Lab-2026!, then save. Leave unrelated timing controls at their existing defaults.

:::expected
The saved security page shows WPA2-Personal and AES. This exercise does not require WPA3 support on the WRT model and makes no claim that a different Packet Tracer controller provides it. An existing client profile may need updating before data works.
:::

steps.title: — Join the laptop and request an address
steps.body:
On the laptop, open Desktop → PC Wireless. Refresh the network list and select CCNA-LAB; if the version uses profile creation, create a profile with that exact name, WPA2-Personal/AES and the lab passphrase. Connect. Set Desktop → IP Configuration to DHCP.

Before connecting, predict whether the SSID name, security result, IP lease and HTTP result would establish the same thing. Then inspect the status and run:

```text
ipconfig /all
ping 192.168.80.1
ping 192.168.80.20
```

Open the laptop's Web Browser and request `http://192.168.80.20`. Record a fresh returned page as well as the ICMP results.

:::expected
The client reports the intended WLAN/security and an address somewhere in .100–.149, mask /24 and gateway .1. Do not assume .100 specifically. Both local targets respond after any initial ARP delay, and the configured HTTP page loads. If ipconfig /all is absent, use the IP Configuration GUI. The dotted line alone is insufficient evidence: record the address and successful data tests too.
:::

steps.title: — Save the verified starting point
steps.body:
Save as wireless-principles-baseline.pkt, then Save As wireless-principles-faults.pkt for the experiments. Record the laptop's actual lease, SSID, security and observed status.

:::expected
Two separate files exist, and the recorded baseline includes successful pings and a fresh HTTP page. Continue only when the initial secure WLAN works; otherwise troubleshoot that state before adding a fault.
:::

steps.title: — Optional security refresher: observe a wrong client key
steps.body:
This bounded refresher supports the radio/security distinction; chapter 38 owns the fuller WLAN-security workflow. Predict which old fields can remain visible despite failed new key establishment. Change only the laptop's saved passphrase to Cedar-Lab-2025!. Disconnect/reconnect using its wireless utility so a new security exchange is required. Keep the router and DHCP settings unchanged.

Try a fresh HTTP request to `http://192.168.80.20`, try its ping, and inspect client security status. Record this state before restoring anything.

:::expected
The wrong shared secret prevents successful WPA2 key establishment and normal protected data access. The SSID may remain visible, and the laptop may retain its previous IP lease. A stale address does not prove security succeeded; an association indicator does not necessarily mean the four-way handshake completed.
:::

steps.title: — Optional security refresher: restore and verify
steps.body:
Restore Cedar-Lab-2026! in the laptop profile, reconnect, and request DHCP again if needed. Repeat both baseline pings and a fresh request for the same HTTP page.

:::expected
The known settings restore access. Record recovery separately from the fault observation. If failure remains, compare SSID, mode and AES selection before changing addressing or channels.
:::

steps.title: — Change the channel without changing the WLAN identity
steps.body:
First predict whether changing a channel must also change the SSID, passphrase or IP subnet. On WRT300N, change only the standard channel from 1 to 6 and save. Refresh/reconnect the client when necessary. Record the SSID, reported channel and IP address, then ping the server and request its HTTP page again.

:::expected
The WLAN name and passphrase remain the same while the channel changes. A brief reconnection may occur. Successful recovery demonstrates configuration compatibility; it does not measure improved throughput or reduced interference. Keep this channel-6 observation separate from the restoration in Step 10.
:::

steps.title: — Restore the channel and optionally compare a second cell
steps.body:
Restore WRT channel 1, save, reconnect if needed, and repeat the same HTTP request. Record the restored setting and service result before the optional extension.

Optional: add AccessPoint-PT and cable its wired Port 0 to WRT Ethernet 2 with copper straight-through. In its radio/Port 1 settings, use CCNA-LAB, channel 6, WPA2-PSK, AES and the same passphrase. If this model lacks that security combination, leave it disconnected and use the lesson's ESS diagram as the worksheet instead.

Use available client status/scan information to distinguish the cells. You may move the laptop in the Physical workspace to encourage a change, but do not assume the simulator performs a particular roaming algorithm.

:::expected
The required restoration returns the original channel and working HTTP service. In the optional extension, both cells bridge toward the same LAN/DHCP server. If the client changes serving BSSID, record that evidence and retest .20 by ping and HTTP. Its lease may remain valid; do not claim guaranteed seamless roaming from an unchanged SSID. A real AP can have a management IP while still forwarding as a Layer 2 bridge.
:::

steps.title: — Compare RF evidence before deciding on a change
steps.body:
Complete the following paper worksheet before opening its answer. These values are supplied exercise data, not measurements of the Packet Tracer project.

1. Three mutually neighboring APs must use ordinary North American 2.4 GHz 20 MHz channels. Propose a nonoverlapping plan and explain why 1/2/3 differs from your choice. They may share an SSID; does that change the RF overlap?
2. At one receiver, signal is −68 dBm and noise −94 dBm. At another comparable location, signal is −58 dBm and noise −64 dBm. Calculate both SNRs and distinguish stronger signal from better signal-to-noise ratio.
3. A 5 GHz AP occupies bonded component channels 36/40/44/48 at 80 MHz. A neighbor uses 20 MHz channel 44. Are the occupied ranges independent? Would different SSIDs make them so?
4. A client has a strong received signal but slow transfers at lunchtime. Both client count and nearby appliance use rise then; no spectrum data or controlled comparison is available. What facts would you gather before identifying a cause?
5. A receiver reports 600 Mb/s PHY rate and has 24 clients sharing its channel. What application throughput can you establish from those two fields alone?

:::solution Check the RF reasoning
1. Use channels 1, 6 and 11 in the stated plan. 1/2/3 occupy overlapping spectrum. SSID equality or difference does not create independent channels.
2. The SNRs are `−68 − (−94) = 26 dB` and `−58 − (−64) = 6 dB`. The second signal is stronger but has a poorer ratio. Neither ratio alone proves a particular application throughput.
3. The 80 MHz channel includes the neighbor's occupied component. Different primary-channel numbers or SSIDs would not remove that overlap. Choose any change from allowed spectrum and a complete survey, then compare results.
4. Record the affected receiver/band/channel/width, signal/noise where available, utilization and retries, and the same application's results. Correlate authorized controlled changes to distinguish added Wi-Fi load from non-Wi-Fi interference. Timing and proximity alone do not prove the appliance caused it.
5. No exact application throughput. PHY rate is not a per-client reservation or a fixed fraction of useful throughput. Measure the intended service and consider shared airtime, overhead and the rest of the path.
:::

steps.title: — Inspect a real connection without changing it
steps.body:
Optional, on an authorized Windows computer already connected to Wi-Fi, run the following read-only commands. They are Windows commands, not a guarantee of Packet Tracer PC support.

```text
netsh wlan show interfaces
netsh wlan show networks mode=bssid
netsh wlan show drivers
```

Windows may require location permission or an elevated context for particular wireless details. Use the permitted OS settings display if a field is unavailable; do not change networks or expose saved passwords. macOS/Linux inspection is covered in chapter 30.

:::expected
Record only needed fields: SSID/BSSID, band/channel, authentication/cipher and reported rate. A scan is a partial observation, not a complete site survey. Finish by saving the restored simulator file and noting every unsupported step.
:::

### Evidence to keep

- The actual SSID/security, DHCP lease, channel and successful baseline HTTP page; unavailable fields marked as such.
- A prediction and separate observation for the channel change, followed by the restored channel and original HTTP service.
- Optional wrong-key observation and separate recovery, if performed; an old lease is not a fresh security success.
- RF worksheet calculations, channel-range comparisons and a justified next test for ambiguous interference.
- Optional second-cell or Windows observations labeled with their source; no claimed site survey from simulator graphics.

lab.troubleshooting:
- SSID not listed: check model/radio support, power, SSID broadcast, scan refresh and simulated range. The absence of a scan entry does not identify one unique cause.
- SSID visible but data fails: compare security mode, cipher and exact passphrase; then inspect IP configuration and DHCP. Existing leases can outlast a failed reconnection.
- .1 reachable but .20 fails: inspect the server address, link, port and host settings. A gateway mistake on a same-subnet server is not automatically the cause of a same-subnet ping failure.
- Optional second AP fails: verify its LAN cable and matching security. It must not introduce a second conflicting DHCP service.
lab.challenge:
Prepare a fresh **paper** channel and evidence plan for a four-cell training site. The site permits the ordinary North American 2.4 GHz 20 MHz plan. AP-A is fixed on channel 1, and AP-B is fixed on channel 6. All four cells use the same approved SSID/security and bridge to the same client LAN.

The supplied survey establishes these pairs as strongly mutually audible: **A–B, A–C, B–C, B–D and C–D**. A and D are sufficiently separated for the scenario's approved co-channel reuse. No other relevant transmitter appears in this bounded survey. This is explicit survey evidence, not an inference from the drawing or row number.

1. Choose channels for C and D while preserving A and B. Check every listed neighboring pair and explain which channel is reused.
2. A test client measures −64 dBm signal and −90 dBm noise at one location. At a busier location its readings are −59 dBm and −66 dBm. Calculate each SNR; say which reading has the stronger desired signal and which has the better ratio.
3. After a client changes from BSSID A to BSSID C, it reports the same SSID, completed approved security and its original valid lease. What additional checks establish that the intended application still works? Does the unchanged SSID alone prove seamless roaming?
4. Define an acceptance record for an authorized channel change. Include the same locations/test conditions, both radio directions where measurable, retries/utilization, and a fresh application action. State what remains a prediction when no physical RF equipment is available.

:::solution Check the independent plan
C uses channel 11: it hears both fixed A/1 and B/6. D uses channel 1: it hears B/6 and C/11, and the supplied survey permits reuse with A. Every strongly audible pair uses different nonoverlapping channels. This particular reuse decision depends on the stated survey; it is not a universal “fourth AP uses 1” rule.

The first SNR is `−64 − (−90) = 26 dB`. The busier location gives `−59 − (−66) = 7 dB`. The latter desired signal is stronger, but the former has the better ratio. Signal strength alone would select the wrong conclusion about relative noise conditions.

Confirm the intended BSSID-to-AP/forwarding mapping, valid address/mask/gateway, gateway reachability where relevant, and the actual application's fresh result. Record interruption or session behavior if that is a requirement. Identical SSIDs alone do not guarantee identical VLANs, valid addressing or preserved sessions; this scenario explicitly supplies the common LAN rather than asking you to assume it.

Keep before/after channel/width, client location, received/noise measurements where available, both-direction link evidence, retries/utilization and the same application transaction. Apply one approved change, observe it, then restore the known baseline separately if it fails acceptance. In Packet Tracer or paper-only work, channel settings and model predictions can be recorded, but physical coverage, interference and measured capacity remain unverified.
:::

questions.prompt: What does CSMA/CA contribute to ordinary Wi-Fi operation?
options: Listening, waiting and backoff to reduce contention collisions
Full-duplex transmission and reception on the same ordinary radio
A dedicated collision-free channel for each associated station
Guaranteed retransmission-free delivery once a client associates
questions.explanation: Carrier sensing and contention/backoff rules help stations share airtime. They do not eliminate collisions, retries or interference. Modern scheduling enhancements do not remove those basic RF limits.

whyWrong.1: The ordinary same-channel radio model here is half duplex.
whyWrong.2: Association does not allocate an independent radio channel per station.
whyWrong.3: Association is not a guarantee of error-free delivery.

questions.prompt: For neighboring APs using the ordinary North American 2.4 GHz 20 MHz plan, which two statements are correct? Choose two.
options: A 40 MHz channel creates more independent frequency choices
Adjacent channel numbers have centers only 5 MHz apart
Channels 1, 2 and 3 provide three separate occupied ranges
Channels 1, 6 and 11 are the usual nonoverlapping reuse set
A different SSID lets nearby APs ignore shared airtime
questions.explanation: Channel spacing is narrower than the occupied width. The usual 1/6/11 plan separates neighboring cells; increasing width consumes more spectrum.

whyWrong.0: Wider operation consumes spectrum rather than creating additional independent channels.
whyWrong.2: These closely spaced channels overlap.
whyWrong.4: Different network names do not separate RF frequencies.

questions.prompt: Why can an AP using a DFS-required 5 GHz channel leave that channel even when its clients have strong signals?
options: SSID uniqueness requires each AP to change its channel periodically
Radar protection requires it to vacate after a radar detection
A strong client signal causes a mandatory radio power shutdown
A WPA2 key renewal requires a different center frequency
questions.explanation: DFS protects radar users of shared spectrum. Signal strength does not override the regulatory requirement; exact channels and timing depend on the deployment.

whyWrong.0: SSID uniqueness is not a DFS mechanism.
whyWrong.2: Strong signal alone does not cause the stated radar-driven behavior.
whyWrong.3: Security key renewal is separate from channel selection.

questions.prompt: Wi-Fi 6E extends which radio technology into compatible 6 GHz equipment?
questions.explanation: Wi-Fi 6E identifies the 6 GHz extension of 802.11ax. Both AP and client need compatible hardware and local regulatory support.

whyWrong.1: 802.11n operates in 2.4 and 5 GHz.
whyWrong.2: 802.11a is an older 5 GHz technology.
whyWrong.3: 802.11ac is a 5 GHz technology.

questions.prompt: Which pairing is appropriate for the WPA2-PSK configuration taught in the CCNA GUI objective?
options: WPA2-Personal using AES-CCMP and a shared passphrase
WPA2-Enterprise using AES-CCMP and individual EAP credentials
WPA3-Personal using SAE and protected management frames
Original WPA-Personal using TKIP and a shared passphrase
questions.explanation: The required WPA2-PSK exercise uses WPA2-Personal and AES-CCMP. WEP and TKIP are legacy choices, while WPA3 has its own authentication/security requirements.

whyWrong.1: That is an Enterprise authentication design, not the requested WPA2-PSK exercise.
whyWrong.2: That is WPA3-Personal rather than the stated WPA2-PSK setting.
whyWrong.3: Original WPA/TKIP is a legacy alternative, not this WPA2/AES exercise.

questions.prompt: Which two statements describe a WPA3-Personal-only WLAN? Choose two.
options: It uses SAE for password-based authentication
It requires TKIP for compatibility with original WPA
It requires protected management frame support
It requires individual RADIUS accounts for every client
It removes the need to protect endpoints and credentials
questions.explanation: WPA3-Personal uses SAE and requires PMF. These improve wireless protection but do not eliminate endpoint risks or all forms of radio disruption.

whyWrong.1: TKIP is obsolete and is not the WPA3-Personal cipher requirement.
whyWrong.3: Per-user 802.1X/RADIUS is an Enterprise design, not a Personal requirement.
whyWrong.4: Wireless security does not replace endpoint and credential protection.

exhibit.title: netsh wlan show interfaces — representative
exhibit.text:
State: connected
SSID: STAFF
Authentication: WPA2-Personal
Cipher: CCMP
Channel: 44
Receive rate (Mbps): 866.7

questions.prompt: Which security interpretation is supported by the representative report?
options: The client is using an Enterprise EAP method against RADIUS
The client has completed a successful application throughput test
The connection uses TKIP because Personal mode requires RC4
The connection uses WPA2-Personal with the reported CCMP cipher
questions.explanation: The Authentication and Cipher fields establish the reported WLAN security combination. They do not show an application performance test or prove end-to-end service access.

whyWrong.0: The report says Personal, not Enterprise.
whyWrong.1: A link-rate field is not a throughput measurement.
whyWrong.2: The reported cipher is CCMP, not TKIP.

exhibit.title: Windows-style scan — representative
exhibit.text:
SSID: STAFF
BSSID: 02:11:22:33:44:50   Band: 2.4 GHz   Channel: 6
BSSID: 02:11:22:33:44:51   Band: 5 GHz     Channel: 44

questions.prompt: What can be concluded from this representative scan without consulting an AP inventory?
options: Two BSSIDs advertise STAFF; the scan does not establish physical ownership
The different bands require the clients to use two different network names
The two identifiers establish that both radios belong to one physical AP
The similar addresses establish that the second entry is a spoofed radio
questions.explanation: One SSID can appear on multiple radios and APs. BSSID identifies the service set; similar MAC-style values do not establish which physical chassis owns them.

whyWrong.1: Different bands can advertise the same SSID.
whyWrong.2: Address similarity is not a verified physical inventory mapping.
whyWrong.3: A different or similar BSSID alone does not prove impersonation.

questions.prompt: An AP changes from 20 dBm transmit power to 23 dBm. What is its approximate new power?
options: 50 mW
400 mW
200 mW
questions.explanation: 20 dBm represents 100 mW. A 3 dB increase is approximately a doubling, giving about 200 mW; the exact value is about 199.5 mW.

whyWrong.0: About 50 mW corresponds to 17 dBm, a decrease.
whyWrong.1: About 400 mW corresponds to 26 dBm.
whyWrong.3: 1,000 mW corresponds to 30 dBm.

questions.prompt: At one receiver, signal is −65 dBm and noise is −92 dBm over the same observation period. What is SNR?
options: 27 dBm
−157 dBm
27 dB
−27 dB
questions.explanation: Subtract noise from signal: −65 − (−92) = 27. SNR is a power ratio expressed in dB, not an absolute dBm level.

whyWrong.0: The numeric result is correct but the unit is not.
whyWrong.1: Adding the levels does not calculate SNR.
whyWrong.3: This reverses the subtraction.

exhibit.title: Survey worksheet
exhibit.text:
AP-A: channel 1
AP-B: channel 6
AP-C: channel 6
AP-B and AP-C: strong mutual reception; high shared airtime utilization

questions.prompt: All APs use 20 MHz in the North American 1/6/11 plan. The survey shows no other relevant channel-11 source. Which candidate change addresses the displayed reuse and should then be verified?
options: Move AP-C to channel 11 and verify the resulting RF behavior
Move AP-A to channel 6 so all APs can coordinate one channel
Move AP-B to channel 3 to separate it from AP-C numerically
Move AP-C to channel 8 to create a separate center frequency
questions.explanation: The demonstrated problem is AP-B/AP-C sharing channel 6. Channel 11 is a suitable candidate in this stated plan; measurements after the change verify the result.

whyWrong.1: Adding another co-channel AP does not remove the existing contention.
whyWrong.2: Channel 3 introduces overlap rather than using the planned nonoverlapping set.
whyWrong.3: Channel 8 overlaps the neighboring channel-6 occupied spectrum.

exhibit.title: Verified deployment
exhibit.text:
AP1: SSID STAFF, BSSID 02:00:00:00:01:10
AP2: SSID STAFF, BSSID 02:00:00:00:02:10
Both bridge to VLAN 20 through the wired LAN.
The roaming client's address remains 10.20.0.57/24.

questions.prompt: The managed deployment uses the same SSID and security on both APs with a common distribution system. What describes the combined service?
options: An independent basic service set
A single basic service set
An extended service set
A wireless mesh backhaul
questions.explanation: The cooperating infrastructure BSSs form an ESS. The given shared VLAN supports this example's unchanged IP addressing, but identical SSIDs alone would not prove the same result.

whyWrong.0: An IBSS is an ad hoc arrangement without these infrastructure APs.
whyWrong.1: Each shown BSSID identifies a separate BSS.
whyWrong.3: The exhibit specifies wired distribution, not wireless mesh backhaul.

exhibit.title: Authorized diagnostic observations — authored worksheet
exhibit.text:
2.4 GHz client: strong received level, heavy retries while nearby microwave runs
Spectrum observation: non-Wi-Fi energy increases during operation
Controlled appliance off/on trials: impairment repeatedly disappears/returns
5 GHz comparison client: unaffected

questions.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the controlled observations?
options: The noon timing proves a neighboring AP changes channel
A DFS event on 2.4 GHz causes the recorded loss
The operating appliance is a demonstrated interference source
The laptop's strong signal rules out RF interference
questions.explanation: The controlled repeated correlation and non-Wi-Fi energy measurement support the appliance as the source in this scenario. A lunchtime symptom alone would only suggest investigation.

whyWrong.0: No neighboring-AP channel change is shown.
whyWrong.1: The ordinary 2.4 GHz WLAN in this scenario does not use 5 GHz DFS.
whyWrong.3: Strong desired signal can coexist with interfering energy.

questions.prompt: A WLAN design must support revoking one employee's individual credential. Which design directly meets that requirement?
options: Personal mode with one shared passphrase and MAC filtering
Personal mode with one periodically rotated staff passphrase
Personal mode with one shared passphrase and hidden SSID
Enterprise EAP with an individually managed account per employee
questions.explanation: Individually managed Enterprise credentials allow targeted revocation. Enforcement can also require terminating existing sessions according to policy; disabling an account is not a promise that every active session ends instantly.

whyWrong.0: MAC filtering is not an individually authenticated credential and addresses can be copied.
whyWrong.1: Rotating a common secret affects the group rather than one employee's credential.
whyWrong.2: Hiding the SSID does not create individual authentication.

questions.prompt: A surveyed point-to-point link needs a narrow beam aimed at a second building. Which listed pattern best matches that requirement?
options: An omnidirectional antenna covering the room horizontally
A directional dish with an 8-degree specified beamwidth
A broad wall-panel pattern covering a 120-degree sector
An omnidirectional ceiling pattern covering nearby desks
questions.explanation: The stated narrow-beam dish fits the specified point-to-point coverage pattern. Actual suitability still depends on link budget, alignment, clearance and permitted power; antenna names or distance alone are insufficient.

whyWrong.0: Room-wide horizontal coverage does not match the requested narrow beam.
whyWrong.2: The supplied 120-degree sector is much broader than the stated link needs.
whyWrong.3: The supplied pattern is for local area coverage rather than the specified beam.

exhibit.title: Client status
exhibit.text:
Receive PHY rate: 600 Mb/s
Client count on shared channel: 24
Application file-transfer rate: not measured

questions.prompt: Why does the reported PHY rate not establish a 600 Mb/s file-transfer rate?
options: Each associated client is reserved the displayed 600 Mb/s concurrently
The application rate is fixed at exactly half the displayed PHY rate
Changing the SSID isolates this client from the channel's other users
Overhead and shared airtime prevent that link rate from proving throughput
questions.explanation: The link rate describes radio transmission capability for that connection. Useful application throughput depends on airtime, overhead, retries and the rest of the path; no fixed percentage applies universally.

whyWrong.0: The shared radio medium does not reserve the full link rate for every client.
whyWrong.1: There is no universal fixed PHY-to-application throughput ratio.
whyWrong.2: A network name does not create independent radio spectrum.

exhibit.title: Two RF measurements (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Comparable readings at each client during the stated interval:
Client A: signal −54 dBm, noise −66 dBm
Client B: signal −66 dBm, noise −96 dBm
Application throughput has not been measured.

questions.prompt: Which comparison is supported by the two measurements?
options: A has stronger signal and therefore must deliver higher throughput
A has 12 dBm SNR, while B has a weaker 30 dBm signal
B has 30 dB SNR, compared with A's 12 dB; throughput still needs testing
B must use a higher-power AP because its noise floor is lower
questions.explanation: A: −54 − (−66) = 12 dB. B: −66 − (−96) = 30 dB. B has the better signal-to-noise ratio despite its weaker signal, but neither measurement alone guarantees application capacity.

whyWrong.0: Stronger desired signal can coexist with a much higher noise floor.
whyWrong.1: SNR is a ratio in dB; −66 dBm is B's received signal.
whyWrong.3: A lower noise floor does not establish the AP's transmit power.

exhibit.title: Bonded channel comparison (exercise)
exhibit.text:
AP-A: 5 GHz, 80 MHz width; occupied component channels 36, 40, 44 and 48.
AP-B: 5 GHz, 20 MHz width on channel 44.
The cells have strong mutual reception.

questions.prompt: Which channel-width conclusion is correct?
options: Different primary channels prove the occupied spectrum is independent
The 80 MHz radio overlaps the narrower radio's channel spectrum
Renaming one SSID separates these transmissions in frequency
Both must have the same PHY rate because some spectrum overlaps
questions.explanation: The supplied 80 MHz channel includes the component containing channel 44. Different primary-channel labels do not make their occupied spectrum disjoint. Channel width and the actual occupied range matter.

whyWrong.0: The primary-channel number does not describe the entire bonded range.
whyWrong.2: SSID naming does not change occupied frequencies.
whyWrong.3: Overlap does not determine equal rates; capabilities and conditions also matter.

exhibit.title: Measurement location and time (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Laptop receive level from AP-A: −60 dBm at 10:00.
AP-A noise floor: −95 dBm at 10:20 in a different location.
No laptop noise measurement is available.

questions.prompt: Can these two readings establish the laptop's SNR?
options: No: obtain comparable signal and noise readings at the same receiver
Yes: subtract the distant AP's noise reading to obtain 35 dB
Yes: the shared SSID makes noise identical throughout the WLAN
No: negative dBm levels cannot be used in a subtraction
questions.explanation: SNR compares desired signal with noise at the relevant receiver over a comparable interval and band. Combining a laptop's measurement with an AP's measurement elsewhere does not establish either receiver's SNR.

whyWrong.1: The arithmetic mixes different receivers and observation conditions.
whyWrong.2: The SSID does not make RF conditions uniform.
whyWrong.3: Negative dBm values are valid power levels; the issue is measurement comparability.

exhibit.title: Band compatibility requirements (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Approved new WLAN: 6 GHz, WPA3-Personal.
Client vendor specification and driver report: 2.4/5 GHz only.
The business requires this client to retain authorized access; its current hardware has no 6 GHz upgrade path.

questions.prompt: Which deployment change can meet the stated requirement without pretending a setting adds unsupported hardware?
options: Rename the 6 GHz SSID to match the client's saved 5 GHz profile
Provide an approved compatible band or replace/update to documented capable equipment
Select WPA2-only security on the 6 GHz radio for this client
Increase 6 GHz transmit power until the 5 GHz-only adapter can detect it
questions.explanation: The verified client lacks a 6 GHz radio capability. Use a supported, approved band for it or obtain equipment with documented 6 GHz support. A name, power change or security downgrade cannot add the missing radio band.

whyWrong.0: SSID equality does not add a radio capability.
whyWrong.2: WPA2-only is not the appropriate 6 GHz security design and would not add band support.
whyWrong.3: Increasing power does not change the adapter's supported frequency band.

exhibit.title: A direction-specific RF change (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Same stationary client before/after an approved AP power increase:
Client receives AP: −72 -> −61 dBm.
AP receives client: −81 -> −81 dBm; uplink retries remain high.
Security completes; client address/gateway are correct.
Downloads improve, uploads still fail the application acceptance test.

questions.prompt: Which next action best addresses the evidence without assuming more AP power fixes both directions?
options: Raise the AP power again because the client hears it well
Inspect client-to-AP coverage and placement using repeated two-direction tests
Replace the DHCP pool because association implies good radio delivery
Widen the channel before checking the weak client-to-AP path
questions.explanation: The AP's higher transmit power improved only what the client receives. The AP still hears a weak client transmission and uplink retries remain high. Investigate placement, obstructions and client capability in that direction, then compare the same tests before claiming recovery.

whyWrong.0: Further AP transmit power does not increase the client's transmit capability.
whyWrong.2: The supplied valid addressing and directional RF evidence do not identify a DHCP fault.
whyWrong.3: More width does not establish a repair for the weak return radio path.

exhibit.title: Roaming and retained addressing (exercise)
exhibit.text:
AP-A and AP-B advertise STAFF with the same approved security.
Client was on AP-A/VLAN 20 with 10.20.0.57/24, gateway 10.20.0.1.
After moving: BSSID maps to AP-B; security succeeds; signal is strong.
The old IP settings remain, but the gateway and application no longer respond.
AP-B's wired VLAN/mobility mapping has not been verified.

questions.prompt: Which next check best separates the wireless identity from the broken IP path?
options: Treat the shared SSID as proof that both BSSIDs lead to VLAN 20
Raise the client signal threshold because strong RSSI proves DHCP succeeded
Change the server's address because a changed BSSID proves a server fault
Check AP-B's forwarding/VLAN design and the client's valid subnet after the move
questions.explanation: The client changed cells and completed compatible security, but the retained address is not automatically correct behind AP-B. Verify the authorized mapping/mobility design and obtain valid addressing for that path. Same SSID and good signal do not establish the same VLAN or uninterrupted sessions.

whyWrong.0: SSID equality is not proof of an identical wired forwarding domain.
whyWrong.1: Signal strength does not prove a fresh DHCP exchange or correct subnet.
whyWrong.2: No supplied evidence identifies a server addressing change.

exhibit.title: Two plausible interference explanations (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Lunchtime calls deteriorate on 2.4 GHz; signal stays strong.
Scan shows nearby APs; retries increase, but utilization and spectrum were not recorded.
A microwave is nearby, and client load also rises at lunchtime.
Security and IP settings remain valid.

questions.prompt: Which next test would best distinguish the proposed RF causes?
options: Declare the nearby microwave responsible because loss happens at lunch
Replace the shared passphrase because channel scans cannot show passwords
Change every AP to the strongest scanned channel and compare afterward
Record band, retries/utilization and spectrum during controlled authorized comparisons
questions.explanation: The symptoms suggest investigation but do not identify one source. Correlate comparable RF and service evidence, and use an authorized controlled change that separates the suspected non-Wi-Fi source from competing Wi-Fi load. Change one factor at a time.

whyWrong.0: Timing and proximity alone do not establish the cause.
whyWrong.1: No supplied security failure is shown, and password changes do not diagnose RF load.
whyWrong.2: The strongest scanned signal does not identify the least congested channel; changing every AP loses experimental control.

cards.front: Nonoverlapping 2.4 GHz channels in the usual North American 20 MHz plan?
cards.back: 1, 6 and 11. This is a reuse plan; the actual permitted channel list depends on the regulatory domain.

cards.front: Why do neighboring 2.4 GHz channel numbers overlap?
cards.back: Centers are generally 5 MHz apart while the occupied channel is much wider, commonly 20 MHz (legacy DSSS about 22 MHz).

cards.front: What happens when 5 GHz 20 MHz channels are bonded to 80 MHz?
cards.back: It consumes the component channels, overlaps their spectrum and leaves fewer independent choices. A higher possible PHY rate is not guaranteed better application throughput.

cards.front: What is DFS for?
cards.back: Protecting radar users on designated shared channels. Detection can force a channel change; exact channels and timing are location/platform dependent.

cards.front: What must support a 6 GHz WLAN?
cards.back: The AP and client need suitable radio capability and local authorization; use the applicable WPA3 or Enhanced Open security design.

cards.front: What does a +3 dB power change mean approximately?
cards.back: Twice the power. It does not mean twice the coverage distance or twice the application throughput.

cards.front: dB versus dBm versus dBi?
cards.back: dB is a ratio; dBm is power relative to 1 mW; dBi is antenna gain relative to an isotropic reference.

cards.front: How is SNR calculated from dBm readings?
cards.back: Signal minus noise at the same receiver and observation period, expressed in dB. −65 − (−92) = 27 dB.

cards.front: What does Wi-Fi 6E add to compatible Wi-Fi 6 equipment?
cards.back: Operation in the 6 GHz band, subject to AP/client support and local authorization. A label or SSID setting does not add a radio band.

cards.front: SSID versus BSSID?
cards.back: SSID is the WLAN name, up to 32 octets. BSSID is a 48-bit service-set identifier, not proof of a particular physical AP.

cards.front: How do an infrastructure BSS and an ESS differ?
cards.back: A BSS is one AP service and its associated stations. An ESS connects infrastructure BSSs through a distribution system.

cards.front: Co-channel versus adjacent-channel effects?
cards.back: Co-channel cells share airtime; overlapping occupied channels can interfere. Either situation can involve retries; there is no fixed throughput-halving rule.

cards.front: What evidence identifies a non-Wi-Fi interferer?
cards.back: Correlate band, time, spectrum information and a controlled change. A nearby microwave or Bluetooth device is a candidate, not proof by itself.

cards.front: Which protection pair does the WPA2-Personal lab use?
cards.back: A shared passphrase with AES-CCMP. WEP and original WPA/TKIP are legacy alternatives, not equivalent modern settings.

cards.front: What changes with WPA3-Personal?
cards.back: SAE password authentication and required PMF. These do not prevent all disruption, protect every management frame or secure a compromised endpoint.

cards.front: Shared Personal credentials versus Enterprise credentials?
cards.back: Ordinary shared-passphrase Personal access differs from individually managed 802.1X/EAP Enterprise authentication. Session enforcement remains a separate policy issue.

cards.front: Omnidirectional and directional antenna patterns?
cards.back: Omni provides coverage around an axis; patch, Yagi and dish designs focus energy in chosen directions. Use actual beamwidth/gain specifications, not a universal ranking.

cards.front: Does strong received signal prove usable application connectivity?
cards.back: No. Check airtime/noise, security, IP settings and the actual service; signal strength establishes only part of the link.

cards.front: Why might increasing AP power fail to repair client uploads?
cards.back: It improves what the client hears, not what the AP hears from the client. Assess both directions and the actual application.

cards.front: Do different SSIDs create separate airtime on the same channel?
cards.back: No. Nearby transmissions still share or interfere with the occupied spectrum; a network name is not a separate radio channel.

commands.task: Show the current wireless interface status on Windows.
commands.note: Fields and permissions depend on the OS and adapter. Signal percentage has no universal conversion to dBm.

commands.task: Scan and display visible BSSID details on Windows.
commands.note: This is what the adapter currently reports, not every AP in the area. The same SSID can appear on several BSSIDs.

commands.task: Inspect the Windows wireless adapter driver's reported radio and authentication capabilities.
commands.note: Compare current driver/OS capabilities with the WLAN requirements; check documented upgrades before assuming hardware replacement.

tickets.title: Office transfers slow while the neighboring test radio operates
tickets.scenario: The office AP and a separately authorized test AP use 2.4 GHz, 20 MHz channels. A survey first identifies overlap, then the operator repeats an approved on/off test of the test AP while other conditions remain stable. The excerpts below are an authored diagnostic scenario, not a captured simulator run.

exhibits.title: Radio inventory
exhibits.text:
OFFICE-AP: channel 1, SSID OFFICE
TEST-AP: channel 3, SSID TEST
Client near OFFICE-AP: strong desired signal throughout the test

exhibits.title: Repeated controlled observation
exhibits.text:
TEST-AP transmitting: OFFICE client retries rise sharply; transfer rate falls
TEST-AP radio disabled: retries return near baseline; transfer rate recovers
Repeat trials reproduce the same result; the OFFICE channel remains 1

tickets.question: What cause is supported by the combined evidence?
options: A weak desired signal caused by increasing client distance
Interference from overlapping occupied channels 1 and 3
Co-channel contention because the SSIDs have different names
A DFS radar response on the office's 2.4 GHz channel
tickets.explanation: The inventory establishes overlap, and the controlled repeatable test supports its effect here. Strong desired signal does not exclude interference; a scan alone would not establish the causal conclusion.
tickets.fix: Restore the authorized baseline, then choose an allowed nonoverlapping channel using the complete survey. For a small North American 20 MHz plan, evaluate 1/6/11 across both APs. Change one radio at a time, reconnect clients and repeat the same measurements. Record actual retries and application results; do not infer an optimal channel solely from a neighbor's signal percentage.

tickets.title: One client cannot rejoin after the WLAN security change
tickets.scenario: STAFF is changed to WPA3-Personal-only. A failing client's OS/driver report and vendor compatibility check confirm that this installed combination supports WPA2-Personal but not SAE. The passphrase is verified unchanged. Other compatible clients connect. The excerpts are representative.

exhibits.title: WLAN settings
exhibits.text:
SSID: STAFF
Band: 5 GHz
Security: WPA3-Personal only
Authentication: SAE
PMF: Required

exhibits.title: Client capability evidence
exhibits.text:
Radio support: 802.11a/n/ac
WPA2-Personal + CCMP: Supported
PMF: Supported
WPA3-Personal / SAE: Not supported by installed OS/driver

tickets.question: Which mismatch prevents this client's access?
options: The shared passphrase differs even though it was verified unchanged
The presence of an 802.11ax AP necessarily excludes 802.11ac clients
The client lacks the SAE authentication capability required by this WLAN
The client lacks CCMP even though the capability report lists support
tickets.explanation: The security capability evidence establishes the missing SAE support. PMF and CCMP support alone do not make a client WPA3-capable; radio generation names alone do not establish the security method.
tickets.fix: Check whether a supported OS/driver update provides the required capability for this hardware. Otherwise replace the client or use a separately approved migration design. On 2.4/5 GHz, a compatible WPA2/WPA3 transition design can allow older WPA2 clients, but they still use WPA2 and do not acquire SAE's properties. Confirm the exact controller security/PMF settings and client compatibility, document the exception, and retest. Do not apply a WPA2 fallback to a 6 GHz-only WLAN.

chapters.summary: Compare autonomous, controller-based and cloud-managed WLANs, follow CAPWAP discovery and forwarding, and choose AP and controller switchport settings from the traffic they actually carry.

sections.body: A wireless design contains several distinct paths. Administrators need to configure the AP, the AP needs an IP connection to its manager, and clients need a path into their own network. Those paths can share a cable without sharing a VLAN. Before choosing a switchport configuration, draw where each kind of traffic enters and leaves the wired network.

sections.title: Separate management from client forwarding
sections.body:
:::facts
- CAPWAP uses controller UDP port `5246` for control and `5247` for data.
- In a centrally switched WLAN, client traffic reaches its wired VLAN at the controller. With local switching, it reaches that VLAN at the AP.
- Use an access port for one untagged VLAN; use an 802.1Q trunk when the device must carry tagged VLANs. Architecture names alone do not decide the port mode.
- Established Cisco AP–controller control traffic uses DTLS; CAPWAP discovery precedes that protected session. Data encryption is a separate setting.
- AireOS and Catalyst 9800 have different configuration models. Identify the platform before interpreting interface names or configuring aggregation.
:::

The **management plane** provides configuration and monitoring. The **control plane** makes operational decisions, such as maintaining client state and selecting radio parameters. The **data plane** forwards user traffic. These are descriptions of functions, not three mandatory physical cables.

Consider an AP with management address `192.168.10.21` and a wireless client in `192.168.20.0/24`. The AP can reach its controller using VLAN 10 while the client's VLAN 20 is carried inside a tunnel. The switch connected to that AP may therefore need only an access port in VLAN 10. Making it a trunk because the client is in a different subnet would add configuration without addressing the actual forwarding requirement.

Now change the WLAN to local switching. The AP must put the client's Ethernet traffic directly into VLAN 20. If management remains untagged in VLAN 10, the link needs a trunk with native VLAN 10 and tagged VLAN 20. The IP addresses have not changed; the location where client traffic leaves the tunnel has.

sections.title: Compare the three architectures
sections.body:
An **autonomous AP** keeps its wireless configuration and client handling locally. It can bridge a single WLAN to one untagged Ethernet network or map several WLANs into different VLANs. Multiple tagged VLANs require a trunk; an autonomous AP does not inherently require one. Independent administration becomes more work as the number of APs increases.

A **controller-based AP**, often called a lightweight AP, obtains configuration from a **wireless LAN controller (WLC)**. Cisco's **split-MAC** design keeps time-sensitive radio operations in the AP while centralizing other functions. The AP handles such work as radio acknowledgements, retransmissions, beacons, power-save buffering and per-frame wireless encryption/decryption. The controller coordinates WLAN policies, client state, mobility and radio management. The exact division also depends on AP mode and features.

A **cloud-managed AP** obtains configuration through a cloud service such as the Meraki dashboard. That describes its management arrangement. In Meraki **bridge mode**, ordinary client traffic is bridged into the local wired network. Other supported SSID modes include NAT and tunneling to a concentrator. Identify the configured mode before drawing the data path.

| Design | Main configuration location | Example data path | Port implication |
|---|---|---|---|
| Autonomous | Individual AP | Client → AP → local VLAN | Access or trunk, according to tagging |
| Controller, central switching | WLC | Client → AP → CAPWAP → WLC → client VLAN | AP can use access; WLC often needs trunk |
| Controller, local switching | WLC; AP applies local policy | Client → AP → branch VLAN | AP often needs trunk |
| Meraki bridge mode | Cloud dashboard | Client → AP → local VLAN | Access or trunk, according to tagging |

Management availability and forwarding availability are separate questions. Losing dashboard access does not by itself mean every bridge-mode client loses local communication. Conversely, existing configuration cannot replace a failed DHCP server, authentication service or Internet gateway.

```diagram
{"type":"topology","title":"Fig 37.1 — The same client VLAN can leave at different devices","caption":"The central WLAN reaches VLAN 20 at WLC1; the locally switched WLAN reaches VLAN 20 at AP2.","nodes":[{"id":"C1","kind":"laptop","label":"Central client","x":1,"y":1},{"id":"AP1","kind":"ap","label":"AP1","sub":"untagged management","x":4,"y":1},{"id":"SW","kind":"switch","label":"SW1","x":7,"y":3},{"id":"WLC","kind":"wlc","label":"WLC1","sub":"client VLAN 20","x":11,"y":1},{"id":"AP2","kind":"ap","label":"AP2","sub":"local VLAN 20","x":4,"y":5},{"id":"C2","kind":"laptop","label":"Local client","x":1,"y":5}],"links":[{"from":"C1","to":"AP1","style":"wireless"},{"from":"AP1","to":"SW","label":"access VLAN 10"},{"from":"SW","to":"WLC","label":"trunk 10,20","accent":true},{"from":"C2","to":"AP2","style":"wireless"},{"from":"AP2","to":"SW","label":"native 10; tagged 20","accent":true}]}
```

sections.title: Place the controller
sections.body:
A controller can be a physical appliance or a supported virtual deployment such as Catalyst 9800-CL. A centralized campus controller can serve APs in many buildings. A branch may use local switching to avoid sending local printer traffic across a WAN to a distant controller and back.

**Cloud-based controller** and **cloud-managed AP** are different descriptions. A controller VM in a hosted environment still has AP discovery, CAPWAP and platform-specific forwarding requirements. A Meraki dashboard is not simply an AireOS controller VM with a different web address.

You may also encounter embedded controllers in supported switches or APs. These are product-specific designs, not a feature available on every Catalyst device. Cisco's Embedded Wireless Controller running on an AP reached end of sale in November 2024, with IOS XE 17.15.x its final supported software train. Recognize existing EWC-AP and older Mobility Express deployments without treating them as the default new purchase. The separate switch-based embedded offering has its own scope and lifecycle.

For this chapter, concentrate on placement and forwarding consequences. Maximum AP counts, VM sizes, licensing and supported hypervisors belong in the selected product's current deployment guide.

sections.title: Follow CAPWAP discovery and forwarding
sections.body:
**CAPWAP** stands for Control and Provisioning of Wireless Access Points. Its outer IP packet uses the AP and controller addresses. Routers between them forward that outer packet normally; the AP need not share the controller's subnet.

An AP first needs working power, Ethernet and IP configuration. It then discovers controller candidates. Common Cisco methods are local-subnet discovery, previously learned or configured controller addresses, DHCP option 43, and DNS for `CISCO-CAPWAP-CONTROLLER` in the relevant domain. Local broadcasts do not cross an ordinary routed boundary. A previously joined AP may still remember a controller after a subnet move, so the move alone does not prove discovery will fail.

Option 43 is vendor-specific. For Cisco APs that use suboption `241`, `f104.c0a8.0a05` encodes type `f1`, length `04` and one IPv4 address, `192.168.10.5`. Other AP families can require different formats; check the supported AP model rather than assuming that every vendor interprets this string.

```ios R1 — example inside the AP DHCP pool
R1(config)# ip dhcp pool AP-MGMT
R1(dhcp-config)# network 192.168.10.0 255.255.255.0
R1(dhcp-config)# default-router 192.168.10.1
R1(dhcp-config)# option 43 hex f104.c0a8.0a05
R1(dhcp-config)# exit
```

This example supplies a discovery address; it does not make an unreachable controller reachable. Routing, filtering, software compatibility and certificate checks can still prevent a join. Configured primary/secondary preferences help select a controller from reachable candidates.

```diagram
{"type":"sequence","title":"Fig 37.2 — From an IP address to a registered AP","actors":["AP","DHCP server","WLC"],"steps":[{"from":0,"to":1,"label":"Obtain IP settings","note":"lease, gateway and optional discovery information"},{"from":0,"to":2,"label":"CAPWAP discovery","note":"UDP 5246; before the DTLS session"},{"from":2,"to":0,"label":"Discovery response"},{"from":0,"to":2,"label":"Establish DTLS and join","note":"certificate and compatibility checks","accent":true},{"from":2,"to":0,"label":"Configuration and operational state"},{"from":0,"to":2,"label":"Centrally switched client data","note":"UDP 5247; separate data-encryption policy"}],"caption":"A lease proves address allocation; a registered AP record proves that discovery and the subsequent join completed."}
```

The CAPWAP data path encapsulates client traffic for transport to the controller when central switching is used. Do not assume that every implementation carries an unchanged encrypted 802.11 frame. CAPWAP supports different framing arrangements, and the AP performs wireless decryption/encryption.

:::trap Radio encryption is not tunnel encryption
WPA2/WPA3 protect the client–AP radio link. They do not automatically protect client payloads across the wired AP–controller path. CAPWAP data DTLS is a separate capability and policy; application encryption such as HTTPS is also separate. Discovery traffic is not part of the established encrypted control session.
:::

sections.title: Choose the AP operating mode
sections.body:
An AP's mode determines its job. Available modes depend on the AP family and controller release; a Packet Tracer dropdown is not a complete inventory of current hardware features.

| Mode | Main job | Ordinary wireless clients? |
|---|---|---|
| Local | Serve clients, normally using central switching; also gather RF information | Yes |
| FlexConnect | Serve branch WLANs with supported central/local switching and authentication choices | Yes |
| Monitor | Dedicate radios to monitoring rather than normal client access | No |
| Sniffer | Forward frames heard on a selected channel to a capture system | No on the sniffer radio |
| Bridge/mesh | Use supported wireless backhaul between APs | Depends on model/design |
| Rogue detector, legacy AireOS | Correlate wired observations with suspected rogue devices | No |

A sniffer does not capture every frame everywhere: channel selection, receiver sensitivity, encryption and capture loss limit its view. Monitor mode is not a promise that a device will never transmit under any enabled security function.

**FlexConnect local switching** and **local authentication** are independent settings. A WLAN can send data into a branch VLAN yet use a remote RADIUS server for new authentication. If the WAN fails, already connected clients and new clients may have different outcomes. Continued service depends on supported standalone behavior and reachable local services. An available AP cannot provide a lease from a DHCP server that is across the failed WAN.

Changing AP mode may disrupt service. Whether it requires a reboot depends on the transition and release; some current local/FlexConnect transitions do not. Check status after the change rather than teaching a universal reboot rule.

sections.title: Recognize controller interfaces and profiles
sections.body:
Older **AireOS** screens distinguish physical ports from logical interfaces. A port is a connector. A logical interface identifies a function, IP configuration and, where appropriate, VLAN mapping.

| AireOS item | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Management interface | Controller management and, on common newer AireOS platforms, AP-manager/CAPWAP functions |
| Dynamic interface | Map client traffic to a wired VLAN; includes appropriate address/gateway/DHCP-server settings |
| Virtual interface | Internal support for functions such as web authentication and DHCP proxy; not the clients' routed gateway |
| Service port, where present | Separate out-of-band management connection |
| Redundancy port, where present | High-availability communication with a peer |

An AireOS virtual address should not conflict with a real routed host. Cisco documents using a suitable unused documentation address, such as `192.0.2.1`, for this purpose; the number is not inherently incapable of routing. The controller's service-port and redundancy arrangements vary by model.

Catalyst 9800 uses IOS XE interfaces plus **profiles** and **tags**. Its wireless management interface supports AP/controller communication. A WLAN profile holds the SSID and security; a policy profile carries client policy such as VLAN and switching behavior. A policy tag maps a WLAN profile to a policy profile and is assigned to APs. Site and RF tags supply other AP/site/radio settings. A correctly created WLAN still needs an effective assignment to the intended APs.

Learn to translate the purpose, not copy an AireOS “dynamic interface” command into IOS XE. Chapter 38 applies the WLAN settings through the GUI.

sections.title: Configure the AP and controller links
sections.body:
Choose the switchport from a written traffic contract: which frames arrive tagged, which arrive untagged, which VLANs are needed, and whether the device uses one link or a supported bundle.

Also follow platform requirements: Cisco documents an 802.1Q trunk for an AireOS controller's distribution-system connection even when this isolated example carries only one native VLAN. Its separate service port is an access-port connection. This controller requirement does not make an AP carrying only untagged management traffic require a trunk.

For a centrally switched AP sending only untagged management traffic into VLAN 10:

```ios SW1
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 10
SW1(config-if)# spanning-tree portfast
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
```

For an endpoint explicitly configured to send untagged management in VLAN 10 and tagged locally switched users in VLAN 20:

```ios SW1
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/2
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 10
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20
SW1(config-if)# spanning-tree portfast trunk
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
```

PortFast here is for the documented endpoint connection, not an arbitrary inter-switch link. Both VLANs must exist. The AP's actual management-tag setting must agree with the switch's native/tagged treatment.

**Power over Ethernet (PoE)** also matters. Confirm that the switch port and total switch power budget support the AP's documented requirements. A link can be up while the AP operates with reduced radio capability because it received insufficient power. On a supported Cisco PoE switch, `power inline auto` enables automatic power allocation and `show power inline` reports the state and allocation. A non-PoE Packet Tracer 2960 model cannot validate a real AP power negotiation; use the AP's supported external supply in that simulation.

**Link aggregation** is equally model-specific. Legacy AireOS LAG uses a static bundle, so the adjacent switch uses `channel-group 1 mode on`. Catalyst 9800 supports negotiated aggregation on documented platforms. Some dual-port Meraki APs support LACP: for example, the documented MR52/53 design uses an AP in passive mode and an upstream switch in active mode. Configure compatible VLANs and native VLAN on both members and the port-channel. Provision the AP through its primary port first and follow its installation guide before adding the second cable.

Do not configure every two-port AP as a bundle. A second port may have another purpose, and hardware support must be confirmed. Aggregation distributes flows; it does not guarantee that one flow uses the combined link rate.

sections.title: Verify the design one layer at a time
sections.body:
Check power and Ethernet first, then AP addressing and controller discovery, then AP registration, and finally client forwarding. Representative abbreviated records below illustrate the evidence; field layout depends on software.

```output AireOS — show interface summary
Interface Name  Port  Vlan Id  IP Address      Type     Ap Mgr
management      1     0        192.168.10.5    Static   Yes     ← untagged here; switch native VLAN 10; AP-manager function
users           1     20       192.168.20.5    Dynamic  No      ← client VLAN mapping, not an AP address
virtual         N/A   N/A      192.0.2.1       Static   No
```

```output SW1 — show interfaces trunk (abbreviated)
Port    Mode  Encapsulation  Status    Native vlan
Fa0/24  on    802.1q         trunking  10             ← untagged management design in this example
Port    Vlans allowed on trunk
Fa0/24  10,20                                       ← both required VLANs admitted
```

`show cdp neighbors detail` can identify a neighbor and its advertised address; that is not proof of a DHCP lease or successful CAPWAP join. Use the DHCP binding/AP address and the controller AP table for those checks. AireOS `show ap summary` and Catalyst 9800 `show ap summary` summarize registered APs; their detailed commands and columns differ.

A controller's MAC learned in VLAN 20 proves some traffic from that MAC entered VLAN 20. It does not prove that a wireless client's WLAN mapping is correct. Finish with the intended client's IP settings, controller association/security record and a test to a known reachable destination.

sections.title: Exam focus
sections.body:
- Explain where management and client forwarding occur for each architecture.
- Follow discovery, protected control and optional protected data separately; know CAPWAP UDP `5246/5247`.
- Recognize AP modes and the limits of FlexConnect survival during a controller/WAN failure.
- Translate AireOS ports/interfaces to their purposes; recognize the different 9800 profile/tag model.
- Derive access/trunk, native/allowed VLANs, PoE and supported aggregation from the actual AP requirements.
- Treat old AireOS LAG and current LACP-capable platforms as different cases, not one universal controller rule.

lab.title: Build the wired foundation for a controller WLAN
lab.intro:
Practice revised September 2026. If you completed an earlier version, repeat the revised exercise and update its checkmarks.
Build a management VLAN, a separate client VLAN and the links required for centrally switched wireless service. This lab proves the wired foundation and, where the selected Packet Tracer model supports it, AP registration. The next chapter builds and tests the client WLAN.

:::note Simulator boundary
Start with a new file and record your Packet Tracer version. Use a WLC-3504 and LAP-PT if your palette offers them. Their setup pages and exposed features vary. The switch/router work below is independent of those pages. If the controller lacks a required control or the AP cannot register with the available models, complete the explicitly identified controller worksheet using the given values and record “not simulated”; do not record a successful join. No real RF, PoE negotiation, Meraki dashboard or Catalyst 9800 is simulated by this lab.
:::
