In a separate copy, review this proposed change before applying anything. PC-A (`10.1.1.10`) is now the **only** approved remote administrator of R2. PC-B (`10.2.2.10`) must keep ordinary routed ping connectivity but must no longer open new SSH sessions. R2 Gi0/1's approved description becomes `Branch-B users`. Keep both IP networks and OSPF unchanged.

The recovered configuration currently permits PC-B at sequence 10, PC-A at 15, then denies other sources at 20. A proposed plan removes sequence 15, changes the description and reports “successful deployment” after checking only the description. Identify the two problems, write the smallest correct change and choose acceptance tests. Keep console access, establish PC-B's new SSH baseline first, and close old sessions before testing the new policy.

On paper, a cloud-hosted controller applies the reviewed, versioned desired-state file through an automation pipeline. Classify the overlapping management approaches, label the controller's two API directions and distinguish a successful job status from completion of your acceptance tests. No controller or pipeline is emulated here.

:::solution
The proposed deletion removes approved PC-A rather than disallowed PC-B. Checking only the description omits access and forwarding requirements. At R2's console:

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# ip access-list standard LAB-MGMT
R2(config-std-nacl)# no 10
R2(config-std-nacl)# exit
R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R2(config-if)# description Branch-B users
R2(config-if)# end
R2# show access-lists LAB-MGMT
R2# show running-config
R2# show ip ospf neighbor
```

Preserve sequence 15 permitting PC-A and sequence 20 denying other sources; verify the list remains attached to every usable VTY range. Before the change PC-B can attempt `ssh -l observer 10.2.2.1` with the supplied account, then exit. Afterward a **new** PC-B attempt must be denied, while PC-A's new SSH attempt succeeds. Test PC-A → PC-B and PC-B → PC-A pings, OSPF state and the exact new description. These establish different parts of acceptance; one result cannot replace the others.

If a simulator omits named-ACL sequence deletion, stop before editing and record the proposed ordered entries as a worksheet. Do not improvise a broader policy replacement. The required final list is PC-A permit then deny any; no IP, OSPF or transit-interface policy change is needed. Live verification remains unexecuted for that unsupported variation.

The management workflow can be cloud-based, controller-based, automation-based and infrastructure as code simultaneously. The pipeline/application talks to the controller northbound; the controller talks to managed devices southbound. The device CLI used in this lab is device-based administration. A job result records the tool's outcome; fresh device state and all intended service tests establish whether the change is complete.

Save a verified challenge copy only after the tests, accepting each device's save prompt separately. The recovered baseline remains available.
:::

questions.prompt: Which functions learned this route and forward a transit packet using it?
options: The management plane learns the route; OSPF forwards each packet.
The data plane computes OSPF routes; SSH forwards each packet.
OSPF supplies control information; the data plane forwards the packet.
OSPF selects a new path separately for each transit packet.
questions.explanation: OSPF exchanges routing information and computes reachability. The forwarding function uses installed entries; whether that function runs in hardware or software depends on the platform.

whyWrong.0: OSPF learns the route through the control plane; the data plane forwards packets. These roles are not management-plane route learning or per-packet OSPF forwarding.
whyWrong.1: OSPF is a control-plane protocol, while SSH provides management access.
whyWrong.3: Forwarding uses installed information rather than a new OSPF calculation for every packet.

questions.prompt: Which switch activity is a management-plane function?
options: Answering an SNMP request for interface counters.
Forwarding a received frame toward its destination.
Dropping transit traffic against an installed ACL.
Calculating the STP role for a redundant link.
questions.explanation: The SNMP exchange lets a management system inspect device state. A function is classified by its purpose, not merely by whether a CPU is involved.

whyWrong.1: Frame forwarding is a data-plane function.
whyWrong.2: Applying an ACL to transit traffic is a data-plane function.
whyWrong.3: STP role calculation is a control-plane function.

questions.prompt: Which two are data-plane functions? Choose two.
options: Exchanging OSPF link-state advertisements.
Retrieving interface statistics through an API.
Accepting a network administrator's SSH login.
Adding a VLAN tag while forwarding a frame.
Applying a configured ACL to a transit packet.
questions.explanation: The forwarding path processes transit frames and packets using existing forwarding and policy information. Tag insertion and ACL matching are per-traffic operations.

whyWrong.0: OSPF exchanges establish control information.
whyWrong.1: An API statistics query performs monitoring.
whyWrong.2: SSH administration terminates a management session.

questions.prompt: Which comparison is accurate?
options: Traditional control requires hand typing; controllers provide software automation.
Traditional devices hold no topology state; controllers store every forwarding table.
Traditional forwarding uses CPUs; controller-based forwarding always uses ASICs.
Traditional device control can be automated; controllers coordinate network-wide functions.
questions.explanation: A controller can centralize policy or coordination without eliminating every device protocol. Automation is possible with or without a controller.

whyWrong.0: Scripts can automate traditional devices through their management interfaces.
whyWrong.1: Distributed routing protocols maintain topology/reachability state on devices.
whyWrong.2: Implementation hardware does not define the management architecture.

questions.prompt: In the SD-Access example, which technology encapsulates user traffic for overlay forwarding?
options: NETCONF
VXLAN
LISP
SNMP
questions.explanation: VXLAN carries the inner traffic across the underlay. The example distinguishes the data-plane encapsulation from endpoint-location control and management protocols.

whyWrong.0: NETCONF is a configuration/management protocol.
whyWrong.2: LISP provides endpoint/location control information in this design.
whyWrong.3: SNMP supplies management observations.

questions.prompt: The vendor hosts the management service in its cloud. Devices use that service for configuration, while the described user traffic is locally forwarded. Which label directly describes the hosting arrangement?
options: An on-premises management service
Cloud-based management
Infrastructure as code by definition
Device-only management
questions.explanation: Cloud-based identifies the management service's hosting arrangement. The service can also be controller-based or used by automation; the approaches overlap.

whyWrong.0: The service location is explicitly off premises in the vendor cloud.
whyWrong.2: No versioned infrastructure definitions or reviewed code workflow are specified.
whyWrong.3: The service is hosted centrally in the vendor cloud, not only on each device.

questions.prompt: Which workflow best illustrates infrastructure as code?
options: Accept discovered device settings as approved intent automatically.
Manually paste a template without recording its intended scope.
Keep nightly device backups without defining an approved target.
Review versioned infrastructure definitions and apply them with a tool.
questions.explanation: IaC applies software-style practices to infrastructure definitions and changes. A plan and post-change tests are still needed; a repository does not guarantee safe behavior.

whyWrong.0: Discovery does not automatically approve whatever configuration it finds.
whyWrong.1: Manual repetition alone does not establish a versioned code workflow.
whyWrong.2: A backup records observed state but does not by itself define desired state.

questions.prompt: An application reads inventory from a controller over HTTPS. The controller manages switches using NETCONF. Which mapping is correct?
options: Application/controller is northbound; controller/switch is southbound.
Both are southbound because each crosses physical network links.
Application/controller is southbound; controller/switch is northbound.
Both are northbound because each retrieves structured information.
questions.explanation: Direction is relative to the controller's role in the architecture. HTTPS can also appear in a device-facing interface; protocol name alone is insufficient.

whyWrong.1: Physical location and transport do not define northbound/southbound.
whyWrong.2: The application-facing and infrastructure-facing roles are reversed.
whyWrong.3: Data format does not determine interface direction.

questions.prompt: What does this application response establish?
options: The current endpoint data path is healthy because reachability says Reachable.
The controller forwarded a user packet to determine the software version.
The controller API returned a stored inventory observation in JSON.
The switch has just completed a direct NETCONF query from the application.
questions.explanation: The application received structured inventory data from the controller. The collection timestamp limits conclusions about current device state.

whyWrong.0: The supplied timestamp makes freshness relevant, and management status is not an application test.
whyWrong.1: An inventory representation does not imply user packets traverse the controller.
whyWrong.3: The participants and endpoint are an application and controller; no direct device NETCONF exchange is shown.

exhibit.title: Representative controller response
exhibit.text:
GET /inventory
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
{"device":"SW1","reachability":"Reachable","collectedAt":"2026-09-20T08:00:00Z"}
Current time: 2026-09-20T09:00:00Z

questions.prompt: All overlays between A and B fail, while paths to C still work. Which is the best first shared-dependency check?
options: Compare each endpoint's guest address before checking their common transport
Compare controller inventory timestamps before testing the failed forwarding path
Compare each affected VNI assignment before checking their common transport
Compare A–B underlay reachability and usable MTU as a shared dependency
questions.explanation: A shared underlay path is a reasonable first investigation because multiple overlays depend on it. The symptom does not prove the underlay is the cause; tests must establish which dependency failed.

whyWrong.0: Guest addressing can matter, but this broad pair-specific pattern makes their common transport an efficient first shared check.
whyWrong.1: Inventory freshness is a management concern and does not establish this forwarding path's operation.
whyWrong.2: Individual overlay mappings may need investigation later; first examine the shared transport dependency, without assuming it is proven faulty.

exhibit.title: Observed reachability matrix
exhibit.text:
A ↔ B: all tested virtual networks fail
A ↔ C: tested virtual networks work
B ↔ C: tested virtual networks work
No route, MTU or policy checks have yet been performed.

questions.prompt: Approved intent requires exactly NTP servers 10.200.0.10 and .11. What is the smallest configuration correction?
options: Keep both servers and add 10.200.0.11 as a third.
Remove both current servers, then add 10.200.0.11.
Change the approved record to match the device.
questions.explanation: Preserve the matching .10 entry, replace the unintended .19 with .11 and compare again. Separately verify NTP operation; configuration agreement alone does not prove synchronization.

whyWrong.0: The intended set is exact, so leaving .19 preserves drift.
whyWrong.1: The correct .10 server need not be removed.
whyWrong.3: Observed state does not automatically override approved intent.

exhibit.title: Representative current configuration
exhibit.text:
ntp server 10.200.0.10
ntp server 10.200.0.19

questions.prompt: A cloud-hosted controller is updated by a script using versioned, reviewed desired-state files. Which conclusion follows?
options: Automation removes the need to verify operational results.
Cloud, controller, automation and IaC approaches can overlap.
Cloud management excludes infrastructure-as-code workflows.
Controller-based management must move to an on-premises appliance.
questions.explanation: These labels describe different dimensions of the workflow. Hosting, coordination, execution and change discipline can all apply to the same system.

whyWrong.0: Operational verification remains necessary after automation.
whyWrong.2: IaC can use cloud APIs and controllers.
whyWrong.3: Controller describes coordination, not a required physical location.

questions.prompt: An administrator on PC-A opens SSH to R2 through R1. At R1 the packets are ordinary transit traffic; R2 terminates the session. Which classification fits those roles?
options: R1 data; R2 management
R1 control; R2 data
R1 management; R2 control
R1 management; R2 management
questions.explanation: A packet's role depends on the function at the specified device: forwarding at R1, administration at R2.

whyWrong.1: Transit forwarding is not a control calculation, while the addressed SSH session terminates at R2.
whyWrong.2: R1 does not terminate this management session, and R2 is not exchanging a routing protocol.
whyWrong.3: R1 transports the session rather than serving as its administration endpoint.

questions.prompt: A controller is unavailable. The documented design keeps installed forwarding on switches, but new policy deployments require that controller. Existing client tests still pass. Which conclusion fits?
options: The tested existing forwarding works; new controller policy deployment is unavailable
Every new network change is now safe to make without the controller
The forwarding tests prove the controller has recovered
All routing and authentication dependencies are independent of the failed service
questions.explanation: The supplied dependency permits a narrow conclusion about observed forwarding and blocks the controller-dependent operation. It does not prove all future activity.

whyWrong.1: The new deployment explicitly depends on the unavailable service.
whyWrong.2: A working data path is not a controller availability test.
whyWrong.3: The scenario does not establish every other dependency.

questions.prompt: An unwanted network change was already deployed. A reviewer reverts its infrastructure definition in Git. What is still required to restore the network?
options: Delete the last device backup so it cannot reintroduce the change
Wait for the repository timestamp to change every device automatically
Review and apply the resulting recovery plan, then verify configuration and service
Mark the incident resolved because the approved file now matches its older version
questions.explanation: Version control changes the recorded definition. A supported deployment/reconciliation step must update the actual infrastructure, followed by operational checks.

whyWrong.0: Removing evidence does not apply a recovery.
whyWrong.1: Repository changes do not by themselves establish a deployment mechanism or result.
whyWrong.3: Desired state matching an older file is not evidence that deployed state or service recovered.

exhibit.title: Change acceptance record — representative
exhibit.text:
Approved change: exactly NTP servers 10.200.0.10 and .11; device must synchronize
Job: configuration operations completed without errors
Fresh device configuration: .10 and .11 only
After the agreed observation interval: neither server is selected; clock remains unsynchronized
No reachability/source-status investigation performed yet

questions.prompt: A change job reports success. Which acceptance decision follows from all three observations?
options: Accept the job because configuration now matches the intended server list
Rewrite the approved intent to use whichever server the device currently selects
Revert both approved server entries because a successful job cannot leave an operational fault
Keep the change open and investigate time service operation while preserving the verified configuration
questions.explanation: The configuration goal is satisfied but the operational requirement is not. Keep the task open and test reachability, source usability and current status; the job result does not establish synchronization.

whyWrong.0: The stated acceptance condition also requires actual synchronization.
whyWrong.1: Observed failure does not authorize replacing approved intent.
whyWrong.2: A blanket rollback is not justified solely by a result requiring a more specific operational investigation.

cards.front: What is the difference between control and data-plane work?
cards.back: Control establishes forwarding information; the data plane uses installed information to process traffic.

cards.front: Name two clear control-plane operations.
cards.back: Forming an OSPF adjacency and selecting an STP port role.

cards.front: Applying an installed ACL to a transit packet belongs to which plane?
cards.back: The data plane: it applies existing policy while processing traffic.

cards.front: Must data-plane forwarding occur in a hardware ASIC?
cards.back: No. Physical switches often accelerate it; virtual routers can forward in software.

cards.front: What does controller-based networking centralize?
cards.back: Some combination of network policy, management or control; device forwarding and protocols may remain distributed.

cards.front: Common SDN layers, bottom to top?
cards.back: Infrastructure, controller and applications.

cards.front: What is the northbound interface?
cards.back: The application-facing controller interface, often a REST API.

cards.front: What is the southbound interface?
cards.back: The controller's interface to infrastructure, using supported protocols such as NETCONF, RESTCONF or SSH.

cards.front: NETCONF versus RESTCONF at recognition level?
cards.back: NETCONF commonly uses SSH/XML RPCs; RESTCONF uses HTTP mechanisms with YANG-modeled JSON or XML.

cards.front: Does one enable command prove a device API is usable?
cards.back: No. Platform support, authentication, transport, authorization and an actual request must be verified.

cards.front: Underlay versus overlay?
cards.back: The underlay provides transport between tunnel endpoints; the overlay builds logical connectivity over it.

cards.front: Can the five management approaches overlap?
cards.back: Yes. A cloud-hosted controller can be driven by automation using reviewed infrastructure-as-code definitions.

cards.front: What is configuration drift?
cards.back: A difference between approved desired state and observed configuration within the managed scope.

cards.front: What does an idempotent operation do when repeated?
cards.back: It has the same intended state effect; this is a property to verify, not a guarantee for every script.

cards.front: What limits a controller inventory response as current evidence?
cards.back: Its collection time, source device and collection status; a successful API response may contain older observations.

cards.front: Does reverting an infrastructure file in Git restore deployed devices?
cards.back: Not by itself. Apply the reviewed recovery through the management workflow and verify the actual result.

commands.task: Inspect the CEF forwarding entry selected for destination 10.2.2.10.
commands.note: Optional where this view exists; the lab gives a route-table fallback.

commands.task: Display running-configuration lines containing ntp for comparison with approved intent.
commands.note: Configuration evidence must be followed by operational verification.

commands.task: Inspect the named IPv4 management ACL LAB-MGMT.
commands.note: Cumulative matches do not identify every packet's source.

tickets.title: The controller cannot open new device sessions
tickets.scenario: The controller at 10.10.5.20 can ping SW3 10.10.0.13 but its new SSH connections time out. Users through SW3 still work. A console inspection confirms this ACL is applied inbound to every usable VTY range. These are authored diagnostic excerpts.

exhibits.title: SW3 VTY configuration
exhibits.text:
line vty 0 15
 access-class MGMT-IN in
 login local
 transport input ssh

exhibits.title: SW3 management ACL
exhibits.text:
Standard IP access list MGMT-IN
 10 permit 10.10.99.0 0.0.0.255
 20 deny any

tickets.question: Which mismatch is established by the configuration?
options: The controller source is excluded from the device's VTY permit list
The SSH user is explicitly rejected after password authentication
The switch's transit ACL blocks all user traffic through the switch
The controller has no ICMP route to the switch management address
tickets.explanation: 10.10.5.20 does not match the only permit and reaches deny any for VTY access. A VTY access-class does not apply to ordinary transit frames or prove that other management protocols are also blocked. The supplied source and ACL establish the SSH mismatch without attributing unrelated counters.
tickets.fix:
```ios
SW3# configure terminal
SW3(config)# ip access-list standard MGMT-IN
SW3(config-std-nacl)# 15 permit host 10.10.5.20
SW3(config-std-nacl)# end
SW3# show access-lists MGMT-IN
```
Retest a new SSH session from the controller's actual source and then its documented synchronization workflow.
Repeat a user-service test through SW3 as well. A controller synchronization result and preserved client forwarding are separate acceptance observations.

tickets.title: A replacement path passes small tests but stalls larger traffic
tickets.scenario: A controlled VXLAN design carries a 1500-byte inner IP packet with 14 bytes inner Ethernet, 8 VXLAN, 8 UDP and 20 outer IPv4 bytes. No inner VLAN tag is retained. A replacement underlay interface has an effective IP MTU of 1500. The design requires an outer IP MTU of at least 1550 along this path.

exhibits.title: Representative path evidence
exhibits.text:
Small endpoint-locator ICMP tests: successful
1550-byte outer IPv4 test with DF: ICMP fragmentation-needed received
Reported next-hop MTU: 1500
Replacement interface effective IP MTU: 1500
Other tested path interfaces: effective IP MTU at least 1550

tickets.question: What established issue should the approved repair address?
options: The approved overlay identifier is mismatched at the two tunnel endpoints
The return route is absent for packets of every tested size
The replacement interface cannot carry the required outer IP packet
The controller's stored inventory is too old to authenticate the application
tickets.explanation: The required outer IP packet is 1500+14+8+8+20=1550 bytes. Explicit fragmentation-needed evidence and the replacement interface's effective MTU establish the size mismatch. This is stronger than inferring MTU solely from a stalled file copy.
tickets.fix: Use the replacement platform's documented MTU procedure to meet the approved end-to-end design, checking whether a reload or interface action is required. Do not blindly apply a system-wide command to an unspecified model. Recheck the effective MTU, repeat the 1550-byte DF test, and test the actual application and return direction.

chapters.title: REST APIs and JSON
chapters.subtitle: Read requests, responses, credentials and structured network data accurately.

sources.title: Python: JSON parsing and compliance limits

chapters.summary: Interpret REST-style HTTP exchanges and JSON without confusing encoding, authentication, authorization, transport protection or a completed network change.

sections.body: A network API gives software a defined way to request information or operations. Reading an exchange requires several separate questions: which resource is addressed, what operation is requested, how is access established, what does the status mean, and how is the returned data structured? You do not need to become an application developer to answer those questions accurately.

sections.title: Why network engineers read HTTP
sections.body:
:::facts
- REST is an architectural style. HTTP supplies application-level request/response semantics; JSON is a data format.
- Common CRUD mappings: create `POST`, read `GET`, replace/create-at-a-known-URI `PUT`, partial modification `PATCH`, remove `DELETE`. Follow the API contract.
- `Content-Type` describes the message body. `Accept` expresses acceptable response formats.
- JSON has objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and `null`.
- Basic encoding, bearer credentials and JSON formatting do not encrypt a connection. HTTPS uses TLS; certificate and hostname verification matter.
:::

A controller may expose inventory, interfaces, tasks and policies as **resources**. A script reads them using documented paths and data models. Structured output can be easier to process than CLI text, but it still needs interpretation. A field named “reachable” may reflect the last collection; a successful task submission may not mean a device was changed.

The v1.1 objectives ask you to describe REST characteristics and recognize JSON components. The announced v2.0 blueprint does not name those standalone objectives. This chapter remains useful preparation for controller and automation work; it does not claim that deploying a RESTCONF service is required here.

sections.title: What makes an API RESTful
sections.body:
**Representational State Transfer (REST)** describes architectural constraints. Client/server separation gives each side a defined responsibility. A stateless interaction carries the context needed to interpret the request rather than depending on a hidden sequence of conversational steps. Responses indicate whether and how they may be cached. A uniform interface lets clients interact through consistent resource identification and representations. Layering permits intermediaries. Code on demand is optional.

**Stateless** does not mean the server stores nothing. Servers retain resource data, credentials, authorization information and logs. A token can identify an access context without making a client rely on a prior “select device R1” command remembered in an interactive terminal session.

Caching also does not mean every response is safe to reuse forever. Cache instructions and freshness determine whether a stored response can answer a request. Sensitive responses need appropriate handling. A controller inventory record and its timestamp should be interpreted together.

Many products call their HTTP APIs REST APIs while implementing different subsets of REST conventions. An HTTPS endpoint returning JSON is not, by that fact alone, proof of every REST constraint. For CCNA interpretation, know the architecture and read the supplied API contract rather than inventing behavior from a product label.

sections.title: Requests: URIs, verbs and headers
sections.body:
Consider `https://controller.example/api/devices?site=branch1`. The scheme is `https`, the authority identifies the server, `/api/devices` is the path and `site=branch1` is the query. A query's meaning is defined by the API; adding an undocumented filter does not guarantee filtering.

| Method | Common use | Important qualification |
|---|---|---|
| GET | Retrieve a representation | Read semantics; do not use it to request a configuration change |
| POST | Submit data for processing, often create a subordinate resource | Repeating it can create another operation |
| PUT | Set the target resource's representation | Can replace or create when the API permits |
| PATCH | Apply a partial modification | Interpretation depends on the patch media type |
| DELETE | Remove the target's association/resource | A second deletion may return a different response |

A **safe** method does not request a state-changing action. Logging a GET or incrementing a request counter does not make GET unsafe: those incidental effects differ from the requested operation.

An **idempotent** method has the same intended state effect after repeated identical requests. GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent by their HTTP semantics; POST and PATCH are not guaranteed to be. A second DELETE can return `404` after the first returned `204`, yet the intended result remains “resource absent.”

If a POST times out, the request may have succeeded and only the reply been lost. Blindly repeating it can duplicate a job or collide with an existing object. Read the API's status lookup, identifier or idempotency-key facilities. A method label does not remove the need to reconcile an uncertain outcome.

For a JSON body, `Content-Type: application/json` identifies its media type. `Accept: application/json` says the client accepts that format in the response. Neither header grants access. The required schema still determines whether fields such as `enabled` must be boolean and whether a resource name is valid.

sections.title: Responses: status codes
sections.body:
Read the status before trying to parse a success body. An error may have a different JSON structure or even an HTML body supplied by an intermediary.

| Code/class | Meaning | Appropriate interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| 1xx / 2xx / 3xx | Informational / successful / redirection | Follow the specific response semantics |
| 200 / 201 | Successful response / resource created | Read the representation and any Location header |
| 202 / 204 | Accepted for processing / success without content | 202 is not completion; 204 has no body to parse |
| 400 / 401 / 403 | Bad request / valid authentication credentials missing / refused request | Inspect the error and documented authorization policy |
| 404 / 405 / 409 | Resource not found / method not allowed / state conflict | Verify target, supported method and current state |
| 429 | Too many requests | Respect documented backoff and Retry-After when provided |
| 500 / 502 / 503 | Internal error / invalid upstream response / temporarily unavailable | Diagnose and retry only with appropriate safety and backoff |

`401 Unauthorized` indicates that the request lacks valid authentication credentials for the target; the name can be misleading. `403 Forbidden` indicates refusal. Insufficient permission is a common cause, but 403 does not universally prove that the caller was successfully authenticated. A server can also conceal a forbidden resource using 404.

A 4xx or 5xx class helps classify the response; it does not allocate personal blame or prove the root cause. A proxy can generate an error before the controller receives the request. A 503 does not prove every part of the submitted body was valid. Capture the status, relevant headers, safe error detail and request identifier before changing several variables.

:::trap Accepted is not completed
A `202` response can provide a task URL. Inspect that task according to the API contract until it reaches a terminal state. Then verify the required network result; an accepted job is not evidence that every device now has the intended configuration.
:::

sections.title: Authentication and transport protection
sections.body:
**Authentication** establishes an identity or accepted credential context. **Authorization** determines permitted operations. **TLS** protects the channel and normally authenticates the server through certificate validation. These are related but different checks.

| Mechanism | Typical representation | What to remember |
|---|---|---|
| HTTP Basic | `Authorization: Basic ...` | Base64 of username:password; reversible encoding |
| API key | Documented header containing an issued secret | Treat it as a credential; location/lifetime are API-specific |
| Bearer credential | `Authorization: Bearer ...` | Possession grants the represented access; token format is not fixed |
| OAuth 2.0 | Framework for obtaining access tokens | Grants, scopes and optional refresh behavior depend on the flow |

Basic's encoding does not hide a password from someone who can read the header. Use authenticated HTTPS for real credentials. With curl, `--user username` can request a password interactively; embedding a password directly in a command risks shell-history or process-list exposure.

An API key can be carried using a vendor header or, where documented, a Bearer header. A Bearer header alone does not prove OAuth was used. Tokens may be opaque strings or structured formats; they are not necessarily JWTs and do not all expire after one hour.

OAuth is an authorization framework that can support delegated access. Modern suitable flows avoid giving the client the user's password. Not every flow returns a refresh token, and client-credentials flows concern the application's own access. Do not infer a complete OAuth exchange merely from the word “token.”

Cisco APIs provide concrete examples. Meraki documents API-key and OAuth mechanisms. Catalyst Center APIs commonly use an authentication endpoint and an `X-Auth-Token` header. Read the exact product/version documentation for acquisition, lifetime and permissions. This course supplies no supposedly permanent public sandbox password.

When curl reports a certificate failure, inspect trust, hostname, expiry and the system clock. Suppressing validation with `--insecure` removes an important identity check. A lab can use a trusted private CA or a deliberately pinned certificate with the correct name; the existence of a self-signed certificate does not require bypassing verification.

sections.title: JSON: the data encoding you must read
sections.body:
**JSON** is a text representation with six value categories. Object member names are double-quoted strings; arrays preserve item order. Object member order should not carry application meaning.

| Type | Example | Distinguish from |
|---|---|---|
| Object | `{"name":"R1"}` | An array of values |
| Array | `["Gi0/0","Gi0/1"]` | A single comma-containing string |
| String | `"24"` | Number `24` |
| Number | `24`, `1.5` | Hex, NaN or quoted digits |
| Boolean | `true`, `false` | `"false"` or `False` |
| Null | `null` | A missing member, empty string or zero |

```json
{
  "response": [
    {"id": "r1", "hostname": "R1", "enabled": true, "ports": 3},
    {"id": "r2", "hostname": "R2", "enabled": false, "ports": "3"}
  ],
  "next": null
}
```

Start outside and move inward. The top-level object has `response` and `next`. `response` is an array of two objects. Using familiar zero-based path notation, `response[1].hostname` selects `"R2"`. The first device's `ports` is a number; the second's is a string. The characters look similar, but an API schema may accept only one type.

JSON has no comments, single-quoted strings or trailing commas. Booleans and null are lowercase. Strings use escapes for characters such as quotes, backslashes and newlines. A complete JSON document can be any single JSON value, not just an object or array.

Syntactic validity does not establish semantic validity. `{"enabled":"false"}` is valid JSON but may violate an API's boolean requirement. Missing `enabled`, `"enabled":null` and `"enabled":false` can mean three different things. Avoid relying on a programming language's conversion of strings to truth values.

Duplicate member names should be avoided: implementations can handle them differently. Some parsers also accept extensions. Python's default decoder accepts NaN and Infinity, for example, although JSON numbers exclude them. The lab rejects those constants explicitly. Do not call a tool a universally strict validator without checking its options and behavior.

sections.title: JSON, XML and YAML side by side
sections.body:
JSON, XML and YAML are data representations, not authentication or encryption schemes. Their syntax can help identify the format, but each API or tool defines the supported schema.

| Format | Recognizable structure | Common networking use |
|---|---|---|
| JSON | Braces, brackets, quoted object names | HTTP API data |
| XML | Elements such as `<name>R1</name>` | NETCONF messages |
| YAML | Indented mappings and sequence markers | Ansible playbooks and inventory |

YAML supports more styles than indentation alone, and modern YAML specifications accommodate JSON syntax. XML values gain interpretation through the consuming application or schema. The goal here is reliable recognition and reading; Chapter 42 teaches the configuration-management workflow.

sections.title: Reading the output
sections.body:
This authored exchange illustrates an HTTP/1.1 representation. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 encode messages differently; the methods, headers and status semantics remain meaningful.

```output Representative inventory exchange
GET /api/devices HTTP/1.1                         ← method and target
Host: controller.example
Authorization: Bearer fictional-training-token  ← credential representation, not evidence of OAuth
Accept: application/json                         ← requested response media type

HTTP/1.1 200 OK                                  ← successful response
Content-Type: application/json                   ← representation format

{"response":[{"id":"r1","enabled":true}],"next":null}  ← array inside an object
```

Read in order: target and operation; authentication context; response status and headers; body structure and types; then what has actually been established. A `200` inventory response establishes a successful read of that resource, not that a later configuration request is permitted.

With curl, `-i` includes **response** headers; it does not print the outgoing request line and headers. Verbose/debug traces can show outgoing details but may expose secrets. Keep the request description separate from captured response output and redact credentials before sharing diagnostic evidence.

sections.title: Exam focus
sections.body:
- Distinguish REST style, HTTP semantics, HTTPS protection and JSON encoding.
- Interpret CRUD mappings, safe/idempotent methods and uncertain outcomes without blind retries.
- Separate missing valid credentials, refused authorization and unrelated network/TLS failures.
- Read nested JSON types and paths; distinguish syntax from schema validity.
- Treat product-specific endpoint paths, token lifetimes and rate limits as documented implementation details rather than universal constants.

lab.title: Read a local HTTP API and validate JSON
devices: One Windows, macOS or Linux computer
lab.intro:
Practice revised September 2026. If you completed an earlier version, repeat the revised exercise and update its checkmarks.

The required outcome is interpreting requests, statuses and JSON, which you can complete as a 30-minute worksheet using the supplied observations. Running the service is an optional hands-on path; allow about 65 minutes including setup. Mark each recorded result as observed locally or reasoned from the supplied case.

For the hands-on path, run a small, supplied **teaching service** on your own computer. It returns deterministic inventory data and lets you distinguish 200, 401, 403 and 404 without a public sandbox. It is not a production controller, a full REST implementation or RESTCONF. Its fictional tokens protect no real resource. The service binds only to IPv4 loopback and intentionally uses HTTP; real credentials require authenticated HTTPS.
lab.topology:
```diagram
{"type":"sequence","title":"Loopback-only practice","actors":["Terminal B: curl","127.0.0.1:8765 teaching service"],"steps":[{"from":0,"to":1,"label":"GET /api/devices","note":"fictional Bearer token","accent":true},{"from":1,"to":0,"label":"200 application/json","note":"two fixed device records"}],"caption":"Client and service run on the same computer; no router, external link or public account is involved."}
```

| Setting | Exact lab value |
|---|---|
| Bind address | 127.0.0.1 only |
| TCP port | 8765 |
| Inventory path | /api/devices |
| Restricted path | /api/admin |
| Read credential | lab-read-token |
| Write-role credential | lab-admin-token |

The admin endpoint is still a GET and does not change anything. Role names are invented for this exercise. The implemented query is an exact, case-sensitive hostname match. Unknown paths return 404 after credential checking; no matching hostname returns an empty array with 200. No write methods are implemented.

steps.title: Choose the worksheet or local execution path
steps.body:
For a worksheet, skip installing software and copying Python: read the service contract, then record predictions and compare them with the supplied responses in Steps 3–16. For local execution, create an empty folder named `ccna-api-lab` in your documents area and open two terminals in it. Use your text editor to save files as plain UTF-8. Do not place unrelated sensitive files in the folder.

On Windows PowerShell:

```powershell
python --version
curl.exe --version
```

On macOS/Linux:

```bash
python3 --version
curl --version
```

The remaining commands show Windows names; substitute `python3` and `curl` on macOS/Linux. If Windows uses the Python launcher, substitute `py -3` for `python`. If tools are absent, install Python from python.org and curl using its official platform instructions or your OS package manager, then reopen the terminal. No Python packages are needed.

:::expected
Python is version 3.9 or later and curl identifies itself. Windows PowerShell 5.1 may alias plain curl to another command, which is why `curl.exe` is explicit. If installation is unavailable, interpret the expected exchanges on paper and record that execution was not performed.
:::

steps.title: Create the teaching service
steps.body:
Save this complete code as `api_lab.py`. You need not memorize its implementation; the exercise is reading requests and responses.

```python
import json
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer
from urllib.parse import urlsplit, parse_qs

DEVICES = [
    {"id": "r1", "hostname": "R1", "enabled": True, "ports": 3},
    {"id": "r2", "hostname": "R2", "enabled": False, "ports": "3"},
]
ROLES = {"lab-read-token": "read", "lab-admin-token": "admin"}

class Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def reply(self, status, body, challenge=False):
        data = json.dumps(body, allow_nan=False).encode("utf-8")
        self.send_response(status)
        self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
        self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(data)))
        if challenge:
            self.send_header("WWW-Authenticate", 'Bearer realm="ccna-lab"')
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(data)

    def do_GET(self):
        scheme, _, token = self.headers.get("Authorization", "").partition(" ")
        role = ROLES.get(token) if scheme.lower() == "bearer" else None
        if role is None:
            self.reply(401, {"error": "valid lab token required"}, True)
            return
        target = urlsplit(self.path)
        if target.path == "/api/admin":
            if role != "admin":
                self.reply(403, {"error": "admin role required"})
            else:
                self.reply(200, {"role": role, "changed": False})
            return
        if target.path != "/api/devices":
            self.reply(404, {"error": "resource not found"})
            return
        name = parse_qs(target.query).get("hostname", [None])[0]
        matches = [d for d in DEVICES if name is None or d["hostname"] == name]
        self.reply(200, {"response": matches, "next": None})

    def log_message(self, message, *args):
        print(message % args)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    server = HTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 8765), Handler)
    print("Teaching service: http://127.0.0.1:8765 (Ctrl+C to stop)")
    try:
        server.serve_forever()
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        pass
    finally:
        server.server_close()
```

In Terminal A:

```powershell
python api_lab.py
```

:::expected
The service announces 127.0.0.1:8765 and stays running. If that port is already in use, stop only an earlier copy of this lab that you recognize, or choose a different unused port in the script and every later URL. Do not bind to 0.0.0.0 or publish this teaching service.
:::

steps.title: Read inventory with the supplied credential
steps.body:
Before running, identify the method, path, credential header and requested response format. Predict the outer JSON type and distinguish a successful inventory read from permission to change a device.

In Terminal B:

```powershell
curl.exe -i -H "Authorization: Bearer lab-read-token" -H "Accept: application/json" http://127.0.0.1:8765/api/devices
```

:::expected
The response has status 200 and `Content-Type: application/json`. The body contains two records in `response` and `next: null`. Python's small server may use an HTTP/1.0 response line; that does not change these status or JSON meanings. `-i` prints response headers, not the outgoing request.
:::

steps.title: Observe missing authentication
steps.body:
Predict whether removing only the credential changes the resource path or the access decision. Omit the credential:

```powershell
curl.exe -i http://127.0.0.1:8765/api/devices
```

Record the status, challenge header and body before repairing.

:::expected
401, a Bearer `WWW-Authenticate` challenge and the error `valid lab token required`. No inventory body is returned. This result follows the supplied service's contract, not an assumption that every network timeout means bad credentials.
:::

steps.title: Restore the credential
steps.body:
Repeat the successful Step 3 request unchanged.

:::expected
The status returns to 200. You changed the authentication context, not the path, protocol or stored device data.
:::

steps.title: Observe insufficient permission
steps.body:
Predict how missing credentials differ from a valid credential with an insufficient role. Use the valid read credential on the restricted endpoint:

```powershell
curl.exe -i -H "Authorization: Bearer lab-read-token" http://127.0.0.1:8765/api/admin
```

:::expected
403 and `admin role required`. Here the code explicitly authenticated the supplied read token before denying its role. In an arbitrary API, 403 alone does not establish all of those internal steps.
:::

steps.title: Use the correct fictional role
steps.body:
```powershell
curl.exe -i -H "Authorization: Bearer lab-admin-token" http://127.0.0.1:8765/api/admin
```

:::expected
200 with `{"role":"admin","changed":false}`, allowing for spaces. The name admin does not make GET a write operation; the endpoint reports a role and makes no change.
:::

steps.title: Distinguish an empty collection from a missing path
steps.body:
Predict each status and array length, then run separately:

```powershell
curl.exe -i -H "Authorization: Bearer lab-read-token" "http://127.0.0.1:8765/api/devices?hostname=R9"
curl.exe -i -H "Authorization: Bearer lab-read-token" http://127.0.0.1:8765/api/missing
```

:::expected
The documented filter matches no devices and returns 200 with an empty `response` array. The unknown path returns 404. These behaviors are deliberately implemented here; check another API's contract rather than assuming every collection behaves identically.
:::

steps.title: Save and inspect the body without headers
steps.body:
```powershell
curl.exe --silent --show-error -H "Authorization: Bearer lab-read-token" --output inventory.json http://127.0.0.1:8765/api/devices
python -m json.tool inventory.json
```

Open `inventory.json` in the editor. Identify its outer type, array length, `response[1].hostname` and the type of each `ports` value. The next section supplies a parser check with explicit limits.

:::solution Check the saved-body interpretation
Object; two records; R2; first ports is a number and second ports is a string. There are no HTTP headers in the saved file because `-i` was omitted. A saved error body can also be valid JSON, so inspect the response status when diagnosing an actual API failure.
:::

steps.title: Validate syntax and schema separately
steps.body:
Save `validate_lab.py` with this code:

```python
import json
from pathlib import Path

def reject_constant(value):
    raise ValueError("Not a JSON number: " + value)

data = json.loads(
    Path("inventory.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"),
    parse_constant=reject_constant,
)
assert isinstance(data, dict), "Expected an object"
assert isinstance(data.get("response"), list), "Expected response array"
for device in data["response"]:
    assert isinstance(device, dict), "Expected a device object"
    assert isinstance(device.get("hostname"), str), "Expected hostname string"
    assert type(device.get("enabled")) is bool, "Expected enabled boolean"
print("Lab syntax and selected schema checks passed")
```

Run `python validate_lab.py`. This checks the listed schema fields and rejects NaN/Infinity extensions. It is not a complete generic schema validator and does not detect every interoperability problem, such as duplicate names.

:::expected
The supplied body passes. JSON syntax and the selected field types are checked separately; the intentionally different ports types are not rejected because this small schema does not constrain them.
:::

steps.title: Observe a syntax fault before repairing it
steps.body:
In the saved local `inventory.json` only, replace the first lowercase `true` with `True`. Do not modify the service. Predict the failure stage and run `python validate_lab.py`. Record the error before making another edit. A worksheet learner should identify which token violates JSON syntax.

:::solution Check the predicted stage
`True` is not a JSON literal, so decoding fails before the selected field-type assertions. No successful schema decision can be inferred from a parse failure.
:::

steps.title: Restore the syntax baseline
steps.body:
Fetch a fresh body with the Step 9 curl request and run `python validate_lab.py` again. Confirm the first device's `enabled` value is the boolean `true`.

:::expected
The selected checks pass again. This reread from the unchanged service restores the original document rather than leaving another accidental edit in the fault copy.
:::

steps.title: Observe a different, valid-JSON fault
steps.body:
Change the first `true` to `"true"` in the local copy. Predict whether a general JSON decoder and this lab's schema check will agree. Run the validator and preserve its result before repairing.

:::solution Check the two decisions
The quoted value is a valid JSON string. Decoding succeeds, then the selected boolean-field check fails. Indenting or pretty-printing the document would not change that type.
:::

steps.title: Restore and select the operation from its contract
steps.body:
Fetch the unmodified body again and rerun the validator. Then complete this separate paper worksheet; the local service still implements GET only.

| Required operation | Documented contract |
|---|---|
| Create a device; service chooses its ID | POST /devices |
| Replace r7 with a complete representation | PUT /devices/r7 |
| Modify only r7's description | PATCH /devices/r7 with the documented patch body |
| Remove r7 | DELETE /devices/r7 |
| Read job 9 | GET /tasks/9 |

Choose the description-only request. Explain what to do when a create request times out without a response, and what a later 202 with a task URL establishes. Attempt the worksheet before opening the answer.

:::solution Check the operation and its verification
PATCH matches the documented partial update. A timeout leaves the create outcome unknown: use the API's resource/job lookup or documented idempotency mechanism to reconcile it before retrying. A 202 establishes acceptance for processing, so follow that task to a terminal result and verify the intended device behavior. A JSON parser can validate the representation without proving that the requested network operation succeeded.
:::

steps.title: Compare the local service with real HTTPS
steps.body:
Before handling real credentials, identify which protections the loopback exercise did not demonstrate. Explain whether an HTTP 401, a certificate validation failure and connection refusal establish the same stage.

:::solution Check the boundary
This service demonstrated a fictional role check over local HTTP. It did not implement TLS, OAuth acquisition, expiry or a production server. Real access needs the platform's supported authenticated HTTPS setup and credential/authorization policy.

A certificate error concerns TLS identity/trust before a normal protected API response; a 401 is an HTTP response about valid authentication credentials; refusal means the connection did not reach a listening service at that endpoint. Disabling certificate validation does not repair an expired API token. Packet Tracer is not claimed to run this service or RESTCONF.
:::

steps.title: Stop the service and submit the evidence
steps.body:
Hands-on learners press Ctrl+C in Terminal A, then repeat Step 3's inventory request in Terminal B. Worksheet learners state how that result differs from removing the request credential while the service was running.

:::expected
With no remaining lab process listening on that endpoint, the connection fails rather than returning a 401/403/404 document. Preserve that distinction in the record. Stop only the teaching process you started; do not terminate an unrelated listener.
:::

### Evidence to keep

Keep a request/response table containing method, path/query, credential role, status, body type and what the result actually establishes. Include your predictions and separate recovery evidence for both authentication and JSON faults. Identify the selected array entries, the syntax-versus-schema distinction, and one limit of the local service. State whether you executed the service or completed the supplied worksheet. Do not include real credentials in the record.

lab.troubleshooting:
- Connection refused: inspect the server terminal, bind address and port; there is no HTTP status until an HTTP server answers.
- 401 in this service: compare the Bearer scheme and exact fictional token.
- Parser sees leading HTTP text: do not save `-i` response headers into a JSON-body file.
- Valid JSON fails schema: inspect types and required fields; formatting cannot fix an incorrect value.
- Certificate failure on a real API: inspect trust/name/time independently of API authorization.
lab.challenge:
Use this new, supplied API contract; do not send writes to the local teaching service. An inventory read uses `GET /devices?site=west`. Its response is:

```json
{"devices":[{"id":"r7","ports":[{"name":"Gi0/0","enabled":true},{"name":"Gi0/1","enabled":false}]}],"next":null}
```

1. Separate the resource path from the query and give the zero-based path to Gi0/1's enabled value, including its type.
2. The API permits a partial update with `PATCH /devices/r7/ports/Gi0%2F1` and requires a boolean `enabled`. A colleague supplies `{"enabled":"true"}`. Explain both its syntax and its schema result; write the corrected body.
3. A submitted update returns 202 with task `/tasks/21`. The task later reports `{"state":"failed","reason":"device unreachable"}`. State what to record and which outcome remains unproved.
4. Separately, a documented DELETE returns 204. State what the client should do with its absent body.

:::solution Check the independent exchange
The path is `/devices`; `site=west` is the query. `devices[0].ports[1].enabled` selects boolean `false`. The supplied update is valid JSON but its value is a string; the required body is `{"enabled":true}`.

Record the accepted submission and its later explicit failure separately. No device update is established; investigate the reported reachability problem and follow the authorized retry/task-verification process before claiming the intended port state. A 204 is successful without a response body, so the client should not unconditionally parse JSON.
:::

questions.prompt: The API documentation says X-Lab-API-Key carries an issued API key. Which mechanism is shown?
options: An API key in a documented vendor-specific header.
HTTP Basic containing an encoded username and password.
An OAuth authorization-code exchange with a browser redirect.
A TLS client certificate encoded in an HTTP header.
questions.explanation: The supplied contract identifies this header as an API-key mechanism. A random-looking string by itself would not establish how a credential was issued.

whyWrong.1: Basic uses its own Authorization scheme and encodes user:password.
whyWrong.2: No authorization-code flow or redirect is shown.
whyWrong.3: A client certificate participates in TLS; this field is a documented key.

exhibit.title: Authored request excerpt
exhibit.text:
GET /api/devices HTTP/1.1
X-Lab-API-Key: fictional-training-key
Accept: application/json

questions.prompt: Which two HTTP methods have idempotent semantics? Choose two.
options: POST
PATCH
PUT
DELETE
questions.explanation: PUT and DELETE have the same intended state effect when repeated identically. Their responses can differ between attempts, and incidental logging can occur more than once.

whyWrong.0: POST is not guaranteed idempotent; API-specific facilities may make particular operations safe to repeat.
whyWrong.1: PATCH is not guaranteed idempotent, although a particular patch operation can be.

questions.prompt: Which REST constraint requires requests to supply their interaction context without relying on a remembered conversational sequence?
options: Layered-system architecture
Stateless interaction
Response cacheability
Optional code on demand
questions.explanation: Statelessness concerns the interaction between client and server. It does not prohibit resource databases, authorization data or server logs.

whyWrong.0: Layering concerns intermediaries and component visibility.
whyWrong.2: Caching governs reuse of responses rather than conversational context.
whyWrong.3: Code on demand concerns optional executable code supplied to clients.

questions.prompt: What can be concluded from the Basic scheme in this header?
options: Its credential is reversible encoding and needs transport protection.
Its credential is a one-way password hash verified without a password.
Its credential is encrypted by the Basic scheme using a public key.
Its credential proves an OAuth browser grant has completed.
questions.explanation: HTTP Basic encodes user:password with Base64. The sample is fictional; real use requires authenticated HTTPS and careful credential handling.

whyWrong.1: Basic does not replace the password with a one-way hash.
whyWrong.2: The Basic scheme does not provide encryption.
whyWrong.3: A Basic header does not identify an OAuth browser flow.

exhibit.title: Authored header
exhibit.text: Authorization: Basic bGFiOnRyYWluaW5n

questions.prompt: In https://controller.example/api/devices?hostname=R1, which component is the query?
options: /api/devices
controller.example
https
hostname=R1
questions.explanation: The question mark introduces the query, here hostname=R1. The API defines what the parameter means and whether it is supported.

whyWrong.0: That is the path.
whyWrong.1: That is the server authority/host portion.
whyWrong.2: That is the scheme.

questions.prompt: Which request header identifies the media type of a submitted JSON body?
options: Authorization: Bearer example
Content-Length: 128
Content-Type: application/json
Accept: application/json
questions.explanation: Content-Type describes the representation carried in that message. A correct media type does not prove that its fields meet the API's schema.

whyWrong.0: Authorization carries access credentials, not body encoding.
whyWrong.1: Content-Length describes size, not the media type.
whyWrong.3: Accept expresses acceptable response formats.

questions.prompt: Which format best matches the supplied mapping and sequence syntax?
options: JSON using double-quoted names and bracketed arrays.
YAML using indentation and sequence markers.
XML using paired element tags and attributes.
CSV using commas as record-field separators.
questions.explanation: This is a common YAML presentation. Recognize the syntax without assuming that every YAML document must use only this style.

whyWrong.0: These unquoted mapping names and dash sequence syntax are not JSON.
whyWrong.2: There are no XML elements or attributes.
whyWrong.3: The structure is nested rather than comma-separated records.

exhibit.title: Authored configuration text
exhibit.text:
devices:
  - hostname: R1
    enabled: true

questions.prompt: What types are the four values in order?
options: Number, string, boolean and null.
Number, number, string and absent member.
String, string, string and empty object.
Number, string, boolean and empty string.
questions.explanation: The syntax distinguishes all four values. An explicit null member is also different from the member being absent.

whyWrong.1: The second is quoted, false is boolean and last is an explicit null.
whyWrong.2: JSON has built-in value types; not every value is a string.
whyWrong.3: Null is distinct from an empty string.

questions.prompt: A documented POST creates a new resource immediately. Which status most specifically expresses creation?
options: 202 Accepted
204 No Content
409 Conflict
201 Created
questions.explanation: 201 specifically reports creation of one or more resources. Inspect the representation and Location header when provided to identify what was created.

whyWrong.0: 202 says processing was accepted, not necessarily completed.
whyWrong.1: 204 indicates successful handling with no content but does not specifically express creation.
whyWrong.2: 409 identifies a conflict rather than successful creation.

questions.prompt: An API supports PUT for complete replacement and PATCH for a partial modification. Which method should change only an interface description?
options: PUT
GET
DELETE
PATCH
questions.explanation: PATCH matches the stated partial-change contract. The body still has to use the API's documented patch format and authorization.

whyWrong.0: The supplied contract says PUT replaces the representation.
whyWrong.1: GET requests a read, not this modification.
whyWrong.2: DELETE requests removal, not a field update.

questions.prompt: What correction is supported by this controller response?
options: Change the account's role because authentication definitely succeeded.
Obtain a new valid credential through the documented authentication flow.
Change the inventory path because the requested collection is absent.
Request a larger API rate limit before attempting another read.
questions.explanation: The error body states that the supplied token expired. Renew it through the documented flow, protect the replacement credential and retry the read with bounded error handling.

whyWrong.0: The response explicitly identifies an expired credential; permission may be checked later.
whyWrong.2: The supplied error identifies credential expiry rather than a missing resource.
whyWrong.3: No rate-limit error is shown.

exhibit.title: Authored controller response

questions.prompt: Which statement about the displayed JSON is correct?
options: response is an array, and response[1].hostname is R2.
response is an object with keys R1 and R2.
ports is numeric in both records because both contain digits.
version is a number because its characters are 1.0.
questions.explanation: The array contains two device objects. Zero-based position 1 is its second item; JSON types are determined by syntax, not how a value looks to a person.

whyWrong.1: Square brackets make response an array; the hostnames are member values.
whyWrong.2: Quotes make the second ports value a string.
whyWrong.3: The quotes make version a string.

exhibit.title: Authored JSON document
exhibit.text: {"response":[{"hostname":"R1","ports":3},{"hostname":"R2","ports":"3"}],"version":"1.0"}

questions.prompt: Which two syntax faults make this document invalid JSON? Choose two.
options: The member name managed uses single quotes.
The array ends with a trailing comma after 30.
The null value is not enclosed in double quotes.
The true value is written in lowercase.
The member names are not alphabetically ordered.
questions.explanation: JSON requires double-quoted member names and does not allow trailing commas. The boolean and null values shown are otherwise valid.

whyWrong.2: Unquoted lowercase null is valid JSON.
whyWrong.3: Lowercase true is the required boolean syntax.
whyWrong.4: Object member ordering need not be alphabetical.

exhibit.title: Faulty JSON
exhibit.text: {"hostname":"R1",'managed':true,"vlans":[10,20,30,],"site":null}

questions.prompt: A read-only inventory GET returns 503 with Retry-After: 30. Which response is most appropriate?
options: Revise the requested fields before retrying this inventory read.
Obtain a different token before repeating this inventory read.
Wait at least the stated interval, then retry with a bounded limit.
Poll for completion because the server accepted the request.
questions.explanation: 503 is a server-error response indicating temporary unavailability in this scenario. Honor the supplied retry guidance for the safe read, while limiting repeated attempts and retaining useful error evidence.

whyWrong.0: The response supplies temporary-unavailability guidance, not a schema error.
whyWrong.1: No credential-expiry or authentication error is supplied.
whyWrong.3: 503 is not a successful asynchronous submission such as 202.

questions.prompt: What authentication pattern is shown in this documented API exchange?
options: An OAuth redirect flow is proved by the custom header name.
A client certificate is supplied in the token JSON member.
Basic acquires a token; the data call presents that token.
Basic sends the password on both of the shown requests.
questions.explanation: The example shows a product-defined token acquisition pattern. It does not establish a universal token lifetime, token format or OAuth grant.

whyWrong.0: This exchange does not demonstrate an OAuth redirect or authorization code.
whyWrong.1: The member is an issued token, not evidence of a TLS client certificate.
whyWrong.3: The second request shows the token header rather than Basic.

exhibit.title: Authored exchange
exhibit.text:
POST /auth/token
Authorization: Basic <fictional encoded credentials>
Response: {"Token":"fictional-issued-token"}

GET /inventory
X-Auth-Token: fictional-issued-token

questions.prompt: A job submission returns 202 with a task URL. What should the client conclude?
options: Treat the task URL as confirmation that the resource is already changed.
Inspect the task outcome, then verify the intended device result.
Repeat the submission until one response contains the status 200.
Parse the task URL as the location of a deleted resource.
questions.explanation: 202 indicates acceptance for processing. The API's task status and the required operational checks determine whether the intended change actually completed.

whyWrong.0: A queued task can still fail before changing the device.
whyWrong.2: Repeated submissions can create duplicate work; follow the supplied task instead.
whyWrong.3: No deletion or deleted-resource contract is shown.

questions.prompt: The schema requires enabled to be a boolean. Which assessment is correct?
options: The document is invalid JSON because false is quoted.
The document is valid and satisfies the boolean requirement.
The document is valid JSON but fails the stated field type.
The document fails because an object cannot contain one member.
questions.explanation: Double quotes encode a string. Parsing and checking the required field type are separate decisions.

whyWrong.0: A quoted string is valid JSON.
whyWrong.1: The schema requires a boolean, not the string containing its spelling.
whyWrong.3: A JSON object may have one member.

exhibit.title: Syntax versus field type
exhibit.text:
Schema: enabled must be boolean.
Body: {"enabled":"false"}

questions.prompt: Using zero-based array notation, which path selects the enabled value for interface Gi0/1?
options: devices[0].interfaces[1].enabled
devices[1].interfaces[0].enabled
devices[0].interfaces.enabled[1]
devices[0].interfaces[0].enabled
questions.explanation: The first device is at index 0, and its second interface is at index 1. The final member contains boolean false.

whyWrong.1: There is no second device in this document.
whyWrong.2: interfaces is an array; select an element before reading its enabled member.
whyWrong.3: That selects Gi0/0, not Gi0/1.

exhibit.title: Nested device data
exhibit.text: {"devices":[{"name":"R1","interfaces":[{"name":"Gi0/0","enabled":true},{"name":"Gi0/1","enabled":false}]}]}

questions.prompt: What should this client do before attempting to parse a JSON response body?
options: Treat the missing body as a failed write and retry it.
Add Accept: application/json to require an error document.
Replace DELETE with GET so deletion returns an object.
Recognize that 204 completes without a response body.
questions.explanation: 204 is a successful response without content. A client should branch on response semantics instead of unconditionally parsing JSON.

whyWrong.0: An absent body is expected for 204 and does not establish failure.
whyWrong.1: Accept does not require a body on a 204 response.
whyWrong.2: GET reads; it does not replace the intended deletion.

exhibit.title: Supplied API evidence
exhibit.text:
Documented operation: DELETE /api/devices/r8
Response: HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
No message body follows.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion about repeated DELETE requests is correct?
options: The method loses idempotence whenever the response code changes.
The intended absent state can be the same despite different statuses.
The second response must be changed to 204 to preserve the resource.
The client must recreate the object before checking the first result.
questions.explanation: Idempotence concerns the intended state effect of repetition, not identical response bytes. Both attempts leave this resource absent.

whyWrong.0: Identical status codes are not the definition of idempotence.
whyWrong.2: Changing a returned status is not a resource-state operation.
whyWrong.3: Recreation would contradict the deletion goal.

exhibit.title: Supplied API evidence
exhibit.text:
First DELETE /api/devices/r8: 204; resource removed.
Second identical DELETE: 404; resource already absent.

questions.prompt: Why is the proposed credential renewal not supported as the first correction?
options: A 200 response proves the role can perform every write.
A successful GET guarantees that the PATCH body is valid.
The request reaches authorization with a known read-only role.
Changing Accept would grant the missing modification privilege.
questions.explanation: The identity-service check confirms a current token, the successful read exercises it, and the write error identifies missing scope. Compare the operation with authorized role policy rather than assuming expiry.

whyWrong.0: Read permission does not imply write permission.
whyWrong.1: GET success does not validate a different operation or its body.
whyWrong.3: Response-format negotiation does not grant authorization.

exhibit.title: Supplied API evidence
exhibit.text:
Identity check: current token belongs to inventory-reader; not expired.
GET /api/devices/r8: 200.
PATCH /api/devices/r8: 403 {"error":"scope_required","scope":"device.write"}.
Role policy: inventory-reader has device.read only.
Proposed repair: renew the same role token repeatedly.

cards.front: Common CRUD-to-HTTP mappings?
cards.back: Create POST; read GET; replace/create-at-target PUT; partial modification PATCH; delete DELETE, per API contract.

cards.front: Which HTTP methods are idempotent by semantics?
cards.back: GET, PUT and DELETE, among others. POST and PATCH are not guaranteed idempotent.

cards.front: What does safe mean for a GET request?
cards.back: The requested operation is read-only; incidental logging or counters can still change.

cards.front: PUT versus PATCH?
cards.back: PUT supplies the target representation; PATCH applies a partial modification using a defined patch format.

cards.front: HTTP status classes 1xx through 5xx?
cards.back: Informational, successful, redirection, client error and server error.

cards.front: How does 202 differ from a completed API operation?
cards.back: 202 accepts processing. Follow the documented task outcome and verify the required result; acceptance alone is not completion.

cards.front: 401 versus 403?
cards.back: 401 lacks valid authentication credentials; 403 refuses the request, often for insufficient permission.

cards.front: What does 429 require the client to consider?
cards.back: Rate-limit guidance, bounded backoff and Retry-After when provided.

cards.front: HTTP Basic credential representation?
cards.back: Authorization: Basic followed by Base64 of user:password. Encoding is reversible; use authenticated HTTPS.

cards.front: What does Authorization: Bearer identify?
cards.back: A credential presented by possession; it does not prove OAuth, JWT format or a fixed lifetime.

cards.front: What is OAuth 2.0?
cards.back: An authorization framework for obtaining access tokens; grants, scopes and refresh behavior depend on the flow.

cards.front: Content-Type versus Accept?
cards.back: Content-Type identifies this message's representation; Accept expresses acceptable response formats.

cards.front: Does stateless REST prohibit server databases or logs?
cards.back: No. It constrains interaction context, not storage of resources, credentials or operational records.

cards.front: Six JSON value categories?
cards.back: Object, array, string, number, boolean and null.

cards.front: Why is {'enabled': True} invalid JSON?
cards.back: Member names need double quotes, and the boolean literal must be lowercase true. These are syntax faults, not formatting preferences.

cards.front: In {"ports":[3,8]}, what does ports[1] select?
cards.back: The second array value: number 8. Array indexes start at zero in this notation.

cards.front: What body should a client expect after HTTP 204?
cards.back: No response body. Do not unconditionally parse JSON after every successful status.

cards.front: Why can valid JSON still fail an API schema?
cards.back: The API can require particular fields and value types. A valid string such as "false" does not satisfy a boolean field.

commands.task: In Windows PowerShell, show response headers and body from the running local lab inventory using Bearer lab-read-token.
commands.note: The credential is fictional and the HTTP service is loopback-only.

commands.task: Pretty-print inventory.json with Python's built-in JSON tool using the Windows python command.
commands.note: Useful for reading syntax; default Python parsing accepts some non-JSON constants, so use the lab validator for its stated checks.

tickets.title: Inventory reads stop succeeding after several polls
tickets.scenario: A documented controller API requires X-Auth-Token. This deployment's issued credential includes expires_at 03:00:00 UTC. The service obtained it at 02:00 and never renews it. The server reports token_expired after the stated expiry; no fixed lifetime for other products is assumed.

exhibits.title: Authored credential metadata and request log

tickets.question: Which repair follows the supplied evidence?
options: Use a different header without consulting the API contract.
Obtain a current credential and verify a new inventory read.
Increase the account role while retaining the expired token.
Change the collection path while retaining the expired token.
tickets.explanation: The supplied expiry and explicit error establish an expired credential. This does not require guessing a product-wide one-hour lifetime. Use the documented renewal/acquisition flow, protect the new token and retry the read with limits rather than looping indefinitely. Role or path changes do not address the explicit token_expired evidence; changing header convention is unsupported by the given contract.
tickets.fix: Replace the expired credential through the deployment's approved authentication flow. Record only safe expiry/error metadata, verify a new read, and implement renewal according to the API contract. A renewal failure should surface for investigation instead of exposing passwords or retrying without a limit.

tickets.title: A repeated creation request returns a conflict
tickets.scenario: The API contract says POST /vlans creates a VLAN and returns 409 if that VLAN ID already exists. A network interruption makes the first response unavailable to the client. The supplied server audit and follow-up GET establish what happened.

exhibits.title: Authored server/client evidence
exhibits.text:
Server 09:00:00: POST VLAN 30 committed; response 201 generated
Client 09:00:01: response timeout
Server 09:00:02: repeated POST VLAN 30 → 409 already_exists
Follow-up GET /vlans/30 → 200 {"id":30,"name":"LAB"}

tickets.question: Why did the retry conflict?
options: The first request committed even though its reply did not reach the client.
The follow-up GET returned a proposed object that has not been created yet.
The repeated request was rejected before the server parsed its credentials.
The first timeout rolled back the object, leaving only a stale client copy.
tickets.explanation: The audit explicitly records the first creation and the GET confirms the object. POST is not guaranteed idempotent, so repeating after an uncertain response collided with the existing ID under this API's contract. A timeout by itself would not have proved either success or failure. The GET and server audit describe an existing committed object, not a proposed object or client cache. The supplied conflict does not indicate credential rejection.
tickets.fix: Reconcile the returned object against the exact intended attributes before treating it as complete. Use documented task/resource lookup or idempotency support for future uncertain outcomes. Do not delete an existing object merely to make a blind retry succeed.

chapters.title: Ansible & Terraform
chapters.subtitle: Build an inventory, run verified commands, and understand what a plan and its results mean.

sources.title: Ansible: ios_command implementation and documented boundaries
Ansible: IOS CLI plugin command execution
HashiCorp: Sensitive state and plan data
Ansible: Release and Python support matrix

chapters.summary: Recognize configuration management capabilities, use Ansible to collect IOS command output, and follow a local Terraform plan/apply cycle. Learn the setup, authentication, state, and verification checks that make the results useful.

sections.body:
An automation task still needs a precise networking purpose. “Collect the software version and interface state from the branch routers” is specific enough to implement and check. “Make the network correct” leaves the target, intended result, and acceptable changes undefined. Ansible and Terraform help carry out repeatable work; the engineer remains responsible for choosing and verifying that work.

The current v1.1 objective emphasizes recognizing Ansible and Terraform capabilities. The announced v2.0 objective requires using configuration management mechanisms such as Ansible to execute commands. This chapter therefore develops a complete Ansible collection task and uses a small, local Terraform exercise to explain its different approach. Cloud provisioning, elaborate roles, and configuration pipelines are optional further study.

sections.title: Why configuration management is useful
sections.body:
:::facts
- Ansible uses an **inventory** to identify targets and **YAML playbooks** to organize tasks.
