steps.title: — Inventory, cable and prepare the external service
steps.body:
Create a new Packet Tracer project named `capstone-build.pkt`. Place the nine devices and connect them using the cable/address tables. Decline the routers' initial setup dialog. Renaming an icon does not set its IOS hostname; the command blocks do that separately.

On SRV-HQ, Desktop → IP Configuration: address `10.255.20.10`, mask `255.255.255.0`, gateway `10.255.20.1`. Enable Services → NTP and SYSLOG. Use its time only as this isolated lab's reference; it is not a trusted Internet clock. On SRV-REMOTE set `198.51.100.10/24`, gateway `198.51.100.1`, DNS `198.51.100.10`. Enable HTTP and DNS; add the A record `portal.capstone.test` → `198.51.100.10`.

```ios ISP
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname ISP
ISP(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
ISP(config-if)# ip address 203.0.113.2 255.255.255.0
ISP(config-if)# no shutdown
ISP(config-if)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
ISP(config-if)# ip address 198.51.100.1 255.255.255.0
ISP(config-if)# no shutdown
ISP(config-if)# end
ISP# show ip interface brief
```

From SRV-REMOTE's Desktop → Command Prompt run `ping 198.51.100.1`. Repeat after address resolution if needed.

:::expected
ISP Gi0/1 and the server link become up/up; the server reaches its gateway. ISP Gi0/0 is not expected to be up/up until R2 is configured. Do not require an exact intermediate up/down combination. Stop and repair addressing or cabling if the directly connected test fails.
:::

steps.title: — Create VLANs and endpoint ports
steps.body:
Configure each switch separately. The 2960 uses 802.1Q without a trunk-encapsulation selection command. The inter-switch links are still unbundled during this step; default STP may block one to avoid a loop.

```ios SW1
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW1
SW1(config)# vlan 10
SW1(config-vlan)# name STAFF
SW1(config-vlan)# vlan 20
SW1(config-vlan)# name GUEST
SW1(config-vlan)# vlan 99
SW1(config-vlan)# name MGMT
SW1(config-vlan)# vlan 999
SW1(config-vlan)# name NATIVE-UNUSED
SW1(config-vlan)# exit
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 10
SW1(config-if)# spanning-tree portfast
SW1(config-if)# spanning-tree bpduguard enable
SW1(config-if)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 999
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,99,999
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show vlan brief
SW1# show interfaces trunk
```

```ios SW2
Switch> enable
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# hostname SW2
SW2(config)# vlan 10
SW2(config-vlan)# name STAFF
SW2(config-vlan)# vlan 20
SW2(config-vlan)# name GUEST
SW2(config-vlan)# vlan 99
SW2(config-vlan)# name MGMT
SW2(config-vlan)# vlan 999
SW2(config-vlan)# name NATIVE-UNUSED
SW2(config-vlan)# exit
SW2(config)# interface fastethernet0/2
SW2(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW2(config-if)# switchport access vlan 20
SW2(config-if)# spanning-tree portfast
SW2(config-if)# spanning-tree bpduguard enable
SW2(config-if)# end
SW2# show vlan brief
```

:::expected
Both VLAN databases list 10, 20, 99 and 999. SW1 Fa0/1 belongs to VLAN 10; SW2 Fa0/2 belongs to VLAN 20. Gi0/1 has the intended trunk configuration, but may be absent from operational trunk output while R1 Gi0/0 remains administratively down. A cable alone does not enable the router port.
:::

steps.title: — Bundle the links and establish management reachability
steps.body:
Before entering commands, predict which switch should become root, whether two passive LACP ends would initiate a bundle, and whether a management SVI alone proves its VLAN crosses the link. Keep your prediction beside the actual output.

Use LACP active at both ends with matching trunk properties. The newly created port-channel inherits compatible member settings; confirm the logical interface and both members after configuration.

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface range fastethernet0/23 - 24
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport mode trunk
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport trunk native vlan 999
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,99,999
SW1(config-if-range)# channel-group 1 mode active
SW1(config-if-range)# exit
SW1(config)# spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst
SW1(config)# spanning-tree vlan 10,20,99,999 priority 24576
SW1(config)# interface vlan 99
SW1(config-if)# ip address 10.10.99.11 255.255.255.0
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# exit
SW1(config)# ip default-gateway 10.10.99.1
SW1(config)# end
SW1# show etherchannel summary
SW1# show interfaces trunk
```

```ios SW2
SW2# configure terminal
SW2(config)# interface range fastethernet0/23 - 24
SW2(config-if-range)# switchport mode trunk
SW2(config-if-range)# switchport trunk native vlan 999
SW2(config-if-range)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,99,999
SW2(config-if-range)# channel-group 1 mode active
SW2(config-if-range)# exit
SW2(config)# spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst
SW2(config)# interface vlan 99
SW2(config-if)# ip address 10.10.99.12 255.255.255.0
SW2(config-if)# no shutdown
SW2(config-if)# exit
SW2(config)# ip default-gateway 10.10.99.1
SW2(config)# end
SW2# show etherchannel summary
SW2# show spanning-tree vlan 20
SW2# ping 10.10.99.11
```

:::expected
Po1 is a Layer 2 channel in use, normally shown as Po1(SU), and Fa0/23 and Fa0/24 show bundled (P) on both switches. Po1 carries 10,20,99,999 with native 999. SW1 is root; VLAN 20 displays priority 24596 including the VLAN ID. The switch management SVIs become up/up when VLAN 99 has an active forwarding path, and SW2 can ping 10.10.99.11. The router uplink still depends on Step 4.
:::

steps.title: — Configure the VLAN gateways and request leases
steps.body:
Configure R1. The parent is enabled and unaddressed; subinterfaces bind the tags to the gateway addresses. VLAN 999 remains unaddressed.

```ios R1
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# interface gigabitethernet0/0.10
R1(config-subif)# encapsulation dot1Q 10
R1(config-subif)# ip address 10.10.10.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-subif)# interface gigabitethernet0/0.20
R1(config-subif)# encapsulation dot1Q 20
R1(config-subif)# ip address 10.10.20.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-subif)# interface gigabitethernet0/0.99
R1(config-subif)# encapsulation dot1Q 99
R1(config-subif)# ip address 10.10.99.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-subif)# interface gigabitethernet0/0.999
R1(config-subif)# encapsulation dot1Q 999 native
R1(config-subif)# exit
R1(config)# ip dhcp excluded-address 10.10.10.1 10.10.10.49
R1(config)# ip dhcp excluded-address 10.10.20.1 10.10.20.49
R1(config)# ip dhcp pool STAFF
R1(dhcp-config)# network 10.10.10.0 255.255.255.0
R1(dhcp-config)# default-router 10.10.10.1
R1(dhcp-config)# dns-server 198.51.100.10
R1(dhcp-config)# exit
R1(config)# ip dhcp pool GUEST
R1(dhcp-config)# network 10.10.20.0 255.255.255.0
R1(dhcp-config)# default-router 10.10.20.1
R1(dhcp-config)# dns-server 198.51.100.10
R1(dhcp-config)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
R1# show ip dhcp binding
```

On each PC, Desktop → IP Configuration → DHCP. Then use `ipconfig /all` to record the actual address, mask, gateway and DNS. After requests, repeat R1's `show ip dhcp binding`. From staff, ping its gateway, the guest's actual lease and `10.10.99.12`.

:::expected
The staff lease is an available address within 10.10.10.50–254; the guest lease is within 10.10.20.50–254. Both use /24, gateway .1 in their subnet, and DNS 198.51.100.10. Allocation need not start at .50. Router subinterfaces and the router trunk are now operational; the local tests pass after convergence. External browsing is not yet expected.
:::

steps.title: — Connect HQ and verify OSPF routes in both directions
steps.body:
Draw the forward and return paths for staff-to-HQ traffic. List the client prefixes R2 must learn and the remote prefixes R1 must learn. Predict whether a successful transit ping would prove those routes exist.

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.255.12.1 255.255.255.252
R1(config-if)# ip ospf network point-to-point
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# router ospf 1
R1(config-router)# router-id 1.1.1.1
R1(config-router)# passive-interface default
R1(config-router)# no passive-interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-router)# network 10.10.10.0 0.0.0.255 area 0
R1(config-router)# network 10.10.20.0 0.0.0.255 area 0
R1(config-router)# network 10.10.99.0 0.0.0.255 area 0
R1(config-router)# network 10.255.12.0 0.0.0.3 area 0
R1(config-router)# end
```

```ios R2
Router> enable
Router# configure terminal
Router(config)# hostname R2
R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R2(config-if)# ip address 10.255.12.2 255.255.255.252
R2(config-if)# ip ospf network point-to-point
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R2(config-if)# ip address 203.0.113.1 255.255.255.0
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# interface gigabitethernet0/2
R2(config-if)# ip address 10.255.20.1 255.255.255.0
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# exit
R2(config)# ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 203.0.113.2
R2(config)# router ospf 1
R2(config-router)# router-id 2.2.2.2
R2(config-router)# passive-interface default
R2(config-router)# no passive-interface gigabitethernet0/0
R2(config-router)# network 10.255.12.0 0.0.0.3 area 0
R2(config-router)# network 10.255.20.0 0.0.0.255 area 0
R2(config-router)# default-information originate
R2(config-router)# end
R2# show ip ospf neighbor
R2# show ip route ospf
```

On R1 also run `show ip ospf neighbor`, `show ip route` and `ping 10.255.12.2`. From staff ping `10.255.20.10`. Check SRV-HQ's gateway if the return test fails.

:::expected
Each router reaches FULL with its peer on the point-to-point link; no DR/BDR election is needed there. R2 learns the three branch /24s. R1 learns 10.255.20.0/24 and an OSPF external default through 10.255.12.2. Inspect actual costs instead of requiring a fixed metric or convergence time. Staff reaches HQ. Before PAT, an external client ping can fail because the ISP has no private return route; a timeout alone does not prove the packet reached the server.
:::

steps.title: — Configure PAT and compare sources
steps.body:
Predict which sources the selector below will translate: staff, guest, SW1 management and R1 transit. Explain how the ISP's missing private return routes affect the untranslated cases before running the comparison.

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R2(config-if)# ip nat inside
R2(config-if)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R2(config-if)# ip nat outside
R2(config-if)# exit
R2(config)# ip access-list standard NAT-LANS
R2(config-std-nacl)# permit 10.10.10.0 0.0.0.255
R2(config-std-nacl)# permit 10.10.20.0 0.0.0.255
R2(config-std-nacl)# exit
R2(config)# ip nat inside source list NAT-LANS interface gigabitethernet0/1 overload
R2(config)# end
R2# show ip nat statistics
```

From both PCs browse `http://198.51.100.10`, then `http://portal.capstone.test`. While generating traffic, inspect R2's `show ip nat translations` and `show ip nat statistics`.

For an additional source comparison, run `ping 198.51.100.10` from R1. Then run `ping` alone: accept IP, enter target `198.51.100.10`, accept count/size/timeout, answer `y` to Extended commands, supply source `10.10.10.1`, and accept the remaining defaults. A release that accepts an inline source form can use that instead.

:::expected
Both clients load the page by address and name. Active PAT entries use inside global 203.0.113.1 and each client’s actual inside-local address; ports/identifiers vary. R1’s ordinary transit-sourced test is excluded from translation, whereas the staff-gateway-sourced test is eligible. This comparison depends on the stated route/selector design, not a general rule that routers cannot use NAT. No management or transit source is added merely to make the first test pass.
:::

steps.title: — Install the guest packet policy and test both directions
steps.body:
Draw a staff echo request and its guest echo reply with source, destination and direction at Gi0/0.20. Predict the first matching entry for the reply, a new guest-to-staff request, a DHCP Discover and a guest external HTTP request. A permit for a reply type is not a session table.

First record that the guest can currently ping staff, management and HQ. Install this complete list on R1:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip access-list extended GUEST-IN
R1(config-ext-nacl)# 10 permit udp any eq 68 any eq 67
R1(config-ext-nacl)# 20 permit icmp 10.10.20.0 0.0.0.255 10.10.10.0 0.0.0.255 echo-reply
R1(config-ext-nacl)# 40 deny ip 10.10.20.0 0.0.0.255 10.10.10.0 0.0.0.255
R1(config-ext-nacl)# 50 deny ip 10.10.20.0 0.0.0.255 10.10.99.0 0.0.0.255
R1(config-ext-nacl)# 60 deny ip 10.10.20.0 0.0.0.255 10.255.0.0 0.0.255.255
R1(config-ext-nacl)# 70 permit ip 10.10.20.0 0.0.0.255 any
R1(config-ext-nacl)# exit
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0.20
R1(config-subif)# ip access-group GUEST-IN in
R1(config-subif)# end
R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/0.20
R1# show access-lists GUEST-IN
```

Using actual leases, test guest→staff ping (deny), staff→guest ping (allow), guest→10.10.99.11 and 10.255.20.10 ping (deny), guest→10.10.20.1 ping and external HTTP (allow). Renew guest DHCP with `ipconfig /release` and `ipconfig /renew`, or reselect DHCP in its IP Configuration GUI. Compare ACL counters before and after each new test.

:::expected
The inbound attachment is GUEST-IN. Requests and responses match different entries as specified; DHCP remains permitted. A denied probe may time out or receive an unreachable indication, depending on implementation. The list permits an ICMP reply type, not a tracked session; it does not promise all staff-initiated applications will work or control same-VLAN guest traffic. The next step separately restricts SSH to the gateway itself.
:::

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# logging host 10.255.20.10
R2(config)# logging trap informational
R2(config)# service timestamps log datetime msec
R2(config)# end
R2# show logging
```

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# logging host 10.255.20.10
SW1(config)# logging trap informational
SW1(config)# service timestamps log datetime msec
SW1(config)# end
SW1# show logging
```

```ios SW2
SW2# configure terminal
SW2(config)# logging host 10.255.20.10
SW2(config)# logging trap informational
SW2(config)# service timestamps log datetime msec
SW2(config)# end
SW2# show logging
```

Configure NTP on **R1** and **R2** separately:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ntp server 10.255.20.10
R1(config)# end
R1# show ntp associations
R1# show ntp status
```

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# ntp server 10.255.20.10
R2(config)# end
R2# show ntp associations
R2# show ntp status
```

Wait for observations across polls; check server service and both-direction IP reachability if unsynchronized. Do not set a local master to hide a failed server association. Switch NTP is optional: use `ntp server 10.255.20.10` only if that model/image supports it; otherwise record that limitation and leave its timestamp accuracy unverified.

Generate a controlled event on R1 by creating an unused unnumbered loopback, then administratively shutting it:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface loopback44
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface loopback44
R1(config-if)# shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
```

Inspect SRV-HQ → Services → SYSLOG for the device, interface and severity of the new event.

:::expected
The router status and association identify the selected HQ source and actual stratum; do not require stratum 2 or a fixed one-minute delay. The receiver contains the controlled event if its severity is 0–6 and transport/collection work. If a Packet Tracer model lacks a command or does not emit a documented event, record the feature as unverified and analyse the equivalent evidence from Chapter 27; do not mark a missing event as received.
:::

steps.title: — Remove the temporary interface and preserve the baseline
steps.body:
Remove only the loopback created in the preceding step:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# no interface loopback44
R1(config)# end
R1# show ip interface brief
```

Run the lesson's acceptance matrix, including all four staff logins and both clients' address/name browsing. Record any simulator limitations separately from successful tests. Save on each device individually with `copy running-config startup-config`, accepting its destination prompt before entering the next command. Save the project as `capstone-baseline.pkt`, then Save As `capstone-faults.pkt`. Work only in the fault copy below.

:::expected
The temporary loopback is gone and the original requirements pass. A saved project and saved device configuration are separate checkpoints. The unchanged baseline is available for comparison.
:::

steps.title: — Observe one EtherChannel member failure
steps.body:
On SW1 shut only Fa0/23:

```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/23
SW1(config-if)# shutdown
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show etherchannel summary
```

Check SW2's summary. From guest ping its gateway, then open the external page. Do not repair yet; record channel/member state and any loss.

:::expected
Fa0/23 no longer participates; Fa0/24 keeps the logical channel operational. Guest connectivity should recover/remain through that member. Transient loss is possible; this test does not promise zero interruption or unchanged capacity.
:::

steps.title: — Restore the member and recheck participation
steps.body:
```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/23
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show etherchannel summary
```

Check the other switch and repeat the guest test.

:::expected
Both members return to bundled participation after negotiation. Complete this recovery before introducing the next fault.
:::

steps.title: — Observe a VLAN omitted from the router trunk
steps.body:
```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,99,999
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces trunk
```

From guest try its gateway ping and renew DHCP. From staff verify external HTTP still works. On R1 inspect `show ip interface brief` and `show ip ospf neighbor`.

:::expected
VLAN 20 is excluded at the router trunk even though Po1 still carries it. Guest gateway/lease tests fail; staff and OSPF remain available. R1’s guest subinterface may still show up/up because the physical link remains up. This combination locates the demonstrated fault more precisely than the client symptom alone.
:::

steps.title: — Restore VLAN 20 and renew the client
steps.body:
```ios SW1
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,99,999
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces trunk
SW1# show spanning-tree vlan 20
```

Wait until the VLAN's path is forwarding, renew the guest lease and record its current address. Retest gateway, external HTTP and the guest policy.

:::expected
The allowed/active/forwarding path includes VLAN 20 and the client regains service. Convergence is observed from state; it is not assumed to take exactly 30 seconds or to use legacy listening state on every Rapid PVST+ implementation.
:::

steps.title: — Observe a passive OSPF transit
steps.body:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# router ospf 1
R1(config-router)# passive-interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-router)# end
R1# show ip protocols
R1# show ip ospf neighbor
R1# show ip route
R1# ping 10.255.12.2
```

Check both routers as the change converges. From staff compare HQ/external access with a local VLAN gateway ping.

:::expected
The connected transit ping remains possible while the OSPF relationship and learned remote/default routes are lost. The local change can remove state immediately; the peer may detect lost hellos through its dead timer. Do not insist that both wait exactly 40 seconds. Local VLAN routing remains available.
:::

steps.title: — Restore the active transit and prove the routes
steps.body:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# router ospf 1
R1(config-router)# no passive-interface gigabitethernet0/1
R1(config-router)# end
R1# show ip ospf neighbor
R1# show ip route
```

Verify R2's branch routes and repeat the HQ and external service tests.

:::expected
FULL and the required routes return after convergence. The repair restores the original design; adding an unrelated static route would conceal the OSPF fault instead of resolving it.
:::

steps.title: — Observe an ACL entry that is too broad
steps.body:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip access-list extended GUEST-IN
R1(config-ext-nacl)# 35 deny ip 10.10.20.0 0.0.0.255 any
R1(config-ext-nacl)# end
R1# show access-lists GUEST-IN
```

From guest renew DHCP, ping its gateway and start a new external request. Compare staff service. Recheck counters and R2's translation table while distinguishing existing translations from new traffic.

:::expected
DHCP still matches line 10. The broad line 35 denies other guest packets before the intended narrower rules and final permit, so the gateway and external requests fail. Existing NAT entries may remain until aged; their presence does not prove these new packets reached R2. The staff-to-guest echo reply exception above line 35 still works.
:::

steps.title: — Remove only the unintended rule
steps.body:
```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip access-list extended GUEST-IN
R1(config-ext-nacl)# no 35
R1(config-ext-nacl)# end
R1# show access-lists GUEST-IN
```

Repeat allowed and denied tests from Step 7, plus the guest-gateway SSH denial from Step 8.

:::expected
Removing line 35 restores the intended policy without disabling the whole ACL. Fresh guest external requests can create/use translation state again; intentional internal and management denials remain.
:::

steps.title: — Record a reproducible handover
steps.body:
Save the verified running configuration on all five Cisco devices, handling each copy prompt separately. Save `capstone-repaired.pkt`. Record the actual leases, port map, OSPF routes, translation example, ACL counter observations, four login results, time source and collected log. Include every simulator feature you could not demonstrate.

Include a small acceptance table with columns for source, destination/service, expected allow/deny, observed result and supporting evidence. Include staff-to-HQ, both external URLs from both clients, all four staff SSH sessions, guest gateway ping, guest gateway SSH denial and guest-to-staff denial. Record where help was needed; there is no required cold-build time.

:::expected
The final record separates working requirements, restored faults and unverified features. A repeated independent build is evidence of this topology’s skills, not proof of every CCNA objective or a guaranteed exam result.
:::

lab.troubleshooting:
- Missing lease: inspect the access VLAN, both trunks, R1 subinterface, DHCP pool/exclusions and policy. A missing binding does not prove that the server received no request.
- Missing route with FULL neighbor: check advertised networks and route selection, then topology consistency including both network types. FULL alone does not diagnose one particular fault.
- No external access: compare route, source selector, inside/outside roles, ACL counters and a fresh application request. Separate numeric-address access from DNS resolution.
- Staff SSH failure: check IP return path, active VTY coverage, local account, key/server state and MGMT-SOURCES. A timeout or refusal is not a complete diagnosis.
- No time/log evidence: verify the actual service and appropriate transport, not only ICMP. A simulator limitation must remain marked unverified.
lab.challenge:
In a **fresh** project, use staff `10.20.10.0/24` and guest `10.20.20.0/24`, keeping VLAN IDs, management, transit and server networks unchanged. List every dependent configuration area before building. Verify client services, staff management and all guest denials. Do not edit the only working baseline.

For this variation, allow guest HTTP (TCP destination port 80) to SRV-HQ, but continue denying guest HQ ping and all other guest-to-HQ IP traffic. Enable HTTP on SRV-HQ first and prove staff can load its page. Write the guest ACL entry, its position and both required test outcomes before configuring it. Preserve guest external browsing and staff-to-guest ping.

After your build, diagnose this separate authored incident without changing unrelated settings: staff external HTTP works; guest DHCP and gateway ping work; a fresh guest external request passes GUEST-IN but creates no PAT entry; NAT-LANS contains the new staff prefix and the **old** guest prefix. The ISP still has no private return route. State the smallest repair and the positive/negative controls you will retest.

:::solution Review after your independent attempt
On R1 change both gateway addresses, DHCP exclusions, pool networks/default routers and OSPF network statements. Change guest/staff prefixes in GUEST-IN, including the echo-reply exception and final guest-source permit. On R2 change both NAT-LANS entries. On **R1, R2, SW1 and SW2** change MGMT-SOURCES to permit the new staff subnet. Obtain new leases and update test records. VLAN IDs, trunk allowance, LACP, native VLAN and management addresses stay the same.

With the original sequence numbers, the new HQ exception can be inserted before sequence 60:

```ios R1
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip access-list extended GUEST-IN
R1(config-ext-nacl)# 55 permit tcp 10.20.20.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.255.20.10 eq 80
R1(config-ext-nacl)# end
R1# show access-lists GUEST-IN
```

Guest HTTP to `http://10.255.20.10` should load the page and increment the exception. A new guest HQ ping remains denied by sequence 60. HQ replies leave the guest subinterface, so they do not traverse this inbound list. This service stays on the internal routed path; it does not need the external PAT mapping.

For the separate incident, replace only the retired guest selector through R2's console:

```ios R2
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# ip access-list standard NAT-LANS
R2(config-std-nacl)# no permit 10.10.20.0 0.0.0.255
R2(config-std-nacl)# permit 10.20.20.0 0.0.0.255
R2(config-std-nacl)# end
R2# show access-lists NAT-LANS
R2# show ip nat translations
```

Generate new guest external HTTP by address and name and observe its actual source translation. Retest staff browsing, guest HQ HTTP, guest HQ/staff ping denial and guest gateway SSH denial. A selector miss leaves the packet untranslated; it is not itself an interface ACL drop. The missing private return route explains why that untranslated flow cannot complete here. Preserve the working staff entry and all interface policy.
:::

questions.prompt: On a non-AAA lab router, SSHv2, keys and a local username already exist. Which two commands under every applicable VTY range require local-user login and restrict incoming transport to SSH? (Choose two.)
options: transport input telnet ssh
transport input ssh
password Readiness-Lab-45
login local
ip ssh version 2
questions.explanation: Transport input restricts the accepted remote protocol; login local selects the local username database in this non-AAA configuration. A separate access-class can further restrict client source addresses.

whyWrong.0: This also permits Telnet.
whyWrong.2: A line password alone does not select local username authentication.
whyWrong.4: The SSH version command belongs in global configuration and is already present.

exhibit.title: Representative SW1 SSH state
exhibit.text:
SSH Disabled
Please create RSA keys to enable SSH.
Configured VTY transport: ssh
Configured authentication: login local

questions.prompt: A fresh SW1 has a hostname, domain name, local user and correct SSH-only VTY settings. The output explicitly reports no RSA key. Which action supplies the missing prerequisite?
options: Replace the local account with a VTY line password
Reapply the SSH-only transport setting on the VTYs
Generate a supported 2048-bit RSA server key pair
Increase the VTY idle timeout to keep the session open
questions.explanation: The exhibit identifies the missing server key. Generate it using supported syntax, verify SSHv2 state, then test a fresh authorized login; a failure message without this evidence would need broader investigation.

whyWrong.0: A line password cannot supply missing server key material.
whyWrong.1: The transport setting already exists and does not generate a key.
whyWrong.3: Idle timeout affects an established session, not creation of the SSH server key.

exhibit.title: Representative SW1 channel state
exhibit.text:
Po1(SD) LACP Fa0/23(I) Fa0/24(I)
SW1 members: channel-group 1 mode passive
SW2 members: channel-group 1 mode passive

questions.prompt: Both switches have compatible operational trunk ports in channel group 1, but both ends use LACP passive. Which change initiates negotiation while retaining LACP?
options: Set both ends to channel-group 1 mode on
Set one end to channel-group 1 mode active
Set the native VLAN to 1 at both ends
Set the port-channel to spanning-tree portfast
questions.explanation: LACP passive responds but does not initiate. One active end is sufficient to start negotiation; compatible link and channel settings are still required.

whyWrong.0: On selects static bundling rather than LACP.
whyWrong.2: A native-VLAN change does not provide an LACP initiator.
whyWrong.3: PortFast changes STP edge behavior and is inappropriate for this inter-switch link.

questions.prompt: Both switches use base STP priority 32768 in VLANs 10,20,99,999. SW2 currently wins by MAC address. Which SW1 command makes it preferred over current and future default-priority peers in all four VLANs?
options: spanning-tree vlan 10,20,99,999 priority 32768
spanning-tree vlan 1 root primary
spanning-tree vlan 10,20,99,999 root primary
spanning-tree vlan 10,20,99,999 priority 61440
questions.explanation: Against the stated default-priority peers, root primary selects a lower base priority, typically 24576 on the documented Catalyst implementation. Check the elected root; the macro is not an unconditional 24576 assignment in every existing topology.

whyWrong.0: Leaving the priority at 32768 leaves MAC address as the tie-breaker.
whyWrong.1: Changing VLAN 1 does not select the root for the four named VLANs.
whyWrong.3: A higher numerical bridge priority is less preferred.

exhibit.title: Representative SW1 trunk excerpt
exhibit.text:
Port   Status     Native   Allowed VLANs
Gi0/1  trunking   999      10,99,999
Po1    trunking   999      10,20,99,999

questions.prompt: A guest on SW2 VLAN 20 needs DHCP from R1 behind SW1 Gi0/1. Its access VLAN and Po1 forwarding state are correct, but no lease arrives. R1 Gi0/0.20 is up/up. Which demonstrated fault interrupts the path?
options: VLAN 20 is excluded from the router-facing trunk
VLAN 999 needs an IPv4 address on the switch
The router needs a DHCP helper to its own pool
The guest VLAN must be the trunk native VLAN
questions.explanation: SW1 Gi0/1 excludes VLAN 20, so that tagged path to R1 is unavailable. An up/up router subinterface does not certify the switch’s allowed VLAN list.

whyWrong.1: The unused native VLAN needs no routed address for tagged VLAN 20.
whyWrong.2: The directly attached router is already the DHCP server; a helper to itself is not needed.
whyWrong.3: The guest VLAN can be carried as tagged traffic while another VLAN is native.

questions.prompt: A fresh R1 Gi0/0.20 subinterface will route tagged VLAN 20 as 10.10.20.1/24. Its parent is enabled and unaddressed; the switch trunk already carries VLAN 20. Which two subinterface commands are needed? (Choose two.)
options: encapsulation dot1Q 20
switchport access vlan 20
ip helper-address 10.10.20.1
ip ospf network point-to-point
questions.explanation: Bind the VLAN tag to the subinterface, then assign its gateway address. These are the missing settings for the stated fresh interface; the parent and switch path are separate prerequisites.

whyWrong.1: A routed subinterface uses encapsulation, not an access-switchport command.
whyWrong.3: A helper to the same router is not required to route client traffic.
whyWrong.4: An OSPF network type does not supply the tag or gateway address.

exhibit.title: Representative both transit interfaces
exhibit.text:
R1: Router ID 1.1.1.1, Network Type POINT_TO_POINT, Hello 10, Dead 40
R2: Router ID 2.2.2.2, Network Type BROADCAST, Hello 10, Dead 40
R1 neighbor 2.2.2.2: FULL
Expected remote LAN route: absent

questions.prompt: The two ends of one OSPF transit show the following state. The remote LANs are enabled in area 0, yet expected routes are absent. Which verified inconsistency should be corrected first?
options: Different local OSPF process identifiers
Different IPv4 administrative distances
Different OSPF network types on the link
Different learned external route metrics
questions.explanation: The output directly establishes a point-to-point/broadcast mismatch. Cisco documents cases where incompatible topology descriptions prevent route calculation even with a FULL relationship; FULL alone would not uniquely diagnose this fault.

whyWrong.0: Process IDs are local and no process-ID conflict is demonstrated.
whyWrong.1: No changed administrative distance is shown; it would not fix inconsistent link descriptions.
whyWrong.3: No external metric difference is shown and it is not the observed mismatch.

questions.prompt: R1 already has pool STAFF with network 10.10.10.0/24 and serves that directly attached VLAN. Reserve .1–.49 and supply gateway .1. Which two additions meet those requirements? (Choose two.)
options: ip dhcp excluded-address 10.10.10.1 10.10.10.49 in global mode
ip helper-address 10.10.10.1 on the client interface
network 10.10.10.50 255.255.255.0 in the pool
default-router 10.10.10.1 in the pool
ip dhcp excluded-address 10.10.10.50 10.10.10.254 globally
questions.explanation: The exclusion reserves the low addresses, and default-router supplies the gateway option. Available candidates are .50–.254; allocation order and existing leases are separate matters.

whyWrong.1: The local server does not require a relay to itself.
whyWrong.2: The existing pool network already identifies the /24; a host-looking network line does not define the desired starting lease.
whyWrong.4: That reserves the intended client range instead of .1–.49.

questions.prompt: R1’s external ping is confirmed to use source 10.255.12.1. R2 PAT permits only 10.10.10.0/24 and 10.10.20.0/24; the ISP lacks private return routes. Client HTTP and ping succeed. Which next test compares an eligible source?
options: Add a default route on the clients toward R2 directly
Ping from R1 with source 10.10.10.1 and inspect R2 NAT
Mark R1’s transit as outside to create another translator
Change R2’s selector to permit every source without review
questions.explanation: The staff-gateway source lies in the existing selector and still crosses R2’s inside/outside path. Comparing its result with the transit-sourced test demonstrates why the chosen source matters.

whyWrong.0: The clients already use their correct local gateway and work.
whyWrong.2: An additional translator is not required for this comparison.
whyWrong.3: Expanding translation changes the design instead of testing the stated source rule.

questions.prompt: The ACL is inbound on the guest subinterface. Staff echo requests reach guests, but guest echo replies are dropped. Preserve the deny of new guest echo requests to staff. Which change fits?
options: Permit guest-to-staff ICMP echo-reply before the deny
Move the ACL to the staff subinterface inbound
Replace the final permit with permit icmp any any
Permit guest-to-staff ICMP echo before the deny
questions.explanation: A staff request leaves the guest subinterface; the guest reply enters it. A preceding echo-reply exception permits that packet type while new guest echo requests still match the deny; this is not state tracking.

whyWrong.1: Moving the list changes which traffic is filtered and does not implement the required guest-source policy.
whyWrong.2: A later entry cannot override the earlier deny.
whyWrong.3: Echo matches the request type that the requirement intends to deny.

questions.prompt: With logging trap warnings configured, which listed message is eligible for remote forwarding under that severity threshold?
options: %SYS-5-CONFIG_I
%LINEPROTO-5-UPDOWN
%LINK-5-CHANGED
%LINK-3-UPDOWN
questions.explanation: Warnings is severity 4, so levels 0–4 qualify and 5–7 do not. Eligibility does not prove the collector received the message, and console/buffer thresholds are independent.

whyWrong.0: Severity 5 is outside a threshold of 4.
whyWrong.1: Severity 5 is outside a threshold of 4.
whyWrong.2: Severity 5 is outside a threshold of 4.

spec.title: Branch, HQ and ISP
spec.caption: R1 Gi0/1 and R2 Gi0/0 share area 0; the ISP uses a static route relationship.

questions.prompt: R1 and R2 use passive-interface default and enable OSPF on the branch/HQ LANs and their shared transit. Only the R1–R2 link should form an adjacency. Which two exceptions are needed? (Choose two.)
options: R1 GigabitEthernet0/0.10
R1 GigabitEthernet0/1
R2 GigabitEthernet0/2
R2 GigabitEthernet0/0
R2 GigabitEthernet0/1
questions.explanation: The diagram places the transit on R1 Gi0/1 and R2 Gi0/0. Other enabled LAN interfaces can remain passive while their connected prefixes are advertised through that adjacency.

whyWrong.0: The staff subinterface should not form a neighbor.
whyWrong.2: The HQ server interface should remain passive.
whyWrong.4: The ISP is not an OSPF peer in this design.

exhibit.title: Representative R1 default route
exhibit.text:
O*E2 0.0.0.0/0 [110/10] via 10.255.12.2
R2 design sets external metric 10 explicitly.

questions.prompt: R1 learns an OSPF external default from R2. R2 must advertise it only while it has its configured static default through 203.0.113.2. Which pair of settings expresses that design?
options: An OSPF network statement plus passive-interface default
A static default plus an OSPF router-id statement
An OSPF network statement plus a NAT overload rule
A static default plus default-information originate without always
questions.explanation: The static default supplies the route; default-information originate advertises a default while the required route exists. This does not prove the upstream service is healthy, and the metric is a separate configuration/default detail.

whyWrong.0: Network statements enable interfaces and do not create a default route.
whyWrong.1: A router ID does not cause default-route origination.
whyWrong.2: Neither an interface-selection statement nor NAT generates the needed default.

questions.prompt: Fresh guest gateway and external requests increment the unintended line 35. DHCP still works. The intended policy permits both requests while denying guest-to-staff requests. Which repair preserves the rest of that policy?
options: Remove sequence 35 within GUEST-IN
Detach GUEST-IN from the subinterface
Clear every dynamic NAT entry on R2
Replace the guest subnet’s default gateway
questions.explanation: The preceding broad deny matches the tested guest packets before the intended entries. Removing that single unintended sequence restores the scoped policy; an empty NAT table alone would not identify this cause.

whyWrong.1: Detaching the list also removes required restrictions.
whyWrong.2: Clearing downstream translation state does not remove the upstream deny.
whyWrong.3: The gateway is already correct; the packet matches the router’s ACL.

questions.prompt: DHCP moved to 10.255.20.10. Its staff pool and return route are correct, filtering permits relay traffic, and R1 has no helper on client-facing Gi0/0.10. Which addition forwards that VLAN’s requests to the new server?
options: Add ip helper-address 10.255.20.10 to R2’s server-facing interface
Add ip helper-address 10.255.20.10 to R1 Gi0/0.10
Re-create a competing staff DHCP pool on R1 itself
Set the client’s DNS option to the new DHCP server address
questions.explanation: The helper belongs where the client broadcast arrives, on R1’s staff subinterface. With the stated server and path prerequisites, the relay supplies the staff gateway in giaddr so the server selects the correct pool.

whyWrong.0: The server-facing interface does not receive the original client broadcast.
whyWrong.2: Reintroducing the old local server changes the intended design.
whyWrong.3: The DNS option does not enable a DHCP relay.

questions.prompt: GUEST-IN permits packets from guests to their own gateway 10.10.20.1. R1 must accept SSH only from 10.10.10.0/24, while retaining guest gateway ping. Which additional control fits?
options: Apply a deny ip any any rule inbound on the guest subinterface
Remove the IP address from the guest gateway subinterface
Apply a staff-source standard ACL with access-class on all VTY lines
Mark the staff subinterface as a passive OSPF interface
questions.explanation: A VTY access-class restricts remote terminal clients independently of the interface’s general IP traffic. Keep local authentication and SSH-only transport, then test both an allowed staff login and a denied guest login.

whyWrong.0: That would also break permitted guest traffic including the gateway ping.
whyWrong.1: Removing the gateway breaks the client design.
whyWrong.3: An OSPF passive setting does not control SSH access.

questions.prompt: Two 100 Mb/s members carry Po1. After one is shut, Po1 remains in use and a new guest HTTP request completes. Which handover statement is supported?
options: The channel now provides one 100 Mb/s member path; interruption and application performance must be observed
Each surviving flow retains 200 Mb/s because Po1 still has two configured members
Every packet took the failed member and was retransmitted without any delay
The test proves the branch can tolerate loss of the entire access switch
questions.explanation: The surviving member preserves a path but reduces available aggregate link capacity. A successful request does not measure transient loss, latency or switch-level resilience.

whyWrong.1: A configured but down member contributes no forwarding capacity.
whyWrong.2: The observed application result does not establish per-packet handling or lossless failover.
whyWrong.3: Only one member link was removed, not an entire switch.

questions.prompt: Two guests in VLAN 20 communicate directly through SW2. GUEST-IN is attached only to R1 Gi0/0.20 inbound. What should the acceptance record say about guest-to-guest isolation?
options: The router ACL blocks the traffic because both hosts have a guest source address
The router ACL is not traversed by ordinary same-subnet switching; this requirement is not implemented
The implicit deny blocks the traffic as soon as SW2 learns both source MACs
Adding another deny to the same router ACL will make SW2 inspect those frames
questions.explanation: Hosts in the same subnet resolve each other and send frames across the local VLAN. The routed ingress ACL has no opportunity to inspect that direct path. Client isolation would require an appropriate separate design.

whyWrong.0: A matching source is useful only if the packet actually crosses the attachment point.
whyWrong.2: The router’s implicit deny does not become a switch forwarding rule.
whyWrong.3: Additional entries at an untraversed attachment do not change this traffic path.

questions.prompt: Which next step best separates the cause of the guest failure without changing a working path?
options: Broaden NAT-LANS to permit any source because at least one application failed
Compare the guest DNS setting and a fresh lookup with the DNS server record
Replace the OSPF default because named and numeric URLs use separate routes
Clear every PAT entry because a successful numeric request cannot use PAT
questions.explanation: The guest already reaches the same external HTTP service by address. The missing dependency in the failing name-based test is resolution; inspect it before changing routing or translation. This narrows the investigation without claiming the exact DNS fault is known.

whyWrong.0: The successful guest numeric request already demonstrates an eligible working translation path.
whyWrong.2: The hostname is resolved before IP forwarding; the evidence does not identify a default-route fault.
whyWrong.3: The successful request and corresponding translation argue against clearing unrelated sessions.

exhibit.title: Authored evidence for this case
exhibit.text:
Guest: http://198.51.100.10 loads the expected page; http://portal.capstone.test fails to resolve.
Staff: both URLs load.
R2: a fresh guest TCP/80 translation appears during the numeric request.

questions.prompt: Which action addresses the missing return path while preserving passive client-facing OSPF interfaces?
options: Make every client-facing interface nonpassive so endpoints can form neighbors
Extend PAT to HQ traffic so the route advertisement no longer matters
Enable the staff interface in area 0 on R1 and verify R2 learns the staff prefix
Rebuild the transit adjacency because FULL requires every LAN route to be present
questions.explanation: A passive LAN must still be enabled in OSPF to have its prefix advertised. The supplied interface list shows the staff interface is absent, and R2 therefore lacks that return route. Enable the intended staff interface while leaving it passive, then repeat the staff-to-HQ test.

whyWrong.0: Hosts do not need an OSPF adjacency, and removing passive status alone does not select an interface for OSPF.
whyWrong.1: Changing the NAT boundary avoids the stated routing requirement instead of meeting it.
whyWrong.3: FULL describes database synchronization with that peer; it does not prove every intended interface was selected.

exhibit.title: Authored evidence for this case
exhibit.text:
R1–R2: FULL; matching area, timers and point-to-point type.
R1 route: HQ 10.255.20.0/24 via R2.
R1 OSPF-enabled interfaces: Gi0/1 and Gi0/0.20 only; passive-interface default.
R2: guest 10.10.20.0/24 learned; no staff-prefix route; lookup for 10.10.10.50 selects the ISP default.
Staff ping to HQ fails; guest-to-HQ policy is intentionally denied.

questions.prompt: A change permits guest HTTPS to HQ host 10.255.20.10, while all other guest-to-HQ traffic remains denied. GUEST-IN is inbound on R1 Gi0/0.20 and currently has sequence 60 denying guest traffic to 10.255.0.0/16. Which change and test pair meets the request?
options: Insert a TCP destination-443 permit before sequence 60; test guest HTTPS and a still-denied guest HQ ping
Append a TCP destination-443 permit after sequence 60; test only the new entry’s configuration
Insert permit ip to the HQ host before sequence 60; test only a successful guest ping
Permit TCP source port 443 before sequence 60; test a guest request whose source port is ephemeral
questions.explanation: A guest request enters with an ephemeral source port and destination 443. A specific permit before the broader deny admits only that requested service. A new allowed application test and a denied control test establish both sides of the requirement; the HQ service and return route must also work.

whyWrong.1: The earlier matching deny prevents the appended permit from being reached.
whyWrong.2: Permit ip also admits unrelated protocols to the host, including the ping that must remain blocked.
whyWrong.3: The initial request is addressed to server port 443; its source is not normally 443.

questions.prompt: After staff is renumbered from 10.10.10.0/24 to 10.20.10.0/24, a client reaches all management addresses and external HTTP. A console check shows local accounts, keys and SSHv2 are healthy; every device still permits only 10.10.10.0/24 in MGMT-SOURCES. Which repair and verification meet the design?
options: Replace the local account on R1 and use the old staff gateway as the SSH source
Remove every VTY source filter permanently and rely on successful authentication
Change the NAT selector to translate staff SSH into the old subnet
Update MGMT-SOURCES on all four managed devices; test fresh staff logins and a denied guest login
questions.explanation: Routing and SSH prerequisites have been independently checked. The source policy still refers to the retired prefix on every managed device. Update all four lists through the retained consoles, then verify authorized and unauthorized sources.

whyWrong.0: The supplied evidence rules out a missing account and the old source is no longer the intended staff identity.
whyWrong.1: This removes the staff-only management requirement.
whyWrong.2: Internal management should use the routed staff source; the external PAT rule does not repair each VTY policy.

questions.prompt: SW1 at 10.10.99.11 reaches HQ through R1/R2. R2 translates only 10.10.10.0/24 and 10.10.20.0/24 on its external path; the ISP has no route to 10.10.99.0/24. No other filter or NAT rule applies. Why does SW1’s external ping fail?
options: The switch lacks a usable gateway for all remote subnets
The HQ interface needs to be marked as NAT outside
The SVI cannot originate a packet to a routed destination
Its source is untranslated and the private return route is absent
questions.explanation: The selector does not match the management subnet, so this rule leaves the packet untranslated. The explicitly missing return route explains the failure; the selector itself is not an attached deny filter.

whyWrong.0: The stated successful HQ test uses the same remote gateway path.
whyWrong.1: Making the internal HQ segment outside would change the intended NAT boundary.
whyWrong.2: An addressed management SVI can originate routed traffic through its gateway.

cards.front: What selects sources for the lab’s interface PAT?
cards.back: Inside/outside roles, the NAT-LANS source selector and interface overload mapping. An unmatched source is not denied by that selector alone.

cards.front: Why can a router ping fail while translated client traffic works?
cards.back: The router may select a different source address excluded from NAT. Confirm that source, routes and policy, then compare a sourced test.

cards.front: What is the capstone guest ACL’s order?
cards.back: DHCP permit; guest echo-reply to staff; specific internal denies; permit the intended guest source to other destinations. This is a packet policy, not session tracking.

cards.front: What separate checks establish usable SSH management?
cards.back: Server keys/version, local or AAA authentication, every VTY’s transport/source policy, IP return path and a fresh authorized session.

cards.front: An OSPF peer is FULL but a needed route is absent. What next?
cards.back: Check prefix advertisement, competing routes, topology consistency and return reachability. A network-type mismatch is one possible cause, not a conclusion from FULL alone.

cards.front: Why collect several verification outputs for one service?
cards.back: Layer 2 state, lease, routes, translation and ACL counters answer different questions. A successful application test ties them to a real flow.

cards.front: Can a router subinterface stay up when a trunk excludes its VLAN?
cards.back: Yes. Parent/subinterface state does not confirm the neighboring switch’s allowed and forwarding VLANs.

cards.front: What does one surviving EtherChannel member demonstrate?
cards.back: A remaining forwarding path and reduced aggregate capacity; the failover is not guaranteed to be lossless.

cards.front: Does a guest interface ACL necessarily prevent gateway SSH?
cards.back: No. Evaluate the gateway destination explicitly; the lab also uses a staff-only VTY access-class.

cards.front: Why preserve a baseline before injecting a fault?
cards.back: It provides known state to compare and a recovery reference. Change one condition, observe, then restore and retest.

cards.front: Does an active PAT entry prove an HTTP request completed?
cards.back: No. It proves translation state exists; check return traffic and the client’s application result.

cards.front: What belongs in a test of a narrowly scoped policy change?
cards.back: A fresh request that should now succeed, a comparable request that must remain denied, and evidence from the actual attachment point. Retest the application; a configuration line or stale counter alone is insufficient.

commands.task: On the selected compatible switch ports, initiate LACP in channel group 1.
commands.note: Active initiates negotiation; verify both participating ends and bundled members.

commands.task: On new Gi0/0.999, identify untagged traffic as native VLAN 999.
commands.note: This lab leaves the native subinterface unaddressed and matches the switch’s native VLAN.

commands.task: Set the two-router Ethernet transit to OSPF point-to-point.
commands.note: Configure the same intended type at the peer and verify it; this type does not elect a DR/BDR.

commands.task: Originate an OSPF default only while this lab router has a default route; use default parameters.
commands.note: Without always, origination depends on the route’s presence. It is not an upstream service-health probe.

commands.task: PAT sources permitted by NAT-LANS to the Gi0/1 address, sharing it among sessions.
commands.answer: ip nat inside source list NAT-LANS interface gigabitethernet0/1 overload
commands.note: The inside/outside interfaces and route must already fit the design; the selector is not an attached traffic filter.

commands.task: Attach GUEST-IN to packets entering this guest subinterface.
commands.note: A guest reply enters here; a staff request toward the guest leaves here.

commands.task: Display channel groups, protocol and member flags on this switch.
commands.note: Read the legend and compare both switches. A defined channel can exist without all members bundled.

commands.task: Display this router’s current NAT/PAT translations.
commands.note: Generate fresh eligible traffic. Entries can expire, and an existing row is not proof the newest request succeeded.

tickets.title: Guests on SW2 cannot obtain leases
tickets.scenario: In this isolated branch variation, one guest on SW1 works and a guest on SW2 fails. Both access ports are in active VLAN 20. R1 is the DHCP server behind SW1 Gi0/1; its pool has free addresses. Before a change, both clients obtained correct leases.

exhibits.title: Representative SW2 trunk state
exhibits.text:
Po1 trunking; native VLAN 999
Allowed VLANs: 10,99,999
VLAN 20: active in local VLAN database
Guest access port Fa0/2: VLAN 20, connected

exhibits.title: Representative SW1 state
exhibits.text:
Po1 allowed VLANs: 10,20,99,999
Gi0/1 allowed/active/forwarding VLANs: 10,20,99,999
Local VLAN 20 client: valid DHCP lease

tickets.question: Which demonstrated change is needed on the SW2 path?
options: Add a DHCP helper to the management SVI
Allow VLAN 20 on SW2 Port-channel1
Change the native VLAN to the guest VLAN
Move the DHCP pool to the external router
tickets.explanation: SW2’s logical trunk excludes the client VLAN. The functioning local guest and healthy router trunk help isolate the failed path to the inter-switch link; a local VLAN entry alone does not place it in the trunk’s allowed list.
tickets.fix:
On this lab switch, restore the intended list and inspect member/logical consistency:

```ios
SW2# configure terminal
SW2(config)# interface port-channel1
SW2(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,99,999
SW2(config-if)# end
SW2# show interfaces trunk
SW2# show etherchannel summary
SW2# show spanning-tree vlan 20
```

Verify the VLAN is forwarding, renew the SW2 client and confirm the actual lease and gateway. Do not change the working DHCP server. Then confirm a fresh guest external HTTP request succeeds and a guest-initiated staff ping remains denied. Record the new client address if renewal changed it.

tickets.title: HQ routes are missing despite an established neighbor
tickets.scenario: R1 and R2 are the only routers on a dedicated Ethernet transit. The approved design uses point-to-point at both ends. Both required LAN interfaces are enabled in area 0 and passive. HQ access failed after an image migration. The following authored evidence was collected.

exhibits.title: Representative R1 observations
exhibits.text:
Gi0/1: Network Type POINT_TO_POINT; Hello 10; Dead 40
Neighbor 2.2.2.2: FULL
Required HQ route: absent

exhibits.title: Representative R2 observations
exhibits.text:
Gi0/0: Network Type BROADCAST; Hello 10; Dead 40
Required HQ interface: up/up, enabled in OSPF area 0
Intended transit network type: point-to-point

tickets.question: Which repair addresses the explicit configuration inconsistency?
options: Make the transit passive at both routers
Change both local process IDs to the same value
Restore point-to-point on R2’s transit interface
Redistribute all connected routes on both routers
tickets.explanation: The interfaces disagree about the OSPF topology model. Cisco documents route-calculation failures with such mismatches even when a FULL relationship is observed. The conclusion relies on the displayed types and intended design, not FULL alone.
tickets.fix:
Restore the intended type on R2:

```ios
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R2(config-if)# ip ospf network point-to-point
R2(config-if)# end
R2# show ip ospf interface gigabitethernet0/0
R2# show ip ospf neighbor
R2# show ip route
```

Allow convergence, compare R1’s type and routes, then test HQ and its return path. If the route remains absent, continue with advertisement and route-selection evidence instead of assuming this one change proves service. From the authorized staff client, repeat the original HQ ping and numeric/name HTTP to the external server. Keep the guest-to-HQ denial intact.

tickets.title: Guests receive leases but cannot use external HTTP
tickets.scenario: Guest gateway ping and external HTTP stopped after a named ACL edit. Staff service still works. GUEST-IN is inbound on R1 Gi0/0.20. The intended policy denies guest requests to staff, permits guest DHCP and permits external access.

exhibits.title: Authored before/after probe record
exhibits.text:
Guest DHCP renewal: succeeds
Line 35 count before new gateway/external probes: 40
Line 35 count after probes: 48
Staff external HTTP: succeeds

tickets.question: Which minimal repair preserves the intended restrictions?
options: Remove sequence 35 in named-ACL configuration
Remove the inbound attachment of GUEST-IN
Permit all sources in R2’s NAT selection ACL
Add a second default route on the guest PC
tickets.explanation: The broad sequence 35 matches the failing requests before the intended entries. DHCP survives because an earlier permit matches it. Removing the whole list would also remove the required staff protection.
tickets.fix:
```ios
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip access-list extended GUEST-IN
R1(config-ext-nacl)# no 35
R1(config-ext-nacl)# end
R1# show access-lists GUEST-IN
```

Repeat a new gateway ping and HTTP request, renew DHCP, and confirm a guest-initiated staff ping remains denied. Existing NAT rows may outlive the fault; evaluate new traffic and counters.

tickets.title: Branch clients reach HQ but lose external access
tickets.scenario: The branch still reaches HQ but cannot reach the external server. The approved edge design uses a default route through 203.0.113.2 and advertises it conditionally to R1. R2’s ISP interface is up/up and that next hop answers a connected ping. The following state was collected after maintenance.

exhibits.title: Representative R1 state
exhibits.text:
Neighbor 2.2.2.2: FULL
O 10.255.20.0/24 via 10.255.12.2
Gateway of last resort is not set

exhibits.title: Representative R2 state
exhibits.text:
router ospf 1
 default-information originate
Gi0/1 203.0.113.1/24 up/up
show ip route 0.0.0.0: network not in table
Approved next hop: 203.0.113.2

tickets.question: Which repair restores the documented conditional default design?
options: Add always to origination despite the missing route
Change R1’s VLAN gateways to the ISP address
Make R2’s ISP interface an OSPF area 0 peer
Restore the approved static default on R2
tickets.explanation: R2 has no default route, so default-information originate without always has nothing to advertise. HQ reachability and the FULL neighbor isolate the missing external route from the functioning internal routing relationship.
tickets.fix:
```ios
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 203.0.113.2
R2(config)# end
R2# show ip route 0.0.0.0
```

After OSPF convergence, verify R1 learns the default and repeat numeric/name HTTP from both clients. Restoring a route is necessary here but still does not by itself prove the external service is healthy.

chapters.title: Exam readiness
chapters.subtitle: Check your skills against the right blueprint, rehearse unfamiliar tasks, and prepare for the appointment.

sources.title: Cisco: Stay on track before the CCNA refresh

chapters.summary: Build an evidence-based revision plan, practise timed configuration and interpretation, and check the official exam and delivery requirements.

sections.body: Finishing a course gives you a set of resources and completed exercises. Readiness requires another check: can you apply the ideas when the addresses, outputs and requirements change? This chapter turns that question into a practical revision plan. Its checkpoint is a mixed sample of networking skills, not a full mock exam or a prediction of your result.

sections.title: Confirm the appointment requirements
sections.body:
:::facts
- As checked on **24 September 2026**, Cisco lists CCNA **200-301 v1.1** at **120 minutes**, in English or Japanese, with a listed price of **US$300**. Confirm the amount, applicable taxes, eligibility and allotted time when booking.
- Cisco announces **v2.0 for 3 February 2027**; v1.1 remains the published track through **2 February 2027**.
- Cisco does not publish a fixed passing score. Course percentages and completion badges are not Cisco scores.
- Prepare to interpret, configure and troubleshoot according to your selected blueprint. Do not base pacing on a promised item count or a fixed number of labs.
:::

Use the [official exam page](https://www.cisco.com/site/us/en/learn/training-certifications/exams/ccna.html) to reach scheduling. Check the appointment's exam, date, time zone, language and delivery method. Resolve profile or identification discrepancies before exam day. Keep the confirmation and the instructions that apply to that appointment; rescheduling deadlines can differ by delivery method, so an old blanket “24-hour rule” is not a sufficient reference.

For a test center, Cisco's published policy calls for two forms of identification with signatures, including a government-issued photo ID. Read the appointment's country-specific admission instructions. Online delivery has its own ID and equipment rules; do not assume the two processes are interchangeable.

For OnVUE, run the [Cisco program's system test](https://www.pearsonvue.com/us/en/cisco/onvue.html) on the actual computer and connection you intend to use. Its current rules require an approved single-screen setup, camera, microphone and speakers, and prohibit VPNs and virtual machines. It provides a digital whiteboard; ordinary paper notes are not allowed. Follow the current program page for exceptions and accommodations. A successful system test is preparation, not permission to leave other prohibited software running.

Keep appointment logistics on a separate checklist from technical revision. A subnetting exercise will not uncover an expired ID, a wrong time zone or an unsupported laptop. Checking those items early gives you time to resolve them without disrupting your study plan.

sections.title: Choose the correct blueprint
sections.body:
An **exam blueprint** states the skill areas and their relative weights. The verbs matter: “describe” calls for an explanation, “interpret” calls for reading evidence, and “configure” or “troubleshoot” requires practical work. A familiar acronym alone is not evidence that you can perform the requested task.

The two versions use the same exam number but different domain groupings. These are separate lists, not a row-by-row equivalence:

| v1.1 domain | Weight | v2.0 domain | Weight |
|---|---:|---|---:|
| Network Fundamentals | 20% | Network Infrastructure and Connectivity | 25% |
| Network Access | 20% | Switching and Network Access | 25% |
| IP Connectivity | 25% | IP Routing | 20% |
| IP Services | 10% | Network Services and Security | 20% |
| Security Fundamentals | 15% | AI, and Network Operations and Management | 10% |
| Automation and Programmability | 10% | — | — |

Read the actual [v1.1](https://learningcontent.cisco.com/documents/marketing/exam-topics/200-301-CCNA-v1.1.pdf) or [v2.0](https://learningcontent.cisco.com/documents/marketing/exam-topics/200-301_CCNA_v2.0_Exam_Topics_PDF.pdf) topic list. V2.0 explicitly adds or changes depth around OSPFv3, secure file transfer, DNS diagnosis, Ansible command execution and AI-assisted operations. It does not list every older objective, such as the v1.1 WLAN GUI configuration task. Foundational knowledge remains useful, but revision priorities should follow the applicable list.

Use this app's track selection and Blueprint map to locate lessons and practice. A chapter may provide supporting knowledge without a direct objective tag. Likewise, one tagged question covers only one aspect of an objective; it does not certify that the whole skill has been learned. The capstone combines several topics but does not exercise every blueprint item.

```diagram
{"type":"sequence","title":"Fig 45.1 — From objective to evidence","actors":["Blueprint","Practice","Review"],"steps":[{"from":0,"to":1,"label":"Choose the verb and topic","note":"For example: configure an IPv4 ACL"},{"from":1,"to":2,"label":"Record a new attempt","note":"Configuration plus allowed and denied traffic tests","accent":true},{"from":2,"to":1,"label":"Change the scenario and repeat","note":"Different subnet, direction or service"}],"caption":"A repeatable result on a changed scenario is stronger evidence than recognizing an answer you have memorized."}
```

sections.title: Work through items deliberately
sections.body:
Cisco's published introduction to performance-based items describes labs alongside multiple-choice and drag-and-drop formats, and states that candidates cannot return to a previous item after moving on. Read the current tutorial and the on-screen instructions before testing. The introduction's historical design estimate is not a guaranteed time allowance for each future lab. It does not establish a fixed lab order, universal partial-credit formula or exact number of questions.

Practise making a decision before advancing. For a selected-response item, identify what is asked, note how many answers are required, and eliminate choices using the evidence. Do not spend the whole budget trying to infer undocumented scoring. If uncertain, choose the best-supported response consistent with the item instructions and move on.

For a configuration task, read the requirements, topology and restrictions before changing anything. Confirm the device and mode, inspect relevant existing state, make the requested change, and verify its effect. A command can be syntactically accepted while producing the wrong behavior. Save when the instructions require persistence; this course does not assert an undocumented grading rule for running versus startup configuration.

```ios R1
R1# show ip interface brief
R1# show ip route
```

These are examples of useful inspection commands, not mandatory first commands for every task. If the problem is a switchport's VLAN, begin with the relevant switch evidence instead. Read the destination and prefix lengths before comparing the route attributes in this **authored, abbreviated** example:

```output Representative R1 routing entries
S* 0.0.0.0/0 [1/0] via 203.0.113.1
O  10.1.0.0/16 [110/20] via 10.9.9.1
S  10.1.3.0/24 [1/0] via 10.9.9.2
>> O  10.1.3.64/26 [110/30] via 10.9.9.3  ← destination 10.1.3.77 matches this most-specific prefix
C  10.9.9.0/24 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0/0
```

For ordinary destination-based forwarding, `/26` wins over `/24`, `/16` and the default for `10.1.3.77`. Administrative distance helps choose route sources for the same prefix; it does not let a less-specific static route override that installed `/26`. A forwarding decision also does not prove the remote host has a return path.

Use **remaining time divided by remaining items** as a rough checkpoint when the interface supplies those values. For example, 60 minutes for 40 items averages 90 seconds each. That is a planning average, not an equal budget: an output question may take seconds and a lab several minutes. Reassess periodically and avoid a rigid “finish item 70 by minute 90” rule based on an invented exam length.

:::trap A correct answer for the wrong reason
If you chose the `/26` because “OSPF beats static,” record a learning gap even though you selected the right next hop. A different prefix arrangement will expose that misunderstanding. During practice, explain why the closest competing choice fails.
:::

sections.title: Measure readiness with evidence
sections.body:
Use a small **evidence ledger** for each objective. Record the task, date, result, help used and next action. “Read Chapter 21” describes activity. “Built an OSPF neighbor relationship, identified a passive-link fault, then verified the remote prefix” describes demonstrated work.

| Level | Evidence for the objective's stated verb |
|---|---|
| 0 | Cannot explain or attempt it yet |
| 1 | Can complete it with notes, worked examples or hints |
| 2 | Can complete a familiar variation independently and explain the result |
| 3 | Can handle a changed scenario, verify it and explain plausible wrong alternatives |

A descriptive objective does not require configuring a feature that its blueprint only asks you to explain. For example, compare hypervisors, VMs and containers through a deployment scenario. For a configuration objective, an explanation alone is insufficient: create the state and inspect it. For troubleshooting, begin with a symptom and show how the evidence narrows the fault.

You can summarize revision needs with a weighted score: `sum(domain weight × level / 3)`. For v2.0 levels `2, 2, 3, 2, 1`, the result is `(25×2 + 25×2 + 20×3 + 20×2 + 10×1)/3 = 70%`. This is a course planning measure, **not a calibrated probability of passing**. Keep the per-objective gaps visible; a strong domain average can conceal one unpractised required skill.

Prioritize by both importance and weakness. A simple planning measure is `domain weight × (3 − level)`. A 25%-weight domain at level 1 scores 50; a 10%-weight domain at level 2 scores 10. The ratio is five, not four. It suggests where effort may help, but does not prescribe exact hours or justify ignoring an entire lower-weight domain.

Separate first attempts from repeated attempts. Repeated practice is useful for fluency, while fresh scenarios help assess transfer. Review wrong answers and correct guesses, then wait before trying a changed example. A high score immediately after reading an explanation is weak evidence of durable recall.

sections.title: Review rules with their conditions
sections.body:
Build a compact personal reference from your actual errors. Keep the condition next to every number: “OSPF broadcast default hello/dead 10/40 seconds” is useful; “OSPF is 10/40” hides other network types and configurable intervals. Use the earlier chapter as the authority when a short flashcard needs explanation.

| Review area | Useful self-check | Course reference |
|---|---|---|
| IPv4 and IPv6 | Derive a range, choose a route, distinguish prefix from interface identifier | [Subnetting](#/chapter/subnetting-vlsm), [IPv6](#/chapter/ipv6-addressing) |
| Switching | Trace VLAN tags and calculate a root path using the stated costs | [Trunks](#/chapter/trunks-dtp), [Spanning tree](#/chapter/spanning-tree) |
| Routing | Explain neighbor state separately from route installation and return reachability | [OSPFv2](#/chapter/ospfv2), [OSPFv3](#/chapter/ospfv3), [FHRP](#/chapter/fhrp-hsrp-vrrp) |
| Services | Distinguish lease, name resolution, time synchronization and translation evidence | [DHCP](#/chapter/dhcp), [DNS](#/chapter/dns), [NAT/PAT](#/chapter/nat-pat) |
| Security | Evaluate both directions of a flow; distinguish authentication from authorization | [ACLs](#/chapter/acls), [AAA](#/chapter/aaa-tacacs-radius), [VPNs](#/chapter/vpns-ipsec) |
| Wireless | Separate radio selection, security negotiation and IP configuration | [Wireless principles](#/chapter/wireless-principles), [WLAN security](#/chapter/wireless-security-config) |
| Automation | Interpret structured data, target a command safely and evaluate generated advice | [REST/JSON](#/chapter/rest-apis-json), [Ansible](#/chapter/ansible-terraform), [AI](#/chapter/ai-in-network-operations) |

For each missed rule, create one changed example. After misreading an ACL wildcard, calculate a different block and test its first and last matching addresses. After confusing a NAT selector with a filter, trace a packet that does not match the selector. After confusing association with useful wireless connectivity, identify which additional evidence would establish IP reachability.

Avoid turning the final review into an unbounded list of obscure defaults. Concentrate on the values and mechanisms that support the published tasks. Be able to use command help during practice and to interpret output even when spacing, counters or interface names differ from a screenshot.

sections.title: Plan the final revision period
sections.body:
The following two-week schedule is a suggested study arrangement, not a claim that fourteen days will repair any skill gap. Adjust it around your evidence ledger and available time. If major configuration objectives remain unpractised, allocate more preparation rather than repeatedly taking the same question bank.

| Days before the appointment | Main work | Record before moving on |
|---|---|---|
| 14–12 | Review the correct blueprint; sample each domain with unfamiliar work | Missing objectives and three priorities |
| 11–8 | Rebuild weak topics; practise one fault at a time | Commands, evidence, cause and recovery |
| 7 | Rehearse a timed mixed session using legitimate practice material | Time used, misses and correct guesses |
| 6–4 | Review each miss; repeat with different values or requirements | Evidence that the underlying error is resolved |
| 3–2 | Complete another bounded rehearsal and the appointment checklist | Remaining gaps and a realistic next step |
| 1 | Brief retrieval practice, logistics and rest | Ready equipment, identification and appointment details |

Use a reasonable session length and stop to analyse repeated mistakes. Rushing through twenty nearly identical questions can reinforce a bad shortcut. One carefully explained failure and a successful changed example can be more valuable.

The guided lab below offers a small independent build, a verification checklist and a separate reference solution. Attempt the specification before reading the solution. Record elapsed time without treating this exercise's duration or point total as Cisco's grading scheme. The wireless, IPv6, automation and other tasks omitted from that topology still need their own evidence.

sections.title: Exam day and next steps
sections.body:
Review your appointment instructions before leaving or beginning check-in. For online delivery, Pearson currently asks candidates to start check-in 30 minutes early. Stay within the proctor's rules, and do not assume an unscheduled break is permitted. Raise delivery problems through the provided help channel; do not spend the remaining exam time silently troubleshooting the exam computer.

Cisco provides an exam score report with performance information. Use the official record rather than trying to reverse-engineer a passing score from domain percentages. If unsuccessful, identify the weakest objectives and repeat relevant work with new evidence. Cisco's current policy requires five calendar days of waiting, counted from the day after a failed associate attempt; a passed exam with the same number has a 180-day minimum retake interval.

CCNA is normally valid for three years. After earning it, track its expiration. The current associate recertification route requires 30 eligible Continuing Education credits; qualifying activities and exams are listed in the [current recertification policy](https://www.cisco.com/site/us/en/learn/training-certifications/certifications/recertification/index.html). Complete requirements before expiry and check the recorded new date. Do not assume any higher-level exam automatically qualifies.

Continue practising useful small changes: a new VLAN, a verified route, a narrowly scoped ACL or an inventory command. Keep your own configurations and explanations, while respecting Cisco's confidentiality rules for actual exam material. The course's questions are original teaching exercises, not recalled examination items.

sections.title: Exam focus
sections.body:
- Choose the blueprint for the actual appointment date and use its objective verbs.
- Demonstrate the requested skill with fresh evidence; reading completion and repeated-question scores have limits.
- Read the whole task, inspect the existing state, make the required change and verify it.
- Pace from the current instructions and remaining work, not a promised lab order or question count.
- Review the reasoning behind correct guesses as well as wrong answers.
- Use official appointment and policy pages for logistics; the networking facts in this chapter's mixed practice link back to their teaching chapters.

lab.title: Independent build, verification and fault diagnosis
lab.intro:
Use the specification for an independent attempt, then compare with the reference configuration. The suggested 50-minute attempt plus 10-minute verification is a practice budget, not the length, content or scoring of an actual CCNA lab item. Allow additional time for reference review and the fault exercise. These instructions are documentation-reviewed; no simulator run is claimed.

Practice revised September 2026. If you completed an earlier version, repeat the revised exercise and update its checkmarks. The full exercise includes review and a later changed attempt; split it into sessions as needed. The closed reference panels are available after the first attempt, not part of its evidence.

| Device / interface | Address | Notes |
